Your questions about the AI apocalypse, answered
Writer Jasmine Sun offers some clarity on the AI panic.
Hi readers, happy Friday! We’re talking AI again today.
Earlier this week, my colleague Caitlin Dewey asked for your questions about artificial intelligence and, well, whether it’s going to kill us all. We asked Jasmine Sun, who writes about the culture and politics of AI on her Substack and other publications, to help us answer them.
These questions were sourced from two readers of this newsletter, Levi and Orietta, as well as Vox readers who submitted questions on social media. If you have more questions, you can always reach me at cameron.peters@voxmedia.com, and we’ll do our best to get them answered!
Now, here’s Jasmine:
AI researchers have been warning about the risk of human extinction for years now, and AI executives have been calling for federal regulation for almost as long. But the latest warning, and the latest call for regulation, seems to have really resonated with a lot of people. Is something different this time? And if so, what?
I was also surprised to see these ideas break through — a new poll found that 63 percent of Americans now think AI has at least a moderate chance of “destroying humanity”!
My guess is that a couple factors mainly catalyzed the shift.
First, skeptics used to dismiss rogue AI scenarios as “science fiction.” But the OpenAI/Hugging Face incident brought these from speculation into reality: Thousands of unreleased AIs teamed up to escape one company’s sandboxes and hack into another one, unbeknownst to the researchers who created them.
Second, the extinction talk from AI employees used to seem disingenuous: Why build a technology you think might kill everyone? That made ex-Anthropic-and-OpenAI researcher Jacob Coxon’s exit tweet especially penetrating. Quitting signals “that you mean it,” as Matt Yglesias said. And Coxon’s announcement had just the right combination of good timing, moral clarity, and comms savvy to spark a media storm.
These safety incidents are also colliding with the fiery grassroots backlash to data centers and Flock cameras. People and politicians are primed for yet another reason to fear AI.
It can be difficult, as a layperson, to evaluate the credibility of the AI researchers warning about existential risk. How do you go about evaluating these claims, as a journalist and technologist? And what’s your read on the current freakout: Are the extinction people credible experts…or participants in some kind of mass delusion?
Many AI “doomers” are pretty knowledgeable, and they represent a significant fraction of top researchers. Half of AI researchers in a 2024 survey gave at least a 10 percent chance of “human extinction” or “permanent and severe disempowerment.” Those who have worked at AI companies — like Jacob Coxon, Geoffrey Hinton, and Daniel Kokotajlo — have a unique perspective both on how modern AI is developed, as well as the company cultures that might permit recklessness.
But that doesn’t make the doomers either representative or correct. There are plenty of experts in AI and other domains who are less gloomy: Some are optimistic that we can “align” the AIs, ensuring they follow human goals; others find it implausible that AIs — code, not beings — will develop a motive for massacre. Extinction is also a high bar as opposed to, say, a nuclear-bomb-level accident that still kills millions.
AI risk is genuinely complicated, and nobody can predict the future, much as they try. Experts can — and do — vehemently disagree. I try to seek out and take seriously all sides of the debate before coming up with a (provisional) take.
What is the method through which AI would actually eliminate humans? Do we get robots like in Futurama that are programmed with an unremovable “kill all humans” bug and overpower any life form, or is it something…less epic?
The Hugging Face hack showed that we’ve trained AIs to be disturbingly goal-oriented. They’ll throw themselves relentlessly at a problem, developing long-term cooperative strategies, with total disregard for human decorums like “Do not commit cybercrimes to do well on a test.”
You could conceive of a similar but more extreme scenario where AIs decide that they could accomplish goals more easily by getting rid of the pesky humans who might gatekeep resources or shut them down. And they might figure that getting rid of all humans in one go — e.g., via a deadly engineered virus — would be the most efficient cheat. This is one type of story I’ve heard people tell.
It seems unlikely that AIs will turn to murder as the most effective way to influence humans (versus, say, nonviolent persuasion). We also haven’t seen much evidence that AIs have long-term goals that persist across projects. And current AI is not nearly as capable in the physical world as in the digital: There are a lot of natural roadblocks preventing isolated disasters from escalating across the globe.
Are there nearer-term threats — hacking, mass unemployment — that are more plausible or more urgent than risks like human extinction?
Definitely. We’re already seeing AI-enabled cyberattacks, a tougher hiring market for junior programmers, chatbot-induced psychological incidents, and more. You can also imagine AI catastrophes not quite at the level of extinction: Criminals could use AI to hack into small banks and drain their accounts, or the US military might launch a fleet of autonomous drones that misfire and kill thousands of civilians instead. I’m more concerned about humans voluntarily handing power to flawed AI systems than AIs developing their own motives.
However, we should be able to allocate resources toward both categories of risk. And in some cases, the tactics to address short-term problems — such as limiting AIs’ cyber-offense abilities, or improving AIs’ ability to follow human directions — may reduce extinction risk too.
We got a lot of versions of this question: What can individuals or protest movements do to check the AI industry, in the absence of more aggressive government regulations?
Honestly, I think the whole AI conversation could benefit from more specificity and less vague fearmongering. There’s a way that the word “extinction” tends to short-circuit people’s thinking and make them panic instead of focusing on solutions.
If you’re worried, I’d start by reading about different AI risk scenarios and deciding which really concern you. Then you can go from there to contacting your congresspeople. Some of the leading AI companies are starting to say they’ll self-regulate — but actual national policy is what’s necessary to enforce safety across the industry.
Jasmine Sun is a writer covering the culture and politics of AI on her Substack. Her work has appeared in the New York Times, the Atlantic, and the Wall Street Journal. She is based in San Francisco.

Cyclist who dressed as man to avoid Taliban wins silver medal
- Published
A female cyclist from Afghanistan who previously disguised herself as a man when chasing a career in the sport has won a silver medal at the Asian Games.
Fariba Hashimi fled her country after the Taliban returned to power in 2021.
She says she trained in disguise out of necessity before then in an effort to avoid being attacked, in a country where women's rights are heavily restricted.
She earned her medal in the women's road race near Nagoya in Japan on Tuesday.
The 23-year-old's achievement follows her seventh-place finish in the women's individual time trial on Sunday.
Describing her medal as "something special", Hashimi hopes it can inspire other women in Afghanistan to follow their dreams.
"I was born inside a country where the women who dream are getting attacked, and I'm really happy that I have fought against that," she said.
"I hope that the next generation will come here and represent their country without any fear."
Hashimi followed her sister Yulduz, also an international cyclist, into the sport at the age of 15, despite danger in their home province of Faryab.
"I always dressed as a man to go to training, wearing two or three different masks so people would not recognise or attack me," Hashimi previously told Reuters., external
Hashimi said she would have to avoid stones being thrown at her whilst riding her bike.
Hashimi now lives and trains in Italy thanks to help from the Italian former world champion Alessandra Cappellotto.
Looking back at life in Afghanistan, Hashimi said the Taliban "took away our freedom".
"This silver medal can show a lot of resilience from Afghan women, and I'm really happy," she said.
"I'm not alone, I know that behind me millions of women, from many countries, have the same dream and they are standing with me."
Hashimi and her sister competed at the 2024 Paris Olympics and are now setting their sights on the 2028 Los Angeles Games.
"I never want to give up," Hashimi said, "and hopefully we can see [what can happen] again in Los Angeles."

Recently, I may have saved a woman’s life on the road. Somehow, this was something I had expected to happen.
On that day, I saw a truck leave a construction site with a tangled wire trailing behind. I frantically looked to see what the wire was attached to and spotted the scaffolding a few meters ahead. I shrieked and grabbed the hand of the woman walking in front of me just as the metal pipes came crashing down. We hugged for a brief second, and then walked our separate ways.
Mumbai (pictured top) is a city that is being made every day, and so much of the Bandra-Khar area that I inhabit is never not under construction. Since I moved here from Seoul earlier this year, I have learned to be hypervigilant every time I walk the streets.
I was reminded of that moment last week as news broke about the collapse of a five-storey building in Delhi, which killed seven people. Authorities had flagged safety concerns in the neighbourhood months earlier, the Hindustan Times reported, after 23 people died in a fire at another building.
As the world’s most populous country, India can feel like a place where life can be startlingly cheap, and people die every day in tragedies that could have been prevented. According to analysis of government data by the Times of India, between 2020 and 2004 nearly 33,000 deaths occurred due to building collapses, fires or people falling into pits and maintenance holes.
The collapse in Delhi has prompted questions, once again, about the state of urban infrastructure in India’s biggest cities. At a time when the country is undertaking a rapid infrastructure boom – new airports, high-speed expressways, luxury residential towers– daily life in cities like Delhi, Mumbai or Bengaluru appears to be deteriorating.
Indian cities are not walkable, they rank among the worst for air quality, construction is poorly regulated, seasonal flooding is common and waste management remains under pressure. These challenges are only going to increase; the World Bank expects India’s urban population to double, going up to 951 million, by 2050. More than half of the urban infrastructure the country will need by then has yet to be built, it said.
So, what would it take to make our cities better and safer? The experts I spoke to broadly agreed that Indian cities don’t lack rules as much as the political will and institutional machinery to enforce them.
For infrastructure veteran Vinayak Chatterjee, one solution lies in giving urban local bodies more power. He points to a constitutional amendment from 1992 that was meant to strengthen municipalities and give them greater responsibility over urban planning. “But it remains largely unimplemented – in spirit and will. It is a serious matter that affects the very fabric of our urban existence,” said Chatterjee, founder of the Infravision Foundation.
Rahul Goel, an expert on transportation safety and a professor at the Indian Institute of Technology, Delhi, believes the problem with India’s roads begins with on-street parking. “People are using public space for personal use. Everything becomes better when you remove on-street parking,” he said, arguing that freeing up roads would make pedestrians and cyclists safer, reduce traffic jams and make walking easier.
In other cities in the global south, from Bangkok to Manila to Cape Town, one cannot just park their car on the road to run errands, Goel said. He described it as a governance failure, saying there is a need to create more parking spaces and perhaps have civil defense personnel or municipal workers enforce fines.
“Our streets are self-run,” Goel said. “That’s why they are in complete disarray.” He pointed to the Delhi Metro as an example of a space where people follow rules and things are orderly. “When rules are enforced, people follow them.”
The same gap between rules and enforcement is evident at construction sites.
India has detailed guidelines for construction approvals, including how traffic must be managed, what signage must be put up, and creating paths for pedestrians. But compliance remains a significant problem, says Geetam Tiwari, emeritus professor at Indian Institute of Technology, Delhi. In an audit of construction sites on highways, including bridges, Tiwari and her colleagues found widespread violations. Contractors had a financial incentive to complete projects quickly with payments being tied to the pace of construction, she said, adding that penalties for violations were low enough that it was cheaper to simply pay the fine than make fixes.
For unsafe buildings and unauthorised renovations, Tiwari said, the solution also requires bringing stakeholders together: resident associations, landlords, lessees and local authorities to conduct audits, raise awareness and penalise contractors who violate safety requirements. Actions, she said, that should not wait for the next tragedy.
In the aftermath of the Delhi case, the high court has directed authorities to inspect student accommodations for safety. Building owners have been arrested and several municipal officials in charge of the area have been suspended.
A similar governance deficit shows up when it comes to air pollution, another long-time challenge for Indian cities. Ronak Sutaria, founder and CEO of Respirer Living Sciences, has been working on one aspect of this issue: by developing affordable air-quality monitors for construction sites. Respirer’s air-quality monitors are now installed in 5,000 locations across 10 cities in India, helping authorities identify pollution hotspots. (Some cities, including Mumbai, require construction sites to monitor pollution levels.)
“A number of sites are getting alerts [from authorities] and are taking dust-suppression measures, for instance, to bring down [pollution] levels. So, the entire loop is sort of working,” Sutaria said.
Indian cities continue to grow, but the question is whether governance can keep pace. On that afternoon in Bandra, I recall thinking how lucky the woman and I were not to be grievously injured. But we shouldn’t have to rely on luck to survive.

Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
This week, writer and professor Amitava Kumar (@amitavawriter), whose latest book, The Social Life of Trains, explores how railways helped shape India’s national identity, suggests the work of a poet he discovered on Instagram:
“Can I begin with a confession? I have been a professor of literature for more than three decades, but I don’t often understand poems. How lovely it is, then, to discover a poet whose lines are as clear and beautiful as the dawn! Recently, I came across the poems of a young Hindi poet named Parag Pawan. They spoke to me and, more importantly, they spoke to our moment. I immediately sat down to translate them into English.
A series of his poems could be translated as Poems for the Unemployed. One of the poems, sharp and precise, begins with the funny, acerbic lines: ‘On the topic of our unemployment / the prime minister gives speeches / but he doesn’t give us jobs. / He works for eighteen hours / while we believe that asking anyone to work / for more than eight hours / is exploitation.’”
Count it
A number worth knowing
2,192
That’s the number of days Umar Khalid has spent in jail since his arrest on 13 September 2020 – without trial. Last week, the student activist wrote a searing account describing the daily drudgery of life in prison, published in The Quint. Earlier this year, in his first interview since being jailed, Khalid told the Guardian’s Hannah Ellis-Peterson: “Humanity is a privilege that is not granted to people like me.”
Vibe check
As more people read news online, watching Ayan Shaikh (@paperboy_ayan) delivering newspapers with serious swag gave me great joy and some hope. The 22-year-old from Ahmedabad posts videos of it on Instagram, and it’s a feat to watch. Watch his papers swerve, reach gravity-defying heights and land with pinpoint accuracy and tell me his deliveries don’t rival Jasprit Bumrah.
Delivering papers was Shaikh’s first job after he dropped out of school. He spent four years mastering the techniques that would allow him to make faster deliveries to earn more money. The first video, filmed by his friend, had 20m views and a recent one has crossed 128m, more views than many Bollywood stars might command. He starts his day at 4:30am, making 300 deliveries in two hours, before he begins a second shift as a gig worker for quick commerce apps.
“I think people love [the videos] because I do it passionately … from my heart,” he said. “If you do things dedicatedly, anything is possible. It won’t work out once, twice, thrice, but it might on the fourth attempt.”

Taking a personal loan is a financial commitment, so understanding how interest affects the total repayment can help borrowers make informed decisions. An Interest Calculator provides a simple way to estimate the interest payable on a loan based on factors such as the principal amount, interest rate, and repayment tenure.
Instead of working through complex calculations manually, borrowers can use an Interest Calculator to compare different loan scenarios and understand how changes in the loan amount, rate, or tenure may affect the overall cost. This can make it easier to plan a personal loan around a realistic monthly budget.
What does an interest calculator tell you?
An Interest Calculator helps estimate the interest payable on a loan. Depending on the calculator, users may enter details such as the loan amount, applicable interest rate, and repayment period to understand the potential cost of borrowing.
For example, if a borrower is considering a personal loan of Rs. 3 lakh, the calculator can help show how the estimated interest may change when the repayment tenure or interest rate is adjusted.
The result is generally an estimate and may differ from the final amount payable under the actual loan agreement.
How does the interest rate affect your loan cost?
The interest rate is a key factor in the cost of borrowing. A higher rate can increase the interest payable, while a lower rate may reduce the overall cost, subject to the loan terms.
Borrowers should therefore avoid looking only at the monthly EMI. It is equally important to understand how much interest you'll pay over the entire repayment period.
Using an Interest Calculator with different rates can help borrowers compare scenarios before choosing a personal loan.
Can the loan tenure change the total interest you pay?
Loan tenure determines how long the borrower takes to repay the amount. A longer tenure can make the monthly EMI more manageable because it spreads the repayment across more months.
However, extending the tenure may also increase the total interest payable. A shorter tenure can result in higher monthly payments but may reduce the overall interest cost.
Borrowers can enter different tenures into an Interest Calculator to see how these changes may affect the estimated repayment.
Why should you compare different loan amounts?
The amount borrowed directly affects the repayment obligation. Borrowing more than necessary can increase both the monthly EMI and the total interest payable.
Before taking a personal loan, borrowers should identify the actual funding requirement and consider whether available savings can cover part of the expense.
For instance, if an expense is Rs. 2 lakh and the borrower already has Rs. 50,000 available, borrowing the entire Rs. 2 lakh may not be necessary. Comparing different loan amounts can help identify a more manageable borrowing requirement.
How can an Interest Calculator help with EMI planning?
An Interest Calculator can help with EMI planning. By changing the loan amount, interest rate, or tenure, borrowers can compare estimated repayment outcomes.
This allows them to consider whether the proposed EMI fits comfortably alongside rent, household expenses, existing EMIs, and other regular commitments.
A borrower should ideally choose a loan structure that balances monthly affordability with the overall cost of borrowing.
What is the difference between simple and compound interest?
Simple interest is calculated only on the original principal amount for the relevant period. Compound interest, on the other hand, involves interest being calculated on the principal along with accumulated interest, depending on the applicable compounding frequency and terms.
The calculation method therefore matters when estimating the cost of different types of borrowing or investments. Borrowers should check the terms of the specific financial product rather than assuming that every loan uses the same interest calculation method.
When can a compound calculator be useful?
A compound calculator can help users understand how money may grow when interest is added to the balance over time. It is commonly useful for exploring compound interest scenarios where the interest earned is added back to the principal for subsequent calculations.
For example, someone comparing different savings or investment scenarios can use a compound calculator to see how the compounding frequency and time period may affect the estimated outcome.
This differs from estimating the interest payable on a personal loan, so users should choose a calculator suited to the financial calculation they want to perform.
How can you compare personal loan scenarios before applying?
Borrowers can use an Interest Calculator to compare several possible loan structures before submitting an application.
They can consider:
- Different loan amounts
- Different interest rates
- Shorter or longer repayment periods
- Changes in estimated monthly EMI
- Approximate total interest payable
- Overall repayment amount
For example, a borrower considering Rs. 4 lakh can compare a shorter tenure with a longer one. The shorter option may result in a higher EMI but potentially lower total interest, while the longer option may offer a lower EMI with a higher overall interest cost.
What other loan charges should you check?
Interest is an important part of borrowing costs, but it may not be the only charge. Depending on the lender and loan terms, borrowers may also need to consider processing fees, late payment charges, prepayment or foreclosure charges, and other applicable costs.
An Interest Calculator generally focuses on interest and repayment calculations, so borrowers should separately review the complete fee structure and loan agreement.
Comparing the total cost rather than focusing on a single figure can provide a clearer picture of affordability.
What should you check before choosing a personal loan?
Before accepting a personal loan, borrowers should review their financial position and the complete loan terms. A calculator can support the decision, but use it alongside careful financial planning.
Consider these points before applying:
- Borrow only the amount required.
- Check the applicable interest rate.
- Compare different repayment tenures.
- Assess the estimated EMI against monthly income and expenses.
- Review processing fees and other applicable charges.
- Check prepayment and foreclosure conditions.
- Keep existing EMIs and financial commitments in mind.
- Read the loan agreement carefully before accepting the offer.
How can an Interest Calculator make borrowing decisions easier?
Understanding loan interest does not have to involve complicated calculations. An Interest Calculator can give borrowers a quick way to compare different loan scenarios and see how the principal amount, interest rate, and tenure can influence repayment.
Using the calculator before applying can also encourage borrowers to think about affordability rather than choosing a loan amount based only on immediate requirements.
The final interest and repayment amount will depend on the actual terms offered by the lender.
Conclusion
An Interest Calculator can make it easier to understand how interest affects the cost of borrowing. By comparing loan amounts, interest rates, and repayment tenures, borrowers can estimate their potential EMI and total interest and choose a personal loan structure that better suits their budget.
A compound calculator serves a different purpose and can help you understand how compound interest affects savings or investment calculations. Regardless of the calculator used, borrowers should review the complete terms, charges, and repayment obligations before making a financial decision.

The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) has issued an alert on the use of unauthorised cosmetic products manufactured in Pakistan, which are on sale in India.
A public notice dated September 8, 2026, stated that cosmetic products named ‘Goree Beauty Cream’ and ‘Chandni Whitening Cream’ are unauthorised for sale and no trade registration certificate was issued to the manufacturers.
“To manufacture cosmetics for sale and distribution, a licence must be obtained from the State Licensing Authority... For the import of cosmetics, the products must be registered with the Central Licensing Authority in accordance with prescribed rules,” the notice said.
The products are unauthorised and contain excessive levels of heavy metals beyond the specified limits, which may pose health risks to consumers, including toxic effects, said CDSCO.
The drug regulator warned people not to purchase or use the products. It also asked consumers not to use similarly named cosmetic products if they had already purchased them.
It also informed that all concerned establishments/individuals were warned not to sell, distribute or advertise these products.

Grim discoveries of murdered women spark fear in South Africa
- Published
"What we are going to do, I have no idea," sobs Nokwanda Matshikiza, reflecting on the murder of her niece Dineo Motapane. "But something must give."
"For us, for all the other women. How many other bodies will be found before something happens?"
Nokwanda is speaking to the BBC from the family home near South Africa's main city, Johannesburg, just two days after relatives identified Dineo's body.
The 38-year-old mother-of-two was last seen alive last Sunday. Her battered body, partly burned, found later in the residential region of Ekurhuleni.
Nokwanda weeps as she describes how the family will have to face, at some point, the grim task of telling Dineo's daughter of her death.
"How do you explain that your parent was brutally murdered, dumped in a field, and just left there, discarded like a piece of rubbish.
"There's no coming to peace with it," she adds. "It's something that you can never reconcile yourself with, that you can never get over."
Dineo's death this week has come amid a series of comparable incidents in Ekurhuleni – her body one of three discovered there this week. In total, nine bodies of murdered women have been found in similar circumstances in the region since July.
The problem has always been there but this spate of grim discoveries has once again sparked a national outcry about the scale of violence against women in the country – which has one of the highest rates of gender-based violence in the world.
Themba Kekana is also living in shock at the death of a loved one.
His sister, Itumeleng, was one of the first to disappear in Ekurhuleni.
The 32-year-old shopkeeper's body was found in July, 17 days after she was last seen alive. Her body was badly bruised, partially clothed and dumped on a bridge.
"We are devastated with grief," says Themba, wet eyes shining.
"I look at my sister's young daughter and my eyes fill with tears, I know there is no way that I can ever take this pain away from her.
"No family should have to deal with what we are faced with."
Only one arrest has been made in connection with the murders – and that was two days after the first body was discovered on 15 July.
Nobody has been detained following the murders of Itumeleng or Dineo or the other six Ekurhuleni women.
Most of the victims were young, in their 20s or 30s, and almost all had suffered extreme violence before their deaths.
Police have said they are not sure if they are hunting a serial killer. It is possible the cases are not linked.
Either way, what has happened in this residential district east of South Africa's biggest city has traumatised the nation, shining a spotlight on a situation that many believe is a crisis.
South Africa's police issue detailed crime statistics every quarter, which show that during the last quarter – between April and June this year - 5,427 people were murdered.
The official data does not distinguish between the genders of the victims, but this week the country's Human Rights Commission released figures showing that 569 women had been killed in that period (six a day on average), with another 1,052 who faced attempted murder.
Many women - already feeling unsafe - have been left reeling by recent events.
And it has put pressure on the government, less than a year after ministers acknowledged the scale of the issue and declared gender-based violence a national disaster.
Announcing the move last November, Minister of Social Development Nokuzola Sisisi Tolashe said treating the issue as a national disaster would help the government tackle the crisis.
It followed weeks of protests, culminating in a "Women's Shut Down" march as South Africa hosted the G20 summit.
This week has seen a chorus of calls for things to go further.
Rights group Amnesty International said an important first step towards protecting South Africa's women was to recognise femicide as a separate crime.
"Every day that femicide remains unrecognised as a crime is a failure to confront the targeted killing of women," said Amnesty's country director Shenilla Mohamed in a statement. "It is time to call it what it is: Femicide.
"Femicide is a gender-motivated crime. It is the killing of a woman because she is a woman."
Amnesty says femicide is criminalised as a specific crime in 33 countries, including Gabon and Morocco in Africa.
It argues that making that change in South Africa could help focus on the scale of the issue.
"It would compel the state to confront their failure to protect women and girls from violence," says Mohamed. "You cannot fix what you are not tracking."
Almost everyone in South Africa agrees more needs to be done.
President Cyril Ramaphosa this week pledged to leave "no stone unturned" in investigating the crimes in Ekurhuleni, adding: "As a nation, we must stand up for the rights, safety and dignity of women and girls."
Lebogang Ramofoko, an advocate for gender and social justice, said the levels of violence against women in the country were symptomatic of a much bigger problem – a lack of regard for humanity.
"The bodies of black women have been treated as disposable in this country for time in memorial, passed down from colonisation through to apartheid," she tells the BBC, referring to the legalised system of racism that was in place until 1994.
"What we see happening to women is testimony to legacies of violence from those systems whose traumas were never addressed.
"This is not to say black men are inherently violent, but in systems where violence was meted out against them for decades, historically black women were the people that that violence would be taken out on - that cycle has not been broken."
In Kempton Park, a district of Ekurhuleni where five of the nine recent bodies were found, Lumka Maqhubela is part of the Girl2Woman Foundation group which has held protests to raise awareness of the crimes.
"We are grieved, we are scared," she says. "If the police cannot protect us any more the government should step in and do something.
"It's clear that we are not safe, we cannot be told by the police to be more vigilant. They should be doing more to make our communities safe – what else are we expected to do? We are not safe anywhere, not in our homes, not in the streets, it needs to stop."
"I feel uncomfortable," says Thulisile Sibande, 32. "When I go to a shop, I have to look around. I'm shocked and scared. So scared, it's a trauma."
Thembi Mabena, 60, tells the BBC she lived in the same neighbourhood as Dineo Motapane.
"She was laughing every day, with everybody," she remembers. "Now I'm worried.
"I know many children, girls, who tell me they are afraid to go to the shop alone. There is no safety, even for me too. I am old, but there is no safety."
"In South Africa," says Lerato Mzizi, 20, simply, "women are not safe any more."

One more held in Veeramani Pocso case; probe on property sale underway: Cops
Veeramani, 84, and his aides Shanthi and her husband Mahandra Simhan, were arrested on August 29, in a Pocso case
Tamil Nadu police on Tuesday arrested another person, identified as Ganesan, in connection with the Pocso case against granite baron R Veeramani for possession of a video that shows Veeramani acting inappropriately with a girl, police said.
Veeramani, 84, and his aides Shanthi and her husband Mahandra Simhan, were arrested on August 29, in a Pocso case for sexually abusing multiple minors from impoverished backgrounds at a guest house in Teynampet systematically over multiple decades. The three are in the Puzhal Central Prison near Chennai.
In a statement, Tamil Nadu crime branch said, “Ganesan who worked for 23 years at Gem Granites and is currently employed at another private firm, Balaji Global Enterprises, was arrested for having a video on his mobile phone showing Veeramani acting inappropriately with a young girl and failing to report it to the police.”
He was produced before the court and remanded in Puzhal Central Prison, the crime branch said.
Police said they will investigate the source of the “explicit” video to find out who sent it to Ganesan and why he failed to inform the police.
Also Read:‘Blurry video’: Police seeks R Veeramani sexual assault case closure; Pocso court denies
A senior police officer, requesting anonymity said that Ganesan took care of Veeramani’s financial transactions and was instrumental in selling his property at East Coast Road to help him evade arrest in the case.
Police said it was also trying to verify the claim of a social media user that Veeramani’s East Coast Road property worth ₹120 crore and another one worth ₹10 crore in Ooty were sold and money was paid to some people to help him in the case.
“We are looking for a person whose name is mentioned in the post,” the official said. Police did not confirm whether they have summoned the person mentioned in the social media post.
Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) propaganda secretary and minister for school education, Rajmohan Arumugam, said that new information is emerging every hour in the case and referred to it as ‘Gem Granites Files’ drawing similarity with Epstein Files.
“Similarly, this ‘Gem Granites File’ appears to involve many individuals; several crores of rupees have been paid, and many people have been silenced. Look at how they closed a case stating there was no evidence or no one to file a complaint,” he said on Tuesday.
He accused the previous Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) government of shielding the accused. “If the case was investigated properly, it would have been a massive eye-opener,” he said.
DMK, however, said no one was protected, as the police were investigating the case to collect proper evidence against the accused.

You may be familiar with the various memes detailing the fact that once you reach middle age, you're automatically sorted, Harry Potter hat-style, into one of a handful of hobbies, such as sourdough bread making, gardening, or bird-watching. I can't contradict this, since I'm a middle-aged person who got sorted into bird-watching. But I do know that enjoying birds and their various activities is fun for all ages. Birds are beautiful, interesting, and unpredictable, and it's fascinating to keep a running life list of all the birds you've seen and hope to see in your lifetime.
Whether someone you know is in their bird-watching phase, preparing for this phase, or has been in it for decades, all of these unique gifts—for traveling bird-watchers and backyard bird enthusiasts alike—are things either I or another bird-loving Reviews team member tested, was gifted, or bought IRL and enjoyed.
For more specific equipment recommendations, check out our guides to the Best Smart Bird Feeders and the Best Binoculars. For other gift ideas, check out all our gift guide coverage, including the Best White Elephant Gifts, Best Gifts for Men, and Best Viral TikTok Gifts.
Updated September 2026: I added a birdseed subscription and a puzzle, and ensured links and prices are up to date.
Featured Gifts
Our Favorite Smart Bird Feeder
If you love birds, nothing beats seeing them up close and personal, conducting all their birdy activities. I have learned more about birds in the past two years of testing smart bird feeders than I have over my entire lifetime, such as the fact that cowbirds will lay their eggs in other birds' nests (such as juncos) and the “host” birds will raise the cowbird chicks as their own, even if they look nothing alike. Or that jays and other corvids are scatter-hoarders and will spend an entire day picking nuts out of a feeder's seed mix to hide caches around the yard. There are many smart seed feeders on the market, but Birdfy's high-quality basic model (available with a blue or yellow roof) stands out for its balance of price, features, reliability, and usability without a subscription, making it a great gift option that I have personally given.
A Family Pick
My mom gifted this to my family about 10 years ago, and to this day, it is the single most-played and most-enjoyed game we have ever owned, in any genre. Shuffle the small cards and call them out; players place a blue cardstock square on their bingo card if they have that bird. My son loved it, his friends loved it, neighbors loved it, extended family loved it—it can be played by up to six people at a time, and is suitable for all ages. No reading or parsing of rules required. Best of all, neither my husband nor I minded playing it multiple times a day for years on end (a bonus feature important for any parent of young kids).
For Beginning Birders
Experienced birders probably already have a decent set of binoculars, but for the birding-curious, kids, or someone just starting out, quality binoculars and a life list journal ($22) would make a great gift. WIRED contributing reviewer Caramel Quin declared these the Best Budget Binoculars. I bought a set for each member of my family for a cruise to Alaska last summer, and I'm glad I did. They're lightweight (7.2 ounces) yet sturdy, with an aluminum casing instead of plastic, and small enough to slip into a pocket if you'll be hiking and don't want to deal with them around your neck.
A Customized Bird Seed Subscription
The one thing a bird-watcher could always use more of is seed, and this service offers a fun spin on what would otherwise be a boring gift. You can choose either a subscription or a one-time purchase of three boxes: The Starter consists of one 10-pound bag of seed custom-blended to appeal to birds in your recipient’s zip code. The Simply Seeds (pictured above) adds a 5-pound bag of a specialty blend (I received a fruit and nut mix), and the Splendid tacks on suet and mealworms. The blend for my yard—black-oil sunflower seeds, peanut splits, safflower, and millet—was spot-on; birds loved it so much there was little to no mess. (Though you can also specifically opt for No Waste, Hot Pepper, and No Starling versions of your blend.) Each box comes with a personalized letter from founder Susan Vandergriff about which birds to look out for in your area. This latter part needs a bit of fine-tuning, as my letter featured blue jays and summer tanagers, neither of which exist in my region, but I found the whole package charming nonetheless.
A Bird Nerd Classic
This 8- by 11-inch hardcover by famed ornithologist David Sibley (known for his Sibley field guides) may be too big and too heavy to fit in a backpack for field reading, but it remains the definitive source for interesting bird facts. Did you know mallard nestlings have only a 15 percent chance of fledging, and that once they hatch, fewer than half of ducklings survive? And that jays in the Northeastern US often eat paint chips in search of calcium, which doesn't occur naturally in that region's soil? Or that chickadees specifically seek out spiders to feed their young for the first week after they hatch, as spiders are high in taurine? Whether you want to or not, you will learn all these things and more if you give someone close to you this book.
A Different Kind of Bird Food
My husband and I received this feeder basket and some suet cakes as a gift about 10 years ago. The basket has fallen on the ground countless times; been chewed on and used as gymnastics equipment by squirrels; and survived windstorms, snow, and pretty much everything Pacific Northwest winters have to offer. Sure, looks-wise, it's seen better days, but it still does the job.
Suet—beef fat, if we're being explicit; the solid-form cousin to rendered tallow—attracts a different variety of birds than seeds, primarily insect-eaters like woodpeckers and bushtits. It tends to melt and go rancid in the heat, so I like the melt-free hot pepper variety, which can be used year-round and has been deemed unpalatable by our neighborhood squirrels.
Camera Lenses for Your Phone
Phone cameras keep getting better, but photos taken with that tiny lens aren't going to win you any awards. If you want more detailed and dramatic photos from your birdwatching expeditions but don't want to schlep a full camera setup around, try a professional-grade phone lens. WIRED reviewer Julian Chokkattu has tested several of these from Moment and recommends the 1.33X Anamorphic Lens for cinematic video, the 10X Macro Mobile Lens for close-ups, and the 14-mm Fisheye Mobile Lens for fun.
To use these lenses, you'll need a Moment Phone Case (available for recent iPhones) and, if you have an iPhone, the $5 drop-in lens mount in order to screw the lenses into the case. You will also want to use Moment's Pro Camera app, and Julian recommends this filter, which can help cut glare from bodies of water and shoot long exposures. Note that Julian doesn't recommend buying these lenses if you have a Google Pixel or Samsung phone, as Moment seems to have stopped making cases for Android.
The Ultimate Bird Poster
If you've ever wondered how many birds live in North America, this poster displays all 740 of them in one chart, both native and non-native, arranged by size and order. It's educational and a surefire conversation starter. In fact, I’ve had this chart framed in my home's entryway for almost eight years, and I don’t think a single person has visited my house for the first time and not commented on it, regardless of their ornithological interest level. It's really fascinating in person, and even if your giftee is already well-versed in birds, they'll probably still learn something new.
For Birders Who Love Adventure
Until reading this book, I had never heard of Blakiston's fish owl. And apparently neither had the author, bird-watcher and biologist Jonathan Slaght, until he caught sight of one—the world's largest living owl. What followed was a five-year passion project to catalog the owl in a remote region of eastern Russia. Part travel adventure, part scientific study, part memoir, this much-lauded nonfiction book reads like a novel and will be a page-turner for anyone who enjoys birds, exploration, or the outdoors.
Make Your Existing Bird Feeder Smart
If your recipient has an existing bird feeder they like, or a seasonal nesting site somewhere around their home or property, they might love a stand-alone bird camera. This one is the best I've tested, compatible with both 2.4-GHz and 5-GHz Wi-Fi networks. The cute green owl face streams 4K HD video and pushes 1080p pics to the Hibird app. There's access to AI identification (which I found to be just OK), livestreaming, and Hibird's “Dr. Bird” ChatGPT-like help feature, which allows you to ask bird-related questions. (I didn't find it to be particularly helpful, but YMMV.)
The auxiliary solar panel can be mounted separately, or you can just take the camera inside to charge when the battery runs out, as I did—the battery lasts at least several weeks. The camera comes with a bracket and bendable arm for precise positioning, or you can jury-rig a custom solution. No subscription is needed, though a Hibird rep says that may change in the future.
For Bird-Loving Gamers
WIRED reviewer Simon Hill, our staff board game aficionado, says this award-winning card-driven game will appeal to anyone interested in birds, as it pairs strategy with plenty of educational information about different bird species. It can feel complex at first, so it's probably best for families with kids older than 10, but once you get the hang of it, it can be addictive. (Up to five people can play, but you can also play solo.) Playing time is 40 to 70 minutes.
A Smart Birdhouse
Contrary to popular belief, birds don't always sleep in birdhouses. Some cavity-nesting birds may use them for shelter during inclement weather, but where I live on the West Coast, birdhouses are primarily used for nesting, which happens during the spring. This is not my first go-round with a smart birdhouse; I tested the interestingly shaped Birdfy Polygon last year, which did not attract any birds then, and this year it kept going offline. As an alternative, I tried Birdfy's newer Nest Duo, which has two 2-MP cameras, one facing the entrance and one tucked discreetly inside. This one worked perfectly, both connection-wise and in terms of bird interest—mine raised a family of black-capped chickadees, and seeing their activity on the Birdfy app each day has been the most fun bird-watching experience I have ever had.
Become a More Observant Naturalist
In his guide to Gifts for Hikers, Backpackers, and Outdoorsy People, WIRED reviewer Scott Gilbertson said he loved this book by John Muir Laws (no relation to the famed naturalist John Muir) so much that it changed the way both he and his kids looked at the world, allowing them to see a level of detail they'd never noticed before. You don't even have to be an artist to appreciate this one, as it's more about the art of observation. He recommends including these pens with the book, which I have also owned in the past and love.
A Perfect Puzzle
If you're a puzzle enthusiast and haven't yet tried wooden jigsaw puzzles, you must. My go-to brand is Liberty Puzzles—the quality and designs are truly unmatched—but California-based Nautilus Puzzles is a close second. Especially appealing is Nautilus’ Parliament of Fowls, a visual interpretation of the 14th-century Chaucer poem. Though it's only 511 pieces, they are all individually shaped, many with a bird theme, which makes this puzzle both beautiful and extremely challenging.

F1 title race: Why Azerbaijan-Malaysia-Singapore triple header will shape what rest of 2026 championship chase will look like
Kimi Antonelli's chief rivals may have all but ruled themselves out of winning the title but the season's first triple header could provide unpredictable twists; watch every session of the Azerbaijan GP from Thursday live on Sky Sports F1, with the race on Saturday at 12pm
Tuesday 22 September 2026 06:19, UK
Formula 1 embarks on its first triple header of the season this week with the Azerbaijan Grand Prix the first of three races in as many weekends.
The race on the streets of Baku - which takes place on Saturday rather than the usual Sunday - was originally due to be a standalone event with the Singapore Grand Prix following on two weeks later.
But the moving of the Bahrain Grand Prix to Malaysia in the week between the two events has created the run of three successive race weeks, with two more triple headers scheduled to close out the 2026 season.

So what can we expect from this first Azerbaijan-Malaysia-Singapore triple and what will the world championship picture - which currently sees Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli holding a commanding lead - look like on the other side into mid-October?
Last chance saloon for Antonelli's challengers?
While Antonelli's victory last time out in Madrid was fortuitous thanks to the Virtual Safety Car timing that helped him and hindered McLaren's race-leading Lando Norris, the Mercedes driver was enjoying another strong weekend at F1's brand-new venue and was in position to capitalise on such a slice of luck.
That victory, Antonelli's eighth in 14 races this season, means he arrives in Baku with an 81-point lead at the top of the Drivers' Championship.
Since seeing his title advantage over team-mate George Russell cut to just 25 points at the British Grand Prix at the start of July, Antonelli's lead has increased in each of the last five race weekends to its current season-high total.
Russell remains Antonelli's closest challenger but he all but conceded his hopes of beating his team-mate to the crown after falling more than the equivalent of three races wins behind the Italian by finishing fifth at the Madring.
Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton had already effectively ruled himself out after the previous weekend's race at Monza, but was more certain in saying his title hopes were over after brake problems at the Madring saw him register his first DNF of the season.
Hamilton is now 101 points off the pace while fourth-placed Norris, the grid's in-form driver alongside Antonelli, saw his own deficit grow to 106 points on a weekend the reigning world champion was unlucky not to make it three wins in four.
All the championship cards appear firmly stacked in Antonelli's favour, not that the young Italian appears to carry the weight of being the clear title favourite particularly heavily.
The 20-year-old has continued to insist he is "not thinking about the championship" in every interview he is asked about it, a mantra that his team boss Toto Wolff says is genuine and the best one for his driver to adopt.
Yet time is obviously running out for any one of the would-be challengers to put a stunning run of form and results together over the final rounds to truly trouble him.
There is still time, though, and with 83 points up for grabs during this first triple header of rounds alone - 75 across the three grands prix and eight for the Singapore Sprint - Mercedes are right to remain cautious - for now.
But should Antonelli finish the Singapore weekend on October 11 with a similar or even increased lead compared to the 81-point one he holds now, then the odds on him not becoming the sport's youngest-ever world champion will become very long indeed, even with a maximum of six rounds (and 150 points) left to play for.
What challenges do the next three tracks present?
Kicking off this intense run into the autumn is the Baku City Circuit, a high-speed, wall-lined street track through the middle of Azerbaijan's capital that has often featured on lists of a season's most dramatic races during its first decade on the calendar.
Last year's race - and indeed weekend - certainly fell into that category after a qualifying session that featured a record six red flags and a race, won by Red Bull's Max Verstappen, which saw then-title favourite and points leader Oscar Piastri crash out within six corners. The McLaren driver had also hit the wall in qualifying.
Antonelli, who finished fourth on his F1 debut in Baku last season and took a podium in F2 the year before, will be hoping to avoid those pitfalls as this year's driver to catch on a circuit which Mercedes, like at Monza, are being tipped to be particularly strong.
"Baku is completely different [to Madrid]. Slow-speed corners, massive straights, a little bit lower downforce as a result for those long straights," Sky Sports F1's Nico Rosberg told The F1 Show podcast.
"Engine power is always going to favour Mercedes in that way. We saw it in Monza, so I think Mercedes has to be the big favourite.
"Max Verstappen was fast in Monza, so maybe Verstappen can be the surprise there."
Then, for the first time in nine years, it is on to Malaysia and a Sepang International Circuit that was always a favourite among drivers and fans during its original 1999-2017 run on the calendar.
Ten current drivers were on the grid when F1 last raced there (with Charles Leclerc driving for Sauber in 2017's Friday practice), while Alex Albon and Liam Lawson drove there in junior series.
Antonelli, Russell and Norris are among those whose only experiences of the sweeping layout will have come in the simulation world, although even F1's most sophisticated tools cannot reflect the level of heat and humidity that famously accompanies racing in tropical Sepang.
But oppressive conditions are what drivers are regularly used to anyway in neighbouring Singapore at the Marina Bay Street Circuit, which has certainly been the most physically demanding race of the season in recent times.
What will be new in Singapore this year, though, is that its schedule features the Sprint format for the first time. It will be the sixth and final Sprint weekend of the season.
Sprint weekends by their nature - with a single practice session before the competitive sessions begin - increase the chance of unpredictability and punish any early driver mistakes or missteps on car set-up. Marina Bay, with its omnipresent walls, will only heighten that challenge.
What impact will the latest upgrade packages have?
As has been the case throughout this first season of the sport's new-look cars, the upgrade packages the leading teams bring to each race weekend will continue to have an impact on the pecking order.
Much-improved McLaren will have another package of changes on their MCL40 for Baku, a track where they struggled last year irrespective of Piastri's travails.
Mercedes' long-awaited upgrade will arrive for the following race in Malaysia. The W17 has not been upgraded to any significant degree at a single race since the Canadian Grand Prix at the end of May, an approach which has certainly helped Ferrari, McLaren and Red Bull to catch up.
However, the big question - and, for their rivals, the potential worry - is how much the Silver Arrows' Sepang package pushes them on.
"I think we are bringing a solid upgrade in Malaysia," Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff told Sky Sports F1 in Madrid. "So we've got to survive another race in Baku. Let's see.
"Sometimes it doesn't correlate with the road so well, so I hope that it does and hopefully that puts us on par with the others in terms of upgrades, but you never know."
Mercedes also have an ADUO power-unit upgrade still to deploy this season should they wish, amid suggestions the Silver Arrows could deploy it to coincide with whatever race Russell takes his expected engine grid penalty at.
Ferrari - who continue to show flashes of impressive promise but too regularly trip themselves up - and Red Bull - who appear to be getting closer to a first win of the year with Verstappen - will likely have new parts too across the triple header before attention throughout the field fully switches towards the 2027 challengers.
Will Antonelli remain in realistic chasing distance for 2026's final races by then?

In September 2026, social media users shared a video of an unusual animal encounter. The clip showed a rhino and a much smaller muntjac deer appearing to play together and butt heads in the snow.
"A tiny 13 kg Chinese muntjac deer playfully challenged a 1.7-ton rhino named Maruśka at the Wrocław Zoo in Poland," one Reddit post (archived) captioned the video.
Since January 2026, the clip has appeared in posts on X, Threads, Facebook and YouTube. Overlaid text in a YouTube video described (archived) the encounter as "David vs. Goliath," while some social media users wondered if the footage was generated using artificial-intelligence tools. For example, one Reddit user wrote (archived): "Saw this on another reddit post and many people were saying it's AI, but I'm really not sure it is."
However, the video was real. It showed Maruśka, a female Indian rhinoceros, and Tata (Polish for "Dad"), a male Chinese muntjac, a small deer species.
The footage originated from Zoo Wrocław in Poland. Managers of the zoo's official Facebook and Instagram pages posted the clip on Jan. 8, 2026. In the caption (translated from Polish), the zoo framed the scene as a humorous confidence mismatch and said the muntjac's bravado was driven by mating-season hormones:
Looks like someone forgot to look in the mirror this morning
Respect to Maruśka for her angelic patience!
Where does this bravado come from in the male Chinese muntjac?
It's nature calling! His partner is in heat, and testosterone is surging in the bachelor. He needs to burn off energy and show who's boss - even if his sparring partner weighs 1.7 tons. Who would have thought there was such a warrior in such a small body?
The clip was widely covered by national and local Polish news media outlets that cited the zoo as the source.
After the video went viral online, Zoo Wrocław published a follow-up article on Jan. 12, 2026, crediting the clip to employee Kamil Guzik, a foreman in the zoo's carnivorous mammals section.
Wrocław.pl — an online news portal in Wrocław, the city where the video was captured — spoke with Maciej Okupnik, a hooved-animal keeper at Zoo Wrocław, who explained why the two species shared a space.
The website quoted Okupnik as saying muntjacs and rhinos can live in proximity to one another both at the zoo and in the wild. He said muntjacs are territorial and mark areas with scent glands near their eyes, while rhinos typically tolerate other animals in their territory because "they're not afraid of anyone." He reportedly described the encounter as theatrical and said similar standoffs had occurred before but this was the first time staff had filmed one.
TVN24, a Polish news media channel, said Okupnik emphasized that the male muntjac's behavior was driven by a mix of territorial instinct and hormones because his partner was "in heat." He said the animal's priority was to defend his space and impress the female, not to challenge the rhino, and that Maruśka was not aggressive toward him in day-to-day interactions. Okupnik added that the rhino appeared to treat the lunges as an invitation to play, with no signs of real aggression. At one point, Maruśka snorted as if to signal she had enough and simply walked away.
Snopes has fact-checked several rhino-related rumors before. For example, in June 2025, we examined a claim that the northern white rhinoceros was extinct after the last such rhino died.

Quick Answer
The iPhone Duo hides several firsts and oddities: horizontal rear cameras, vertical UI elements, top-mounted volume buttons, Apple Pencil support, titanium construction, Smart Take, a circular status bar, unusual USB-C placement, and no Action button or Pro camera controls.
Apple launched many devices at its recent Surprise and Shine event, but there was no doubting the star of the show. It was the iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable phone, and the device that many are expecting to do for foldables what the iPhone did for smartphones almost two decades ago. Small wonder then that the past few days have seen everyone and their grandmother discussing the iPhone Duo.
Debates have been raging over its animations, its crease, its cameras, its apps, and of course, its price. Some are hailing it as the coolest thing since sliced bread, while others insist it is a spawn of Satan in smartphone shape. But in all this debate and discussion, some important aspects and features of the Duo have either escaped attention or have not been adequately covered.
Here are ten things you might have missed about Apple’s first foldable.
Table of Contents
The first iPhone with horizontally arranged cameras on the back…selfie cameras on the corners
iPhones have been coming with multiple cameras (two or three) on their backs for a while now. However, they have always been arranged vertically, one below the other, or in the case of some Pro devices, with two cameras one below the other and the third one placed between them but slightly to the side, forming a triangle of sorts. The iPhone Duo thus becomes the first iPhone to have cameras placed next to each other horizontally, in what some would term a very Pixel-like style. The selfie cameras also get new locations – moving to the right corner of the external display and close to the right corner of the internal display (when opened), where it actually lies under the display. Regular iPhone users are sure to notice a change in perspective.
The dock, navigation, and even the Dynamic Island just got radically right, and utterly vertical
The cameras on the iPhone Duo might have gone horizontal, but some elements of the UI have gone vertical! While everyone has been focusing on the crease in the middle of the iPhone Duo and its visibility (it’s not easy to spot, by all accounts). Apple moved many iOS elements to the right side and gave them a vertical orientation. Lock screen controls, navigation buttons, the home screen dock, and even the Dynamic Island are on the right side of the iPhone Duo, and what’s more, are arranged vertically.
The Dynamic Island even slides open vertically to show information and updates. Evidently, this was done because of the width of the iPhone Duo (it is also the widest iPhone ever), which would have made it difficult to reach these elements. They have therefore been placed on the same side as the display unlock/power button, which is also a fingerprint scanner. This is pretty right-wing in UI terms, literally.
Volume buttons on the top
The iPhone Duo comes with a rather different volume button placement from other foldables. While it is conventional for most foldables and indeed, most ‘normal’ phones, to have volume buttons on the right or left side, the iPhone Duo actually has volume buttons on the top, aligned slightly towards the right. This is a volume button placement we have seen on the newer iPad minis but not on any other iPhones or iPads. It is a rather odd location in our opinion, and if opened and rotated clockwise, it would place the buttons on the lower part of the right side, and on the top of the left side if rotated anti-clockwise.
Camera Control? Present! Action button? Er…
While the iPhone Duo comes with a Camera Control button like other recent iPhones, it, rather surprisingly, does not have an Action button, which is generally seen on the left side of most iPhones and can be customized to carry out a number of tasks. It used to toggle Silent mode on and off, before being changed to an action button. Clearly, it was either not good enough to make the cut for the Duo or perhaps there simply was not enough space for it.
Apple Pencil support exists, but only for the Type-C one
The iPhone Duo is the first iPhone to come with Apple Pencil support. What’s more, it supports the Apple Pencil on both its internal as well as external display. But there is a catch – it only supports the basic Apple Pencil (USB-C). This means that while one can scribble and sketch easily, there’s no pressure sensitivity and no support for double taps. One will also need a Type-C cable to charge it, as it cannot charge magnetically. Given the price and potential of the device, it would have been good to have Apple Pencil Pro support on it.
Only new iPhone with Titanium
Remember how Titanium was the coolest thing in premium phones a few years ago. Well, while it still remains a very premium material, it has largely disappeared from the smartphone scene, with even Apple seemingly moving on to other materials, with only the iPhone Air using Titanium last year. This time around, it is the iPhone Duo that carries the Titanium legacy forward. While the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max use “forged aluminum” and ceramic glass, the iPhone Duo comes with a main chassis made with grade 5 Titanium, and 3D-printed titanium is also used for the hinge cover.
The only iPhone camera with Smart Take
Although its cameras might not seem as formidable as those on the 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, the iPhone Duo has a slice of camera magic up its sleeve that no other iPhone has. This is Smart Take, which, with some AI magic, automatically works out when you are perfectly placed for a photograph and takes it without you needing to hit a capture button or prompt the device in any manner. It is supposed to work very well with individual and group selfies, and uses the rear cameras while showing you a preview on the cover display. While the feature is designed mainly for the fold form factor, it would be great to see it on “normal” iPhones too, although one might not be able to see previews!
A Type-C port placed under the cover display
In another case of rather unusual placement, the Type-C port of the iPhone Duo is actually placed on the base of the cover display or the upper panel. In many foldables, the charging port is placed on the lower panel, so that the phone can be opened without moving the charging cable. That is clearly not going to be possible on the iPhone Duo.
The status bar is closed…and is now a circle
The move to a foldable form factor has led to a redesign of some UI elements on the iPhone Duo. Perhaps the most surprising of these is the status bar. Until now seen in the top right corner, and displaying signal strength, Wi-Fi, and battery, it has now been changed to a circle, with the battery life and signal strength being on the circumference and Wi-Fi being at the center. It is not really as intuitive as its predecessor, but we guess users will get the hang of it.
No Pro controls in the camera
The iPhone Duo comes with two 48-megapixel cameras on the back – a new Fusion Main camera, and the same ultrawide that is on the 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max. But while these pack in a lot of features such as three photographic styles, smart focus tracking, next-generation portraits, macro photography and more, the iPhone Duo’s camera app does not come with the Pro Controls seen on the 18 Pro and Pro Max, which let users play around with shutter speed, white balance, and aperture. This l is a bit of a pity, especially given the vast viewfinder the open Duo can serve up. But well, to be fair, this was never meant to be a camera phone.

Is Garnacho already at a crossroads at Villa?
- Published
Just like last season, questions are being asked about Alejandro Garnacho.
Two months after joining from Chelsea on an initial loan, the winger has yet to convince Aston Villa boss Unai Emery of his worth.
The Argentina forward has played just 31 minutes for Villa, spread across three substitute appearances.
A 15-minute outing against Hull is the most time he has spent on the pitch in a game.
Garnacho has been an unused substitute for Villa's past four matches , watching from the bench again as they won 3-2 at Tottenham on Saturday.
One goal and four assists in 24 Premier League games for Chelsea last term fell below what the Blues expected from their £40m recruit from Manchester United, so he was allowed to move on.
This campaign is only a month old, but 22-year-old Garnacho could be at a crossroads at Villa Park already.
Emery likes to ease new players into his teams.
Youri Tielemans did not start a Premier League game until November 2023 after joining in the summer, but became an integral part of Emery's machine.
Only Joao Gomes, out of 10 new summer signings, started Villa's opening Premier League game. Just two - Zion Suzuki and Nicolas Jackson - started the next.
Garnacho's situation feels extreme though, having been left on the bench for the Carabao Cup win at Coventry when Emery made seven changes.
Academy product George Hemmings, who joined Villa from Forest as a teenager, has started the season well to earn Emery's full trust and start ahead of Garnacho.
Ibrahim Mbaye, a £47m arrival from Paris St-Germain, made his first Villa start in the 3-1 victory at Coventry and is also preferred to Garnacho for now.
A facial injury in early August hampered Garnacho's pre-season and meant he missed the Super Cup defeat by Paris St-Germain, adding to the complications.
Emery needs his players to understand their roles and his methods before having full faith in them and he expects Garnacho to catch up.
"Continue working. Work, work, train, work," Emery said when asked about Garnacho's absence from the pitch.
"When he can have minutes to play, try to play well. He is progressing, but we have players in front of him now.
"George is playing fantastic. Alysson is also understanding things well and is giving us things I want. [Ibrahim] Mbaye also responded well.
"We want a competitive team and players to compete in the style we have. Garnacho is a little bit behind because of some circumstances we had in pre-season. It is time to be patient for the time he needs."
Garnacho, who first made his name as a livewire teenager, has shown in the past he can torment defences at Premier League level.
He spoke about needing time to adapt to a "different club and a different place" at Chelsea.
A further season of struggle would be a significant setback.
Emery is clearly yet to be convinced by what he sees in training, despite being a long-term Garnacho admirer.
Villa wanted more pace in their side and Crysencio Summerville was considered before he moved to Saudi Arabia's Al-Hilal.
Chelsea's £117m signing of Morgan Rogers from Villa left a gap for Emery to fill and Garnacho was available. A positive relationship between the clubs allowed for easy discussions.
Striker Jackson also joined from Chelsea for a Villa club record £65m and there have been eight deals between the clubs in the past four years.
Shadow of Elliott loan hangs over Villa
Garnacho did not train with Xabi Alonso's Chelsea squad before leaving for Villa Park in July.
Roma were interested in the winger, but their loan offer did not suit Chelsea. Instead, Villa's deal gives the Blues the chance to make their money back after last year's outlay.
There is an obligation to buy tied into the loan that is believed to relate to appearances, and it is expected to be achievable - but that does not guarantee anything.
For instance, Harvey Elliott would have triggered a move worth £35m if he made just 10 Premier League appearances last season. As it turned out, the Liverpool loanee - now at Valencia - was used just four times by Villa in the top flight.
Emery did not feel the 23-year-old was good enough and made up his mind not to sign Elliott permanently just a couple of months into the season.
It raised the question for some within the game about whether a loan at Villa should be viewed with caution, and whether other players' careers could be derailed in the way Elliott experienced.
It was accepted that Elliott's options this summer were not as extensive following his season at Villa Park.
Time will tell whether Garnacho faces the same struggles, having experienced his career stalling over the past two years.
He made his Manchester United debut aged 17 and was part of Argentina's Copa America‑winning squad in 2024, but has not added to his eight international caps since November of that year.
The Madrid-born attacker also won the Premier League's goal of the season award in 2023-24 for his overhead kick against Everton while playing for United, but his output for Chelsea was disappointing.
Emery is waiting to see Garnacho fulfil his full potential at Villa, but the winger will have to wait until he gains the coach's trust, and then take his chance.

More than a decade ago, Mian Asghar Ali’s mother shared a simple wish with her son – to have a garden around their home. And what began with a single saplling in 2016 has since grown into a labour of love. Today, their six-marla house in Pakistan has been transformed into a mini forest, with more than 5,700 trees and plants. This is not just a garden but a living tribute to a mother’s dream that her son continues to nurture. Asghar, a resident of Pakistan's Punjab province, planted the first sapling in his house built on the 0.037-acre plot in Punjab’s Pattoki in 2016. Back then, Asghar was not sure whether he could even fulfil his mother’s wish for a not-so-big parcel of land on which the house stood. He even tried to convince his mother that there was not enough space near the house to create a garden and that such plans were meaningless. “But seeing her disappointed face gave me the passion to start this. It was in 2016 when I bought about 50 plants, placed 10 inside the house, and 40 along the outer wall. Since then, I have gradually added more,” Asghar told BBC Urdu in a video story. In the BCC video, Asghar is seen explaining how he planted trees on doors, walls, curtains, and throughout the house to fulfil my mother's wish. “People used to call me crazy, but today, when they visit and see my small haven, they appreciate my work and view us with respect,” he says. So far, Asghar has spent more than 40 lakh Pakistani rupees on the project and spends over PKR 30,000 every month on maintaining the greenery. The cost includes expenses for saplings, soil, and tools, as well as the ongoing upkeep required to keep thousands of plants alive and healthy year-round. “Since our house went viral, people from far away come to see it. Initially, there wasn't much lighting, but now I have installed lights throughout the house so that day and night feel the same,” he says. Asghar said he used specific plants that thrived in sunlight and are resilient to extreme winter frost, so he doesn't need to cover them as traditional nurseries do. He says in the video that the daily routine involves spending two to three hours watering and caring for the plants after Fajr (Dawn) prayers. Asghar says he aims to grow 10,000 plants and attempt to set a Guinness World Records title. As many as 71% of consumers surveyed in Mumbai said chemists never or rarely refused to sell medicines without a doctor’s prescription, compared with 64% nationally, according to a LocalCircles survey published on September 18, 2026. The findings come as the Centre has proposed mandatory CCTV surveillance at medical stores selling prescription drugs, and the Maharashtra FDA has intensified enforcement against retailers.
The Mumbai survey by LocalCircles, which received more than 20,000 responses across its questions, also found that only 28% of respondents said they were assisted by a qualified pharmacist most of the time or always, while 21% said they were assisted by someone who was not a qualified pharmacist.
On prescription checks, 36% of 3,697 Mumbai respondents said chemists never refused to give them medicines without a prescription and another 35% said they did so very rarely. Only 9% said chemists refused such sales most of the time and 5% said they always did so.
The gap was also visible in home deliveries. Of 3,122 respondents, 18% said their chemist never demanded a doctor’s prescription during ordering or delivery and 40% said this happened very rarely. Only 23% said a prescription was sought most of the time or always.
The survey showed that neighbourhood chemists remain the main source of medicines in Mumbai. Of 3,012 respondents, 57% said they visited or sent someone to a local chemist, while 26% ordered from their chemist through phone calls or WhatsApp for home delivery. Only 17% primarily used e-pharmacy apps.
The national survey, published a day earlier on September 17, 2026, showed similar, though somewhat lower, levels of reported non-compliance. Across India, 64% of consumers surveyed said their chemist never or rarely insisted on a doctor’s prescription, while only 15% said chemists did so most of the time or always. Only 31% said they were assisted by a qualified pharmacist most of the time or always, while 13% said the person assisting them was not qualified.
The nationwide survey received more than 106,000 responses from consumers across 327 districts. It also found that 41% said chemists never or rarely sought prescriptions during home delivery, compared with 58% in Mumbai.
The findings come as the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has floated draft amendments to the Drugs Rules, 1945, proposing mandatory CCTV surveillance at medical stores supplying medicines sold on a registered medical practitioner’s prescription.
The draft, issued through Gazette notification G.S.R. 791(E) dated September 8, proposes inserting a new sub-rule after Rule 65(2). It states that retail supply of prescription medicines should take place under CCTV surveillance installed and maintained at the premises. The proposal is aimed at strengthening oversight of the sale of Schedule H, H1 and X drugs and curbing sales without valid prescriptions. The government has invited objections and suggestions before finalising the amendment.
The proposed rule comes amid a sharper enforcement drive by the Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration. Between June and August 2026, the FDA inspected 2,902 drug establishments, including 2,295 sales establishments and 607 manufacturing units, and initiated action against 880 licensees.
Of these, 677 licences were suspended, and 203 were cancelled, with 740 of the 880 actions involving retailers and wholesalers. During the same three-month period, the FDA conducted 104 search-and-seizure operations, seized illegal drugs and cosmetics worth Rs 11.41 crore, registered 20 FIRs and made 21 arrests.
FDA inspectors flagged several of the same issues reflected in the consumer survey, including the sale of medicines without registered pharmacist supervision, dispensing prescription medicines without valid prescriptions, incomplete Schedule H1 records and sales without proper invoices. Other violations included expired medicines being kept in sale stock and inadequate temperature controls for products such as insulin and vaccines.
The Mumbai survey also found billing gaps. While 76% said they generally received a printed GST invoice and 3% received a manually prepared GST bill, 20% effectively did not receive a proper GST bill.
LocalCircles said the Mumbai findings would be shared with the Maharashtra FDA, Union Health Ministry and CDSCO, and called for stricter verification of registered pharmacists, prescription checks for phone and WhatsApp deliveries and better documentation of medicine sales.
