India’s higher education policy framework increasingly talks about inclusion. The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 (RPwD Act) places obligations on educational institutions to promote inclusive education, while the University Grants Commission (UGC) has, over the years, developed guidelines and institutional mechanisms intended to ensure that students with disabilities (SwD) can participate in higher education on an equal basis.
Despite these measures, the dearth of remedial support makes them vulnerable to academic exclusion and widens existing educational inequalities. Limited digital access further restricts their access to online learning resources, digital libraries, academic databases, and other educational platforms, hindering participation in technology-enabled learning and limiting their ability to make full use of academic opportunities.
(Sign up for THEdge, The Hindu’s weekly education newsletter.)
Most recently, the Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities listed the Accessibility Guidelines and Standards for Higher Education Institutions and Universities, issued by the Department of Higher Education, Ministry of Education, on June 25, 2024. The UGC describes these guidelines as part of its effort to ensure equal participation and inclusion of persons with disabilities in higher education.
Importantly, the UGC states that every higher educational institution (HEI) is expected to develop an effective accessibility mechanism extending from the admission process through the completion of the course. The Commission issued fresh directions to universities to furnish a report along with statistical information in respect of students admitted, teaching and non-teaching recruitment, as well as fellowships/scholarships provided to PwD students through the Universities Activity Monitoring Portal (UAMP) by September 30, 2026. It calls for the need to form an Internal Committee comprising teachers, staff, students and parents to take care of the day-to-day needs of persons with disabilities.
Yet institutional attention to disability often becomes focused on admission, reservation, and physical infrastructure. The more difficult question of what happens to the student after admission receives considerably less attention.
“The national statistical architecture measures how many students with disabilities enter higher education but does not adequately measure what happens to them after they enter colleges and universities,” disability rights activist and Professor at University College of Medical Sciences, Delhi, Dr. Satendra Singh told The Hindu.
Students with disabilities may enter higher education with varying levels of exposure to accessible learning environments. Some may require additional academic assistance, remedial classes, note-taking support, assistive technologies, or additional time and flexibility to engage with coursework. A student who misses classes because of disability-related issues may not have access to a structured academic mechanism to navigate the backlogs. The result is a form of exclusion that is not visible in institutional statistics.
Supportive system needed
The RPwD Act itself points to Section 16, which requires not merely admission without discrimination, but reasonable accommodation, necessary support, and monitoring of participation, academic progress, and completion. The UGC’s own accessibility framework similarly speaks of an accessible mechanism covering the student journey from admission to completion. But the lack of adequate remedial support has a direct bearing on how students with disability perform academically.
“Majority of the HEIs do not have a rights-based understanding of reasonable accommodation. They are still stuck with ramps, braille and talking books,” Dr. Singh said.
Pointing to the 2023–24 AISHE data, he said, “Of the 4.50 crore students enrolled in HEIs, the reported 54,080 students with benchmark disabilities (SwBD) represent approximately 0.12% of total higher-education enrolment. This is about 12 SwBD per 10,000 students. The AISHE reporting does not provide a detailed disability-type categorisation. This is a significant data gap because ‘SwBD’ is an extremely heterogeneous category. A student who is blind, a deaf student who uses Indian Sign Language (ISL), a student with dyslexia, an autistic student, and a student with psychosocial disability can have completely different accessibility and academic-support requirements.”
Dr. Sanjay Kant Prasad, Director of the National Centre for Disability Studies at IGNOU and former Deputy Chief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities, echoes his views. He said, “Higher education must recognise that the 21 categories of disabilities identified under the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act have diverse and often distinct educational needs. While some disabilities may require limited remedial support, students with blindness, low vision, hearing impairment, deafness, cerebral palsy, autism and learning disabilities, among others, may require specific forms of academic and assistive support.”
He stresses that inclusive education does not mean eliminating specialised support. Rather, it is about creating an accessible environment in which the same educational curriculum can be accessed by students with different needs.
“In higher education, teachers may not require specialised training for every disability, but they should at least be oriented to disability-related needs and know how to make classrooms, teaching methods and learning materials accessible. This could include tactile materials and Braille for students with visual impairments, appropriate seating and mobility support, hearing aids or visual aids for students with hearing impairments, and the use of assistive and digital technologies such as text-to-speech software,” Dr. Prasad said.
Citing IGNOU’s efforts to provide study material at students’ doorsteps, counselling through teleconferencing and facilities for submitting assignments using computers, while following government and UGC guidelines, Dr. Prasad feels students’ ability to remain in education depends on broader social and economic support, not just classroom accommodations. Housing, awareness of available services and support from disability organisations are important factors.
Progress has been made over the past several decades from exclusion towards inclusion, but implementation remains uneven, and continued awareness, teacher training, and institutional support are needed to navigate the barriers.
In schools, the structures for remediation are more readily available than in higher institutions. The multi-tiered systems of support are a comprehensive framework that help provide individualised support to students.
Under this tiered system, the first level of support is the universal support that is offered to all students to help them learn better; the second level is classroom-based strategies and only the third level involves intensive care such as remediation.
“Often, students who reach higher education come equipped with an understanding of their own needs, have developed learning strategies, and carry an arsenal of tools that have been offered to them since school. Therefore, not every SwD requires remediation; some might require accommodations and modifications. Here is where inclusive EdTech, digital access, and online learning resources come in handy,” Dr. Rajeshwari Muthukumaran, Assistant Professor at the Centre for Neurodiversity Research and Innovation at Christ (Deemed-to-be University), said. She runs a support group aimed at fostering a sense of belonging and building a community on campus with students with disabilities, and neurodiverse students.
Although SwD might already come with their specific digital tools/modified equipment, they may still need guidance and access to software and tech tools often used in their domain.
Significant resource gaps persist, including the availability of Braille-translated materials and books in accessible typefaces. These constraints make it more challenging to design and implement tailored remediation programmes.
Additionally, institutional resource limitations, including a shortage of faculty with both subject expertise and training in developing accessible curricula, pedagogical practices, and assessment methods, as well as limited spaces and opportunities for one-on-one student-faculty support, further compound the problem.
Drawing from experience, Dr. Muthukumaran said, “I have met students who often enter higher education with a mix of hope, anxiety, and anticipation, and are seeking a supportive and approachable guide/mentor/peer who can offer them a safe and understanding space and serve as a support system. While guiding them in classrooms, I often end up recommending students to mental health professionals/supportive online communities where they can exchange ideas and converse with individuals with similar experiences to help them deal with campus life overall.”
Evidently, more colleges have now started looking into strategies, establishing specialised cells and centres that further look into research and student support. “While there is a long way to go, this scattered chatter needs to grow louder, unanimously, to shape future education and move towards evidence-based inclusive practices,” Dr. Muthukumaran added.
The digital divide
Considering that higher education has become increasingly dependent on digital infrastructure, learning management systems (LMS), university portals, digital libraries, online journals, e-books, recorded lectures, online assignments, examination portals, email systems, and virtual classrooms are now integral to campus life. For many learners, this digital environment offers greater convenience, flexibility, and access to educational resources. But for students with disabilities, digital technologies can be either powerful enablers or, when accessibility is inadequate, can become significant barriers to participation and academic success.
A university website that cannot be navigated effectively with assistive technology can make admission and administrative processes more cumbersome. A PDF that is simply a scanned image may not be usable for a blind student. An online learning platform without appropriate keyboard navigation, captions, transcripts, or alternative texts can prevent students from participating on equal terms.
Digital exclusion can widen the educational divide even when the physical campus is accessible. This is particularly important because UGC’s own framework requires online programmes to meet accessibility standards for learners with disability. If education is delivered digitally, its accessibility must be inclusive.
The lack of adequate data makes it difficult to assess the enormity of students’ plight. “There is no AISHE, NAAC or NIRF indicator reporting the percentage of students with disabilities in higher education who have access to accessible LMS platforms, screen-reader-compatible material, captions, Indian Sign Language interpretation or accessible e-books,” Dr. Singh said.
Without such indicators, institutions may be able to report enrolment and infrastructure without demonstrating whether students with disabilities can actually access, participate in, and benefit from digital learning on an equal basis. The absence of systematic data also makes it difficult to identify gaps, assess institutional performance, or hold institutions accountable for meeting accessibility requirements.
“We need a stricter implementation protocol for higher education institutions as there is mostly a lack of awareness and enforceable rules that institutions should follow,” says Deepa Palaniappan, Disability Inclusion practitioner, highlighting the need for more discussions, training, and handholding, as well as forming national task forces and committees to track effective inclusion of students with disabilities in higher education institutions across the country.
Reality check
For Delhi University (DU) alumnus and disability rights activist Ashutosh Singhal (24), the challenges of being an undergraduate and later postgraduate student of Political Science were harrowing. ‘’I use a regular, mainstream computer with a screen reader that reads out the text and other information displayed on the screen. This means that questions appearing on the computer can be read aloud to me, enabling me to access and answer them independently,” Ashutosh said, who suffers from late-onset visual impairment (retinitis pigmentosa), a condition in which the vision can gradually deteriorate.
Beating the odds, he managed to use a computer to write his Political Science BA and MA exams in Hindi, which was the first instance of its kind.
“Initially, they gave me a computer that crashed. The computer instructor apparently knew that there were problems with the computer but did not inform me beforehand. A substitute computer was eventually provided, but by then considerable examination time had been lost. I was told that I would receive additional time to compensate for the lost time, but this was not implemented adequately. Since the examination authorities had to collect and pack the answer scripts at a fixed time, I was under pressure to finish and submit my answers immediately,” he added. Ashutosh was also made to sit in a computer lab during the exam where the constant noise made it difficult to detect the sounds of the screen reader, disrupting his flow of thoughts.
Ashutosh’s experience made him realise that the biggest difficulty for students with disabilities is often not the technology itself which is already available. It is about getting institutions to recognise and implement accessibility provisions consistently.
A student may have to repeatedly explain their requirements, submit applications, approach different departments, contact outside organisations, and persuade officials to make arrangements that should ideally be part of a standard accessible examination system. “For me, the computer and screen reader made it possible to access examinations independently. But the institutional process surrounding the technology created many obstacles. Accessible examination systems should be implemented proactively rather than requiring students with disabilities to repeatedly request, justify, and negotiate for accommodations each time they have an examination,” he added.
(Rajlakshmi Ghosh is a journalist with over three decades of experience in media houses and educational institutions)

WHO and Switzerland have announced the renewal of their cooperation strategy for the period 2024-2028. In 2013, Switzerland became the first high-income country in the WHO European Region to pilot a cooperation strategy with WHO (hereafter referred to as the WHO-Switzerland Cooperation Strategy). An Australian man accused of murdering a Thai teenager and putting her body in a suitcase pleaded not guilty on Friday in a hearing in the seaside resort city of Pattaya, a court official said.
Simon Peter Carman, 45, was arrested in June after 17-year-old Tunchanok Donhomla was reported missing in Pattaya City, about 150km south-east of Bangkok. A suitcase containing her body was found shortly after.
Police said she died of suffocation.
Carman appeared on Friday at Pattaya provincial court, where he pleaded not guilty to all charges, a court spokesperson said.
He had been charged with murder, concealing a body and taking a minor for indecent purposes. The next court date was set for 12 October.
Police previously said CCTV footage showed him entering a condominium in Pattaya with the girl in the early hours of 25 June, and leaving that evening carrying a large black suitcase.
In a police interrogation video shared online by Thai media, Carman has said he was acting in self-defence because the girl was threatening him with a knife.
The case put the spotlight on Pattaya, which is popular with foreign tourists for its beaches and nightlife, but also has a reputation for sex tourism.

PATIALA: A 34-year-old foreign coach attached to the Indian cycling squad has been booked under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (Pocso) Act for allegedly raping a minor cyclist at the National Centre of Excellence (NCOE), housed within Netaji Subhas National Institute of Sports (NSNIS) campus in Patiala.
Patiala police have issued a look out circular (LOC) against the accused, Maxat Ayazbayev, a former professional road cyclist from Kazakhstan.
He has been untraceable since the complaint surfaced last week. Police have seized his passport and formed two teams to track him down.
According to investigators, the alleged assault took place on September 13.
The survivor had been stationed at the Patiala facility for a high-performance training camp. After her complaint, an FIR was lodged at Civil Lines police station on Sept 18 under relevant sections of the 
Pocso Act
 and rape provisions.
Civil Lines police station SHO Winnerpreet Singh said the mandatory medico-legal examination of the survivor had been conducted at Govt Rajindra Hospital, Patiala, and psychological as well as legal counselling had been extended to her in accordance with child protection protocols.
"We registered a criminal case immediately upon receiving the complaint from the athlete," Patiala senior superintendent of police (SSP) Harmandeep Singh Hans said. 
"The accused coach was in Delhi at the time and has since been untraceable. Two special teams have been constituted to trace him.”
Police revealed that the LOC has been opened at all international transit points to prevent him from fleeing the country.
Ayazbayev had been scheduled to accompany the Indian cycling contingent to Japan for Asian Games, but his travel clearance was revoked once the allegations emerged, said police.
Taking cognisance of the matter, the Cycling Federation of India (CFI) reportedly suspended Ayazbayev with immediate effect and marked the matter to its internal complaints committee (ICC) for an inquiry.
Patiala SP (city) Mohit Aggarwal said raids were under way across multiple locations in Delhi and the National Capital Region to apprehend the coach.

This story is based on an interview with Katie Rosier, 48, who is on disability after leaving her procurement job. It has been edited for length and clarity.
Four years ago, at age 44, I was newly discharged from the hospital with a stent in my heart, and I thought about the five strokes I'd had and the poor state of my health overall.
I looked down at my hands to see myself holding a glass of bourbon. Despite everything I'd been through over the last few years — including a stay at a homeless shelter — I was still drinking.
It was one of many rock bottoms during my past 32 years as an alcoholic. This time, however, I knew it was get sober or die.
I started drinking early
I became Dad's drinking buddy at the tender age of 12. My 10 older siblings had flown the nest, so it was only him and me after my mother died.
He was an alcoholic, and it was almost inevitable that I'd follow the same path. We drank cheap wine and beer before I graduated to vodka.
It led to my not prioritizing school, constantly missing deadlines, and being written up for behavioral issues, such as getting into fights. I was part of the stereotypical bad crowd.
I got three DUIs within nine years
I went to college while working, including a kitchen job at a casino. The money allowed me to afford more expensive brands of whiskey. I was consuming anything between a fifth and a handle of whiskey on my days off.
Over the years, I got into so much trouble with the law. I got my first DUI at 17, my second at 21 — when I nearly T-boned a police car — and my third at 26. I went to jail twice.
The habit soon crept into my working hours. I had monster hangovers and was barely functional. Eventually, the drinking won, and I left my job.
Then things looked up a bit, and I managed to attend graduate school and earn an MBA in supply chain management. It helped me get my procurement position in 2017.
My alcohol consumption didn't diminish. I didn't really care. The constant thought that I was drinking myself to death didn't stop the urge.
Then, I had an accident at home. It wasn't related to alcohol, but my declining health had me taking FMLA from work, and then leaving my job completely.
In the summer of 2021, I was homeless and stayed in a Salvation Army shelter for four months. Then I qualified for housing. partly because because I'd been diagnosed with congestive heart failure.
But my drinking continued for the next 12 months. The stent surgery took place in August 2022.
I called several rehabilitation centers
It was a few days later, when I stared at that half-full glass of bourbon in my hand, that I knew enough was enough.
I couldn't keep going on as I was. Something had to change.
I called several rehabilitation centers before choosing one that fit the bill and accepted my insurance. I checked myself in on September 20, 2022. which marked the beginning of my sobriety.
The detox process wasn't fun, but I got through it OK. Then I had intensive psychiatrists' appointments and counseling sessions with other addicts like me.
To help my body stay on track, a doctor suggested I try a Vivitrol injection. The medication treats alcohol dependence by affecting the opioid pathways in the brain.
There's a school of thought that it takes 21 days of sobriety to gain clarity. For me, it took three days. I no longer craved slamming down a beer or tasting whiskey. It no longer occupied my mind.
I was finally able to focus on my health, eating healthily at last, and getting regular exercise.
People drink around me, but I'm no longer tempted
A nurse gives me the injection in my backside every month. My doctor said I'll keep having them as long as I need.
In the four years since I got my first shot, I haven't looked back. My whole world has opened up. I have renewed my interest in pinball, which I've loved since I was a child, and joined a league.
Some of the tournaments take place in bars — my former favorite haunts. But it doesn't bother me in the slightest. People drink around me, but I've never been tempted since starting the injections.
I joke that, if I could afford it, I would buy everybody with an alcohol problem a shot — a shot of the medication, not whiskey. It worked for me, and I hope it does the same for others.

Senegal job an 'absolute dream' for new boss Vieira
- Published
Patrick Vieira says it is "an honour" to become Senegal head coach, with the decision to take the job "one from the heart".
The 50-year-old was born in the West African nation but subsequently represented France as a player, winning the 1998 World Cup and the 2000 European Championship with Les Bleus.
The former Arsenal midfielder spoke of his "immense pride" to begin his first international job, following stints with New York City, Nice, Crystal Palace, Strasbourg and Genoa, at his unveiling by the Teranga Lions on Friday.
"Being head coach of the Senegal national team is an absolute dream," he told a news conference in Dakar.
"I was born here, my parents were born here, and it really is a homecoming.
"From the very first meetings I had with the [Senegal football federation] president, I accepted this challenge straight away, because there was also an exceptional generation of players.
"I realise the expectations of the people - all 20 million Senegalese. And I know that with the experience I have, with the determination I have, I'll be able to see this project through."
- Vieira named new Senegal head coach 
  - Published18 August
Taking over after the dismissal of Pape Thiaw, Vieira inherits a Senegal side which exited the 2026 World Cup in dramatic fashion in the last 32, throwing away a 2-0 lead after 85 minutes against Belgium before losing 3-2 following extra time.
Before that the Teranga Lions claimed the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) title with a 1-0 extra-time win over Morocco in January.
However, the ultimate destination of the trophy will be decided by the Court of Arbitration for Sport after a walk-off by some Senegal players and staff protesting against a penalty decision in the final resulted in the trophy being handed to the North African hosts instead in March.
"Today, Senegal is among the major nations in world football," Vieira said.
"Senegal's objectives aren't what they were 10 or 15 years ago. On the back of its recent results, Senegal has moved forward, has reached new levels.
"The demand for results has also stepped up. We need to lay solid foundations."
Vieira plans to build a side with "a very precise structure" which can play with "intensity and aggression".
"What matters to me isn't starting again from scratch," he added.
"It's about respecting what the federation has put in place over the last few years and building the next stage, opening a new chapter.
"A new chapter meaning my job isn't to tear everything down, it isn't to throw everything out of the window.
"It's about keeping this team's strength: its identity, its unity, its ability to suffer together.
"To make this project work, I'll need the whole nation united. I'll work heart and soul to restore the team's pride."
Starting with two away trips
Vieira has been thrust straight into competitive action in qualifiers for the 2027 Afcon with two fixtures in this international window, two more in November and the final two rounds in March 2027.
His stint in charge was due to begin with a home match against Mozambique on Friday, 25 September but the fixture has been reversed as Dakar is in the midst of preparations for the 2026 Youth Olympic Games.
"Of course, I'd have preferred to play the first match here in Dakar but unfortunately, with the federation, we all felt the best decision was to postpone the match and go and play in Mozambique," Vieira explained.
"Those are difficulties we're going to accept and deal with."
Senegal will be without several notable names for the trip to Maputo and the subsequent away game against Ethiopia on 29 September.
Long-time number one Edouard Mendy, 34, has retired from Teranga Lions duty and Vieira said talismanic forward Sadio Mane will be absent with "a bit of a physical issue".
Despite previous speculation that Mane, also 34, could follow Mendy into retirement, Vieira said the former Liverpool and Bayern Munich man will "surely" be part of his next selection, fitness permitting.
Right-back Krepin Diatta has been left out because he is currently without a club, while forward Ismaila Sarr, who is yet to feature for Crystal Palace this season because of transfer speculation and a groin injury, is also absent.
'No doubt' about his managerial ability
Vieira's career as a player was trophy-laden but he has found the same kind of success hard to come by as a manager.
He departed Palace in March 2023 with a record of 22 wins from 74 games in all competitions and, after a season at Strasbourg, has been out of work since being sacked by Genoa in November last year with the Italian club bottom of the table.
He had guided them to safety in Serie A in the 2024-25 campaign but was then dismissed after six defeats in nine league games at the start of last season.
"When you talk about my coaching career, or a certain amount of experience, I've always been someone who stays positive," Vieira said.
"That means you learn, and there are always positive things to take from it. I'm a better coach today than I was in my last spell at Genoa, because that experience helped me grow and made me realise certain things.
"Given the experience I have as a manager, I've got no doubt about my ability to meet the expectations of fans."
Vieira was warmly received when he arrived in Dakar on Thursday evening, with video clips posted on social media showing him holding a Senegal flag aloft while shaking hands with a throng of fans gathered at the capital's airport.
"I couldn't have been given a warmer welcome. I saw the supporters' enthusiasm and I thank them for it.
"Taking charge of this national team isn't just a new stage in my career - it's coming back home."

Nearly a year after releasing Premiere for iPhone, Adobe is finally bringing its redesigned video-editing app to Android. The app has been in beta for several weeks but is now available as the official successor to Premiere Rush, which the company will stop supporting on September 30.
Eric Snowden, senior vice president of design at Adobe, tells WIRED the feedback for the iOS app has been “incredibly positive” (to his credit, it has a 4.8-star rating out of 5 on the App Store with more than 25,000 ratings). The goal with the Android version wasn't just to port the iPhone app experience, but to make it feel really native to Google's platform.
That includes making sure the app works just as well on every kind of Android device out there, whether it's a Samsung foldable or a candy bar Google Pixel. Yes, when you open up a folding phone with the Adobe Premiere app, you can view your footage on the left and see the multi-track timeline on the right, maximizing space. Snowden suggests optimizing the app for Android foldables will help the company with the iPhone app for the upcoming iPhone Duo.
And if you're wondering whether this app will work well on Google's new Googlebook laptop platform, Adobe says its apps—Acrobat, Photoshop, Lightroom, and Premiere—are optimized for the new laptops, meaning they'll take advantage of the larger screen, but can’t quite deliver the “desktop-grade” experience you’ll find on Windows or macOS.
Equally important is ensuring the app runs on lower-power devices, though Premiere has a minimum requirement of 5 GB of RAM (phones will also need to run Android 13 or later).
“We wanted this to run on as many devices as possible, so the team spent a ton of time making sure that this is not just for flagship phones,” Snowden says. “This is for a really broad range of Android devices.”
Launch the Adobe Premiere app and you will see all your footage from your camera roll on the home screen. From there, you can choose creator-made templates—ranging from lifestyle to beauty to templates for foodies—to get started on an edit, or start from scratch if you'd like.
It's easy to add your footage, then opt for the mini editor or the full editor. The former lets you easily trim or replace your footage, and even choose a filter to apply a specific color style to all of your clips. You can export directly to YouTube Shorts without leaving Premiere. The full editor gives you a multitrack timeline for more granular edits, like layering text, music, and effects.
Several AI tools are on board, like Enhance Audio, which can boost the subject's voice and cut background noise. If you want to add a voice-over, you can speak into your phone's mic and see your footage in real time so it all matches up. Adobe says the app has Firefly-powered AI features, like Generative Fill, Image-to-Video, and Generate Sound Effects. However, these require generative credits, aka a subscription, if you run out of your monthly allotment.
Some features are still “coming soon,” like the Continue Editing function so you can wrap up an edit on desktop after starting it on mobile, or support for Adobe Fonts.
Uniquely (for an Adobe product), you do not have to log in or subscribe to Adobe's creative suite to use Premiere on Android. Like the iOS version, the app is free to use.
“What we're seeing with a lot of mobile apps right now is that there are these huge barriers to entry to using it for the first time,” Snowden says. “We really wanted to get away from that, and I think part of the accessibility and simplicity of the app—the onboarding process is part of that—and we just want to get people in and using it."

It always creates apprehension because the sight is somewhat gory, but a nosebleed, in general, isn’t a cause for major concern. Occurring mostly in the under 10s and the over 45s, nosebleeds are very common: about 60% of the population is estimated to experience one in their lifetime. They can occur in one or both nostrils, but usually affect one. The medical term for a nosebleed is epistaxis.
How do they occur?
Our noses are lined with a moist, delicate tissue, the nasal mucosa. This lining cleans the air that we breathe in, and also warms and moistens the air. The mucosa is made of many tiny blood vessels, lying to close to the surface. These blood vessels can easily be irritated, injured and broken. When they break, they cause a nosebleed.
There are two types of nosebleeds: anterior and posterior. An anterior nosebleed, which is the most common type, starts at the front of the nose. These types of nosebleeds can mostly be treated at home. A posterior nosebleed takes place place deep at the back the nose, may cause heavier bleeding and could result in blood going down the back of the throat. This type of nosebleed requires medical attention.
Why do they occur?
Common causes include the inside of the nose becoming dry, usually due to a change in temperature, picking the nose, or blowing the nose too hard.
When the air is very dry, it causes the nasal mucosa, which is meant to be moist, to dry out, making it prone to crusting and bleeding. Dry air can occur in hot places with low humidity, areas of high altitude and in air-conditioned or heated spaces. People with upper respiratory infections, sinus infections, allergies or other ailments such as rhinitis may also sneeze, cough or blow their nose frequently, making them more prone to bleeds. The frequent use of medications such as antihistamines, nasal sprays or blood thinners, could also make people vulnerable to nosebleeds, as could breathing in strong fumes.
Nosebleeds can also occur due to injuries to the nose, the insertion of objects into the nose, a deviated septum, recreational drug use as well as less common causes such as having blood disorders, alcohol use, nasal polyps or tumours.
Being pregnant may also increase the chances of nosebleeds.
When to see a doctor
In general, nosebleeds aren’t serious and can be treated at home. In some circumstances, however, it is best to consult a medical professional. You should see a doctor if: the nosebleed has followed an injury or accident; if there is heavy bleeding or the bleeding lasts longer than 30 minutes; blood has been swallowed; if there is a feeling of weakness, dizziness, lightheadedness or if you have breathing difficulties, chest pain or a rapid heart rate. A doctor should also be consulted if the person with the nosebleed has other health issues such as a bleeding disorder, or high blood pressure, or if the person is a child under two years old.
How to stop a nosebleed
To stop a nosebleed, there are some first-aid measures that can be taken:
- Sit upright so the head is above the level of the heart, lean forward slightly
- Breathe through the mouth and gently blow the nose to clear it
- Use the thumb and index finger to pinch the both nostrils shut. Do this for 10 minutes.
- Use an icepack on the bridge of the nose at the same time as the pinching
- Check in 10 minutes, and if the bleeding has not stopped, repeat the pinching for another 10 minutes
- Once the bleeding has stopped, lean forward and clean the nose with lukewarm water
- See a doctor immediately if the bleeding does not stop in 30 minutes
Preventing nosebleeds
Using a humidifier in the house especially in dry air conditions, trimming children’s fingernails, managing allergies, using a nasal saline spray or petroleum jelly to keep the inner lining of the nose moist and avoiding smoke exposure can all help prevent nosebleeds.

McPake's 'colourful' journey from club-less to Scotland call-up in three years
- Published
Three years ago, Josh McPake was without a club. Twenty months ago, he was in the shop window but "no-one wanted him".
This week, he's involved in his first Scotland camp following a heroic start to life at Hearts, where, to the tune of Abba's Dancing Queen, the supporters sing he is "having the time of his life".
His call-up to Sebastien Poconogli's squad for the upcoming Nations League games caps an eventful few years for the 25-year-old winger.
From Rangers academy's next big thing, to dropping into Scottish League 1 with Stirling Albion, to being shelved at St Johnstone, it's been a colourful - and at times chaotic - career so far.
But, "I wouldn't change my journey for anything," McPake insists.
He now appears at home in Gorgie and many have hopes he will be just as comfortable when he gets the opportunity to represent his country.
His story is one of resilience and patience. And it's paying off.
BBC Sport Scotland charts the fall and rise of McPake as "he can pass, he can score, having the time of his life, Josh McPake, watch him play on a Saturday".
- Sesko among three injury absences for Slovenia against Scotland 
  - Published10 hours ago
- Scotland call for Montgomery as Tierney & McLean drop out 
  - Published16 hours ago
- How is Scotland squad shaping up for Pocognoli debut? 
  - Published16 hours ago

  - Published19 hours ago
Academy starlet - football nomad - League 1 outlier
His story starts like many others, in the Ibrox academy from a young age, where he was awarded player of the year in 2019 by working up through the reserves to the fringes of the first team.
A matter of months after collecting the gong, he was given his first - and only - run-out for Steven Gerrard's side.
His appearance off the bench in Rangers' rout against Gibraltar's St Joseph's in Europa League qualifying was not a sign of things to come, as he was sent out on his first of six loan moves just one month later.
Dundee, Greenock Morton, Harrogate Town, Morecambe, Tranmere Rovers and Queen's Park all had a taste of McPake but nothing permanent was made.
He swiftly became a bit of a football nomad.
While on Tayside, he scored the winner for Scotland Under-19s against Germany, but still he was flung from pillar to post.
On 1 September 2023, he left Rangers and, though he trained with a number of clubs - where he endured some "knocks and setbacks" - he didn't find a home for another near-six months, until Stirling signed him on a short-term deal.
A dunt down to earth, no doubt, but McPake didn't allow any ego to get in his way, as then-Binos boss Darren Young recalled.
"He came into training and he was brilliant - he couldn't have done any more," former Aberdeen midfielder Young told BBC Scotland.
"He worked very, very hard. He helped put balls away after training, he was always doing extra bits of shooting and finishing - I joked to him once or twice, 'if you don't get your finger out then you'll end up back here part-time' but it was one of those where you could see his ability, he was head and shoulders above the guys.
"It was just a case of him then doing it and getting into the kind of situation where a club - and the right club - would come and get him."
He scored on his debut for the League 1 side - though that was little surprise to Young who was left "wondering why he had not been signed up" when he got the move in motion.
"We had an eye on him as he was free but it looked like he was going to sign at a higher level but another player got injured and then the move wasn't going to happen," he explained.
"He sort of found himself in limbo but I think there's a lot of positives that can be learned from that.
"He kind of said, 'well, I don't want to be in this position and I don't want to be back down there again' and the only way to do that is by working hard and working on weaknesses, which he did."
It'll be of no surprise McPake didn't lack anything in the attacking sense. A wee bit of fine tuning on his tracking back was all that was required during his time at Forthbank to fire him back to where he wanted to be.
"I didn't need to tell him how to go by a player and put it in the top corner - he had all that," Young said.
"I was just trying to say if he could fit into the structure here, work as hard at going back as he did forward, then he'd get, hopefully, an opportunity to kick on again.
"Some players don't, some players kind of have that attitude of, 'I can do it going forward, I don't need to do it going back,' but the penny dropped and he realised to improve and progress, that's what he had to add.
"He worked hard for it and he's got what he deserved."
Resurrection & ‘wake-up call’ at Saints
The reward for knuckling down - and dropping down - was a move back to the top flight with St Johnstone - despite suffering relegation with Stirling Albion.
A two-year deal was agreed but he failed to force his way into Craig Levein's team, and had similar struggles when Simo Valakari took over in October 2024.
His mettle was being pushed to the max yet again.
The Finn revealed last year, external that McPake was made available in the winter transfer window while Saints were fighting for their Premiership life, but they "couldn't find him any clubs".
"We made Josh available in January and offered him to many clubs because he needed to play," Valakari said.
"The truth is, nobody wanted him. We couldn't find him any clubs.
"And, for me, that was the wake-up call for Josh. That was when he decided things had to change.
"If things had stayed the way they were then football was done for him. He would have had to go and get a normal life."
What followed was far from normal.
McPake started his first Premiership game for St Johnstone in the first of their five post-split games and kept his place until the end of the season as he registered three assists.
Saints were ultimately relegated but it set him up for the season of his dreams.
He set the tone for the Championship campaign he dominated with a hat-trick on the opening weekend against title rivals Partick Thistle.
In the second tier, his blistering pace, immense physicality and dancing feet were flung back into the spotlight. His eye for a goal - 16 all told in the division - was evident, too.
Such qualities caught the attention of then Premiership leaders Hearts, who agreed a pre-contract back in January.
But there was no head-turn from the winger, who remained fully focused on repaying the club who resurrected his career by ensuring they would be an opponent of his this season.
He ended the campaign with the mantelpiece packed with trophies and, while the personal accolades were appreciated, it was all about the Championship winners' medal for Tynecastle-bound McPake.
Back to the big time with ‘more to give’
Ensuring adversity remained an ever present in his tale, the footballing gods - seemingly - threw another curveball McPake's way.
Though Derek McInnes was in charge when he agreed the move, the head coach had headed for Rangers by the time he got going in Gorgie.
But, despite sitting out the Champions League qualifiers against Sturm Graz and the first league game of the season under Wouter Vrancken, the Belgian has quickly found out why Hearts snapped up the Saints showman when they did.
With eight goal involvements in 11 games - his best contribution a goal and assist in the Edinburgh derby - he has made the step back up to the Premiership a seamless one and, as such, made it nigh impossible for Pocognoli to leave him out of his plans.
"I've loved every part of the journey," McPake said after answering his country's call.
"Personally, I feel I needed those experiences to become the player I am now.
"There were a lot of setbacks but going down the levels, proving myself and working my way back up taught me a lot.
"If you want something enough and work hard for it, you can achieve it.
"I don't want to stop here. I feel I've still got more to give and I'll continue working hard to show what I can do."

The 2026 Urban Local Body elections were held recently in Rajasthan for 309 urban local bodies and 10,244 wards, with polling held on 09 and 11 September and counting on 14 September. The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) won 4,182 wards, followed by the Congress with 3,619, while Independents secured 2,273 wards. The results also saw the BJP secure majorities in several municipal corporations, while Congress and Independent candidates won in some others (here, here).
In this context, a video is circulating on social media (here, here, and here), claiming it shows a BJP candidate crying after receiving just one vote in the Rajasthan civic elections. The post also alleges that even his own family members did not vote for him. Let’s verify the claim made in the post in this article.
Claim: The video shows a BJP candidate crying after receiving just one vote in the 2026 Rajasthan civic elections.
Fact: It is true that a BJP candidate named Kailash Chandra received one vote in the 2026 Rajasthan civic elections. However, the viral video is unrelated to this incident. The man seen in the video is Rashtriya Janata Dal (RJD) leader Shivchandra Ram, who was seen crying during a press conference in June 2026 after being denied an MLC ticket in Bihar. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to several media reports (here, here, here, and here) published in June 2026 featuring the same video. According to these reports, the person seen crying during a press conference is RJD leader and former Bihar minister Shivchandra Ram, who broke down in tears after being denied an MLC ticket. RJD’s Sunil Singh had filed the nomination for the Grand Alliance for one of the 10 seats in the Bihar Legislative Council, which reportedly angered Ram. He alleged that the party had promised to make him an MLC but had betrayed him, following which he announced his resignation from all RJD posts, while clarifying that he had not left the party. This confirms that the viral video is unrelated to the 2026 Rajasthan civic elections.
To investigate the claim that a BJP candidate received only one vote in the 2026 Rajasthan civic elections, we conducted a Google keyword search and found multiple reports (here, here). According to these reports, BJP candidate Kailash Chandra received only one vote in Ward No. 13 of the Parbatsar Municipality in Rajasthan’s Deedwana-Kuchaman district. Congress candidate Hina Khanam received 376 votes, while Independent candidate Rasheed Khan received 195 votes. The reports also state that Kailash Chandra was a voter in Ward No. 12 but was fielded by the BJP from Ward No. 13, meaning he could not vote for himself.
We then checked the election results available on the official website of the Rajasthan State Election Commission. The results for the Parbatsar Municipality show that Kailash Chandra, the BJP candidate from Ward No. 13, received one vote.
To sum up, an unrelated video of a Bihar RJD leader crying is falsely linked to the BJP candidate who received one vote in the 2026 Rajasthan civic polls.

Get better at: Persuading others
Today's move
If you want to get your boss or colleague on board with an idea, think about what they care about and frame the pitch around that.
Why it works
Amanda Nimon-Peters, a leadership professor and author of "Working With Influence," said that people often resort to using rational arguments when they want to persuade someone else. While you may have strong reasons for why the other person should be invested, you may be better off appealing to their interests.
Nimon-Peters said persuasion isn't about getting people to do things they don't want to do; it's about finding ways to make the outcome and success that you're after also appealing to them.
Try it today
Before you talk to the person you need to convince at work, write down the answer to this question: "What's in it for them?"
Maybe your idea or pitch saves them time, maybe it makes their job easier, or it creates a solution to a problem they've been frustrated with. Then center your pitch around that.
The bottom line
Research suggests that rational arguments aren't the only effective strategy for persuading others.
A 2017 report published in The Leadership Quarterly analyzed 49 studies on how people influence others at work. It found that rational arguments can work, but other approaches, like showing someone what they stand to gain, were also linked to positive outcomes.
Instead of proving that you're right, you should try to show the person why they should care.

Five reasons to stick with your iPhone 17 Pro instead of upgrading to the 18 Pro
The iPhone 18 Pro is an impressive phone, but you won't notice a big difference compared to the 17 Pro.
September means new iPhones are out in the wild, and while all eyes are on the fancy iPhone Duo, we shouldn't forget about the iPhone 18 Pro. This generation isn't radically different from the iPhone 17 Pro, but some folks might still consider upgrading — especially if you get a good deal from your carrier.
But is it really worth moving from the iPhone 17 Pro to the iPhone 18 Pro? In most cases, no. You'd likely be better off saving the cash and sticking with your current device for now. All told, these two units aren't that different.
They look pretty much the same
As we noted in our full review of the iPhone 18 Pro, you'd probably have a hard time spotting the differences between it and the 17 Pro if it weren't for the new colors. The iPhone 18 Pro comes in a new deep Burgundy and a light Glacial. There's also a black model, which a lot of people had been asking for after its absence in the 17 Pro lineup. But aside from the colors, the design is pretty much identical. In fact, the iPhone 18 Pro is a few grams heavier than its predecessor, which might not sit well with some.
There actually is a design change between them, though it's hard to notice at a glance. The Dynamic Island is smaller now, thanks to a new infrared sensor hidden beneath the screen. Sure, this is cool, but it's also not something that will change how you use your iPhone. It's more of a nice-to-have feature than a must-have, since the prior setup of the Dynamic Island works just fine.
The iPhone 17 Pro is still extremely fast
Apple talked a lot about performance during the iPhone 18 Pro presentation. No wonder, since it comes with the A20 Pro chip, which is the first built on a 2-nanometer architecture. This chip is fast — extremely fast. Its extra GPU core compared to the A19 Pro delivers up to 40 percent better graphics performance. There's also a second Neural Engine to better handle AI. But in normal usage, you might not notice that difference that much.
The iPhone 17 Pro is still a highly capable phone. And while the leap in performance is impressive, it won't matter when it comes to opening Instagram or streaming Apple Music. If you're not a heavy user who's always editing RAW photos or playing intensive games on your iPhone, the A19 Pro still gets the job done with ease. And even then, a year-old phone is hardly obsolete for this kind of work.
Most cameras haven't changed
Perhaps the most notable change in this year's Pro iPhone models is the new camera. For the first time, Apple is using a wide-angle camera with a variable aperture lens. Just like with the lenses on a DSLR camera, you can adjust the aperture to let the sensor receive more or less light. It's great for changing how the photo looks, as well as the depth of field. The new, wider aperture also improves photos and videos taken in low light.
But aside from the main camera, all the others are identical. The iPhone 18 Pro uses exactly the same ultra-wide and telephoto sensors as the iPhone 17 Pro. Even the front-facing camera is the same, so you won't be missing out on much if you don't upgrade. Also, some of the new photographic styles Apple showcased during the keynote are expected to arrive on certain older iPhones with a software update.
You already have Apple Intelligence and Siri AI
If you have an iPhone 17 Pro, you already have access to all the latest iOS features. This includes Apple Intelligence and Siri AI, Apple's virtual assistant built into iOS 27. Both the iPhone 17 Pro and 18 Pro offer the same functionality here, so you aren't getting major exclusive software features if you upgrade. The new Siri app, contextual conversations, enhanced Siri voice adjustments, improved dictation and ability to extend and reframe photos are all also available on the iPhone 17 Pro.
Of course, the future is unknown, and Apple may add some exclusive features to the iPhone 18 Pro down the road. It could put that extra Neural Engine to use for better AI performance. But right now, that doesn't mean much to most people.
The iPhone 18 Pro is a bigger upgrade for those with older iPhones
Getting new tech is always enjoyable, especially for enthusiasts. And having an iPhone with longer battery life and a more advanced camera will sound exciting to many people. But for the vast majority of those who already own the iPhone 17 Pro, the iPhone 18 Pro is a minor upgrade. Sure, it performs better, but it doesn't change how you use your iPhone every day.
The iPhone 18 Pro is best viewed as an upgrade for those with older iPhones, like the iPhone 15 Pro. That way, you'll get all the improvements from the last three years, like the vapor chamber, a new design and improved zoom. If you have a newer model, save some money and wait for next year's iPhone — or maybe consider the iPhone Duo.

Five baby orangutans have been found in a forest in India, prompting authorities to investigate if they were trafficked into the country from south-east Asia.
The orangutans, native only to the islands of Borneo and Sumatra and known for their shaggy red fur, were found in Balasore district of Odisha state, thousands of kilometres away from their natural habitat.
Odisha’s environment minister, Ram Singh Khuntia, said wildlife investigators were trying to establish how the rare apes reached India.
“We suspect that an international racket might be involved in this,” Singh said.
International commercial trade in orangutans is prohibited under Cites – a global agreement governing trade in endangered wildlife.
The five babies were found by forest department officials who were patrolling in the Jaleswar range in Balasore district.
Officials believed the orangutans had been in the area for just a few days, and they have now been placed in quarantine at a zoological park in Odisha.
According to the World Wildlife Fund, about 104,000 orangutans remain in Borneo and Sumatra, down from more than 230,000 a century ago.
The Tapanuli orangutan (Pongo tapanuliensis), a third species, is classified as critically endangered, with fewer than 800 believed to survive in the wild.
In November, conservationists found the Tapanuli population had been reduced by 7% after severe flooding in Indonesia.
Between 33 and 54 Tapanuli orangutans were estimated to have been killed in widespread floods and landslides in North Sumatra province.
Previous research has suggested annual losses of 1% of the Tapanuli orangutan population would be sufficient to lead to eventual extinction.
The entire Tapanuli population dwells solely in the West Block of the Batang Toru, a forest threatened by mining, palm oil plantations and a large hydropower project.

Info Edge Ventures backed NBFC Ascend Capital’s profitability improved significantly in the fiscal year FY26, growing 6.25X to ₹10 Cr from ₹1.6 Cr in FY25. As per ratings assigned by ICRA, the Jaipur-based EV-focused lender’s total income for the fiscal jumped about 131% to ₹50.3 Cr in FY26 from ₹21.8 Cr in FY25. Its total managed assets (AUM) also expanded 46% to ₹238.6 Cr from ₹163.7 Cr during the period. ICRA noted that the cumulative collection efficiency from Ascend’s securitised EV loan portfolio, comprising of three-wheeler EVs like e-autos, loaders and L5 vehicles, stood at 97.5% as on July 2026, while the 90+ days past due (dpd) delinquency stood at 1.3%. Its gross non-performing assets (GNPA) increased to 2.6% in FY26 from 1.7% in FY25 while capital-to-risk weighted assets ratio (CRAR moderated to 34.8% from 41% a year earlier, though it remained well above the regulatory capital requirement. Despite the healthy pool performance, ICRA highlighted that the NBFC poses risks such as limited operational history and geographical concentration. As of September 2025, Ascend Capital was present across 60 cities in five states and UTs, although its top three states made up for 87.5% of the portfolio. Its total borrower base stood at 18,975 at the time. Tapping The Growing EV Demand Founded in 2019 by Lokesh Chandra and Gaurav Maheshwari, Ascend Capital extends loans of up to ₹2-4 Lakh to consumers looking to buy EVs and batteries for e-rickshaw and L5 vehicles. Ascend originates EV loans through its NBFC and funds its lending book through a mix of institutional debt and securitisation, where pools of EV loans are packaged into securities and sold to investors, allowing the lender to recycle capital into fresh loans. To overcome underwriting and collection challenges related to EV financing, the NBFC has developed an internal benchmark for valuing batteries and maintains a data repository covering OEMs, distributors and drivers. It started disbursing loans against e-autos and e-loaders in January 2024. The NBFC’s PAT stood at just ₹0.1 Cr in FY24, while income stood at ₹13.7 Cr, highlighting a notable acceleration in its scale over the past two years. It also raised ₹50 Cr in equity funding from Info Edge Ventures and Asha Ventures in 2024. The investors own a 24.8% stake in the NBFC as of now. The development comes as a growing set of specialised lenders targets the financing gap in India’s EV ecosystem. A record 24.5 Lakh EVs were sold in India in FY26, up 25% YoY, with electric three-wheelers accounting for 8.31 Lakh units, or 34% of total EV sales, as per Vahan data. E3Ws also crossed a 60% share of India’s overall three-wheeler sales during the year.

UK to offer Saudi Arabia aerial refueling to counter Houthi attacks
Prime Minister Andy Burnham says Britain has agreed to provide limited military support to Saudi Arabia to repeal attacks by Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen
ABOARD THE BRITISH PRIME MINISTER’S PLANE -- Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Monday that Britain has agreed to provide limited military support to Saudi Arabia to repel attacks by Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen.
Burnham told reporters as he flew to the United Nations General Assembly in New York that he had agreed the Royal Air Force will provide air-to-air refueling of Saudi planes. The agreement is for a matter of weeks, but Burnham said it will be kept under review.
The conflict between the Houthis and Yemen’s Saudi-backed government has reignited, with the Houthis aiming missile and drone strikes at Saudi Arabia, including one that targeted Riyadh on Saturday before being intercepted. The Houthis also declared a blockade on Saudi shipping in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the Red Sea, attacking Saudi-linked vessels and oil facilities inside the kingdom, the world’s top oil exporter.
The Houthis advanced inside Yemen earlier this month, seizing the crucial port city of Mokha and key Red Sea islands allowing them to better monitor shipping traffic through the Bab el-Mandeb, through which some 12% of world trade normally passes.
Burnham said he was “acting to secure the interests of Britain and the wider region" at a moment when Saudi Arabia is facing attacks and it is critical to keep passages for oil open.
Britain has condemned the Houthi attacks and said the U.K. will “work with partners to support regional stability, protect civilians and support humanitarian access.”
U.K. officials had previously declined to comment on “operational matters” but noted that Britain and Saudi Arabia have a close defense partnership.
The U.S., which bombed the Houthis under the Biden and Trump administrations, has shown no interest in getting involved militarily this time around.
U.K. officials say the agreement will start in the coming days, and involve one RAF Voyager refueling Saudi planes on “defensive” missions.
The Associated Press reported last week that Saudi Arabia has asked its allies, including France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt to deploy air-defense support to the region to help defend against missiles and drones fired by Houthis and other Iran-backed groups on the kingdom.

15 సెప్టెంబర్ 2026న ఉత్తర అరేబియా సముద్రంలో భారత్, పాకిస్తాన్ నావికాదళాలకు చెందిన యుద్ధనౌకలు ఒకదానికొకటి ఢీకొన్నాయి. తమ నౌక సాధారణ నిఘా విధుల్లో ఉండగా పాకిస్తాన్ నౌక వేగంగా, ప్రమాదకరంగా దూసుకొచ్చిందని భారత్ పేర్కొంది. దీనిపై నిరసన తెలుపుతూ సెప్టెంబర్ 16న పాకిస్తాన్ దౌత్యాధికారికి భారత్ సమన్లు జారీ చేసింది. అయితే, పాకిస్తాన్ మాత్రం ఇందుకు భిన్నమైన వాదన వినిపించింది. తమ ‘SEASPARK-26’ నావికా విన్యాసాల్లో ఈ ఘటన జరిగిందని, భారత నౌక ఉద్దేశపూర్వకంగా తమ నౌక సమీపంలోకి వచ్చిందని ఆరోపించింది.
ఈ నేపథ్యంలో, భారత, పాకిస్తాన్ యుద్ధనౌకలు ఢీకొన్న దృశ్యాలంటూ ఒక వీడియో (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) సోషల్ మీడియాలో ప్రచారంలో ఉంది. దీంట్లో ఎంత నిజముందో ఇప్పుడు చూద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: 15 సెప్టెంబర్ 2026న భారత్, పాకిస్తాన్ యుద్ధనౌకలు ఒకదానికొకటి ఢీకొన్న దృశ్యాలు.
ఫాక్ట్: ఈ వీడియో 15 సెప్టెంబర్ 2026న భారత్, పాకిస్తాన్ యుద్ధనౌకలు ఢీకొన్న ఘటనకు సంబంధించినది కాదు. వాణిజ్య నౌక ‘ఎంవీ సూయజ్’కు భద్రతగా వెళ్తున్న సమయంలో 2011లో పాకిస్థాన్ నౌక పీఎన్ఎస్ బాబర్, భారత నౌక ఐఎన్ఎస్ గోదావరిని ఢీకొన్న పాత సంఘటనకు సంబంధించిన వీడియో ఇది. కావున, పోస్టులో చేయబడిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పుదోవ పట్టించే విధంగా ఉంది.
ముందుగా వైరల్ వీడియోలోని దృశ్యాలను రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, ఇదే వీడియోని 16 అక్టోబర్ 2014న “mix” అనే యూట్యూబ్ ఛానెల్లో అప్లోడ్ (ఆర్కైవ్) చేసినట్లు గుర్తించాం. ఈ వీడియోలో పాకిస్తాన్ నౌక బాబర్ భారత నౌకతో పోటీ పడుతుందని పేర్కొనబడింది. ఏడెన్ అఖాతంలో (Gulf of Aden) ‘ఎంవీ సూయజ్’ అనే వాణిజ్య నౌకను రక్షించే సమయంలో తీసిన భారత, పాకిస్తాన్ నౌకల దృశ్యాలను ఈ వీడియో చూపుతుందని వివరణలో రాసి ఉంది. దీన్ని బట్టి, వైరల్ వీడియో సెప్టెంబర్ 2026 నాటి ఘటనకు సంబంధించినది కాదని, అది దశాబ్దానికి పైగా పాతదని స్పష్టమవుతుంది.
దీనికి సంబంధించిన మరింత సమాచారం కోసం ఇంటర్నెట్లో వెతకగా, ఇదే ఘటన గురించి చెప్తున్నా 2011 నాటి NDTV వార్తా కథనం లభించింది. ఈ కథనం ప్రకారం, ఈ ఘటన 16 జూన్ 2011న జరిగింది. వాణిజ్య నౌక ‘ఎంవీ సూయజ్’కు భద్రతగా వెళ్తున్న సమయంలో, భారత నావికాదళానికి చెందిన ‘ఐఎన్ఎస్ గోదావరి’ నౌకను దాటి వెళ్లే ప్రయత్నంలో పాకిస్తాన్ యుద్ధనౌక ‘పీఎన్ఎస్ బాబర్’ దాని వెనుక భాగాన్ని ఢీకొట్టింది. సముద్రం అల్లకల్లోలంగా ఉన్న సమయంలో ఐఎన్ఎస్ గోదావరికి అతి సమీపంలోకి వచ్చిన పీఎన్ఎస్ బాబర్ రాసుకుంటూ వెళ్లిందని, దీనివల్ల భారత నౌకలోని హెలికాప్టర్ డెక్కు నష్టం వాటిల్లిందని ఆ కథనం పేర్కొంది. నౌకలు ఢీకొన్న తర్వాత పాకిస్తాన్ నౌక సిబ్బంది సంబరాలు చేసుకుంటున్న దృశ్యాలను కూడా ఆ కథనం చూపించింది.
18 జూన్ 2011న భారత విదేశీ వ్యవహారాల మంత్రిత్వ శాఖ ఒక పత్రికా ప్రకటన విడుదల చేసి పాకిస్తాన్ తీరుపై నిరసన వ్యక్తం చేసింది. పీఎన్ఎస్ బాబర్ చేసిన ప్రమాదకరమైన విన్యాసాలు ఐఎన్ఎస్ గోదావరి నౌక, దాని సిబ్బంది భద్రతను ప్రమాదంలో పడేశాయని అందులో పేర్కొంది. అంతేకాకుండా, పాకిస్తాన్ చర్యలు అంతర్జాతీయ సముద్ర భద్రతా నిబంధనలను, అలాగే సైనిక విన్యాసాలకు ముందస్తు సమాచారం ఇవ్వాలనే 1991 నాటి ఇండో-పాక్ ఒప్పందాన్ని ఉల్లంఘించాయని భారత్ స్పష్టం చేసింది.
చివరిగా, వైరల్ వీడియో 2011లో భారత్, పాకిస్థాన్ నౌకలు ఢీకొన్న పాత ఘటనకు సంబంధించినది.
