How unarmed 911 teams are reshaping public safety in nearly 100 cities
On a recent Wednesday in Durham, N.C., Rob Crisp and Allie Craft were on a mission, equipped with snacks, bottled water and hygiene kits. They are part of Durham's unarmed community response team, and they were looking for a man someone called 911 about.
"Our notes say we got a trespasser on a business property. He has a bunch of belongings, and he's refusing to leave," Crisp said.
In a parking lot on the side of a strip mall, they found the man, wearing a McDonald's T-shirt and a backward baseball cap and toting several full garbage bags and a sofa with him. Crisp approached the man, who looked tense. He said he didn't want anyone to touch his things.
Crisp, a peer support specialist who has struggled with drug addiction in the past, took his time talking with him.
"I can relate to not having anything," Crisp later told NPR. After a few minutes, he calmed the man down.
"I was like, 'We're not trying to bother you, but hey, we do have some supplies while we are here. Is it all right if we get you a bag together?' Little things like that to say, 'Hey, I don't have a gun. I don't have a badge. I'm here because I feel for you, brother,'" Crisp said.
Crisp and Craft, a mental health clinician, gave the man water and a fresh pair of socks. They convinced him to haul his things off the property and onto a nearby vacant lot. It was not a long-term solution, but it resolved the immediate conflict.
Just five years ago, police would have most likely been dispatched to respond to this 911 call.
But since the police killing of George Floyd in 2020, dozens of cities around the United States have made the same calculation: that calls like this don't always need an armed officer.
In 2020, there were only six programs in the U.S. that sent unarmed responders, such as mental health clinicians, to certain 911 calls instead of police officers. Now, these programs — sometimes called alternative or community response — are in nearly 100 cities.
"They're not police officers, but they are a part of the public safety net"
Durham's program — the Holistic Empathetic Assistance Response Team (HEART) — launched in 2022 and has since responded to more than 25,000 911 calls.
The community response team now operates citywide. The program also has a limited co-response team, in which mental health clinicians are paired with a police officer on patrol, as well as a mental health clinician embedded in the city's 911 call center.
"Honestly, I would say if you can send a social worker to a call that you could send a law enforcement officer and you got the same results, then it's already a success," says Ryan Smith, director of the Durham Community Safety Department, which runs the program.
Recent research suggests Durham is seeing signs of success: A preliminary study from researchers at Duke University last year found that the program has increased 911 calls, a potential sign of growing public trust.
A study this year by the Research Triangle Institute (RTI) found that the city's program is also associated with fewer arrests, that most police officers find it helpful and that police are rarely called for backup.
Elsewhere, other community response programs have also been studied. A 2022 Stanford University study of a program in Denver found evidence that it reduced reports of certain crimes by more than a third. A 2025 study found that a program in Eugene, Ore., reduced the likelihood of a 911 call resulting in an arrest and increased access to medical care.
Still, relatively few of these programs nationwide have been studied, and they're not always an easy sell.
In Durham, Patrice Andrews, the city's former chief of police until earlier this year, helped launch HEART. She says at the time, police officers in the city had concerns, even though many agreed that they were not always needed at a 911 call and that forgoing certain calls could potentially free them up to investigate other crimes.
"Their heartburn was, "OK, are we going to have to protect these people that are unarmed? They don't have the knowledge that we have with law enforcement tactics,'" she says. "And then there was the political side of it — that this was this ultra-uber-liberal idea being pushed down our throats. This was 'They're not backing the blue.'"
Over time, Andrews says, police officers began to accept the program as a fourth and equal wing of 911 response, alongside police, fire and emergency medical services. It helped, she says, that police and HEART are on the same radio channel for dispatch: Police officers can hear the unarmed responders, and vice versa.
"That allowed our staff to be able to see that they are a part of the public safety team. They're not police officers, but they are a part of the public safety net," Andrews says.
How many 911 calls can an alternative response program handle?
In some cities, fatal police shootings in recent years have revealed the limitations of their alternative response programs.
In New York City, for instance, the 2024 fatal police shooting of Win Rozario, who was experiencing a mental health crisis, raised questions as to whether its program was answering as many calls as it could. According to a 2025 audit by the Office of the New York City Comptroller, the majority of the city did not have access to the city's program.
In Baltimore, an investigation by The Baltimore Sun after the 2025 police killing of Pytorcarcha Brooks, who also was suffering from a mental health crisis, found that the number of 911 calls diverted to mental health services had fallen by more than 50% in recent years, even as the total number of mental health calls had surged. The city is now considering modeling its program after Durham's.
One way to measure success is to assess how many 911 calls a program is handling per capita, says Amos Irwin, who studies community response programs at the Law Enforcement Action Partnership (LEAP), a criminal justice reform nonprofit. Durham HEART, for instance, handles around 28 calls per 1,000 residents according to LEAP, which ranks the city in its top 10 U.S. programs by call volume.
"It is the easiest data point to get and to compare programs," Irwin says. "It's a shortcut. It doesn't tell you the quality and whether they manage to make a long-term difference in the lives of the people that they served."
But researchers also caution that because almost all of these programs are just a few years old, it's hard to say what the ceiling is in terms of how many 911 calls they could safely take or what a good goal would even be.
"Many of us are still trying to figure that number out, but we anticipate it's far more than what any city is handling at this point," says Mariela Ruiz-Angel, director of community safety initiatives at Georgetown Law's Center for Innovations in Community Safety.
One limitation some programs face, Irwin says, is that they simply are not funded enough to answer a higher number of calls. Another point of failure, he says, is when community response teams are authorized to respond to only clear-cut mental health crises.
"There are all kinds of calls that responders can handle that do not have mental health on the surface," he says. "No one calls and says somebody is in a mental health crisis. They call and say there's somebody panhandling really aggressively here. There is somebody loitering around my store, refusing to leave."
In Durham, before the HEART program even began, the city, in partnership with RTI, analyzed three years of 911 data. They also held conversations with community members, other first responders and other similar community response programs across the country.
The city zeroed in on which types of calls rarely ended in violence. Those included certain mental health crises but also things like trespassing, panhandling, intoxication, indecency and welfare checks. Those 911 call types became the ones that HEART responds to. Irwin says all the leading programs are handling calls like that.
Leigh Mazur, an assistant director in the Durham Community Safety Department, says the decision for whom to send to a call cannot be subjective. When it is, she says, a 911 dispatcher is "more often than not going to — of course and understandably — err on the side of caution and likely send the police to calls that they didn't necessarily have to send them to."
"Why aren't you fixing homelessness?"
On another recent call in Durham, Rob Crisp and Allie Craft, the two HEART responders, handled a dispute involving a mother and adult daughter who called 911 on each other. Brittney, the daughter, didn't want to use her last name so she could discuss her family situation more freely.
When HEART arrived on scene, Brittney told Crisp and Craft that she was hoping HEART could help her find new housing, because she didn't feel safe or comfortable where she was currently living. As Brittney listened from the back seat of the van, the HEART responders told her that the only housing immediately available was a homeless shelter. Brittney declined.
Calls about housing are common, Craft later told NPR, and it can feel frustrating that there aren't more options. Ruiz-Angel, the Georgetown researcher, says this is a frequent limitation for programs across the country.
"People are constantly like, 'Why aren't you fixing homelessness?' And I will say that in 2020, that was not the call to action. The call to action was 'We don't want another George Floyd situation to happen,'" she says.
Ruiz-Angel founded the community response program in Albuquerque, N.M. Very quickly, she says the team realized many of the people they encountered did not have their basic needs met.
Every community response program, she says, eventually faces a choice: Should it stay in a narrow lane, answering 911 calls and managing immediate crises, or should it try to tackle the deep-seated causes of those crises, like homelessness?
"They all come down to poverty issues, and there's just not enough resources at this point. There's not enough housing. There's not enough everything out there," she says.
Durham is choosing that more ambitious path: The city launched a division last year within the Durham Community Safety Department called Stabilization Services.
"The aim of the 911 response is to de-escalate the situation and leave everybody in a somewhat stable place. That does not mean that whoever's left there has a connection to the right resources," says Anise Vance, the leader of the city's new initiative.
His aim now, he says, is to connect people with resources — to offer them a deeper, more systemic path after the initial moment of crisis has passed.
"Those services have to include some of the basic things in life. They have to include housing. They have to include medical care. They have to include behavioral health care. They have to include food. Those are all key ingredients," Vance says.
It's too early to say whether it will be a success. But the idea is that, over time, fewer 911 callers will need a team like HEART in the first place.

An Islamic State group member was sentenced on Wednesday to 20 years in prison for aiding the terrorist organization that took credit for a suicide bombing that killed 13 US service members and about 160 Afghans at the Kabul airport five years ago during the US military’s chaotic withdrawal from the country.
A federal jury in Virginia had convicted Mohammad Sharifullah in April of providing material support to the IS affiliate known as Islamic State Khorasan Province (ISKP). But jurors could not agree whether he bore some responsibility for the airport bombing on 26 August 2021.
US troops were conducting an evacuation operation at the airport when a suicide bomber detonated an improvised explosive device near an entry point known as Abbey Gate. Sharifullah’s role in the attack was scouting a route to Hamid Karzai international airport, prosecutors said.
Sharifullah, 28, received the maximum sentence for his one-count conviction in an international terrorism case that Donald Trump heralded last year during a speech to a joint session of Congress.
Sharifullah did not testify at his trial and declined to address the court before the US district judge Anthony Trenga imposed the sentence. The judge said the defendant was a “dedicated terrorist” who expressed no remorse for the “unfathomable” grief and suffering that he had caused.
Trenga heard victim impact statements from several parents of US service members. From a podium only a few feet from where Sharifullah sat, they took turns paying tribute to their children’s sacrifices and describing how the attack has shattered their families.
Mark Schmitz of Missouri asked Sharifullah to turn and look at him as he spoke about the life and death of his 20-year-old son, Marine Corps L/Cpl Jared Schmitz.
“They may have taken his life, but they’ll never take his legacy,” Mark Schmitz said. “A bomb killed my son. It did not kill what he stood for.”
Paula Knauss-Selph, whose son, army SSgt Ryan Knauss, was killed in the Abbey Gate bombing, said the family was “forever changed” by the attack.
“No justice will ever be enough to mend my broken heart,” she said.
Sharifullah requested a 17-year prison sentence, while prosecutors sought 20 years. His lawyers said he was never an ISKP leader and had not been convicted of any conduct related to the airport suicide bombing.
“He was brought here because the government believed he participated in the Abbey Gate attack, a theory which it was unable to prove at trial,” defense attorneys wrote.
Prosecutors said in their sentencing memo that “from his teenage years, when he pledged an oath of allegiance to [ISKP], Sharifullah’s carnage was driven by hate. Hate towards Americans.”
Jurors convicted Sharifullah of providing material support to ISKP. They deadlocked on whether any deaths at the airport “resulted from” that conspiracy. Sharifullah could have faced a possible life sentence if the jury had unanimously decided that question.
According to prosecutors, Sharifullah told a journalist that he wanted to “catch and kill the crusaders” from the United States for invading his country after the attacks of September 11. They said Sharifullah was involved in dozens of other attacks, including a March 2024 assault on a Moscow concert hall that killed roughly 140 people.
Defense lawyers argued that prosecutors failed to present any evidence tying Sharifullah to the Kabul bombing besides his own words during hours of FBI questioning. His team said Sharifullah told FBI agents what he thought they wanted to hear, possibly because he was afraid of being tortured in Pakistani custody before he was brought to the US.
A review by US Central Command found that the Abbey Gate bomber was Abdul Rahman al-Logari, an IS member who had been released from an Afghan prison by the Taliban. According to an FBI affidavit, Sharifullah recognized the alleged bomber as an operative he had known while incarcerated.

Bhopal (Madhya Pradesh): After fulfilment of MBBS interns' demand for a stipend hike, AYUSH interns staged a protest at the collectorate on Tuesday to seek a raise in their stipend.
They stated that the government currently provides a monthly stipend of Rs 9,383, which is the lowest among 15 states in the country. The intern doctors were stopped at the main gate of the collectorate.
Police forces were deployed at the site. Intern doctors have warned that if no action is taken within 15 days, they will go on strike and stop attending OPD duties. OPD services will be suspended.
A three-day protest was recently held in Bhopal by MBBS interns from Gandhi Medical College (GMC) demanding a stipend hike.
During the protest, they blocked roads. Subsequently, the government acceded to the demand and raised the interns' stipend by 50%, bringing it to Rs 21,500 per month.
As per AYUSH interns, monthly stipend for AYUSH interns in West Bengal is Rs 33,099, in Odisha it is Rs 30,000, Telangana (Rs 29,792), Bihar (Rs 27,000), Andhra Pradesh (Rs 25,906), Kerala (Rs 23,000), Karnataka (Rs 22,500), Assam and Maharashtra (Rs 18,000), Chhattisgarh (Rs 15,900), and Punjab and Uttarakhand (Rs 15,000).
In Rajasthan, interns receive a stipend of Rs 14,000 along with dearness allowance (DA), while in Haryana and Himachal Pradesh, the stipend is Rs 10,000. In Madhya Pradesh, only Rs 9,383 is provided.

Henry Pollock: England star signs new multi-year deal with Northampton Saints to stay with defending PREM champions
Henry Pollock's contract with Northampton Saints had been due to expire at the end of the 2026-27 season; the England international previously said he was open to exploring all options over his future
Tuesday 22 September 2026 10:03, UK
Henry Pollock has signed a new multi-year contract extension with Northampton Saints that will see him stay at his boyhood club beyond this season.
Pollock has been a key part of the Saints side since bursting through as a 17-year-old in 2022, delivering a Player of the Match performance during their Gallagher PREM final victory last season.
The back rower already has 13 England caps and five British & Irish Lions caps to his name, with his growing appeal seeing him become the first rugby player to join Eddie Hearn's Matchroom Talent Agency earlier this year.
- Eddie Hearn values Henry Pollock at £1m amid contract talks
- Latest rugby union news, headlines, results and reports
- Get latest Sky Sports deals or stream with no contract
Pollock previously said he had an open mind about next steps in his career, with Hearn labelling him worth at least £1m a year, but the 21-year-old is now looking forward to extending his time at Saints.
In a statement, Pollock said: "I'm massively happy to re-sign with Saints, my boyhood club. It's an exciting place to be right now. We're in a great spot as a team, but it feels like there's still so much more growth in us.
"I'm still young, and we've got a young squad with a brilliant group of lads. Some of my best mates are here, and every day everyone pushes each other to improve and be the best players and team we can be. For where I am in my career, this is exactly where I want to be.
"I feel like we're only just getting started. We won the PREM last season and we want to go again. Winning the Champions Cup is another huge ambition for us. We came so close a couple of years ago, and achieving that together would be incredibly special.
"I just want to enjoy every moment of this journey. I'm playing for my boyhood club, surrounded by great people, and that's something I never take for granted. The connections within this group are what make it such a special place."
Saints' Director of Rugby, Phil Dowson, added: "We're delighted that Henry has committed his future to Saints.
"Over the last few years, everyone has seen the quality he brings on the pitch and the speed of his rise through the game - but just as importantly, he's a young man of outstanding character.
"Keeping someone with both his talent and mindset is hugely important for the club."
'Rugby not used to Pollock and Hearn's contract posturing'
Sky Sports News' James Cole:
"Henry Pollock's transfer stand-off with Northampton divided the club's fanbase. The England flanker is a generational talent. The friction wasn't just financial - it was also cultural.
"Rugby isn't used to the sort of public posturing that Pollock and his agent Eddie Hearn have engaged in over this new deal. It's very un-rugby. Very un-gentlemanly.
"Some will say that the sport and the attitude of its fans need to evolve. Others will say these are the core values that drive people to play, watch and fall in love with the game.
"The new £400,000-plus contract is likely to represent a three-fold increase in Pollock's salary and make him one of the top-earning flankers in the Premiership.
"It's not the seven-figure sum Hearn thinks his client is worth - but within the parameters of the league and its salary cap, it's an excellent deal. The 21-year-old has the potential to become one of the sport's all-time greats, but he's not there yet."

Teen social media bans are hot these days, with new regulations installed or soon to come in Australia, Indonesia, and the European Union. But how will we know these rules are working? And what does “working” even mean?
Researcher Camilla Iannone asked a group of young people for advice on how to answer those questions. Their feedback reframed the whole debate for her. “Rather than focusing solely on whether social media is harmful and whether we need a ban, they repeatedly asked us to look at what role social media currently plays in young people’s lives, and what might replace it if access is restricted,” she writes in a new First Opinion.
Read more on the questions teens had for researchers, and what kinds of data they’d like to see.
We write a lot at STAT about artificial intelligence and medicine. But I hadn’t seen a paper quite like this one before. In it, Penn State researchers probed how AI would choose whoshould receive a donor kidney, one of the thorniest issues in medical ethics. “Often, there is no single objective correct answer,” the researchers wrote. “Rather the decisions rely on nuanced human and moral judgements.”
But when they asked several prominent large language models to choose between possible kidney recipients, they found that AI diverged from human judgement in a few key ways: The AI was less indecisive than humans, “tending toward deterministic recommendations even when abstention is explicitly permitted.” It also rarely chose against the majority choice, which could “fail to capture the plurality inherent in moral values.”
I’m curious whether and how AI is finding its way into medical ethics, and whether this research lines up with real-world experiences. How are you thinking about AI and medical ethics? Thoughts, examples, and other research welcome!
Congress pushes back on effort to let political appointees control NIH grants
The fight over science grant funding boiled over at an Oval Office meeting Friday, when Office of Management and Budget head Russell Vought pushed to give political appointees more direct control over National Institutes of Health funding. According to The Washington Post, Vought encouraged Trump to sign an executive order establishing a commission of political appointees to review all grants coming out of NIH, saying current research is too “woke.” In response, lawmakers on both sides of the aisle released statements warning that such a move would be “contrary to congressional intent.”
It’s the latest example of Vought trying to exert more political control over the types of research projects funded by the NIH. Where is NIH Director Jay Bhattacharya in all this? Anil Oza and Chelsea Cirruzzo have the scoop.
Should it be ‘Pinky and the Brains’ now?
We all know about left brain and right brain. But a new paper suggests a more surprising division — our brains might have developed from two distinct organs.
To draw that conclusion, Stanford University researchers examined how the brains of mouse embryos develop. They found that at the earliest stages of growth, the hindbrain expresses discrete genes and a different chromatin configuration than the midbrain and forebrain. That raises some interesting possibilities.
“Although the brain is often construed as a single organ, the brain may itself derive from two parallel progenitors that emerge early in development and that, respectively, form the forebrain/midbrain versus the hindbrain,” the researchers write. “Analogously, the heart derives from two parallel progenitors, the first and second heart fields, which converge to form a single organ.”
The researchers hope their discovery will make it easier to grow hindbrain neurons, which support the study of diseases like spinal muscular atrophy and ALS. Read more here.
New federal autism committee head has financial ties to leucovorin
Move over, Sylvia Fogel. It’s John Gaitanis’s turn to steer autism research.
Health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has installed Gaitanis, a pediatric neurologist, as the new chair of the Interagency Autism Coordinating Committee, which helps the federal government decide how to allocate roughly $2 billion in autism research.
Gaitanis, who recently began a stint at the National Institutes of Health’s child health institute, is best known for co-founding Meadow Biosciences. The telehealth startup is centered around helping autistic kids access leucovorin — a drug that President Trump touted during a news conference last year even though the clinical evidence that it helps improve speech is sparse.
Fogel will remain on the autism council. During her tenure as chair, she got into testy exchanges with other autism committee members, pushed for doubling autism research funding, and oversaw the creation of a new strategic plan that ditches genetic research for investigations into environmental causes, including vaccines. — O. Rose Broderick
‘I have people, moms, showing up who hate vaccines, but they like me’
If you want a window on how health related issues are playing this election, look no further than Ohio. As Sarah Todd writes in her dispatch from the state, the gubernatorial race could be “the most direct test of where public opinion in the heartland currently stands on health care, trust in science, and the lasting legacy of the Covid pandemic.”
Sarah spent the day in Cleveland attending rallies for both Democrat Amy Acton, the physician who led Ohio’s aggressive response to Covid-19, and Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, the billionaire founder and former CEO of biotech company Roivant. The sobering number in the CDC’s latest mortality report
This morning, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention released new demographic data on 2024’s leading causes of death. Most of the killers — heart disease, cancer, and unintentional injuries top the list — remained unchanged from 2023. But suicide moved into the top ten, accounting for 1.6% of all deaths in 2024. It was the seventh most common cause of death for men, and the second leading cause of death for Americans between 10 and 24.
Johns Hopkins professor Paul Nestadt, medical director of the Center for Suicide Prevention, offered some helpful context, writing in an email that suicide has crept up the cause of death list “more because Covid deaths shrank than any particular increase in suicide rates.” What has been rising, he said, is the proportion of suicides by firearm. “Right along with that, we see increases in suicide specifically in the populations that are having the most new increases in firearm ownership: Black Americans,” he added.

73 goals from dropping deep - we ask Kane to break down how he did it
- Published
As Harry Kane's career has progressed, the 33-year-old has taken an increasingly complete role, popping up to collect the ball as deep as his own box.
Many wonder why a talisman tasked with scoring doesn't spend more time closer to goal, but last season the England and Bayern Munich striker scored 73 goals - the highest tally of his career - while playing deeper than he ever has done.
When I mention this paradox, a grin spreads across his face.
"Until you really understand football and understand what we've been talking about, it's so easy to say 'stay high, you're going to score' but it doesn't work like that," Kane says.
I sat down to speak to Kane about the finer details of his game, shedding light on his unique role.
Watching Kane train, his professionalism is palpable. England's record goalscorer is one of the first out on the pitch. The younger players indulge in playful kick-ups as he watches, engaged in conversation with a member of staff.
From a distance, that makes it easy to confuse him with a coach but, given his role on the pitch, it is a fitting mistake.
Kane's style of play reflects who he is as a person, with those who know him saying he is well-rounded and humble on and off the pitch.
The season is in its infancy but Kane isn't basking in the success of the past 12 months. With only five days of pre-season training under his belt, the England captain completed 90 minutes of Bayern's 2-1 win over Borussia Dortmund to lift the German Super Cup.
As demanding as his roaming role is, he has taken the physical demands of it in his stride. Across the past six seasons, STATSports - a sports technology company Kane has invested in - found his distance covered, high-speed running and accelerations were up 8%, 22% and 42% respectively.
And given how the tactical landscape has changed over that time, it is particularly impressive Kane has been able to not only keep up, but stay ahead.
"Over the last five or six years, man-to-man pressure has become bigger," Kane says.
"European football is physical and top teams are trying to win the ball back high, trusting their defenders and midfielders to defend man for man to win their battles."
Given that change, the best teams have recruited physical athletes and brilliant dribblers who can beat their man when the game becomes a series of one-against-ones.
Kane, not known for his dribbling - and by his own admission "not the fastest", has thrived on his own terms.
Against Dortmund, there was a specific moment Kane dropped deep, looking to arrive in space unmarked. Recognising the danger, two players converged on the Englishman.
Kane's dribbling is cerebral. His speed of thought provides him solutions to problems others would attempt to solve with their feet alone.
After getting low and using his strength to shrug centre-back Waldemar Anton off him, Kane rose, slightly adjusting his body to the right. These micro-adjustments are a hallmark of his game and through them he is able to shift an entire team's momentum.
Fooled by this feint, Daniel Svensson and Jobe Bellingham found themselves wrong-footed as Kane snapped the ball back the other way, opening up the entire pitch from within Bayern's half.
1 of 4
Earlier this year, Bayern boss Vincent Kompany shed light on Kane's unique role, explaining it as being 50% coached and 50% Kane deciding what to do.
"I think it's partly instinct, using my football brain and getting the feeling on the pitch," says Kane. "If, for example, I want to drop and see if the centre-back really wants to commit, he might commit into midfield, but is he going to commit if I drop all the way to my box?
"After the first five or 10 minutes you really get an understanding of how the opposition are going to play, which dictates how I play."
There is a shared understanding at Bayern of an approach that allows team-mates to make sense of rotations that, to the naked eye, appear random.
Kane, who is given more freedom than most, is at the centre of it.
"I feel like my position now is as one of two 10s, and you work together," he says. "You can double up on one side to overload, which causes the opposition centre-backs a problem of who to mark.
"If they want to mark both, they've got to go man-to-man and then that leaves space for our wingers or full-backs to run into.
"It's posing all these questions to the opposition but, personally, I love having someone close to me who I can link with."
Kane built his reputation playing as a lone number nine, so it is interesting to hear him identify instead as a number 10 - in a front two.
"When you're the number nine on your own you can get marked by two centre-backs and you struggle to get touches on the ball," he says. "You're relying on everyone else to find you with the ball."
Showing Kane two clips from last season, I ask him to talk through what was going through his head.
"The thing with our formation is, as long as there's someone in each position, it doesn't really matter who it is. Lucho [Luis Diaz] in this clip is playing as one of those 10s.
"I've come off to try and create a bit of space and Lucho's gone through the centre."
Distracted by Kane's dropping-deep movement, one of the opposition midfielders is pulled towards him. This creates space, allowing Joshua Kimmich to punch the ball through to Diaz.
"I think it's Serge [Gnabry] making the run in behind which takes the defenders back, which allows me and Lucho that space in between. Lucho lays it off and whenever I'm in that position, around 20-25 yards out, I'm always looking if I can get my shot off."
It is one of many examples of Kane initially dropping deep before scoring.
"By playing deep when the play develops, I end up coming into a number 10 spot when everyone's dropped," he says. "I can get shots off from the edge of the box, which is a big strength of mine, or I'm running off the back of players where no-one's picking me up - because the midfielder finds it hard to [track]."
1 of 3
The second clip is from Bayern's Champions League tie against Club Brugge.
Usually Kane is marked by an opposition centre-back, but the Belgian club give that responsibility to their holding midfielder - something he recognises and exploits.
Lennart Karl scores without Kane touching the ball, but the striker's involvement is undeniable.
"These are the little runs, again, not everyone sees," Kane explains. "With Jamal Musiala and Lenny, they're so good at receiving the ball and dribbling so there'll be times where I will actually stay higher and let those guys get on the ball a bit deeper, and I'll try and make runs in behind.
"Without changing my game too much, I try and complement the players around me.
"I know Lenny is so good in those pockets and when he gets there, I'm more thinking of running in behind because, one, he can play me in and I can go through on goal, or two, he can dribble with the ball and do exactly what happened here.
"As soon as Lenny gets in that pocket I make the run and not always to get the ball, sometimes it is just to drag the defender away.
"Now he's one-against-one with a centre-back in the middle of the pitch and that's dangerous for any centre-back."
1 of 3
With the Ballon d'Or announcement on the horizon, Kane's name is in the conversation, primarily for the sheer volume of goals he has scored. What is easier to miss in that debate is the rest of his game.
Kane plays for the team in each phase of the game across the entirety of the pitch, while at the same time producing extraordinary individual numbers that match the likes of Cristiano Ronaldo, Lionel Messi and Erling Haaland.
He has described himself as playing in the role of a number 10, nine and six at times.
In a football world of specific and heavily drilled tactical roles, that is quite the achievement.

A leaked document has provided the clearest picture yet of how Oracle's latest layoffs have reorganized its vitally important cloud business.
Oracle began a new round of layoffs last week as the tech giant continues to cut costs amid an expensive AI infrastructure push.
Business Insider obtained a previously unreported document showing the scale and scope of the cuts at Oracle's cloud infrastructure division.
It shows the job titles and ages of 546 employees in Oracle's America Cloud Infrastructure organization who were laid off, representing around 7.6% of the 7,185 employees listed. Of those, managers, engineers, software developers, and workers in the company's data center maintenance and servicing division were most affected.
Oracle said in the document that the information was provided to comply with federal age discrimination laws.
It provides an insight into the type of roles the company is eliminating in its second major round of job cuts this year. Oracle has not said how many people it laid off in total last week.
The document states that it includes all employees in Oracle America's Cloud Infrastructure organization eligible to receive severance benefits.
Business Insider could not determine if the document listed all the employees laid off from Oracle's cloud infrastructure org. The company did not respond to a request for comment.
Oracle previously disclosed that its workforce declined by 21,000 employees, or 13%, in the 2026 fiscal year ended May 31, and the company said it had 141,000 employees before the most recent round of layoffs.
How Oracle's cuts break down
Oracle's cloud infrastructure organization is one of the most important parts of its business, with the company reporting in its most recent earnings that quarterly revenues from the division had soared 121% year over year.
Of the employees listed in the document, the cloud org roles hit hardest by the layoffs were software developer III, with 57 workers made redundant, followed by program manager IV and principal core infrastructure engineer.
Software developers were heavily affected, according to the doc, making up around 17% of the roles cut.
Developer roles have long been predicted to be especially vulnerable to AI, especially as AI tools have become increasingly proficient at coding, with some forecasting that Big Tech companies could eventually cut as many as 50% of their engineers.
So far, that scenario has not come to pass, despite a growing number of companies citing AI in their layoff announcements — and recent data from job site Indeed suggests there has been a modest increase in software engineering job postings.
Oracle's layoffs also fell heavily on the company's data center support services, which provide maintenance and tech support for the company's data centers.
Forty-one employees from Oracle's data center support services were selected for termination, around 7.5% of the total, including the vice president of the division and two senior directors.
The layoffs come as Oracle continues to double down on its investments in AI data centers.
The company has racked up tens of billions of dollars in debt and expects to spend $90-$95 billion this year on building new data centers as it bets demand for AI will continue to surge.
Managers hit hard
The recent layoffs also eliminated 128 roles containing the word "manager" across the cloud infrastructure division, according to Business Insider's analysis of the document, around 23% of the total cuts.
Program manager was among the roles that saw the highest number of terminations, with 61 employees eliminated in total.
It comes as other Big Tech companies — including Meta, Snap, Coinbase, and Block — have increasingly cut management roles to pursue "flatter" organizations with fewer layers of bureaucracy.
Managers were by far the hardest-hit group when Meta cut 10% of its workforce earlier this year, although Business Insider recently reported that the company had begun asking some employees in its Applied AI division if they want to take on management roles again.
An analysis of the Oracle layoff document also showed how the company's cuts in this group fell more heavily on older, experienced workers.
The majority of employees affected in Oracle's cloud infrastructure division were over 40, Business Insider's analysis found, and around 16% were 60 or over.

As Trump and Zelenskyy talk about potential energy truce, Russia and Ukraine unleash new wave of strikes
Both countries traded fresh attacks overnight
Ukraine and Russia traded fresh strikes on their respective energy infrastructure overnight, underscoring the gap between the high-level talk of an energy ceasefire in the ongoing war and the reality on the ground.
Ukraine struck two Russian oil refineries, while Russia launched a barrage of missiles at southern Ukraine, hitting several targets, including an oil and gas facility that officials say is now so badly damaged it cannot be restored.
The strikes come as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy prepares to meet U.S. President Donald Trump on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York.
The two leaders spoke by phone on Sunday, and Trump reportedly raised concerns several times about soaring diesel prices. Zelenskyy said afterward that there are “ideas on the table for bringing peace closer, starting with strong de-escalation steps.”
But Zelenskyy has also said any agreement must protect Ukraine’s food exports and critical infrastructure, not just energy facilities.
- Putin's ruling party romps to win in wartime Russian election
- Norway PM 'prepared, but not afraid' of Russian incursion
The Kremlin has previously said it is open to a moratorium on attacks against energy infrastructure, but has insisted that Western sanctions must also be lifted.
Last week, Trump said both sides had agreed to an energy ceasefire. But the agreement appeared to exist largely on his social media feed, because strikes continued.
For many Ukrainians, this has left little reason for optimism.
“I don't really believe in it, I don't, because there are rockets flying,” said Mykola Nechyporenko, a 55-year-old energy worker who spoke to CBC News as he and a crew repaired a damaged electrical cable in Kyiv on Tuesday, ahead of the winter.
“This whole process is uncontrollable.”
Strikes deepen pressure on Russia's fuel supply
Overnight, Ukraine hit a refinery in Russia’s Samara region, about 500 kilometres southeast of Moscow, as well as a refinery in Ufa, more than 1,100 km from the capital.
Those strikes followed what Moscow's mayor called Ukraine's largest drone attack yet on the capital. On the weekend, Kyiv launched more than 400 drones at a refinery in the city.
The attacks are part of a broader Ukrainian campaign against Russia’s energy infrastructure. In recent months, repeated strikes have contributed to fuel shortages, prompting Moscow to ban diesel exports and begin importing fuel from other countries, including India.
In a recent report, the International Energy Agency (IEA) says Russia’s gasoline output is down 20 per cent compared with 2025 levels, while diesel production is estimated to have fallen by nearly 30 per cent.
The IEA says Russia has 32 major refineries, some of which have been attacked as many as 15 times since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
In the first eight months of 2026, a Russian refinery was hit, on average, once every three days, according to the agency.
The disruption is being felt by Russian drivers. Videos posted on social media have shown shortages at gas stations, with frustration at times boiling over into fistfights at the pumps.
The pressure on fuel supplies has also contributed to higher diesel prices internationally, according to the IEA.
Russia targets Ukraine's energy system
While Ukraine strikes deep inside Russia, Moscow has kept up its attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
Overnight, Russia launched several ballistic missiles at southern Ukraine, including at an energy facility in the Poltava region.
The facility is owned by Naftogaz, Ukraine’s largest oil and gas company. The company said at least five missiles struck the site. It had already been shut down, but Naftogaz said the latest damage was so severe that it would no longer be possible to restore and operate the facility.
The state-owned company also operates a network of gas stations, called Ukrnafta. Some are now being fortified with barriers in an effort to reduce damage if they come under attack.
Russia has already targeted several gas stations with drones, including one in the city of Boryspil on Aug. 20.
“There was an alert, and we went with the others behind the petrol station and then there was an explosion in the air and shrapnel came down,” said Valentyn Krasnopir, 63, whose leg was severely injured in the strike. He spoke to CBC News on Saturday from a hospital bed in Kyiv.
Krasnopir said he has lost hope in negotiations.
Iryna Panina, 36, feels the same sense of exhaustion. She was startled awake overnight by what she described as the sound of an aircraft falling, followed by a large explosion.
The windows in her apartment were blown out and furniture was thrown across the floor when a neighbouring five-storey building was hit in the attack. The first floor of that building caught on fire. Two people were injured, and all of the residents were evacuated.
On Tuesday afternoon, as residents gathered alongside emergency crews to try and start the cleanup, air defences rang out in the Ukrainian capital as crews attempted to shoot down a swarm of Russian drones.
“This war has continued too long for us. I don't know what to say, because we are all tired of this and we want some peace,” Panina said in an interview with CBC News.
“I think most of us don't believe in these [Trump/Zelenskyy] meetings. Just talking … that's all. I don't think that something will change.”
New challenge for Ukraine's air defences
The latest attacks come as Ukraine faces another challenge on the battlefield: Russia’s use of jet-powered drones.
Kyiv has adopted a strategy of sending multiple waves of drones toward a target at once in an effort to overwhelm Russian air defences. But Ukrainian forces are struggling to intercept Russian jet-powered drones, which travel too quickly for some of the country’s existing systems.
The attacks have raised concerns about another difficult winter if Russia continues to target Ukraine’s energy grid.
“It's like a neverending story,” said Panina.
“I think we will make some damage for [the Russians], they will for us, and how long it takes? I don't know."

The story so far: The Union Health Ministry has said that stem cell therapy for Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) cannot be offered as routine or commercial treatment and can be used only as part of a duly approved clinical trial. The advisory, issued on September 16 to States and Union Territories that have adopted the Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulation) Act, 2010, follows a landmark Supreme Court judgment in January that examined the use of stem cells for autism.
What exactly has the government said?
The Health Ministry has reiterated that stem cell therapy can be offered as standard clinical care only for disease conditions or indications included in the Ministry’s approved list. Autism is not among those indications.
For ASD specifically, the Ministry has said that therapeutic use of any type of stem cell must remain restricted to duly approved clinical trials, following the National Guidelines for Stem Cell Research, 2017, and other applicable regulatory requirements. It should not be offered as a routine, standard or commercial clinical service.
The advisory is an attempt to ensure enforcement of an existing regulatory framework, particularly after the Supreme Court ruling.
Why is this significant for autism?
Autism is a neurodevelopmental condition. There is currently no established stem cell treatment that has been shown to cure autism or to provide sufficient evidence of benefit to make it a standard treatment.
The Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), in its evidence review on stem cell therapy for ASD, examined the available scientific evidence and concluded that it did not support using stem cells in addition to behavioural and supportive therapies. It recommended that stem cell therapy for autism should not be offered as standard or routine therapy and that its therapeutic use should be restricted to approved clinical trials.
This distinction is important — a treatment being investigated in a clinical trial does not mean that it has been established as an effective treatment. A clinical trial is the mechanism through which safety and efficacy are tested.
What did the Supreme Court say?
The issue came before the Supreme Court in Yash Charitable Trust & Ors. v. Union of India & Ors., decided on January 30, 2026.
The petition raised concerns about the commercial promotion and administration of stem cell “therapy” for autism. The court examined the scientific and regulatory position and held that, given the evidence available at present, stem cell therapy for ASD could not be offered by medical practitioners as a clinical service outside an approved and monitored clinical trial or research setting.
The court also said that, until further research establishes stem cell therapy as a sound and relevant medical practice for ASD, offering it as routine clinical treatment would not meet the reasonable standard of care expected of medical practitioners.
The court recognised the difficult situation faced by families of people with autism who may look for experimental treatments when conventional interventions do not produce the hoped-for results.
It therefore also addressed patients who were already undergoing such treatment before the judgment. Rather than abruptly discontinuing treatment, the court directed the Health Ministry to work out a mechanism, in consultation with AIIMS and the National Medical Commission, to provide the best possible solution and facilitate their continuation until they could be redirected to institutions conducting clinical trials.
So is all stem cell therapy prohibited in India?
No, that is not what this latest advisory states. The latest advisory does not say that stem cells can never be used clinically. It draws a distinction between approved standard care and experimental use.
The Ministry’s current approved list covers 18 adult and 14 paediatric indications. These include several blood cancers and blood disorders, as well as conditions such as multiple sclerosis and systemic sclerosis. For these indications, the relevant treatment is haematopoietic stem cell transplantation performed appropriately; the Ministry’s list specifically states that mesenchymal stem-cell transplantation is not recommended for any disease condition.
Autism is not on this list.
The 2017 National Guidelines for Stem Cell Research also make a fundamental distinction between established haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation and experimental applications. They state that, apart from approved indications, stem-cell use in humans must be within an approved and monitored clinical trial.
What is the way forward for use of stem cells in children with autism?
The advisory states that this therapy cannot be simply prescribe or administer as a routine therapy/treatment.
If stem cells are being investigated for ASD, the treatment has to be part of a properly designed and approved clinical trial. Such research requires the appropriate regulatory and ethical approvals. Depending on the nature and manipulation of the stem cells, different regulatory requirements apply.
This is the key difference between research and treatment being that a clinic cannot describe an experimental intervention as an established therapy and charge patients for it as ordinary clinical care.
What about clinics already offering it?
The Health Ministry has asked State and District regulatory authorities to ensure compliance and to disseminate the Supreme Court’s directions to government and private clinical establishments involved in stem cell research, treatment, promotion or administration.
The National Medical Commission (NMC), in an advisory dated September 5, has separately reiterated that stem cell therapy can be offered as standard clinical care only for approved indications. It has said that unauthorised administration, prescription, promotion or advertisement beyond those indications would constitute professional misconduct. State Medical Councils have been asked to examine complaints and take disciplinary action where professional misconduct is established following due process.
There can also be consequences for clinical establishments. The Health Ministry has referred to Sections 32 and 40 of the Clinical Establishments Act, which provide for cancellation of registration and penalties in applicable jurisdictions.
What should parents understand from this?
The advisory does not mean that research into stem cells and autism has stopped. It means that such research has to remain research until there is convincing evidence that establishes safety and efficacy.
For parents, perhaps the most important distinction is between a clinic saying that stem cells are being studied for autism and saying that stem cells are an established treatment for autism.
The first is a legitimate area of scientific investigation, subject to approvals. The second is not supported by the present evidence or India’s regulatory framework. ICMR’s assessment remains that stem-cell therapy should not be offered as routine treatment for ASD.
The September advisory puts renewed emphasis on enforcing the distinction between an experimental intervention being tested under scientific oversight and a commercial treatment being sold to families as established care.

China's Alibaba unveils new powerful chip and ambitious AI model plans
China's Alibaba has unveiled new plans for its AI model and new chip technologies, including what it claims is China's most powerful AI chip
HONG KONG -- China’s Alibaba unveiled new artificial intelligence chip technologies and plans for more powerful models on Tuesday, including what it said was China's most powerful AI chip, days ahead of a meeting between Chinese and U.S. leaders at which competition to lead on AI technology is expected to be a major theme.
Alibaba’s announcement came as U.S. AI leaders, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, are warning that China's development of AI poses a threat to the United States and calling for an overall slowdown on development of the technology.
Chinese leader Xi Jinping is set to arrive in Washington on Wednesday for a state visit and meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump, at which AI, trade and tariffs are expected to be discussed.
At its annual flagship conference in Hangzhou, Alibaba rolled out a new AI chip and describes its plans for the next generation of its AI model.
CEO Eddie Wu said the new Zhenwu V900 chip is the “most powerful AI chip in China today” and can deliver three times the performance of the company's previous generation Zhenwu M890 chip.
Such chips power frontier AI model training and “inference,” a term for the calculations a trained AI uses to deliver responses to users. Alibaba's Zhenwu chips are used in its data centers, providing computing to the company and its cloud clients.
Alibaba also said it plans to train a new AI model at the scale of five to 10 trillion parameters, a measure of an AI's learning capacity. Its latest Qwen3.8-Max model, the most powerful of its Qwen AI series models, has 2.4 trillion parameters.
Chinese AI company Moonshot says that its Kimi K3, released in July, is the world's largest open model with 2.8 trillion parameters.
Alibaba also highlighted plans to expand the data centers that power its cloud computing business, citing “exponentially” rising demand for AI computing. The company said it expects to have over 20 gigawatts' worth of computing by 2032.
SpaceX has approximately 1.4 gigawatts of AI computing capacity as of mid-this year and says it aims to reach over 10 gigawatts in 2027.
Recent Chinese advancements in AI are giving Beijing more leverage in its upcoming talks with Washington, some analysts believe, as China steps up its self-reliance push even as U.S.-led export restrictions have barred it from accessing some of the world’s most cutting-edge technologies, including AI chips and chipmaking machines.
Open Chinese models, which are often more affordable than cutting-edge closed models from leading U.S. AI labs, have also been making inroads globally, including in the U.S.
Chinese technology giant Huawei last week also unveiled new chip technologies as it looks to challenge global leaders like Nvidia.
Alibaba is “mobilizing every resource” to meet customers’ demand for AI, CEO Wu said in his speech.
Global shortages across the AI data center supply chain, for example, “are currently limiting the speed at which we can scale our compute infrastructure” for AI, he added.
Wu also likened AI growth to the industrial revolution and said “machine intelligence” will rapidly outgrow human thinking capacity.
While “machine intelligence today is not a substitute for human intelligence,” he predicted that, eventually, machines will be able to produce over 1,000 times more “thinking” than all of humanity combined, up from less than 3% currently.

In a three-day strategic dialogue, Belgium and WHO reviewed progress in their longstanding partnership, and agreed to further boost their collaboration on universal health coverage, health-systems strengthening and equitable access to essential vaccines, medicines and health technologies.
The Belgian delegation – headed by H.E. Christophe Payot, Ambassador of Belgium to the United Nations and other international organizations in Geneva – discussed issues of strategic importance, exchanged views on how to smoothly align WHO strategic directions and Belgium's development cooperation priorities in the context of an evolving global health landscape.
The partners exchanged updates on Belgium's support to global health areas brought in the spotlight during the Belgian presidency of Council of the European Union in 2024. WHO was represented by leadership and technical experts from Headquarters and from the Regional Offices for Africa and for Europe.
"After listening to the leaders and experts of WHO we now better understand how they are navigating these challenging times", said Mr Koen Van Acoleyen, Minister Counselor at the Permanent Representation of Belgium to the UN. "We are honoured that we can walk this road together."
Accelerating equitable access to vaccines, medicines and health technologies
The partners reviewed the current status and the most noticeable results achieved by the Access to Medicines programme funded by Belgium. WHO illustrated its work and challenges with an example of country-level implementation in Senegal. It also explained WHO's policies and work on equitable access and local production. Both parties recognized a shared goal for sustainability of the Access to Medicines initiative, as market shaping is key to ensure long-term success.
Health emergencies and pandemic prevention, preparedness and response
Discussions covered WHO's role in strengthening the global architecture for health emergency prevention, preparedness, response and resilience, including the pandemic agreement negotiations and the One Health approach. WHO's crucial field work on health emergency response was demonstrated by presenting the activities in Gaza. The debate also touched upon threats posed by acceleration of biological risks and zoonoses, along with WHO engagement, in particular, risk mitigation.
Universal Health Coverage (UHC)
Elaborating on progress made on UHC-Partnership, the participants reviewed results achieved by WHO with Belgium support in the period 2021-2024, specifically in Belgium's partner countries. They discussed the way forward, exploring the potential for enhanced collaboration at country level, including eventual alignment between WHO country office programmes and Belgium's country level bilateral cooperation. Examples included a summary of the work and challenges at country level from the Democratic Republic of Congo. The visitors listened to a recap of WHO's policies and work on mental health in the context of primary health care.
The partners also reviewed progress in other areas of collaboration on WHO programmes supported by Belgium, such as Neglected Tropical Diseases and Sexual, Reproductive Health and Rights. The review underpinned the importance of an evidence-based approach in these areas.
WHO appreciates Belgium's commitment and engagement, displayed by the participation of representatives of the country's Federal government as well as the Flemish and Walloon governments. "We thank you for your support, honesty, and strong engagement for global health", said Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Director-General, External Relations and Governing Bodies. "Your efforts in supporting our work in Mozambique and Senegal are clear examples of the crucial work we accomplish together".
Looking into the future
The partners discussed ways forward for the Belgium-WHO collaboration framework and multi-year agreement, including progress towards a renewed WHO-Belgium Country Cooperation Strategy.
The enhanced collaboration between Belgium and WHO will support a strong global health agenda under the WHO 14th General Programme of Work (GPW14). There was a shared vision that UHC and health systems strengthening being at the heart of GPW14 ambitions will be taken as essential scope in WHO's ongoing prioritization work.
"We recognize WHO as a trustworthy partner in global health. We felt proud hearing how crucial our support is to the Organization and how it is having a positive impact at country, regional, and global levels", said Mr Dirk Brems, Director of Thematic and Multilateral Cooperation, Directorate-General Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Aid. "It's important we continue these discussions as we tread uncharted territories, and we look forward to working together for strong and sustained multilateralism".

After Meta, tech giant Google has reportedly has agreed to report child abuse content hosted on its platforms to appropriate law enforcement agencies in India. The central government has increased its scrutiny on tech platforms in a bid to safeguard children. Authorities are urging tech giants such as Google and Microsoft to report child abuse content involving India directly, Reuters reported citing government sources, amid concerns that the existing reporting system causes significant delays. Google has increased its investments significantly to detect, deter, remove, and report child sexual abuse material. To note, the company regularly takes down hundreds of thousands of pieces of content and accounts in India via automated detection tools to prevent the spread of CSAM and extremist material. As of the last available public record, January 2024 saw Google take 63,975 removal actions following user complaints in India, with copyright accounting for 61,180 of them. Inc42 has reached out to Google for comments on the development. The story will be updated based on their response. The government and regulatory bodies are closely monitoring social media intermediaries’ social media platforms regarding their content moderation policies and legal compliance. It has warned that action would be taken against platforms that fail to introduce adequate measures to protect children online. The development comes about a week after social media major Meta agreed to report instances of child sexual abuse to the appropriate law enforcement agencies in India. One unresolved issue is the persistence of harmful AI-generated material. The government has questioned why such content can reappear after being flagged, and why AI-generated videos without appropriate labels remain accessible on Meta’s platforms. In an earlier meeting, officials also pressed Meta to increase human oversight of content moderation, particularly for Indian languages and material shaped by local cultural and social contexts. To protect children from predatory practices online, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) issued notices to multiple social media platforms to remove child sexual abuse material (CSAM) on their websites in 2023, and warned that non-compliance with the order will entail strict action, including withdrawal of safe harbour protections. Meanwhile, the Gujarat High Court (HC) issued notices to global tech giants Meta, Google, X, Reddit and Scribd in a case pertaining to the spread of AI-generated content hosted on these platforms, earlier in April. The petition flagged the growing circulation of AI-generated videos online, warning that the “widespread creation and circulation of AI generated videos on digital platforms” poses a “serious threat to public order and functioning of a healthy democracy.”

Quick Answer
Wanderlog, Stippl, Polarsteps, and TripWaffle can turn flight, hotel, train, and other confirmation emails into organized travel plans. They differ in AI planning, maps, collaboration, trip tracking, alerts, and pricing, so the best choice depends on how you travel.
While traveling is something we all look forward to, the preparation behind it is sometimes quite grueling. Especially when you are doing everything by yourself. You book a flight on one site, a hotel on another, and a rental car through a different source, maybe through a referral link sent to you on WhatsApp. Traveling isn’t just about downloading the right apps before you board the flight. It is also about having all your important info at your disposal.
Just to know whether your hotel booking said 2 PM or 12 PM, you have to dig through your inbox. This is such a universal travel headache that an entire category of apps has been developed just to fix this. This list contains 4 AI travel planner apps that can convert your forwarded emails into a clean, day-by-day plan — flights, hotels, activities all lined up in order.
Table of Contents
Best AI Travel Planners
I went over the internet and actually dug through four of the more talked-about names in this space — Wanderlog, Stippl, Polarsteps, and the newer, scrappier TripWaffle. These apps were put to the test to see what they are genuinely good at, where they fall short, and which one deserves a spot on your phone before your next trip. Let us go through them one by one.
Wanderlog: The one that does almost everything, and does most of it well
For me, Wanderlog has become the default travel planner app, and for good reason. The email trick works two ways here. You can either forward your flight and hotel confirmations email to a special address Wanderlog gives you, or you can just link your Gmail account and let it quietly scan your inbox for bookings automatically on its own. The details show up straight in your itinerary, and it eliminates typing in flight numbers and copying and pasting confirmation codes.
However, there is one thing that makes Wanderlog stand out from a plain inbox-scanner. After your bookings are in, Wanderlog does not just leave them sitting there as a list. It pins everything onto an actual map. You can drag your stops, reorder your day, and there is a route optimizer that can rearrange your stops to save you driving time. Wanderlog also works like a shared Google Doc. Add your travel companions by email, and everyone will have access to edit the same trip at the same time, see live changes, and more. For a group trip, this is a great thing to have.
Community members also contribute travel guides right inside the app, so you have all the interesting information about a new city you have landed. Speaking of the cons, some users have reported that once a trip is created, there is sometimes no way to edit locations cleanly, forcing them to delete and redo it. Then there is the paywall issue, where features such as offline access and automatic Gmail scanning are locked behind the Pro subscription.
Download Wanderlog: Android | iOS
Stippl: The AI-first planner that tries to be your whole travel toolkit
Stippl leans hard into AI to get there. You just need to tell it what kind of trip you want (relaxed, adventurous, culture-heavy, offbeat) and it generates out a full day-by-day itinerary for your destination in under two minutes. If you already have a rough plan and just need a day filled in, you can use Stippl for that too. Simply tap a single day, and it will generate activities, restaurants, and transport suggestions just for that slot.
For emails, it works the same familiar way. You just need to forward your booking emails, and Stippl will pick up flights, hotels, trains, and restaurant reservations and feed them to your trip automatically. Everything also gets synced to the calendar, so your itinerary shows up right alongside your regular meetings and reminders. Stippl sets itself apart from the other three by the fact that it leans into being a memory-keeper as well as a travel planner.
There is a scratch map feature that adds every country you have already visited. It gives the feel of a passport stamp collection you can show off. It can also stitch your trip photos into an automatic travel reel or photobook once you are back home, no editing required from your end. You can also purchase an eSIM from the app. Coming to the con, the AI-powered itinerary generation and offline mode sit behind a paywall. Some users have reported having run into crashes, slow email imports, and the odd date or flight not saving correctly, especially with overnight flights or long layovers. Do keep that in mind.
Download: iOS
Polarsteps: Built for tracking your journey, now sneaking in planning too
Polarsteps is a bit different than the other three apps on this list. It did not start as a booking organizer at all but as a way to automatically track where you have already been and turn it into a beautiful, shareable map, eliminating manual check-in anywhere. You just have to carry your phone, and the app quietly traces your route in the background using WiFi and mobile data with constant GPS pings. That said, Polarsteps is also slowly gaining proper trip-planning tools, and the confirmation-email feature is now part of it. You can forward your hotel or flight booking to the app, and it pulls out the address and other details automatically.
Polarsteps has also introduced an AI-powered itinerary builder. There is also the ability to manually add flights by looking them up by airline and flight number, though you cannot book through the app. Since tracking is Polarsteps’ specialty, once your trip ends, it can turn the whole route into a digital travel book that you can order and keep.
Speaking of the shortcomings, compared to Wanderlog or Stippl, Polarsteps’ booking-import feature is newer and less complete. Polarsteps traditionally allows just one person to add content per trip. This means that if you are planning a group trip, Polarsteps, as a travel planner, won’t be a good option. It is meant for solo travelers and backpackers, who care as much about documenting the journey as planning it.
TripWaffle: The newcomer that’s focused on one job
TripWaffle may be the least-known name here, but that is one of the reasons why it makes it to this list. It’s built by a small, independent team (led by a single developer, Guy King, based in Australia). Instead of trying to be a do-everything travel app, it does one thing and focuses on, which is turning forwarded confirmation emails into a clean itinerary.
The setup is about as simple as it gets. You sign up and send your booking confirmations to it from providers. Using AI, TripWaffle reads the email, pulls out the dates, times, confirmation numbers, and addresses, and puts everything into a day-by-day timeline with time zones and connecting flights already planned out.
TripWaffle earns its keep in the details that it can keep. You get live flight tracking with real position updates, alerts about delays, gate changes, and a “flight reliability score,” which tells you how a specific flight number has historically performed. You receive a pre-trip checklist email covering visa requirements, weather, and packing suggestions just a day before your departure. TripWaffle is completely free with no ads, no Pro tier, and no upsell, which is something none of the apps in this list provide. You do not get crowd-sourced attraction guides or any AI-generated itineraries from scratch.
So which one should you actually download?
Honestly, it depends on what kind of traveler you are. I travel a lot, and most of my stay is outside my home country. I would suggest you try multiple apps and then decide on the one that you want to keep. Nani, Sonali Kulkarni, Kayadu Lohar and Raghav Juyal attended the press meet of The Paradise in Mumbai. Mostly, actors of Pan-India films come on stage and answer pre-decided questions asked by the host. But the actors of The Paradise, in a rare instance, decided to take questions from the media as well. As expected, Nani stole the show with his replies, especially his remarks on Shah Rukh Khan and his iconic 1993 film.
The Paradise Mumbai press meet: Nani calls Baazigar his “favourite commercial film”; reveals, “Shah Rukh Khan and I have the EXACT same measurements; wish we had the same PAYMENT as well!”
Nani said, “The Paradise is an extremely intense film. Nowadays, when we see a commercial film, emotions or intensity are presented in a light manner; thoda touch karke aa jaata hai! This is because songs or fights are forced into the narrative and in the process, they don’t explore the emotions. But in our childhood, our favourite commercial films like Baazigar and many others, the emotions were very intense in these films. But in commercial films of today’s times, we don’t feel the essence. Yes, the hero is beating up the villain. But you are not shouting ‘Maaro usse’! You don’t feel the anger or the depth of the situation.”
He continued, “But The Paradise attempts to catch that intensity. If somebody is in pain on screen, you’ll feel that pain too. If some character is in love, you’ll be able to relate. From the time the film begins, you’ll be transported into its world. You’ll forget your surroundings for 3 hours!”
During the Q-and-A session with the media, Raghav Juyal was asked, “What’s common between Nani and Shah Rukh Khan?” The actor’s next, King, stars SRK. Before Raghav could answer, Nani replied, “Our measurements!”
Nani smiled and explained, “I worked in Yash Raj Films’ first South film, Aaha Kalyanam (2014). When I went for the photoshoot, that’s the first thing they have told me, ‘Sir, you have exact measurements as Shah Rukh sir’! I was like, ‘Nice’. I have the exact measurements but not the exact payment (laughs). I wish it was the exact payment as well!”
Raghav then revealed, “Both treat everyone equally on the sets. They are very respectful with every single unit member. They are calm. I love those who have patience. Mere mein bilkul nahin hai. I am too impatient (smiles).”
The Paradise releases in cinemas on September 24.
