Two men that the Trump administration expelled to Equatorial Guinea were bound, fitted with bags over their heads, beaten and pushed down a flight of stairs, all in plain view of other US deportees, according to witnesses and human rights lawyers.
The men – one from Egypt and one from Eritrea – were then taken to a prison. About 30 detainees from the US remain trapped at a hotel in the outskirts of the coastal city of Malabo after being deported from the US. Detainees have said they believe the men were beaten for telling the press and human rights advocates about the poor conditions and violence inside the hotel, and that they are haunted by flashbacks and terrified they will be retaliated against next.
Human rights advocates and experts have warned for months that conditions at the Hotel Bamy – a run-down establishment that has served as a detention center for US deportees – are dangerous.
The US has sent at least 66 people from different African countries, Cuba and Brazil to Equatorial Guinea, which has received $7.5m as part of a deal to cooperate with the US deportation program. The Trump administration has pursued dozens of similar deals with countries to take in immigrants that the US cannot deport directly to their home countries, where judges have deemed they would face torture or persecution. In the past, the US government allowed those people to live and work in the US indefinitely.
The Trump administration, however, has sought instead to expel them to third countries where they have no ties, do not speak the local language and have no legal status – trapping them in limbo.
Advocates have been especially concerned for deportees sent to Equatorial Guinea, where the authoritarian government is notorious for human rights abuses, including torture, according to the US state department. Detainees held at Hotel Bamy have told the Guardian that armed guards keep watch over them 24/7, and that they have not been provided any medical care or even fresh clothes since arriving there. One of the detainees, who has a severe stomach hernia that requires visits to the hospital to drain his stomach due excessive fluid build-up, said he has been unable to see a doctor since arriving at Hotel Bamy.
Other detainees have managed to obtain medication for HIV, diabetes and other conditions via human rights lawyers, but remain fearful that access to medications will be arbitrarily cut off.
The two men who were tortured – Ahmed Soliman, 31, of Egypt, and Samson Birhane, 47, of Eritrea – have since been transferred to a prison in Malabo. Multiple witnesses recounted that the police officers shouted, “Where is the phone? Where is the phone!” as they beat the men, who had initially been accused of breaking a mirror at the hotel before they were pulled aside and arrested.
The beating, which occurred on 11 September, followed the release of a video first reported by Reuters showing conditions at the hotel and the violent behavior of the guards. The detainees had been using cellphones to communicate with lawyers and the media about the conditions they were facing.
In the video taken by Soliman, which lawyers shared with the Guardian, authorities are seen pointing guns at the deportees. A Cuban man asked the officer for the return of his confiscated mobile phone so he could contact relatives and a lawyer, but was ignored. When officers noticed Soliman filming the exchange with his mobile phone, multiple officers rushed at him and others standing nearby, pointed their guns, and told Soliman to remain on his knees with his hands up for 10-15 minutes.
In another video, Soliman was able to film authorities forcibly sending US deportees to Ethiopia, where they are likely to face torture. When deportees resisted going with authorities, officials gave them the option to “go back to their home country” or “go to prison”. At least 12 people have been returned by Equatorial Guinea to their home country, where they face persecution.
In May, human rights experts at the United Nations issued a rare public appeal asking Equatorial Guinea to halt plans to return deportees to their home countries and to comply with international human rights standards and avoid refoulement, or the expulsion of people to countries where they face persecution.
“This is a human rights catastrophe,” said Bella Mosselmans, director of the Global Strategic Litigation Council, who represents several of the deportees at Hotel Bamy. The US and Equatorial Guinea “must be held accountable for the atrocities they are committing”, she added.
In the week since Soliman and Birhane were beaten, police have also been searching the other detainees’ hotel rooms for cellphones, and have confiscated them. They have also barred lawyers from seeing the deportees. Authorities have told the 29 US deportees who remain at Hotel Bamy that they may never see Soliman or Birhane again, according to lawyers. One detainee who witnessed the beating said authorities treat them as if they are “blanks” who “don’t even exist”. Another detainee said an officer told her: “You will disappear from the earth. I am the law.”
Witnesses said they feared for the lives of Soliman and Birhane, who came to the US as children.
Soliman is a gay man from Egypt who had lived in Phoenix for most of his life. He had a green card, but lost status after he was convicted of drug possession. He served time for his crimes, and in October, a judge had determined he would face persecution and torture if he were to return to Egypt due to his sexuality.
Birhane had come to the US as a refugee when he was 13, but lost status after a conviction for robbery when he was in high school, in 1988. He was allowed to remain in the US after a judge ruled he faced torture in Eritrea, and had been regularly checking in with Immigration and Customs Enforcement as required.
Lawyers for the deportees shared copies of multiple emails they had sent to the US embassy in Equatorial Guinea alerting them to threats and violence against those detained at Hotel Bamy, but those messages have gone unanswered, they said. In July, amid a lawsuit challenging conditions for deportees, the African Commission issued an urgent interim order instructing the government of Equatorial Guinea to refrain from deporting, transferring, or relocating deportees against their will.
The US Department of Homeland Security did not respond to the Guardian’s request for comment.
A spokesperson for the state department said: “The US government will use all legal means to remove those with no right to remain in our country.”
The agency did not respond to questions about whether it was aware of how Equatorial Guinea was treating US deportees, nor would it acknowledge whether any measures have been taken to intervene.
“As a general matter, we do not comment on the details of our private diplomatic communications with other governments,” the spokesperson said.

In December 2025, as social media’s potential impact on youth mental health faced growing scrutiny, Australia became the first country to ban social media for people under 16, with Indonesia quickly following. The European Union is taking a slightly different approach, banning social media for children under 13 and personal accounts for people under 15 after pressure from several E.U. nations.
Elsewhere, big tech companies are being challenged in the courts. Meta recently agreed to pay up to $18 billion to resolve claims in the U.S. that Facebook and Instagram harmed children. Meta will also introduce “safety by design” features for young people, such as concealing the number of “likes” on posts. But will these features meaningfully change young people’s behavior or experiences online? Will the bans have their intended effect?
With major changes being introduced around the world, researchers must seize this opportunity to conduct robust independent evaluations of how social media — and its regulation — impacts teenagers’ mental health, wellbeing and social lives. With almost half of all mental health problems emerging by the age of 18, this research is crucial.
One size might not fit all
Ultimately, the question is not simply whether social media is inherently “good” or “bad,” or whether restrictions “work” or “don’t work.” Instead, researchers need to look at whether changing young people’s digital environments leads to meaningful changes in their mental health and wellbeing.
The evidence increasingly suggests that there is unlikely to be a single “social media effect” that impacts all teenagers in the same way.
Social media restrictions will likely affect individual young people differently, based on factors such as their age, whether they have existing mental health problems, and their sleep patterns. It could have different effects based on teenagers’ gender, their socioeconomic background, or where they live (for example, whether they come from an urban or rural area).
Social media can be an important source of community, so restrictions may affect people from marginalized backgrounds in different ways, including those who identify as LGBTQ+. It will most likely also depend on the specific way that a person uses (or previously used) a given platform.
If restrictions do bring changes in teenagers’ mental health, researchers need to understand the mechanisms behind the change. For example, if some young people experience an improvement in their mental health following the restrictions, might it be because they are meeting up more with friends in real life, or are they getting more sleep? The answer to the why question could shape future policies that support youth mental health.
Lessons from Australia
Early findings from Australia suggest that age verification from social media companies is a significant challenge in implementing the ban.
An evaluation published in the British Medical Journal found little evidence of substantial reductions in social media use three months after Australia implemented its ban. It found that many young people were continuing to use restricted platforms and finding ways around age-verification systems. Meanwhile, a report by Australia’s online watchdog found that more than 80% of children were still using a restricted online platform.
Behavioral economist Leonardo Bursztyn and colleagues found that many teenagers continued to believe their peers were using restricted platforms and reported they would be more willing to stop if more of their peers stopped, too. This shows the importance of peer influence in adolescent decision-making, which will be a factor in the restrictions globally.
The difficulties in implementing the ban in Australia mean that it is still too early to say whether it has improved young people’s mental health and in what ways it has worked. Still, this raises an important point that implementation will be a major factor across the world.
Assessing the change in the U.K.
In the U.K., the government is planning to introduce a social media ban in spring 2027.
I work at Wellcome, a global philanthropic foundation based in London and one of the biggest funders of mental health research in the world. We are going to be funding evaluations of the impact of the social media ban in the U.K. on youth mental health, with research teams working with tens of thousands of teenagers. All our work is guided by young people with experience in both social media use and mental health problems, so that research best reflects their concerns.
In this case, we consulted with a group of young people to ask for advice on how best to design and implement the research on social media restrictions. The young people reframed the whole debate. Rather than focusing solely on whether social media is harmful and whether we need a ban, they repeatedly asked us to look at what role social media currently plays in young people’s lives — and what might replace it if access is restricted.
Young people are not oblivious about the risks of social media, such as misinformation and harmful content, but they also recognize it as infrastructure for learning, connection, support, creativity, and belonging. They highlighted that evaluating the restrictions requires understanding how teenagers’ time is otherwise spent. For example, they said, researchers should look at whether young people are spending time in a positive way by cultivating outdoor hobbies, friendships, sleeping better, and studying more. Or will they simply spend the time being bored, or find themselves in unregulated online spaces?
In short, the young people were asking researchers to evaluate changes in their lives, rather than simply looking at changes in their screen time.
They suggested that the evaluation should not only focus on how to reduce harm, but also on understanding what kinds of social environments best support young people’s mental health and wellbeing.
A global opportunity
We are not simply trying to evaluate the U.K. government’s policy on banning social media. We are trying to understand a much broader and fundamental question: How do changes in the digital environment impact young people’s mental health and wellbeing, and why?
While we are focusing on the U.K., this is a globally relevant question. Comparing what happens in Australia and the U.K., with the results in the E.U., where they will be cracking down on certain practices, and elsewhere in the world, via Meta’s new tools, will be illuminating. Perhaps we will end up learning that bans are the solution. Perhaps some tools will be more effective than others.
There is a seismic opportunity for research teams around the world to join forces to evaluate how social media and its restrictions impact youth mental health. The answers that emerge could influence how we intervene in youth mental health for generations to come.
Camilla Iannone is research lead in the mental health evidence team at Wellcome.

Boks power & All Blacks of old - what did we learn from series?
- Published
South Africa further cemented themselves as the world's best team with a 3-1 victory over New Zealand in the Rugby's Greatest Rivalry series.
After losing the opening Test in Johannesburg, the world champions won three straight games, comfortably claiming the series with a 43-28 win in Baltimore.
The fourth Test, played in the United States, came after three Tests in South Africa where the All Blacks continued to show promising signs under Dave Rennie.
With the Rugby World Cup next year, what did we learn from the series, which replaced this year's Rugby Championship and will be played again in 2029?
Power remains Springboks' trump card
New Zealander Tony Brown's arrival as attack coach in 2024 pointed to South Africa's ambition to dominate in all facets of the game.
The former Highlanders head coach, who will join the All Blacks in 2028, is known for creating a cohesive attacking shape built on sharp ball movement.
But having been outscored in terms of tries over the first two Tests, the Springboks flipped their pack-power trump card - pivotal to their back-to-back World Cup successes - to prevent a repeat of New Zealand's victorious 1996 series win in South Africa.
Nothing illustrated that more than a monster maul that started just inside New Zealand's 22 and ended with Malcolm Marx peeling off to score the decisive try under the posts.
That came after a penalty try from a scrum in the first half. In Baltimore, their power again proved too much.
"South Africa have tried to play expansively a couple of times when we have dominance after hurting teams in the maul or scrum," Schalk Brits, a 2019 World Cup winner, told BBC Sport.
"New Zealand didn't have that dominance in the forwards, but people said they played beautiful rugby. I don't care if it is beautiful or not.
"Beauty is in the eye of the beholder and I love a maul and scrum."
Fly-half Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu, who was injured at the end of May, returned to start all four Tests. He was initially named on the bench for the second match, only for Handre Pollard to withdraw.
Despite improving as the series went on, the 24-year-old lacked his usual flashes of individual brilliance.
It remains to be seen whether South Africa turn back to 32-year-old Pollard, as they did in 2023, on the biggest occasions to close out games.
Rassie Erasmus' experienced back-to-back World Cup winners - Marx (32), Eben Etzebeth (34), Pieter-Steph du Toit (34), Siya Kolisi (35), Damian de Allende (34), Cheslin Kolbe (32) - all remain regular starters.
The world champions have proven they can also play an exciting brand of attacking rugby, but appeasing the masses will not matter if a familiar formula can bring them three straight World Cups.
All Blacks return to what made them great
Scott Robertson's dismissal in January after two years as head coach sunk New Zealand to a new low.
Rennie, not the flashiest appointment, had to hit the ground running, and a stunning Test win over South Africa at Ellis Park was a case of doing just that.
The 33-16 victory injected jeopardy into a series which many had the Springboks winning comfortably, given their home advantage and recent dominance.
Hurricanes half-backs Cam Roigard and Ruben Love, both aged 25, were trusted by Rennie to instil a return to the All Blacks way - the ability to score from transition from anywhere on the field and compound scoreboard pressure.
Four or more tries in each Test in South Africa showed just that, with the third Test all square at half-time.
"Scott Robertson was a good culture coach but maybe not a brilliant technical coach. Dave Rennie is a brilliant technical coach," former England wing Ugo Monye told Rugby Union Weekly.
"After the Nations Championship, you could see the structures and how they want to play. I think the All Blacks' backline is the most skilled in World Rugby."
Love struggled to have the same commanding impact in Tests two and three, with fly-half Richie Mo'unga returning for the Baltimore game, his first Test since the World Cup final.
The 32-year-old Mo'unga, who is back after a stint in Japan, was not at the standard that made him one of the best fly-halves at the 2023 World Cup.
However, getting him back up to speed will be an All Blacks goal over the next 12 months.
Former England scrum-half Danny Care said: "Imagine what New Zealand would do with a platform and some dominance. It is great for the game that they are coming back to be the All Blacks of old, and the next 12 months will be fascinating."
World Cup rivals: France 'can play multiple styles', and be 'careful of Ireland'
South Africa live for must-win games. That is when, according to Brits, the Boks "come alive".
Defeat at Ellis Park cost them their world number one status - which was quickly regained - but also exposed a vulnerability.
South Africa, who lost matches in the pool stages of the past two World Cups, are currently the favourites to win next year's tournament in Australia, bringing a pressure they have not experienced previously.
"We hate being the favourite, we almost have to have our backs against the wall," Brits said.
"We prefer not to have the eyes on us and move under the radar. I think that is the best way for any team."
Back-to-back Six Nations champions France sent a weakened side to Christchurch in July and lost 34-32 to New Zealand.
When matched against the Springboks last November, France were beaten emphatically, 32-17.
Brits believes France are "the most settled" and offer tactical flexibility similar to that of the world champions.
"I feel like South Africa have an advantage as they can play multiple styles, and it feels like most other nations don't have that capability," Brits said.
"The only team that can play multiple styles is France, as they can grind it out with the forwards, play the kicking game and the expansive game as well."
He added that England still need to become what they are "supposed to be" and to keep an eye on Ireland, who are travelling "under the radar" after peaking in previous World Cup cycles prior to the tournament.
"Ireland still have amazing rugby players and coaches – the best coaches out there - and a top-four squad," Brits added. "Be careful of Ireland."

The 18th BRICS Summit was held at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi on 12–13 September 2026, with leaders from BRICS member and partner countries in attendance. In this context, a selfie purportedly showing Russian President Vladimir Putin, Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Chinese President Xi Jinping, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, South African President Cyril Ramaphosa, and former Iranian President Ebrahim Raisi is being widely shared on social media (here, here). Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: A real selfie image featuring world leaders at the 2026 BRICS Summit.
Fact: The image is AI-generated. It includes individuals who did not attend the summit. The image also features former Iranian President Ebrahim Raisi, who died in a helicopter crash in May 2024. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
While reviewing the post, we noticed several inconsistencies in the viral image. The presidents of Brazil, the UAE, and Türkiye did not attend the 2026 BRICS Summit. Brazil was represented by Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira, while Crown Prince Khaled bin Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan represented the UAE. The image also features former Iranian President Ebrahim Raisi, who died in a helicopter crash in May 2024. Therefore, the presence of these individuals in a purported selfie from the 2026 BRICS Summit raises questions about the authenticity of the image.
Additionally, we ran this image through AI detection tools. Hive Moderation showed this image was 99.9% AI-generated. Sightengine also showed it was 99% AI-generated.
Pictures of the leaders who participated in the conference can be seen here and here.
To sum up, this AI-generated image is being shared as a real photo of world leaders at the 2026 BRICS summit.

A decades-old shady eucalyptus, an elm beloved by thousands of commuters, and a type of gingko once thought to be extinct in the wild are among the finalists for Victoria’s tree of the year.
The competition run by the National Trust of Victoria started in 2016 as a way to raise awareness about trees around Victoria and advocate for their protection by celebrating significant trees.
To be eligible, the trees must be listed on the National Trust significant tree register, which it recognises up to 10,000 important trees in Victoria for their cultural, scientific, and historic value.
This year it had more than 40 nominations, which were narrowed down to nine finalists by a panel of 12 experts and arboriculturists.
The executive manager of gardens at the National Trust, Justin Buckley, said the trees nominated for the registry have been there for generations, and the people who nominated them often remember playing under them and climbing them, along with their children.
“It’s not always just the biggest or most impressive tree that wins; it’s often one that has a lot of community support behind it.” Buckley said.
The 2026 finalists are:
The famed myrtle beech in Apollo Bay may be the result of two or three trees growing together and visitors are able to wander through the complex structure: a parallel to the web of life they support.
Although flooded gums only naturally grow north of Newcastle, and especially in very wet areas like the Daintree, this specimen most likely planted in the 1960s or 70s in Carlton North is a landmark of pride for the community.
These trees were planted as a experiment by the Melbourne Metropolitan Board of Works in the 1930s in order to see if conifers could clean drinking water in a landscape which had been extensively cleared. Growing much taller than any other trees, they offer visitors an awe-inspiring experience.
The ginkgo was planted in Geelong Botanic Gardens in 1859, and is more than 167 years old. Gingkos, also known as maidenhairs, were thought to be extinct in the wild for many centuries before being revived.
The Indian bean tree is located in the botanical gardens in Castlemaine. Originally from Central America, the tree is known to herald the season by covering itself in large white flowers in spring and growing a full shady green canopy of large leaves in summer and long seed pods in winter.
This smooth-barked apple myrtle in Prahran is the biggest of its kind in cultivation. Located in the middle of urban Melbourne and surrounded by construction works, there are hopes that architects will let the tree continue to grow for many years to come.
Planted by 1867 Jacob Bernstein, a member of Ballarat’s Hebrew community, this Canary Island pine is the second-eldest recorded tree among the finalists and is a recognisable feature in the landscape of Ballarat. Canary Island pines are known for their longevity and ability to survive changes in climate.
The competition is the trust’s most successful advocacy campaign and helps bring awareness to important trees in Victoria, Buckley said.
“In the 40-odd years that we’ve been keeping the significant tree register, they’re potentially under more threat than they ever have been with densification of cities and more housing; we think protection of trees is as important as it’s ever been,” Buckley said.
Voting for the competition closes at midnight, 22 October, with the winner announced on 27 October.

Researchers at the BRIC-Rajiv Gandhi Centre for Biotechnology (BRIC-RGCB) here have developed a nanopore-based sensing technology that could pave the way for early detection and monitoring of biomarkers linked to neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson’s disease and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).
A research team led by Mahendran K.R., with contributions from PhD student Varsha Shaji and postdoctoral researcher Neethu Puthumadathil, designed the ‘self-assembling dual-diameter’ nanopore sensors that are capable of detecting such biomarkers with high sensitivity, the RGCB said in a statement.
The research published in Nature Nanotechnology represents a significant advance in nanoscience and biomolecular sensing, the RGCB said.
Indicators of diseases
Biomarkers are indicators of diseases that can be used for early detection. Nanopores are extremely small hollow structures. Detecting biomarkers at an early stage using conventional techniques, however, remains challenging as many of these biomarkers occur at extremely low concentrations.
“In the new approach, the researchers designed short peptides that form pores of varying sizes, providing a versatile platform for sensing biomolecules with different shapes and dimensions. The sensors distinguish disease and non-disease-associated forms of the biomarkers, even when they were present in complex protein mixtures at very low concentrations,” according to the RGCB.
In future, these sensors can be used to develop point-of-care devices that detect biomarkers associated with various diseases, such as cancer, directly from biological fluids, including blood, the institute said.
Major challenge
Early and accurate detection remains a major challenge in managing neurodegenerative diseases, BRIC-RGCB director Beena Pillai said. “The nanopore sensor platform demonstrates how advances in nanotechnology and biotechnology can come together to address a critical unmet need in health care,” she said.
The work was carried out in collaboration with Ulrich Kleinekathöfer’s group at Constructor University, Germany, and Krishnananda Chattopadhyay’s group at CSIR-Indian Institute of Chemical Biology (CSIR-IICB), Kolkata. The study was supported by grants from the Department of Biotechnology, the Department of Science and Technology, the Indian Council of Medical Research and the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research.

WHO and Netherlands Strategic Dialogue in The Hague, Netherlands 10 April 2024. Credit: Michel Mees Photography
The WHO and the Netherlands convened in The Hague on 10 April 2024, to discuss joint priorities and alignment between the Dutch Global Health Strategy and WHO’s key strategic goals, marking a new milestone in their longstanding partnership.
Rooted in the Netherlands' unwavering commitment to global health, human rights, and universal access to comprehensive health services, the collaboration between the WHO and the Netherlands is instrumental in addressing global health challenges and fostering health and well-being, worldwide and in the country.
Against the backdrop of ongoing conflicts, disasters, and the escalating impact of climate change, and the interconnectedness of the Dutch public health landscape in the Netherlands with global health challenges, this year’s Strategic Dialogue emerged as a critical platform for reflecting on this partnership’s long-term vision.
“In this Strategic Dialogue, throughout all sessions, WHO and the Netherlands showed a commitment to cooperation and to deepening their partnership based on the strong alignment between their respective priorities and objectives”, said Ms Marjolijn Sonnema, Director General for Public Health at the Netherlands’ Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport.
A key outcome of the Strategic Dialogue was the recognition of the alignment between the Dutch Global Health Strategy and the WHO's forthcoming 14th General Programme of Work, paving the way for synergies in areas such as health system strengthening, pandemic preparedness, climate change and health, anti-microbial resistance (AMR) and mental health support.
"At a time when inequity in health and in access to essential health services and financial protection is increasing, disproportionately impacting the poor and most vulnerable, the Netherlands stands as a global health leader and trusted WHO partner. With shared priorities and commitment to sexual and reproductive rights, gender equity, health systems, security, climate resilience, and mental health, we look forward to strengthening our partnership to enhance the health and well-being of all, globally and in the Netherlands", said Dr Bruce Aylward, WHO Assistant Director-General, Universal Health Coverage, Life Course.
WHO acknowledged the Netherlands' global leadership as a flexible donor, with an agreement around the imperative to ensure WHO's financing is more sustainable, through the inaugural WHO Investment Round. This WHO initiative aims to mobilize predictable, sustainable and flexible resources essential for the WHO to respond swiftly and effectively to global health challenges and improve health outcomes, particularly for vulnerable populations.
Addressing contemporary challenges such as geopolitical tensions while seizing opportunities for advancing global health objectives were also on the table during the dialogue. Both parties stressed the importance of sustained collaboration to address pressing health issues comprehensively.
Taking stock of the joint achievements since the previous strategic dialogue in 2022
In 2022, the Strategic Dialogue between the Netherlands and WHO called on both partners to enhance synergies between WHO priorities and the new Dutch Global Health Strategy. Implementing this approach, the Netherlands and WHO:
- Expanded their cooperation to new areas of joint interest, e.g., climate change and health;
- Renewed their longstanding cooperation on Water, Sanitation and Hygiene and Mental Health and Psychosocial Support in health emergencies and humanitarian settings;
- Improved the flexibility and predictability of the Netherlands’ financial support through renewed General Arrangements with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (2022-2025) and the Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport (2024–2028) demonstrating the Netherlands’ commitment to WHO’s sustainable financing;
- Hosted together the 2nd World Local Production Forum in the Netherlands;
- Continued and deepened their technical cooperation through secondments, Junior Professional Officers and the Collaborative Centres.
The outcomes of the 2024 dialogue will inform future collaboration between the Netherlands and the WHO, so that efforts are aligned, and the optimal use of resources is helps achieve improved health outcomes worldwide. The enduring partnership between the Netherlands and the WHO stands as a cornerstone in the global health landscape, reflecting a shared commitment to advancing health and well-being globally.
-----------------
The Netherlands is a key supporter and strategic partner of the WHO.
In 2022- 2023, the Netherlands was one of the top five flexible WHO contributors with nearly US$ 19 million in core voluntary contributions. Overall, the Netherlands contributed more than US$ 106 million to the WHO in 2022 - 2023, of which US$ 93 million, nearly 90%, was voluntary funding.
The Netherlands also supports the WHO's technical expertise through secondments of staff and helps boost young people's careers in public health via the WHO's Junior Professional Officer Programme.
This demonstrates the Netherlands' commitment through its Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport to the WHO’s central role in the global health architecture.
Through this support, the Netherlands contributes to crucial activities in the areas of sexual and reproductive health, water and sanitation, mental health in emergencies, emergency preparedness, tuberculosis, One Health, primary health care, antimicrobial resistance, while facilitating cooperation with top Dutch institutions.

Anthropologists and community leaders from Nagaland, a remote state in north-eastern India bordering Myanmar, have expressed joy and relief that human remains belonging to their ancestors that had been on display in a British museum for nearly a century are finally being returned.
On Monday, the Pitt Rivers Museum in Oxford announced that 39 pieces of human remains – including parts of skulls, a finger and a piece of skin with hair – belonging to the Naga tribes, will be returned to Nagaland after six years of negotiation between the community and the museum.
For the Nagas, the repatriation is not just about “bones and ancestral remains … It is about memory returning to where it belongs,” the community said in a statement.
“We are at peace,” said A Peihwang Wangsa, an Indigenous Konyak man involved in the repatriation negotiations. “Our forefathers are coming back.”
Wangsa, whose ancestors’ remains are among those being returned, added that the homecoming would be a moment of “mourning and celebration”.
NT Thamlong Phom, a Naga community leader from the Phom sub-tribe, said: “I feel joy, I feel blessed.
“Ever since the announcement was made, my entire community has felt happy,” he said. “Our ancestors’ spirit will have a final resting place.”
Thejao Vihienuo, who is also part of the repatriation discussions and went to Oxford in 2025, said he had been “angry and unhappy” to see the remains of his ancestors, which he said had been “taken in a most dubious manner”.
“It was displayed as if it was a trophy, but they silently spoke of the atrocities the British committed on our people,” he said.
The return caused “mixed feelings”, he said, but added: “We owe it to our ancestors to bring their remains back and put them to peaceful rest. And also to our younger generation to decolonise their minds and show that our children are not inferior to any white man.”
The Nagas are a transnational Indigenous group of tribes living in India’s north-east and parts of Myanmar, once associated with headhunting but now predominantly Christian.
The Pitt Rivers Museum, home to one of the world’s largest ethnological collections, has more than 6,500 Naga objects, 898 of which were on display. Most of the collection was “coercively” acquired by the colonial administrators James Philip Mills and John Henry Hutton.
The human remains were displayed at the museum for 80 years. In 2020, they were put into storage during a revamp aimed at addressing the institution’s colonial past and how exhibiting human remains “reinforced racist and stereotypical thinking” of other cultures.
The museum said in a statement: “Thirty-nine Naga ancestors will soon begin their journey home from Oxford to Nagaland.”
In November, a Naga delegation will visit Oxford for a handover ceremony and the remains are expected to arrive in Nagaland before the end of the year. They will be laid to rest in a traditional community ceremony in the state capital, Kohima.
The repatriation negotiations were led by representatives from all of the Naga tribes.
“It has been a journey of redemption,” said Prof Dolly Kikon, a Naga anthropologist. “This shows that we are no longer victims of colonial violence. We embrace our roles as people who find redemption and healing by giving dignity and honour to a very violent past.”
The negotiations started in 2020, when Kikon wrote to the museum after reading “an article in the Guardian that they were doing an ethical review” of the collection. “They replied within 24 hours,” said Kikon.
That was just the beginning of a lengthy process that soon expanded into a wider community-led campaign.
The Forum for Naga Reconciliation, a community peace group, assembled a team known as Recover, Restore and Decolonise, bringing together Naga volunteers from across the region to work on the repatriation effort.
“They travelled to villages and organised meetings to inform people about the remains,” said Arkotong Longkumer, a Naga anthropologist who worked closely with Kikon to lead the initiative, which he described as “open and transparent”.
“It was an intergenerational journey that brought together students, civil society, tribal leaders and the church,” said Longkumer, who teaches at Edinburgh University.
A Naga delegation, including tribal leaders, visited Oxford in 2025 to officially register a claim to the remains.
“I had never known our ancestral human remains had been taken away like that,” said Wangsa. “I felt angry when I saw them.”
Laura Van Broekhoven, director of the Pitt Rivers Museum and a professor of museum studies and ethics at Oxford University, said the museum was completing paperwork to enable the return of the remains.
“We will then start working towards the ceremonial aspects so we can have everything ready,” she said. “In our experience, handover ceremonies can be very emotional.”

At least 16 killed after vehicle loaded with explosives rams into Pakistan mosque
- Published
At least 16 people, including five police officers, have been killed after a vehicle loaded with explosives rammed into a mosque in north-western Pakistan, according to a senior police official in Peshawar.
A gun battle is still ongoing between attackers and security forces at the mosque, near police headquarters, in the Kohat district of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
One of the assailants has reportedly been killed, an officer says, and a rescue operation is under way.
In a statement, Pakistan's President Asif Ali Zardari expressed "his best wishes for the swift recovery of those injured in the explosion."
Khyber Pakhtunkhwa police chief inspector general Zulfikar Hameed described the attack as a "suicide attack", according to Reuters news agency.
There has been no immediate claim of responsibility.
Prime Minister Muhammad Shehbaz Sharif also condemned the blast.
Militancy in Pakistan's border areas has risen sharply in recent months, targeting the military and police.
Islamabad says militants use safe haven in Afghanistan to train and plan attacks in Pakistan. Afghanistan's Taliban government denies the accusation and says militancy is Pakistan's domestic problem.

Do USB extenders really work and are they safe to use?
Getting a longer USB connection is easy. Getting the connection you actually expected takes a little more care.
USB extenders do work. The less convenient answer is that the term "USB extender" can mean anything from a passive cable to an active repeater or a CAT/fiber extender. They all extend the USB connection, but don't necessarily preserve the same speed, power or features. They're generally safe to use, as long as a unit is properly rated hardware within its stated limits.
This is important when you get past connecting a keyboard and mouse. A 4K webcam, external SSD or USB-C dock can require significantly more bandwidth; a dock can also transmit video and power. An extender can thus "work" while switching to a slower USB mode, disconnecting from time to time or losing a feature you thought you had.
Distance decides what kind of USB extender you need
A passive extension cable simply adds more length between the computer and device. This is okay for shorter runs, but as the cable length increases, maintaining signal integrity becomes difficult. USB 2.0 is fairly tolerant up to approximately 16 feet (5 meters) and passive USB 3.x runs are typically kept to around 10 feet (3 meters) before active hardware becomes the more intelligent choice.
Active extenders include electronics to regenerate the signal. For instance, StarTech offers a 33-foot active USB 3.2 Gen 1 cable with a 5 Gbps speed rating and says two of them can be daisy-chained for a ~66-foot run. Icron's Raven 3104 takes it a step further, delivering up to 5 Gbps speeds at a max distance of 328 feet, using a CAT 6a or CAT 7 cable.
The device at the other end is still important. Compared to a keyboard, devices like storage drives, VR headsets, webcams and docks are more likely to reveal connection issues, as they may need more bandwidth or multiple USB features simultaneously. Shopping is even more puzzling with USB-C, as the connector itself provides little indication of the speed or capabilities behind it.
Power is a separate problem from data
Power transmission is where only checking the connector on the box can become costly. Up to 240W is possible with USB Power Delivery, but the source, device and cable must all support that power level. The source advertises its capabilities and the connected device requests power before the higher-power contract is established. USB-IF requires USB-C-to-USB-C cables passing its compliance program to carry either a 60W or 240W power marking, and all except USB 2.0 cables must also show their supported data rate.
For a given cable, those numbers may not be close at all. Anker offers a 10-foot USB-C cable with 240W charging support, but its data transfer speed tops out at 480Mbps. Icron's 328-foot extender does the opposite: It supports up to 5Gbps, but offers just 6W per remote USB port. There's no guarantee of fast data with fast charging, and vice versa.
Passive USB-C male-to-female extensions need extra caution. C-to-C cables, Type-C-to-legacy cables and adapter assemblies are listed in USB-IF's passive Type-C compliance document, while generic male-to-female Type-C extension cables are not. But that doesn't mean USB extenders are illegal.
If you're looking for USB4, display output or high-power charging, getting the USB-C connectors to fit together is just the beginning of the compatibility test. If the actual issue is that your charger doesn't reach the wall outlet, a properly rated AC extension cord may be cleaner for a temporary setup than extending the USB connection itself.

Hong Kong lacks a climate narrative to unify its efforts
Hong Kong does not mention ‘climate change’ in its five-year plan, yet it already has many ingredients of climate leadership
Hong Kong deserves credit for its first five-year plan, accompanied by a detailed policy address. The plan establishes a useful framework beyond the annual policy cycle. Precisely because this is an important first effort, it is worth asking what could make the framework even stronger.
One striking omission is that the five-year plan never explicitly mentions climate change. This does not mean Hong Kong is failing to act.
Consider the binding indicators. They include the long-standing reduction in carbon emissions per unit of gross domestic product and increasing the proportion of zero-carbon energy in electricity generation. The plan also addresses cleaner power, electric vehicles, green maritime fuels, sustainable aviation fuel, energy efficiency, hydrogen, waste reduction and carbon trading.

Tom Brady, Kirk Cousins, Fernando Mendoza and the Las Vegas Raiders' surprise start to the NFL season
Sky Sports NFL presenter Neil Reynolds explores the early impact of Kirk Cousins in leading the Las Vegas Raiders to a surprise unbeaten start through the first two weeks of the season; Cousins starred in Sunday's win over the Los Angeles Chargers as he plays mentor to Fernando Mendoza
Tuesday 22 September 2026 14:50, UK
As I walked out of Allegiant Stadium in the middle of last November, following the Las Vegas Raiders' miserable home defeat to the Dallas Cowboys, I looked at all the downcast fans trudging away and I thought, why does Tom Brady want to be involved with this?
As many of you know, the seven-time Super Bowl-winning quarterback has a top front office job with the Raiders, as well as being a TV commentator, and it's his job to try to build the silver and black back into a contender. But they felt miles away from contention on that night in November.
They'd just lost 33-16 to the Cowboys, Geno Smith was ineffective a quarterback and arguing with fans in the stands, star defensive end Max Crosby was so frustrated at the final gun that he launched his helmet about 40 yards across the field.
That stadium in Las Vegas is nicknamed the Death Star, and as I walked away that night, I was reminded of the very first Star Wars film and thought, like the original Death Star, this thing needs to be blown up. Not the stadium, but the football program.
Head coach Pete Carroll was in the final throes of his potentially Hall of Fame career, and it's kind of fitting that he was in Las Vegas. It's the place where legendary names go to sell tickets, and I felt like that was what was happening there with the Raiders last year with Pete Carroll at the helm.
But this team is now laying down what seem to be proper foundations. They had the first overall pick in the NFL draft, and they used it well with the obvious selection of Fernando Mendoza out of Indiana.
And then you think, well, that means they're going to throw him into the fire straight away. That's been the way it's been done in the NFL in recent years. There aren't many teams that take a patient approach anymore.
Rookie quarterbacks are thrown to the wolves occasionally. Look at Cam Ward last year with the Tennessee Titans. Beaten from start to finish of the season, then spends the first part of the offseason rehabbing a shoulder injury that he suffered in Week 18.
The last really patient approach of quarterback that was notable was probably the Kansas City Chiefs resisting the temptation to put Patrick Mahomes in as a rookie, having him sit and learn for a year under an unselfish proven veteran in Alex Smith. And the Raiders have replicated that model, and so far it's worked.
They brought in Kirk Cousins, and the relationship between Cousins and Mendoza is not only endearing and quirky, it's also going to be very valuable. Cousins will have some limitations as a quarterback, but he is a safe pair of hands, and he knows how to get you in and out of the huddle. He knows how to win games.
Even this past week, as the Raiders moved to 2-0 on the season, you saw some of the veteran smarts that are going to help the Silver and Black this year.
On one of his touchdown passes against the Chargers, pre-snap, Cousins was constantly looking behind, signaling to the running back time and time again. Now yes, he could have been calling out protections, but it's also a good chance he was trying to pull the defense into thinking a running play was coming, and then he tosses the ball into the end zone for a touchdown.
So the Raiders are 2-0, one of the surprising teams to be with that record in the early stages of this season, and they can now really take their time in bringing Mendoza along. I spoke to Cousins in the summer, and he talked about why he was excited for this opportunity in Las Vegas, and I got the impression it was because this is his job for this year if things go well.
I could see a scenario where we have a wire-to-wire Cousins situation with the Raiders, and how he works with Klint Kubiak, the new head coach, he's got it all laid out before him. It's going to be fascinating to see.
The thing with Kirk as well is he's one of the most unselfish and nicest guys in the NFL. So even if it's to his long-term detriment, he is going to bring Mendoza along. He is not going to close himself off in the quarterback room. He's never going to keep secrets and tips and advice to himself.
He will be an extra coach in effect for their franchise quarterback in waiting. So it feels like there's a newer approach with the Raiders, a more patient approach.
I think Kubiak has time now to build the program the right way. He's got young players who he can work with for many years. Ashton Jeanty at running back, Brock Bowers at tight end. If they can keep Maxx Crosby healthy and productive on the other side of the ball, then there are pieces in place.
But the most important piece for the Raiders this season is a quarterback that very few teams around the NFL wanted anymore, and that's Kirk Cousins. He has a mighty role to play for the Silver and Black this season, but how he operates in the coming months could set the stage for this team to be competitive in many, many years to come.

About two years ago, education entrepreneur Boris But had what he calls a “penny-drop moment” – that, like countless others in China, his company needed to embrace AI before it was made obsolete by it.
His clients, well-off parents looking to send their children to study overseas, had begun arriving in his office reeling off information and opinions gleaned not from rival firms, but from chatbots.
In response, he started developing his own AI study tool, concluding: “If you can’t beat them, join them.”
The pace and quality of AI development in China is second only to the United States, with the two superpowers locked in an intensifying rivalry as the stakes rise with each new model’s capabilities.
Analysts generally agree that frontier, or cutting-edge, US models are still some way ahead of their Chinese counterparts.
But over the last few weeks the mood music from Silicon Valley has been decidedly sombre, as insider after insider has warned of the potential catastrophes that could result from “loss of control” of the most advanced AIs.
And last Saturday Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei pitched a “worldwide pacing of the frontier” – something he said would “require cooperation with China”.
“China is definitely not receptive” to a slowdown on US firms’ terms, though, said Lian Jye Su from technology research group Omdia.
For the government, AI is a “core sovereignty capability”, and Beijing will not want to jeopardise the progress made in closing the gap with US frontier models.
“It sees these calls [for a slowdown] as a bid to lock in US advantage,” said Su.
Amodei made this explicit, mentioning China specifically when arguing it was key “to keep democracies’ AI lead over autocracies as large as possible”.
He advocated for measures including continued export controls to China on advanced chips and machinery – the existence of which some argue already amounts to a forced unilateral “pacing”.
China’s foreign ministry responded to Amodei’s piece by saying “fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance”.
However, several analysts told the Guardian it would be a mistake to assume this suggested a rejection of the broader concerns raised by the essay.
This week China released the third iteration of its AI safety governance framework – a document that functions as a “mapping of the AI risk landscape and roughly what one should do about it”, said Gabriel Wagner, a researcher at Concordia, a Beijing-based AI safety consultancy.
Included in the updates are the risks posed by agents, the cybersecurity threats from frontier models and the issue of recursive self-improvement – an as-yet hypothetical scenario where AI becomes advanced enough to improve itself.
“In many ways, I think there is more common ground than people might assume between what Amodei is saying and what the Chinese government is saying,” said Wagner.
That contrasts with US president Donald Trump, who this week called fears AI could wipe out humanity a “hoax”.
Trump is set to meet counterpart Xi Jinping in Washington next week, with AI expected to make the agenda, though analysts are sceptical a major breakthrough will happen.
The ruling Communist party, finely attuned to risks to its political control, has been proactive in ensuring the new technology has developed within boundaries set by the state.
Centralised authority over critical infrastructure and commercial activity means China is generally better placed than the United States “to address any AI disaster”, said Omdia’s Su.
However, Chinese companies do less voluntary monitoring and evaluation work than US ones, said Leia Wang from the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace (CEIP).
Neither government seems prepared for a loss-of-control incident like those outlined over the last few weeks, she said.
China’s regulation, though, is “iterative … they are quick to adapt and release new measures”, she added.
China has had an algorithm registry since 2022, but warnings on agents released this year suggest a switch in focus “from controlling what AI says to controlling what it does”, per Concordia AI.
Beijing also issued national regulations this year aimed at curbing emotional dependency on companion AIs.
At the same time, AI is being actively encouraged across the economy to promote growth, enshrining this goal in its latest Five Year Plan.
Local governments are offering funding and low rents to companies to help achieve this – entrepreneur But was recently invited to pitch his company, Hampshire Education, to a small city three hours from Shanghai set on establishing a reputation as a tech hub.
Factories across the country’s huge manufacturing base are being encouraged to convert their processes into the AI era.
“Safety and controllability are certainly major concerns, and they are actively discussed,” said a spokesperson for Black Lake Technologies, an industrial agent platform that says it has worked with 40,000 factories globally.
“But in manufacturing, these concerns tend to be much more concrete and operational … what companies care most about is whether the AI is reliable.”
Daily life in China is already highly digitised, with traditionally less discourse around data privacy helping with widespread adoption.
For example, digital health service A-fu, which features AI chatbot versions of prominent doctors trained on real clinical studies, recently hit 150 million users.
“Most people treat AI as an already-useful everyday tool, not an abstract threat, so the practical attitude is to live with it,” said Ni Tao, founding editor of tech website yangtzeer.com.
“There is real anxiety about jobs and misinformation, but it coexists with a strong belief that China must master AI rather than slow down.”

David Jiang, cofounder and CEO of smart glasses company Viture, tells me about how he used to yell at his kid.
His 10-year-old son played tennis. During tournaments, Jiang says he had a habit of shouting and criticizing his son’s mistakes as he played. He wanted to apply pressure to make him succeed—it was the way he’d been taught to raise kids, after all. It made sense.
But then, unprompted, his smart glasses sent him a message. The AI assistant in his company’s newest wearable had picked up on what he was doing, recognized that his behavior wasn’t helpful, and messaged him about what he should do differently. Stop shouting. Stop criticizing. Just be there, be present, and show that you support your son. That worked, Jiang says, and being called out like that has supposedly made him a better father and improved the relationship with his kid, all thanks to his yet-to-be-released Vonder AI glasses.
“I didn't know this until Vonder could find my pattern,” Jiang says. “This is not only a tool that can summarize your life, but also a tool that can help yourself to be a better person.”
Viture, a San Francisco-based company known for its plug-in virtual display glasses, announced its first pair of spectacles with no virtual display on Tuesday. The glasses instead look remarkably like normal glasses, but aim to map out your memories, ideas, and goals and plop them on a digital vision board, all without embedded cameras.
Now co-headquartered in California and Beijing, Viture has made glasses like the Viture One and the Viture Beast—wearable face computers that connect via USB-C cable to a device to project its screen right before your eyes. The company's products have primarily targeted gamers or anyone interested in big-screen entertainment. They work well for that purpose, but their chunky design means they fall short in comfort and fashion.
The new glasses are a bit of a pivot. They're called Vonder, you know, like “wonder” but with a V, and they don't have cameras. The glasses' arms feature mics and speakers that can play music, dictate map directions, and let the wearer make phone calls. Vonder also features a built-in AI assistant that combines the top large language models. It can trigger OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Anthropic’s Claude, Google’s Gemini, or even DeepSeek. Based on the task’s complexity, Vonder AI will source the answer from whichever model is the quickest and most economical.
They cost $299, can be fitted with prescriptions, come in a variety of frame shapes and colors, and can have clear, transition, or shaded sunglass lenses. Preorders launch September 28, and they’ll ship in November.
The company, like other smart-glass brands Xreal and Even Realities, is trying to make it very clear that it is not Meta, distancing itself from the ire Meta’s Ray-Bans have generated for their privacy-encroaching features. Viture says above all else, it wants its smart glasses to be a good pair of glasses. Ones that operate privately—the kind of frames people will willingly wear without worrying about being labeled a creep.
A blue indicator light turns on when the glasses are recording audio. It’s a small dot on the arms of the glasses, less central and less immediately noticeable than the indicator light on the Ray-Ban Meta glasses.
But Viture stands apart because most of the time, the glasses can collect data only when the wearer is speaking. You can trigger a meeting mode, and it will use on-board microphones to record the environment around you, but the rest of the time, they use bone-conduction sensors in the frames that can passively pick up the audio vibrations of the person wearing them all day long. (The Vonder glasses get about 16 hours of battery life.)
Once it collects information about your day and what you talk about, the assistant generates a personal memory graph that tracks your memories—things like what coffee shops you’ve been to, what sports you play, or whatever else you choose to confide in the glasses. As long as you’re talking about something, the glasses will pick that up and try to interpret the context to make a broader picture of what you’re up to. In the app, it displays all those connections in a big web graphic.
In a demo of how the glasses work, Jiang showed that the Vonder glasses he's wearing have kept tabs on his life over the past three months. He can ask it where to find coffee shops based on his caffeine preferences or have it help figure out why he's felt so stressed lately. The tech is also preemptive, pulling up topics he's been thinking about, like help with hiring decisions he's been mulling over and a plan for announcing his new smart glasses a day before Meta Connect. It also pulled up a dossier on me that it presented to him the morning he came to visit. It clearly knew who I was, what I write about, and had suggested some topics for him to prepare for.
“We just want to mimic the way your brain works,” Jiang says. “This is not a transcript or a summary. This is just how your memory organizes in your brain, even better than your memory.”
The Vonder glasses raise a question of how self-indulgent the information you’re collecting across your day is. It only records one perspective, after all—yours. That means you have to be comfortable sharing your thoughts with the glasses if you want them stored in the memory graph or have conversations with others all day.
I ask Jiang about this: how you make sure the information in your mind web considers other factors than your own perspective. Jiang says if he wants something to stick, he tends to repeat what someone else said.
“In a conversation, a human tends to repeat because a conversation is turn by turn—if you have a question, I follow up your question and then AI knows what the question is,” Jiang says, “Even though there's a missing part, it's not 50 percent missing. It's maybe only 10 percent or 15 percent.”
I ask what he’d do if we were arguing right now. If I’d felt one way and he another, and then he went back to his mind web and tried to revisit the conversation. Would it bias him if his own voice was only the information it was given? This is what prompts him to talk about his kid playing tennis. That the glasses had outright told him he was wrong about something.
“The problem right now is that AI has really, really powerful somatic knowledge, but the missing part is the human episodic memory there,” Jiang says. “In the past three months I’ve used these glasses, I feel my life has been changed or improved.”

“Treatable conditions can masquerade as Alzheimer’s disease, including autoimmune disorders and thyroid inflammation,” said Ennapadam S. Krishnamoorthy, founder and behavioural neurologist and neuropsychiatrist, Buddhi Clinic, stressing the importance of a specific diagnosis in people presenting with cognitive symptoms.
He was speaking at The Hindu Wellness Series webinar on Alzheimer’s dementia and the promise of brain stimulation, held on Sunday by The Hindu in association with Buddhi Clinic, marking World Alzheimer’s Day.
Dr. Krishnamoorthy said a detailed, case-based assessment was important to distinguish Alzheimer’s disease from other conditions that can cause cognitive symptoms and may be treatable. He also stressed the need to tailor care to the individual, noting that some medications may offer limited benefits or cause harm in certain patients. He said non-pharmacological interventions also had an important role in dementia care.
Vivek Misra, senior consultant – Neuromodulation and Clinical Neurosciences, Buddhi Clinic, discussed the potential of non-invasive brain stimulation as part of dementia care. The technique uses external stimulation to modulate activity in specific areas of the brain. “It does not require sedation or seizure induction and can be done in an outpatient setting,” Mr. Misra said.
He said brain stimulation should not be viewed as a standalone treatment, but as one component of a broader, precision-based approach to dementia care, with interventions tailored to the individual’s clinical profile and needs.
The session was moderated by Athira Elssa Johnson, Senior Reporter, The Hindu.

A Show That Lovingly Pokes Fun at Gen Z
Culture and entertainment recommendations including Adults, Emmylou Harris, and more
This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.
Welcome back to The Daily’s Sunday culture edition, in which one Atlantic writer or editor reveals what’s keeping them entertained. Today’s special guest is Emma Williams, an associate editor who helps oversee the magazine’s social media and has also written about her home state of Texas.
Emma is a habitual rewatcher of Normal People, a show that she says has resonated with her differently over time. She also enjoys listening to her namesake Emmylou Harris, laughing over Adults episodes, and watching Hailee Catalano’s comforting cooking videos.
— Stephanie Bai, senior associate editor
The television show I’m most enjoying right now: The first scene of FX’s Adults tells you pretty much everything you need to know about the show: It’s crass, crude, absurd, and indulgently hilarious. Adults pokes fun at Gen Z without being judgmental or predictable, and it features some familiarly ridiculous plights. Maybe don’t watch it with your grandmother—but your spunky aunt is probably okay.
A quiet song that I love: I discovered the British DJ Fred Again when I was going down an NPR Tiny Desk Concert rabbit hole years ago. I was immediately struck by his talent—but over time, I have come to better appreciate the emotion he evokes through his performances. Even in his natural habitat, behind the DJ booth, Fred isn’t what you might normally expect from an EDM artist: He samples spoken-word poems, Zoom calls, and random internet videos to create songs that you can just as easily dance to as you can cry to.
I know I’m cheating a bit by saying that his entire Tiny Desk production is my favorite quiet song, but the fact that he was able to pull off an acoustic EDM performance is remarkable. To re-create the sound of electronic beats, he used the marimba, the vibraphone, and the piano; he also pounded and tapped on a desk and layered in his soft, husky voice. It is gentle, engrossing, and stupidly impressive.
 
 A loud song that I love: The first time I heard “Dance Yrself Clean,” by LCD Soundsystem, I was confused. My best friend played it for me, and by minute two, I was enjoying the song, but I could not comprehend how this hazy and somewhat repetitive tune could continue for another seven minutes and be as “life changing” as she had promised.
 
 Then I hit 3:05 on the track. I felt the ba-da-da-dum in my bones before James Murphy’s newly impassioned voice flooded through the speakers. This is now my song for any moment when I need to drown out my thoughts. Whether I’m going through a breakup, a bad day, or an existential crisis, I’ll put on “Dance Yrself Clean” and itch through the first three minutes, eagerly anticipating the rush of euphoria that hits after the beat drops.
 
 Years later, that same friend and I heard the song live. I have no idea whether we were crying or laughing or shouting, but I know we were dancing with abandon—and letting the music wash over us.
A cultural product I loved as a teenager and still love: I watched Normal People for the first time when I was 19, and I’ve rewatched it at least once a year every year since. I have never wavered in my fondness for it, but my reaction to the characters and storylines has evolved with time.
 
 When I first saw the show, based on Sally Rooney’s novel of the same name, I fell madly in love with Connell, barely registering that his cold avoidance of Marianne in public was wrong. I just thought he was broody and complicated; therefore, to my teenage mind, he was perfect and dreamy. I’m glad to say that I have moved past that (kind of), and I now find it difficult to watch his treatment of Marianne in the first few episodes.
 
 In my 20s, I resonate more with Marianne’s college arc. Specifically, her need to become the coolest, most stylish, most successful version of herself—even if it comes at the cost of her own happiness.
 
 Marianne and Connell’s lack of clear communication is always maddening. But I understand it more with age. Sometimes vocalizing what you really want can be more terrifying than staying quiet.
A musical artist who means a lot to me: I have to pay homage to my namesake, the inimitable country folk artist Emmylou Harris. Her music reminds me of my home state of Texas. Listening to her song “Boulder to Birmingham” transports me back to long drives through the plains of West Texas and the seemingly endless miles of wind turbines. I hear my parents’ voices, lovingly calling me Emmylou and Emmy-lou-lou. Whenever I feel adrift, her music pulls me back to the ground.
A YouTuber, TikToker, Twitch streamer, or other online creator I’m a fan of: I have an embarrassing confession: There is a cooking influencer whom I’m really obsessed with—as in, I went to a meet and greet of hers, and I send her the occasional tipsy Instagram DM. (Sometimes she even responds!)
 
 Hailee Catalano is a James Beard–winning chef. Her food is fresh and unique, and her video style isn’t gimmicky or aggressive like that of so many other cooking accounts—it’s simple and personable. My favorite series of hers is called Friday Night Dinner, which is a collaboration with her partner, Chuck Cruz, who is also a chef and content creator. They film themselves making a new meal every week, and I can only describe their vibe as homey. The videos sometimes have awkward pauses and funny asides (and, of course, clips of their dog, Gus), and watching them makes me feel like I’m sitting at the kitchen counter as two of my friends prepare something delicious for us to eat.
A poem, or line of poetry, that I return to: The older I get, the more I find myself recalling the lines of Langston Hughes’s poem “Harlem.” Hughes asks: “What happens to a dream deferred?” I recently turned 25, and the “quarter-life crisis” is certainly hitting me. I think about all of my childhood hopes that have dissipated, and all of the ones I still have that I’m not sure will come true. I, too, wonder what happens to these dreams.

Math Can’t Go On Like This
By Kai Williams
In late July, one of the world’s most famous mathematicians issued a warning to his field. Math is entering a “turbulent period,” the UCLA professor Terence Tao said in front of a packed lecture hall at the International Congress of Mathematicians. AI is getting so good at math, he said, that it’s causing a “crisis in our mathematical values and practices.”
Earlier in the same week that Tao gave his talk at math’s most prestigious conference, a researcher at Anthropic had used Claude to disprove an 87-year-old math conjecture. Still, when I asked mathematicians at the conference about their experiences with AI, most hadn’t thought deeply about the topic. Many seemed a little surprised that a journalist was asking them about it at all.

US President Donald Trump is moving from his earlier ambition of acquiring Greenland to a security arrangement that would significantly expand the US military footprint on the Arctic island.
Trump is due to meet Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenland Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen at the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Tuesday (September 22) to sign the trilateral agreement.
Reuters reports that the pact is expected to allow the US to establish military facilities at Narsarsuaq in southern Greenland and Mestersvig on the east coast, in addition to the existing Pituffik Space Base.
Quick answers to key questions
The new agreement allows the US to establish military facilities at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig in Greenland, significantly expanding its military footprint on the island.
Greenland is strategically important due to its position between North America and Europe, which aids in monitoring military activities and securing resources as Arctic ice melts.
The deal represents the biggest expansion of US military infrastructure in Greenland since the Cold War, adding two new military sites to the existing Pituffik Space Base.
Denmark asserts that the agreement respects its sovereignty and Greenland's right to self-determination, placing Arctic security under NATO's collective responsibility instead of solely with the US.
Trump claims the agreement grants the US permanent control over Greenland’s security, preventing adversaries from establishing military bases without US approval, although its legal implications remain unclear.
The agreement marks a major shift from Trump's earlier demand for US control of Greenland. But it also leaves important questions unanswered: the full text has not been made public, and it remains unclear whether the arrangement changes the existing 1951 US-Denmark defence framework or creates a new legal structure.
Trump's interest in Greenland dates back to his first presidency, when he publicly floated the idea of the US purchasing the territory in 2019.
The issue returned with far greater force after Trump was elected again. In December 2024, he described ownership and control of Greenland as an “absolute necessity”. In January 2025, he refused to rule out military force to obtain the territory, triggering a diplomatic crisis with Denmark and concern among NATO allies.
Greenland's leaders repeatedly rejected the idea of the island becoming part of the United States. Denmark also insisted that Greenland was not for sale.
Negotiations eventually shifted from the question of who owns Greenland to who is responsible for its security.
The result is the agreement now due to be signed.
The most immediate change is expected to be a substantial expansion of America's military presence.
The US already operates Pituffik Space Base in northwestern Greenland, a strategically important installation that supports missile-warning, space-surveillance and other defence activities.
Under the new arrangement, Washington is expected to gain access to two additional sites:
Narsarsuaq: A former US Cold War airbase in southern Greenland. The US closed the Bluie West One base there in the 1950s, and the local population has since dwindled to only a few dozen.
Mestersvig: An outpost on Greenland's east coast currently used by Denmark's Sirius Dog Sled Patrol, an elite special-forces unit responsible for patrolling the remote Arctic territory.
The expansion would represent the biggest increase in US military infrastructure in Greenland since the Cold War. During that period, Washington maintained 17 installations and more than 10,000 personnel on the island. Today, Pituffik is the principal US military installation, with roughly 150 American personnel.
One of the biggest uncertainties surrounding the deal is what Trump means by “permanent control”.
Trump has said the agreement gives the United States “permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland.” He has also said US adversaries would not be allowed to establish bases, maintain military forces or make sensitive investments on the island without Washington's approval.
Copenhagen says the agreement respects Danish sovereignty and Greenland's right to self-determination. Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen has said Arctic security will be placed under NATO's collective responsibility rather than left solely to the US and Denmark.
Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen has similarly said the arrangement recognises Greenland's interests and its right to self-determination.
The actual legal meaning of the US security commitment therefore remains one of the most important unanswered questions.
The world's largest island sits between North America and Europe, at the intersection of the Arctic and North Atlantic. Its location gives it strategic importance for monitoring activity across the Arctic and North Atlantic.
The island also has substantial mineral and energy resources, making it increasingly important as Arctic ice retreats and competition for resources and shipping routes intensifies.
For Washington, Greenland's geography also makes it relevant to monitoring potential military activity by Russia and tracking developments in the increasingly contested Arctic.
Trump has repeatedly cited concerns about Russia and China gaining a foothold in Greenland.
The US administration says the agreement will prevent Washington's geopolitical rivals from establishing military bases or deploying troops on the island. It also seeks mechanisms to restrict sensitive investments.
China's growing interest in Arctic resources has particularly concerned US officials.

Man accused of 16 killings caught dressed as a woman after forest manhunt
A man accused of killing 16 people in a remote part of Brazil avoided capture by hiding in the woods, police say
A suspect accused of slaughtering 16 people in a remote region of northeastern Brazil evaded capture by hiding out in makeshift forest camps, police revealed Monday.
Lead investigator Douglas Garcia, who spearheaded the two-day manhunt that ended with the Sept. 13 arrest of 33-year-old Jorlan Lopes da Silva, told The Associated Press that the suspect used his knowledge of the dense bush to elude authorities. The killings tied to da Silva all took place over a three-month span in the isolated territory of Mulungu, located in Paraiba state roughly 1,553 miles north of Rio de Janeiro.
Locals dubbed da Silva "Mosquito" due to his frail frame—a physical trait Garcia said unexpectedly worked to the suspect's advantage.
"That allowed him to evade capture for years," Garcia said. "Jorlan lived mostly in the woods; that’s why it was so hard to find him and link him to crimes that didn’t seem to be connected at first."
Detectives finally connected da Silva to the string of murders after he allegedly gunned down an 18-year-old victim in a public square. While da Silva claimed to investigators that he exclusively targeted criminals, police said evidence collected so far disproves his assertion.
During questioning, da Silva reportedly confessed to additional offenses beyond the current charges. Garcia noted that several closed cold cases are being reopened, though specific victim details remain confidential to protect ongoing prosecutions.
Da Silva's eventual arrest yielded surreal circumstances: police intercepted him wearing a black-and-white striped dress, a wig, and painted fingernails while carrying an unrelated infant.
"This is a very different person; he said he killed for the first time at age 13," Garcia said. "We caught him because he wasn’t able to reach his tent in the woods, so he, out of desperation, got that disguise, took that baby that is not his and was ultimately arrested."
Authorities previously alleged da Silva belongs to an organized criminal syndicate responsible for dozens of regional homicides. However, da Silva denied any gang ties upon his arrest, telling officers he was simply engaged in a "personal war."
