Wanna buy an entire town? It can be yours for just $5 million
The historic 15-person settlement features a two-story resort, saloon, schoolhouse and rental cabins — all going on the market for the first time in more than 30 years
An unincorporated mountain outpost deep in northern California's Feather River Canyon has been put on the market for $4.75 million as its long-time owner prepares to leave after more than five decades.
Belden, an 87-year-old historic gold rush settlement in Plumas County, is currently owned by Ivan Coffman. The former mason from Fresno, Coffman bought the property in 1989 after decades spent mining the local waters.
He is now selling the entire compound, which includes a two-story resort and lodge, restaurant, bar, general store, mechanics garage, schoolhouse and colorful rental cabins.
The decision to sell comes after a series of personal shifts and tragedies for Coffman, as reported by SFGate. The Dixie Fire in 2021 burned surrounding hillsides and destroyed the nearby town of Greenville, but Belden survived because Coffman’s son and several employees stayed behind to combat the flames.
Coffman’s son died earlier this year due to health complications, prompting Coffman to finally put the property up for sale.
“Oh, I guess all the people you meet over the years,” Coffman told SFGate when asked what he loved most about the place. “And you know, as time goes on, you look back on a lot of things.”
Coffman originally stumbled upon Belden during a week off from his masonry work in 1970. Following a major flood that shifted the riverbed, he discovered rich deposits of gold nuggets at the junction where Yellow Creek enters the Feather River.
“That year, we had a terrific flood that washed a huge bar of gravel off down into this hole, and that’s what left all that gold layin’ there,” Coffman said. “It’d been hidden for all them years.”
During that single trip, Coffman recovered roughly 50 ounces of gold — worth about $35 an ounce at the time, compared to modern values of around $4,400 an ounce. He called his business partner to say he was extending his trip and never returned to his masonry career, expanding instead into jewelry making, private lending and eventually real estate.
Belden’s history dates back to the California Gold Rush, when it operated as a bustling camp of roughly 1,000 residents. As gold mining waned, the area transitioned into a logging and railroad outpost before turning to tourism and river fishing.
Mid-20th-century dam construction along the Feather River altered the local ecology and reduced fish populations, driving the area into economic decline.
By the time Coffman purchased Belden in 1989, a 1970s fire had left most of its original structures in ruins. Coffman rebuilt the property, transforming it into an off-grid haven for travelers, Pacific Crest Trail hikers and motorcyclists.
Author Cheryl Strayed highlighted her arrival at the compound in her 2013 memoir “Wild,” describing her relief at reaching the remote resort during her trek. In recent years, the secluded location has also gained popularity as an all-night music festival venue, according to SFGate.
Despite its tiny permanent population of 15, the property operates as a self-contained community off Highway 70. The main lodge houses an array of vintage items, including historical taxidermy, art and an antique slot machine.
Josie Litchfield, a friend helping Coffman market the listing, noted his enduring role as the host of the property.
“Who wants to be the next mayor of Belden Town?” Litchfield wrote in an email regarding the listing.
Coffman remains known for his casual hospitality toward passersby, frequently opening the closed lodge to assist travelers. During a recent visit, he offered a free bottle of water to a cancer survivor who required bottled water due to treatment.
“Well, even though we’re not open now, I can grab you a bottle of water if you need something right now,” Coffman told the visitor, refusing payment. “I’ll just give it to you, how’s that?”

A video showing a large crowd gathered on a road and a flyover is being widely shared on social media, claiming that it shows the crowd at Congress leader Rahul Gandhi’s ‘Chhatron Ki Goonj’ event in Indore on 19 September 2026 (here, here, here). Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Video shows people gathered for Rahul Gandhi’s ‘Chhatron Ki Goonj’ event held on 19 September 2026 in Indore, Madhya Pradesh.
Fact: The viral video is old and unrelated to Rahul Gandhi’s event. It shows a rally organised in Indore on 9 August 2026 to mark World Tribal Day. Hence, the claim made in the post is MISLEADING.
A reverse image search using keyframes from the viral video led us to a Facebook post by Vinoddj Vlog posted on 10 August 2026. The account confirmed in the comments that the video was recorded during the Adivasi Diwas (World Tribal Day) celebrations in Indore. Further, we found a YouTube video uploaded on 9 August 2026 by @DineshSolanki_indori, which features the same truck and location seen in the viral video. This video also identified the visuals as being from the World Tribal Day celebrations in Indore. This confirms that the video predates Rahul Gandhi’s ‘Chhatron Ki Goonj’ event, which was held in Indore on 19 September 2026.
Further, we also found similar visuals shared by Lokesh Mujalda, president of Jai Adivasi Yuva Shakti (JAYS), on Instagram on 9 August 2026. The post stated that a large number of people had gathered in Indore for World Tribal Day celebrations.
We identified the location seen in the viral video as Bhanwarkuan Square in Indore, which was one of the locations along the route of the World Tribal Day procession. A comparison between both can be seen below.
Media also reported that thousands of people participated in the World tribal day procession that took place in Indore (here, here). Actual visuals showing the ‘Chhatron Ki Goonj’ event can be seen here and here.
To sum up, an old video of the World Tribal Day rally is being shared as visuals of crowd at Rahul
Gandhi’s Indore event.

We are in the midst of a loneliness epidemic: More than half of Americans say they feel isolated, and we’re getting together less and less. In 2023, only about 4 percent of adults said they went to a party on a weekend or holiday.
Why we should all be partying more
The historical case for partying it up, explained.
According to Imogen Willetts, a party historian and author of the book Up All Night: A History of Going Out, this moment is an outlier.
“For most of human history, the experiences that we associate with nightlife — drinking, dancing, music, hedonism — those experiences were simply part of religion because religion was so all-encompassing,” she told Vox.
If parties are so ingrained in humankind, then, what are we missing when we don’t get out the door on a Friday night anymore? And what lessons can we learn from the turnups of yore? We get into all of that and more — including how to throw a great party and how to be a good guest — on the latest episode Explain It to Me, Vox’s weekly call-in podcast.
Below is an excerpt of my conversation with Willetts, edited for length and clarity. You can listen to the full episode on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or wherever you get your podcasts. If you’d like to submit a question, send an email to askvox@vox.com or call 1-800-618-8545.
Can you talk about the role religion played in early nightlife? Because I think we often think of religion and partying as two separate things, but that was not the case for all of history, was it?
[Religion] contained people’s hedonistic instinct. There was nothing really outside of it. And so there’s even evidence, which I love thinking about this, that the churchgoing experience in medieval England was actually quite rowdy and quite raucous.
On feast days there would be drinking, there would be dancing. And there’s one theory that wooden pews were introduced in Wells Cathedral in England to subdue the dancing because it was so raucous. And so in some sense, it takes us a while to get to nightlife because we sort of didn’t need it for a very long time. Religion contained hedonism quite comfortably within it.
Seventeenth-century Japan, I would say, is the beginning of modern nightlife because we have these commercial party scenes, nightlife environments, which have nothing to do with religion,
“Whether it’s at a sports match or a concert stadium, and even within religion — that is collective effervescence.”
Crucially, they’re also separate from court. Another part of party scenes is court spectacle — think Louis XIV and Versailles and all of that stuff that was contained within these monarchical structures. So the first real nightlife destination is Yoshiwara, which was built on the outskirts of Edo, which is now Tokyo.
The idea of church being a place to party is so interesting. I do get the same feeling I get at church when I’m on the dance floor and I hear Kaytranada. I can imagine how these religious experiences allowed people to access that feeling of release through music and through dance.
An expression that I came across when researching the book that I think really wonderfully kind of captures the essence of nightlife and partying is this term coined by the sociologist Émile Durkheim in 1912, which is “collective effervescence.” That’s the feeling that we experience during peak communal experiences.
Whether it’s at a sports match or a concert stadium, and even within religion — that is collective effervescence. That is the same sensation, that surge of euphoria that people feel on dance floors. I think parties and nightlife are such an important way to access this very important human feeling, particularly in societies that are increasingly atheist or increasingly secular.
We need nightlife to have these communal euphoric experiences and feel part of something bigger than ourselves.
You’ve written about how, yes, parties are fun, but they’re also at the epicenter of some pretty important cultural and societal shifts.
I think nightlife is very uniquely poised to allow for experimentation and innovation and transgression. Also, in a very practical way, if you’re part of the abstract expressionist scene of mid-century New York or something, you need somewhere to meet and talk to people and figure out how you’re going to sell your work that’s like nothing people have ever seen before.
These social spaces play a really, really important role in culture. The abstract expressionist artists were hanging out in the Cedar Tavern, and then you have things like the Viennese Secession Movement and Cabaret Fledermaus was part of that meeting space.
Similarly, you get things like dance and music that’s very much created for dance floors, for clubbing, for nightlife: the can-can and then disco and then techno. Nightlife has been so crucial to the propulsion of culture.
A lot of this is happening in the club, but what about parties happening in private homes?
One of the great examples of people opening up their homes in a sense of turning the home into a club was turn-of-the-century New Orleans. On Saturday nights, people would host fish fries: Basically, when you would open up your home to the public, you would charge entry at the door. Once inside, people were treated to this amazing spread of food, drink, and there would be bands that would perform. It was often a way for households who were struggling with rent payments to earn some extra cash.
It happened again in Harlem in the 1920s. Langston Hughes writes about the Saturday night rent parties, where people’s apartments would be opened up in the exact same way. He said they were more interesting than anything that was going on in the cabarets and the clubs. He was going to those as often as he could and collecting the invitations for them.
People would write their address on business cards, leave them in different shops and pubs and hairdressers or whatever, and then you would pick them up and then go to the party. Langston Hughes collected them, and they now are randomly in a Yale archive of all places.
As you think of parties over the centuries, are there elements that all the best parties have in common?
At their very core essence, you need good music, you need good lighting, and I think also you need to create this atmosphere where the sense that anything can happen. What you want is for the people that are at your party to feel like they can behave differently or do something a little bit wild.
I think that there’s something very satisfying in experiencing a domestic world upturned. I think seeing the kitchen become a gloomy cocktail bar, the living room becoming a dance floor — there’s something very satisfying in experiencing that.
It goes back to what the heart of nightlife culture or party culture is all about. We want to shed our daily lives. You want that sense of slight disorder that makes people feel alive.

Rogue Liberal senator Alex Antic says he will give “back some voice” to party members now that he has been elected as state president in South Australia.
Many of those members are part of “Alex’s Army”, the evangelical and Pentecostal Christians the federal MP recruited into the operational wing of the party.
That has given the rightwinger a huge amount of influence in a state that for years was the scene of turf wars between the conservatives and the moderates.
Over the weekend, Antic beat upper house leader Nicola Centofanti 119 to 73 votes to take the presidency.
The prospect of Antic as president led some to speculate that the federal party might forcibly take over the state branch because of concerns over the senator’s close relationship with One Nation and whether Antic was likely to improve the beleaguered party’s vote.
Pollster Tony Barry, the RedBridge director of corporate affairs and communications, has branded Antic a “vote-losing machine” for the party.
Since his ascendancy, the Liberal party has been smashed at a federal and a state election.
After SA’s March election, the Liberal party was left with just five lower house seats. Moderates are concerned that opposition leader Ashton Hurn’s attempts to turn around the party’s fortunes will be made more difficult if she is constantly asked about Antic’s musings on topics including vaccinations, trans issues and climate change.
On Monday, Antic posted to X that his win was a “great result”.
“It’s proof positive that getting involved in politics can achieve outcomes, grassroots political action as it’s known, people joining up, turning up to vote,” he said.
“And … we’re going to give the members of this party back some voice into the machine”.
It’s not clear how he would deliver on that promise.
The organisational wing of the party “cannot dictate policy”, the party says, “but consults with and advises the parliamentary wing, particularly on the development of longer-term policies”.
However, Antic could use his power to force constitutional change, to pre-select candidates that are ideologically aligned, or to pressure sitting MPs to adopt more rightwing policies.
Trish Worth, a state council delegate and Howard government parliamentary secretary, told the ABC the party “should always be selecting the people with the most experience and loyalty”, and criticised his recent moves to change the No Jab, No Play legislation.
He was the only Coalition senator to vote for that change, but was joined by the four One Nation senators and United Australia Party senator Ralph Babet.
On Monday, state health minister Blair Boyer called on Antic to declare whether he would seek to form a coalition with One Nation.
“The transformation is complete,” Boyer said.
“The South Australian Liberals are now the Temu version of One Nation – just as extreme, just as dangerous, just less genuine.”
One Nation’s SA leader, Cory Bernardi – who was snapped enjoying a beer with Antic earlier this year – welcomed Antic’s win, and said he looked forward to their ongoing “constructive relationship”.
Liberal senator Anne Ruston wished Antic the best, now he had two “enormous” jobs as president and senator.
Antic’s close conservative colleague Tony Pasin told the ABC on Monday the Liberal party and One Nation should “work together to defeat the Australian Labor party”.
Pasin said the advantage of the presidency was “there might be an opportunity for people to look a little closer at what Alex says from time to time”, for example on vaccination.
In June, Antic claimed in the senate that pharmaceutical companies were using the bird flu to push people to get the flu jab.
“These birds are almost like the bell ringing on the pharmaceutical company’s guilt trip, saying: ‘We’re entering the winter season. We’re about to lean on you to get your flu shot, and now we’ve found two birds with the sniffles’”, he said.
Pasin said he agreed with Antic, but that he was merely saying that the flu jab did not protect against bird flu.
Asked whether people in the Liberal party might be “concerned about repercussions” from Antic’s election, Pasin said the party “should be focused on winning elections”.
Antic did not respond to questions by deadline, and said on X that he had “no intention” of dealing much with the media.

MP Police issue sweeping guidelines restricting online activities of personnel
Police chief Kailash Makwana issued the guidelines to maintain discipline and protect the force’s public image
The Madhya Pradesh Police on Tuesday issued sweeping guidelines restricting social media use and monetisation by their personnel.
An officer, who did not wish to be named, said police chief Kailash Makwana issued the guidelines to maintain discipline and protect the force’s public image after complaints about comments linked to caste and religion, which raised trust issues.
The guidelines, issued days after chief minister Mohan Yadav met top police officers, prohibit uploading reels, photos, or videos in uniform or indecent attire during or after duty. They require the removal of any previously posted inappropriate content. “Family-related posts that compromise dignity or feature uniforms, police vehicles, or weapons are also banned. ...personnel is barred from posting or reacting to caste, religion, or gender-based discriminatory content, as well as obscene, malicious, erroneous, or unverified information in online groups,” say the guidelines.
Police personnel cannot follow or befriend people with criminal records or suspicious reputations, nor can they share photos or videos with them. They are prohibited from using political symbols, organisational logos, or protest imagery, and from participating in online polls.
The personnel have been instructed against commenting on matters related to national security, governance, or policy. Self-promotion of successes and achievements, paid promotions, or advertising are banned. “If any income is generated through social media, details must be reported within 30 days,” say the guidelines.
The use of social media has been banned during duty hours, including posting or live-streaming of VIP security, weapon training, raids, or drills. The guidelines say that police personnel are prohibited from using AI tools for official purposes, uploading government or sensitive documents to platforms such as ChatGPT or Gemini, or creating personal accounts using Closed User Group SIMs, government Wi-Fi, or official email IDs.
“During sensitive duty, personnel must keep geo-tagging and location services active on their mobile phones. They are barred from posting unsealed photos/videos of seized goods or weapons during investigations.”
The guidelines say that police personnel cannot reveal any techniques and tactics. “These must remain confidential. Disclosure of police strategies, field craft, or investigative methods requires prior approval from competent authorities. “
The guidelines strictly prohibit sharing information related to ongoing investigations or court cases that may affect proceedings, as well as posting photos/videos of victims, witnesses, or accused persons during inquiries or public hearings.

On Friday, The Washington Post reported on a contentious White House meeting in which the director of the National Institutes of Health (NIH), Jay Bhattacharya, tried to fend off yet another effort to place funding decisions under political control. The move came from Russell Vought, head of the Office of Management and Budget (OMB), which has sought to limit and control research funds. The Post suggested that Bhattacharya ended up on the losing side of the fight.
This initial leak has been confirmed and expanded on by outlets such as The New York Times and Politico. It now appears that the administration is drafting an executive order that would give Vought veto power over every individual grant awarded by the NIH.
If at first you don’t succeed
The NIH is the largest funder of biomedical research on the planet, and its $47 billion budget is larger than that of the next 10 research funders combined. Its funding, distributed largely through grants to academic researchers at universities, supports everything from basic biological research to clinical trials and has helped the biotechnology industry flourish.
But Vought seems to feel that it has funded a lot of “woke” research. Immediately after Trump re-entered the Oval Office, the agency terminated a broad range of grants on topics like pandemic preparedness and health disparities and proposed a budget that would shrink the NIH by nearly half. That cut was rejected by Congress, and the policy behind the NIH grant terminations was also voided by a court. Vought responded to these setbacks by proposing new grant funding rules that would make political considerations key determinants in which grants get funded. Congress put that rule on hold, too.

Change in Canada's citizenship law hitting U.S. archives
Archivists in several archives reporting sharp increase in request for records, backlogs and processing times
Sitting in their archive in Lafayette, Louisiana, Barbara Dejean and Stephanie Simon first heard about a change in Canada's citizenship rules in December, when they read an online news story.
Then the calls started coming in.
Calls from Americans who wanted to document their Canadian ancestry to apply under the new rules for Canadian citizenship certificates.
"It started a bit earlier in January, but now we have over 450 requests waiting to be processed," said Simon, associate archivist at the Diocese of Lafayette, whose records include those of many Acadian families.
"The same day that we mail out 40, 40 more come in the mail, so it's not like we can make some headway on it. It's just kind of keeping up with them."
Dejean estimates their two-person archive has received 1,350 requests for records since Bill C-3 went into effect on Dec. 15, 2025. Turnaround time for those requests is currently 12 to 16 weeks.
It used to be two to three days.
"They're from all over, all over the United States where we've been getting requests for our records," said Dejean. "A lot of them are no longer here. The families have branched off and moved on."
Lafayette's archive is not alone.
Citizenship demand spreads to U.S. archives
While the increase in requests for genealogical records has not yet made it onto the radar of national associations of archivists in the U.S., many American archives — both large and small — are experiencing unintended consequences from Bill C-3.
Bill C-3 allows Canadian citizenship for those who can prove they're descended from a Canadian ancestor, even if that ancestor left the country several generations back. It was adopted after the courts ruled that limiting citizenship to the first generation born outside Canada was too restrictive.
It has become very popular — particularly with Americans.
According to the most recent figures available from Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, 6,635 people received Canadian citizenship certificates as a result of Bill C-3 between Dec. 15, 2025 and June 30, 2026. More than half of the newly recognized Canadian citizens under Bill C-3 – 3,510 people — were born in the United States.
Another 19,160 people have received certificates as a result of having a Canadian parent — 9,150 of them from the U.S. Prior to the bill's adoption, those who were born outside Canada had to have a Canadian parent to qualify for citizenship.
The certificates allow the 25,795 newly recognized Canadian citizens to apply for Canadian passports and live and work in Canada.
However, the backlog of applications for Canadian citizenship certificates has soared. It currently stands at 136,000 applications, with an estimated processing time of 33 months.
Last October, Immigration Minister Lena Metlege Diab told the House of Commons immigration committee that she didn't expect a flood of applications for citizenship certificates once Bill C-3 went into effect and she only expected "volumes in the tens of thousands over time."
Estimates of just how many people could qualify for Canadian citizenship as a result of Bill C-3 vary widely.
Some point to a period spanning more than 100 years, in the 1800s and 1900s and even earlier, when hundreds of thousands of Canadians — particularly from Quebec — crossed the border for jobs in the U.S.
Small archives struggle with the workload
One area that saw an early influx of French-Canadian immigrants was southern Illinois, where Mike Heithaus serves as a part-time archivist with the Diocese of Belleville.
He said the number of requests began to climb around May or June before subsiding a bit in September.
"From roughly June 1st to the beginning of September, I had 32 requests, which I know doesn't sound like a ton," Heithaus said. "But when it's just me and I'm here 10 to 15 hours a week, that is basically consuming all my time to do those."
Heithaus said the diocese debated whether to continue responding to the requests. Instead of refusing requests, it decided to increase Heithaus's hours from 10 to 15 a week and more than triple the fee for requests from $10 to $33 US.
Pressure reaches larger archives, too
The U.S. National Archives and Records Administration's (NARA) collection includes different kinds of documents that can help establish ancestry, such as naturalization records, census records, passenger records and Canadian border-crossing records.
While NARA's public affairs department declined an interview, sources who spoke on condition of anonymity because of concerns for their jobs said archivists are seeing an increase this year in requests from people seeking Canadian dual citizenship under Bill C-3. They are also seeing an increase in requests from Americans who could qualify for dual citizenship in other countries, such as Italy or Germany.
Archivists have a variety of tasks, and the increase in requests by prospective dual citizens has created a backlog and led to longer processing times.
"It's become untenable," one source said. "It's become an unstable situation. People are seeking these records out and it's become most of our job."
- Canadian citizenship certificate applications now facing nearly 3-year delays
- Demand for Canadian citizenship certificates soaring, fuelled by Americans
Anderson Smith, an archivist with the Acadian Archives at the University of Maine at Fort Kent, said the number of requests related to documents for Canadian citizenship jumped from one each in 2024 and 2025 to 72 in 2026. However, a change to IRCC regulations in June that spelled out the need to provide original or certified copies of documents led to a decline in requests.
"Early on, we were getting a lot more traffic from people because I think we were able to provide the records that they needed but then those regulations kind of changed in June and so we saw a decrease in the amount of people who were coming in with requests for these records."
Smith said staff at the archives are now helping requesters find the original sources or locate the original institutions that can provide certified copies of the records they need.
American archives aren't the only ones feeling the impact of Bill C-3.
Normand Deragon is president of the American French Genealogical Society based in Woonsocket, Rhode Island, which helps people research their French-Canadian roots. He says it has processed an estimated 200 requests since Bill C-3 came into effect and currently has a backlog of about 150 more.
"We're an all-volunteer organization, nobody gets paid," said Deragon. "Our libraries open only two days a week, so you can see how it would be easy for us to get backlogged…. But we do the best we can. We're cranking them out as quickly as we can."

Neutral venues and no 'away' fans - how Israel v Republic of Ireland became so contentious
- Published
An elite-level European football match will be played on Sunday at a neutral stadium, with no 'away' fans, and reduced television coverage.
That the match is even taking place had been in doubt - one side had to vote on a motion confirming whether or not they would participate amid significant opposition from fans, pundits and politicians.
But the vote confirmed the fixture would go ahead, and now the Republic of Ireland will travel to Debrecen, Hungary, for a Uefa Nations League 'away' match against Israel, played against a backdrop of ongoing and increasingly volatile disagreement between the two countries about Israel's military offensive in Gaza.
And on 4 October, the Republic will face the same opponents in a 'home' match in Backa Topola - a small town in Serbia.
No tickets have been sold to Irish fans for either fixture, and Irish public broadcaster RTE will air a stripped-back version of match coverage, with no commentators, pundits, or half-time analysis.
So how did a Uefa Nations League match become one of the most contentious fixtures in football?
Venue changes have not quietened protests
As soon as the Republic of Ireland were placed with Israel - plus Austria and Kosovo - at the Nations League draw in February, the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) faced calls from some to boycott the matches because of Israel's military action in Gaza.
The FAI eventually took a vote of its delegates in July, in which 75 members voted to play the matches and 32 voted to boycott.
Not playing the matches could have harmed Irish football in the long-run, the FAI said, amid the possibility of Uefa sanctions for refusing to fulfil the fixtures and the potential loss of millions of euros in income.
As well as curtailing its coverage, RTE will not take advertising or sponsorship income from the matches, saying it will only "meet its contractual obligations" to broadcast the fixtures.
No tickets are being sold to Irish fans for either the 'home' or 'away' matches, with a small allocation available for Israeli fans for the first fixture, which has been the case at multiple previous Israel home games held in Hungary.
Hungary has been deemed a suitable host nation for Israel matches because the two nations enjoy stronger diplomatic ties than those between Israel and many other European nations, and it has been willing to provide the necessary policing and security arrangements for matches to operate smoothly.
The FAI decided in the summer to play its 'home' fixture against Israel at a neutral stadium, citing "operational challenges that could impact on the delivery of the game on home soil".
Reports have claimed the FAI was concerned protests could prevent the match from taking place in Dublin.
The FAI gave no official reason for the selection of Backa Topola, but choosing a venue in Serbia - in a town so remote - in theory renders security management easier and reduces the possibility of protest.
In 2025, Serbian foreign minister Marko Duric described Israel as one of Serbia's "closest friends and strategic partners". Serbia has also purchased military equipment, including drones and missiles, from Israel in recent years.
The decision to play in neutral stadiums has not curtailed opposition.
Fans of various Irish clubs have demonstrated against the matches during domestic fixtures in recent weeks, and on Monday more than 160 Irish athletes signed an open letter by the Irish Sport for Palestine group urging a boycott. The signatories include boxer Tyrone McKenna and former European champion athlete Ciara Mageean.
FAI CEO David Courrell said last week Uefa had rejected a request for the teams to be kept apart in future draws, director of football John Martin described the games as a "very uncomfortable situation for everyone". Manager Heimer Hallgrimsson, meanwhile, said playing the match did not constitute legitimisation of Israel's "genocide".
"We're not playing with genocide, we're playing against genocide," Hallgrimmson said. "We're playing against Israel, we're not playing with Israel."
In response, the Israel Football Association accused Hallgrimsson of "ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity".
The Republic of Ireland faced Israel in Women's EuroBasket qualifiers last autumn and earlier this year after "extensive deliberations".
Irish support for Palestinians is long-standing
The Republic of Ireland has been among the European countries to most keenly show support for Palestinians since the start of Israel's military offensive in Gaza in October 2023.
More than 73,000 people have been killed in Israeli attacks, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations (UN).
In May 2024, alongside Spain and Norway, Ireland officially recognised a Palestinian state, and later that year joined South Africa's Gaza genocide case against Israel in the International Court of Justice.
The country has also boycotted Eurovision since 2025 because of Israel's ongoing participation in the song contest, was the first EU country to ban goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank, and has issued travel bans for Israeli government ministers.
On Monday, Irish foreign minister Helen McEntee said: "Ireland's view is clear - international law is being breached. We are seeing an attempt to erase a population."
Israel has criticised Ireland's standpoint and claims its actions in Gaza constitute self-defence, after the armed Palestinian group Hamas attacked Israel on 7 October 2023, killing about 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages.
Last summer a UN commission of inquiry found that Israel has committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, and this year a further investigation determined that the country has deliberately targeted children with military force, resulting in genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes in Gaza and the occupied West Bank.
Israel has repeatedly rejected allegations it has committed genocide.
The Republic of Ireland is not the only nation to have expressed reluctance to face Israel in international football.
In 2024, Belgium refused to host Israel on home soil, and the match was held instead in Debrecen.
The president of the Norwegian Football Association, Lise Klaveness, made a public statement last year saying Israel should be suspended from European competitions, and Turkey also called for Israel to be banned.
BBC Sport reported last autumn that Uefa executives were considering a vote on whether to ban Israel, under pressure from representatives from a number of nations.
But any plan to hold a vote was pulled when the first phase of a ceasefire was announced last October.

UN chief calls for AI curbs and end to wars in his last assembly address
United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres' address capped a decade-long tenure in which he sought to position the UN as a mediator in conflicts and a forum for governing emerging technologies, even as major powers increasingly bypassed the organisation.
UNITED NATIONS: United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres used his final address to the General Assembly on Tuesday (Sep 22) to urge world leaders to regulate artificial intelligence, end wars, focus on climate change and overhaul UN institutions he warned are struggling to confront mounting global challenges.
The former Portuguese prime minister, whose second five-year term ends on Dec 31, reiterated his calls for global oversight of AI risks, just as the UN's 15-member Security Council prepares to host AI leaders for a briefing on the powerful technology.
Guterres also reflected on the gridlock within the organisation, as nearly 130 world leaders gathered in New York, and Chinese President Xi Jinping and others - including leaders from South Africa, India and Germany - skipped the diplomatic meeting.
Delegates responded with sustained applause when Guterres defended a two-state solution for Israelis and Palestinians, demanded that "polluters must pay" for climate change and pressed for reforms to international institutions, causes he has championed throughout his decade leading the United Nations.
The address capped a decade-long tenure in which Guterres sought to position the UN as a mediator in conflicts and a forum for governing emerging technologies, even as major powers increasingly bypassed the organisation and Washington slashed its funding.
"Those countries leading this technological revolution must share information on emerging safety risks, cooperate on testing and evaluation - and work towards common safeguards that protect us all," Guterres told the assembly.
He called on the leaders gathered in New York to "advance the conditions for the responsible pacing of AI and the additional safeguards needed to address risks" and to "work towards a multilateral AI risk management framework, supported by credible and independent oversight".
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Sunday that Washington had proposed a new AI safety notification mechanism for US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi to consider at their summit this week. The proposal emerged from talks on establishing a US-China AI dialogue and would cover AI-related incidents with national security implications.
A CHAMPION FOR GLOBAL GOVERNANCE OF AI
Guterres has long pushed for global governance of AI. In 2023, the UN created a 39-member advisory body on AI, with members including tech company executives, government officials and academics from countries such as the US, Russia and Japan.
The Security Council, which is charged with maintaining international peace and security, met for the first time on the risks of artificial intelligence the same year, when China said the technology should not become a "runaway horse" and Washington warned against its use to censor or repress people.
On the Middle East, where the conflict has widened as Houthi gains along the Red Sea coast threaten shipping routes and tensions persist in the Strait of Hormuz, Guterres called for "de-escalation and dialogue".
"Together, let's send a clear message from this hall: The fighting must stop. Humanitarian aid must flow. And navigational rights and freedoms must be fully restored in accordance with international law," Guterres said.
On the UN system, criticised by Trump and others as bloated and ineffective after Washington withdrew from several UN agencies and slashed funding, Guterres said, "our mechanisms for collective action are under growing strain" and global institutions "continue to reflect the power realities and interests of a largely bygone age".
Guterres used the address to bid farewell to most of the global leaders he has worked with over the last 10 years.
"So, on January 1st, when I am no longer secretary-general, be sure of this. Wherever I will be, whatever I will be doing - I will keep championing the conviction that peace is possible," he said. "I will continue to stand up for the values of the United Nations Charter and I will never, ever give up. Thank you."

Doctor in court to face Rwanda genocide charges
- Published
A 65-year-old doctor has appeared in court, the first person in the UK to be charged over the genocide in Rwanda in 1994.
Dr Vincent Brown, formerly Dr Vincent Bajinya, who is in custody, confirmed his name and address from the dock at Westminster Magistrates' Court.
He was charged following a seven year British investigation into the killings.
He was told he faced a charge of conduct ancillary to genocide and six offences of conduct ancillary to murder, as a crime against humanity.
The case was passed to the Old Bailey for a hearing on 9 October. A bail application will be considered later on Tuesday.
The 1994 killings in Rwanda lasted 100 days, during which Hutu extremists carried out a campaign of slaughter against Tutsis and other moderate Hutus.
The charges against Brown relate to an alleged slaughter in the Rugenge district of Kigali between 6 April and 13 April in 1994.
Brown is accused of "killing, directing or encouraging" the deaths of members of the Tutsi ethnic group, as well as intending to destroy the group "as a whole or in part."
Prosecutors said he was being charged with genocide under the 2001 International Criminal Court Act and the alleged killings were "part of a widespread or systematic attack, directed against a civilian population, with knowledge of the attack."
Three members of the same house were allegedly murdered, along with a taxi driver, a mother and her young son.
The alleged victims were Dominique Mukurarinda, Immaculee Mukankusi, Gerasi Rurangirwa, Leandre Mbogoye, Charlotte Kamaguja and Olivier Tuyishime.
Brown is a medical doctor who qualified in Rwanda in the 1980s. He later became head of the country's Department of Family Health in Kigali and lived in a suburb there with his wife and young son.
In 2006 he was worked at Praxis, a London-based charity which helps refugees from places like Rwanda.
He has also served on the Refugee Nurses Task Force, which was set up in 2003 to advise the UK government.
Senior police officers have previously stressed the UK should not be a safe haven for alleged war criminals, and investigators have been trained in international war crimes legislation.
Sam Blom-Cooper, a barrister for Brown, told the court his client denied the allegations and was intent on going in front of a jury to clear the "stains of these appalling allegations."
He said the defendant had hoped for, longed for, and prayed for the best part of 20 years, for this day."
"These are appalling crimes, terrible murders committed in 1994 but this is the beginning of the end for Dr Brown."
Inquiries continue into other alleged genocide offences in Rwanda.

A year ago, President Trump pledged to lower Medicaid drug prices. Has that happened?
What's the latest with the Trump admin's promise on lower drug prices in Medicaid?
When President Trump talks about accomplishments of his second term, he often mentions the deals he's struck with pharmaceutical companies to lower drug prices.
"We went from the highest prescription drug prices, by far, anywhere in the world, to the lowest prescription drug prices anywhere in the world," Trump said during his remarks at the midterm Republican National Convention in Dallas on Sept 10. "And that alone should get us a big victory in our midterms that are coming up."
Last year on Sept. 30, the president and his health officials gathered in the Oval Office to announce a major agreement with Pfizer — the first of what he said would be a series of deals with pharmaceutical companies. Eventually, the White House said 26 companies signed agreements, but they have not been made public.
Trump refers to these agreements as "most favored nation" deals, meant to bring U.S. drug prices in line with what other wealthy countries pay for drugs.
The most buzzed-about part of the first announcement was the creation of TrumpRx, a website for consumers to find discounts on some drugs if they choose not to use their health insurance. But, as NPR has reported, the drugs available are limited, and most consumers will get a better price if they just use their insurance and pay the copay.
But Trump's announcement also included another promise, for the low-income and disabled Americans who are covered by Medicaid:
"Today Pfizer is committing to offer all of their prescription medications to Medicaid," he said on Sept. 30, 2025. "And it will be at the most favored nation prices. It's gonna have a huge impact on bringing Medicaid costs down like nothing else."
And Trump said he expected other drug companies would do the same.
Medicaid covers 66 million Americans, and its net spending on prescription drugs grew by 46% between 2019 and 2024, costing taxpayers $46 billion dollars that year, according to the nonpartisan health policy research group KFF.
But turning Trump's promises into an operational program has been difficult. A year later, that effort has been plagued by uncertainties, delays and a general lack of transparency.
The pilot program relies on voluntary participation, by both drug companies and individual states, which means the number of drugs that will be discounted, and the number of patients who will have access to those prices, could be lower than what Trump originally promised.
Companies might not offer all of their drugs
Because the administration has refused to release the actual pharmaceutical agreements, it's not clear if participating companies have to offer Medicaid most-favored nation discounts for all their drugs.
NPR reached out to Pfizer and 16 other major drug companies that struck pricing deals with the Trump Administration over the past year. None would confirm to NPR that all of their drugs would be discounted in Medicaid, or say exactly which ones would be discounted.
Gilead told NPR it is working with states to make "selected covered products available," including drugs that treat hepatitis C, hepatitis B and HIV.
Sanofi said it would make the discounted pricing available for "certain wholly owned medicines that treat diabetes, cardiovascular and neurological conditions, and cancer."
Eli Lilly said it didn't have a final list but expected "many" of its medicines to be part of the pilot program at a discount. It said "any" of its "eligible covered outpatient drugs " could be selected — except for its GLP-1 medicines that are part of another pilot program in Medicare.
Genentech would only say that "certain medicines" would be a part of the Medicaid program.
Two companies told NPR the terms of the Medicaid agreements were confidential.
The federal regulatory agency, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid, wouldn't tell NPR how many of each company's drugs would get Medicaid discounts either.
This fact that companies aren't discounting all of their drugs as part of this pilot program is worrisome, said Dr. Thomas Hwang of Brigham and Women's Hospital in Boston. It makes it easier for companies to game the system, he said
"Companies have every incentive to cherry-pick [for this program] the products for which they already give Medicaid the best discounts and for which the international price may not be that much lower," Hwang said. In other words, the companies might publicly get credit for discounts that are actually negligible.
"So there would be an incentive for companies to try to limit their liability and pay less to Medicaid," Hwang explained. "That gaming is what worries me about this backsliding over the past months — from the initial messaging that all drugs will be offered from participating manufacturers, and now to maybe only certain drugs will be offered."
The discounts won't reach all states
Even if pharmaceutical companies do end up offering lower prices on a wide range of products, those new prices won't simply take effect nationwide. Instead, the discount program is being set up as a voluntary pilot. That means every state has to decide whether to opt-in, and then agree to certain conditions.
The pilot is called the Generous model. And the ramp-up has been slow. Deadlines for drug companies and states to sign up were originally set for the spring and summer, but they've been pushed back.
"It's always a bad sign when you keep pushing back your deadline," said Ameet Sarpatwari, a professor of population medicine at Harvard, and a drug policy researcher.
Why states might hesitate to commit
Even though the aim of the Generous pilot program is lower drug prices, a state that signs up could be exposing itself to some financial risks.
The federal government splits the cost of Medicaid with the states. In most states, Medicaid is the biggest part of the state budget, after education.
But unlike the federal government, states have to balance their budgets every year, according to Jack Rollins, who directs federal policy at the National Association of Medicaid Directors.
Even if a prescription drug is expected to save money on projected health care costs over many years, a state Medicaid program might not have enough budgeted to pay for every patient who needs the drug in a given year.
"Everything in Medicaid is going to be a trade-off," he said. "There's no silver bullet to the drug costs that we're navigating."
State budget managers already try to control Medicaid costs using various coverage rules for drugs with high price tags.
For example, some drugs might require a doctor to submit a "prior authorization" request to the state Medicaid program. Another rule is to require patients to try cheaper drugs first, to manage their condition, before trying a more expensive brand.
But in the Generous pilot program, states would have to toss out their own coverage criteria and accept a standardized system, if they want the negotiated price.
That would mean states that previously had some coverage limitations on certain drugs might be forced to offer unfettered access, says Sarpatwari.
"Then all of a sudden your state Medicaid plans might be spending a whole lot more because a whole lot more people might be getting the drugs," he says.
The deadline for states to apply was Sept. 10, and a few states like Massachusetts said publicly that they would opt-in. California officials said they would apply, but as a means to see more details before committing. States have until September 30 to finalize and sign binding agreements.

The Congress on Tuesday (September 22, 2026) alleged that the government withheld data on suicides at the Indian Institutes of Technology (IITs) and claimed that more than half of the students who died by suicide in the premier institutions over the past five years belonged to Scheduled Caste (SC), Scheduled Tribe (ST) and Other Backward Classes (OBC) communities.
Congress general secretary (organisation) K.C. Venugopal alleged that the Ministry of Education had deliberately excluded suicide-related data from its response to a parliamentary question he had raised in December 2025.
“When I raised this question in Parliament in a question to be tabled on 8th December 2025, the Ministry gave a vague response and evades disclosing specific numbers,” Mr. Venugopal said in a post on X.
He said an Under Secretary in the Ministry had written to the IITs on December 1, 2025, seeking the relevant information, but the data was not included in the Minister’s response.
“This shows that their intentions were to lie to the people, to hide the extent of discrimination taking place at elite government institutions,” Mr. Venugopal alleged.
He was reacting to a news report which claimed that 53 students had died by suicide at IITs over the past five years and that more than 50% of them belonged to SC, ST and OBC communities.
Citing IIT-B student death
The Congress leader linked the issue to the death of Sahil Wakode, who was from an SC community and a student of IIT-Bombay, and demanded an explanation from the government on why the data was not disclosed.
“When Sahil Wakode’s death has shocked the entire nation, hiding such data makes the government complicit in creating the atmosphere that caused Sahil’s death,” he said.

“Sahil’s life mattered. His dignity mattered. His family deserves truth, justice and accountability,” Mr. Suresh said in a post on X.
The Congress demanded that the government disclose the data and spell out measures to address concerns among students from marginalised communities at the IITs.

For much of my career in cancer care, I have seen a contradiction play out in the exam rooms of my colleagues and across the country. Cancer patients ask how to manage pain, fatigue, anxiety, immune suppression, and the daily toll of the disease. Clinicians often prescribe only medication, even though they know other evidence-based treatments could help: acupuncture for chemotherapy-induced nausea; exercise and nutrition counseling to improve clinical outcomes; and mindfulness-based programs to ease distress, sleep problems, and even immune dysfunction.
When doctors and patients do discuss these treatments, too often the conversation ends with a shrug: “Insurance doesn’t cover that.”
This disconnect is indefensible.
Over the past two decades, the field of integrative oncology — the evidence-informed use of mind-body practices, lifestyle interventions, and selected complementary therapies alongside conventional cancer treatment — has evolved from a fringe idea into a mature clinical discipline. The field now has clinical practice guidelines jointly developed by the Society for Integrative Oncology (SIO) and the American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO), and recommendations embedded throughout the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines.
When ASCO and NCCN agree that a treatment is effective and safe, that should carry decisive weight in coverage decisions. Yet coverage remains inconsistent, fragmented, and inequitable. This is no longer primarily a scientific problem. It is a policy failure.
Integrative oncology earned legitimacy by embracing science and evidence-based medicine. Leaders in the field demanded better research, standardized methods, and clinical trials to confirm safety and efficacy. We studied what patients were already using, rigorously tested what worked, and built clinical guidelines grounded in evidence rather than ideology.
That approach paid off. Randomized clinical trials and meta-analyses now show that specific integrative interventions meaningfully reduce cancer-related pain, fatigue, anxiety, depression, sleep disturbance, neuropathy, hot flashes, and treatment-related nausea. Many of these outcomes are not subjective. Integrative oncology therapies can influence immune function, inflammation, stress hormones, and patients’ ability to tolerate and complete lifesaving therapies. Better symptom control often means patients stay on treatment longer and recover better.
This evidence base is why ASCO endorses integrative oncology guidelines and why NCCN incorporates integrative therapies throughout symptom management pathways. Acupuncture is recommended for pain and nausea. Mindfulness-based interventions are recommended for anxiety, depression, and fatigue. Exercise and nutrition counseling are no longer optional extras. They are foundational components of comprehensive cancer care.
We now tell patients these interventions work, then ask them to pay for them out of pocket.
In the United States, access to integrative oncology often depends on where a patient lives, which insurer they have, or whether their employer negotiated the right benefits. Two patients with identical diagnoses can receive very different supportive care based not on science, but geography.
That inequity has no place in evidence-based medicine.
If a therapy is recommended by SIO, ASCO, or NCCN guidelines, it should be covered. At a minimum, coverage policies should align with the same evidentiary standards used to develop those guidelines. These guidelines are built using the standards applied to chemotherapy, radiation, and supportive medications. Insurers routinely cover extraordinarily expensive drugs with modest benefit. Failing to cover lower-cost, evidence-based integrative therapies makes little clinical or economic sense and perpetuates a two-tiered system of care.
Even on economic grounds alone, failing to cover these evidence-based services undermines both efficiency and value-based care. Acupuncture sessions cost far less than nerve blocks. Group-based mindfulness programs cost a fraction of an emergency department visit for uncontrolled symptoms. Exercise and nutrition interventions reduce downstream costs related to deconditioning, metabolic disease, and hospitalizations, not to mention progression or recurrence of disease.
Coverage gaps are not accidental. They reflect deliberate choices.
Many insurers still view integrative therapies as optional, rather than as evidence-based components of cancer care, despite recommendations from major oncology organizations. Some coverage policies may also reflect outdated perceptions of these interventions rather than the current state of evidence. In addition, many of the benefits appear as avoided complications, better symptom control, fewer
hospitalizations, and better treatment adherence, making them less visible than the
immediate cost of providing the service.
As integrative oncology has matured, so have the research questions. Early work focused on symptom relief and quality of life. That research was essential and remains so. But the field is now asking deeper biological questions and doing so using the most rigorous scientific methods. Some of this work remains in an early stage, but it reflects a broader shift toward applying rigorous methods to previously untested questions.
One of the most controversial areas of recent investigation involves biofield therapies: approaches such as reiki and healing touch, where practitioners gently touch clients or hold hands above the skin without touching. For decades, these therapies were dismissed by mainstream researchers because they relied on subjective outcomes and lacked plausible biological mechanisms. Recently, researchers have started investigating more objective outcomes, studying immune markers in clinical trials and controlled preclinical experiments designed to eliminate placebo effects. This line of inquiry reflects how integrative oncology has evolved as a discipline: by applying modern scientific tools to questions patients have long been asking.
My colleagues and I have examined whether biofield therapy could produce measurable biological effects in a series of preclinical studies. In work we recently reported in Cancer Medicine, we found that biofield therapy delivered through a standardized protocol was associated with significant inhibition of growth and invasiveness of pancreatic cancer cells in vitro, along with reduced liver metastasis in mouse models. At a cellular level, this included changes in mitochondrial structure, cell cycle regulation, membrane voltage potential, and key oncogenic pathways, including FOXM1, a major driver of cancer proliferation and metastasis. Our earlier studies in lung cancer models showed changes in immune cell infiltration, macrophage balance, and tumor necrosis, findings consistent with others.
We do not yet know what these findings mean clinically. That uncertainty is exactly why more careful study is essential.
The uncertainty exists alongside a clinical reality many health care professionals already recognize. The Department of Veterans Affairs now includes biofield therapies such as reiki, healing touch, and therapeutic touch among its integrative health offerings. Across major U.S. hospitals, these approaches are quietly becoming part of routine supportive care, often delivered by trained nurses working alongside conventional medical teams.
Cancer patients are already exploring these therapies. Ignoring that reality does not protect them; it abandons them. The ethical responsibility of medicine is not to prematurely endorse unproven approaches, but neither is it to dismiss promising signals because they challenge existing frameworks.
If biofield therapies ultimately prove ineffective in clinical settings, patients deserve to know that so they can direct their time, energy, and money elsewhere. If they prove helpful for specific outcomes or populations, we have an obligation to define those boundaries clearly and responsibly. Either way, we need more study, not silence. The worst option is intellectual inertia.
Integrative oncology’s future no longer hinges on scientific credibility. That work has largely been done. What remains is a lack of political will.
The evidence has advanced. Coverage policies have not. Medicare, Medicaid, and private insurers should update coverage policies to reflect NCCN and SIO-ASCO recommendations, just as they update coverage when other standards of cancer care evolve.
Mandating coverage aligned with these guidelines would immediately expand access, reduce disparities, and bring cancer care closer to what it claims to be: evidence-based and patient-centered. Our health care system must keep pace.
Cancer patients deserve care guided by evidence, not by what insurers choose to cover. So do the clinicians trying to practice evidence-based medicine within a system that has not yet caught up with the science.
Lorenzo Cohen, Ph.D., is a distinguished professor and integrative oncology researcher at a cancer center in Houston, co-author of “Anticancer Living: Transform Your Life and Health with the Mix of Six” (Penguin Random House), and a stage 3 melanoma cancer survivor.

With cases of mumps being reported from various parts of Thrissur district in Keralam, the District Medical Officer (DMO) has urged the public to remain vigilant.
Mumps is a viral infection that spreads through air, particularly through droplets from coughing and sneezing, nasal secretions and close contact with infected persons. The disease is most contagious from about two days before the onset of swelling to four to six days after the swelling appears.
Children between five and 15 years are commonly affected, although adults can also contract the infection. The disease can be more severe in adults.
Symptoms
The most prominent symptom is swelling on the sides of the cheeks, below the ears. The swelling may affect one or both sides of the face. Mild fever and headache are among the early symptoms, followed by difficulty in opening the mouth, chewing and swallowing. Loss of appetite and fatigue may also occur.
The DMO has advised patients to seek treatment for fever and pain, drink plenty of fluids and take adequate rest. If proper precautions are not taken, the infection can, in some cases, affect the brain, testicles, ovaries, pancreas and prostate. Complications such as encephalitis may occur if the infection spreads to the brain. In adults, complications involving the reproductive organs can, in some cases, affect fertility.
Avoid contact
Teachers should immediately inform parents and health workers if children develop symptoms. Infected persons should remain at home until they have recovered. They should avoid close contact with others. Children with mumps should not be sent to school.
Disinfecting items used by infected persons, wearing masks, maintaining physical distance and washing hands with soap are among the measures recommended to prevent the spread of the infection. The illness usually subsides within one to two weeks.
MMR vaccine
The DMO has advised parents to ensure that children receive the MMR (measles, mumps and rubella) vaccine at 16-24 months of age, as it provides protection against the three infections.
Anyone developing symptoms has been advised to consult a doctor promptly and seek appropriate treatment.

AI solved one of math's hardest problems. Humanity learned nothing (so far)
When OpenAI announced its AI had solved one of the world's toughest math problems earlier this month, its tone was celebratory:
"A major goal of our work is to empower scientists to advance research and technology that benefits all of humanity," the company wrote.
But mathematicians say that, so far, humanity has learned very little from the solution the company's AI model purportedly found. Although they believe the proof to be technically correct, the dense, 166-page manuscript drafted by AI is proving to be a difficult read.
"So far it's been very difficult to really extract any human understanding from this new AI proof," said James Maynard, a mathematician at the University of Oxford.
"The paper is not written for humans," said Javier Gómez-Serrano, a mathematician at Brown University who uses AI in his own research. He said he believes the proof could help advance the field after "some serious re-writing," but "as of today, the paper doesn't teach us much."
The solution came as AI appears to be rapidly gaining mathematical insights. AI has exploded onto the math scene over the past six months, academic mathematicians contacted by NPR said. For the first time, large language models appear capable of producing real results that could lead to new mathematical discoveries.
But few see OpenAI's announcement, which came as human mathematicians were closing in on a solution, as an example of how AI and mathematicians can work together.
"This whole episode could have been a wonderful proof-of-concept of the power of collaboration between humans and AI," said Maynard, who signed a statement by 25 winners of the prestigious Fields Medal. The statement, which was published September 11, decried "misaligned goals" between the AI companies and the mathematics community.
"Unfortunately, because of the decisions of humans involved, it became this scrappy, messy battle," he said.
Rush to discovery
The problem OpenAI apparently solved is considered among the most important unanswered questions in mathematics.
Known as the "Navier-Stokes problem," it concerns a set of equations used to describe the flow of fluids. The equations are used every day across physics and engineering, said Tristan Buckmaster, a mathematician at New York University.
And yet, at a fundamental level, researchers really don't understand why they work. Buckmaster says that getting deeper insights into Navier-Stokes would likely yield "a new toolkit to understand complicated solutions to fluids." That in turn could lead to better models of things like turbulence in fluids and lift in aircraft.
In order to find a better version of Navier-Stokes, researchers had been looking for scenarios where the equations "broke down," or stopped working. Describing such scenarios became one of the $1 million Millenium Prize Problems, which were established in 2000 by the Clay Mathematics Institute.
Mathematicians had been working towards an answer to the Navier-Stokes problem for years, and the community could sense they were getting close. "Among the seven Millennium Problems … Everyone agreed that this would be the next one that got solved," said Martin Hairer, a mathematician at EPFL, a top European technical university located in Lausanne, Switzerland who also signed the statement.
Buckmaster and his collaborator, Levent Alpöge at Anthropic, were among the human mathematicians who were inching closer to finding a scenario where the equations stopped working. The two were using AI tools, including OpenAI's chatbot to work towards a solution.
Then OpenAI caught wind that the problem might soon be solved.
"On Tuesday, September 1, we heard rumors that two Millennium Prize problems had been resolved," the company wrote. "Inspired by these rumors and by the step change in performance of our internal model, we launched an effort to evaluate it on all open Millennium Prize problems and a few other high-impact problems."
The company marshalled some 10,000 AI agents to work on the Navier-Stokes problem. The agents worked for 88 hours, using around 130 billion output tokens, or units of text and characters generated by the model. According to OpenAI's pricing for its most advanced publicly available model, the solution to the Navier-Stokes problem cost the company somewhere around $6-$10 million to compute. (Overall, the company says it used 300 billion tokens, closer to $15-20 million, looking for solutions.)
The announcement of OpenAI's solution sparked controversy after Buckmaster issued a public statement describing how the company had approached him. According to Buckmaster, they said they would put him on their paper if he dropped Alpöge, his collaborator at rival company Anthropic.
Buckmaster told NPR he believes OpenAI was tipped off to the approach he and Alpöge were using to try and find the solution to Navier-Stokes.
"There's so much circumstantial evidence that they had far more knowledge of what we were doing than they let on," he said. He added that the word "they" doesn't necessarily mean a person. "It could mean the agents," he said.
OpenAI has denied that they used Buckmaster and Alpöge's prompts or proofs in its search for a solution.
Regardless, the hurried results seem muddled. Several mathematicians who looked at OpenAI's paper said it was virtually unreadable.
"It's a terribly written paper," Buckmaster said.
"The paper doesn't explain what parts are important. What parts are routine? How does the idea feed into other places?" added Gómez-Serrano.
Buckmaster said that OpenAI's decision to rush out an answer forced him to publish his own heavily AI-influenced preliminary results. Those too, he said, are not very well written. "Everything was rushed out," he said. "It's still not at the level I'm happy with, but at least the introduction has all the key ideas."
Computers check computers
While OpenAI's 166-page proof is taking weeks to untangle, few mathematicians believe it's wrong. That's because in addition to publishing the proof, the company also produced a piece of computer code called a Lean formalization. Lean is a programming language used in mathematics to check if proofs are correct. If the code can be compiled, then the proof is considered complete.
The Lean code produced by OpenAI's tools did compile as expected, Gómez-Serrano said. Based on that, "the community seems to have the consensus that it is correct."
Gómez-Serrano, Buckmaster and other mathematicians contacted by NPR all said they envisioned a future for AI in mathematics. The field is open to new tools, in part because for decades, it's ceded much of the day-to-day computations required for making advancements to computers.
But this episode is a reminder that mathematics is about more than just finding a solution, said Maynard. "It wasn't about only answering this problem, it was about the human understanding behind it," he said.

The United Nations looks broken. Is it?
A major UN meeting kicks off this week in New York, one year after President Donald Trump asked if the UN had a purpose.
It’s time for yet another United Nations General Assembly meeting in Manhattan — just one year after President Donald Trump appeared at it and asked, bluntly: “What is the purpose of the United Nations?”
Every year around this time, roughly 130 leaders from around the world convene at the UN to deliver speeches, hold diplomatic meetings, and debate issues like AI, climate change, and the wars in Ukraine, Gaza, and Iran. Trump is scheduled to speak this week, as are Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu (...despite New York’s chilly reception).
Even more important than those big public speeches, however, are the one-on-one talks between foreign leaders. Trump has a packed meeting schedule on Monday and Tuesday, featuring the likes of Zelenskyy, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, and new British Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
In Trump’s famously bizarre speech last year, he attacked several US allies, called climate change a “con,” and suggested the UN itself was irrelevant. Increasingly — as we’ll get into below — that’s an accusation echoed by many UN critics.
Go a little deeper
This week’s meeting comes at a moment of crisis — or at the very least, inflection — for the United Nations.
The UN faces a severe budgetary shortfall this year, caused largely by Trump’s refusal to pay America’s full dues. At the same time, the UN has battled searing criticism of its inability to end conflicts in places like Ukraine, Iran, and Gaza.
Under the organization’s founding charter, any of the five permanent members of its Security Council — the body responsible for maintaining international security — can block important resolutions unilaterally. In 2022, Russia controversially used that power to torpedo a resolution condemning its attempted annexation of parts of Ukraine. Three years later, the US similarly vetoed a demand for a permanent ceasefire in Gaza and an increase in unrestricted humanitarian aid.
Critics point to impasses like these as evidence the UN no longer works; even UN Secretary-General António Guterres has said the Security Council needs reform. But it would be a mistake to conclude the UN is somehow irrelevant or newly ineffectual.
For one thing, Security Council gridlock isn’t a recent development — it’s the historical norm. (Check out all the Cold War-era vetoes in the chart above.) The UN is also far more than its Security Council — it’s a sprawling humanitarian apparatus that provides food, cash aid, medical care, and other assistance to millions around the world.
In Gaza last year alone, for instance, the UN says it provided clean water to 1.6 million people, operated dozens of makeshift schools for Palestinian children, and distributed almost $55 million of humanitarian cash assistance.
Those efforts probably won’t make headlines this week. But they help answer Trump’s 2025 question.
