Guatemala’s Democracy Dilemma
A reformist president weighs the pressure to move fast against the imperative to restore institutions his people can trust.
Just over three years ago in Guatemala, a coalition of young and Indigenous voters helped propel Bernardo Arévalo, a reformer who campaigned against corruption, to an astounding presidential win. Guatemala had not only refused the global trend toward populist authoritarianism; it had also defied what its citizens called “the pact of the corrupt,” a loose alliance of politicians, judges, criminal networks, and crony capitalists that had gained control of the country’s institutions.
Today the mood in Guatemala is less hopeful. Some of Arévalo’s former allies, and many of those who voted for him, are dejected, convinced that the president missed a once-in-a-generation opportunity to transform the country. When I met with Arévalo in Guatemala City in May, he defended the pace of his administration’s progress and suggested that the alternative would have been to abuse the powers of a government he was elected to reform.
In Latin America, “we never truly got used to understanding that the rule of law is fundamental,” he told me. “Rule of law is not the same as rule by law. Rule of law is when we all accept that we are subject to the law and we operate within that framework to solve problems. Rule by law is when I use the law that’s at my disposal as part of my political arsenal.”
Had he crossed that line, Arévalo insisted, he would have risked being ousted by his opponents and replaced by someone willing to do much worse. His critics disagree.
Arévalo’s personal integrity is undisputed. But some of the reformers who helped elect him now argue that he may be too scrupulously rules-respecting to deal effectively with the “pact of the corrupt” and the institutions it captured—too much of a liberal democrat to save democracy. When he leaves office in 2028, they fear that the pact will quickly retake control of the few institutions it has lost, or that voters will choose an autocrat who promises to crush crime without concern for legality.
Guatemala’s predicament points to a more universal problem. Can liberal reformers unwind authoritarian state capture without, themselves, engaging in at least a little bit of illiberalism? The dilemma is not Guatemala’s alone. Move too aggressively, and you risk being branded an autocrat, or even becoming one. Move too cautiously, and you risk obstruction, sabotage, and ineffectuality. South Africa’s Cyril Ramaphosa chose a gradualist approach to reversing Jacob Zuma’s state capture and disappointed many of his supporters. Placing the opposite bet, Poland’s Donald Tusk bent rules to try to undo the damage done by the right-populist Law and Justice party—and stood accused of undermining the rule of law. Hungary’s post-Orbán leader, Péter Magyar, seems to be following Tusk’s example.
In a way, both Arévalo and his critics are right. Guatemala has avoided a democratic breakdown. But the president’s rules-bound approach has also left many Guatemalans feeling that he has not fought for them forcefully enough. The question now is whether Arévalo has preserved democracy as an ideal that Guatemalans believe in and, if necessary, will defend.
In Guatemala City, I watched as hundreds of people gathered outside the country’s public prosecutor’s office, a bunker-like building ringed by a huge black-steel fence put up three years before, allegedly to shield the occupants from nonviolent democracy protesters. The crowd had come to celebrate the long-awaited end to the term of María Consuelo Porras, the country’s attorney general and, to many citizens, the personification of the pact of the corrupt.
For the past eight years, Porras had been a figure of fear. She used the power of her position to investigate and jail critics of state corruption. When Arévalo was elected in 2023, her office tried to overturn the results, alleging irregularities that international observers found baseless. That effort looked likely to succeed—until indigenous Maya communities organized peaceful demonstrations that lasted 106 days and drew the participation of nearly 2 million Guatemalans. Arévalo was inaugurated.
That he did not take extralegal action to remove Porras from her post has given rise to some of the fiercest criticism against him. She opened an investigation into Arévalo’s party, the Seed Movement, for relatively minor party-registration irregularities. Although the probe did not produce formal charges, it led to the party’s dissolution and thus thwarted any hope of its controlling Congress. Porras also brought more than 75 legal cases or complaints against the president and his supporters, including the arrests of two of the Indigenous leaders behind the 2023 protests, and even a cabinet minister. Now Porras was finally leaving, and a new attorney general was taking over.
The Guatemalans gathered outside the office had waited for this moment. What they had not anticipated was how long Porras’s departure would take, and how few people would come out to celebrate it. Thousands had massed in the same street just a few years before.
When I met Arévalo a few days later, he justified the delay by explaining that his government had arrived “with an enormous level of public legitimacy, but without control of the Congress, and with the justice system positioned against us.”
Legally, he had no authority to simply eject the attorney general. He sent a bill to Congress to grant him that power, but the opposition blocked it. “If, in that scenario, I make a political miscalculation, the result isn’t that I go with a hundred people to pull Consuelo Porras out of that building and that this is sustainable and produces results,” he said. It was that “I go to prison or into exile, and someone else comes in, one of them, to take power.”
Like much else in Guatemala, the colossal, mint-green presidential palace where Arévalo sat down with me is a holdover from a bygone era of authoritarianism. It was built by Guatemala’s Hitler-admiring, yet U.S.-backed dictator, Jorge Ubico, who rose to power in 1931 and was forced to resign amid mass protests in 1944.
Arévalo, before winning the presidency, was best known as the son of the man who succeeded Ubico, in Guatemala’s first truly free elections. Juan José Arévalo, an educator and a social democrat, returned to Guatemala from exile in 1944 to run for president against the ex-dictator’s favored candidate. As his son would later, he won by a landslide, and Guatemala’s “democratic spring” began, a time of expanded rights and education. But after his freely and fairly elected successor, Jacobo Arbenz, went further, carrying out a land reform that threatened the interests of wealthy families and the powerful U.S.-based United Fruit Company, the United States organized a coup that put the military in power in 1954. Nine years later, a guerrilla leader asked Arévalo to help spearhead armed resistance to the regime, and the former president refused, saying that confronting the military head-on would turn Guatemala “into a lake of blood.”
He was right. In the name of crushing the greatly outnumbered guerrillas, the military and its allies killed or disappeared more than 100,000 Guatemalans over the next three decades. It massacred leftists, labor leaders, and residents of more than 400 Maya villages suspected of supporting insurgents. Guatemalan courts eventually deemed the latter crime a genocide.
Bernardo Arévalo, born in exile in Uruguay, returned with his family in the middle of the dictatorship period, and he began a career as a diplomat at its tail end, as the country formally returned to elections and civilian rule in 1985. He later left the diplomatic service, earned a Ph.D., and worked in international peace-building.
The wood-paneled presidential office where we met was decorated only with two portraits: his father’s, in black-and-white, and his own, beside it, in color. Arévalo’s demeanor was professorial.
“We are in a process of recovery,” he said. “Democracy doesn’t develop in a linear, unidirectional way; it has leaps and twists, not only here, but everywhere in the world.” For much of the 1990s and 2000s, Guatemala had been twisting its way toward democracy, but corruption networks and drug traffickers had insinuated themselves into the country’s institutions. “Part of what we set out to do is to recognize the serious damage this had caused the country—this corrosion, this penetration of political-criminal networks” that served no “ideological interest,” Arévalo said, but rather “the highest bidder: whoever could pay for impunity.”
Dislodging these forces from the machinery of the state has been neither swift nor straightforward, and even those most anxious for change are hard-pressed to offer practical solutions. The president told me that some supporters had asked him to use the military to remove Porras. He found the suggestion unsettling: “Are you really asking us to go back to the years of military dictatorships of the 1970s, when armies were the only solution?”
I asked Arévalo about the Indigenous protest leaders, Luis Pacheco and Hector Chaclán, who had then been imprisoned for more than a year while under investigation on terrorism charges. “I would like the people who say ‘But the government could have done something else’ to tell me what,” Arévalo replied, exasperated. “What they’re venting is the frustration we all feel.”
He assured me that the pact of the corrupt was weakening incrementally as its networks lost access to the state: first the executive branch, then the public-works contracting system, now the prosecutor’s office. “Without tools, they aren’t powerful. And our task is to keep removing those tools from them.”
Arévalo can point to some successes. Young lawyers have worked to clean up corruption in the judicial selection process. Appointed in March, the new bench of the Constitutional Court, which rules on the constitutionality of laws and policies, is more favorable to reformers than the one it replaced, as is the new electoral tribunal, which oversees elections. I spoke with the new attorney general a few days after he assumed his post: He was so busy firing Porras’s apparatchiks and preparing for the institution to resume serious criminal investigations that he was sleeping only four or five hours a night. An anti-corruption commission that Arévalo formed early on has already filed more than 200 criminal complaints against former officials.
Arévalo was tasked with not only freeing a state captured by kleptocrats, but also strengthening one that was fundamentally weak. The bureaucracy he inherited had little capacity to provide public services, reduce poverty, or fight organized crime. In this, too, his administration has made some progress. It has hired more than 15,000 new teachers, and built or refurbished more than 150 rural-health clinics (his predecessor built just six in four years, Arévalo said). The government has also replaced dirt floors with cement in more than 75,000 households in the country’s poorest rural municipalities, and has distributed water filters and cleaner-burning stoves.
Still, much else that Guatemalans had hoped for has failed to materialize. Congress, which remains dominated by the old-guard pact forces, has blocked or stalled bills aimed at curbing corruption—for example, bills to modernize public-works contracting, require shell companies to disclose who owns them, and protect whistleblowers. Partly because the contracting system remains dysfunctional, the government has made little visible progress toward repairing the country’s crumbling highways. And, unwilling to buy votes in Congress outright, as his predecessors did, Arévalo has resorted to pork-barrel spending and raising congressional salaries to win legislative support. Such tactics are deeply unpopular with the public.
Another limiting factor has been the Trump administration. Although Arévalo’s cooperation on crime and drugs has kept the relationship cordial, his opponents have courted President Trump to try to tip the scales against reformers. In April, the U.S. ambassador to Guatemala personally called reluctant Guatemalan lawmakers to pressure them to approve a Constitutional Court judge favored by pact elites and conservatives, a top lawmaker, Luis Aguirre, told me. This tied the court between reformers and their opponents, leaving Arévalo without a reliable majority.
The young reformers who campaigned with Arévalo knew that he would face constraints, but some wish that he had more often tested those limits.
Samuel Pérez, 34, is a member of Congress; he was also the head of the Seed Movement bloc in Congress before it was dissolved. I went to see him in a building plastered with missing-persons flyers for those who were disappeared during the military dictatorship decades ago. The flyers are a common sight in Guatemala City, posted and reposted by the victims’ families.
Pérez told me that Arévalo was elected not only “to overthrow the regime, but also to construct something new, and that isn’t happening.” Now Pérez was creating a party, called Raíces, to which most of the lawmakers formerly associated with the Seed Movement had defected. They would still support Arévalo, but they would advocate for a more confrontational approach. “The president interprets power and good government as doing things a little better and a little more than what already existed. For me, no. You don’t use power to administrate what’s already there, but to transform what isn’t working,” Pérez explained.
I’d last seen Pérez during Arévalo’s presidential campaign in 2023. He’d told me then that if the Seed Movement won, the government’s greatest difficulty would be managing popular expectations. But he hadn’t predicted that he himself would be among the disappointed. Arévalo should have rallied the public to pressure Congress to pass the law removing Porras, Pérez said. He should have conceded less to business elites, and done more to free Pacheco and Chaclán. Pérez was particularly upset that the police had come to arrest the two men in a white van with tinted windows—a symbol of the dictatorship, which used such vehicles to disappear its victims—and that the government had not stopped this.
Several young Guatemalans in the reform movement suggested to me that the political caution of their parents’ generation was a product of the fear instilled in them during the years of military rule and internal armed conflict. Some speculated that Arévalo’s aversion to escalation emanates from that experience, too, given his youth in exile and the persecution of many of his father’s supporters in the years after the 1954 coup. “I think he is a son of his circumstances,” said Andrea Reyes, a young lawmaker helping Raíces organize.
Arévalo readily locates his most formative influences in that era—as a source not of fear, but of strengthened conviction. He spoke to me of his father’s refusal to abandon democratic principles: “Even when the world began to change around him, he kept his convictions, which today we see were the correct convictions, after all, 80 years later.”
Arévalo, too, has found his convictions under pressure—not only from former allies who worry that his reforms have gone too slowly, but also from constituents and conservative politicians who want a government that will ignore constitutional limits in cracking down on crime. In this they compare him unfavorably with the autocrat next door: Many Guatemalans who live in daily fear of extortion and kidnapping see gangs, not illiberal state capture, as the biggest threat to their basic freedoms, and they see President Nayib Bukele’s El Salvador as a beacon of safety.
Bukele, first elected in 2019, took an almost opposite approach from Arévalo’s to governing. He purged institutions of his political rivals, packed them with loyalists, and then cut secret deals with gang leaders before cracking down on their followers. His mass roundups virtually eliminated violent crime in his country, by jailing more than 90,000 people suspected of gang ties, many without due process. Arévalo is unwilling to pursue such methods. He has, however, seized record quantities of cocaine, extradited crime bosses, hired thousands of new police officers, and begun building the country’s first new maximum-security prison in 40 years. But murder and extortion rates have proved stubborn, and many are now demanding more-radical methods.
“Guatemalans are searching for their Bukele,” said Alvaro Arzú Escobar, a conservative lawmaker sanctioned by the Biden administration for allegedly trying to undermine Arévalo’s inauguration. Arévalo “isn’t radical in his ideas or his actions,” Arzú told me. But, he added, “the country’s biggest problem right now is a lack of authority. As president, he doesn’t exercise the power he holds. There is a lot of rhetoric, but little action.”
The Mariscal Zavala military prison sits on a pine-covered ridge on the outskirts of Guatemala City. A former army base, it houses the state’s highest-profile prisoners. I went there to meet Pacheco and Chaclán, the Indigenous leaders who’d played such an instrumental role in safeguarding the 2023 presidential election. Both had been on the board of the 48 Cantones of Totonicapán—one of the country’s oldest Indigenous self-governing bodies, in rural western Guatemala—when the attorney general’s office had moved to annul the vote. Pacheco and Chaclán canvassed rural villages on foot, helping gather some 50,000 signatures calling for Porras’s resignation. Later they helped organize protests in the capital.
“The 48 Cantones is also a democracy, with elected leaders and term limits,” Chaclán told me. “For us, democracy is sacred, and although Guatemala often doesn’t reflect it much, we must respect it.”
In April 2025, Porras ordered him and Pacheco into pretrial detention. After that, their court hearings were repeatedly delayed, seemingly intentionally, and when I met them in May, they had no idea when the next one would be.
I asked them whether they believed Arévalo should have rallied protesters or found some other tool to remove Porras, and thus to free them. Pacheco responded, “I would have liked it at first, but later I realized it would have only changed the person, not the form of doing justice.” Chaclán added, “This is nothing simple, and surely he is doing what is best for the country. We have faith we have already passed the majority of our time here.”
Chaclán was right. On August 5, a judge released Pacheco and Chaclán to house arrest, reuniting them with their families. Around the same time, the prison-like, black-steel fence was taken down from around the public prosecutor’s office.
Guatemala’s next presidential election is just nine months away. Right-wing candidates are beginning to emerge, some imitating Bukele, and many sure to court the White House, in the hope that Trump will try to tip the scales. Arévalo’s and Pérez’s reformists claim that they will join forces behind a unity candidate, but such a figure has not yet surfaced. Democracy is twisting its way forward, in Arévalo’s words. No one thinks it is leaping.
But the passage of time may provide a different perspective. On one of my last days in Guatemala City, I walked by a cathedral I had passed dozens of times before. I had never previously noticed the tiny engraved names of more than 13,000 victims of the internal armed conflict, so small as to be illegible from even a short distance, on its stone columns.
For much of the 20th century, Guatemalans who advocated for self-government, equality before the law, and the welfare of the majority—that is, social democrats—knew that the state might try to kill them. Today, social democrats govern. Reformers may disagree as to whether Bernardo Arévalo made the most of the opportunity he was given. But that such an opportunity could ever arise is more than many members of his father’s generation likely thought possible.

A shopkeeper’s alleged murder in West Bengal’s Titagarh on September 11 has triggered a controversy after Barrackpore BJP MLA Koustav Bagchi attempted to give it a communal spin by describing the victim as a ‘Sanatani’ murdered by ‘jihadis’.
In a 33-secong-long video that has now gone viral for over a week, the MLA’s claim was challenged on camera by the victim’s son, who interrupted Bagchi to say that there was nothing communal or political about his father’s murder.
The victim, Ramji Shaw, used to run a small corner shop from a portion of his home in the GC road area of Ward 18 of Barrackpore Municipality. He was allegedly killed after he refused to sell cigarettes on credit.
According to the locals, on September 11 afternoon, Shaw was trying to protect his son, who was allegedly being assaulted by three young men who were demanding to buy cigarettes from the shop without paying money on spot. As Shaw declined to sell cigarettes on credit, the men allegedly began attacking him and his son.
In the physical altercation, Shaw was pushed and heckled and lost consciousness. His family members rushed him to Barrackpore B N Bose sub-divisional hospital, where he succumbed to his injuries. According to locals, the three accused have been identified as Banti Ghosh, Sk. Sahil and Md. Nasir. Shaw’s wife had told Bengali news channel ABP Ananda that the accused had assaulted their son in the past.
Deceased’s Son Corrects MLA
As news of the alleged murder spread in the locality, Bagchi visited the deceased’s family the same day. Speaking to news channels while at Shaw’s home, he attempted to present the murder as communally motivated, specifically targeting the identity of the two accused who belong to the Muslim community.
In the viral clip, Bagchi can be heard saying (translated from Bengali), “This incident is not just related to an altercation over payment. Three Jihadis have killed a Sanatani. They wouldn’t have killed someone from their own religion.” However, even before Bagchi could finish his sentence, the deceased’s son corrected him, (translated from Bengali), “Sir, there is nothing related to religion in this case. The accused had come to my shop, looking to buy things on credit. When my father objected, they beat him up.”
The BJP MLA, seeming baffled by the interruption, responded: “I am speaking! Why are you not letting me speak!”. A few moments later, a person in purple shirt can be seen escorting the son to another room. While leaving the scene, the son stated, “This is not a matter of party politics.”
‘Politicians Inciting Locals for Electoral Gains’
Alt News visited the locality to independently verify the claims surrounding the murder and Bagchi’s allegation of a communal motive. While the bereaved wife and son both declined to speak, Shaw’s daughter Rikita confirmed to Alt News that it was indeed her brother who was seen correcting Bagchi in the viral video.
Sheikh Afroz (Ripon), who is Shaw’s immediate neighbour, said that the people in the area lived in communal harmony, as Hindus and Muslims co-existed there for generations. He added that politicians were, in fact, attempting to incite hostility between the communities. He also confirmed that Shaw’s son was seen in the video. “After the tragic incident, locals started to protest against the ‘gundagardi’ culture, and police officers had to come and pacify the situation. As the area is predominantly occupied by Muslims, most of the protesters were also Muslim. Does this not prove that this was not a communal incident?” asked Afroz.
A few metres from Shaw’s house, Md Mansoor, who runs a mobile repairing shop, said that Shaw’s shop used to have ‘ittar’ (perfume) and ‘surma’ (kohl) which were not found anywhere else in the area. “Every Eid, people from the Muslim community thronged to his shop to buy these products. Given that this was the reality which we saw every day, we don’t understand where this communal angle is coming from,” he said.
According to Mansoor, the accused youths were “known troublemakers”. “It is unfair to malign the name of an entire area and community for the wrongdoings of a select few. One of the accused is a Hindu, but the MLA still went on to claim that Shaw was murdered by Jihadis. Most of the shops in the neighbourhood, which is a predominantly Muslim area, were all shut in protest of Shaw’s murder for a few days after, only because there is no feeling of communal tension in this area,” Mansoor added.
No Communal Motive: Police
Alt News spoke to Titagrah officer-in-charge (OC) Atanu Chakraborty. The police station is located 1 km away from the crime scene. The officer confirmed that three people had been arrested in connection with the case. He said police did not find any communal motive behind the incident. The accused had pushed and beaten Shaw, following which Shaw suffered a stroke and died, he added.
“The accused are Sk Sahil, Md Nasir and Banti Ghosh. We have primarily booked them under sections pertaining to murder and further investigation is on. We couldn’t find any communal angle behind the crime,” he said, adding, the accused have been involved in public nuisance in the area in the past.
The police account, therefore, refutes Bagchi’s claims of a communal motive behind the alleged murder.
My Comments Twisted, Victim’s Son Apologised later, Claims MLA
Speaking to Alt News, Bagchi alleged, “There is no confusion. Some people are trying to do mischief with my quote. If I wanted, I could have done a lot of things over this issue, but I restrained myself considering the situation of the family. The area where this family lives are surrounded by Muslims — 90 out of 100 people living here are Muslims. The Hindu’s are constantly under a lot of pressure. So, whatever they said that day is due to fear.”
“I have a video of Ramji Shaw’s son. He had made a video and had sent it to me, clarifying their position. He also called me and apologised. Since my comments are being twisted, now I feel I have to publish the video that I have. I told his son that I can understand his emotions, his pain and fear. In the video, he also said that Hindus in that area are very few in number compared to the Muslims. However, they haven’t yet realised that the TMC government is gone and they [Hindus] are safe. I told him to be fearless,” Bagchi claimed, adding, “There definitely is a communal angle to this incident. The Muslims have kept the Hindus in that are terrorised.”
When asked about the one Hindu accused and how he could confidently claim that Shaw was murdered by ‘jihadis’, Bagchi said, “Banti Ghosh is a rowdy element and he mixes with them [the other two accused]. However, the main culprits are the two Muslims men. They have continued this for long, and you won’t find them attacking any Muslim.”
Alt News’ interactions with the locals and an observation of how they live, however, contradict Bagchi’s ‘fear of Muslims’ narrative. Shaw’s house is 550 metres from the Titagarh railway station. About 200 metres from the station, beside G C Road, stands a Muslim shrine (mazar), and next to it, a Ganesh Puja pandal has been erected. The two structures are separated only by a food stall.
A search on Google Maps of the area brought up an image from two years ago, in which a Durga Puja pandal was erected right next to the same Muslim shrine.
Further down the road, opposite to Mansoor’s shop, is Hasanjan Sporting Club, and a Hindu temple stands right next to it.
Pointing towards the narrow path beside the club, Mansoor said, “Ten families live there. Six are Muslim and four are Hindu.”

Liquor case: Reporter TV MD Anto Augustine granted bail by Kerala high court
Justice Kauser Edappagath passed the order on the petition for bail, filed by Augustine’s counsel, after noting that recovery in the case had already been made
The Kerala High Court on Tuesday granted bail to Reporter TV managing director (MD) Anto Augustine in the case booked by the excise department against him for possession of liquor beyond permissible limits at his home in Wayanad district.
Justice Kauser Edappagath passed the order on the petition for bail, filed by Augustine’s counsel, after noting that recovery in the case had already been made and that the accused did not have criminal antecedents. A detailed order is awaited.
Excise officials had seized around 67 litres of liquor, including foreign-made foreign liquor, Indian-made foreign liquor (IMFL) and wine, during raids conducted on September 16 at Augustine’s home in Muttil in Wayanad district. The seizures far exceeded the permissible limits for possessing liquor in domestic premises.
Also Read:Reporter TV MD Anto Augustine jailed after 67 litres of liquor seized from Kerala home
Excise officials will also investigate if a portion of the seized liquor is illicit in nature. Augustine has been charged under sections 55(a), 55(i) and 58 of the Kerala Abkari Act.
The liquor seizure took place as part of statewide raids on Augustine’s premises, including at the Kochi bureau of the news channel he heads. The raids by the Kerala police were part of its probe into alleged irregularities in connection with the visit of football legend Lionel Messi and the Argentine football team to the state, an event which did not materialise.

Reporter Broadcasting Corporation is part of Augustine’s corporate assets and was planned as the private sponsor for the event.

Mira Murati was trying to speak. Women swished around in evening gowns, men in tuxes. Giant piles of carved meat rested like sleeping babies on banquet tables draped in linens as red as a handmaid’s robe. Bartenders served up a cocktail named Zero to One, a nod to the philosophy of Peter Thiel.
It was a recent Saturday night in a converted church in San Francisco, and the Foundation for American Innovation, a center-right think tank, was hosting a black-tie affair to hype the new religion of AI.
Murati, the founder and CEO of Thinking Machines Lab, was talking about the history of revolutions to a crowd of more than 350 people. The Albanian-born executive had for several years kept a relatively low profile as a VP and then CTO of OpenAI before participating in an unsuccessful coup against Sam Altman and then launching her own $12 billion AI startup. Now, with chatter bouncing off the church walls, Murati’s efforts to get her points across were about as successful as that coup: No one seemed to be listening. The woman interviewing Murati asked more than once for people to stop talking or take their conversations outside.
I whispered to the friend sitting next to me that this was the second time in a week that I’d seen a woman getting drowned out. She sighed. Both of us were there to actually hear what Murati had to say. I tried to restrain myself from what I said next, but I sensed my friend was holding back too. “Her hair is amazing, though,” I hissed. “Oh my God, I know,” she replied immediately. Murati’s hair has achieved AGI. Her jaw cuts glass.
Soon after, President Donald Trump’s top science adviser, Michael Kratsios, took the stage. The crowd quieted down. We are all part of the problem.
Over the past three months, I’ve been asking anyone and everyone about the most powerful women in Silicon Valley, a club to which Murati clearly belongs. Ask who the most powerful man in tech is and many quickly say “Elon.” Or “Jensen.” Or “Sam.” Wait a beat and you might hear the name of a billionaire VC whose financial capital has been broadly and ruthlessly deployed to advance an agenda, like “Peter” or “Marc.” Ask who the most powerful woman is, and most people respond with a thoughtful pause. A thinking-face emoji. “Gwynne?” “Lisa?” “Daniela, maybe?”
An astute observer of the Valley might posit that the most powerful woman has to jet-set between SV and DC, like Ruth Porat, the president and chief investment officer of Google, or Dina Powell McCormick, Meta’s president and vice chair. WIRED’s top editor—a woman—said at one point, “Isn’t it obviously Gwynne Shotwell?” Then a Silicon Valley CEO told me that whenever she mentions the SpaceX president and chief operating officer, her friends say “Gwynne who?”
Some people seemed allergic to my question. They don’t view tech as gendered, they told me, or didn’t have much to say. Who cares? Just put your head down and do the work.
Still, the question provoked reactions. My conversations—which took place on the phone and Zoom, in boardrooms, in San Francisco coffee shops, in a Palo Alto home where my source dozed off on the couch—produced a wealth of options, ranging from founders and CEOs to venture capitalists and philanthropic ex-wives. Some of those women, both CEOs and those who call bullshit on CEOs, spoke to me at length.
I realized that the real question is not who is most powerful, but why this question is still, in 2026, so difficult to answer. What’s missing from their lives or résumés? Why is there no woman Elon? Why don’t we have our own all-powerful heroine or supervillainess?
In June, a friend and former Slack executive suggested to me that power in Silicon Valley contains multitudes of capital—financial, intellectual, political, and social or cultural.
We agreed that the mononymous men score high in all categories. Their influence has been stunning, alarming even, in its contagion. They write blog posts that are referenced for decades. They dox people with a single post on X. They sway elections. They deliver sermons. They are asked to sign a woman’s breasts at a trade show in Taiwan, like some ’80s hair-metal frontman. They suggest that a young woman trying to save the planet is the antichrist.
Does any woman in tech come close to achieving this cult of personality, to spreading the seeds of their capital in this way? There is no “Time to Build” manifesto that the women of the Valley are rallying around. The last time women in tech had a manifesto, things didn’t go as planned.
On a recent drive to Lake Tahoe, I downloaded the audiobook of Sheryl Sandberg’s Lean In. I’d read the book when it came out in 2013, and I wanted to see how its ideas had aged. By the third chapter I had heard enough.
My brief listen reminded me, though, of why the book had been influential for nearly a decade. Sandberg, who clocked 14 years as chief operating officer of Meta, put words to a lot of bad workplace patterns. Women were treated as second-class at the office. We were prone to self-doubt and backed away from opportunities that seemed incompatible with family life. And for God’s sake, we should be paid as much as men.
But Sandberg’s book suffered from too many unrelatable anecdotes and simplistic solutions. It largely put the onus on women to sit closer, speak louder, marry better. Perhaps most crucially, what began as a guidebook for a select group—relatively privileged women clawing their way up the corporate ladder—was marketed as the answer to a whole host of women’s issues. Start a “Lean in Circle.” Create a hashtag, like #BanBossy. Run for office. Small actions can, of course, catalyze movements, but in a post-pandemic world, legions of frustrated working women opted to lean out instead.
Aileen Lee, a prominent VC who often hosts private gatherings of women in the industry, said she “appreciates” what Lean In brought to the foreground. It presaged a series of events that led Silicon Valley to examine its bro-topia. There was the Ellen Pao trial in 2015, in which Pao alleged gender discrimination and retaliation by her former firm, Kleiner Perkins. (A superior court jury eventually ruled in favor of the firm.) Then came Susan Fowler’s revelatory 2017 blog post about the way she was treated while working at Uber. And, later that year, reports emerged that a male VC had made unwanted sexual advances toward half a dozen women he interacted with while doing business.
Tech firms responded by hiring investigators and crisis comms squads and suddenly found high-profile roles for the women in their ranks. But “the 2010s was the era of lip service,” says Timnit Gebru. “‘Look at how many women we have on our team!’ And if there was one woman on the team, that woman got advertised to death.”
She would know. In 2018, Google hired the Ethiopian-born Gebru to colead a project on ethical AI. Gebru did what she was hired to do: She called out biases in AI via a now-infamous research paper that Google said didn’t meet its standards. Her subsequent termination caused a firestorm. Now she heads a group called Distributed Artificial Intelligence Research that investigates some of the harms caused by tech giants and AI.
Gebru noted that the 2010s weren’t all a wash. Women were forming networks behind the scenes. Ifeoma Ozoma, who left her job at Pinterest due to pay disparities and racial discrimination, successfully cosponsored California’s Silenced No More Act, which protects employees who speak out about workplace discrimination.
But then came the backlash to the backlash. Some men had been itching to declare their sacred workplaces free of distracting social politics. When Elon Musk bought Twitter in 2022, the app morphed into a platform where men in tech were more emboldened to share their rightward beliefs, while Musk himself became even more of a “hardcore” icon. Once Trump was reelected in November 2024, all bets were off.
“The industry focused so much on the topic of ‘women in tech’ for a few years that it backfired along with a broader backfiring against DEI,” said one founder, speaking anonymously. She observed that it’s not only men who avoid discussing identity and gender. “Women don’t want to talk about it, either,” she said.
Fortunately, I managed to find exceptions to that rule. Which is how I ended up on the front stoop of a home in Palo Alto, ringing the doorbell for 18 minutes, wondering if I was at the right place. A yellow wooden W on the stoop indicated that I was. Then Anne Wojcicki, in athletic shorts and a tank top, rolled up to the house on one of those bizarro outdoor elliptical bikes and waved at me.
“Is my mom not home?” she asked.
This was where Anne and her two sisters grew up; where a young Ruth Porat came over to swim in their backyard pool. The Wojcicki matriarch, Esther, was a well-known journalism teacher at the local high school. She later wrote a book about raising her immensely successful daughters: Anne, the founder and CEO of 23andMe; Janet, an epidemiologist; and Susan, who was the CEO of YouTube before passing away two years ago from lung cancer.
Anne welcomed me in, offered me a glass of water, and kicked off her shoes, revealing mismatched fluorescent socks. Then she plopped down on the floor of the living room. I followed suit.
Esther arrived soon after and took a regal seat on the couch. I asked them both if anything had gotten better for women in the Valley over the past 15 years.
“I do think it has improved,” Esther said. “Men don’t shake their heads and say ‘My God, what a ridiculous idea’ if a woman heads up a company. But there’s still hesitancy.”
She continued, “I remember all of the battles that my poor daughter Susan went through when she moved from Google to the head of YouTube.”
Anne spoke up. “Look, Susan took over YouTube, and she was very comfortable with herself. She had a strong vision, and she was a tough negotiator. You’re always going to have different groups that make your life difficult. Susan was really good at just powering through … Whenever I would complain about something, Susan would tell me, ‘Just ignore them and move on.’”
Anne may have had her sister’s mantra in mind when she hit a recent road bump. In 2025, her genetic testing startup, 23andMe, went bankrupt, and Anne stepped down as CEO. Customers deleted their accounts, concerned that their genetic data would end up in a new owner’s hands (23andMe had experienced a major data breach before). But she managed to buy the company back, a power move if there ever was one. It’s now controlled by a nonprofit public benefit corporation that Anne runs.
Many of her earlier investors declined to support her, Anne said. Someone like Adam Neumann can whittle his commercial real estate company down to a fraction of its peak value and still raise hundreds of millions for his next act.
But there’s more to power than money, Esther said firmly. You need cultural capital. “You have to be on X. You have to be out there,” Esther said. “If you can’t get a word in …”
Anne disagreed, calling X a distraction. She does post on Instagram; lately, her Stories have centered on lung cancer research, in honor of her sister. But she dismisses X as “male-dominated.”
“Do you have to be out there creating a lot of noise versus just using social media to show a little bit of what you do?” Anne said. “Gwynne Shotwell is powerful because she’s the leader of this incredible company, but a lot of people don’t know who she is. She’s not always out there on the conference circuit. She’s heads down, executing.”
Some of what Anne said struck me as true. Over twenty-plus years Shotwell grew SpaceX into an $800 billion business prior to its IPO this year. To the public she’s elusive, but not to the world’s power brokers: She zips around the globe to try to obtain regulatory approval for her technology. On SpaceX’s first earnings call in August, she took the lead on answering questions about Starlink, the company’s cash cow.
What she doesn’t do, except rarely, is post on X.
I got the sense that the Wojcickis were antsy to get back to their work. As I made my way out, I noticed the family portraits and framed magazine covers on almost every surface of the home. Many photos featured the three sisters, now just two. Social capital, financial capital, old media, new media were all on display; a stunning collage of power and a sobering reminder that no amount of it can control certain outcomes.
It’s impossible to talk about power in Silicon Valley without talking about venture capital. Anne Wojcicki was clearly haunted by her attempts to raise enough of it to buy back her company.
In July I headed to an event on the San Francisco waterfront for women entrepreneurs and VCs. When I arrived, I found hundreds of well-heeled women and a handful of men grazing on prosciutto skeins, dried apricots, and cubes of cheese, swanning around an airy space misnomered Shack15.
Event sponsors had set up tables with goodies. An experiential marketing firm offered a K-beauty snail mucin sheet mask to anyone who followed the firm on its socials. The event’s swag bag included a pack of Popo Band, a “gentle mouth tape” meant to encourage nasal breathing during sleep. I imagined future historians asking why we women tucked ourselves into bed glistening with snail slime, our mouths taped shut.
The soiree, titled Funded Female Founders, was the brainchild of a man named James Gee. He was appropriately brief and charming in his intro speech, joking that he’d just learned what K-beauty was. Mabel Chan, the founder of an events company called Superconnected, reminded attendees that the goal was to increase deal flow. “Our ethos is high-signal rooms, not performative panels,” Chan said.
Then the evening’s emcee, AJ Thomas of Good Trouble Ventures, took the mic. She asked the crowd to snap their fingers and began belting out a revised version of “Ain’t No Mountain High Enough”:
“Ain’t no startup hard enough,
Ain’t no valley low enough,
Ain’t no founder strong enough,
To keep us from running the world, babe …”
The singing portion of the evening was brief, for better or worse. The panel conversations that followed were lively and instructive; you might even say they were high-signal. Libby Leffler, who founded a legal tech platform called First, said she was giving discounts on prenuptial agreements. Literal cheers.
The belief that the tech industry has entered a brave new AI world was palpable. But most of the entrepreneurs speaking that night emphasized that fundraising is still hard for women, particularly when they pitch VCs who have “preconceived notions.” Capella Kerst, who has a PhD in mechanical engineering and runs an adhesives company, told the room that a potential backer once suggested she take business classes.
The financial data platform PitchBook has tracked VC fundraising trends since 2007. This year, it reported that female-founded or -cofounded startups had raised “a record $73.6 billion in 2025—even exceeding pandemic-era highs—capturing an unprecedented 27.7 percent of total US venture deal value.” In 2022, the firm estimated that solely woman-founded companies raised 2 percent of VC capital for US startups.
Yet despite the gains since then, the overall deal count for women declined last year, PitchBook noted. The companies in its dataset might have had male cofounders who led the fundraising. And a huge fraction of last year’s VC funding went to two startups with women cofounders, Anthropic and ScaleAI. Alas: Despite the record high, it’s not clear that those billions mark progress.
In the gap between the two panels, a lawyer named Dobrina Ustun stepped up to give a short talk on immigrant visas. The audience seized the moment to migrate to the back of the room, where they replenished their wine, scored some K-beauty, and struck up conversations. The noise reached a fever pitch. Thomas, the emcee, asked the crowd to quiet down and listen to Ustun. They declined. How rude could we be to our own? Very, it turns out.
Venture capital is not Silicon Valley’s only currency, but it is a signifier. It’s status. “It’s definitely not 2013 anymore, where someone raises a round and it’s on the front page of Fast Company,” Catherine Bracy told me over the phone. “But there’s still real cachet in raising funding, and it would be better for women if they could raise more.”
Bracy is the CEO and cofounder of an activism group called TechEquity and the author of a 2025 book on venture capital titled World Eaters. She noted that VC is typically an “alpha male” game. Its “testosterone” culture lends itself to a high-risk, high-reward investing style: VCs are OK with a 90 percent failure rate, provided the remainder pays off big time. It’s often the overconfident founder, with an outlandish story of potential success, who gets backed. And those founders, she said, tend to be men.
“If VCs were more willing to set up smaller funds, where you can still make market-beating returns but at smaller margins across 30 to 40 percent of your portfolio companies, you would naturally see more women and founders of color in those cohorts,” Bracy theorized. “It would open up the industry to more risk-averse founders and a totally different set of companies.”
Aileen Lee told me that her firm, Cowboy Ventures, receives hundreds of inbound notes and pitches each month from AI entrepreneurs. Only a fraction are coming from women. “It’s really low,” Lee said. She told me she sometimes jokes with friends that they should create a “World Wildlife Fund” for the endangered species of women entrepreneurs.
“You did this,” Sarah Guo said across the table at Tartine Bakery, down the street from her VC firm, Conviction.
Guo drank two glasses of water, while I downed coffee and ordered a toast that turned out to be half a loaf of bread. She broke off a small piece. “The entire problem with the last era of tech is that you made women out to be a special thing. You made a generation of people take an entire class of people unseriously.”
“Do you mean ‘you’ as in the media, or—,” I began.
“Yes!” Guo said. “But also, the people writing … those books,” she said, waving her hand.
I had been chasing Guo for months, trying to schedule a meeting. People kept telling me she was someone I should know. And now she was basically telling me off. (I later told Guo that I was terrified to compliment her appearance, like her sparkling tennis bracelet or collared navy midi dress, fearing that I was reverting to old tropes.)
“The girlboss era aesthetically did not appeal to me,” she said. “I’m not embarrassed about being female. I also think it has absolutely nothing to do with what I’m trying to achieve.”
Guo belongs to a class of women at the intersection of capital and internet culture. She’s hyper-energetic, extremely online, obviously wealthy, politically astute, and pals with the guys. She doesn’t pretend that traditional power structures don’t exist, she told me. She just honestly believes that anyone can win in Silicon Valley.
She invests in defense tech companies. She hosts a podcast, No Priors, on which tech legends like Jensen Huang appear. Her husband is a prominent venture capitalist, though that does not define her. (Guo told me a story in which she and her husband, Pat Grady, showed up at a private opera event, hosted by Huang. “Are you two together?” Huang asked them. “Only for the past 10 years and four kids,” Guo replied.)
“Look, my firm is majority women,” Guo said. “And if you publish that I’ll be so annoyed with you. Because it doesn’t matter. I don’t know if you noticed, but we’re fucking winning.”
Guo’s fund has raised over $330 million and invests between $1 million to $25 million in early-stage AI companies. Its portfolio includes Harvey, Mistral, and Sierra—buzzy AI startups with multibillion-dollar valuations. It’s a hugely impressive group.
Guo told me several times that she didn’t believe she was the person to ask about powerful women. Yet during our meeting she fired off a list of names and sent more later via WhatsApp. Two were from Anthropic: Daniela Amodei, cofounder and president, and Ami Vora, chief product officer. Jayshree Ullal, chairperson and CEO of Arista Networks. Fidji Simo, most recently the CEO of AGI Deployment at OpenAI, and before that, the CEO of Instacart.
“Fidji is amazing. Very mission-driven,” Guo told me. “She’s a girl’s girl.”
“She seems well liked throughout the industry,” I said, then caught myself. “And there you go. ‘Well liked.’ Is Elon well liked?” I mused aloud.
“No, Elon is revered,” Guo corrected me. “But Fidji is both.”
Knowing of Guo’s connection to Huang, I opened an email on my iPhone and slid it across the table. In July I’d emailed Huang, asking who he thought was the most powerful woman in tech. Huang replied an hour later: Dina Powell, Ruth Porat.
“How often (if at all) do you interact with Ruth and Dina, and what impresses you most about them?” I wrote back. “See them when I’m in DC,” he replied. I tried again: “What about Gwynne Shotwell?”
“Oh my gosh, absolutely. I forgot! My bad. You are right,” Huang responded, as though a Jensen AI had wrested control of his inbox.
“Oh yeah,” Guo said when I showed her the email. “Gwynne Shotwell is amazing. Dina, too.”
“Is Gwynne powerful partly because she’s juxtaposed with Elon?”
“What does it matter?” Guo shot back.
I asked her whether spending significant time in Washington, DC, had become more essential to tech power. It’s hard to miss the parade of executives jetting to the White House. Guo said she has traveled to DC more in the past three years than in the decade prior. So yes: Politics is part of the game.
“I can’t make the US government do anything. What person has that power? I think it’s a nonsense concept,” Guo said. I decided not to interrupt her with “Elon” once again. “However, I can ask questions, and I can influence if it makes sense for me to do so,” Guo continued.
A recurring theme in my interviews is that the most powerful women are cultivating allies in DC—on behalf of their companies. When I spoke to AMD’s CEO and chairperson Lisa Su last year, she told me she doesn’t weigh in on social issues, because that’s not her “value add,” as she put it. “But when it comes to technology policy and where semiconductors are in the world, yes, we have to participate.” (Su declined to participate in this article.)
Another woman I spoke to pointed out that Mary Barra, the CEO of General Motors, introduced Trump at a rally at the GM Proving Ground in Milford, Michigan, in July. “She needs the company to survive,” this person said. “Now is definitely not the time to use your dry powder.”
A decade ago some large tech companies did wade into social issues; Salesforce, for example, threatened to pull back from states where LGBTQ+ rights were under fire. Now, if you’re one of the many tech companies in Texas, it’s of no concern that rates of pregnancy-related sepsis and maternal deaths have spiked since the state essentially banned abortion in 2021. You cannot stick your neck out and be a suffragette for women broadly. You have thousands of people to employ. You have deals to make.
Guo stood up to leave, and I indicated I was staying behind to work. To my surprise, she offered me a hug. “I don’t know if any of this was helpful,” she said.
I thanked her and assured her it was. “I do love your outfit, by the way.”
“Thanks! It’s vintage Fendi,” Guo said, and floated out the door.
Here’s a non-exhaustive list of powerful women, sourced largely from other women in tech: Gwynne Shotwell, Lisa Su, Michelle Zatlyn, Fei-Fei Li, Safra Catz, Meredith Whittaker, Melanie Perkins, Fidji Simo, Jayshree Ullal, Reshma Saujani, Tekedra Mawakana, Aicha Evans, Ruth Porat, Dina Powell McCormick, Sarah Friar, Amy Hood, Colette Kress, Rachel Whetstone, Liz Reid, Sarah Guo, Theresia Gouw, Timnit Gebru, and Mira Murati. Laurene Powell-Jobs, MacKenzie Scott, Melinda Gates, and Cari Tuna, if you consider the origins of their immense wealth. Kara Swisher, if you count lambasting tech bros.
And one name that came up more often than most: Daniela Amodei.
Amodei is arguably the most important person at Anthropic, the nearly $1 trillion “startup” that has created some of the most powerful large language models. She’s also one half of the Amodeis. Her brother, Dario, is CEO and a cofounder. His novella-length encyclicals on AI and nutty-professor mannerisms have captivated people in the industry and the press that covers it. Either he or the savvy communications professionals behind the duo have positioned the Amodeis as cherubic foils to a Machiavellian Sam Altman.
Given tech’s long record of power imbalances, I was curious how the benefits of the AI future will be distributed across genders. Amodei was more than happy to discuss this with me over Zoom in early August. The number one thing she tells people, she said, is: “Do not let AI become a tool that’s just for the guys. It’s our job, and the job of other model providers, to not make this technology gendered, right?”
Anthropic has a remarkable number of women in its leadership ranks. Its chief product officer, chief people officer, head of public policy, head of design for Claude, head of platform engineering, head of product for coding, head of product for research labs, and head of “personality alignment” for AI models (yes, that’s a thing) are all women.
(More recently, another woman close to Anthropic has emerged as something of a power player. According to The Information and The Wall Street Journal, Dario’s longtime partner, Cami Clark—who reportedly tried to get Jeffrey Epstein to invest in her porn company—was instrumental in connecting him with some of Anthropic’s early financial backers.)
In a June interview with Bloomberg’s Emily Chang, the Amodeis revealed that Dario largely sidesteps having direct reports, while Daniela runs the day-to-day operations. All of the leadership team reports to Daniela. “That sounds like a pretty sweet job,” Chang said to Dario, her brows raised. “It’s incredibly freeing,” Dario replied, with his trademark enthusiasm. “It lets me do all the things that I do, much more easily than I would otherwise.”
“And she does all the work?” Chang replied. Dario faltered in his response.
I asked Daniela what she makes of Chang’s points and the responses they elicited. (“I saw that interview, and it just showed me how much Dario thinks he’s a special boy,” a friend in one of my group chats fumed.)
“Dario and I very much run the company together,” Amodei insisted. “I think everyone who knows the company really well or works here knows it’s a two-person ship.” She believes it would be hard for one person to run a company at the “level of consequence” of Anthropic.
Daniela has amassed considerable financial, intellectual, and cultural capital. She is not, however, the face of Anthropic’s political agenda. That’s her brother and, more recently, Anthropic cofounder Tom Brown.
“I worked on Capitol Hill before, and I know enough to be dangerous,” she told me. “I do go to Washington, and I think it’s a matter of what’s happening in the headlines versus behind the scenes.” She engages on topics like trust and safety or how AI will impact future generations—things viewed “not necessarily as the most sexy,” she explained.
And who arbitrates the “most sexy” issues in artificial intelligence? We already know the answer to that.
With her fleet of women executives and her stated ethos of non-gendered AI, Amodei may emerge as a historic figure in Silicon Valley, depending on the fate of her company. What she’s built may signal a new era of corporate culture and achievement for women. But when I asked other people if the AI boom presents ample opportunities for women, their outlook was less rosy. Bracy, who wrote World Eaters, flatly said, “No.”
Gebru told me that “the AI industry is worse for women than whatever the tech industry was in the 2010s.” People still don’t want to listen to women, she said, and many of the most hyped companies are still led by men.
She is correct. Outliers like Amodei and Shotwell are the industry’s high-
profile heroines. They’re also complex examples of power. They are operational masterminds and the steady hands guiding the men in charge, much like Sheryl Sandberg was.
I thought about the powerful figures now schlepping to DC on a regular basis to try to bend the ear of a man and his army of acolytes who regularly minimize and degrade women. A few names on that non-exhaustive power list jumped out at me as women who aren’t afraid to say exactly what they’re thinking, consequences be damned. Significantly more women told me it’s not worth it to post their politics on X or to say the spicy truth in interviews or to try to be a podcast bro. It would compromise their focus on the work.
Women now possess all kinds of capital, which is in itself remarkable. But they are choosing not to fully enter the matrix. And really, why would they? What awaits them on the other side?
Gebru was still going, and now she flipped my question on its head. “How successful women are in AI is not my measure of power or success for women. Why do women have to join the terrible thing men are doing? They’re accelerating harm. They’re talking about littering the world with data centers. The kinds of arguments I thought were fringe, like AGI, they’ve mainstreamed.”
“What does power mean? Does it mean you have to trample on your own people in a terrible system in order to succeed in your career?” Gebru said to me over the phone.
She was sitting somewhere outside, in Boston, and kids were shrieking in the background. At one point she apologized for the noise and asked if I could hear her. I assured her I was listening.

New book by Princess Diana's brother prompts war of words with King Charles III
LONDON — A new book published Tuesday by the brother of the late Princess Diana has made headlines around the world with its damning allegations about Diana's ex-husband, now King Charles III, and reopened decades-old wounds within Britain's royal family.
In "Swan Song: Diana, My Sister," Charles Spencer alleges that he argued with the then-Prince Charles over palace plans for Prince William and Prince Harry, then 15 and 12, to walk behind their mother's coffin during her 1997 funeral procession.
Spencer says he told Charles that Diana, who was killed in a car crash in Paris at the age of 36, would not have wanted her boys to undergo the ordeal. He claims the prince "went ballistic" during the argument, and told him: "Rest assured, we'll forget her soon enough." Spencer also accuses Charles of having "contempt" for his ex-wife and of sounding "elated" after her death.
After excerpts of the book were published last week, Buckingham Palace responded with a strongly-worded statement that's rare by the measured standards of the royal household.
"His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and color memory in ways others do not recognize, even many years after such a loss," it said.
Spencer has stood by his claims, insisting to the BBC that he is telling the truth. On the royal rebuttal, he asked: "Is he furious? Is he furious or is he embarrassed?"
War of words draws renewed attention to Charles and Diana's stormy history
Charles, then 32, married 20-year-old Lady Diana Spencer in a lavish ceremony at St. Paul's Cathedral in 1981. The couple divorced in 1996, and a decade later Charles married Camilla Parker Bowles, now Queen Camilla.
Charles Spencer, the 9th Earl Spencer, has long clashed with the royals over their treatment of his older sister.
Tensions between the palace and the Spencer family following her death were dramatized in the film "The Queen" and the Netflix series "The Crown."
In a searing eulogy at his sister's funeral, Spencer vowed that her "blood family" would carry on her "imaginative and loving" legacy in raising her two sons. The speech was widely considered a swipe at the royal family.
At the time, many in Britain and beyond felt Queen Elizabeth II and the royals were too slow to acknowledge the global outpouring of grief over Diana's death and that the monarchy was deeply out of touch with the public mood.
Charles Spencer says press treatment of Harry echoes that of his mother
The royals have spent decades putting that period of crisis behind them. The warmer, more personable approach of William and Harry — and, in recent years, the king — is a legacy of that time.
In his book, Spencer also criticized the royals for what he described as a "lack of obvious care" for the then 12-year-old Harry.
He recounted how "tiny, and slight, and bereft" his nephew looked after the funeral. "He needed Diana's hugs, of course, and they would forever be denied him," he wrote. "But instead of calm and nurture, he was allowed to spin out of control."
Some critics have questioned why Spencer felt the need to revisit the pain and trauma 30 years on.
The aristocrat said he wanted to write down his own thoughts and memories about Diana, "once and for all, rather than having the discomfort of again reading the opinions of others, many of which are based on untruths."
Asked if the relationship between the press and Harry and his wife, Meghan, mirrors the way the media treated his sister, Spencer told the BBC: "(Diana) was really brought low by all that criticism. I suppose it's a pity when I see echoes of that now."
Penguin Press said the book will be published globally and translated into 12 languages.

Srinagar, Sep 22: BJP legislators staged a walkout from the Jammu and Kashmir Legislative Assembly on Tuesday after disrupting Question Hour amid heated exchanges with ruling party members.
The developments came after BJP MLA S S Salathia asked the Speaker to direct the government to respond to issues and questions raised by BJP members during the first day of the autumn session.
Amid the exchanges, a Congress MLA accused the BJP members of repeatedly disrupting the proceedings and said the party had “ended the dignity of the House.”
“We come here to raise public issues, but they disrupt the House,” the legislator said.
Speaker Abdul Rahim Rather urged members to maintain order and assured them that adequate time would be provided to discuss the issue of holidays.
“I will give you appropriate time to discuss the issue of holidays in the House, but allow the House to run smoothly,” Rather said.
The Speaker also cautioned members against bypassing parliamentary procedure while raising issues.
“Everybody is trying to act like a Speaker here. I won’t allow this to happen here,” Rather said, adding that there was a proper procedure for discussing issues and seeking answers from the government.
The BJP members subsequently staged a walkout from the House after disrupting Question Hour.
As the BJP legislators walked out, ruling party members, including Congress MLA Irfan Hafiz Lone, raised slogans of “Chanda Chor” inside the House.
The walkout came amid continued tension in the Assembly over remarks by NC MLA Majid Larmi regarding restoration of holidays associated with Sheikh Abdullah, which had earlier triggered noisy scenes in the House. (With inputs from Syed Rizwan Geelani)

The Centre has told the Delhi High Court that an adult can nominate a partner, including one in a non-heterosexual relationship, to make medical decisions if they become incapacitated, potentially opening the way for same-sex partners to act for each other despite existing rules not clearly recognising such arrangements.
The submission comes in a case filed by Arshiya Takkar, who has been in a relationship with her partner since 2015 and married her in New Zealand in 2023. Her plea highlighted that in the event of a medical emergency, she could be left without any legal mechanism to make critical decisions for her partner, despite the couple having lived together in Delhi since 2018.
Responding to her plea, the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and the National Medical Commission said that allowing a competent adult to nominate a partner, including one in a same-sex relationship, to take medical decisions in the event of incapacity was “substantially capable of being accommodated within the existing legal and ethical framework”.
“Permitting a competent adult to nominate his/her partner, including a partner in a non-heterosexual/same-sex relationship, to take medical decisions on his/her behalf in the event of incapacity would constitute a logical and tailored extension of the same principle,” the affidavit said. It added that such a nomination could be subject to appropriate safeguards and the applicable law.
The Centre said decisions concerning an adult patient who is unable to make or communicate a decision must be considered in light of the nature of the treatment, the circumstances requiring the decision, the patient’s own wishes, and the legal framework governing such representation.
It further submitted that where a competent adult has nominated or otherwise authorised their partner to act on their behalf in the event of incapacity, “there appears to be no medical or ethical rationale for excluding such person merely on account of the sex, gender or sexual orientation of the partners or because their union does not fall within the conventional understanding of marriage...”.
The Centre also said it recognised and respected the constitutional guarantees of dignity, privacy, autonomy, equality and individual choice available to all persons, including members of the LGBTQIA+ community.
The petition is likely to come up for hearing on Thursday (September 17, 2026).
Ms. Takkar, in her petition filed last year through advocates Manjira Dasgupta and Bhargav Ravindran Thali, highlighted the lack of a clear legal framework or common law recognising “partners in a union”, making it difficult to provide consent during medical treatment or emergencies.
The plea stated that the existing regulation, Clause 7.16 of the Indian Medical Council (Professional Conduct, Etiquette, and Ethics) Regulations, 2002, mandates consent for medical procedures or treatment from a “husband or wife, parent or guardian in the case of a minor, or the patient himself”.
“This lack of explicit recognition of partners in a union renders the petitioner effectively powerless to make critical medical decisions for her partner, or vice versa, a right readily available to heterosexual partners under the current regulations,” it stated.
The petition contended that despite the Supreme Court directive for a high-powered committee to address entitlements of LGBTQIA+ couples, including their recognition as “family” for medical decision-making, the authorities have failed to take expeditious measures.
“This inaction leaves the petitioner and other same-sex couples vulnerable and unable to exercise the fundamental right to care for each other in medical emergencies,” the plea said.

Fiji has declared an HIV national emergency after data showed one in 60 people in the South Pacific island nation is now estimated to have the bloodborne virus.
The country says it is boosting testing and treatment efforts to fight a surge in new infections, which have increased 12-fold over the last 15 years, according to the Joint United Nations Program on HIV and Aids (UNAIDS).
Latest figures showed there was about 9,000 people living with HIV in 2025 in a country which has less than a million people, according to the UN agency. It said only 39 per cent of patients knew their HIV status and just 22 per cent were receiving antiretroviral treatment.
Fiji said that one in every 60 adults in the country has HIV, compared with one in 167 five years ago.
"This means HIV is now a national crisis and the government is treating it like one. No more business as usual," Fiji's Health Minister Antonio Lalabalavu said in a video statement on Facebook. “More people in Fiji are living with HIV than ever before.” The government said it was finding more cases because its testing efforts are reaching more people. It will provide more free testing, clean needles for drug users and free treatment for people who test positive.

ED files prosecution complaint against former chairman, 6 others in CGPSC case
The 99-page prosecution complaint, along with documents running into around 3,700 pages, was filed before the Special PMLA Court in Raipur
The Enforcement Directorate (ED) on Tuesday filed a prosecution complaint against seven persons, including former Chhattisgarh Public Service Commission (CGPSC) chairman Taman Singh Sonwani, in a money laundering case linked to alleged irregularities in recruitment examinations conducted during the previous Congress government.
The 99-page prosecution complaint, along with documents running into around 3,700 pages, was filed before the Special PMLA Court in Raipur, ED counsel Sourabh Kumar Pande said.
Besides Sonwani, the complaint names businessman Shravan Goyal, then CGPSC Deputy Controller (Examination) Lalit Ganvir, Utkarsh Chandrakar, nephew of K K Chandravanshi, a former personal assistant to former chief minister Bhupesh Baghel, Vikas Chandrakar, Anil Chandrakar and Chetan Borghariya, a state services officer who was posted as an officer on special duty (OSD) in the office of former chief minister Baghel.
Borghariya is the seventh accused named in the prosecution complaint.
This is the first prosecution complaint filed by the federal agency in the case.
According to ED, Goyal allegedly gave the bribe to an NGO, Gramin Vikas Samiti (GVS), associated with Sonwani, as part of an arrangement to facilitate the selection of his son and daughter-in-law in CGPSC examinations.
The agency has also alleged that when the CGPSC recruitment rules were amended in 2021, Ganvir played a role in removing the word “nephew” from the definition of “family”, which allegedly facilitated the selection of relatives of then chairman Sonwani.
Utkarsh and Vikas Chandrakar allegedly arranged preliminary and mains examination papers for candidates and collected money from them, the agency has alleged.
Sonwani was arrested by ED in July this year in the money laundering investigation that stems from an FIR registered by the Chhattisgarh Economic Offences Wing (EOW), a subsequent complaint filed by the CBI in July 2024 and three chargesheets filed in 2025. The suspects have been accused of involvement in corruption, question paper leaks and manipulation of examinations conducted by the commission in 2020 and 2021 for posts including deputy collectors and deputy superintendents of police.
According to ED, question papers were leaked and the selection process was manipulated in exchange for illegal gratification to facilitate the selection of Sonwani’s relatives and other favoured candidates for senior government posts, including deputy collector and deputy superintendent of police.
Sonwani was also arrested by the CBI in 2024. The CBI case was registered after the Bharatiya Janata Party defeated the Congress in the state elections and formed the government in Chhattisgarh in November 2023.

Developing El Niño becomes strongest on record weeks before expected peak
- Published
The developing El Niño climate phenomenon is now the strongest on record, according to scientists monitoring Pacific Ocean temperatures.
Daily sea surface temperatures in a key region of the central-eastern Pacific were 3.05C above average on 19 September - exceeding the previous record of 3.02C set during the very strong El Niño of 2015.
Some longer-term measures of El Niño have not yet hit record levels but this is likely to change, with the peak not expected until later this year.
El Niño can cause major shifts in weather patterns around the world, with the Met Office saying many of the expected impacts are already being felt.
- El Niño set to be 'strongest in living memory', says Met Office 
  - Published21 August
- What is El Niño and why could it mean record temperatures? 
  - Published11 June
What is El Niño and how is it measured?
El Niño is a naturally-occurring pattern, which happens about every two to seven years and tends to last for around a year.
Trade winds that typically blow from east to west across the Pacific Ocean can weaken or even reverse, allowing warm water to spread eastwards.
Heat is then released from the ocean into the atmosphere which can boost global temperatures and drive changes in weather patterns around the world.
Forecasters track the development of El Niño by watching temperatures in a key region of the Pacific Ocean. When these are consistently 0.5C above normal, an El Niño is declared.
There are different ways of measuring the strength of El Niño, however.
The records that have now been broken relate to daily measurements of sea surface temperature compared with the long term historical average.
This is called the Oceanic Niño Index (ONI).
Many scientists - including forecasters in the USA and Australia - also consider an alternative measure known as the Relative Oceanic Niño Index (RONI).
This measures how warm the key El Niño region is relative to the rest of the tropical oceans, meaning it takes into account the background warming caused by climate change.
By the RONI index the current El Niño is not yet a record-breaker - but it is likely that more announcements will follow in the coming weeks.
Professor Adam Scaife, Head of Long Range Prediction at the Met Office, said: "We have been signalling for months that the developing El Niño will be an unprecedented event.
"The fact that it has already exceeded previous records – with several weeks to go before it peaks later this year – shows the enormity of this El Niño."
Impacts of El Niño already being felt globally
Every El Niño is different, therefore impacts on global weather patterns are not guaranteed.
And the unprecedented strength of this El Niño does not necessarily mean it will have unprecedented impacts on the weather.
Professor Scaife said: "Scientists are still assessing whether the impacts will be in proportion to its magnitude, but we are already seeing expected effects worldwide."
El Niño increases the odds of storms and floods in some regions and of drought and wildfires in others.
El Niño years tend to bring below-average monsoon rainfall in India, which is already being reflected in this year's data.
Statistics from the India Meteorological Department show that, until 22 September the southwest monsoon had brought 15% less rain than normal.
Another typical impact of El Niño is reduced hurricane activity in the Atlantic due to changes in wind patterns high in the atmosphere.
So far in 2026 there have been no Atlantic hurricanes, setting a new record for the latest date without a hurricane forming since satellite monitoring of storms began.
Other possible effects - some of which are already being felt - include the increased risk of floods in coastal parts of Ecuador, Peru and the southern USA, and the enhanced threat of drought and wildfires in Brazil, Australia and Indonesia.
These weather impacts can have significant knock on effects for on crop yields, food security and economies around the globe.
Will there be an impact on UK weather?
The UK is thousands of miles from the tropical Pacific and so the effects of El Niño tend to be less clear-cut than in other regions.
However, it does bring the increased chance of wet and stormy conditions across north-west Europe during the late autumn and early winter.
A forecast released by the Met Office this autumn stated that there were already "signals for increased rainfall and storminess in autumn here in the UK", especially into November and December.
The winter of 2015 and 2016, which coincided with a very strong El Niño, brought a succession of major storms delivering what experts at the time described as the most extreme flooding on record.
In addition to storminess, El Niño can also be associated with UK cold spells in the late winter - but the link is not a strong one and the past evidence is mixed.
The so-called Big Freeze of winter 2009/2010 was, at the time, the coldest in three decades - and this coincided with an El Niño.
However, 2006/2007 was also an El Niño winter and that was unseasonably warm.
As this unprecedented El Niño approaches its likely peak towards the end of 2026, scientists will continue to monitor its development - and its impact on weather around the world.

Scotland: Sebastian Pocognoli has 'good mix' as new head coach targets winning start in Nations League
The new head coach takes charge for the first time against Slovenia in the Nations League on Saturday; Scotland are also away to N. Macedonia with games against Switzerland and Slovenia at Hampden during this international break; six newcomers are included in the Belgian's first squad
Tuesday 22 September 2026 15:42, UK
New Scotland head Sebastien Pocognoli has told Sky Sports it was time for change, believing he has a "good mix" in his first squad.
The Belgian is meeting his players for the first time this week as they train in the La Manga sunshine ahead of their Nations League opener against Slovenia.
Five players were handed their maiden full Scotland call-ups in his initial squad, with Blackburn Rovers midfielder Kristi Montgomery drafted in following the withdrawals of Kieran Tierney and Kenny McLean.
- Five newcomers included in Pocognoli's first Scotland squad
