New Delhi, Sep 22: Union Home Minister and Minister of Cooperation Amit Shah today inaugurated the 3rd National Conference of Anti-Narcotics Task Force (ANTF) Heads of States/UTs in New Delhi. On this occasion, the Union Home Minister launched Television Commercials (TVCs) to spread awareness against narcotic substances and laid the foundation stone of new zonal complexes of the Narcotics Control Bureau (NCB) in Lucknow and Dehradun. During the event, the best-performing ANTF of States and UTs were also honoured. In addition, the Union Home Minister launched the newly designed website of the NCB. In the two-day conference organised by the NCB, ANTF heads from 36 States and Union Territories, along with representatives of concerned government departments and other stakeholders, are participating.
In his address, Union Home Minister Amit Shah said that under the leadership of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, we have for the past five years been taking one step after another in an effort to achieve the difficult goal of a drug free India. He said that the time has now come to deliver a decisive blow against narcotics, which have become the most serious threat to the country and the world, and to achieve victory through collective efforts. Shah said that by 31 December 2029, we will collectively succeed in uprooting the drug trade from India.
Shah said that in the past five years we have achieved success against several challenges such as terrorism in Kashmir, insurgency in the Northeast and the problem of Naxalism. The Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) with the cooperation of all the states, we have ended these major problems that have confronted the country for decades. He said that the fight against drugs is the most difficult of all battles, but we cannot abandon this fight. Shah said that to build a Viksit Bharat by 2047, to save future generations and to connect the youth with India’s development, the only option before us is to make India drug-free. We will have to fight this problem unitedly and with passion, and we must achieve victory.
Union Home Minister said that the ‘Vision Document 2026-2029’ is like the Gita for all those involved in this fight. This Vision Document has been prepared with great effort after discussions with more than 35 departments. He said that we have prepared the complete roadmap after taking suggestions from all stakeholders, and it has been given to everyone with definite targets. Targets and timelines have also been fixed in it. The Home Minister said that it will also be reviewed after some time. Shah added that the MHA or the NCB cannot do all this alone. We all have to fight this battle with top priority and complete dedication, and we have to win it as well.
Shah said that it should be our shared responsibility and resolve to end this menace of drugs that is hollowing out future generations. Our resolve should be that we will not allow even one gram of drugs to enter the country from anywhere in the world, nor will even one gram of drugs go from our country to the world. He said that we have prepared this roadmap with a resolve for the welfare of youth across the world. Shah said that we will have to work for a drug-free India with sensitivity, with an understanding of its importance, and as the topmost priority. He said – Meet once the parents and siblings of even one young person afflicted by drugs. Until you meet them, intensity in this fight cannot arise in you. A weeping, wailing mother, a younger sister, and a boy who ranked in the top 10 in the Class 10 board examination is slowly moving towards death, while his helpless parents watch. There can be no greater sorrow than this for anyone, and for us too it is a national loss. A talented child who was going to contribute to India’s development in the days to come - his life is ending midway. There can be no greater loss than this for us and for the country.
Union Home Minister said that we have to fight the battle against drugs with clarity. He said that the focal points of this fight have already been identified, and a roadmap has also been prepared at the state level to take intelligence, investigation, financial action and prosecution in one direction. Shah said that in the first ANTF conference we had created an institutional mechanism and strengthened it. In the second ANTF conference, we discussed capability, action and execution in order to convert that mechanism into action. Today, the third ANTF conference will convert this roadmap into a decisive battle.
Shah said that whatever we have done so far is not enough. Until the Principal of every school, the Patwari of the village, the PSI of the police station, the Director General of Police and the Chief Secretary of the state, and even the Home Secretary of the Government of India, work in one direction, we will not achieve success. He said that today’s conference is the most important because this time we will move forward towards complete victory by fixing Target, Timeline and Accountability.
Union Home Minister said that we now have to move from Meeting to Mission, from Reporting to Result, from Seizure to the dismantling of Networks, and from Case to Conviction. He said that until all departments of the state governments and the Government of India engage in this work, we cannot move forward.
Shah said that Prime Minister Narendra Modi has set the target of building a Viksit Bharat by August 15, 2047 before the 140 crore citizens of the country, when India will be at the forefront globally in every sector. He said that if we are to achieve this goal, we cannot do so with a youth power and future generation hollowed out by addiction. He stated that India is the youngest country in the world, which is why the threat is also the largest for us in the global context. This is our necessity because the health, skills, labour, and thinking capacity of the youth alone can lead the country to that goal, and drugs damage all four of these capacities.
Union Home Minister said that for emerging challenges such as synthetic drugs, diversion of precursor chemicals, new communication technologies, dark-net, drug markets, crypto, dead-drop delivery systems, and international drug networks, a team of officers who think 'out-of-the-box' should be constituted in every state, and success should be shared and implemented across the entire nation.
Shah stated that the Vision Document 2026–2029 rests on four pillars: Enforcement, intelligence & operations, Control of precursor & synthetic drugs, Demand & harm reduction, and Capacity building & coordination. Over 100 targets have been categorized across these four pillars. Under the target of registering 1 lakh Nashamukt Mitras outlined in the Vision Document, various ministries have registered 46,780 Nashamukt Mitras so far, and they are already operational. To take this campaign to the grassroots level, Nashamukt Mitras will visit 10 lakh schools, colleges, and institutions across the country in the coming days to caution the youth and sensitize campus directors.
Shah said that today we are discussing converting the roadmap into results, and the most crucial element of the brainstorming taking place over these two days is compassion. Our goal should be to transform the ANTF into an ‘Anti-Narco Mission Command’, and State Chief Secretaries will need to adopt a different approach regarding manpower, technology, budget, and other resources. The Home Minister added that the Government of India is emphasizing technology and forensics in capacity building.
Union Home Minister and Minister of Cooperation stated that instead of maintaining a seizure-centric approach, we must move forward with the objective of dismantling entire networks. Our priority, along with backward-forward investigation, must also include financial investigation and tracing digital links. Our strike must hit the funds earned by drug dealers. Shah said that cartels must be targeted at three levels: the entry point, the inter-state distribution system, and the local sales networks within districts. Further, districts will be categorized into three clusters: those where drugs are manufactured or enter the country, those serving as transportation corridors, and those where consumption takes place.
Union Home Minister stated that we must increase the utilization of PITNDPS, as there is a strong need for it in the country. A complete roadmap from investigation to conviction must be formulated in coordination with public prosecutors. A dedicated campaign must be launched to deport foreign accused present in India and blacklist them so they can never re-enter the country. Moreover, the fugitives who are supplying drugs to the country from abroad should be caught and brought before the Indian courts. By targeting borders and production centres, all loopholes must be plugged. Every ANTF should integrate the entire process of converting information to actionable intelligence into the work culture of their respective state police force. The Home Minister expressed confidence that we will succeed in this fight against drugs and emerge victorious.
Participation in this national conference will assist states, departments, and agencies under the 'Whole of Government Approach' to move forward with renewed resolve to effectively combat drug trafficking across the country over the next three years.
The deliberations held during the conference will help strengthen the effective enforcement of drug control laws and make the strategies adopted to protect the country's youth from drugs more impactful. This national event will provide an effective platform to bolster a future-ready partnership between the NCB and ANTFs of States and Union Territories to tackle drug abuse and fulfil the pledge of a Nasha Mukt Bharat.

What Were My Dreams Trying to Tell Me?
To make sense of my deepest experiences, I needed a new way of talking about the soul.
When I was 20 years old, I started to sense a hole inside me. The feeling was utterly concrete, though the result of no medical condition that any of the various doctors I saw could identify. The hole felt like a viscous emptiness—a paradox, admittedly, as any real emptiness should have felt like nothing. This was a nothing, but its nothingness very much felt like something—and something that was growing.
Accompanying this feeling of an expanding hole at the center of me was a sense that I was losing more and more of myself to it, like shoreline eroded by rising waters. To lose myself felt less like oblivion than instability. I observed in myself a new susceptibility to the opinions of others, and a new recklessness, as if some dark, decisive action might either quiet my doubts about my fundamental worth or end my longing once and for all. I recall one particularly dangerous, drunken night that had me well over the legal limit, both aware that I was getting into a car that could kill me and others, and also not believing that any of it mattered.
The onset of my devolving well-being was strange and sudden, and seemed connected to childhood in some way I couldn’t understand. I hadn’t been a tortured child but rather placid, if introverted. My parents always said that I had been easy to keep happy. It sometimes seemed to me as if the hole I was experiencing was one where some piece of my childhood had once resided.
My friends found my behavior disturbing. I was missing class in college, showing up to theater rehearsals drunk. A caring young woman I was dating could take no more of my savage, ranting mood swings and persistent despair. She broke up with me over tea at the student union and implored me to seek help. I knew she was right. Even sleep was now fraught with violent, terrifying dreams—of rocket ships out of control, conflagrations and invasions, and, yes, holes into which I would disappear. But exactly what sort of help I might need, I didn’t know.
I confided my woes to a friend who’d grown up on a farm in Kentucky. He never missed Sunday Mass, and when I told him about the hole inside me, he pulled a copy of The Seven Storey Mountain from his bag and handed it to me. Thomas Merton, he said, had written about something similar. It was what had led him to leave the world and become a monk.
I found deep resonance in the book’s harrowing account of Merton’s time at Cambridge and Columbia—the intense restlessness and emptiness, the disgust and torpor and despair. But Merton’s solution was theistic: a turn to God that I could only read as naive and distorting. I didn’t have any interest in God. Even the passages that approached the specificity of my own experience were charged with personification that read as anachronistic at best:
The room was very quiet. It was rather dark, too. And as I lay in bed, in my weariness and pain and disgust, I felt for a moment the shadow of another visitor pass into the room.
It was death, that came to stand by my bed.
I kept my eyes closed, more out of apathy than anything else. But anyway, there was no need to open one’s eyes to see the visitor, to see death. Death is someone you see very clearly with eyes in the center of your heart: eyes that see not by reacting to light, but by reacting to a kind of a chill from within the marrow of your own life.
I knew this experience: a central chill, a lightlessness connected to the doomed feeling of some ultimate end. But I resisted any characterization that departed from the fundamental sensation itself—of a growing hole inside me. For no reason I knew, I was convinced that remaining honest with myself about this basic fact was the only thing I could do to help myself.
My parents were worried. They flew out to visit me at school and figure out what was wrong. Over a meal they prepared for me in a hotel room with a kitchen, I confided in them. There was a hole inside me that I needed to address, I said. They were understandably perplexed. My mother found me a psychiatrist, an avuncular Brit who was more interested in my sex life than my interior void, which I insisted was more real than he seemed willing to allow. But something important endured from the handful of sessions I had with him. A volume on the shelf over his left ear drew my fascination, and would soon fill weeks of my life: Freud’s The Interpretation of Dreams.
That book began a process in me, what I’ve often called “curiosity” when I’ve told this story, but which is probably better described as a form of relationship. The nightly tumult of disturbing dreams persisted, and even if I couldn’t be sure whether Freud was right about how to make sense of them, simply attempting to do so seemed to help. Paying attention made it easier to remember my dreams, and to remember more of them. In one, I was carefully drawing an empty circle on a page of the Quran that my grandparents had given me as a boy, a circle through which—impossibly—I could reach and touch cool water. I awoke with the feeling that the hole inside me might be leading to something better, however unknown.
Even so, it wasn’t until I mentioned that I was interested in dreams to a teacher I admired that I started to keep a detailed nightly log. This teacher had done a great deal of dream-work, and suggested that I tie a pencil to my finger to remind me, in those brief moments of stirring between sleep cycles, to write down whatever fragments were stirring in hypnagogic consciousness. So I did. What resulted was a daily haul of interior riches. The vividness of my unadulterated hopes and sorrows, the unusual expansiveness and wonder I experienced by night, lived on in the often-paradoxical images I would recall throughout the day.
My study of Freud led to a similar scouring of the work of other psychoanalysts—and, later, mystics such as Emanuel Swedenborg, Ibn Arabi, and Rabbi Nachman—for clues about what kind of sense to be making of my dreams. In my final year of college, I encountered, in a late work of Carl Jung’s, the advice to treat dreams as meaningful psychic events, a technique to facilitate what Jung called their “compensatory” function—balancing the biases and limitations of one’s conscious attitudes. I took this to mean treating a dream’s images as real in their own right. Whether doing so had any such balancing effect on me, I can’t be sure. But my persistent despair seemed to be dimming; the hole inside me felt different the more I was able to gaze patiently into it for whatever was coming through. The dream-work was paying dividends, though what exactly was paying them out, I had no clue.
I know how what I’m about to share is likely to come off; it isn’t the first time I’ve spoken it aloud. I started to dream of things that hadn’t happened yet, to “see” things at night that then appeared in my life during the day. One of the earliest and most startling of these uncanny doublings took place in my first year after college. I was living and working in a small town in the Tuscan countryside, without a phone, before the internet. I dreamed that a friend I knew in Paris showed up on my doorstep with skis on his back. Two days later, I awoke to the sound of my name being called from down in the piazza, outside my front window. I opened the worn balcony doors to find the very friend I’d dreamed of; he’d gotten my Italian address from a mutual friend and seen that the town I was living in wasn’t too far out of the way as he made the trip from Rome up to the city in the Alps where he planned to spend a few days skiing. I resisted speaking of what had happened, lest I be impelled to name whatever in me had seized my bewildered attention.
The Tuscan episode was not the last time dream and day seemed to cross wires. Years later, I would dream of a terrorist attack on Manhattan two days before 9/11, and of a malign, cough-inducing fog slowly engulfing the world several weeks before the eruption of the coronavirus into my (and the world’s) awareness—improbable coincidences I struggled to accept as such. And yet, these visions became the occasion to doubt any picture of the universe that failed to make room for what could only be experienced as a kind of magic.
If the prognosticating mode had been the only benefit to accrue from my attention to my dreams, I might not have been so diligent in my recordkeeping. After all, I wasn’t seeing stock prices or lottery numbers, the only rationale many might have accepted for my habit of destroying every good night’s rest. For at that point, I was waking up every 45 minutes to reach for the bedside pad on which I made notes about whatever was moving around inside me. But my night work was opening up creative vistas. One mentor, well-versed in working with the unconscious, suggested that it was enlarging the space of what she kept calling—despite my confusion about what she really meant by it—my psyche.
Indeed, a growing spaciousness was now my sense of the interior core where the hole had opened up. The hole itself wasn’t gone, but it had changed character, less a wound now than an opening, though I couldn’t always tell the difference. And yet, the trajectory seemed to be shifting. That pliant, receptive brightness bearing the imprint of something more than just my name, the self, began to feel heightened, enlarged. I had learned that some cultures conceived of the self as containing two parts: a smaller, individual, daily self, and a larger, multiple, primordial one. This greater self, it was believed, was the one that dreamed. Something about this way of thinking felt more useful—and more reflective of my experience—than any of the latest studies in neuroscience I read about the physiological functions of dreams.
Psyche : Greek for “soul.” Which felt like a more appropriate frame of reference—despite my continued resistance to the language of theism—for experiences that so evidently defied the materialist doctrines of my late-20th-century education. To privilege the Newtonian model of classical mechanics—one object pushing or pulling another, all the way down to the molecules that formed consciousness—over the actual data of my experience felt like intellectual laziness. I understood that others would see my willingness to abide more patiently in the mystery as irrational. My usage of the Greek term started to give way to its English corollary. The word soul seemed to make better sense of whatever was expanding inside me, a rising that was also a deepening, married to the uncanny knowing of what seemed like prognostication, and, more valuably, to a natural empathy for others. And in case this comes off as more altruistic than seems reasonable: Less blinded by myself, more porous to others, I found, too, that I was becoming a better writer.
Soul was, for me then, a mode of being mostly experienced in images by night that shaped my understanding by day—for example, that a close friend was like the abandoned dog I dreamed he was, long neglected by his family, never allowed into the house; an image that helped me navigate his touchiness, providing readier access to the wellspring of loving loyalty that coursed beneath his habitual choler. I found in the use of soul a capaciousness that not only accounted for this richer relationship to others and the world—and to myself—but served as a bridge to deeper mystery, and to a new patience that allowed me to acclimate to it.
There were other benefits, too. Just as the vital, vivid stuff of my brain’s nightlife enriched my being—to use a word that joined soul in the lexicon of descriptive terms of dubious provenance—so did my immersion in dream dross seem to feed my capacities with language. There was a stronger tether now between word and thing, a tether, paradoxically, that operated simultaneously in many directions and layers. The webbed, protean mode of associative thinking—one thing reaching for another, in opposing vectors at once—was less an effort than a reflex, more instinctive than the ordinal fixity of my usual habits of mind. Shakespeare, whom I’d long struggled to apprehend, now made easier sense, even as the experience of reading him felt like perpetual entry into undiscovered country, the phonetic expatiations, the dense semantic clusters, the sounds and images opening up more and more effortlessly into a particular state of absorptive flow, a pleasing emotional and intellectual static that I took to calling “linguistic space.”
I started taking a yoga class on the Upper West Side. Our becalming teacher spent the better part of our weekly hour teaching us to meditate. Setting aside my irritation with her hushed and holy tones, I found myself growing more susceptible to her instructions. I could catch a gap between thoughts that felt curiously similar to a rich blankness that resulted from hours spent in linguistic space. The fixed point of focus on the breath sharpened my mind and filled it with something closer to light than thought. On my own, I began to sit—sometimes for hours—in this pregnant blankness, exhibiting a facility for what the yoga teacher called “practice” that I couldn’t explain.
My weekly hour with that yoga teacher sparked an interest in meditation that led to weeks, and years, of working with other instructors of inner techniques. I learned to visualize and hold in memory shapes derived from Gnostic practices and colors derived from Sufi ones. Intoning Abulafia’s list of Hebrew names for God at the proper pitch and volume shook the bones in my ear and nerves along my neck. Calm was promised, and often followed, though I wondered whether this said more about my susceptibility to suggestion than the practices themselves. Sometimes what followed was stranger. Once, as I sat in a darkened room at dusk, observing the breath going in and out of me, I felt that breath begin to breathe itself. In the half shadows, with my eyes closed, a startling brightness waxed and waned with the movement of air. What was this light? I wondered. Was this just the room’s faint light filtering through my eyelids, brightening and dimming as my pupils dilated and contracted with each breath? If so, was this suggestion too? I would come to no definitive answer. The inner light continued to strobe.
If it was all suggestion, I didn’t mind. It was getting me further than faith had. From Meister Eckhart I learned to recognize in my meditative blankness a silence clean of longing, one that, if I could remain in it, would release an astonishing vitality. Others I studied with found it strange that my interest in meditation would be piqued by dream-work and quickened by pentameter. They sometimes remarked that what I was up to resembled anthropology more than devotion. They were only partly right. To me, it was all a study in being, or soul, or spirit (the latest addition to my lexicon)—which is to say, an inquiry into the substance and nature of the interior life.
My reading, too, reflected the scavenging of a magpie in search of material from which to build its nest: the Phaedrus and Patanjali and Mulla Sadra; Being and Time one month, Mathnawi the next. What exactly I thought I was doing was not a matter of concern as long as I kept to myself about it. What I’m compressing into paragraphs here took so much longer, of course, and was hardly as sequential as telling makes it sound. I kept at it for the reward of the work itself. I had experiences of rapture (and sorrow) so deep, of pleasures so unprecedented, it was sometimes hard to return to the dishes and the rent. But I had studied with a remarkable Vedic teacher who warned me about seeking states rather than the truth. “What is the truth?” I once asked him as we sauntered along a Tennessee creek. He pulled his orange robe tighter against a rising spring wind. He was too smart to oblige. “The truth is not like knowledge about that tree,” he said, pointing to a blooming magnolia. “Only the tree knows its truth.” I didn’t want to pretend I understood him. “You write stories,” he said. “Inside the story is a meaning that is the reason for it. Not words that carry it, but the wordless substance of its truth you take away.”
Despite my customary reticence about such things, I had occasions to compare notes with fellow travelers. One evening, at a fundraising function downtown, I found myself sharing martinis with a physician whose lived-in eloquence about his Zen practice felt like an opening. I was not expecting the lesson in brain science he proceeded to impart: I’d become addicted, he said, to activating certain parts of my cerebral cortex. Like an addict—I flinched at that word—I was pulling on neurological switches, training my brain to release its own pleasure chemicals through a growing grab bag of inner tricks. Clearly he didn’t approve. I was too embarrassed to ask why, even as I recalled my teacher’s warning not to chase states, but rather to seek the wordless substance of truth. I resisted the physician’s account even as I couldn’t ignore the unease it stirred in me.
My fellow traveler was right, at least as far as neuroscience went. Studies were beginning to show that meditation—a loose term for the various practices of inner focus I was involved with—activated and deactivated specific parts of the human brain. In the 1990s, the neuroscientist Andrew Newberg studied advanced Tibetan monks and Franciscan nuns as they entered deep meditative states. The results were strikingly similar. In both groups, areas of the brain believed to be responsible for orienting us in space and time showed markedly decreased activity, as if the neural basis for the boundary between self and other had gone quiet. They were using very different techniques, but the results, neurologically speaking, were nearly indistinguishable. Each group, however, described the experience differently: the nuns as a feeling of union with Christ, the monks as a state of emptiness.
I knew enough about Buddhism to recognize in that word, emptiness, something very different from the hole that had opened up inside me during early adulthood. For the Buddhist, perception of the nature of reality discloses the identity of emptiness with form, and form with emptiness. It’s a perception described in other traditions by other means, and sometimes, in Christianity, as an annihilation of the individual personality in the presence of God. The maps and words and techniques were different; somehow, the underlying experience itself, beyond words or ideas, was the same.
Not quite in the words of my Vedic teacher: The brain scans were a story containing a truth known only to the one inside them.
For a long time, all of this felt like little more than a motley, life-enhancing assortment, which is not to downplay the valuable place it had in my life. Rightly or wrongly, I attributed the return of my fundamental stability after the harrowing years of early adulthood—and the return of the placid, placable self I’d known much earlier in life—to my commitment to daily practice. I would come to think of inner work as an adult corollary to the joyous absorption of childhood play. I’d found a way to play again, I concluded, and somehow this had seemed to “fill” the hole again.
But the life of the spirit was not what I took my real life to be. I was a writer. I wanted to know the broken world that was, not the healed one that could be. I had no fundamental interest in escaping the human condition. To the extent that spirit—or soulfulness—anchored my curiosity, quickened my perceptions, deepened my empathy, I rationalized its creative and analytical utility. In truth, something less tangible than optimization bound me to practice. It kept me in the company of more eternal conundrums, questions of consciousness and origin and meaning for which, of course, I expected no answer. But proximity to the unknown—living contact with it, if you will—seemed like a worthy form of knowledge.
In this, I was like many friends who took psychedelics; I wanted to recover the awe and mystery I recognized in their accounts when they shared them. For the most part, though, I was still doing what my teacher had warned me against—chasing states. In part, this was a function of resisting meaning. I had been too respectful of my teacher back then to tell him I wasn’t sure that a story’s meaning mattered to me the way he assumed it would. But I felt the slow accretion of a wordless substance inside me, not well-being or certainty or the rapture of some fugitive sublime, but something I might call intimacy: intimacy with an inwardness spied only indirectly, whose purer acquaintance I seemed to be making very slowly indeed.
With the hindsight of decades, I can track a tectonic shift away from the visible to something more diffuse and sustaining, an interior through line that has both warned me against the tyranny of acquisition—of things, of states—and provided the means of finding sustenance in absence. Whatever this is, whatever name I might give it, I can’t deny that it all seems to have proceeded from that perception of a hole I felt or imagined when I was younger. William James might have called it a “sick soul”; I still don’t feel entirely confident about what word to use for the continuity that I’ve found or constructed, though some word has always been necessary. I had spent years resisting every vocabulary that exceeded the raw data of sensation, only to find that this austerity, too, had to be exceeded.
Too much of what mattered most in my own life had remained unspoken not because it was unreal, but because I did not know how to bring it into language without betraying it. For decades, I steered conversations away from these inner experiences, obedient to the rule that such things could not be talked about without sounding foolish or deranged. But my reticence began to feel like capitulation to falseness. It took me years to understand that my silence was not only protective but deforming—for without others to hear it, the still, small voice within was so much harder to discern. And yet, the silence was not my own to break. With so little room in our common life for such things, we have no common language for them either.
Ralph Waldo Emerson knew the problem. In “The Over-Soul,” he wrote that language could not paint this “subtile” order of our experience in its own colors; but he knew how important it was to keep trying. The great Russian novelists knew it too, treating soul not as a word reserved for Sundays, but as the moral substance of life. I’ve found myself mourning not their metaphysics but their seriousness, their acceptance of the inscrutable boundlessness of the inner life—unruly, morally consequent—as a subject for public speech.
What matters to me now is less the defense of any particular term than the search for a language in which such things can be spoken of seriously, in fiction and elsewhere, without piety or diagnosis. Without a language for speaking openly together about the inner life, what often matters most to us remains locked away, inaccessible to the inquiry and challenge vital to all knowledge.
As I finished a draft of this essay, I had a dream. In it, I stood at the edge of a well—another hole, I realized as I made note the following morning—where there was no bucket to draw water. Around it moved countless people in a flurried hubbub, shepherds and masons and architects, all of us trying to figure out how to draw the water whose surface we could see in the faint shimmering at the bottom.
It was going to take time, I thought, before we figured it out—just as I awoke.

The first S in CSS stands for “style.” Think colors and fonts, borders and shadows, rows and columns, animations and transitions. CSS is the programming language that makes a website look pretty (or pretty ugly, often). It’s what makes this very webpage look like itself—look WIRED.
One paragraph in, a certain reader will already be smarting at my description of CSS. “It’s a style sheet language,” I can hear them say, “not a programming language.” (The second S indeed stands for “sheets,” and the C, if anyone cares, for “cascading.”) Or, “it’s a domain-specific language, not a general-purpose language.” Also, “it doesn’t execute” and, of course, “it’s not Turing complete” (although … ). Granted, CSS is a little different. There’s no compile step, and it doesn’t throw errors at run time like other languages. But that’s all beside the point.
The gatekeeping over whether CSS is a “real” programming language exists partly because it’s so simple to start—anyone can grok “background: red” right away. But simple does not mean easy, as the programmer-writer Jeremy Keith observed, and calling CSS easy or unserious should be tired by now. There were about 50 properties in the initial CSS specification in 1996 (like “color” and “font-size”); today there are at least 10 times as many (get ready for “hanging-punctuation”). The language has changed so much in three decades, and by now it is just so capable. One programmer recently re-created Doom in CSS. Others have used it to build holographic Pokémon cards and 3D-rendering engines. Cassidy Williams, who competed in this year’s inaugural March MadCSS tournament, built an experimental database-query engine entirely in CSS. When she demo’d it at Microsoft Build, even the emcees—seasoned programmers themselves—took a cheap shot at CSS. “You’re one of the people that likes it,” they snarked. “You might be the only one.”
Why is the lore of JavaScript’s creation so famous (Brendan Eich, Netscape, 10 days) and yet hardly any programmer would recognize the name of CSS creator Håkon Wium Lie? It might have something to do with Lie being a Norwegian guy with a diacritic in his name, not an American in Silicon Valley like Eich nor a Brit like Tim Berners-Lee, who invented HTML. And to be fair, JavaScript and HTML each have a chip on their own shoulder to worry about. But in the browser’s holy ternary of JavaScript-HTML-CSS, people tend to treat CSS as less than or purely decorative. Styling can be decorative—and wonderfully so—but the legibility and rich design it affords are important. People care how things look!
There’s another, uglier explanation for the CSS disrespect: It’s considered a “feminine” language. CSS developers work on the frontend—the part of a website you can actually see. There’s the obvious undertone that dealing with style and beauty is Female Work, along with the recycled joke that a CSS developer is “a freak in the style sheets.” How seriously a language is taken has knock-on effects on programmer salaries, what skills are sought out and tested in job interviews, and how accessible websites are for people with disabilities.
I recently talked to a friend, a talented backend engineer, about this. In college, she got an internship at a reputable software company in San Francisco doing entirely backend work. “I’d never expressed any interest in frontend at all, almost to an extreme extent,” she told me. “I don’t like frontend.” And yet, when she joined the company full-time after graduation, she was immediately assigned … a frontend role. She eventually worked her way back to the backend, and by now she’s used to the skepticism. “I’ve been in a million and one conversations with the classic man engineer who doesn’t think I know what I’m talking about until they work with me for six months and see my first backend project.”
I didn’t know this specific story when I first asked my friend if, maybe, I dunno, she had any experience with people assuming she was a CSS girlie. But the “coincidence” is really more of a probability. To overcorrect for such situations, she’s taken to branding herself as unmistakably backend-y. When we worked together, whenever it came time to distribute tasks among our team, she made it quite clear that she did not want to touch the frontend. (I don’t think we ever played Nose Goes, but that was the spirit.) I’d have been seriously obtuse to make the same mistake her manager did.
That same friend used to teach at Kode With Klossy, a tech camp for young women and gender-expansive students started by supermodel Karlie Kloss. Her experience there was all about the other, optimistic side of the coin: CSS can be a gateway into software for those who don’t fit the nerdy-computer-boy stereotype. “These girls would come in who had no interest in coding but just thought that Karlie Kloss was cool, and they would have so much fun,” she said. “They would grow to care more about, like, OK, how does this work?”
Within the industry, the Klossy approach is reflected in slightly better (but still really bad) gender diversity in front-of-the-frontend engineering jobs, compared to back-of-the-frontend and pure backend roles. Of a few thousand respondents in the State of CSS survey last year, 11 percent were women and 3 percent were nonbinary or gender-nonconforming. Pathetic, I know. But the State of JavaScript reported only 6 percent female and 1 percent nonbinary.
Another downstream consequence of CSS neglect is the sameness of websites across the internet, especially in Startup-land. If CSS is what makes a website look like itself, then the more recent fast fashion of frameworks is what makes them all look alike. There was a Bootstrap era, a Tailwind look, and now a distinctive Claudeslop aesthetic. Frameworks are athleisure, and if you’re not into fashion, they’re a shortcut to looking OK. Fair enough. But it does bum me out, in the same way the grayification of American cars bums me out compared to those old photos of technicolor parking lots.
WIRED was one of the first major, high-traffic sites to adopt CSS. It was a “Site for Your Eyes,” WIRED declared, and it was. But back then, there was no Flexbox nor Grid, no custom properties, and no @keyframes, transitions, and transforms for JavaScript-free animations. In this decade alone, so many powerful CSS features have landed in browsers that it’s hard to keep up. I’m no CSS expert, but I know enough to be past the overconfidence cliff in the Dunning-Kruger curve and into the valley of respect and reverence. I delight in one-off goodies like “text-wrap: pretty” (which prevents an orphan word stuck on its own line from ending a paragraph) as much as broad improvements like nested declarations. In the last few years alone, we got container queries, the :has() pseudo-class, and new color spaces like oklch(). CSS supports right-to-left languages, like Hebrew and Arabic. It interpolates positioning of the pieces of a web page to create buttery animations and gradients. And now, with if() conditionals and @function in development, even the “well, technicallyyy” explanations of why CSS isn’t a legit programming language might finally be put to rest. This is not your mother’s CSS.
The fact that CSS is simple to start, yet deep to explore and master, is part of why I love it so much. It’s the closest language we have to end-user programming, the idea that software should be customizable by any user. Style sheets are like spreadsheets in that way: A novice can build something useful in an hour, and experts can build fucking Doom.

How to add extra Ethernet ports if your router doesn't have enough
You don't need a new router to get more Ethernet ports; the solution is much simpler.
With more and more devices offering internet connectivity, running out of Ethernet ports on your router is a common frustration. A few ports aren't enough to connect your smart TV, game consoles, desktop computers, NAS drives, home office equipment and more. If you're maxed out, you might assume you need a new router, but that's not the case.
The real solution is simpler, more affordable and takes only minutes to set up: an Ethernet switch. This (often compact) plug-and-play device connects to one of your router's LAN ports and immediately expands your wired network capacity. Depending on the model, a single switch can add four, seven, 15 or even more ports to your setup — all without replacing your router or reconfiguring your network.
This matters because while Wi-Fi has improved significantly over the years, a wired Ethernet connection still delivers a better, more consistent performance for activities like online gaming, 4K streaming and large file transfers. Let's go over how Ethernet switches work and how they differ from routers, which port to use and what alternatives exist if running new cables isn't an option.
An easy fix to your home's network issues
Most home routers come with four LAN ports and one WAN port. The WAN port is for connecting to your modem (if you don't have a combo unit), which leaves four for your use. Even if this was enough when you bought your router, needs can change. For instance, maybe smart TV starts buffering when you upgrade to a 4K streaming plan, so you don't want it to use Wi-Fi anymore.
If all ports are already in use, an Ethernet switch (not a splitter) will add more connections to your existing router. Then you can enjoy the full internet speed you're paying for on more of your devices, while also enabling more direct connections between devices. The switch acts as an expansion to provide more LAN ports, much like an HDMI switch or USB hub. They're most commonly sold with five, eight or 16 ports, but the usable number is one fewer since one slot connects the switch to your router.
For most people, an unmanaged switch is the way to go as they require zero setup and come at a lower cost. Managed switches have advanced features like monitoring and virtual networks, which aren't necessary when all you want is more ports.
How a network switch works
A router's job is to direct traffic between devices on your home network and the internet. When data comes in from the outside, your router sends it to your phone, laptop or other device as needed. A basic switch doesn't do this; it simply provides more Ethernet ports for the router and makes sure data sent from devices connected to it goes to the right place. A switch doesn't replace your router or affect Wi-Fi performance.
If running new cables through your walls isn't realistic, there are a few alternatives to get a wired-style connection without the mess. You could use MoCA adapters to send broadband over your home's coaxial wiring, or powerline adapters that do the same using your electrical outlets. Alternatively, surface-mounted fiber optic kits allow you to run super thin cables along baseboards for a high-speed performance without signal degradation. However, this is more expensive and requires careful installation to avoid damaging the cables.
How to know which Ethernet port to use
Not every port on your router serves the same purpose. Aside from the WAN and LAN distinction mentioned earlier, you also need to check the speeds that each port supports. Ethernet performance is affected by the standard of the ports on both your router and device, as well as the cable itself.
If your computer and router both have a 2.5 gigabit Ethernet port and are connected by a cable that supports 2.5 Gbps, adding a switch that only supports 1 gigabit speeds will bottleneck performance for devices connected to it. Most unmanaged switches today offer at least gigabit speeds, so unless you have extremely fast internet, this shouldn't be a huge concern. If your router's ports don't have any indication of their standards (like 1G or 2.5G), check the manual or online documentation.
Generally, plugging your Ethernet switch into the router's highest-speed port that it can take advantage of is wise. Keep in mind that your connection speed to the internet and back will be capped by your ISP plan, though this doesn't affect direct connections on your network (like your PC communicating with a NAS).

Country singer Rick Sollo and three others missing after helicopter disappears in Brazil
A Black Hawk military helicopter has been deployed to search for a possible crash site in a rural mountainous area
Musician Rick Sollo was among four people on board a helicopter that has disappeared in Brazil, it has been reported.
The twin-engine Bell 430 aircraft had departed from Porto Belo heading towards Sao Joaquim on Monday afternoon when the pilot lost contact with air traffic control, according to G1 Globo.
The three passengers have been identified as Sollo, 59, from the country music duo Rick and Renner, influencer Bruno Avelar and videographer Paulo Soares, according to a statement shared on Avelar’s social media. The pilot has not yet been named.
“To date, there is no official confirmation of an accident involving the aircraft,” it added. A further post said there were five people on board, bit did not identify the fifth person.
This came hours after Sollo posted a video on his Instagram story showing him boarding and landing an aircraft alongside Avelar.
A search and rescue operation has been launched in the mountainous region of Urubici, where air traffic last detected the helicopter.
In an appeal to residents, Avelar’s team urged them to listen out for “loud bangs and noises” and report any sightings of smoke and debris.
The Santa Catarina Fire Department first received a call about a possible aircraft crash at around 4pm on Monday.
At the time, a red weather alert for thunderstorms and heavy rainfall was issued for Urubici.

“Rainfall between 30 and 60 mm/h or 50 and 100 mm/day, strong winds (60–100 km/h), and hail. Risk of power outages, crop damage, fallen trees, and flooding,” said a downgraded weather warning issued at midnight.
The Brazilian Air Force (FAB) has deployed a Black Hawk military helicopter and an SC-105 Amazonas in the rural Vacas Gordas area to search for a possible wreckage, according to Sapicua Radio Agency.
Lieutenant Colonel Heloisa, commander of the 5th Military Fire Brigade Battalion of Santa Catarina, said about the search and rescue late last night: “The first search point is the point of the aircraft's last communication. A team has already arrived at the location, and nothing was found.
“We also have information on the last cell phone signal point of one of the people who were on that aircraft. At this moment, teams are moving to that location to carry out searches.”
Fire crews are expected to be carrying out searches in the area Tuesday, but the weather conditions are understood to be slowing down the operation.
The air forces added that "the priority of the operation is to locate the aircraft and its occupants in the shortest possible time, concentrating search efforts in the areas of highest probability and continuously adjusting the plan as new information is obtained."

Addressing the United Nations General Assembly and marking the 250th anniversary of American independence, United States President Donald Trump detailed his administration's domestic and international policy agenda. Domestically, Trump highlighted United States economic metrics, poverty reduction, and border security enforcement. In foreign affairs, Trump reiterated that Iran will not be permitted to obtain a nuclear weapon, referencing military strikes on Iranian nuclear sites, the destruction of Iranian naval vessels, and United States naval escorts in the Strait of Hormuz. Trump reviewed the cessation of hostilities in Gaza, the release of hostages, and the formation of a multilateral Board of Peace backed by the United Nations Security Council. He outlined diplomatic mediation across international disputes, including India and Pakistan, Cambodia and Thailand, Kosovo and Serbia, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Rwanda, Armenia and Azerbaijan, as well as ongoing negotiations between Russia and Ukraine. Additionally, Trump detailed United States military operations in Venezuela, the apprehension of Nicolás Maduro, and an agreement involving 65 billion barrels of oil. He announced an accord with Denmark regarding Greenland to construct two military bases for Arctic defense. On technological policy, Trump stated that the United States government will prioritize super intelligence over traditional artificial intelligence terminology. The address concluded with calls for United Nations structural reforms, spending reductions, opposition to international carbon taxation, and the rejection of International Criminal Court jurisdiction.

The technologies that increasingly determine national security are being developed not only by governments but by private companies and universities. This creates a dilemma for liberal democracies like Japan: How can governments secure strategically important technologies without undermining the autonomy and innovation of the private sector?
Investment in dual-use technologies — those with both civilian and military applications — is increasingly seen as an efficient way for states to acquire critical capabilities. But because these technologies are often developed outside government, securing them requires more than technological capacity. It requires a way to govern dispersed capabilities without stifling them.
This is the challenge of technology sovereignty. Countries increasingly speak of AI sovereignty, digital sovereignty and data sovereignty. Technology sovereignty provides a broader framework for understanding these efforts.

క్లెయిమ్: బీహార్ ప్రభుత్వ పాఠశాలలో బీజేపీ మంత్రి సమక్షంలో విద్యార్థినులు సినిమా పాటలకు డ్యాన్స్ చేస్తున్న దృశ్యాలు.
ఫాక్ట్: వైరల్ వీడియోలో ఉన్న వ్యక్తి బీజేపీకి చెందిన మంత్రి కాదు, ఆయన ప్రతిపక్ష RJD నేత డాక్టర్ సంజీవ్ కుమార్. అంతేకాకుండా, ఈ వీడియో విద్యార్థినులు వాస్తవానికి ‘బేటీ హూ మై బేటీ’ అనే స్ఫూర్తిదాయక గీతానికి ప్రదర్శన ఇస్తుంటే, ఆ స్థానంలో బాలీవుడ్ సినిమా పాటను ఎడిట్ చేసి జోడించారు. కావున, పోస్టులో చేయబడిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పు.
ముందుగా, వైరల్ వీడియోను పరిశీలించగా, అందులోని వ్యక్తి రాష్ట్రీయ జనతా దళ్ (RJD) పార్టీ నేత డాక్టర్ సంజీవ్ కుమార్ అని గుర్తించాం. ఆయన 2020-2025 మధ్య కాలంలో జనతాదళ్ యునైటెడ్ (JD(U)) పార్టీ తరఫున ఎమ్మెల్యేగా పనిచేశారు. అనంతరం, 2025లో ఆయన RJD లో చేరారు. ఇక వీడియోలోని దృశ్యాలను రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, దీనికి సంబంధించిన పూర్తి వీడియోను (ఆర్కైవ్) 10 సెప్టెంబర్ 2026 లో ‘Dr. Sanjeev Kumar’ ఫేస్బుక్ ఖాతాలో అప్లోడ్ చేసినట్లు గుర్తించాం.
అయితే, ఈ అసలు వీడియోను పరిశీలించగా, వైరల్ వీడియోలో వినిపిస్తున్న ‘ఆంఖోం సే తూనే క్యా కెహ్ దియా’ అనే బాలీవుడ్ సినిమా పాటకు బదులుగా ‘బేటీ హూ మై బేటీ’ అనే పాట ఉండటాన్ని గమనించవచ్చు. ఇది ఒక స్ఫూర్తిదాయకమైన హిందీ గీతం. గుజరాత్ బోర్డుకు చెందిన ఏడవ తరగతి హిందీ పాఠ్యపుస్తకంలో కూడా ఈ గీతం ఉన్నట్లు గుర్తించాం.
ఇక వైరల్ వీడియోపై వివరణ ఇస్తూ సంజీవ్ కుమార్ ఒక వీడియోను విడుదల చేశారు. తాను ఒక పాఠశాలలో జరిగిన సాంస్కృతిక కార్యక్రమంలో పాల్గొన్న వీడియోను కొందరు ఉద్దేశపూర్వకంగా ఎడిట్ చేసి, తప్పుగా షేర్ చేస్తున్నారని ఆయన తెలిపారు. వాస్తవానికి, ఆ కార్యక్రమంలో విద్యార్థినులు మహిళా సాధికారతకు సంబంధించిన పాటపై ప్రదర్శన ఇస్తున్నారని చెప్పారు. అలాగే, తాను మంచినీళ్లు తాగుతున్న దృశ్యాలను మద్యం సేవిస్తున్నట్లుగా వక్రీకరించి తప్పుడు ప్రచారం చేస్తున్నారని ఆయన స్పష్టం చేశారు. ఇటువంటి అసత్య ప్రచారాలకు పాల్పడిన వారిపై సైబర్ క్రైమ్ పోలీసులకు ఫిర్యాదు చేసినట్లు ఆయన పేర్కొన్నారు.
చివరిగా, బీహార్ మంత్రి విద్యార్థినులతో సినిమా పాటలకు డాన్స్ చేయించాడంటూ జరుగుతున్న ప్రచారంలో నిజంలేదు.

Worldwide, traditional medicine is used by billions of people for their health and well-being. At a signing ceremony in Geneva, the Government of India committed US$ 85 million over 10 years, 2022–2032, to support the programming of the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre. India’s 10-year financial contribution will support a cross-sectoral program of work to strengthen the evidence base for traditional medicine by providing data and evidence on traditional medicine policies, practice, products, and public use.
The WHO-India donor agreement is part of a US$ 250 million investment from India in support of the establishment of the WHO Global Centre of Traditional Medicine in 2022, which includes financial support for the workplan of the Centre, interim premises and a new building. This support will scale up WHO’s capacities on traditional medicine across technical divisions and regions in the spirit of global collaboration and solidarity. Part of this substantial contribution from the Government of India will also be included in WHO’s Investment Round to resource WHO’s core work during 2025–2028.
Photo: WHO/Lindsay Mackenzie
“India’s commitment and leadership in expanding the evidence-based contribution of traditional medicine to the health and well-being of all people and the planet, comes at an opportune moment,” said Dr Bruce Aylward, Assistant Director-General of the Universal Health Coverage and Life Course division of WHO. “Traditional medicine, supported within national health systems, can allow us to reach those most often left behind. Integration of traditional practice and knowledge is critical to achieving health for all.”
“The signing of this donor agreement is a major milestone towards achieving the shared vision of Honourable Prime Minister of India Shri Narendra Modi and WHO Director-General Tedros for the development of the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre at Jamnagar in India,” said Vice Minister Vaidya Rajesh Kotecha, Secretary of the Ministry of Ayush, Government of India.
“India remains committed to supporting WHO in its work to strengthen traditional medicine systems globally for achieving universal health coverage and serving the entire humanity, especially through this Global Centre in Jamnagar, which would help focus these efforts to benefit all Member States,” said Ambassador Arindam Bagchi, Permanent Representative of India to the UN and other International Organizations in Geneva.
The WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre is is a knowledge hub focusing on five inter-connected areas of work: research and evidence; primary health care and universal health coverage; Indigenous Knowledges and biodiversity; digital health applications; and the biennial WHO Global Traditional Medicine Summit and collaborations. The Centre is led by Dr Shyama Kuruvilla, Director a.i.
The first WHO traditional medicine global summit was held in August 2023 in Gujarat, resulting in the a multistakeholder action agenda, the Gujarat Declaration. The next WHO Global Summit is planned for November 2025, following up on the anticipated launch of the 2025–2034 Global Strategy for Traditional Medicine at the 78th World Health Assembly in May 2025.
India’s support for traditional medicine has been expressed through a variety of long-standing partnerships with WHO. In 2023, India signed a five-year agreement to support the technical work of WHO’s Traditional, Complementary and Integrative Medicine (TCI) unit. The unit is supporting the development of the Member State-requested new WHO traditional medicine global strategy (2025 - 2034), and publishes key benchmark documents, standardized terminologies, and other evidence-informed technical products to support the safe and effective integration of traditional medicine in national health systems.  
The Centre and TCI collaborate closely with teams across WHO to advance WHO’s multisectoral agenda on traditional medicine, including through regular meetings of the WHO Technical Expert Network, coordinated by the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre and TCI, to promote a One WHO approach on traditional medicine across headquarters, regional and country office.

Kim Woo Young was left dealing with a very unique problem when he first arrived in Japan following the Tokyo Summer Games five years ago, to begin working as coach of the country’s Olympic rifle shooting program.
“Although I was supposed to coach the shooters, I wasn’t allowed to touch any of their guns,” he recalls. It might seem strange but it was the law.
“The rules are very clear. If you don’t have a Japanese instructors license, then even a coach can’t touch guns that belonged to someone else,” recalls women’s rifle shooter Taichi Hinata, one of the first athletes he trained.
The only way Young, former national coach in South Korea could explain technique to his shooters was through words and gestures. “I could talk to them and I could show them what I needed them to do with pictures. It was very unusual but that is the law,” Young recalls.
Young would eventually have to study for 10 months to get a Japanese instructors license before he was allowed to handle his students shooting instruments. “I remember thinking it would be easier to simply take shooters and coach them outside Japan. It was very frustrating.” he recalls.

Young wasn’t having any trouble as he sat in the coaches chair behind his athletes at the Asian Games, though. Coming off a blank in Hangzhou in 2023, Japan’s already had one of their best ever performance in shooting events at the Asian Games in recent years.
On the opening day of competition, Taichi Hinata stunned Olympic champion Ban Hyojin of Korea, India’s Elavenil Valarivan and China’s triple gold medallist at last years World Championships Wang Zifei in the women’s 10m air rifle final. Hinata also partnered with Misaki Nobata and Shiori Hirata to take team bronze, ahead of South Korea’s vaunted women’s team on the opening day.
Then on Tuesday, Nobata partnering Naoki Hanakawa denied India a place on the podium, taking bronze in the 10m air rifle mixed team events. At the end of the rifle events, Japan has three medals – one of each kind – while Hinata’s gold is only the second in shooting since 2010 (the other came in the women’s trap). Currently Japan are only second to heavyweights China on the shooting medal tally.
It’s a performance that’s all the more impressive when you consider the hoops Japanese shooters and coaches have to jump through in their sport. Young’s journey to put his hands on his student’s air guns isn’t even that extreme, for Japanese gun laws are some of the strictest in the world and sporting instruments even for air guns are highly regulated.
There’s no distinction made between air guns used in the 10m rifle events or guns that fire explosive rounds like those used in the 50m event. Licenses are long, arduous and require applicants to clear multiple police verifications, get neighbours to vouch for character, written exams and psychological tests. Pistol licenses are capped at a number nationwide, junior shooters aren’t even allowed to own their own air guns and fire lasers at targets rather than pellets while the decision even to replace a gun requires months of paperwork.
There are hoops to be cleared that seem designed to dissuade all but the most determined.

“It’s very hard to be a sports shooter in Japan,” admits Nobata. “First of all, competitive shooting is a very niche sport in Japan, so most young people don’t even know about it. Because of this, the participant base is very small. Also the age at which people start tends to be higher. Due to licensing regulations, you can only own an air rifle yourself from age 18, and the same applies to small-bore rifles—you can’t possess one unless you’re 18 or older. So, the fact that the starting point is delayed creates a significant hurdle,” she says.
While there are shooting clubs around the country, they don’t train with the air guns of the sort that can be found across ranges in India. “We have shooting clubs in Japan but if you are under 18 years old, you aren’t even allowed to touch a gun. You can’t fire pellets out of an air gun. You train on laser simulators,” says Naoya Okada who competed in the men’s team and individual event.
When shooters turn of legal age and want to buy their own gun, they need to purchase it from specific stores only after getting a police license for that specific weapon. But first they need to clear a written exam and extensive police verification that lasts months.
“In the test, you have to be able to have to identify the various parts of the gun, you need to know what’s the weight of the trigger and other very minute details. But the test was also created at a time when it was thought that most guns were going to be bought for hunting purposes so you also have to answer questions on where to fire the gun. Later you have to appear before the police three times and you also need to get your neighbours to vouch for your character,” says Hiroka Monagan, a former national level shooter who is involved in press operations at the Aichi Prefecture shooting range where the shooting events of the Asian Games are being held.
If the licenses for rifle shooters are hard, they can get almost prohibitive for pistol shooters since that weapon has an unfortunate reputation with crime.
“There is a limit on the total number of pistol licenses available at any one time. The only time you can get a pistol license is if someone who already had it gives it up. The gun license rules are strict and they get stricter depending on which prefecture you are getting your license in. The rules in Osaka are particularly strict because there is a history of Yakuza (Japanese organised crime) over there. But it is very strict everywhere in Japan,” says an official who didn’t want to be named since he wasn’t authorised to speak to the media.
And while shooters elsewhere – as was the case with India’s Vidarsa Vinod - can simply swap weapons if they need to, that’s a lot harder in Japan. “Your gun license is specific to your gun. So if you want to use another weapon, you need to go through the procedure for another license for that once again,” says Hiroka.
Then there is the problem of finding a place to train. “We only have one shooting range for each prefecture. So if you don’t live nearby, it’s hard to train,” says Naoya.

Indeed most shooters don’t train nearly as much as their international counterparts. “I think it’s very difficult for most shooters to train at a range for more than two days a week. For the rest of the time they have to do dry firing or practise with a gun that fires a laser,” says coach Young.
When informed that many Indian shooters have constructed impromptu ranges in their homes, there’s a sense of disbelief.
“Indian shooters have ranges inside their home? I don’t think you could do that in Japan,” says Japanese men’s shooter Naoki Okada. While the specifics aren’t always known, Japanese shooters are conscious they are at a disadvantage when it comes to simply practising their sport. It takes some getting used to. “I know India, for instance, has a huge number of people participating in the sport. Just like that, I used to feel intimidated when looking at the shooting scene overseas. I was surprised by how easy it was to be a competitive shooter out of Japan. but now I feel confident that I can compete at that level and count myself among the top athletes,” says Nobata.
Even with multiple medals including gold at the Asian Games, shooters like Nobata and Taichi don’t expect much to change with the sport in Japan. “I think it will get a little more popular on instagram or social media but it will still be a niche sport,” Taichi says.
But despite the challenges, the sport will continue to have takers in the country. “Compared to other sports, physical attributes like height or build don’t give you a massive advantage or disadvantage. I find it really appealing that we can compete on a level playing field right from the start. It’s hard to get a gun but what really matters is the person behind the gun,” says Nobata

Autopsy shows Hayden Panettiere died from a drug overdose
- Published
Child star Hayden Panettiere died from the toxic effects of fentanyl, Xanax and several other drugs in her system, according to an autopsy completed by the Greenville County Coroner's Office in South Carolina.
The coroner's office said Panettiere's death was an accident and that no signs of trauma were discovered that would have contributed to her death.
Panettiere died last month at the age of 36 after she was found unresponsive at a South Carolina residence.
The star of US TV shows Heroes and Nashville had spoken openly about her struggles with substance abuse.
The coroner's office also found methocarbamol - a prescription muscle relaxant - and quetiapine - an antipsychotic medication that is used to treat certain mental health conditions.
Fentanyl is a synthetic opioid that has killed hundreds of thousands of Americans over the past five years alone.
The coroner's office said emergency responders had "initiated advanced cardiac life support measures; however, resuscitation efforts were unsuccessful".
The US Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA) was reportedly joining the local police department's investigation into the child star's death.
Panettiere's ex-boyfriend, Brian Hickerson - who has admitted to abusing her - and his brother Zack were with Panettiere when emergency services came, according to a police report from the day she died.
Just months before her death, Panettiere published a memoir where she discussed at length her issues with addiction and postpartum depression.
Panettiere has said she was introduced to drugs around the age of 16 during a red carpet appearance for Heroes when a member of her professional team gave her something called a "happy pill" for energy.
"I had no idea that this was not an appropriate thing, or what door that would open for me when it came to my addiction," she told People Magazine. "As I got older, the drugs and alcohol became something I almost couldn't live without."
Panettiere's brother, Jansen, died aged 28 from a heart condition. Panettiere revealed in her book that her brother also struggled with substance abuse and used heroin and cocaine leading up to his death.

India's government on Thursday told the Supreme Court it was open to tougher red warnings on food packaging after health activists said its earlier proposal was too easy on companies, in a potential blow to the $100 billion food industry.
After years of delays, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) last month suggested a two-phased labelling programme, starting with red-coloured hexagonal warning labels on products that exceeded limits in at least two of three categories — added sugar, salt or saturated fat. Stricter rules would be introduced in a second phase, it said.
The announcement came as India's federal and state food regulators pursued an aggressive enforcement drive, with surprise raids on eateries uncovering poor hygiene and leading to many forced closures, stoking anger among consumers.
Health experts criticised the FSSAI proposal, however, saying the two-nutrient approach was an "industry-friendly loophole" that disregarded public health, as many products would escape scrutiny.
Supreme Court Justice J.B. Pardiwala questioned why the FSSAI was taking a two-phased approach, as he questioned a government lawyer during Thursday's hearing.
"It has to be sugar and salt. Only then will you ask them to put a label?" Pardiwala said, stressing the word "and".
The FSSAI's lawyer, Additional Solicitor General of India Brijender Chahar, responded that after hearing the court, it was now suggesting it could roll out the phases "in one go."
That would effectively mean foods high even in one of the three nutrients — added sugar, salt or fat — would have a red hexagon.
The Supreme Court has been hearing a plea by health group "3S And Our Health" demanding stricter labelling, drawing the FSSAI and the industry to court.
The nationwide debate on food safety has intensified since Reuters reported last month that India's government opted for a weaker labelling regime after lobbying by Coca-Cola and groups backing Nestle and PepsiCo, which argued warning labels were ineffective. Many companies, however, have implemented such measures voluntarily in European markets.
Food industry raises concerns
India's food and drinks market is key for foreign players including Nestle, Unilever, Mondelez and Mars, whose food products compete in a thriving industry that also includes big Indian firms such as ITC and Dabur.
On top of that, thousands of smaller businesses sell snacks and sweets, which remain hugely popular among millions of Indians.
All India Food Processors' Association, which represents dozens of Indian and foreign food giants, has called for a review of the planned health labels on packaging, saying many staples risk being covered in warnings that will tarnish the image of Indian food globally.
During Thursday's hearing, the group's lawyer held a food packet to explain its position, saying "nobody can eat 100 grams of pickle", and so the warning labels should be decided on a per-serve basis, not by analysing salt and sugar in 100 grams of a product as the authorities have proposed.
The United States, for example, has proposed per-serve front-of-pack labelling, which Indian industry favours, though many other countries use the 100-gram benchmark.
Rising obesity rates and the consumption of fatty foods are a growing concern among health experts and the Indian government. Some 450 million Indians could be obese or overweight by 2050, according to a recent study published in the Lancet medical journal.
"We are concerned with the health of people, more particularly growing children. We have taken it up very seriously. We expect one and all to extend their cooperation to a cause which is in national interest," the Supreme Court said on Thursday.
The judges said they will issue a written order before Friday.

Nvidia boss rejects AI extinction fears as 'doomsday narratives'
- Published
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has described warnings that AI could lead to humanity's extinction by the next decade as "doomsday narratives".
"2030 is not going to be the end of the world. There is 0% chance that's going to be the end of the world", Huang said in an interview with CBS News, the BBC's US partner.
Huang added: "Scaring people is unnecessary. It is irresponsible."
Warnings from researchers in recent weeks about potential risks posed by the technology escalated the debate about AI safety, with some industry executives calling for a slowdown in developing models.
His remarks follow claims posted on social media by former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon that AI developers believe the technology "could kill us all by the end of the decade".
Coxon's concerns sparked debate about the technology's risks, including calls by top executives like Anthropic boss Dario Amodei and OpenAI's Sam Altman urging for AI's development to slow down.
Huang said that such predictions are "not grounded in science", adding that it is in Nvidia's best interest to ensure the industry builds its products responsibly.
"Our company's success is directly connected to the safe deployment of products and services," he said. "If we don't continue to do that, our value would be diminished."
Huang suggested AI firms talking about a "slow down" could be seeking liability protections for harms their products may cause.
"Go and read between the lines," he said. "They're actually not asking for more laws. They're asking to be relieved of the laws we do have, and I think that that's a problem."

Srinagar, Sep 22: The Lieutenant Governor Manoj Sinha today launched the book “Sardar Patel and Kashmir: The Untold History”. He paid homage to the foresight and nation-building genius of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel and expressed gratitude to Bhagwan Shri Swaminarayan Ji. The Lieutenant Governor commended the Maninagar Shree Swaminarayan Gadi Sansthan for its unparalleled contributions to spiritual upliftment, education, and humanitarian service. He also congratulated Dr. Rizwan Kadri for editing and publishing this important work.
In his speech, the Lieutenant Governor described Sardar Patel as the “architect of modern India,” whose indomitable will and practical wisdom ensured the integration of 562 princely states into a united country. He emphasized that Sardar Patel’s vision of “Ek Bharat, Shreshtha Bharat” continues to define the essence of India’s democracy and unity in diversity. The Lieutenant Governor recalled Sardar Patel’s firm stance on Jammu Kashmir, noting his declaration that “we will not give even an inch of Jammu Kashmir’s territory to anyone.” He reflected on Sardar Patel’s deep understanding of the nation’s pulse and his ability to connect with the common people, workers and communities across India.
“Through his indomitable willpower, clear vision, selfless diligence, and skilful organisational strength, he ensured that the dream of an undivided India became a reality. I also believe that had Sardar Patel been given the responsibility for Jammu Kashmir, perhaps the problems that the people here endured for more than six decades would not have arisen,” he said.
The Lieutenant Governor highlighted the book’s significance as a serious attempt to re-evaluate history with honesty and impartiality. He cautioned that for too long, historical narratives were shaped by ideological biases that overlooked the decisive contributions of leaders like Sardar Patel. He urged the new generation of writers to treat history as a mirror of truth, not as a tool for glorification, and to learn from past decisions to guide the future.
He also described the abrogation of Articles 370 and 35A in August 2019 as the fulfilment of Sardar Patel’s unfinished dream. The Lieutenant Governor noted that this constitutional change was not merely legal but a profound step towards psychological and emotional integration, ensuring equal rights and opportunities for all communities in Jammu Kashmir.
“In August 2019, under the leadership of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, the nation witnessed a historic constitutional change. New possibilities of education, employment, entrepreneurship and development opened up for the youth.
The Prime Minister’s decision proved that when national interest becomes the supreme priority, no obstacle remains permanent. This is the same firm willpower whose glimpse we saw in Sardar Patel’s nation-building efforts in 1947. I believe that by consigning the era of Article 370 to history, Jammu Kashmir now stands at the threshold of a new future,” he said.
The Lieutenant Governor also outlined 4 priorities for Jammu Kashmir’s future- peace through zero tolerance towards terrorism, rapid development through infrastructure and connectivity, empowerment of youth by linking them to India’s digital economy and startup culture, and revival of cultural heritage to strengthen tourism and human values. He envisioned Srinagar, Jammu, and other cities of the Union Territory as vibrant centres of education, trade, and innovation.
He described the book as a “lighthouse” that illuminates Sardar Patel’s dream of a united, confident India. He called upon citizens to dedicate themselves to the ideals of unity, integrity, and patriotism, and to build an India that leads the world not only economically but also through moral leadership, cultural richness, and democratic values.
Acharya Shree Jitendriyapriyadasji Swamiji Maharaj; Kishor Makwana, Chairperson, National Commission for Scheduled Castes; Dr. Rizwan Kadri; Swami Bhagwat Priya Das Ji; Brij Mohan Sharma, Principal Secretary, Culture Department; senior officials, prominent literary personalities and office bearers of Maninagar Shree Swaminarayan Gadi Sansthan attended the book launch ceremony.

- Control Resonant Artifacts provide passive bonuses that can improve Dylan's combat or survival abilities.
- Find an Untapped Artifact and the required materials before crafting it at Artifact Formation in The Gap.

Artifacts can give Dylan useful passive bonuses that can shape how you approach combat and survival in Control Resonant. You will find several of them throughout the game, each offering a different effect for your build. Here is everything you need to know about finding, crafting, and using Artifacts in Control Resonant.
What Are Artifacts in Control Resonant?
Artifacts are items that provide passive bonuses to Dylan. Once crafted, they can be equipped through the Loadout menu and used to fine-tune your build.
To craft an Artifact in Control Resonant, you first need to find its corresponding Untapped Artifact in the world. You then need the required materials and Source. The Untapped Artifact is consumed when you create the finished Artifact.
Some Artifacts belong to the same family. Artifacts from the same family cannot be equipped together, so you will need to choose which effect fits your build. You can also recycle Artifacts that you no longer need to recover materials.
How to Craft Artifacts in Control Resonant
When Control Resonant release time is here, it is better that you know how to craft Artifacts. You can craft Artifacts at the Artifact Formation station located in The Gap. Interact with the station to open the Artifact Formation menu, then select the Artifact you want to create.
- PC: Approach the Artifact Formation station and press F to interact.
- Controller: Approach the station and press L1 when the interaction prompt appears.
Once inside the Artifact Formation menu, select an Artifact from the list to view its required materials and effect. If you have everything required, you can craft it at the station. Before you even check the crafting methods, check if Control Resonant system requirements fit your device specs so there are no blockades in the middle.
All Control Resonant Artifact Recipes and What They Do
Now that you know what the Artifacts are and how to craft them, here is the full list and their recipes in Control Resonant:
| Artifact Name | Recipe | What It Does | 
|---|---|---|
| Brass Dusters | Untapped Brass Dusters 8 Edible Glob 750 Source 5 Violent Echo | Combat Abilities deal +50% Raw Damage, but have no Filter at all. |

| Amulet | Untapped Amulet 150 Source 3 Odd Echo | Increases Critical Chance for all Melee attacks by 5%. | 
| Face Mask | Untapped Face Mask 150 Source 3 Mourning Echo | Gives Dylan resistance to Infected by increasing the time it takes for the status effect to build up. |
