Can you equip multiple Control Resonant Artifacts from the same family?
No. Artifacts that belong to the same family cannot be equipped together, so you must choose between them.
Can you recycle Artifacts in Control Resonant?
Yes. You can recycle Artifacts you no longer need to recover materials.

Seoul – Two members of North Korea’s delegation to the Asian Games in Japan are looking to seek asylum, South Korea’s Monthly Chosun magazine reported on Tuesday.
Citing a source it identified as an official from Japan’s Cabinet Intelligence and Research Office, the magazine said the two were among a 180-member North Korean delegation attending the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, which opened Saturday.
The two North Koreans expressed a preference to seek asylum in Japan rather than South Korea and have communicated their intention not to return home, the report said.
Their identities and positions within the delegation were not disclosed, and it remained unclear whether their reported outreach would ultimately lead to a defection, according to Monthly Chosun.
The magazine said the information was obtained through a source connected to Japan’s intelligence apparatus and linked to the pro-Pyongyang General Association of Korean Residents in Japan, known as Chongryon.
North Korea sent about 180 athletes and officials to the Games, including Sports Minister Kim Il Guk, according to media reports.
Reporters could not immediately reach the Japanese government for comment on a national holiday in Japan.

At least 11 injured in shooting at Turkish high school
- Published
At least 11 people have been injured in a shooting outside a high school in Turkey after an attacker opened fire before fleeing the scene.
The incident happened at the Inci Uzmez Vocational and Technical Anatolian High School in Turkey's western province of Manisa at about 08:00 local time (05:00 GMT) on Tuesday.
The attacker has since been detained, according to the local governor's office.
Local media reported that two of the victims taken to hospital were in critical conditions.
CCTV footage posted online appeared to show a male on a street near the school carrying a firearm, with other clips apparently showing him fleeing still carrying the weapon.
The motive behind the attack was not immediately clear.
It has been reported in Turkish media that the gunman is a 15-year-old student, though that has not been officially confirmed.
In a statement, Turkey's education ministry said the incident had "deeply saddened our nation, and our educational community in particular".
It said that three national investigators from the ministry had been sent to Manisa.

The last of Peter Handscomb’s 20 Test appearances came more than three years back, at the Narendra Modi Stadium in Ahmedabad during the 2022-23 Border-Gavaskar Trophy.
The Victoria wicketkeeper-batter was dropped subsequently but has since gradually built a reputation for his steady contributions in the Sheffield Shield.
Since the 2023-24 season, no batter has amassed more than Handscomb’s tally of 2,010 runs in 59 innings. He has managed four centuries and 11 fifties in that span. Only Jordan Silk of Tasmania has more fifty-plus scores than Handscomb.
The rich yields have brought him back in the reckoning for a Test return and got him his first Australia-A selection since 2018.
As Australia embarks on a busy Test calendar, which includes a five-match Border-Gavaskar Trophy in India in early 2027, Handscomb talks to Sportstar about the labours of domestic cricket, the changing conditions in Australia, learning from his international failures, and what still makes him Australia’s go-to choice to dominate spin bowling in the subcontinent.
Q. Despite conditions favouring bowlers, you have been one of the most consistent batters in the Sheffield Shield over the last three seasons. Have you had to make any technical adjustments in order to perform better, or is it a mental shift in approach?
A. I think it’s a bit of both. I’ve done a fair bit of work over the last four or five years on my technique and changing a few things.
But also the mental challenge [of it] and making sure that your gameplan is clear. It’s something I’ve worked pretty hard on as well. Understanding where you can and can’t score and what shots you can and can’t play on certain wickets. That’s something that I’ve tried to be really strong at. I think that’s helped me over the last few years.
Q. Is it important not to pay too much attention to others’ opinions and to simply cut the noise?
A. Yeah, absolutely. You can acknowledge that and understand that it probably is tough to bat. But when it gets to the crunch time, when you get out there, you’ve got to put that aside. If you get beaten by a good ball, it’s okay because you’re still out there, and understanding that ugly runs are still runs.
So, finding a way is more important than looking pretty. Do not worry as much about your technique but try to get through your process and stick to that as best as possible.
Q. What is your opinion on the balance shifting drastically in favour of bowlers in Australia? Do you think it takes away from the game a little bit?
A. Yeah, I think the balance has been a little bit one-sided. But then you look maybe 10 years ago, and it was probably one-sided in favour of the batters. I think the game naturally shifts through generations where it becomes too flat.

So then the push is to make seam-friendly or spin-friendly wickets. And then it goes too far and you’ve got to bring it back. So I think we’re just at a stage where we’re hopefully bringing it back. And we can get a more even battle between bat and ball.
Q. Considering all these challenges of batting in Australia right now, do you think you’re at your best version as a batter?
A. It’s an interesting question because 10 years ago I was making a lot of runs. But potentially the wickets were a little bit different then. I think the biggest change from then to now is just my mental state, my mental game. I feel like I’m prepared for any experience that we find out in the middle.
And then I think I can deal with failure a lot better now. Having had a lot of failure but a lot of success throughout the career as well, you start to understand that they go hand-in-hand and that’s part of the game.
Q. Has a topsy-turvy international career helped you get in a space where you’re happy accepting things?
A. I guess so. I mean, I wish it hadn’t been topsy-turvy. It would be nice if it had been one nice straight line. But, no, that’s part of the game. I think failures absolutely help you deal with future failures.
Once you’ve been through that, you understand it’s not the end of the world. You come out the other side and you’re still okay and the sun’s still shining. Yeah, that helps.
Q. Do you consider playing for Australia again as some sort of an unfinished business, where you want to have that sustained run in the team and play the Ashes again?
A. [The last time I played an Ashes Test in 2017] It was one of the low moments of my international career, getting dropped out after that. And that was a good learning moment as well. It’s an interesting one. I’ve done a lot in my career, but there’s still stuff that I want to do.
But I also understand that if those things don’t happen, then it’s not the end of the world. I’ll still be pushing as hard as I can to do that. But I’m pretty lucky with everything that has happened.
Q. Just from speaking to you now, you seem composed and accepting of things. But technically speaking, as a batter, how would you say you’re better now than when you debuted for Australia?
A. I think I’ve just been exposed to more conditions now. I’ve played a lot more County cricket. And that’s helped me with seam and swing bowling, which I was able to take back to Australia and help in those conditions. So, it’s a hard one to teach, but it’s more about just having experience and having learnings from all these different conditions and finding out what’s worked and what hasn’t worked.
ALSO READ | Lakshmipathy Balaji to be India A head coach for Australia A series
So that’s probably where, technically, I’ve found a few things now. If I look at a wicket and I have a guess at what it’s going to do, then I know what I need to do or where I need to bat or what my game plan is for that moment.
Q. You’ve led Victoria in the Sheffield Shield previously. Does being a captain help in that regard – understanding your game better as well?
A. I think it can help as long as you’re able to focus on your game as well. I think as a captain, you spend a fair bit of time thinking about other people and their game, which can help you a lot because you start to understand what other people are thinking and how they want to take their wickets and what they’re seeing. So you can bring that into your game. But yeah, just as long as it doesn’t take anything away from it.
Q. You’ve said it multiple times in the past that you don’t want to be seen as just a one-trick pony. But it’s hard to overlook how good you are at playing spin. Recently, even Indian batters have struggled to play spin. India has lost series to New Zealand and South Africa because of that. What is it that helps you survive spin in spin-friendly conditions – Is it about intent to just attack, about reading the bowler well, or just sheer preparation?
A. Well, to start with, I think I’ve been really lucky in the way that I grew up with my dad. We did a lot of work on playing spin and using my feet and being able to get out of my crease and deal with any ball that came down at me. And then we worked for years on that. And then that progressed into First-Class cricket, where I was able to dominate spin when I came in.
That was something that I wanted to keep strong and make stronger. So, then when I had these tours over in the subcontinent, I was able to work on that again and find clarity around a gameplan.
So having experienced a lot of conditions here in India now, I’ve got a very clear gameplan on how I want to play based on the wicket. And then it’s just trying to implement the right play at the right time.
Q. Just to add to the previous question. You play with the Kookaburra ball in Australia, but it’s SG here. Does the preparation change for both with respect to spin?
A. Probably not so much the ball, more just how the wicket reacts. The SG stays harder, so it has a little bit of sharper turn, but that’s also due to the wickets. So there’s a little bit of both in that.
Q. You’re captain of an Australia-A side that has some promising young batters like Sam Konstas and Campbell Kellaway. How are these guys coming up and how are they different from when you were a 23, 24-year-old?
A. Well, I think this next generation has so many more shots than I’ve ever had. And I think that’s awesome to see how the game is growing and what batters are doing and how they’re able to access different parts of the ground.
So, yeah, first and foremost, I think they’re more talented than I’ve ever been with what they can do, which is awesome. It’s awesome to watch and see how that’s changing. And then, yeah, [my role] it’s just about how they go out and want to implement their gameplans and how clear they are in doing that.
Q. You spoke about the younger batters having more shots and variety. Do you think that’s necessary for taking the game forward and making First-Class cricket more captivating, say something like a Bazball approach?
A. I mean, yes and no. I think the shots are great. I think there’s a time and place for them. But there’s also something to be said for just a proper five-day grind in a Test match. It’s not that easy coming over here and getting a draw.
Not everything has to be a result. Sometimes a fighting draw is something special. So, yeah, having the shots is important. Understanding when and where to use them is the trick.

British Columbia has sued OpenAI in California, saying a mass shooting at a school in the province could have been prevented if the company had warned local law enforcement that the shooter had used ChatGPT to plan the massacre.
The lawsuit filed in San Francisco federal court on Monday names OpenAI and its CEO, Sam Altman, as defendants. It is seeking damages to fund recovery efforts in the province after the February attack, as well as an order directing changes to the way the company handles ChatGPT conversations that could lead to violence.
Nine people, primarily children, were killed in the school shooting in Tumbler Ridge, British Columbia. The shooter, Jesse Van Rootselaar, had been flagged by the company’s safety team after her conversations about gun violence, but the company did not alert police.
Altman published a letter to the community saying he was “deeply sorry” OpenAI had not contacted law enforcement. He promised reforms, but never followed through, despite efforts from British Columbia’s attorney general to engage, the lawsuit says.
The school where the shooting took place is in the process of being demolished, and the province has been forced to absorb the costs of a replacement school, mental health care and other effects of the shooting, according to the lawsuit.
A spokesperson for OpenAI, Drew Pusateri, called the Tumbler Ridge shooting an unspeakable tragedy. “OpenAI remains committed to working collaboratively with government and law enforcement officials, and continuing to advance our ongoing safety work.”
British Columbia’s lawsuit comes after more than 30 family members of victims and others affected by the attack filed lawsuits in California, accusing the company of opting out of a chance to prevent the shooting.
Van Rootselaar shot her mother and stepbrother at home before killing an educational assistant and five students aged 12 and 13 at her former school on 10 February, according to police. Van Rootselaar, who was 18, then died by suicide.
Van Rootselaar’s interactions with ChatGPT were first flagged by the company in June 2025. Safety team members recommended contacting police, but Altman and other OpenAI leadership overruled them, the lawsuit says, citing OpenAI whistleblowers who spoke to the Wall Street Journal in the wake of the shooting.
The shooter’s account was deactivated, but she was able to get a new account and continue using the platform to plan her attack.
After publication of the Wall Street Journal article, the company said the account was flagged by systems that identify “misuses of our models in furtherance of violent activities”, but the issues did not meet its internal criteria for reporting to law enforcement.
The lawsuit comes after a series of cases against OpenAI have been filed in US state and federal courts in recent months over claims ChatGPT facilitated violence, including lawsuits related to a mass shooting at Florida State University last year.
In June, Florida became the first state to sue OpenAI over safety risks, accusing the company of misrepresenting the safety of its ChatGPT platform, which the lawsuit said had harmed children by providing information to school shooters, offering guidance on self-harm and addicting young users.
OpenAI, which has denied the claims, has said it trains its models to refuse requests that could “meaningfully enable violence”, and notifies law enforcement when conversations suggest “an imminent and credible risk of harm to others”.

"In connection with the video circulated on social media, an FIR has been registered at Gondia Police Station. An investigation is underway," Dhenkanal Superintendent of Police Abhinav Sonkar told PTI.
He said two persons have been detained based on the preliminary investigation. Further action will be taken after prima facie evidence is found against them, the officer said.
Pratap Dalei, the inspector-in-charge (IIC) of Gondia block, told NDTV that the identities of some of the people involved in the incident have been established and strict action will be taken, pending an investigation.
Police have not yet established the full sequence of events or the total number of people involved.

Jamui horror
The Odisha case comes days after a similar incident in Bihar's Jamui district sparked widespread outrage. Two accused in the harassment of a boy and a girl were nabbed by police on Tuesday following an encounter in which both were injured. With their arrests, the total number of people held in connection with the September 19 incident reached five.
The victims in the Jamui case, who were reportedly studying at the same coaching centre, were allegedly caught by a group on a road and harassed. Videos circulating on social media purportedly showed the girl being groped.
Although the victims did not lodge a police complaint, the incident came to light after clips of the alleged harassment, apparently recorded by one of the perpetrators, went viral on social media.
police subsequently took suo motu cognisance of the matter, traced the victims and formed a Special Investigating Team.

Of the 13 reported acts of kindness in the Facebook post, nine were true, mostly true or probably true.
Two of the claimed acts of kindness were false, and one was unproven. Lynne Patton, a former Eric Trump Foundation employee whom Trump appointed to roles in both of his presidential administrations, carried out one of the reported acts.
In September 2026, a Facebook post (archived) circulated online that listed 13 claimed "acts of kindness" that U.S. President Donald Trump purportedly carried out before running for office.
The introduction to the post read:
For thirty years before he ran for office, Donald Trump quietly paid mortgages, flew sick children across the country, and wrote checks to strangers who needed help. You will not find those stories on the evening news. So here they are.
Start with what people who knew him before politics say. He has never had a drink. He has never smoked. He has never used drugs. He built his business on long hours, and the people who worked for him will tell you he outworked all of them. Nobody called him a bigot until the day he announced for president. That timing tells you something about the accusation.
Now to the record.
The claim about Trump's reported acts of kindness spread on Facebook (archived, archived), X (archived) and Threads (archived). Snopes readers contacted us, asking if the claim was true.
Of the 13 reported acts of kindness in the Facebook post, nine were true, mostly true or probably true, two were false and one was unproven. One of the alleged acts was actually carried out by Lynne Patton, a long-time employee of the Eric Trump Foundation whom Trump later appointed to roles in both of his administrations.
Given the above, we rate this claim a mixture of true and false or unproven elements. Below, we investigate each claim in the post.
Annabel Hill's farm: True
In 1986, a Georgia widow named Annabell Hill was about to lose the family farm at a foreclosure auction. Trump saw her story on the news, picked up the phone, called the auction, and stopped the sale. Then he sent her the money to keep the farm.
Snopes investigated this claim in September 2026 and found it to be true. According to reporting at the time, Hill's farm had been up for auction twice. Her husband, Leonard D. Hill, died by suicide in February 1986 to try to save the farm using the payout from his life insurance. That sum did not cover the debts, and his widow faced a second auction that September.
That was reportedly when Trump stepped in, called the bank to block a foreclosure auction and started fundraising for Hill. The fundraising was successful, with Trump himself covering at least $39,000 of the $170,000 needed. Because of the fundraising efforts, Hill's family was able to keep the farm.
A private plane for Andrew Ten: True
In 1988, an Orthodox Jewish family in Los Angeles had a three-year-old son named Andrew Ten who needed treatment in New York. The boy could not survive without a full life-support setup, and no airline would carry it. His father asked Trump for help. Trump put the family on his own jet and got them there.
Snopes previously investigated this claim in 2015 and found it to be true based on a report published by the Jewish Telegraphic Agency in 1988 that said Ten's father had appealed to Trump for help transporting his ill son to access medical treatment in the New York area.
The Times of Israel later reported that Ten died in 1998. In 2014, the Securities and Exchange Commission fined Ten's father, Harold Ten, in an alleged scheme to "profit from the imminent deaths of terminally ill patients in nursing homes and hospice care."
Trump sent plane to fly Marines: False
In 1991, two hundred Marines came home from Desert Storm to Camp Lejeune and found out the military had no aircraft to fly them the rest of the way to Florida. Trump's airline, the Trump Shuttle, made two runs between North Carolina and Miami and got every one of them back to their families.
Snopes previously investigated this claim in 2016 and found it false. Though some Marines did fly from Miami to North Carolina on a Trump-branded plane after Operation Desert Storm in 1991, Trump did not own Trump Shuttle or its planes at the time because he had defaulted on the loans he used to buy the fleet. Rather, the military chartered some of the planes that still bore the Trump logo to fly the Marines without involvement from Trump.
A flat tire and a mortgage payment: False
In 1995, a passing driver in New Jersey pulled over to help change a flat on Trump's limo. Trump asked what he could do in return. The man only wanted flowers sent to his wife. A few weeks later, the story goes, the flowers came with a note saying the couple's mortgage had been paid off. People have been repeating that one for three decades.
This claim is an urban legend that Snopes first debunked in 1998. It has also circulated using other celebrities' names. According to an Aug. 15, 1997, report in the Toronto Globe and Mail, an assistant at Trump's New York office told the paper the story "isn't true."
Mar-a-Lago welcomed Black people and Jews: True
In 1996, Trump sued the town of Palm Beach, Florida. The town had been leaning on his Mar-a-Lago club for one reason. He let in Jewish members and Black members, and the older clubs did not. Abraham Foxman, who ran the Anti-Defamation League at the time, said Trump shined a light on the ugly side of Palm Beach that the glitter usually hid. Foxman also said other clubs started admitting Jews and Blacks after Trump forced the issue.
Snopes investigated a similar claim in 2016, finding it true that Trump allowed Black people and Jews to access Mar-a-Lago while other clubs in Florida did not. The Wall Street Journal reported in 1997 that after Trump sued Palm Beach alleging discrimination against his club because it admitted Black and Jewish members, other clubs had started to admit Jewish patrons.
However, the WSJ reported in April 1997 that Palm Beach denied it was discriminating against Mar-a-Lago because of its membership and that restrictions imposed on the club were part of a zoning matter. The outcome of the lawsuit was unclear.
Ultimately, Trump's decision to allow Jewish and Black members turned out to also benefit his business, helping him fight Palm Beach's restrictions and also allowing him to attract a different crowd than existing clubs already catered to.
According to the Wall Street Journal article, Foxman did speak the quote the Facebook post attributed to him, saying Trump "put the light on Palm Beach. Not on the beauty and the glitter, but on its seamier side of discrimination."
Money for a girl with brittle bone disease: True
In 2000, Trump was watching Maury Povich and saw a little girl named Megan who lived with brittle bone disease. He said her attitude got to him. He called the show and sent her family a large check.
According to a recording of a Dec. 19, 2000, episode of "Maury," the talk-show hosted by Povich, an 11-year-old girl named Megan and her mother received a check and video greeting from Trump.
The clip of the show Snopes viewed did not elaborate on Megan's illness or the exact size of Trump's check. During the clip, Trump called Megan "beautiful, inside and out" and told her to "keep up that attitude."
Povich, when handing over Trump's check to Megan, said Trump didn't give out "chump change" and referenced "all those zeros" but did not say the exact amount.
In 2020, to mark the 30th anniversary of the Americans with Disabilities Act, Trump's campaign shared a news release that highlighted several moments he reportedly supported Americans with disabilities. One of these highlights was about Megan and said she had brittle bone disease.
Jennifer Hudson stayed free at Trump hotel: Probably true
In 2008, Jennifer Hudson's mother, brother, and nephew were murdered in Chicago. Trump moved Hudson and her family into his Chicago hotel at no charge and had his security team watch over them while they grieved.
Snopes previously investigated this claim in 2016. E! Online reported on Oct. 31, 2008, that Hudson checked into the Trump International Hotel & Tower on Oct. 24, following the murder of her mother, brother and nephew by her former brother-in-law.
The outlet reported that Trump himself was paying for the stay, something Trump also told People magazine on Nov. 10. It was unclear how long Hudson stayed at Trump's hotel.
Hudson has never publicly refuted Trump's claim that he paid for her stay or named herself or anyone else other than Trump as having paid.
A check for bus driver who saved woman from suicide: True
In 2013, a Buffalo bus driver named Darnell Barton saw a woman standing at the edge of a bridge. He stopped the bus, walked over, put an arm around her, and talked her back to safety. Trump read about it and mailed Barton a check, because he thought a man like that deserved a reward.
Snopes found this claim to be true in 2016. A Buffalo radio station reported photos from a ceremony on Nov. 7, 2013, during which Barton received the $10,000 check (archived) that Trump had promised on social media after Barton's Oct. 18 rescue of an apparently suicidal woman he spotted while driving his bus.
Money for a Marine arrested in Mexico: True
In 2014, Marine Sgt. Andrew Tahmooressi spent seven months in a Mexican prison after he took a wrong turn at the border with legally owned guns in his truck. President Obama never placed the call to Mexico that the sergeant's family begged for. Trump sent Tahmooressi a check for $25,000 to help him rebuild his life once he got home.
Snopes previously investigated this claim in 2018. We found at the time that Tahmooressi was arrested after he crossed the Mexican border while carrying guns and ammunition that he legally owned in the U.S. — but wasn't permitted to carry in Mexico — and was imprisoned for seven months.
We could not substantiate his claims about abuse and mistreatment by Mexican authorities that also circulated at the time.
The House Committee on Foreign Affairs reported on Oct. 31, 2014, that Tahmooressi had been released from Mexican jail. Trump pledged (archived) on social media on Nov. 10, 2014, that he would send Tahmooressi a check for $25,000. We reported in 2016 that Trump made good on his promise the next day, writing to Tahmooressi:
You have served our country with fortitude and dignity, and we are fortunate to have someone like you as a brave Marine and protector of our wonderful nation. We are proud of you and I wish you and your family the very best for many years to come.
According to the House Committee on Foreign Affairs and reporting by the Los Angeles Times, Republican and Democratic politicians alike had pushed for Tahmooressi's release. Any involvement or lack thereof by then-President Barack Obama was unclear.
College money for beauty queen's son: True
In 2016, Melissa Young stood at a Trump rally in Wisconsin and cried while she thanked him. She had competed as Miss Wisconsin USA in 2005, then got sick with an illness that has no cure. During her worst stretch, a handwritten note arrived from Trump calling her the bravest woman he knew. She said the doors Trump opened for her ended up giving her Mexican-American son a full ride to college.
During a Trump campaign rally in Janesville, Wisconsin, on March 29, 2016, Young told the then-candidate that his organizations, including the Miss USA pageant and the since-defunct crowdfunding platform FundAnything.com, had helped secure her Mexican-American son a full ride to college.
Young, who competed as Miss Wisconsin in the Miss USA pageant in 2005, said she suffered from an incurable illness and that at one point when she was in hospital, Trump sent her a handwritten letter addressed to the "bravest woman I know."
In 2016, Snopes reported on Young's story and the open letter to Trump she posted on Facebook (archived) in July 2015. That letter explained that Miss USA 2005 Chelsea Cooley had started a fundraiser for Young's son after attending the launch of FundAnything.com, which would allow him a full ride to college.
It was unclear whether Trump personally paid anything into Cooley's fundraiser for Young's son. (The claim does not say specifically that he did.)
Young posted (archived) on Facebook in August 2026 that her son would be a high school senior that coming school year.
Lynne Patton's reply to claims Trump was racist: True
That same year, Lynne Patton, a Black executive at the Trump Organization, put out a video answering the people calling her boss a racist. She admitted she had fought addiction for years. She said the Trump family never pushed her out. They stood by her the whole way.
Patton, who was at the time the vice president of the Eric Trump Foundation, spoke at the July 20, 2016, Republican National Convention in Cleveland, Ohio. Before she took the stage, a five-minute video essay played in which Patton criticized "repeated and reprehensible" attempts to "align my boss and his family with racist hate-mongering groups campaigns and messaging" (time code 0:14).
Patton called the Trump family, "one of the most generous, compassionate and philanthropic families I've ever had the privilege of knowing" (time code 0:39).
Patton's video essay and following appearance did not include mention of addiction. This part of the claim may have come from her later media appearances. For example, in April 2025, Patton discussed her history with cocaine addiction with Lara Trump, Eric Trump's wife, on Fox News. During that interview, Patton also talked about how the Trump family had supported her through her addiction.
After Donald Trump won the 2016 presidential election, he appointed Patton to a role in the Department of Housing and Urban Development overseeing a region covering New York and New Jersey. During his second administration, Trump appointed Patton as deputy assistant to the president and director of minority outreach.
Patton previously served a suspension from government work for a violation of the Hatch Act, which regulates the partisan political activities of federal employees, during her time at HUD.
Cancer treatment for campaign volunteer's father: Mostly true
Also in 2016, a young Illinois volunteer named Shane Bouvet told reporters that Trump had stepped in to cover his father's cancer treatment. His father, Donald Bouvet, beat the cancer. Trump has stayed in touch with the family ever since.
Trump met with Bouvet and his father, Donald, on Feb. 9, 2018. The president said he had first read about Shane Bouvet in The Washington Post ahead of his January 2017 inauguration.
The Post reported at the time that Bouvet was a Trump supporter and volunteer social media coordinator for the Trump campaign in Illinois. The article noted that Bouvet's father had cancer and that Bouvet and his mother both faced layoffs and difficulties finding well-paid work.
Trump said in February 2018:
I said, "I'd like to meet him." Nice young man, had a lot of difficulty. And I gave him some money for himself — $10,000. His father, Donald — good name — was suffering and really on a pretty final path toward losing his life with cancer. Shane took the $10,000, and, rather than spending it on himself, he gave it to his father. And his father went to a very good cancer clinic or hospital because he was at hospitals before and they didn't do so well.
Trump continued:
And they did a fantastic job, and Donald is now cancer-free. And I think it's an incredible story where a son would give 100 percent of the money to his father, who he loves, obviously.
As such, though Bouvet ended up spending Trump's money on cancer treatment for his father, Trump suggested that was not how he intended the money to be spent when he gave it to Bouvet. It was unclear whether Trump remained in contact with the Bouvet family at the time of this writing.
Loans to Black entrepreneurs: Unproven
And there is a story that has floated around New York business circles for years. A Black business owner could not get a loan anywhere in the city. Someone told him to go see Trump. Trump lent him the money and told him to pay it back when he could. The man came back later with a check and said the business was doing well. Trump tore the check up.
Snopes could not determine the source of this rumor. An oft-cited source was the Joe Brown, a former TV judge, who appeared on a podcast in 2019. When asked on the podcast whether Trump was a racist, Brown said (time code 1:07:43):
I don't think so. I have talked to a number of Black entrepreneurs who, back in the late '80s and '90s were, early '90s, were trying to get financing. They couldn't. Somebody told them to go check with Donald Trump. So they come back and tell me they got a loan from Donald Trump. He gave him a term loan: Show up with the interest in the principal [unintelligible] but they had to go see him in person. They independently relayed this tale that when they saw him he said, "That's what you're supposed to pay me, this is our agreement?" say "Yeah," and then tore the check up, shook their hands and "Congratulations, now run your business."
We found no evidence that Trump, his campaign or individual business owners had ever publicly confirmed giving or receiving such loans. We attempted to contact Brown to ask if he could put us in contact with Black business owners who received loans from Trump in the early 1990s. We also contacted the Trump Organization to ask about the rumor. We await replies to our queries.
Snopes' archives contributed to this report

United Nations, Sep 22: UN chief Antonio Guterres on Tuesday delivered a powerful clarion call to global leaders to reform the UN Security Council to ensure that it reflects today’s world and has the legitimacy to deal with current geopolitical challenges.
This is the final high-level UN General Assembly week for Secretary General Guterres, whose second five-year tenure as head of the United Nations ends in December 2026.
“We must also reform the Security Council so that it reflects today’s world with the legitimacy and effectiveness that today’s challenges demand,” Guterres told world leaders Tuesday in his address to the opening of the General Debate at the 81st session of the General Assembly.
Guterres, delivering his last address to the high-level UNGA debate as UN Chief, said the Security Council was designed in the aftermath of World War II. “But the world has fundamentally changed since then. A change that is far from reflected in the Security Council.”
He said the “most stunning example” of this is Africa.
“When the UN was founded, most of Africa was still under colonial rule. Today, Africa still has no permanent seat on the Council.
A 21st-century Security Council without permanent African representation is unjust and indefensible. This must change,” he said, to applause from the leaders in the UNGA hall.
After ending his nearly 35-minute and final address, Guterres received a standing ovation from world leaders, Foreign Ministers, ambassadors and diplomats and senior UN officials as he exited the podium.
“…Our institutions and systems of global governance continue to reflect the power realities and interests of a largely bygone age. That is the defining challenge before us. At the very moment when humanity faces an unprecedented convergence of threats, our mechanisms for collective action are under growing strain,” he said.
The call by Guterres to reform the 15-nation body was among the strongest by him as the powerful UN organ remains deeply divided and polarised, failing to stop conflicts and fulfil its responsibilities of maintaining international peace and security.
With sharp divisions among its five permanent, veto-wielding members - China, France, Russia, the UK and the US - the Council has remained ineffective as conflicts rage from Gaza to Russia.
India has been at the forefront of years-long efforts to reform the Security Council, including expansion in both its permanent and non-permanent categories, saying the 15-nation Council, founded in 1945, is not fit for purpose in the 21st Century and does not reflect contemporary geopolitical realities.
Delhi has consistently underscored that it rightly deserves a permanent seat at the horse-shoe table. India is vying for a non-permanent seat at the UN Security Council for the 2028–29 term, elections for which will be held in June next year.
As he addressed world leaders gathered in the iconic UNGA hall, Guterres voiced concern over deepened geopolitical divides, intensified inequalities and frayed trust.
“The climate crisis went from distant warning to daily reality. And artificial intelligence moved at a speed that has blindsided even those who created it. These are not separate crises. They are chapters of the same story. The story of power. Who has it. Who is denied it. How it is used. And how it is changing,” he said.
Guterres said that at a time when new centres of economic, political and technological influence have emerged, and humans are increasingly handing over power to machines, “our institutions and systems of global governance continue to reflect the power realities and interests of a largely bygone age."
“That is the defining challenge before us. At the very moment when humanity faces an unprecedented convergence of threats, our mechanisms for collective action are under growing strain,” he said.
Guterres emphasised that “we are clearly moving towards a multipolar world. And that movement is irreversible,” but cautioned that there are different ways that multipolarity can take shape.
“One possibility is a world of fragmentation and transactionalism. A world of rising tensions and deepening mistrust. Of fractured markets and weakened institutions. Of shrinking cooperation and zero-sum calculations. In many respects, that is the trajectory we are on today,” he said.
He also showed the international community the possibility of another path that goes towards networked multipolarity.
“A world built on interdependence – and sustained by a dense web of economic, political, social and technological connections. A world in which multiple centres of influence coexist within a common framework of international law and shared rules,” he said.
Guterres said such a world could help avoid hegemonic tendencies and what he described as the "Great Fracture: The division of the world into two rival blocs with separate economic, technological and security systems."
“A networked world recognises that no power can solve today’s challenges alone. Of course, competition will remain a permanent feature of international relations. But competition does not mean confrontation,” he said.
Noting that healthy competition can drive innovation, strengthen resilience, and expand opportunity, Guterres said building such a future begins with a recognition, especially by superpowers that their power isn’t so super.
"Their power has limits. The events of recent years have made that unmistakably clear. Military power alone cannot secure peace. Economic power alone cannot command stability. And technological power alone cannot guarantee security.
“A networked multipolar world can create the conditions for more balanced and representative global problem-solving. But it requires a multilateral system centred in the UN that is balanced and representative. Strong, effective institutions that reflect the realities and the progressively changing relative weight of countries and economies in today’s world – not the power arrangements of 80 years ago,” he said.

Suspect in Belleville, Ont., shooting is dead, SIU says
Sean Ward, 29, was critically injured near synagogue Sunday night
Ontario's police watchdog says 29-year-old Sean Ward, the man accused of shooting at city police near a Belleville, Ont., synagogue on Sunday night, has died.
Yom Kippur services were underway inside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue when Ward allegedly opened fire on Const. Jeff Smith with a shotgun, Belleville police Deputy Chief Sheri Meeks and Kristy Denette, a spokesperson for Ontario's Special Investigations Unit (SIU), said during a Monday news conference.
Smith had been parked outside Sons of Jacob at the request of the synagogue, its president told CBC News.
Ward had been in life-threatening condition.
Smith, who has been with Belleville's police service since 2013, suffered serious injuries during the shootout and is recovering in an intensive care unit where he remains in critical but stable condition.
More to come.

U.S. shouldn't buy 'blood potash' from Belarus, Sask. premier says
Moe defends Sask. potash in post aimed at Trump's latest trade threat
Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe defended the province's potash industry as ethically and economically superior to other international exporters after U.S. President Donald Trump threatened to source more of his country's fertilizer from Belarus.
"Buying blood potash from Belarus is supporting Russian aggression," Moe said in a post on social media. "It’s wrong and it doesn’t make sense."
Moe's post on Monday afternoon was a response to a Trump social media post from earlier that day.
"The United States is working on a massive Deal with respect to the purchase of Potash from Belarus," Trump said on Truth Social. "The pricing would be for substantially less than we are currently paying to Canada, very good news for our Farmers and Ranchers."
Potash is mainly used in fertilizers. In 2024, almost a third of the world's potash production came from Canada and all of the country's 10 active potash mines are in Saskatchewan, according to Natural Resources Canada.
"More than 40 countries — Canada and its allies — have sanctions against Belarus for supporting war criminal Putin’s invasion of Ukraine," Moe said in his social media post.
"Does anyone believe Belarusian blood potash shipped through Russia is going to be more affordable, more sustainable or more ethical than potash shipped from Saskatchewan — right here in North America?"
Nutrien Ltd., The Mosaic Company, Compass Minerals, and K+S Potash Canada are responsible for all of Canada's potash production. BHP is building the Jansen potash mine in Saskatchewan and expects to start commercial production in mid-2027.
Nutrien is the largest potash fertilizer producer in Canada and one of the largest in the world. The Saskatoon-based company referred CBC to Fertilizer Canada when asked to comment on Trump's post.
U.S. farmers have used Canadian potash for decades, said Fertilizer Canada, an industry trade group, in an emailed statement to CBC News.
"Reliability, proximity, transportation infrastructure, product availability and the ability to deliver during critical application windows all matter," the statement said.
"A strong and integrated North American fertilizer supply chain helps support farm productivity, affordability and food security on both sides of the border.”
Last year, Nutrien announced plans to build a potash export terminal at the Port of Longview, Wash., to handle expected growth in international demand for its fertilizer products.
The opposition NDP called Trump's social media post "infuriating" in a statement on Monday.
"He is looking at signing a deal with an authoritarian Russian satellite state that is supporting Putin’s brutal war against the people of Ukraine," the NDP statement said.
"This is a bad idea that will only hurt families and communities on both sides of the border."

It could have been a scene from Cape Fear: a quiet evening, an ordinary home, a sudden intrusion by a stranger convinced that the law has betrayed him.
In early July 2022, Democratic representative Pramila Jayapal of Washington and her husband were watching television at their Seattle home when men drove past their house screaming threats: vile, racialized, and unmistakably political. They called the police. The men left. Thirty minutes later, one returned, blasting music and approaching the porch. When officers arrived, they found him armed with a loaded handgun, a round already chambered. A neighbor heard him shout, “Go back to India. I am going to kill you.”
Jayapal later described the episode not as an aberration but as evidence of a broader transformation in American politics—a climate in which grievance increasingly functions as permission and intimidation is framed as justified political expression. The threats did not stop. Nor is Jayapal alone. For years, Representative Marjorie Taylor Greene of Georgia lived under constant threat as one of Donald Trump’s most aggressive defenders in Congress. She reported hundreds of death threats, largely from ideological opponents.
But when Greene publicly broke with Trump—over the Epstein files, Gaza, and what “America first” had come to mean—the direction of the threats shifted. After Trump labeled her “Marjorie Traitor Greene,” messages arrived threatening her son by name. One threatened her assassination. Another claimed that a plane ticket had already been purchased. In November 2025, Greene announced her resignation from Congress, citing threats to her family. “I think that comes to a point,” she said, “where any American can look at that and say that’s a high bar and way too much to ask.”
What Jayapal and Greene have in common is not ideology, temperament, or policy; it is exposure. Both became targets in an era in which political violence is no longer confined to the fringe, no longer clearly condemned by leaders, no longer monopolized by either the right or the left—and increasingly treated as a legitimate instrument of political pressure.
What happened to Jayapal and Greene is no longer exceptional; it is revealing. Their experiences point to a deeper transformation: Political violence has moved closer to the center of American political life, touching elected officials across parties and becoming a recurring feature of contemporary conflict rather than a rare deviation.
Since 2016, Americans have argued fiercely not only about whether political violence is rising but about who is responsible. One dominant narrative attributes the problem primarily to the radical right: white nationalism, militias, election denial. A competing narrative insists that violence emanates just as strongly from the radical left, manifested in riots, assaults on police, and organized disruption in cities and on campuses. These claims are not merely rhetorical; they shape public trust, elite behavior, law enforcement priorities, and—most dangerously—the willingness of partisans to condemn violence committed by those they regard as allies. But what does the evidence actually show?
America’s political violence problem is neither one-sided nor symmetrical. Taken together, the evidence from federal threat assessments, terrorism databases, protest incident data, and congressional security records points toward the same conclusion. Political violence in the United States declined for nearly two decades after the 1990s and then rose sharply beginning around 2016. For decades prior to that year, politically motivated violence was concentrated overwhelmingly on the far right. Today, violence associated with the right and left is closer to balance, even as it takes very different forms. Right-wing violence has been substantially more frequent and far deadlier than left-wing violence since 2016—aimed at elections, federal institutions, and public officials—while left-wing violence has been more common in mass protest settings, from the 2020 George Floyd unrest to clashes over immigration enforcement, typically involving property destruction and confrontations with police.
Although uncertainty remains at the margins, the evidence strongly suggests that since roughly 2016, political violence on both the right and the left has reached levels unseen in the United States since the upheavals of the 1960s. These patterns reflect not a single ideology but the deeper forces of violent populism: hardened identities, perceived existential threats, collapsing institutional trust, and elite rhetoric that frames politics as a struggle between enemies rather than fellow citizens.
Much of the public disagreement about whether political violence is rising and who is responsible for it stems not from ideology alone but from competing definitions about what should be counted.
In scholarly literature, political violence is generally defined as the use or credible threat of physical force for political ends. Those ends may include coercion, intimidation, punishment, or symbolic signaling intended to influence public behavior, political outcomes, or institutional authority. Under this definition fall assassination attempts, armed assaults on public officials, bombings, arson attacks, violent intimidation, riots against buildings with explicit political aims, and organized plots to use force against political targets.
Just as important are the exclusions. Political violence does not include ordinary criminal activity lacking political motivation, interpersonal violence driven by private disputes, or lawful protest—even when protests are disruptive, angry, or unlawful. Nor does it include harsh rhetoric alone, however inflammatory, unless it is paired with a credible threat of force. These boundaries matter, because collapsing political violence into crime or protest obscures its distinct causes and consequences.
The hardest problem is determining intent. Political violence is defined not only by what happens but by why it happens—and intent is often ambiguous. When a crowd burns a police precinct, is the act political rebellion, criminal opportunism, or both? When a gunman attacks a synagogue, is the motive ideological antisemitism, personal grievance, or mental illness layered atop political belief? When an individual sends a death threat to a lawmaker, is it expressive rage, partisan trolling, or preparation for real-world violence?
Reasonable scholars answer these questions differently, often using dissimilar evidentiary thresholds. Some datasets require explicit ideological statements; others infer political intent from targets, symbols, or timing. Some classify riots as political violence only when their organizers articulate political goals; others focus on behavior rather than rhetoric. None of these choices is neutral, and each shapes the resulting picture.
These definitional choices explain why prominent datasets sometimes appear to disagree. Federal law enforcement datasets emphasize lethality, capability, and threats to national institutions. Protest-oriented datasets capture frequency and geographic spread. Terrorism databases prioritize ideological framing and tactical similarity to global movements. Each captures something real—and each misses something important.
For this reason, no single dataset can settle the debate. Accordingly, my work triangulates across several sources, combining federal threat assessments, incident-level databases, congressional security data, and survey research. The goal is not to produce a definitive body count but to identify patterns that recur across independent measures: who is targeted, how violence is carried out, how lethal it is, and how those patterns have changed since 2016.
This approach does not eliminate uncertainty. But it does attempt to move beyond partisan narratives and toward a more accurate understanding of how political violence in America has evolved—and why arguments over its meaning have become almost as intense as the violence itself.
The most authoritative window into political violence in the United States comes not from media tallies or advocacy groups but from the federal agencies charged with tracking national security threats—above all, the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). Yet even here, readers encounter a fundamental problem: There is no single, formal US government definition of “political violence.” Instead, federal agencies operate with overlapping categories—domestic terrorism, domestic violent extremism, hate crimes, threats against officials, and antigovernment violence—each shaped by legal constraints, investigative mandates, and statutory language rather than a unified conceptual framework.
This definitional fragmentation matters. Unlike many countries, the United States does not criminalize “domestic terrorism” as a stand-alone offense; the relevant statute (18 U.S.C., § 2331) defines “international terrorism” and “domestic terrorism” descriptively but does not by itself create a prosecutable offense. As a result, the FBI does not report a simple annual count of domestic terrorism incidents. Instead, the statistics reflect investigations, disrupted plots, arrests, and threat assessments organized around ideological motivation, such as racially and ethnically motivated violent extremism, antigovernment or antiauthority extremism, and hostile acts against government structures. The absence of a single metric has fueled public confusion and partisan cherry-picking, with critics on all sides accusing the FBI of either exaggerating or minimizing particular threats.
Despite these constraints, a consistent picture emerges from FBI testimony, annual threat assessments, and congressional reporting since 2016. Across political administrations, FBI directors have warned that domestic violent extremism is a persistent and elevated threat, with particular emphasis on right-wing ideologies—especially white supremacist and ethno-nationalist violence—as the most lethal category among domestic violent threats. This assessment is grounded not in ideology per se but in outcomes: The majority of fatal attacks tied to political or ideological motives in recent years have originated in right-wing ecosystems, often carried out by lone actors inspired by online propaganda rather than formal organizations.
At the same time, federal reporting makes clear that political violence is not monopolized by the right. The FBI and DHS have also documented significant spikes in violence associated with mass protest movements, assaults on law enforcement, arson, and attacks on government facilities during periods of intense unrest—most notably in 2020, when protests following the killing of George Floyd were accompanied by substantial violent confrontations in many cities. These events are more commonly linked to left-wing or anti-authority contexts, tend to cluster geographically, and are far less likely to result in mass casualties. The distinction federal agencies draw is therefore not between “violent” and “nonviolent” sides but between forms of violence that differ in frequency, lethality, and strategic orientation.
A further frustration is temporal. Much of the FBI’s publicly accessible data lags behind current events. Detailed breakdowns often stop several years short of the present, while ongoing investigations limit transparency about more recent trends. As a result, scholars and policymakers must rely on testimony, qualitative assessments, and partial datasets to infer patterns after 2021—a gap that has widened in the wake of intensified threats against public officials and institutions. This delay has created a disconnect between the lived experience of escalating threats—particularly against elected officials—and the statistical record available to the public.
These limitations should not be mistaken for insignificance. On the contrary, the persistence of the same core warnings across multiple administrations, political contexts, and leadership teams suggests institutional continuity rather than partisan distortion. While the FBI cannot provide a clean annual count of “political violence,” its threat assessments provide something arguably more important: a comparative judgment about which forms of violence are most likely to kill, destabilize institutions, and undermine democratic governance.
When federal threat assessments are read alongside terrorism databases, incident-level coding, congressional security data, and survey research, the contours of political violence since 2016 come into focus—even if the exact numbers remain contested. The challenge is not the absence of evidence but the difficulty of integrating imperfect sources into an honest and comprehensive account.

Geneva 17 October 2024 – This afternoon, His Excellency Mr Jérôme Bonnafont, Permanent Representative of France to the United Nations in Geneva, and WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus met in the WHO headquarters for the signing of seven contribution agreements.
The contribution totalling €24 million comes through the Ministry of Europe & Foreign Affairs. It fits in the France–WHO Framework Agreement for 2020 to 2025, which provides both a strategic framework for engagement, aligned with WHO priorities, while providing legal, administrative and financial instruments for operationalizing collaboration.
This latest contribution includes a generous €4.5 million in fully flexible voluntary funds for the Core Voluntary Contributions Account (CVCA).
Additionally, France will support key areas of WHO’s work, addressing some of the most pressing health challenges, including non-communicable diseases (NCDs), urban health labs, One Health, funding for the WHO Contingency Fund for Emergencies (CFE), and several emergencies, such as the WHO response in Gaza, response to cholera outbreaks and mental health support in Ukraine.
France will also continue to support the WHO emergencies centre in Lyon which is playing a crucial role in preparedness and response to epidemics.
Ambassador Jérôme Bonnafont underscored the importance of this collaboration: “France remains deeply committed to supporting the World Health Organization in its efforts to tackle critical global health challenges. These agreements reflect our shared priorities of promoting health equity, responding to emergencies, and strengthening healthcare systems worldwide.”
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of WHO, expressed his gratitude, stating, “We are immensely grateful to the French Government for its steadfast support to WHO, continued partnership and leadership in global health. This contribution will enable us to address key health threats, from non-communicable diseases to emergency response, helping to save lives and protect the most vulnerable populations.”
France is a strong supporter of a fully and flexibly financed WHO, providing leadership and support to the increase of assessed contributions to the Organization. France is also one of the co-hosts to WHO’s first Investment Round towards the mobilization of predictable and flexible resources for WHO’s core work on the Fourteenth General Programme of Work (2025–2028), approved by the World Health Assembly in 2024.
This signing ceremony marks another milestone in the strong and longstanding partnership between WHO and France, reinforcing their joint commitment to a healthier, safer world.

India survived a scare against Japan on Tuesday, edging the hosts by two runs in a rain-hit one-off T20 International that was reduced to five overs per side at the Sano International Cricket Stadium.
Japan needed six runs from the last four balls while chasing India's 32 for 4. But the match took another turn when a wide call was reversed after protests from India.
Left-handed batter Alexander Shirai-Patmore attempted a reverse-hit against 
Axar Patel
 and missed the ball, which went well down the leg side. The umpire called it a wide. The same sequence was repeated off the next delivery, with another wide called.
The second wide decision was also initially given, but after Axar and India captain 
Shreyas Iyer
 protested, the umpire spoke to the leg umpire, New Zealand's Chris Brown, and reversed the decision.
The equation then returned to six runs from three balls. Japan could score only three more runs and finished on 30 for 3, with India winning by two runs.
The result gave India the record for the lowest total successfully defended in T20 cricket. It was also the first men's T20 meeting between India and Japan.
India had struggled with the conditions after choosing to bat. The surface was sluggish and the outfield was slow, making it difficult for the batters to score freely. 
Iyer was the only Indian batter to reach double figures, scoring 16.
What do the laws say?
In white-ball cricket, a delivery that passes down the leg side is generally called a wide. The rule is intended to prevent negative bowling in limited-overs cricket.
However, the rise of reverse sweeps and switch-hits has led to questions over how the rule should apply when a batter moves across and attempts such shots.
The 
MCC's Law 22.4.1 says, "the umpire shall not adjudge a delivery as being a Wide, if the striker, by moving, either causes the ball to pass wide of him/her, as defined in 22.1.2 or brings the ball sufficiently within reach to be able to hit it by means of a normal cricket stroke."
The laws do not specifically mention reverse sweeps or switch-hits, leaving some room for interpretation when a batter changes position and misses a delivery that would otherwise have been called wide.
The MCC also sets out when an umpire can change a decision.
 Law 2.12
 states: "An umpire may alter any decision provided that such alteration is made promptly and does not contradict Law 20.6 (Dead ball not to be revoked). This apart, an umpire’s decision, once made, is final."

A claim (archived) circulated online in September 2026 that a U.S. Secret Service agent said working for President Donald Trump had "ruined" him because of the president's kindness.
According to one Facebook user, the agent in question said:
Trump RUINED me for this job. Not because he's difficult — but because he's completely different. Trump knows my NAME. Other Presidents called me "agent." Trump calls me by my actual name.
The same claim, text and image also circulated elsewhere on Facebook (archived, archived, archived, archived).
We previously investigated this rumor in March 2026 and found it false. We found then that the rumor originated from the "Garvit pandey" Facebook page, which appeared to mass-produce baseless stories about Trump using unrelated images. Snopes had previously found another such story from that page to be false.
There was no credible reporting to support the claim at the time of this writing (archived, archived, archived).The text and images that accompanied the claim appeared to have been generated or edited using artificial intelligence. This, taken together with the unreliable nature of the claim's source, led us to rate this claim false.
Users who create content like the story about the alleged Secret Service agent capitalize on social media users' willingness to believe and share the made-up claims, profiting from advertising revenue on external websites to which the posts link. (Snopes has previously reported on the business strategy.)
A Secret Service spokesperson told Snopes via phone in March 2026 that they could not comment on the interview's authenticity without an agent's name, which neither "Garvit pandey" nor later posts included.
We contacted a manager of the "Garvit pandey" Facebook page ask for more details about the story or an explanation of why it shared the alleged quote without a disclaimer that it was false. We had not gotten a reply by September 2026.
Text and images provided clues to story's falsehood
The post on the "Garvit pandey" Facebook page displayed several signs of AI-generated text. For example, the text used all caps on some words for emphasis, a tool not generally used in traditional reporting. Pangram, a highly regarded artificial intelligence detector for images and text, assessed the Facebook post's text to be fully AI.
Let us note here: These types of AI detection tools are fallible. Snopes cautions people against using them for definitive answers on media's authenticity without supporting evidence.
Aside from likely AI-generated text, the post that circulated in September 2026 appeared to use edited or fake images that showed Trump with Secret Service agents.
Two of the images in the collage showed agents surrounding Trump at a rally in Dayton, Ohio, in 2016. However, the Facebook post used a version of one of those photos with a different background.
An authentic portrait of James M. Murray, a Trump-appointed former head of the Secret Service who stepped down in 2022, also appeared with a different background in the September 2026 Facebook post. Another image that showed Trump looking down with an agent standing behind him (upper left corner) also appeared to have been enhanced from the original and given a different background.
Pangram found the entire collage to be fully AI.
'Garvit pandey' page spreads fake stories about Trump
Snopes previously investigated the "Garvit pandey" page that originally shared the false story in March 2026. Our review found several users accusing the page of posting AI-generated stories. We also found that posts on the page contained common markers of AI-generated stories like excessive use of emojis, repetition of one core message and calls to action. The story about the Secret Service agent included all of these markers.
The above factors led us to conclude that stories on the page were either falsified or misattributed.
The fictional story about the Secret Service agent heaping praise on Trump resembled glurge, which Dictionary.com defines as "stories, often sent by email, that are supposed to be true and uplifting, but which are often fabricated and sentimental."
Snopes has previously investigated other rumors involving the Secret Service, including whether a "reptilian" agent guarded former U.S. President Barack Obama and whether the service went "broke" paying for agents to guard the Trump family.

'Real fear Littler could walk away' - darts would be loser in booing row
- Published
At just 19, Luke Littler has won almost every major trophy in darts.
He is a multi-millionaire with lucrative sponsorship deals and his own TV show.
But has his rapid rise turned some against him?
This past weekend the teenager was once again subjected to boos and whistles from sections of the crowd as he took to the stage at the World Series of Darts in Amsterdam.
What is surprising though is that it came as 'The Nuke' was on a quest to complete a darts clean sweep by becoming the first player to win all 10 major televised tournaments in a calendar year.
Littler suggested afterwards that, if the booing continues, he will not attend events held in the Netherlands.
But Samuel Gill, editor of Dartnews.com, suggests Littler's future in the sport could be at stake.
"There's a real fear that within a few years he'll just turn around and walk away from the sport," Gill told BBC Sport.
"So, I think for fans, 'Don't bite the hand that feeds you'. If people keep taunting him and don't want him to win, he might end up just walking away and not bothering anymore."
Amsterdam was the latest tournament where Littler has faced what some might describe as an overly hostile reaction from fans.
A vibrant pantomime-style atmosphere is part and parcel of the darts experience and Dutch and German crowds are amongs the most raucous - but it is clear Littler believes he has been unfairly targeted.
The referee stopped the match during his narrow win against Nathan Aspinall in the last-16 on Saturday to warn the hostile crowd about its behaviour, before play resumed.
It followed Littler also being booed during his win against home favourite Danny Noppert on Friday.
The teenager's quarter-final defeat to Jonny Clayton ended Littler's quest for the clean sweep, but the Warrington native clearly felt fans had been unduly harsh towards him.
Littler has now withdrawn from a series of upcoming events.
"Just no point in me travelling, wasting my time while I'm getting booed," said Littler.
'Not a unique experience for Littler'
Littler has also been jeered at numerous events in the UK.
His phenomenal rise saw him reach the PDC World Darts Championship aged just 16 in his debut year as a professional.
He captured the title the following year and the trophies, sponsorship deals and six-figure winners' cheques have continued to flow.
But increasingly so have whistles and boos during his performances.
"I don't think people expected him to reach the heights that he has so quickly," Gill said.
The darts journalist - who became aware of Littler when the sport star was 14 - says this level of attention is not just unique to the British player.
"Michael van Gerwen was the same for a long time when he dominated the sport. He barely lost a game in about five years, and he was hoovering up titles for fun and it was similar," said Gill.
"Everyone wanted to boo him and even me as a viewer before I got into this role, growing up watching Van Gerwen, I wanted him to lose because it's something different for the sport every single week."
Currently ranked number one in the world, Littler is so far ahead of his closest rivals that he already has the advantage of only having to play in selective tournaments.
His boycott threat could end up being a blow to tournament organisers.
"They don't like him because he's that good. And he's got a bit of swagger to him," said Karl Holden secretary of St Helen's Darts Academy - where Littler honed his skills from the age of nine.
"Luke's got a bit of a character to him. For me, he's the ultimate professional. He might give a little bit of the large sometimes, but you need that, otherwise darts would be totally boring."
Darts the loser if Littler walks away
It seems remarkable that the future of Littler's career in the sport is even being debated.
More so when you consider his age and the fact he only turned professional two years ago.
However, Gill believes that Littler's rapid haul of trophies, coupled with the huge amounts of money now in the sport, could result in the teenager leaving in the next "four to five years" should the boos and whistles continue.
Gill believes Littler's impact on the darting world is immeasurable.
Tickets to events featuring him are often sold out, applications to darting academies are reported to be at an all-time high and the Briton has transcended the sport.
Gill therefore feels that, if Littler was to walk away, the sport would be the real loser.
"He's the one who is bringing this sport to a completely different level. Nowadays, he is back-page news wherever you go," Gill said.
"He might just decide 'I just want a quiet life now and just live off his money'."
Littler has barely known anything other than winning. His challenged now is maintaining that victorious streak while keeping fans - whose interest helps fund his prize money - happy.
Tricky when some are paying with the hope of seeing him lose.
"If he was on that stage, everybody liked him and he just threw darts, I think I'd get bored of watching him," Holden said.
