This 'fire amoeba' pushes the limit of what's possible for complex life
Angela Oliverio, a microbiologist at Syracuse University, studies the edge of what's possible.
"There's a very deep curiosity and desire to understand life at its limits and at its most extreme," she says. "And where that boundary is and what truly are our constraints."
It's not unlike ultra-elite athletes who push themselves "to the absolute max of what we think is humanly possible," she says. "But in this case, we're just expanding it to life more generally" — specifically, microscopic life.
Oliverio studies organisms called extremophiles, so named because they thrive in unusually harsh conditions, like high temperatures. The title holders in this regard are simple organisms like bacteria and a group called Archaea, with certain species living at or above 212°F, the boiling point of water.
But Beryl Rappaport, a PhD student in Oliverio's lab, says that until now, that same ability to beat the heat has been less studied in eukaryotes — a group whose members include many different species, from humans to single-celled amoebas. These organisms have more complex cells that contain a nucleus and other structures.
Rappaport says part of the reason may simply be that scientists haven't found the right eukaryotes yet. "So few have been described, especially in detail. We have a lot to learn from them."
Now, she and her colleagues have added a remarkable new organism to the pantheon: a species they call the fire amoeba that nudges a key temperature limit for complex cells upwards by another five or so degrees. The findings were published in the journal Cell.
This may seem like a modest improvement, but Oliverio considers the sub-4-minute mile for runners, which was long thought to be impossible. Once one athlete achieved it, however, it was just weeks before it happened again.
"It wasn't so much the incremental amount that this record was broken by, as much as the proof that it was possible," she says.
A little cell that likes it hot
To make this discovery, the researchers and their colleagues went on something of a fishing expedition in Lassen Volcanic National Park in northern California.
"It's one of the least-visited national parks in the US," says Oliverio.
"It's super beautiful," adds Rappaport. "Very mountainous. All of the pines. A lot of butterflies flitting around. It did experience some pretty rough fires in the past decade, so a lot of new understory growth. And then just these little steaming geothermal pockets."
One such pocket is a tributary of a little waterway called Hot Springs Creek, "that you would almost miss because it's surrounded by a lot of tall grasses," says Rappaport.
The research team decided to take some samples there by using extra-long barbecue tongs to grip a series of vials that Rappaport dipped into the steaming water.
Later, in the lab, she put the water samples under a microscope, filmed them, and sped up the footage. And that's when she saw something moving. It seemed to protrude, retract, and fluidly change its shape — as if it were performing a single cell's version of hot yoga.
"That's definitely an amoeba," she recalls thinking. "That's characteristic amoeba movement."
This amoeba, however, was able to replicate at temperatures up to 145°F. This is a new record for a complex organism. It can also continue moving around up to 147°F and protect itself in waters as hot as 158°F. When Rappaport and her colleagues studied its genome, they realized they had a new species on their hands.
The team named it Incendiamoeba cascadensis, which translates to "fire amoeba of the Cascade mountain range."
An extremophile with lessons to share
The next question the researchers investigated was how the fire amoeba can thrive at such high temperatures.
When they compared the genome of the new species to those of other amoebas, they observed that the fire amoeba had ways of keeping its proteins and membranes stable at higher temperatures.
It's a finding that could be used to expand the search for life. "Thinking about not only what are the limits of life and what is possible here, but also what might be possible elsewhere," says Oliverio.
In addition, she argues the amoeba's temperature resilience could offer clues to help create heat-resilient crops or drugs that are stable across a wider range of temperatures.
"I can tell you from experience it's really hard to find a really cool exotic organism and actually turn it into something that has a major impact on other species," says Debashish Bhattacharya, an evolutionary biologist at Rutgers University who wasn't involved with the research.
"But there's always the potential of finding something amazing, that's for sure," he adds.
Bhattacharya says that in other extremophiles, their genomes have become more compact. "It's called genome streamlining," he says, "so they can then compete with bacteria which have smaller genomes and live in these harsh environments."
This isn't the case with the fire amoeba, which has a larger genome than its relatives. "It's taken a different path," says Bhattacharya, "so I think that's really interesting."
Oliverio finds it similarly interesting. And now that the fire amoeba has been documented, she thinks it's just the start. More scientists, she hopes, will now go looking for other complex organisms with these extreme abilities.
"Perhaps the upper temperature record will be broken again soon," she says.

Leh, Sep 22: Ladakh Chief Secretary Ashish Kundra said a new framework is being worked out under Article 371 to provide constitutional safeguards suited to the Union Territory's specific requirements.
"A new model is being worked out considering the aspiration of the Ladakhis which does not exist anywhere else in the country. The draft would be discussed in the next meeting (of the Ladakh representatives and Ministry of Home Affairs) proposed to be held in the first week of October," the chief secretary said at a consultative meeting with the members of the Civil Society.
The Centre has proposed inserting a new chapter K under Article 371 of the Constitution to provide special safeguards to Ladakh.
Kundra convened the meeting in Leh to discuss key administrative, developmental and political issues concerning the Union Territory, including constitutional safeguards, land rights, employment, culture, environment, education, drug abuse and other matters of public importance, an official statement said on Tuesday.
Addressing the meeting, Kundra expressed that there is a broad agreement on the need for constitutional protection for Ladakh.
"The important thing is that constitutional protection is required for Ladakh. The protection should cover our land, employment, culture, environment and natural resources," he said.
Referring to Centre-Ladakh talks, the chief secretary said direct elections to the proposed UT-level body were among the key suggestions emerging from the discussions.
Further steps, including consideration of the proposed constitutional amendment by Parliament, would follow after consensus is reached on the framework, he said.
He also explained that a separate legislation would subsequently be required to provide detailed provisions regarding the powers, functions and institutional arrangements of the proposed body.
The chief secretary also highlighted various recent administrative initiatives, including strengthening of the district-level administrative structure, posting of officers in the districts, upgradation of hospitals to district hospitals, and progress towards Panchayat elections.
He informed the participants that Ladakh has recorded more than four lakh tourist arrivals so far this year, compared to around 3.35 lakh during the entire previous year.
The meeting also featured presentations on a range of developmental and social issues concerning Ladakh.
Ladakh DGP Anand Jain, on behalf of the police, made a presentation on drug-related issues and sought the support of civil society members in creating awareness among the masses.

Alzheimer’s blood tests are advancing diagnosis. What can they really tell us?
Blood tests such as p-tau217 and p-tau181 can help identify changes linked to Alzheimer’s disease. Neurologists explain what these tests can detect, how they aid diagnosis and what the results can and cannot tell patients
For now, the important question is not simply whether a blood test is positive or negative, but what the result means in the context of the person’s symptoms, clinical assessment and the specific test used.
| Photo Credit: AFP
Changes in the brain linked to Alzheimer’s disease can begin years before memory and other cognitive symptoms appear. Blood-based biomarkers offer a less invasive way to detect some of these biological changes. These include phosphorylated tau (p-tau), such as p-tau217 and p-tau181, and amyloid-beta measures such as the Aβ42/Aβ40 ratio. However, these tests do not directly measure memory loss, brain-cell loss or the severity of cognitive impairment.
Tau is a protein found in nerve cells. In Alzheimer’s disease, abnormal tau is linked to the formation of neurofibrillary tangles. The build-up of amyloid-beta is another biological change associated with the disease.

Tata Sons: India's corporate crown braces for upheaval amid boardroom revolt
- Published
This week, the board of Tata Sons - one of India's oldest conglomerates and owner of iconic British brands such as Jaguar Land Rover and Tetley Tea - defied its largest shareholder, Tata Trusts, by reappointing N Chandrasekaran as chairman and backing a public listing of the holding company.
Tata Trusts, which owns 66% of Tata Sons called the decision "illegal" under its articles of association and also opposed the listing, setting the stage for a period of prolonged upheaval and possibly a protracted legal drama at Bombay House, the headquarters of the 158-year-old company.
For the Tatas, who are no strangers to boardroom battles, a cloud of uncertainty now prevails at multiple levels.
The resolution to reappoint Chandrasekharan, while approved by the board, could be defeated at the company's Annual General Meeting as Tata Trusts is likely to vote against it, putting a question mark over his future.
The meeting has to take place before 31 December as per reports, after the previous one was adjourned for lack of quorum, but no new date has yet been announced.
"The Nomination and Remuneration Committee (NRC) of the Board of Tata Sons which reappointed him has no power to take this decision. They can only make a recommendation. Also, their decision flies against the governance code of the company that requires executives to step down from active roles at 65. These are serious lapses," Nitin Potdar, a prominent Mumbai-based corporate lawyer told the BBC.
Chandrasekharan, who got a five-year extension, will turn 65 in 2028.
Tata Group stocks first soared and then crashed as the tensions mounted, reflecting hope and uncertainty about leadership and business continuity amid several high-stakes but loss-making bets by Chandrasekharan in sectors like semiconductors and airlines.
But beyond the leadership tussle, the bigger question to contend with is the group's public listing, "which now looks increasingly inevitable", Nirmalya Kumar, who previously headed strategy at Tata Sons, told the BBC.
In 2022, India's central bank, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), classified Tata Sons as an "upper layer non-banking financial company" because of its systemic importance and investment activities. This created a listing obligation on the group.
Tata Sons sought to get out of this classification by repaying their debt and arguing that they do not borrow directly from the public markets.
But after sitting on its application for over two years, the RBI rejected the company's bid to get out of the framework earlier this month, pushing the group closer to a stock market debut.
In a statement, Tata Trusts reiterated its long-held opposition to going public and said "all available options and not a listing alone" are being explored even though its trustees are no longer unanimous in their position on the matter.
Potdar says the regulator has no power to force any company to go public and the issue will almost certainly be legally challenged by Tata Trusts.
The RBI meanwhile has pre-emptively, external approached the courts seeking to be heard first in any matter related to the listing.
The issue has sharply divided opinion among corporate pundits.
Many in the group, including the late Ratan Tata and veteran director NA Soonawala, have long argued strongly for keeping the group private.
A publicly held Tata Sons could significantly reduce the control and special rights the Tata Trusts wield over the group.
They say the Tatas have a unique operating structure where the majority shareholder is a charity which uses dividends received from commercial arms to fund hospitals, universities and research.
A listing, they say, will destroy its character by making it accountable to outside shareholders whose focus would be financial returns.
"A new group of shareholders might say, 'Don't declare dividends; we need to reinvest this money in the companies.' What happens then? The first casualty will be the hospitals they run," said Potdar.
Opponents of the initial public offering (IPO) also worry that bringing in public investors will weaken the group's internal support function to rescue distressed businesses and expose the company to quarterly performance pressures.
Moreover the timing is another crucial factor.
"The group currently faces large financial commitments from recently formed subsidiary companies, including Air India, investments in long gestation projects, and losses in newer ventures," Soonawala wrote, external in a piece for Times of India.
"The current situation in the case of Air India would be an acid test. All these would need to be disclosed fully in an IPO prospectus. Consolidated financial statements – reflecting subsidiary losses and borrowings – may not present an especially attractive picture to sophisticated investors, pointing to wrong timing for an IPO at the present time."
Many, including Potdar, also argue that globally, industrial foundations are being protected as sources of patient capital - money that can be committed for years to fund long-gestation projects and social goals. By forcing the Tatas to list, India is going the other way.
But supporters of a listing say it would bring much-needed transparency and accountability to a group that is systemically important to India.
"There should be tougher scrutiny of their capital-allocation decisions being so central to the Indian business ecosystem. Everybody wants complete control over their empire and the freedom to take capricious decisions, but that is not a good thing for the organisation," said Kumar.
Collectively, listed Tata companies including Tata Motors and TCS have a market capitalisation of more than $260bn and influence over 17.7 million retail shareholders, pension funds, insurers and mutual funds, investment advisory firm InGovern said.
"[It] cannot reasonably remain outside the governance and transparency expectations increasingly associated with systemically important financial and industrial conglomerates," the report added.
It also argued that shareholders of listed Tata companies are indirectly affected by Tata Sons' decisions, even though they have no direct voting rights in the holding company.
Moreover, given that the Tatas have recently made several high stakes global bets, making iPhones for Apple, partnering with Nvidia on artificial intelligence and Boeing, Airbus and Singapore Airlines on aerospace and aviation, InGovern says, a "flexible and transparent capital structure increasingly important".
Some experts say a listing may now be the only way to ease increasingly fractious relations between the board and shareholders - tensions that are hurting not just the group, but India more broadly.
Tata Trusts hold controlling economic interest and veto rights over Tata Sons board appointments and capital allocation decisions above a certain threshold.
It's hard to imagine the latter can function effectively on crucial issues of national interest - such as turning around Air India or raising funds to pay off a large minority shareholder like the SP Group which is in urgent need of cash to avert a potentially ruinous default - if it can no longer see eye to eye with its biggest shareholder.
Whatever happens on the listing front, experts say India's biggest trophy asset is entering totally uncharted territory. As Kumar suspects, "a new twist" can be expected every week.

Following the seizure of counterfeit drugs, especially those used to treat cancer, Health Department officials are now tracking patients to check the current status of their health.
Licences of 16 retail and wholesale pharmaceutical firms were cancelled and eight licenses were suspended.
Speaking to The Hindu, U.T. Khader, Minister for Health and Family Welfare, said, “Officials will track records of cancer patients from various private hospitals across the State. We will call them up and check the status of their health. They may have unknowingly bought these counterfeit drugs.”
“We don’t sell fake drugs at government hospitals, hence there is no question of tracking patients to know their status,” he added.
Mr. Khader stated that in order to make it easy for laboratories, doctors, and pharmaceutical firms to differentiate between fake and original drugs, the department has written to the headquarters of Pfizer to release their reference standards.
“When the fake drugs are sent to labs for testing, we need to have the company’s reference standards. It will make the process of drug testing easier for our department. However, the company hasn’t replied to our email so far. Hence, we have written to the Union government to take a note of the increasing number of fake drugs and medicines in the market, measures to identify them, and stop them from being sold in medical shops. State governments have a minor role to play in giving permissions to drug manufacturers and what is brought into the market for selling,” he said.
He added that the investigation of counterfeit drugs is ongoing, while the department is contemplating booking fake drug manufacturers, distributors, pharmaceutical firms, and medical store owners under Section 105 of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), according to which if the act is done with the intent to cause death or bodily injury likely to cause death, the punishment is either life imprisonment or imprisonment for five to 10 years and penalty depending on the nature of offence.
An all-India health conclave will be hosted in Bengaluru in the third week of October, said Health Minister U.T. Khader. “Health Ministers from across all the States, FSDA officials from State governments, FSSAI officials and other stakeholders will be part of the conclave. We will not only discuss and debate but take some strong decisions to tackle issues like counterfeit drugs across the country,” he said.

Quick Answer
You can build an Android app with Google Antigravity by designing the UI in Google Stitch, generating the app with Gemini using Expo React Native, previewing it through Expo Go, and creating an APK with Expo EAS. You can also connect Supabase for cloud sync.
Building apps on software is now everyone’s cup of tea, thanks to AI. Even if you have never written a single line of code before, you can just go to any AI tool and build the app you want. However, the real complexity lies in making those apps useful instead of AI slop. To help you out, we have created this series where we help you learn how to build fully functional and reliable apps using AI tools.
To start with beginners, in this guide you will learn how to create an Android app using Google Antigravity.
There are multiple ways to create an app. However, this guide explains how you can create Android apps using Expo, a cross-platform builder that lets you easily build apps and share them between Android and iPhone, and you can also run Expo apps on the web. In the future, you will learn how to create Flutter apps, which offer more flexibility.
Table of Contents
Prerequisites
To create Android apps, you need:
- A Google AI Pro subscription
- Antigravity installed on your Mac or Windows
- An Android phone
- Download the Expo Go app. You can install it for free from the Google Play Store
- An Expo account (which you can sign up here for free)
How to Create Android apps Using AntiGravity
Step 1: Get Google Gemini AI Pro
First, opt for Google Gemini AI Pro. This subscription gives access to the Google Gemini models inside Antigravity. If you are looking for a totally free way with a generous limit to create Android apps, you can view our tutorial on how to create Android apps using Google AI Studio for free.
If you already have a Google One AI Premium subscription, you can directly install the Google Antigravity application and get started.
Although Google isn’t the best at its coding models, it offers very generous free terms compared to other models. Moreover, Google’s recently launched Gemini 3.8 Flash is also reliable for building apps if you guide it in the right way.
Step 2: Create the app UI using Google Stitch
Once you have opted for a Google AI Pro subscription, go to this website: stitch.withgoogle.com to design the UI of the app you are building. It is a free tool, and if you have a Google AI Pro subscription, you get better rate limits.
Stitch is a UI design website similar to Figma, but it relies more on an AI approach, which lets you generate UI for apps and websites just by prompting.
In my experience, Google Stitch, in most cases, produces generic UI designs, but it’s a great start for someone to get started with the app UI.
You can also skip this step if you have reference images. Most AI models are very good at replicating designs and understanding the structure. However, if you want a structured approach and a little customization, you can follow this process: Generate your initial designs using Stitch, then edit and modify them. Finally, use those references in tools like Google Antigravity to generate apps with the best UI, exactly the way you need.
To create a UI design, you can view our full, detailed tutorial on how to create UI designs using Google Stitch.
Step 1: First, open Google Stitch and enter the prompt for the app you want to create.
In this case, let’s create a to-do list app because that is a very good starting point, even for beginners. Remember to select “app” as an option while creating, because Google Stitch supports both app and website designs.
Step 2: Now, enter a prompt to generate the UI of the app. Then tap on Enter
Step 3: Now wait until Google Stitch provides a full UI design of the app.
Step 4: You can tap on any element or use AI to describe the changes you want, or you can just use the built-in basic tools to edit sections, text, and much more.
Step 5: If you dont like the design, you can click on the plus icon and tap on upload files, and then you can upload the reference files.
Step 6: To preview how the app works, you can tap on the prototype option to preview how the full app works
Step 7: And once you have the design, tap on Export, and you can export directly to Google Antigravity or save it as a ZIP file.
I recommend downloading it as a ZIP file because sharing to Google Antigravity doesn’t work in most cases.
Step 3: Open Google Antigravity
Now open Antigravity and set it up as a CLI. You can also use it as an agent for UI; Antigravity supports both, but I prefer the CLI experience. Now tap on Open Folder and create a new app, or you can select an existing folder. For those who are unaware, all app files will be stored in this folder.
Now open the CLI, and on the right, you can see the chat interface. Now, in the chat, you can tap on the model’s name and select Google 3.8 Flash High. For your information, Google 3.8 Flash is better than the Pro series. It is the latest model and very good at AI generation, especially if you have reference images.
Step 4: Add your UI reference images
Now, click on the plus icon and attach the images. You can attach up to five images at a time.
Now enter this prompt to ask Google Antigravity to create an app.
Please build an Expo React Native app in TypeScript based on the attached UI designs.
Requirements:
Replicate the layout, typography, colors, and components from the attached screenshots as closely as possible.
Use standard Expo packages (@expo/vector-icons, @react-native-async-storage/async-storage, expo-linear-gradient, react-native-safe-area-context).
Implement full client-side state with local persistence using AsyncStorage so added tasks and items persist across app reloads.
Keep the code modular with clean components in a src/ folder.
Ensure there are zero TypeScript compile errors.
Step 5: Create the app using Gemini
Once you are done, wait for some time until Google Gemini 3.8 Flash creates an app.
Since it runs on Expo, you can preview the build on your Android phone. Simply enter this prompt, and it will generate your QR code in the terminal. If you want to make any changes, you can ask Google Gemini to do that for you.
Step 6: Preview the app on your Android phone
Now, open your Android phone and install the Expo app. Open the Expo app on your Android phone and tap on “Scan QR code,” and the app will be installed on your device. Now you can preview all the changes that you have made.
If you want to make any changes, you can enter the prompt with the required changes. Maybe also include better UI references to help the Google Gemini model understand better. In my experience, Google models hallucinate a lot. Once everything is finished and you are happy with the output.
Step 7: Create an Expo account
Now, before that, you need to go to Expo.io and create a free account. If you have already created one, you can just sign in. Now, Expo EAS will use your Expo account to create the build.
Now, once the account is created, there are two ways to connect Expo Go with your Google Antigravity. First is using a local authentication session, which is stored in your home folder. You can run login in Terminal at any time to connect.
To do that, open Terminal in Antigravity and then run this command
Command: npx eas-cli login
Now enter the username and password you created for your Expo account. Google Antigravity will remember these credentials for all future builds. So this is a one-time process; you don’t need to do this for every new app build.
If you don’t want to submit your credentials, you can create an Expo access token (perhaps for one-time use, or if you are sharing with a friend). You don’t need this if you are using it personally on your device.
However, if you want to connect your Expo account through an access token:
- Go to expo.dev/settings/access-tokens.
- Create a token, name it “Antigravity”, and generate the new token.
- Open the terminal and run this command:
Commad: export EXPO_TOKEN="your_copied_token_here"
Step 8: Build the Android app
You can simply enter the prompt and wait for some time until Google Antigravity starts an Expo build in the Expo build app. Once it finishes, it will give you a direct download link for the app.
Prompt:
Since you are using a free version, Expo offers some free rate limits, and then later it uses buffer time to build the app, which averages between 1 and 7 hours, depending on the traffic. If you are lucky enough, the app should be ready in less than 5 minutes. Once it’s ready, Google Antigravity will offer a direct download link.
Step 9: Download the app
You can copy the download link and paste it into any app on your Android, tap on it, and install the app. Alternatively, you can just download the app on your PC and share it to your Android.
Once the build process is completed. you can see the app download link. You can directly share the download link to an Android device.
Step 10: Scan the app before installing
Even though the app is built by you, I highly recommend scanning it before installing it on your Android phone. You can use any free online scanners to scan the app and confirm there are no security issues or malware within your app. Once you are done, you can install the app.
Step 11: Install the app on your Android phone
If this is your first time installing a third-party app, Google Chrome will block the app download from unknown sources. When prompted, you can enable unknown sources; once enabled, you can use the package installer to install the app on your Android phone.
Connect your Android app to Supabase (Optional)
Now that the basic Android phone app has been set up and will successfully run on your device, if you want to back up data in the cloud, you can connect it to Supabase.
Supabase is a free database hoster that lets you host small files in the cloud so that your app can use this data, allowing you to use the same app on other devices with sync enabled.
Step 12: Enable Supabase Integration
To connect it to Supabase: Go back to Google Antigravity and enable Supabase MCP. Next, open this URL and create a new account in Supabase. Now, in Supabase, create a new project. Example: my-to-do-app.
Once a project is created, go to your project settings and then API, and copy the following details:
- Project URL – You can go to Project Settings > General
- Publishable key (Go to Supabase project settings > API and find the key here: Publishable key
Step 13: Connect the app to Supabase
And now, once you have connected your Supabase account to Google Antigravity, open Google Antigravity and enter the following prompt: Next, ask Google Antigravity to create a new Supabase database to use for storing the data.
Prompt:
“I want to sync this app’s data with Supabase.
Here are my Supabase project details:
Supabase URL: https://your-project-id.supabase.co
Supabase Anon Key: your-anon-key-here
Please do the following:
Install @supabase/supabase-js.
Create a Supabase client configuration file in src/services/supabase.ts.
Provide the SQL table definition script I need to run in the Supabase SQL Editor for our tasks and projects.
Update our data context so that it fetches from and syncs with Supabase when online, while falling back gracefully to offline local storage.
Now wait for some time until your app is connected to the Supabase free plan. Once done, your application successfully uses and stores data in the cloud, and it fetches it to your app in real time.
Step 14: Test the Expo build again
To confirm again, you can ask Google Antigravity to use this prompt to access the Expo build on your Android device, so that you can check everything. And once you’re done, you need to rebuild the app.
Step 15: Rebuild the app
Enter this prompt, and Google 3.8 Flash will start the build on Expo Application Services (EAS). Wait for some time until it provides a direct app download link. Once it does, you can download it on your PC and share the app directly to your Android, or share the link directly to your Android.
This time, you will see an update prompt instead of an install prompt, since you have already installed the app on your Android phone.
That’s it. On a high level, this is how easily you can create an Expo Android app on your Android phone using Google Gemini. Except for getting access to the Google Gemini models, every other process is free to use.
Since you are using Expo, in the future, if you want to build an iOS version from the same app, you can just open Google Antigravity and start the iOS app build. In the future, we will learn a detailed way to create iOS apps for Siri.
But for now, I hope you find this guide helpful. If you are facing any issues while installing the app, you can comment below, and I am happy to help you.

MinLaw aware of police investigations arising from LawSoc audit, says council members will cooperate fully
The Law Society had said in August that it would release the full report of the audit after a redaction process, following calls from its members and Law Minister Edwin Tong to do so.
SINGAPORE: The Ministry of Law (MinLaw) confirmed on Tuesday (Sep 22) that the police are investigating matters referred to in the recent audit into workplace allegations at the Law Society of Singapore (LawSoc).
The ministry declined to comment further on the ongoing investigations.
“The Law Society and its council members will no doubt cooperate fully with the police on this investigation,” said a spokesperson for the ministry.
The police also confirmed on Tuesday that a report had been lodged in relation to issues raised in the audit and that they were "looking into the matter".
In response to queries from CNA about the specific matters under investigation and whether this meant it would eventually not release the audit committee’s report, the Law Society also said it had no comment at this time.
In an email to members on Sep 21 seen by CNA, the Law Society said that the police had recently notified them that they were currently investigating certain matters referred to in the report.
According to the email, the Law Society was instructed not to further publish or distribute the contents of the report, or comment on such matters before investigations conclude.
It promised members an update “in due course”.
The society had said in August that it would release the full report after a redaction process, following calls to do so from its members and Law Minister Edwin Tong.
The report is a result of investigations arising from an anonymous email to MinLaw and the Ministry of Manpower containing what Mr Tong described as “concerning allegations and complaints” against certain people and practices within the Law Society between 2022 and 2025.
The Law Society represents lawyers and maintains standards of the legal profession in Singapore. Its current council, led by Senior Counsel Professor Tan Cheng Han as president, took office in 2026.
Council presidents from 2022 to 2025 were the late Mr Adrian Tan, Senior Counsel Jason Chan and Ms Lisa Sam.
After receiving the email, MinLaw referred the allegations to the Law Society council, which then appointed an audit committee to investigate the matter. The committee, made up of members and non-members, conducted its investigation independently of the council.
"While the audit did not find evidence of deliberate financial impropriety or an intentional cover-up, it nevertheless identified significant failings in leadership, workplace culture and governance during the relevant period," said Mr Tong in parliament in August.
"These failings have no place in an institution such as LawSoc. They undermine confidence within the organisation, affect the well-being of its employees, and risk eroding the trust that both the legal profession and the public place in it."
Later in August, he also called on the Law Society to release the full report to its members, following a petition and heated closed-door meeting where the members demanded its release.
Before that meeting, hard copies of the audit committee's report, containing a summary of findings and recommendations, were circulated to members and had to be returned before the session ended.
Days later, the Law Society said it would release the full report “as soon as practicable” as long as the confidentiality of interviewees was protected and those facing material allegations were given a chance to respond.

Learning another language is a highly complex mental activity. It requires people to remember words, distinguish unfamiliar sounds, recognize patterns, work out grammatical rules, and retrieve the right expression at the right moment. All of this happens while listening, interpreting, and preparing a response.
Could all this mental activity also help keep an aging brain healthier? Research suggests it can.
Concerns about memory and dementia can send aging adults looking for ways to exercise their brain and maintain cognitive function, whether it is solving crossword puzzles or playing a musical instrument. Language learning might not seem like the same kind of brain exercise, but it is a complex activity that engages several mental processes at once.
I am a linguist who studies language acquisition, use, and loss. My new book, Beyond Words: How We Learn, Use, and Lose Language, examines language and the mind across people’s lifespans.
Research increasingly suggests that language learning and bilingualism can offer cognitive benefits—including for older adults. Learning another language can also create opportunities for communication and social connection.
A workout for the brain
A person’s brain remains capable of change throughout their life. This ability to adapt in response to experience is known as neuroplasticity.
Learning unfamiliar sounds, vocabulary, and grammatical patterns requires the brain to form and strengthen connections. Language learning engages several mental processes at once, requiring people to absorb and retrieve information, notice when something does not work out, and adjust. This sustained mental effort makes language learning a particularly rich form of cognitive exercise.

The Confrontation That Broke New York
A new book sheds some light on the death of Jordan Neely and the trial that divided a post-pandemic city.
In the spring of 2023, a young Black man stepped onto a subway car in Manhattan. He screamed, threw garbage at passengers, and announced that he was prepared to die. New Yorkers often encase themselves in psychological armor on the subway, but for many of the riders in that car, this was too much.
Terror flooded in. A woman hid her face in a friend’s chest; a mother tried to hide behind her stroller with her toddler. One man began to pray. Then a 24-year-old white man, an ex-Marine, grabbed the screaming man and put him in a neck lock, and five minutes later—by mistake? Intentionally?—left that man dead on the floor of the subway car.
To read the new book on that killing, Man in the Mirror: Hope, Struggle, and Belonging in an American City, by Anand Giridharadas, is to recognize that the membrane separating safety and fear on the New York City subways appeared in danger of rupturing by 2023. In the preceding few years, dozens of people had been pushed onto subway tracks, suffering injury or death. Murder and assault had risen sharply. The tension between chaos and order—often evident in New York—could be acute. And in those five minutes, it snapped.
Before anyone could sort out the facts, too many people rushed to impose narratives. Jordan Neely became the homeless Black man with the too-disposable life; Daniel Penny became the muscular vigilante who grew up in the white-bread suburbs. Leftist activists howled racism; right-wing sorts adjusted their ties and talked tough. “In a civilized society, the strong protect the weak,” a member of The Wall Street Journal’s editorial board wrote. “A Marine uses his strength to fight for those unable to fight for themselves.” Liberal politicians divined morality tales. Brad Lander, at the time the city comptroller, who lives in a prosperous liberal precinct in Brooklyn, proclaimed: “We must not become a city where a mentally ill human being can be choked to death by a vigilante without consequence.”
I wanted to say: Stop, please. Forgo reading your political catechisms. Try not to talk of consequences and militarization and the menace of the streets until we have a clue about how to prevent this from happening again.
There is pathos enough to be found in basic facts. In his book, Giridharadas takes on the considerable challenge of telling a story that encompasses conflicting narratives and the voices of nearly every player: defense attorneys, people living on the street, public-health officials, both Neely and Penny. His writing is most powerful when he traces the threads of tragically entwined lives. Whereas some in the media reduced Neely to a trope—the mentally ill homeless man—Man in the Mirror invests his life with complication and nuance. His mother was killed by her boyfriend; in a gothic twist, that boyfriend cross-examined young Jordan while representing himself at his trial. In time, Neely drifted further and further away from those who wanted to offer him succor. The reader learns about outreach workers and prosecutors who were ambivalent on how to treat his illness, and about well-meaning bureaucrats whose actions fell short.
Here and there, the author stumbles when inserting liberal punctuation points. He argues that addressing crime is an inescapable fact of life for Democrats, even if the fear that crime is out of control is “based in nonreality.” The biggest problem, he writes, is a nation “awash in anxiety and fear: of change, of the social advancement of marginalized populations, of losing control of children, of losing control of the border, of losing cultural status and centrality, of the Other, of chaos.” This strikes me as too easy.
Change, demographic and otherwise, has swept through and revitalized New York City for centuries. And the subways are arteries that give life to us all. I grew up riding the rails to see girlfriends and basketball games. My schoolmates and I rode to a Bronx public high school in train cars so encased in graffiti, we had to peer out of the opening doors to see if we’d reached our stop. Slowly, however, that system grew cleaner and safer.
When the coronavirus pandemic overtook New York City, that momentum seemed to reverse, and the subways began to feel menacing again. My claim here is reality-based, drawing on statistics and personal experience. Assaults on the subway increased by 65 percent from 2020 to 2025, and the number of murders in the system spiked as well. And a year after Neely died, a man shoved a friend of my family onto the subway tracks. He suffered multiple fractures, and his rehabilitation stretched across brutal months.
One morning in the spring of 2023, I was riding the Q train to the Upper East Side when I heard a booming voice and saw a great block of a man enter the subway car and ask for money. I returned to my reading. As the man approached, the timbre of his voice grew agitated. I fixed a side eye on him. When the train stopped in the middle of a tunnel, the panhandler stood over a young man who sat across from me. He put out a massive hand.
“You’re giving me money,” he announced. Silence followed as the young passenger kept eyes downcast. “Mutherfucker, I’ve got a big-ass knife”—the man patted his shaggy overcoat—“and I’m going to gut you from your balls to your throat.” I made eye contact with other men on the train. What the hell do we do if he pulls out that knife? If we are lucky enough to pull him to the floor, how do we keep him there?
I offer none of this to sound macho. I’m a 60-something man with a strong desire to remain alive. I harbored no illusions about my ability to wrestle this man to the ground. As it happened, the train started and pulled into the next station and he got off, but not before loudly vowing to gut us all.
I can venture a reasonable thumbnail sketch of this man. He was probably homeless. He was likely known to social-services caseworkers and to police. If he had been prescribed medications, he did not seem to be taking them. His inner resources had been eroded by life’s dysfunctions and the brutal reality of too many days on the street.
In a 2024 column about Neely and Penny in The New York Times, Emmett Rensin noted that the prevalence of “madness”—“those serious and spectacular forms of mental illness”—on the streets and in the subways “creates a dilemma between two principles of a liberal society: the sovereignty of individuals and the collective right to public order.” When those values can’t be reconciled, the city can feel perilous. I have a desperate desire not to live in a Death Wish version of New York, in which residents take it upon themselves to mete out justice, but what happens when you are caught in a moral pincer without a third party to adjudicate? Had that man on the Q pulled a knife, and had we hurt him before he hurt us, would we have been branded vigilantes?
The worst of those times appear to have passed. Murders and shootings in New York City have plunged in the past few years, and it remains one of the nation’s safest big cities. But statistics comfort only to a point. The continuing presence in public of so many people with seemingly untreated mental illness—including those who still push strangers onto the tracks—is unignorable.
To read Man in the Mirror is to inoculate yourself against the belief that the larger crisis is over. Giridharadas’s book illuminates the conundrum posed by those with Neely’s behavioral profile. On a good day, he could be a gentle busker. He was the Michael Jackson impersonator with a moonwalk step and a sweet smile. But Neely’s mental illness most often went untreated, and it had festered as he evaded caseworkers. He was becoming dangerous. In 2019, he punched someone on a subway platform. Two years later, he slugged a 67-year-old woman as she emerged from a subway station, breaking her nose and fracturing her eye socket; for this, he served a sentence at Rikers Island.
Locking away the Neelys of our cities in Kafkaesque asylums was a more common solution until the 1960s and ’70s; the practice was ultimately rejected for urgent and humane reasons. Yet discerning which mentally ill person poses a threat has not gotten any easier, and letting the most afflicted roam the streets untreated does not constitute a sustainable policy.
Giridharadas writes sensitively about this, and illuminates debates between hopeful public-health officials who yearn to transform society—changing “everything ‘out there’”—and hardheaded pragmatists. The latter group supports a sensible program in New York, now in its early stages, to pair public caseworkers with police officers, marrying the compassion of the former with the practical authority of law enforcement—the better to offer the right kind of help in any situation. There is also an effort to make it easier for families to commit mentally ill relatives for care.
Unfortunately, when Giridharadas moves away from the man who died in the confrontation and the questions that arise from the incident, his analysis grows less subtle. He devotes substantial pages early in his account to the Black activist Al Sharpton without mentioning the extent to which the reverend is a sometimes-unreliable narrator. Sharpton can speak movingly of the lives of the Black forgotten and of those who suffer from police abuse; he also has served as an FBI informant, been on a first-name basis with mobsters, and embraced an outright hoax about a racist conspiracy. And in his politics, he is in some ways an outlier. Many Black New Yorkers, as well as Latinos and Asians, have told pollsters that they favor more, not less, police presence, and that safer subways are an urgent concern. That perspective could have enriched the book.
The author also succumbs in places to class-based stereotypes, particularly when writing of Penny and his family of white suburbanites, people who are unlikely to share his political priors. Such missteps limit rather than expand our understanding of Penny’s background and worldview. Penny grew up in West Islip, on Long Island, a town where, Giridharadas writes, “you had your little yard, your little fence, your little deck, maybe you had your little boat.” He adds that “nothing was beautiful and nothing was ugly.” He casts a cold eye on Penny’s mother, Gina, mocking her working-class accent and writing that she had “so much to express” on Facebook, “but not necessarily the skill or will to express those things in any personal, authentic, or original way.”
The book reaches a crescendo with Penny’s trial. Defense lawyers portrayed a city lost to dysfunction; the police were too late to show up, and only Penny was left to put his life on the line to save “perfect strangers.” The prosecutor—who several times during the trial referred to the former Marine as “the white man” and “the white defendant”—acknowledged what activists and liberal politicians could not: Penny had “started out trying to do the right thing,” until he kept his choke hold in place too long and Neely died. A majority of the jurors were white, but at least four were not. They took 24 hours—not very long, given the case’s complexity—to acquit Penny of criminally negligent homicide.
Afterward, Lander warned that the verdict would “valorize vigilantism.” The left-wing Working Families Party called it a “modern-day lynching.” But all of the jurors rode the subway at least semi-regularly; several had spoken before the trial of their own upsetting experiences on the train, and in the end they appeared disinclined to punish a man who acted to forestall what might have been imminent violence.
It is a virtue of this book that Giridharadas, even while seeming to harbor sympathies for the prosecutors, applies an empathy for New Yorkers who try to thread their way through the divides created by this case. “They shared the sense of being undefended. They shared the sense that the calvary was not coming,” he writes. “They shared a sense that the system was rigged,” and so “shared the sense of their own powerlessness.”
Just hours after the verdict, Penny walked along 30th Street, and people recognized him. “Almost to a person,” Giridharadas notes, “they shook his hand and thanked him.”
It’s tempting to think of this, three years after the incident, as a snapshot of a more turbulent city. But as I finished this essay, I learned of a new horror: Early this month, Erin Piacenti was walking through Times Square, having freshly returned from maternity leave, when Pamela Cisneros, a middle-aged mother of three who appeared lost to madness, fatally stabbed Piacenti in the abdomen. Cisneros, who had suffered decades of mental-health issues, then tried to stab police officers; they shot and killed her. And for Piacenti, the young, innocent woman who lost her life, no one was there to save her.

Public trust in science, and in health institutions in particular, has been in decline for years.
On one hand, disinformation and cultural shifts have led people to lose faith in medicine and institutions that are critical for individual and public health. On the other hand, it is not hard to find examples of institutions that have lost the public’s trust for good reason. For nearly 11 years here at STAT, our journalists have been doggedly reporting on misdeeds, scandals, and crimes perpetrated by some of the biggest companies and names in the U.S. health care system.
Understanding the importance of trust while recognizing that distrust is not irrational either is central to our work here at STAT. For that reason, we have recently brought on journalist Nicholas Florko as our first-ever trust-in-science reporter.
“My goal is really to get to the bottom of why people distrust science, the forces behind it, and what we can do to hopefully build up some trust in science where needed,” he told me in a recent conversation.
In this first STATus Report after our summer hiatus, Florko joins me to discuss the importance of trust and how he’s approaching this brand-new beat.

'Alarming' - does WSL have a homegrown problem?
- Published
When London City Lionesses beat Manchester United on the opening night of the 2025-26 season, it suggested times were changing in the English women's game.
For some, that had become clear about an hour before kick-off in Bromley when the team news revealed a starting XI without any English players - the first time a Women's Super League side had done so on the first day of the season.
Two days later it happened again, when Scotland striker Kirsty Hanson was the only British player to start for Tottenham in their win over West Ham.
Both instances speak to the increasing ability of WSL clubs to attract top talents from across the globe, creating a league many now view as the world's best.
But, with the Women's Champions League returning this week, is what's good for the WSL good for homegrown players, and by extension the home nations?
Or is it, as The Guardian's Tom Garry puts it, "alarming" for the hopes of the home nations?
Arsenal v HB Koge, Women's Champions League
Tuesday, 22 September, 20:00 BST
Listen to BBC Radio 5 Live commentary and follow text updates of the matches featuring English teams on the BBC Sport website as the Women's Champions League returns
The changing make-up of the WSL
Ten years ago when current champions Manchester City last won the WSL title, they did so with an all-British starting line-up.
Much has changed since.
In 2018, the WSL went fully professional, the subsequent success of the Lionesses in the 2020s rapidly grew the game's audience and revenues have increased accordingly.
As a result, clubs have expanded their scouting pool and been able to attract players from a wider variety of nationalities - with transfer fees exploding since the turn of the decade.
Over recent windows, WSL clubs have recruited heavily from Germany and Sweden, while two-time Ballon d'Or winner Alexia Putellas exchanged the trophies of Barcelona for big-spending London City this summer.
The proliferation of players from Japan and Australia also highlights the WSL's attractiveness for those at the top of the game as those clubs with the deepest pockets pack their squads with players from across the globe.
"Our league has grown significantly and attracted world class athletes from all over the world," says Birmingham City manager Amy Merricks. "Unfortunately that blocks some of the pathways for the youngsters coming through.
"We need [this] talent in our league because our league is growing, but at the same time we have got to try and address this issue."
Looking at the proportion of homegrown players (English, Scottish, Welsh and Northern Irish) to start 11 or more matches, half of a WSL season, the data shows a steady decline over the past three seasons to under a third.
The first three weeks of 2026-27 have offered a bump on last season, but that can partly be attributed to the WSL's expansion from 12 teams to 14 teams and the greater proportion of homegrown talent in the promoted trio of Birmingham City, Crystal Palace and Charlton Athletic.
It is a downward trend that is not mirrored across other major European leagues.
For 2025-26, 61% of those to start half or more of Premiere Ligue matches in France were French, 63% of those in Frauen Bundesliga games were German, and 69% of Liga F players in Spain were Spanish.
And, while WSL managers say they appreciate the importance of cultivating homegrown talent, the reality of the job ensures it is not their first priority.
"The club has a responsibility to raise young players, give our own talents possibilities to be in the squad and compete every week," says Manchester City boss Andree Jeglertz.
"But when it comes to team selection, I always need to pick the team that gives us the best chance of winning the game. If that contains eight young and promising English players or zero, I don't care. I just want to win the game."
What is the potential impact on the national team?
1 of 4
It feels like a crossroads has been reached between clubs wanting to be competitive, the WSL continuing to grow, and the need to regenerate an England squad that has not changed much over the past three major tournaments.
After all, England are the two-time European champions but seven of the team that started against Spain in June also played in the Euro 2022 final against Germany - while two of the remaining starters in this year's game were on the bench four years ago.
Sarina Wiegman's side were outclassed in Majorca, losing 4-0 to miss out on automatic qualification for the 2027 Women's World Cup in Brazil. They must now navigate two rounds of play-off matches, starting against Greece next month.
Discussions on England's future is pertinent given the biennial Women's Under-20s World Cup is ongoing in Poland.
Last Thursday, Lydia Bedford's young side were dismissed 3-0 from the last 16 by Nigeria, albeit with the caveat a number of players such as US-based Erica Meg Parkinson and Laila Harbert were not released by their clubs to play.
Nevertheless, in 2022 and 2024, like the other home nations, they did not even qualify.
It is a far cry from the class of 2018 where the likes of Alessia Russo, Lauren Hemp and Georgia Stanway led the Lionesses to third place in the Under-20s World Cup, setting the tone for the incredible subsequent success.
Wiegman has handed debuts to 21 players since her arrival in September 2021, but only Lauren James, Hannah Hampton and Lucia Kendall have become established starters.
When England kick off in Crete on Friday, 5 October (20:00 BST), it is likely to be the same faces once again.
- Young Lionesses win European trophy 
  - Published17 April
To try and facilitate the pathway to top level football for young academy players, Football Association rules require WSL sides to include eight homegrown players in their squad lists.
The quota for WSL 2 clubs is higher and works on a sliding scale depending on squad size.
Former England striker Ellen White told the Women's Football Weekly podcast this was insufficient, saying: "We should be updating that quota of eight players, tweaking it to best help and complement our international structure, our homegrown talent."
"I would love to see them go much further - something mandated, a minimum on the pitch at any one time," the Guardian's Garry told BBC Women's Football Weekly. "London City's line-up was alarming.
"It's great for the product over here, but will we see pain in 15 years' time if England are struggling to go deep in major tournaments because we're not developing players?"
Last month, the FA approved a controversial plan to allow some WSL academy sides to play in the National League from 2027-28, saying it would "strengthen the women's football pyramid, raise standards across the league, and improve the development pathway for young players".
The FA believes this reform will address the relative lack of competitive minutes young English players receive.
Chelsea have already confirmed they plan to enter an academy side in the third tier and Manchester City women's managing director Charlotte O'Neill has previously said she would want to enter a team too.

The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) on Tuesday issued an advisory to curb the indiscriminate use of painkillers and antibiotics, highlighting their association with the risk of chronic kidney disease. In a circular, Drugs Controller General of India Dr Rajeev Singh Raghuvanshi noted that all non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and antibiotics must be sold and distributed only on the prescription of a registered medical practitioner or specialist. The country’s apex drug regulator stated that, based on applicability and potential risks, these medicines are placed under Schedules G, H, H1 and X of the Drugs Rules, 1945, requiring medical supervision. Most NSAIDs fall under Schedule H, meaning they cannot be sold at retail without a prescription from a registered medical practitioner, as mandated under Rule 97. Similarly, most antibiotics fall under Schedule H1, requiring labels warning that it is dangerous to take the preparation except in accordance with medical advice and prohibiting retail sale without a prescription. The circular said it is mandatory to ensure these drugs are used only when clinically indicated, in the appropriate dose and duration, and under medical supervision. The advisory outlines specific directions for patients, doctors, chemists, healthcare facilities, and state regulators. The regulator said antibiotics must not be used for self-medication or for conditions where they are not indicated, such as uncomplicated viral infections. Patients must take prescribed antibiotics strictly as advised, avoid sharing them, and refrain from using leftover medicines. People with pre-existing kidney disease or other risk factors for renal impairment must inform doctors before taking NSAIDs, and individuals should seek medical advice when pain, fever, or other symptoms persist rather than self-medicating. For healthcare professionals, the directive states that NSAIDs and antibiotics must be prescribed after assessing clinical condition, age, co-morbidities, concomitant medicines, and risk factors. When prescribing NSAIDs, doctors should consider the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration, particularly for patients at risk of renal impairment, dehydration, or cardiovascular disease. Antibiotics must be prescribed judiciously following stewardship principles, accounting for the causative organism, infection site, severity, microbiological tests, and susceptibility patterns. Doctors must avoid unnecessary combination therapies, incorrect dosing, and prolonged treatment durations. Pharmacists, retailers, and distributors must comply with statutory requirements for Schedule H and H1 drugs, observe label warnings, and avoid encouraging or facilitating self-medication. Hospitals and healthcare institutions have been asked to strengthen systems for prescribing, monitoring, prescription reviews, and patient counselling. State and Union territory drug control authorities have been directed to raise public and professional awareness and enforce compliance with the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, and the Drugs Rules, 1945, to prevent adverse drug reactions, renal complications, and antimicrobial resistance. Priyanka Sharma is a journalist at Mint, where she covers the Union Ministry of Health and the pharmaceutical industry. Her work focuses on explaining government policies and how they impact healthcare and the medicine market in India. With 12 years of experience in journalism, she has built a reputation for providing clear and honest news on important health topics that affect the entire country.

Her educational background includes a journalism degree from the prestigious Indian Institute of Mass Communication (IIMC) and specialized training in public health from the Public Health Foundation of India. Before her current role at Mint, Priyanka worked with India Today, The Pioneer, and ANI. She also served as a lead consultant for the National Health Authority, which gave her firsthand knowledge of how the government manages large-scale health programmes.

Pope to retrace missionary footsteps in Peru and finally visit Argentina in November
Pope Leo XIV is set to return to Peru in November, retracing his steps as a missionary priest
ROME -- ROME (AP) — Pope Leo XIV will retrace his steps as a missionary priest when he returns home to Peru in November in his longest trip to date that will also take him to Uruguay and Argentina, where his Argentine predecessor Pope Francis never returned.
The Vatican on Monday published the detailed itinerary for Leo’s first visit to Latin America as pope. The Nov. 6-17 trip will be a homecoming for the U.S.-born pontiff who also has Peruvian citizenship and spent two decades there as a priest and bishop.
As he showed during his four-nation Africa trip in April, the 71-year-old Leo has no qualms about covering vast distances and working late into the night when he’s on the road. In all, he’ll clock just over 31,000 kilometers (19,000 miles) of flight time during the trip, nearly double the 17,000 kms (10,000 miles) he traveled in Algeria, Cameroon, Angola and Equatorial Guinea.
The visit begins in Uruguay to put Leo in place to mark an important Catholic feast day Nov. 8, associated with the country’s patron saint, of Our Lady of the Thirty-Three. The small statue of the Madonna dates from the 18th century Jesuit missions in the area and currently is housed in the city of Florida, where Leo will celebrate Mass at the National Shrine.
Leo will also honor Argentina’s patron, Our Lady of Lujan, on the second, Argentine leg of the trip. The statue of the Madonna, located in the city of Lujan in the province of Buenos Aires, was particularly dear to Francis.
Francis, who died in 2025, confounded friends and foes alike by never returning to his native Argentina, after he left for Rome for the 2013 conclave that elected him pope.
He had been a divisive figure back home, both as Jesuit superior and archbishop of Buenos Aires, and apparently wanted to avoid fueling the country’s polemics by not giving the ruling party at any given time the political benefits that come with a pope visit.
But Leo seems keen to finally grant Argentina’s faithful a papal visit for the first time since St. John Paul II came in 1982 and 1987.
In Buenos Aires, Leo will visit the capital’s federal prison, perhaps a nod to Francis’ legacy of prison ministry that he developed first as a “slum priest” in Buenos Aires.
The highlight of Leo’s trip will certainly be his return to Peru and especially his diocese of Chiclayo. The former Robert Prevost was bishop of Chiclayo from 2014-2023, when Francis brought him to the Vatican to head the office for bishops.
On the night of his election, Leo gave a shoutout in Spanish to his “beloved diocese of Chiclayo,” from the loggia of St. Peter’s Basilica. He praised its faithful for having “walked alongside their bishop, shared their faith, and given so much to continue being a faithful Church of Jesus Christ.”
Leo is spending the bulk of his visit in Peru, arriving in Lima on Nov. 11 and leaving the afternoon of Nov. 16 after a final Mass in Callao, outside Lima, where he served as a temporary administrator. In between, he’ll spend time in Chiclayo, including having a special private dinner with the diocese’s priests.
He’ll meet with popular groups in Cusco, in the Peruvian Andes, to celebrate the city’s rich history. Cusco was the capital of the Inca empire, an important city of Spanish colonial rule and today remains an important cultural destination with ruins including Machu Picchu.
That same day, Nov. 15, he’ll also honor Peru’s Indigenous peoples by traveling to Pucallpa, deep in Peru’s Amazonian forest, to celebrate Mass.

Just past 6 pm on a recent Wednesday night, half a dozen pet owners logged into a Zoom meeting to confess something they’re afraid to talk about in public: They’re fed up with their dogs.
Before discussion began, Louise Crane, the president and cofounder of Dogs Anonymous, the organization hosting the meeting, recited the seven acknowledgements participants must agree to, the first being, “I admit that life with my dog is not what I imagined.” Crane wore a black T-shirt exclaiming “Abolish ICE” in thick white lettering.
“I may need to be talked off a ledge,” one attendee said as conversation kicked off, mentioning that she wasn’t sure how to handle her dog’s mood swings. Her family had been through a series of new changes: Their other dog died and they were also fostering one, and now their boxer was “unsettled” and “grumpy” to the point he was doing more “demand barking, which has never been like him.”
Other attendees confessed their private shames: a shepherd mix had started engaging in more intense “resource guarding” when around other dogs—the term for when dogs aggressively protect something they value. “He got into it with my sister’s little weiner dog the other day because they both were begging for food.” One woman, who lives in a busy apartment complex, needed advice on how to better handle her dachshund’s constant barking at strangers. (In the spirit of anonymity, Dogs Anonymous asked WIRED to leave out the names and identifying characteristics of its participants.)
Shame is the emotion attendees struggle with the most in these meetings. “The embarrassment of having a dog that’s losing its shit, especially as a woman,” is difficult for some people, Crane tells me when we speak a few days before.
Crane launched Dogs Anonymous, a nonprofit focused on training and emotional support by animal behavior experts, in 2025 in an attempt to help people vocalize their shame.
“We wanted to give people not just a space they could trust for advice on behavior issues or if they are having a crisis with their dog, but also a place where they don’t feel judged to ask questions and admit that maybe it’s a little bit too much for them,” Daphne Mendoza-Tervanis, a cofounder, says.
Sessions are held weekly and span first-time and experienced dog owners, adopters, foster caregivers, and occasionally trainers seeking tips on how to work aggression cases. The meetings are primarily attended by US residents, though previous sessions have attracted dog owners from Singapore, Costa Rica, and beyond.
Jerri Scherff, a cofounder who is 13 years sober, had first-hand experience with recovery programs, and it was important to her that Dogs Anonymous also include some of the same traditions as Alcoholics Anonymous. “We wanted to create something that was repeatable, sustainable, and eventually autonomous, which is the way that recovery groups work,” she says. The most important one was anonymity—what is discussed in the group stays in the group.
The founders say the effectiveness of the group doesn’t necessarily stem from the advice they impart during meetings but comes from members bonding over shared struggles. “The magic of AA the community is that you are going through something that somebody else has either been through or they’re going through the same thing,” Crane adds. This approach, called “sharing your experience, strength and hope,” is a core part of the 12-step recovery program and encourages members to analyze their experience in a way that makes them feel less alone.
According to a survey published in the scientific journal Pets in June examining guilt, burden, and wellbeing among owners of dogs with behavior problems, 53 percent of respondents reported feeling alone, and 78 percent reported “elevated caregiver burden,” a term for the emotional and financial strain of being a caregiver.
During a meeting in August, the group took a beat to dig into the particulars of why shame was the first emotion owners often experience when their dog reacts aggressively. One attendee said it threatened their sense of belonging in a neighborhood they already felt out of place in. Another mentioned how it made them feel judged because others wouldn’t think they were a capable owner. “There’s so much shame when you don’t get Lassie,” Crane says of the fictional TV dog that, for many Gen Xers and millennials, represented the ideal companion.
“I just broke down crying on the way home from my dog’s reactivity training,” one owner in New Orleans posted on Threads last month, writing that she signed up for classes after a woman threw coffee at her “anxious pit” for reacting badly. Dog reactivity is the number one issue most owners deal with. A 2026 study by researchers at the University of Lincoln shows that behaviors group into three main categories—oral attacks, frustration, and posturing—with lunging and barking reported as the most frequent symptoms.
“After three sessions it seems like the main lessons are to avoid triggers and anticipate my dog’s reactions,” the New Orleans owner continued. “As someone who has spent my entire life anticipating human volatility, I’m exhausted. Is there no other way?”
Another Threads user suggested she attend Dogs Anonymous, replying, “Part of what you’ll do here is grieve the dog you thought you would have as you grow closer to the one you have.”
No Dogs Anonymous meeting is the same. Some weeks attendees might discuss what it’s like dealing with their dog’s anxiety issues or ask for advice about going through the euthanasia process. Other weeks, they might vent about life. “The other day we were talking about random things that our dogs had pooped,” Mendoza-Tervanis says. “It was a lot of money and tampons.”
Unlike other support groups for owners of dogs with behavioral challenges, DA prioritizes the owner first. “Why we’re in the problem that we are right now is because we are putting dogs before people,” says Mendoza-Tervanis, who has worked in pet care for 15 years. According to the American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, 2 million dogs were adopted from shelters in 2025, but Mendoza-Tervanis believes the problem is that most owners do not have the actual support they need, especially when the dog doesn’t meet their expectations. “A lot of services are becoming financially inaccessible”—hourly rates for private dog trainers in Los Angeles, for example, can cost up to $300 an hour—“so when someone comes to us the question is not, how much can you pay, but how are you feeling about what happened.”
Social media has also warped the expectations people have around dogs, where colorfully-curated pages of petfluencers @_violasnow, the Husky with 5.8 million Instagram followers, and @tikatheiggy, the Italian greyhound Vogue once called “a new fashion it girl,” can often make owners feel like they are not doing enough. It’s why organizations like DA have become a refuge.
In March, after Scherff’s American bulldog passed, weekly meetings became her safe space to process what happened away from the judgments of social media. Scherff has 283,000 Instagram followers “but with the group, I knew that whatever I said, it was going to stay there and they weren’t going to think anything of me.”
Before Wednesday’s session wrapped, one attendee in Puerto Rico expressed gratitude for the gathering. “I’m just glad we all ended up here through the magic of the internet. It can be such a dark place sometimes. It’s just nice to hear these conversations.”
More than anything, the founders want the weekly Zoom meetings to be a forum that keeps the “toxic outside noise out,” Crane says. “This is a place where you can come and say, I fucking hate my dog today. And there are people who are going to be like, yeah, that was me last Tuesday. Sometimes they drive us crazy and that’s OK.”
