Workers came across human remains – and unearthed a mass grave of 572 people
- Published
When a mass grave was unearthed in northern Sri Lanka last February, it was not by design.
Workers were digging to extend a cremation ground in the Chemmani area of the Jaffna region when they suddenly discovered human remains, prompting an investigation.
By August, archaeologists had completed the third phase of the excavation at the site, during which they found the skeletal remains of 572 people, including children and infants.
Among the dead were artefacts from their lives – bangles, a school bag, a milk bottle.
It is believed to be the largest mass grave site ever uncovered in Sri Lanka.
There had been whispers of its existence before - a soldier on trial for the rape and murder of a young woman during the country's devastating civil war, had spoken about a mass grave which contained hundreds of bodies. Rights groups said they were disappeared civilians
But there was no proof - until now.
And while the discovery is devastating, it has offered hope to people like Jeyaruby Jeyabalan, whose father was among thousands of people who disappeared during the decades-long war. Jeyabalan and families like his hope that answers about what happened to their loved ones lie among the bodies.
Many Tamils believe the grave holds the victims of extrajudicial killings carried out during the civil war. They are calling for an investigation – and for justice.
But the excavation process at Chemmani has moved slowly, testing the patience of families searching for answers about their disappeared loved ones.
The discovery of hundreds of remains near a previously identified mass grave has fuelled anger among the Tamils, who have long-demanded a thorough inquiry into disappearances.
Many fear the mass grave will eventually fade from public attention because of a lack of political will to pursue the truth – and so the grave has become a rallying point for renewed protests in Sri Lanka's north.
Two decades waiting for answers
Sri Lanka, particularly the Tamil-dominated north and east, suffered decades of conflict. The war, which lasted from 1983 to 2009, divided the island-nation along ethnic lines. Tamil Tiger rebels fought for an independent state in the north-east of the country due to what they called systematic discrimination by the Sinhalese-dominated government.
The conflict lasted 26 years and the fighting killed an estimated 100,000 people. It also left about 23,000 – mostly Tamils – missing.
Both the security forces and Tamil Tigers are accused of atrocities and crimes.
In 1995, after a bloody conflict, the Sri Lankan army wrested control of the Jaffna Peninsula from the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE). It was seen as a key turning point in the war, which ended with the defeat of the Tigers in 2009.
As they extended control in the late 1990s, the entire Chemmani region became part of a high-security zone and was dotted with army camps, check points and security posts. There was an army camp in Chemmani close to the cemetery as well.
Some at that time described the Jaffna region as an "open prison" - and the security forces were accused of causing the disappearance of thousands of civilians, something Sri Lankan governments have always denied.
"I was 12 years old when my father was picked up by the Sri Lankan army at a checkpoint close to Chemmani area in September 1996. We still don't know what happened to him," Jeyaruby Jayapalan, who now lives in Jaffna, tells the BBC.
She recalls how, after learning of his disappearance, the family panicked and visited military camps and police stations across Jaffna in a desperate search for information without any luck. He never came back.
Her father, Kandaiah Jayapalan, was a government employee who also ran a roadside café not far from Chemmani.
"I went to Chemmani mass grave with many others hoping that I will find some answers. But we didn't find any material evidence. We want a detailed forensic analysis of the human remains," says Jeyaruby.
Two weeks before Kandaiah Jayapalan vanished, an 18-year-old Tamil school girl, Krishanthi Kumaraswamy, disappeared in the same area.
In 1998, a court in Colombo sentenced five soldiers to death for the rape and murder of Kumaraswamy and for killing three of her family members. The case drew global attention at that time. Their bodies were later found buried in Chemmani area.
It is among the most infamous cases from the conflict – and the grave currently under investigation is within 100 metres of the remains of Kumaraswamy and others were found.
In a startling court testimony, one of the convicted soldiers, Somaratne Rajapakse, alleged that between 300 and 400 people who had been killed in the mid-1990s were buried in Chemmani.
His claim led to the first excavation at Chemmani a year later, during which investigators unearthed more than 10 human skeletons. Human rights activists believed those remains were linked to people who had disappeared during the civil war, but there was little judicial follow-up.
Activists say that because the war with the Tamil rebels was ongoing, the then government didn't pursue the investigation and did not explain why.
The discovery of another mass grave in the same area has revived calls for accountability.
"Preliminary inspections suggest this was not a normal burial site and not consistent with ordinary Hindu burial practices," says Gehan Gunatilleke, a commissioner with Human Rights Commission of Sri Lanka, which conducted inspections at Chemmani last year.
Activists and experts say that while a few dozen bodies appeared to have been formally buried, the vast majority told a different story.
Most of the human remains were found without clothing, packed tightly together and, in some cases, stacked on top of others. The graves were shallow, with bodies buried just one to two metres below the surface.
"There is a reasonable likelihood that the burials were unlawful and pursuant to extrajudicial killings," the Human Rights Commission of Sri Lanka said in a report last year.
Past investigations haven't led to prosecutions
The families of those disappeared during the conflict have responded to the discovery by holding protest meetings and remembrance ceremonies.
Among them is Suseela, a 65-year-old woman who is looking for her son, Gnanaseelan Ravi, who was picked up by the Sri Lankan military in 2007, when he was 24.
"He was my only son, and I keep crying every day remembering him. My life is empty without him," she tells the BBC.
She went to Chemmani grave but couldn't find any evidence, likes clothes or personal jewellery, that suggested her son was buried there. DNA tests on the human remains are yet to be carried out.
All the remains recovered so far from Chemmani have been kept in the Forensic Department of the University of Jaffna campus under court custody.
"We are preparing an interim report, and it will be submitted to the court by the end of September," Prof Raj Somadeva, the chief archaeologist of the mass grave told the BBC.
Some of the samples are expected to be sent abroad for detailed examination to help determine the age of the remains. Separate medical analyses will be needed to establish the possible causes of death.
More than 20 mass graves have been found across Sri Lanka in recent decades, but none have been conclusively linked to enforced disappearances or alleged extra-judicial killings in the north and south of the country – and none have led to prosecutions.
Given the failure of the authorities to investigate previous mass graves, there is scepticism among many Tamil people over what the new investigation might achieve.
They point out to the outcome of the investigation on another mass grave was unearthed in the north-western town of Mannar in 2018 in which more than 350 skeletal remains were found. Investigations proved inconclusive, leaving many families disappointed.
They want Sri Lanka to be referred to the International Criminal Court.
The government of President Anura Kumara Dissanayake insists that it is fully cooperating with the investigation.
After coming to power in September 2024, Dissanayake promised to work towards justice and ethnic reconciliation. But his government vehemently opposes any international mechanism to investigate alleged war crimes committed during the ethnic conflict, disappointing Tamils.
"We will continue with the excavation work at Chemmani," Harshana Nanayakkara, Sri Lanka's justice minister told the BBC.
"We need to analyse the skeletons and find out how these people died. Then we have to carry out DNA tests," he said.
The government, he insists, has also asked the families to give their DNA so that it can be analysed later with the remains.
During his inspection at Chemmani in June, the minister promised investigations to find justice and truth to bring an end to the matter. He also promised that necessary funding will be allocated for the excavation.
The Sri Lankan army spokesman, Brigadier Waruna Gamage rejects allegations that security forces buried civilians after massacring them.
"All the allegations should be proved in court," he told the BBC.
Calls for international assistance
The delays in investigating past crimes have attracted stringent criticism from rights groups.
After years of international pressure, in 2018 the government set up an independent body, the Office of the Missing Persons (OMP), to investigate the disappearances. But those affected say it hasn't made much progress in finding their missing relatives.
"Many cases of forced disappearance, torture and killing remain stalled, while families of victims and human rights defenders face threats and intimidation," Human Rights Watch said in a report earlier this month.
The United Nations has urged Sri Lanka to seek international help in identifying the victims, to find out how they died, and who is responsible.
"This is a situation where victims are deeply frustrated, have lived with pain for decades, have come to distrust past investigations," Rory Mungoven, the Asia-Pacific chief at the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights tells the BBC.
"I think involving international assistance would help to bolster confidence in these investigations," he points out.
Successive Sri Lankan governments have strongly resisted calls for international investigations into alleged wartime atrocities.
During earlier reporting trips to Sri Lanka, I met parents and family members of the disappeared who campaigned for decades to the search for truth. Some have since passed away without ever discovering the fates of their loved ones.
Human rights groups say that President Dissanayake's government now has an opportunity to break from a long-standing pattern of delay and denial and deliver accountability for grave abuses committed during the conflict.
Suseela is determined to know the truth.
"I don't know how long I will live with such uncertainty, but I want closure," she says.
Additional Reporting by: Ranjan Arun Prasadh, BBC Tamil Service in Kandy and Kumanan Kanapathippillai in Jaffna.

There isn’t much that we Indians agree on these days. GDP numbers are no exception. Last week, India released glowing GDP numbers for the latest quarter – 7.8% growth – higher than the forecast 7%. It sparked a furore.
Subhash Garg, a former finance secretary under Narendra Modi’s government and now a critic, reframed what Modi called a “herculean feat” as mere smoke and mirrors. According to Garg, the government revised last year’s current-price GDP downwards to inflate this year’s number – he believes the real growth is only 2.6%.
The assertion, made on a television channel, immediately went viral. A flurry of op-eds and hot takes have been published since. Supporters of the government, predictably, rejected the claims. Those who have questions agree on a more fundamental problem: a lack of transparency and statistical credibility in India’s economic data. So why is there no consensus?
Over the past decade, critics say, the government has systematically hollowed out the integrity of its own data infrastructure, weaponising economic data for political gain and creating a trust deficit. Methodologies have been changed, crucial surveys have faced long delays and there have been attempts to suppress inconvenient findings.
In November, the International Monetary Fund rated India’s national accounts data a ‘C’ on a four-point scale, the second-lowest grade. In its report, the IMF said some of the methodologies are outdated, including relying on an old base year, unexplained discrepancies between GDP calculated from the production and expenditure side, as well as a lack of seasonal data.
India’s statistical system once commanded respect, and its data on economic and social indicators was considered rigorous. There might have been disagreements on the quality of estimates but their independence was widely accepted. That trust appears to have eroded in recent years.
“There seems to be a systematic effort by the government to hide the truth,” said R Nagaraj, an economist who taught at the Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research, adding that some of the other contested datasets include employment numbers, poverty numbers, health data and consumption data. “Over the last 10 years, the government has changed the methodology for many of these, raising questions. They have apparently also removed critical officials who headed some surveys. All of this adds to the scepticism.”
In one of the most prominent examples, from 2019, a Business Standard journalist revealed that the government had not published an official report showing unemployment at a 45-year high of 6.1%. Two expert members of the National Statistical Commission resigned in protest. The government initially denied it, calling it a draft. The figures were only released months later.
Then there is the census, which for the first time since independence, was delayed in 2021. Economists say relying on outdated demographic data means, among other things, inequitable allocation of welfare entitlements. (The first phase of the latest census finally began in April 2026.)
Nagaraj has witnessed some of this first-hand. He served on a subcommittee in 2014 whose report forms a part of the GDP. “The [numbers] we had discussed in the committee and what came out in the final report were different. So, I had to raise a red flag,” he said. The difference was notable: one figure in the published report had been inflated by 108%.
But government economists reject the ongoing criticism of the GDP numbers. Shamika Ravi, a member of the Economic Advisory Council to the prime minister, described it as a “noisy and very ill-informed debate” arguing that political leanings, not data, are behind the criticism.
The IMF rating was expected, she said. “The IMF rating of ‘C’ is the same rating that China has for its statistics. Several large developing or just developed economies have data issues.” Revisions to its calculations that the government was accused of having manipulated, she added, were precisely the sorts of changes the IMF had recommended.
The sticking point, as some including India’s former chief statistician Pronab Sen have pointed out, is the trustworthiness of the underlying data used.
Complicating this debate is the reality for many Indians. This year, young people have taken to the streets in frustration. Protests, which first began over leaked examination papers, have crystallised into a broader reckoning over systemic failures in education, jobs and the promise of a better future.
Almost 40% of graduates under 25 are unemployed, a recent report by Azim Premji University concluded. An estimated 87 million (8.7 crore) Indians between 15 and 29 are neither working, studying, nor doing skill training, a government thinktank reported last month.
That is why we should care about data quality, economists say. Incorrect data means bad policy. As economist Reetika Khera wrote in her recent book, Freebies or Rights: “Data shines the light to guide policymaking and is important for informed public debates.” As evidence, she points to gaps in basic statistics such as urbanisation and literacy numbers due to the delayed census. The consequences, she argues, are not abstract. Because the government still relies on outdated population numbers to decide who gets food subsidies, she estimates approximately 100 million (10 crore) people who should be covered are being deprived.
The controversy is making waves further ashore. In Sri Lanka, where second-quarter GDP figures are expected, the Daily FT newspaper wrote: “One hopes Sri Lankan policymakers and experts are not watching the theatrics in India with watering mouths and dreaming up smart arguments. Spare us such theatre!”

Limp Bizkit is another headline act at the two-day event. Indian artists on the lineup include Ricky Kej (performing with Stewart Copeland) and Aditya Gadhvi.

Earlier this year, Shakira’s concerts in India was postponed. But Rajasthani folk musicians the Ismail Langa Group (@ismaillanga_official) decided the music had to go on, in their own way. Their mashup of the Colombian star’s Hips Don’t Lie with the traditional folk song called Moruda has got everyone grooving (42m views and counting).
It took two months to pull off, says creative director Jagirdar RV. Most artists in the group, aged between 23 and 60, don’t speak or read English and learned the lyrics by rote. The song choice was simple, he said, because it “has a very nice vibe which matched our vibe”.
It’s been a breakout year for the group, which had a semi-final run on India’s Got Talent and are becoming known for taking folk songs to gen Z audiences on Instagram. They are working on their next English mashup – just not spilling which song, yet.

How Kenya won its bid for 2029 World Athletics Championships
- Published
Kenya's President William Ruto says the World Athletics Championship will be "coming home", with Nairobi set to make history after being selected as the first African city to host the event in 2029.
Ruto hailed the winning bid as a "victory for generations of athletes" who have made the nation "synonymous with excellence" on the track and road.
Nairobi beat London and Rome to the hosting rights, with Munich selected to stage the 2031 edition.
After missing out on the 2025 World Championships to Tokyo, a series of factors helped Kenya see off its European rivals this time around.
A sport 'woven into the fabric' of the nation
When World Athletics president Lord Coe announced the decision in Budapest on Tuesday, he described Kenya's bid as "compelling and emotional".
The East African nation is the second-most successful nation in the history of the World Championships with 72 gold medals, placing it behind the United States.
The vast majority of those glories, alongside 38 Olympic gold medals, have come in middle- and long-distance running.
Lord Coe said that athletics is "woven into the fabric" of the nation and that Kenyans have helped "shape the history" of the sport.
He name-checked several runners including two-time Olympic champion Eliud Kipchoge - who was involved in the lobbying for Kenya's bid - men's 800m world record holder David Rudisha and multiple world and Olympic medallist Faith Kipyegon.
A passionate fanbase is also one of the country's great strengths.
Some 68% of Kenyans surveyed by World Athletics rated their interest in athletics as high, compared with a global average of 39%.
Athletics is the country's second-most followed sport, behind only football, and when World Athletics assessed its social media channels, Kenya was the fourth-highest nation in terms of followers.
Upgraded facilities
Kenya's previous bid for the 2025 edition fell down largely on the facilities which the country possessed.
This time around, the Kasarani Stadium will have gone through a complete structural upgrade well before the world's top athletes descend on Nairobi.
The 48,000-capacity venue will be used when Kenya co-hosts football's 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) next June and July alongside Tanzania and Uganda.
"We learned from the 2025 bid because there were areas that we did not score well," Barnaba Korir, who worked on the successful bid, told the BBC World Service.
"Because of that, we managed to improve on those areas.
"I'm happy that the infrastructure that we have already developed will also meet the standards that we have seen all over the world."
Hotel space is one area not expected to be a problem, with Nairobi a regular host for large conventions.
"Kenya is also known for its very dynamic hospitality, the tourism sector," Elijah Mwangi, principal secretary at the State Department for Sports, told the BBC.
"It has a game park within the city, so we are waiting to welcome everybody."
President Ruto made financial and security guarantees in order to secure the Championships.
"We thank World Athletics for the confidence it has placed in Kenya," Ruto said.
"We will honour that confidence by delivering an unforgettable championship worthy of our athletes, our country and our continent."
Expanding athletics
Lord Coe became president of World Athletics (then known as the IAAF) in 2015 and has pledged to grow the sport around the globe.
During his time in office the World Championships have been hosted in Qatar (2019), the United States (2022) and Tokyo, while China's capital Beijing will stage them in 2027.
Kenya has successfully hosted age-grade events in Nairobi and the World Cross Country Championships in Mombasa, while the World Athletics Relays were held in Botswana's capital Gaborone in May.
With Coe's third term in office coming to an end next year, one official involved in Kenya's bid, speaking before the host announcement, said it was "unthinkable" that Nairobi would not succeed.
"With this decision we continue to fulfil our mission of growing athletics worldwide," Coe said.
"It was important that the World Athletics Championships should come to Africa when we had the right host, the right bid and the right circumstances.
Coe hailed the "quality, ambition and commitment" of all four bidding cities.
London, Munich and Rome have all previously held the Olympics, with the World Championships in London as recently as 2017, but the chance to break new ground in Africa was clearly compelling.
UK Athletics chief executive Jack Buckner said his team was "deeply disappointed" to see London miss out.
What is needed next?
Kenya now faces logistical and organisational challenges over the next three years as it prepares to deliver Africa's first World Championships.
With the 2027 Afcon looming large on the horizon, Nairobi will have a chance to test-run getting fans in and out of the Kasarani Stadium, which lies about a half-hour drive from the city's central business district.
The venue does not have any rail connections but Korir says World Athletics officials were "very satisfied" by Kenya's transport plan.
There were instances of overcrowding when the stadium hosted Kenya games at football's African Nations Championships last year, which led to the capacity being reduced for some matches.
Delays in preparations for Afcon have raised concerns, and the funding for the World Championships will come entirely from the Kenyan government.
Mwangi revealed that $78m (£58.5m) is the current estimate for the government's contribution, with sponsorship deals also playing a role.
"We are prepared to ensure that whatever is expected to be paid, it is paid in the due time," he added.
Presidential elections are scheduled for next year, but Korir is confident organisers will secure the "huge" and "legally binding" figure earmarked even if there is a change in government.
"Whatever the government assigns now will be observed by the next government. It is an international agreement," he said.
Then comes ticketing, first to make sure the local population are not priced out and then to ensure the stands are filled.
The cheapest tickets for the Under-18 World Championships in 2017 were priced at 200 Kenyan shillings ($1.15, £1.14) but attendances were low until entry was made free.
World Athletics generated $522m in revenue from Tokyo 2025, with a total of 619,000 tickets sold over the nine days of competition, while London sold a record 705,000 tickets in 2017.
In passing up the opportunity of returning to the British capital, World Athletics has chosen expansion over guaranteed ticket sales, but attendances will be scrutinised - especially after the sparse numbers seen in the stands in Doha in 2019.
Korir, however, is confident the Kasarani Stadium "will be full" on "every day" of competition, including morning sessions, if sales begin early enough.
Meanwhile, Kenya has endured a spate of doping scandals in recent years, with 11 individuals banned by the Athletics Integrity Unit so far this year alone.
The pressure is now on the East African nation to deliver on its promises in the build-up to Nairobi 2029 and ensure the Championships pass off without any major issues.

Lithuania ready to 'fight back' but has evacuation plans in face of Russia threats, PM tells BBC
- Published
Lithuania's prime minister has told the BBC his country has made evacuation plans in the face of threats from Russia, but added they "will not surrender" if attacked.
Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius told Newsnight that Lithuanians feel "constantly threatened" by Russia, in part because of drones entering the nation's airspace.
He told Newsnight if his country was attacked, "we will fight back... we will engage". But he said there were plans for a "variety of scenarios" and used an example of getting elderly citizens out of cities "smoothly" and avoiding traffic jams.
Lithuania, a Nato member, shares a land border with the Russian enclave of Kaliningrad.
"We're thinking about a variety of scenarios, not all of them are being discussed very much publicly," Sinkevičius told the BBC.
"We face concrete threats, not on a daily basis, but we're experiencing them and it's a true reality for us."
Sinkevičius also said the UK needed a "shift in the mindset" in terms of its approach to defence, but noted that Lithuania was "closer to the border and closer to [the] threat".
It comes just a week after Nato fighter pilots shot down a drone that entered Lithuania's airspace.
Though the origins of the drone have not been confirmed, Lithuanian Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas told Newshour that it came from the direction of Belarus, Lithuania's neighbour and a key Russian ally.
The UK's Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said: "Thanks to the swift and professional actions of Lithuanian and Italian forces, Nato once again demonstrated our readiness to protect our airspace.
"We stand united, around the clock, in defence of every inch of Nato territory."
Moscow did not comment on the incident.
Military drone incursions have become increasingly common across Europe since the beginning of Russia's full-scale of invasion of Ukraine.
Residents in Lithuania's capital Vilnius were also forced to take shelter in May after a drone alert was triggered, briefly grounding flights and rail travel.
Nato jets have scrambled multiple times to shoot down stray Ukrainian drones that have crossed into fellow Baltic countries Estonia and Latvia this year.
Ukraine has blamed the stray drones on Russian electronic warfare, technology designed to change the flight paths of Ukrainian drones.
Lithuania, Estonia and Latvia all joined Nato in 2004, becoming signatories to the Article 5 provision that states "an armed attack against one NATO member shall be considered an attack against all members".

The Activision transition is just one part of Xbox’s wider organizational overhaul. Rare and World’s Edge, the studios associated with Sea of Thieves and Age of Empires, will also fall under Activision’s expanded remit.
Meanwhile, a new Fallout game will be released by Bethesda as they take responsibility for Obsidian. Playground Games and Turn 10 Studios are merging to focus on Forza and Fable on Xbox, while King will oversee Microsoft Casual Games. Ninja Theory could also shut down as Xbox failed to find a buyer.
While it’s certain that Activision’s arrival marks a turning point for Halo, and the franchise has entered an entirely new development era.

Rows of hardware and car-part shops line Garstin Bastion Road, with faded signs crammed together above their shutters. By day, the street is one of Old Delhi’s busiest commercial thoroughfares. But as dusk falls, GB Road, as it is known locally, transforms into one of the city’s most notorious red-light districts.
An estimated 2,800 sex workers live and work in brothels that occupy the upper floors of the dilapidated buildings, their entrances tucked behind narrow stairways and unmarked doors. Women sit on plastic stools beneath the stairways, calling out to men passing on the street, while others watch from windows above, their eyes following the movement below before customers are directed upstairs.
The challenges the women of GB Road face are numerous and well documented – from health risks to abuse, debt to poor sanitation. Now they face a new struggle: India’s controversial electoral reform process. The Election Commission’s special intensive revision, or SIR, is a nationwide exercise in which electoral rolls have shrunk by more than 58 million voters across the 13 states covered in the first two of three main phases. In Delhi, covered in the third phase, the scale of exclusion is the highest recorded as a percentage: 4.76 million names – 33% of the city’s previous electorate – do not appear on the city’s draft roll published on 31 August.
The government says SIR is meant to “purify” the electoral rolls by removing ineligible voters, including alleged undocumented migrants, but critics have accused Narendra Modi’s government of using it to target minority voters and reshape electoral rolls in ways that could benefit his Bharatiya Janata party (BJP).
On GB Road, the proportion of those excluded is even higher. Data shared by officials overseeing about 1,300 voters in the area show that about 650 were sex workers on the previous electoral roll. Of these, at least 500 have either been marked as “shifted”, meaning they have moved home or location, or have been unable to establish their eligibility because of missing documentation – more than three-quarters of the sex workers on the local roll.
One of them is 36-year-old Beauty*, who has lived on GB Road for more than two decades. She got her first voter ID in 2008. At the time, the address where she lived and worked as a sex worker and verification by a government official called a booth-level officer (BLO) were enough to put her on the electoral roll. She voted in previous elections.
But under the new rules, voters had to establish eligibility by proving their link to the relevant previous electoral roll or by producing prescribed documents such as a passport, birth or education certificate – a paper trail Beauty struggled to reconstruct. Trafficked at 16 and brought to the brothels of GB Road, she has no contact with her family. She does have an Aadhaar card, India’s biometric identity document used widely to establish identity and access government services, with her GB Road address. But Aadhaar is not proof of citizenship and does not, by itself, establish eligibility to vote under the SIR process.
She tried to get a copy of her matriculation certificate, which is evidence of schooling, from the village in Rajasthan where she grew up. One of her regular customers of the past 10 years – a man she refers to as her husband, agreed to help track down the old record but failed.
“If I had the papers to show my father’s birth certificate, or even my own matriculation certificate, then I could prove who I am,” she says. “But how can I go back to my village to ask for these things when my trafficking has brought so much shame to my family that they no longer accept me?”
Now Beauty has lost hope – and, for now, her vote. Her name was left out of Delhi’s recent draft electoral roll. For her, the voter ID had meant more than a piece of identification. Sex workers, she says, are accustomed to being treated as immoral, degraded and less worthy than others.
“We all shit. That is what makes us equal as human beings. Voting is the same in the realm of rights. When I stand in that queue, nobody is more or less than me. It reminds me that whatever people think about my work, I am still equal to everyone else.”
Beauty is not alone in struggling to prove her eligibility. The SIR requirements have exposed the precarious paper trails of women across GB Road, a roughly 1.5km stretch running between two of Delhi’s historic landmarks, Ajmeri Gate and Lahori Gate.
Of the nine sex workers interviewed for this story, none had successfully completed the SIR process: six said they had never received the enumeration form distributed by BLOs to verify voters’ details and collect information for the electoral-roll revision, while the remaining three were unable to meet the documentation requirements.
According to Kiran Deshmukh, a sex worker and coordinator at the National Network of Sex Workers (NNSW), many have spent years, even decades, in Delhi but possess few documents establishing their family histories or links to earlier electoral rolls. “Some were trafficked as children and lost contact with their families; others never attended school or have moved between rooms and brothels without leaving a stable documentary trail,” says Deshmukh. “It is impossible in such circumstances to prove such rigid eligibility requirements under SIR.”
The process is so cumbersome that even people who are literate and have institutional and organisational support can struggle to establish their eligibility. “The process of receiving the enumeration form, knowing when you have not received it, reaching out, then trying to create a paper trail is so daunting that the entire burden of proving your eligibility is placed on the citizen to protect their own constitutional right,” says Deshmukh.
Sagrika Rajora, a researcher and member of Voter Adhikar Manch, a citizens’ collective, argues that the burden falls particularly heavily on people whose lives do not fit neatly into the categories used by the verification process. “To identify people of such marginality is a tedious task. These categories of ‘shifted’ become an easy way forward for booth-level officers, when finding people on the ground is already time-consuming.”
BLOs are often drawn from occupations such as auxiliary nurses or health workers, adding electoral duties to already demanding jobs. Some have raised concerns about the workload and unrealistic timelines of the exercise. Yet, Rajora says, there has been little effort to streamline the process to ensure that “no eligible citizen is left out”, the aim outlined by the Delhi chief electoral officer, Ashok Kumar.
“There is so much discretion vested in one BLO. Even if you leave citizenship aside and talk only about voter rights, the entire process of delivering and collecting these forms depends on that one person. There are no grounds for entrusting one person with such a huge responsibility without any accountability at all,” Rajora says.
“It is not surprising that sex workers are among those being excluded. When people have lives that are so complex and mobile, you are going to be untraceable, absent from the system. These are the people for whom such a verification system is simply not designed to work.”
The gaps also cause problems for workers’ children when they reach adulthood. “Children may not possess documents establishing parentage in the manner expected for verification. Some are raised by relatives, guardians or members of the community, while others grow up in institutional care, making conventional family records difficult to establish,” says Deshmukh.
For 23-year-old Dinesh*, whose mother was a sex worker, the problem is not abstract. His mother died three years ago, but she never had a birth certificate. Without one, obtaining her death certificate became nearly impossible, leaving Dinesh with little documentation through which to establish his maternal lineage.
When Dinesh submitted his enumeration form, he relied on his matriculation certificate as proof of his identity. But the booth-level officer pointed out that it did not have his father’s name. “If my mother gave birth to me, why do I need a man’s name on any official certificate?” he asks.
Dinesh says his name is missing from the draft electoral roll. He is still unsure why, but suspects the absence of his father’s name may have been a factor.
The NNSW has written to the chief electoral officer seeking special measures to ensure that sex workers and their children are not excluded from the SIR. But the joint chief electoral officer, Balram Meena, told The Hindu there was no separate process for sex workers. “If their mapping can’t be done and there are no documents either, their names will be removed as per the process.”
The fear of losing the vote is not only about voting rights. In West Bengal, where the SIR has already been completed, the BJP government has used lists of voters deleted during the exercise to scrutinise eligibility for welfare schemes. The BJP chief minister, Suvendu Adhikari, says welfare programmes will continue under a “transparent process”, but adds: “No deceased person, illegal infiltrator, or non-Indian individual will be allowed to avail benefits meant for citizens of the state.” The government has excluded about 3 million beneficiaries from its new Annapurna Bhandar welfare for women scheme, using SIR deletion data in its verification process.
In Delhi, the next stage of the SIR process – issuing notices to those whose eligibility or previous electoral-roll details could not be established or matched, and dealing with claims and objections – has now begun and will continue until 29 October. Those excluded from the draft roll can challenge their omission. But Dinesh says he does not intend to.
After years of being asked to produce documents that his family never had, he is unsure what more he can submit to prove that he exists.
“Even if my mother were alive today, I don’t think that would be enough to prove anything. She never had the documents they are asking for. So how am I supposed to get those documents now, especially after her death?”
* Names have been changed. Workers and residents did not permit any photography during the Guardian’s visit

Welcome back to Power Play! Each week, senior writer Molly Taft tackles a topic around this midterm season’s biggest issue: data centers. If you’ve got a question or thought for the column, feel free to shoot Molly an email at [email protected] or reach them securely on Signal at mollytaft.76.
Molly McCann Sanders has a lot in common with many of the other women who helped Donald Trump win a second term as president. A pro-life Catholic who lives in Texas, she has staunchly conservative opinions on immigration and a fierce hatred of eminent domain—the practice of the government taking private property for public use.
Sanders, the president of the Eagle Forum Education & Legal Defense Fund, which was started by Phyllis Schlafly, also describes herself as “a crunchy MAHA mom”—and says she’s been paying particular attention to data centers.
“I'm alarmed by the idea that these data centers can move in and pollute,” she tells me. “I'm not a data center expert. I'm not a tech expert. But I’m suspicious and wary, and want to move slowly.”
She loves Trump, “but I think he’s wrong about data centers,” she says. And she sees the GOP’s effort to court what she calls “the laptop class”—young men who are enthusiastic about technology—at the Republican midterm convention earlier this month as a huge misstep with midterms nearing.
McCann Sanders isn’t alone. More than 60 percent of Americans, including 47 percent of Republicans, say they are opposed to the construction of data centers in a poll released by The New York Times last week. In August, the National Republican Senatorial Committee sent a private memo to AI companies sounding the alarm on how voters perceive data centers, warning that “campaign or party committees can not fix the toxic brand of an entire segment of the economy.” Last week, GOP strategist Tony Fabrizio issued a memo to the party’s candidates claiming that “unqualified support for building more AI data centers is a losing position.”
But the GOP is facing one big hurdle: Trump himself. In recent weeks, facing mounting scrutiny on his policies and support for the industry, Trump has doubled down on his defense of both data centers and AI. In late August, he wrote in a Truth Social post that only communities that wanted to be “backwards and poor” would refuse data centers coming to town.
Last week, he issued yet another series of posts boosting AI data centers. Users on his own Truth Social platform pushed back. An analysis from The New York Times of thousands of responses found that anti-data-center and anti-AI comments—including from staunch MAGA accounts—outnumbered positive comments by four to one.
Sanders says she sometimes “looks past” the wilder things Trump says, but she can’t fully overlook his pro-data-center rhetoric.
“That is not the right way to go about this,” she says of the “backwards and poor” post. “We do have legitimate concerns. There are real problems.”
My colleague Hugo Lowell, who covers the White House and writes our Inner Loop newsletter, says he’s not surprised by Trump’s attitude. “He’s bullish on AI,” he tells me. “He’s been told that restricting data center development means restricting compute, which means the US loses to China.”
The China competition angle is being publicly echoed by tech accelerationists and White House allies, including former White House AI czar David Sacks and investor and Palantir cofounder Joe Lonsdale. The latter debated Steve Bannon’s tech editor Joe Allen—whom I profiled last month—at an auxiliary event during the convention. That conversation between Lonsdale and Allen, Sanders says, was the only time she heard data centers brought up during the entire midterm convention.
There’s some evidence that voters haven’t quite made up their minds on how heavily to weigh the issue—and which party to trust. The New York Times poll found that AI and data centers rank far down the list of voters’ priorities, and almost 20 percent say they don’t know which party would handle the issue better.
And candidates otherwise aligned with Trump may just decide to ignore cues from the White House. Tom Tiffany, the Republican nominee for governor in Wisconsin, has scored Trump’s endorsement. But he’s also attacked his Democratic opponent David Crowley for what Tiffany claims are pro-data-center views.
But despite breaks like Tiffany’s and concerns like Sanders’, Trump “thinks MAGA at the end of the day will back him—on Epstein, on Iran, on AI,” Hugo says.
What We’re Writing
Haven’t you always wished that data centers were a little more cuddly? You’re in luck! My colleague Boone Ashworth wrote about a new server-shaped plushie with gangly limbs and a little smiley face, called Bezzy. (Adorable!) When you squeeze him, he emits a terrible droning noise—real audio recorded by people living next to a data center in Virginia.
Bezzy is part of a larger project designed to raise awareness about data center expansion in the US. The plush toy is one of the many ways the data center backlash is taking shape.
“Personally, I love Bezzy and want to adopt one,” Boone says. “Also, it makes me very grateful I don't live near a data center. I really feel for people who do.”
What We’re Reading
The Washington Sun reports that the Interior Department is considering at least 12 data center proposals across at least 17,600 acres of public land—far more than had been previously reported.
Writer Natalie Fertig traveled to a swing district in Pennsylvania to take the political pulse of anti-data-center organizers there. Despite their success in blocking a big data center project, many of the folks she interviewed in both political parties felt like politicians didn’t care about them.
Amazon admitted this week that it had permanently lost customer data that was stored in data centers hit by Iranian drone strikes earlier this year. Reuters broke the story.
Virginia governor Abigail Spanberger signed an executive order on Friday that creates a state AI task force and may limit data centers. The latter is particularly notable given that the state is home to Data Center Alley, a global hot spot for the facilities. Read more about the order in The Verge.

La Liga president Javier Tebas says claiming there is a refereeing conspiracy against Real Madrid is like "living in another galaxy".
Real manager Jose Mourinho accused officials of making key errors after his side were beaten 2-1 by rivals Atletico Madrid last week.
Mourinho brought printouts of screenshots to the post-match news conference, claiming Atletico should have been given two red cards in the first half.
Writing in response to an article in the Spanish media which claimed there is a "conspiracy" against Real, Tebes dismissed the allegations.

"It's more comfortable to point to a conspiracy than to explain what's happening on the pitch."
Real are fourth in La Liga, six points behind Barcelona who top the table on 21 points after winning all seven of their league games this season.
After defeat by Atletico, where Real went down to 10 men in a feisty encounter after defender Dean Huijsen was sent off, Mourinho blamed the officiating.

You can get Google Pixel’s Rambler AI voice typing on many Android phones without root by patching a supported Gboard version with Morphe. Once enabled, Rambler can clean up speech, remove filler words, fix grammar, add punctuation, and format dictated text using AI.
If there is one feature that truly revolutionized because of AI, it is voice typing. Voice typing did exist way before AI, but it was very basic. It only converted the spoken audio directly into text, which included all the filler words, missing punctuation, grammar mistakes, and more. It basically turned whatever you spoke into text.
But with AI, voice typing goes through one extra step, where all your typing is fed to the AI models, which remove all filler words and format the sentence structure. It fundamentally eliminates the need for you to copy text into multiple apps, fix the grammar and sentence structure, and then copy it again to wherever you need it.
Third-party voice dictation apps went ahead and also included support for different formatting styles based on the app you are using, and they support almost every app.
However, the AI voice dictation feature truly gained traction after Google introduced the Pixel 11’s Rambler feature, which is very similar to AI voice dictation apps that use AI to refine the speech-to-text output.
However, currently, this feature is officially available on Pixel 11 series devices. You can see the full requirements here. But with a single patch for your Google Gboard, you can get this feature on a supported Android device. In this video, you are going to learn exactly how to get the Google Pixel’s Rambler feature on another Android device without root.
Table of Contents
How to Get Pixel 11 Rambler Voice Typing on Any Android Without Root
Before we get started, here are the prerequisites
Download the supported Gboard 18.0.3.954559732-release-arm64-v8a APK from here, or you can skip this if you want to download the supported version directly from Morphe
To use this feature, your smartphone needs to run Android 10 or later. Here are the full requirements:
- Android 10+ (Android 12+ recommended)
- Requires Sideloading enabled
Download the Morphe app for Android. It lets you patch your apps. For those who are unaware, patching is basically modifying the app and adding features that don’t exist.
Step 1: Download the Morphe app on your Android phone. Visit the official Morphe GitHub page and tap Download. Or download directly from the official Morphe site
Step 2: Once downloaded, install the app.
Step 3: Open the Morphe app and tap on Sources.
Step 4: Tap on the Plus icon, paste the following link in the Sources box, tap on Add this link, and tap on Add. https://github.com/jasonwu1994/Gboard-patches
Step 5: Wait for the source to load and tap on the Gboard app.
Step 6: Now tap on Yes, Help me find an APK, tap on Download APK, and download the app. Don’t install it.
Step 7: Now go back to the Morphe app, tap on Open APK file, and select the Gboard 18.0.3.954559732-release-arm64-v8a APK or later you downloaded above, and Morphe will start patching the app.
Step 8: Once patched, tap Install the app and allow Morphe to install the app on your device.
Step 9: Now open the patched Gboard and enable it. You need to set it as the default keyboard on some Android phones to use it, or you can go through the permission setup and switch to this keyboard later.
Step 10: Now open the patched Gboard and tap on Settings, scroll down, and tap on Patches.
Step 11: Tap on Advanced Voice Typing and enable the Enable Advanced Voice Typing option.
Step 12: Once enabled, go back to Voice Typing Settings and then select the Rambler feature.
Step 13: Now, to use the feature, you need to force stop the app. To do that, go to the patched Gboard app, long-press on it, tap on the i icon, then tap on the Force Stop option, and then confirm. These steps may vary depending on your smartphone brand and Android version.
Step 14: Now open any app where you can type, bring up patched Gboard, tap on the microphone icon, and start using Rambler.
This is how you can enable the Google Pixel Rambler feature on a supported Android smartphone without root. Since it is a manual process, I have included details step by step to help you understand.
If you face any issues or errors while using the Rambler feature, or if the Rambler feature is not available on your device, you can comment below. If you face any issues during the steps, comment below, and I will help you.
FAQs on Using Google Rambler on Non-Pixel Phones
1. Is it safe to use a patched version of Gboard with my Google account?
Yes, it is safe to install if you follow my steps exactly and only use the resources I included in this guide. For safety, I also highly recommend checking the app before installing using Google Play Protect or using third-party antivirus scanner tools like VirusTotal.
2. Will Rambler continue working after Gboard or Android gets updated?
Yes, since you are using a separate Gboard patched version, updating the original Gmail app won’t affect this patched version. However, the patched version also needs to be updated in case Google blocks access to the Rambler feature for other devices.
3. Can I switch back to the official Gboard later without losing my keyboard settings?
You won’t lose any settings; you can simply switch back to the original Gboard if you want to anytime.
4. Which languages does Rambler support for AI voice typing?
Google Rambler currently supports Arabic, English, French, German, Hindi, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, Russian, Spanish, and a few other Indian languages,
5. Does Rambler send my voice recordings or typed text to Google for processing?
Yes, the Google Pixel Rambler feature uses cloud processing to fix sentences; however, Google says this data is not saved, stored, or shared and is deleted immediately after the processed text is delivered.

It seems like every chain wants a piece of the dunkable-chicken craze.
McDonald's launched its McCrispy Strips in May 2025, marking the first time chicken strips had been on its menu since the COVID-19 pandemic.
Then, in June 2025, Taco Bell introduced its new Crispy Chicken Strips, with Taco Bell's CMO Taylor Montgomery telling Business Insider that Gen Z was eating more crispy chicken than other generations, and "we need to evolve to where youth culture and the next generation of consumers are going."
I tried chicken tenders from 14 major fast-food chains across the US to see how they compared.
When it comes to my perfect tender, I'm looking for a balance between a satisfying crunch and juicy chicken. I generally prefer thick, all-white-meat tenders with a crisp, flavorful breading over thinner tenders and heavy breading. Plus, amid rising fast-food prices, value for money and portion size have become more important to me than ever before.
Here's how all 14 chicken tenders ranked, from my least favorite to my favorite, based on flavor, texture, and overall value.
Of all the chicken tenders I tried, Whataburger's didn't completely wow me.
A three-piece chicken tender cost $7.48 at Whataburger at the location I visited in Austin.
The tenders were large and perfectly fried.
The tenders could be described as "classic" — they weren't anything out-of-the-box, but I enjoyed them.
The meat inside was juicy, but I thought the fried coating could have had a bit more crunch.
The chicken tenders tasted good on their own and with ranch dipping sauce.
They weren't bad by any stretch of the imagination. However, I did think the other tenders I tried were slightly crispier and had slightly more flavor in the batter.
Regardless, for a relatively low price, I'd definitely order these again.
I also ordered chicken tenders from Cook Out, a regional chain I visited in South Carolina.
The three-piece "snack" cost $4.99, not including tax.
The chicken tenders were crispy on the outside.
They were a good size, and I thought the price was a great deal for the generous portion.
However, there wasn't much chicken meat inside.
These were undeniably classic chicken tenders, similar to those from Whataburger, but a touch too fried for my liking.
Still, I thought they were well-seasoned and had a lot of peppery flavor.
Smashburger's chicken tenders were just slightly too fried for my liking.
An order of three chicken tenders from Smashburger — which has locations in 24 states and Washington, DC — costs $9.99, excluding tax and fees. I thought this was a little pricey, especially compared to other chains' prices.
The chicken tenders were heavily fried and bigger than others I tried.
The breading on the chicken tenders felt thick and crunchy.
Overall, the chicken tenders tasted dry, even when paired with sauce.
The chicken meat inside and the ranch dipping sauce provided could only do so much to offset the intense dryness of the crunchy breading.
The next time I order from Smashburger, I'll stick to the chain's beef offerings.
Next up were the crispy chicken tenders from Sonic Drive-In.
A five-piece order of chicken tenders cost $8.41, excluding tax.
The tenders were evenly fried but on the thinner side.
Rather than thick and juicy, these were flatter. In fact, I'd say these were the thinnest and flattest tenders out of all the ones I tried.
I enjoyed the flavor of the seasoning, but the texture left a lot to be desired.
The chicken was on the drier side, and there simply wasn't a lot of it. I gravitate toward thicker, more shreddable chicken tenders, and these slightly missed the mark for me.
However, the flavor was definitely there — the breading had a peppery essence, and the tenders were evenly fried.
My 10th favorite chicken tenders came from Popeyes.
A three-piece tender combo costs $16.89 before taxes and fees. The meal deal included a large serving of fries, a drink, and a biscuit, along with a choice of dipping sauces.
The chicken tenders from Popeyes were crispy, flaky, and crunchy.
I really liked the crunchy exterior.
The meat inside was flaky and moist.
The batter was flavorful — I could taste hints of seasoning and buttermilk.
However, this meal felt expensive for only three chicken tenders, even though they were large.
I thought the chicken tenders from Bojangles were flavorful and super crispy.
A four-piece chicken tenders combo, including fries, a medium drink, and a biscuit, cost me $10.49, excluding taxes and fees.
The chicken tenders were a good size.
The texture and flavor of the breading made them taste like a cross between Chick-fil-A and Cook Out chicken tenders.
The breading was peppery, just the right thickness, and perfectly encased the juicy white chicken.
I also thought the price was fair, considering the amount of food I received. The chicken tenders paired well with honey mustard but were also tasty on their own.
I would definitely order these again.
Wendy's brought out chicken tenders in 2025.
Wendy's new tenders are available in three- or four-piece options. I ordered a three-piece tender for $8.12, excluding tax and fees, at my local restaurant in Brooklyn, New York.
"Consumers told us what they wanted in a chicken tender, and we listened — taste-tested, fine-tuned, and delivered," Lindsay Radkoski, Wendy's US chief marketing officer, told Business Insider of the 2025 launch.
The tenders were about the same size as the ones from McDonald's, but crispier.
However, I preferred the slightly thinner breading on the McDonald's and KFC tenders.
In terms of flavor, these tenders had a distinct peppery note that paired well with the new signature sauce — which is creamy and peppery — introduced at the time of their release.
These tenders were solid, and I'd order them again.
However, the slight lack of chicken meat inside — at least compared to other chains — and the chunky breading prevented Wendy's tenders from ranking higher for me.
KFC's original recipe chicken tenders really impressed me with their taste and value.
I ordered a four-piece tender meal for $13.65, excluding taxes and fees, in Brooklyn, New York. Although it was more expensive than some other chains, it also seemed like an excellent value for the amount of food I received.
The tenders were well-breaded, though the breading wasn't as crispy or crunchy as others I tried.
The breading stuck closely to the chicken tenders, rather than having a thick or crunchy texture.
However, the chicken tenders paired well with the chain's honey mustard and comeback sauce, which is another creamy, peppery sauce. The breading had a tasty, very peppery flavor that was distinct from the other chicken tenders I tried.
The tenders were flavorful and contained an impressive amount of white meat chicken.
However, the slightly less-crispy texture of the breading meant they didn't come out on top compared to the last six chains I tried.
McDonald's launched its new McCrispy Strips nationwide in May 2025.
At my local McDonald's in Brooklyn, three McCrispy chicken strips cost $10.99, excluding tax and fees.
The chicken strips were large and evenly coated in breading.
The chicken strips differed from the chain's buttermilk crispy tenders, which were discontinued in 2020 at the start of the COVID-19 pandemic.
Chicken tenders haven't been on the menu since, despite fans' pleas to bring them back.
The breading was relatively thin but very crispy.
Unlike some flakier chicken tenders, each bite was evenly coated in well-seasoned, peppery breading. Inside, the chicken meat was thick and juicy.
Paired with the chain's creamy chili sauce, which was created to go with the chicken strips, these packed a decent amount of flavor.
However, on their own, I thought they were a little blander than some of the higher-ranked tenders I tried.
Taco Bell released chicken strips after debuting its crispy nuggets in late 2024.
Launched in June 2025, Taco Bell's chicken strips were available in three types of tacos and burritos, or on their own with dipping sauce.
The chicken strips have been unavailable since January 2026, but Taco Bell frequently discontinues and rereleases items as limited-time offerings, so they could be back at some point.
An order of chicken strips and two sauces cost $9.14, excluding tax and fees.
The chicken strips were thick, juicy, and perfectly crispy.
The chicken strips were marinated in zesty jalapeño buttermilk and breaded with crispy tortilla chips and breadcrumbs, which is the same formula as the chain's chicken nuggets, which I ranked as my favorite across six chains.
These chicken strips packed a lot of flavor.
The crispy breading was flavorful, and I definitely got hints of tortilla chip. The chicken inside was moist and juicy.
My only real complaint was that I wanted more than two.
Chick-fil-A's chicken tenders were crisp and juicy.
When it's not included in a meal deal, a three-piece chicken tender costs $9.69 at my nearest location in New York City. For a meal, the price bumps up to $17.35, excluding tax and fees.
Some of the chicken pieces looked slightly darker and more fried than others.
Small bits of fried breading were scattered on the outside, which I always love with chicken tenders.
The chicken tenders were nicely fried but still juicy on the inside.
Dipped in the chain's signature Chick-fil-A sauce, these tenders were mouthwatering.
They were also great on their own, with the perfect balance of crispy breading and a delicious, briny flavor. The sauce just took them over the edge.
Wingstop's chicken tenders, which were upgraded in 2025, came in third place.
Wingstop revamped its chicken tenders in February 2025.
The chain sells its chicken in various flavors, from original hot to hickory-smoked barbecue and mango habanero. However, I ordered these chicken tenders plain.
I ordered a five-piece chicken tender combo at my local Wingstop in Brooklyn. It cost $15.39 and came with a drink, dipping sauce, and a regular side of fries.
The chain also sells four chicken tenders, which come with one dipping sauce, for $10.69, plus tax and fees.
The chicken tenders were large and well-breaded.
They were deep golden in color and evenly fried, with small clumps of fried breading adding more texture to every bite.
The chicken tender easily tore apart with every bite.
The breading itself was slightly peppery, but not overly flavorful. They paired well with Wingstop's signature ranch — my favorite of any fast-food ranch — and the chain's honey mustard.
Wingstop delivered great classic tenders, though the breading didn't pack as much flavor as the top two chains I tried. Nevertheless, I'd definitely order these again.
My second favorite chicken tenders came from Zaxby's.
Zaxby's, which has locations in 22 states, serves its five-piece chicken tenders with fries, a small drink, coleslaw, and a piece of Texas toast. I also asked for a side of honey mustard and Zaxby's famous Zax sauce.
My meal cost $15.43, excluding taxes and fees.
The breading of the chicken tenders was similar to Chick-fil-A's in consistency, flavor, and texture, but I thought these ones had more meat.
The breading was crispy and flavorful, with a slight sweetness.
The tenders held their own without sauce but were really taken to the next level when dipped in the tangy Zax sauce.
Zax sauce tastes similar to Cane's sauce from Raising Cane's, but I found it to be just ever-so-slightly less flavorful — it didn't have the same kick.
However, the chicken tenders really impressed me. They were a good size, extremely flavorful, and addictively delicious. I found myself craving even more than the five chicken tenders I was given.
In the end, it was a really tough call on whether I preferred Zaxby's or Raising Cane's chicken tenders.
My favorite chicken tenders came from Raising Cane's.
A combo that includes three chicken fingers, fries, Cane's sauce, Texas toast, and a regular drink costs $12.19, excluding tax and any additions or swaps.
The chicken tenders were super crispy.
The chicken tenders were also thick. After biting in, I could actually see the strips of white chicken underneath, which you don't always find with fast-food chicken tenders.
The chicken tenders were crispy and juicy on the inside — I had to give them the win.
I tried the tenders on their own and with the Cane's sauce. On their own, the tenders were simply everything one could ask for: thick, juicy, and crispy on the outside.
The chain is famous for its chicken-complementing sauce, and after taking a bite, I could see why. It had a slight kick, and it was creamy and surprisingly tangy. It paired perfectly with the chicken and was unlike any other sauce I've ever tried.
In the end, Raising Cane's took home the win for me with the chain's near-perfect chicken tenders and fair prices.

IPO-bound B2B seafood brand Captain Fresh crossed the ₹5,000 Cr revenue mark in FY26, while its adjusted EBITDA nearly tripled as the company continued to remain profitable for the second consecutive year. The Bengaluru-based company reported a consolidated net revenue of ₹5,169 Cr in FY26, up 52% from ₹3,397 Cr in FY25. Adjusted EBITDA rose 2.7X to ₹371 Cr from ₹136 Cr in the previous fiscal, it said in a statement. Captain Fresh’s gross margin also expanded to 23.5% in FY26 from 17% in FY25. While the company did not disclose its FY26 bottom line, it claimed it remained PAT-positive. Captain Fresh is yet to file its audited financial statements for the fiscal year. In FY25, it posted a net profit of ₹42 Cr. The company claimed that it is now on track to achieve ₹10,000 Cr in revenue in FY27, with its focus shifting towards scaling its existing portfolio and infrastructure. “FY26 stress tested the industry in the form of tariffs and an unsettled trade environment, and we came out stronger than we went in,” group CFO and whole-time director Mathew George said. Captain Fresh had ₹2,300 Cr debt at the end of FY26, of which ₹440 Cr was long-term debt, while the remainder comprised working capital financing. Its debt-to-equity ratio stood at 1.6 during the year, which it is also targeting to reduce to 1.3-1.5. The company said it carried higher inventory during FY26 to ensure uninterrupted customer supply amid global disruptions. This, it said, was the reason behind its higher working capital requirements during the fiscal. As operating conditions normalise, Captain Fresh expects this inventory build-up to reverse. Captain Fresh said its receivables are insured and that none of them were disputed during the period under review. Zooming Into Captain Fresh’s Business Founded in 2020 by Utham Gowda, Captain Fresh began as a tech-led B2B seafood supply chain platform and has since expanded into a global packaged seafood business. It operates a portfolio of seafood brands across Europe and North America. Its European processing footprint includes Frime in Spain, Koral in Poland, Senecrus in France and CFT in Denmark through a joint venture. In North America, it distributes through CenSea, Ocean Garden and Ocean Edge, largely across foodservice channels. The company sources seafood from more than 30 countries across three oceans. In FY26, Ecuador accounted for 17% of sourcing, followed by Indonesia at 15%, India at 12%, and Vietnam at 9%. Captain Fresh said it serves nearly 2,500 customers, including more than 50 of the world’s largest seafood buyers. Captain Fresh’s Delayed IPO Plans The FY26 performance comes as Captain Fresh continues to prepare for a potential public listing. After converting into a public entity in June 2025, it confidentially pre-filed its DRHP with SEBI for a $400 Mn IPO in August 2025, comprising a $200 Mn fresh issue and a $150-200 Mn offer-for-sale component. However, it withdrew the IPO papers in December 2025, citing delays in obtaining regulatory clearances for a European acquisition. The company said it planned to refile after securing the approvals. The acquisition in question was completed in March 2026, when Captain Fresh acquired Spanish tuna processor Frime. However, it is yet to refile its IPO papers. The company subsequently raised ₹290 Cr in debt from Blue Earth Capital to scale manufacturing, global distribution and hiring. Captain Fresh has raised nearly $250 Mn to date from investors including Accel, Tiger Global, Prosus Ventures, Z47, Evolvence Group, and British International Investment.

Shares of ecommerce major Meesho surged as much as 9.3% during the intraday trading after brokerage UBS maintained its ‘Buy’ rating on the stock and raised its target price to ₹260 from ₹210. The stock touched an intraday high of ₹239.45 on the BSE. It was trading 8.9% higher at ₹238.55 at 11:25 IST. At the current price, UBS’ revised target implies a further upside of around 9%. Meesho’s market capitalisation stood at ₹1.10 Lakh Cr (around $11.5 Bn). The brokerage raised its net merchandise value (NMV) estimates for Meesho for FY29-FY31 by 7%-18%, along with a similar increase in its contribution profit projections. It also increased its EBITDA estimates for the period by 20%-40%. UBS attributed its higher NMV projections to the continued expansion of Meesho’s buyer and seller ecosystems, along with the rapid growth in SKUs and logistics partners. Meesho’s annual transacting sellers jumped 81% YoY to 10.4 Lakh in Q1 FY27, while its annual transacting users rose 29% to 27.4 Cr. The ecommerce platform’s NMV increased 34% YoY to ₹11,614 Cr during the quarter. The brokerage expects Meesho’s earnings to grow faster than NMV over the medium term as the company improves advertising monetisation and its logistics economics. In Q1 FY27, Meesho’s contribution margin expanded to 4.6% of NMV from 4% in the preceding quarter. Its adjusted EBITDA loss narrowed to ₹178.2 Cr from ₹230.1 Cr in the year-ago period. The company also narrowed its consolidated net loss by 54% YoY to ₹132.8 Cr during the quarter, while operating revenue surged 48% to ₹3,707 Cr. Meesho listed on the bourses in December last year. At its current price, the stock is trading nearly 115% above its IPO issue price of ₹111 and about 6% below its 52-week high of ₹254.65.

iPhones and Macs are like two peas in a pod. Apple’s hardware synergy means you can launch iPhone apps right from the macOS desktop, respond to texts without picking up your iPhone, and even copy text on one platform and paste it on the other. That kind of seamless connectivity does not natively exist for Android phone owners at the operating system level.
Google’s trying to change that with Googlebooks, a new class of laptop. First teased in May, the company finally shared more details about the new OS at a media-only event in New York City last week. Like with Android, hardware manufacturers can make their own Googlebooks, provided they hit specific standards set by Google.
Today marks the launch of five new computers that comply with the Googlebooks standard, one each from HP, Dell, Lenovo, Acer, and Asus. These machines are powered by either Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X Elite chip or Intel’s Core Ultra 3 (MediaTek also supports the Googlebook platform with its new Dimensity CX C10 Max chip, but none of the new laptops use the chip yet).
Preorders open today, and the machines hit store shelves on October 4, starting at $899. Every purchase includes a full year of Google AI Pro service with 5 terabytes of storage.
Here are the new laptops, all of which are clamshells except the Acer, which is a 2-in-1 machine:
- Acer Googlebook 14 ($899)
- Dell XPS Googlebook ($1,199)
- HP Googlebook 14 ($1,299)
- Lenovo Googlebook 15 ($1,299)
- Asus Googlebook 14 ($1,299)
Some of the standards Google has set include using “premium materials,” like aluminum, magnesium, or carbon fiber, to make them lightweight. They need at least 16 GB of RAM, deliver more than 45 tera operations per second (TOPS), a touchscreen (LCD or OLED), a backlit keyboard, a haptic trackpad, Dolby Atmos speakers, studio-quality microphones with noise cancellation, and at least 14 hours of battery life. Googlebooks will receive 10 years of software updates.
They must feature the Glowbar—the signature LED strip on the laptop’s exterior that identifies the machine as a Googlebook. It’s a callback to the glowbar Google used on its original Chromebook Pixel. (Speaking of which, Google hasn’t shared whether it’s making its own Googlebook under its Made by Google Pixel hardware division.) Developers can access the Glowbar to customize the lights to specific actions in their apps, and there’s also an Easter egg app consumers can unlock to customize the light color and animation themselves. Like HiLight introduced on the latest Pixel phones, the Glowbar will illuminate when you talk to Gemini.
“There’s a lot the laptop gets right, but much of it was designed decades ago, before mobile devices were invented,” Sameer Samat, president of the Android ecosystem, said at the event. “Reinventing laptops is a multi-year endeavor. Our first step is to focus on the Android community because today there isn’t a laptop that is designed to seamlessly work with your Android phone.”
Googlebook merges Android’s mobile-first operating system with ChromeOS, the OS powering Chromebooks. Google says Chromebooks aren’t going anywhere and will continue to serve schools and act as the budget-friendly option for consumers. While the Googlebook interface feels like a blown-up version of Android, it’s not just an Android-powered desktop. Rather, it’s a distinct OS optimized for x86 and ARM chip architectures.
What’s particularly interesting is how Android apps work on the device. They’re categorized in three ways. When you set up your Googlebook with your Android phone, important data flows seamlessly to the laptop, including Wi-Fi networks, passwords, settings, messages, contacts, and photos. Not all of your phone apps will automatically be installed, though, as Google deems some apps as “better on the web," like Facebook. (You can still install the Facebook app if you want and get the mobile-shaped experience.)
The next tier of Android app is “Optimized for Desktop.” These apps take advantage of the bigger screens with better layouts and a little more functionality. The final tier is “Made for Desktop,” like the desktop versions of Chrome. Google says around 20 or so apps are either optimized for desktop or made for the desktop so far, including CapCut, Adobe Photoshop, Notability, and Fantastical. As the platform grows, Google expects more developers will target Android’s “Made for Desktop” tier and bring their desktop-grade apps from Windows and macOS to Googlebook.
People want to play games on their laptops, and so Google says you’ll be able to access more than 20,000 titles on the Play Store, many of which support cross-device play between mobile, tablets, and laptops. Google says around 50 of the 100 top titles are optimized for keyboard, trackpad, and touchscreen. But since you can’t download AAA games for Googlebooks (yet), especially without a discrete GPU, Google is offering 1 year of Nvidia’s GeForce Now game streaming service, which is optimized for the platform.
New Frontiers
Googlebook is an opportunity for Google to bring artificial intelligence to the forefront of the laptop computing experience, which is why many of the core new features are AI-powered. For example, similar to Android 17, you can generate your own desktop widgets with simple prompts to Gemini.
Magic Pointer is the marquee Gemini feature. Wiggle the mouse pointer over anything, and a Gemini overlay will suggest contextual actions. For example, if you wiggle over an event someone invited you to, you’ll get a prompt to automatically “Create an event” and have it added to your Google Calendar with one tap. Or if you’re wondering what breed of dog you’re looking at (whether it’s a video or photo), wiggle and ask Gemini, “What’s the breed?” If you’re wondering whether an email is a phishing attempt, wiggle over it and ask Gemini.
AI companies are also heavily focused on voice-to-text as the future of computing, which is why Google is injecting its Rambler feature natively into Googlebook. It debuted on the latest Google Pixel 11 smartphones and is a potent AI-powered voice dictation engine that transcribes whatever you say. It intelligently cuts your “ums” and “uhs,” and even knows when you make a mistake and restate something, keeping the parts it believes you want to convey. You can ask it to format sentences in a particular tone, include bullets or emoji, and even mix in different languages. You can call up Rambler with Google’s Quick Insert key, a key found on Googlebook keyboards and newer Chromebook keyboards. Rambler works in any text field.
The rest of the platform leans heavily into Android smartphone continuity. In the Files app, context-aware search lets you find photos by simply typing “dog” instead of the file name—and it searches files on your phone just as easily as local storage. Meanwhile, “Continue on” hands off ongoing tasks so apps open on your laptop right where you left off on mobile, and an app-casting feature lets you stream phone-only apps like DoorDash directly to the desktop.
What if you have an iPhone? Google offers a new “Link to iOS” app that lets users access messages and some notifications on the desktop, but cross-platform limitations mean you can’t enjoy the same breadth of features. Then again, iPhone owners will probably stick to Macs. At least Android now has something comparable.
