On August 17, the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) announced its revamped social media team, appointing Deepak Mhaskey as the national social media convenor, and Priti Gandhi, Shivanand Dwivedi, Alok Bhatt and Arun Yadav as co-convenors.
While curiosity grew as to who these newly appointed individuals were and their past work and association with the party, social media users were quick to notice that immediately after the announcement, Gandhi, Dwivedi and Yadav made their X accounts private and there was no trace of Bhatt on the internet.
While all the other IT cell members are back to being active on X, albeit after deleting hundreds of thousands of old posts, Alok Bhatt is the only one in the group whose X handle remains inaccessible or ‘protected’ even a month after the new team was announced.
The only remnants of Bhatt’s online presence are the now-disabled X account, screenshots from his X posts and some articles in Right-wing outlets like OpIndia, Organiser and Swarajya.
Alt News found that in the past, Bhatt had been called out for controversial tweets several times. In archived screenshots of his posts from the past, the BJP functionary can be seen using sexist, Islamophobic, and derogatory language, some of which can be seen below:
Who is Alok Bhatt?
Bhatt, who claims to hail from Dehradun, has worn many hats over the course of his career. According to his LinkedIn profile, he graduated from Hemvati Nandan Bahuguna Garhwal University (HNBGU) in Uttarakhand and went on to work with several organisations, including NIIT University, where he served as financial controller until April 2010.
In 2010, he founded Nature Connect Outdoors — an education and adventure non-profit organisation that deals in outdoor education and skill development, including treks, camping, and rafting expeditions. According to the website’s bio, Bhatt had “shunned his corporate career” to follow his passion, which culminated in the formation of the NGO. The organisation is still functional.
According to details available on Zauba Corp, Bhatt is a Chartered Accountant (CA) and the partner of a firm of CAs called RSAC & CO LLP, incorporated in May 2021.
Bhatt has also served as the economic adviser to former Uttarakhand chief minister Trivendra Singh Rawat. However, it’s not clear when he was appointed and when exactly his tenure ended. He wrote an article for Firstpost defending the ministry of housing and urban affairs over the controversial Central Vista project. The author bio designated him as ‘Economic Advisor’ to Rawat.
In 2020, after a district officer’s press release promoting inter-caste and interfaith marriages drew criticism from social media users, Bhatt had reportedly tweeted: “No one from the government has spoken in support of promoting interfaith marriages. No one in the BJP government in their wildest dreams will support anything that is made out here.”
We sent an email and called up Bhatt several times to know more from him, but he did not respond.
Long-standing Association With BJP
Bhatt’s X handle, @alok_bhatt, was followed by Prime Minister Narendra Modi. In fact, Modi quote-tweeted one of Bhatt’s posts in 2024, where he urged people to watch the film Sabarmati Report.
Bhatt was also invited to PM Modi’s swearing-in ceremony in the past. In 2024, Right-wing influencer Vikas Pandey shared an image with Bhatt alongside former BJP spokesperson Nupur Sharma, member of the economic advisory council to the PM, Sanjeev Sanyal, and others, with the caption “First swearing in”.

In April 2022, Right-wing influencer Shefali Vaidya, who has been fact-checked by Alt News several times in the past, posted an image with Bhatt on X saying that she had met the latter and “his lovely family” in Uttarakhand.

X Handle Suspended for Violating Guidelines
Alt News found at least three instances, in 2018, 2019, and 2020, where X (then Twitter) had initiated action against Bhatt’s handle for violation of community guidelines, and at least two of those three actions were owing to hateful content.
In 2018, Bhatt declared that all the “killers of Pandits, Rapists of Pandits, Terrorists killing in Kashmir, instigators of Godhra, and bombers of Mumbai were all Muslims, and thus Islam was the problem”. His account had then been ‘limited’.
Why is @alok_bhatt blocked by twitter for a week when blue-ticked racist bigots like Audrey Truschke are still on Twitter despite their naked Hinduphobia? @TwitterIndia pic.twitter.com/3qlnNiVWhj
— Shefali Vaidya. 🇮🇳 (@ShefVaidya) April 20, 2018
In 2019, Bhatt declared in a post that “their boys could take on Jihadis” but needed police action for “rumour mongers” like activist Shehla Rashid. “These jihadi accomplices are running a hate campaign aided and abetted by Media…please help our state dispel rumours,” the tweet read. His account was suspended after this. Political analyst and Right-wing influencer Suresh Nakhua took to Twitter to condemn the move.

The Pamphlet-Savitr Analytics-Alok Bhatt Connection
In 2022, Bhatt took on a directorial role at Savitr Analytics Media and Research Foundation, a company that was incorporated in April 26 that year, with Bhatt and Ashish Nautiyal initially named as directors. According to documents filed with the Union ministry of corporate affairs (MCA), Bhatt holds 9,500 shares, or 95 per cent of the company, while Nautiyal holds the remaining 500 shares, or 5 per cent.
Interestingly, Nautiyal is also the founding editor of the Right-wing media outlet, The Pamphlet.
Savitr Analytics has no website or online presence. We went through its financial records filed with the MCA for the financial years 2022-23, 2023-24 and 2024-25, and found that it was registered as a Section 8 company, i.e., a non-profit. In the 2024-25 financial year, its total revenue from operations was Rs 2.7 crore.
The organisation’s revenue across all three years comes from ‘sale of services’, and the rows for ‘Grants or donations received (relevant for Sec 8 companies)’, present in the 2022-23 and 2023-24 filings, are left blank in 2022-23 and 2023-24. In 2024-25, the row does not exist.
Under ‘Corporate Information’, they state ‘Research and awareness about Indian culture and heritage…’, ‘Promotion of commerce, art, science, sports, education, research, social welfare, religion, charity, and environmental protection…’ and ‘Advancement of education, learning, and skills development…’ as their activities.
There was a category called ‘professional expenses’ in the 2022-23 filing that was later relabeled as ‘content production expenses’. Rs. 41,48,600 was spent in the first year, Rs. 95,36,600 (filed directly as content production expenses) was spent in the second year, and Rs. 1,38,53,200 (also filed directly as content production expenses) was spent in the third year.
Next, we found that an individual named Ridhika Aggarwal stated on LinkedIn that she worked as a content writer for Savitr Analytics Media and Research Foundation until August 2023. We went through her X timeline (linked to her LinkedIn profile) and found that she wrote at least three articles for The Pamphlet during her tenure at Savitr. None of the articles are currently available on the website.
Ridhika is also listed as a non-official member of a steering committee formed by the Union ministry of environment, forest and climate change in 2023.
The Pamphlet, previously known as The Indian Affairs, posted for the first time on Facebook in April 2022, which is the same time when Savitr Analytics was incorporated.
ठीक 2 साल पहले देहरादून में आज ही के दिन @Pamphlet_in ऑफिस निर्माण की शुरुआत हो गई थी, उत्तराखण्ड चुनाव निपटने के बाद मैं २० दिन के अपने नैनीताल और लैंसडाउन प्रवास के बाद दून घाटी में उतरा था।
आज ही के दिन साल 2019 में लोकसभा चुनाव का रिजल्ट भी आया था और प्रधानमंत्री… pic.twitter.com/6lAVSW3twN
— V Ashish Nautiyal (@ashu_nauty) May 15, 2024
The Pamphlet claims to “cut through the noise of the modern information ecosystem by offering readers and viewers clarity, depth and perspective on issues that shape India and the world.” Its reports have seem to be echoing pro-BJP narratives. An August 11 video report, for instance, was captioned: “Questions raised in the public domain regarding the credentials of two CJP leaders, Abhijeet Dipke and Saurav Das, have brought up several serious concerns”. It questioned Dipke’s Boston University degree, academic timeline and funding, as well as Das’ property, tenancy, rent, police verification, and electoral records.
During the CJP protests, another report took a swipe at Mohammed Junaid, who had been feeding protesters, with the reporter noting that “such bhaijaans were also seen” at the protest sites in Shaheen Bagh and Farmers’ stir. Thumbnails of these reports carried AI-generated visuals of individuals critical of the Union government, their faces distorted through AI to portray them in a negative light. This is a tactic common across Right-wing outlets and social media troll handles.
More recently, the outlet, alongside Abhijit Iyer-Mitra, Law Beat, The Jaipur Dialogues and The Sunday Guardian, was summoned by the Delhi high court over a Rs 2 crore privacy suit by Cockroach Janta Party spokesperson Saurav Das, who alleged that they had disclosed his home address and other personal details online. The case will be heard on September 14.
The video below depicts a time when the outlet was still called The Indian Affairs, and Nautiyal (in striped shirt) can be seen with his colleagues alongside educator Pawan Gupta.
The Indian Affairs @ForIndiaMatters Coming Soon
Subscribe our Youtube Channel: https://t.co/orjioxscXy #TIA #TheIndianAffairs pic.twitter.com/v1VVtf83XZ
— The Pamphlet (@Pamphlet_in) July 22, 2022
Nautiyal’s last video with The Pamphlet was uploaded in December 2024. In June 2025, Nautiyal was pictured with the OpIndia team. His first video for OpIndia, an interview with Uttarakhand chief minister Pushkar Dhami, came a month later, in July 2025.
Nautiyal is now the multimedia & digital head and editor at OpIndia, and is no longer listed as a director of Savitr on the MCA website.
It is worth noting that The Pamphlet’s website does not disclose any parent company, ownership, editorial team, funding details or board of directors. Its ‘About Us’ page offers only a description of what it does, while calling itself ‘an independent digital media platform’. The only publicly mentioned funding source we could find was YouTube memberships of The Pamphlet costing Rs. 119 to Rs. 3199 per month.
Nautiyal is not the only link between Savitr Analytics and The Pamphlet. An individual named Shiv Kumar Mishra was appointed the director of Savitr Analytics in April 2023. In March 2023, Mishra was announced as the CEO of The Pamphlet.
Please welcome @shivkmishr, Founder & CEO, The Pamphlet https://t.co/U53aK62Fzo
— The Pamphlet (@Pamphlet_in) March 14, 2023
In other words, two of the three directors of Savitr Analytics Media and Research Foundation have held senior positions at The Pamphlet. And in both cases, the appointments to Savitr and The Pamphlet came in close succession. This raises the question of whether the two entities are formally linked.
We also found that The Pamphlet had an office space from its inception in Dehradun, and it is evident from a photo posted by Nautiyal that it began with a team of at least 20 people. Bhatt, the reader would remember, also claims to be from Dehradun.
While all of this points to a connection between Bhatt and The Pamphlet, there appears to be a concerted effort to keep that relationship under wraps. Hence, we tried to dig more.
Is Bhatt Linked to The Pamphlet? We Asked The Pamphlet
We sent an email to The Pamphlet on September 3 asking them about the relationship between Savitr Analytics and The Pamphlet, and whether Alok Bhatt was connected to The Pamphlet, given that he holds a 95% stake in Savitr Analytics, a company whose other directors have held senior positions at The Pamphlet. We also asked them about their funding sources, since nothing is mentioned on the website.
In reply, they asked us to send our queries to another email ID of The Pamphlet and also to Alok Bhatt, Nirwa Mehta, Ashish Nautiyal and Shiv Mishra. Interestingly, they provided us with the email IDs and phone numbers of each of these individuals. This, in itself, might be considered an indicator of some sort of link between The Pamphlet and Bhatt. It is unlikely for an organisation to provide the direct contact details of someone with whom it has no professional association.
We then sent our queries to all of them.
Nautiyal responded to us saying that his reporting manager, OpIndia editor Nupur J Sharma, “suggested” him “not to give (you) any quotes or information as a matter of policy of not engaging with entities that don’t act in good faith”. A day later, he took to X to let the world know that a woman from Alt News “with a Hindu-sounding name” had approached him with some questions.
Pamphlet editor Nirwa Mehta sent us a 1,071-word response, but did not answer any of our questions. Instead, she sent a detailed set of reciprocal questions concerning Alt News’ funding transparency, the outside associations of its founders and editor, and grants received by individuals associated with Alt News, both currently and in the past. She offered to answer Alt News’ questions in writing once Alt News answered hers first.
It is worth noting that The Pamphlet published a video on Alt News on August 16, 2026, without seeking a response from the organisation.
This correspondent responded to Mehta, stating that questions concerning Alt News’ funding should be directed to its editor, while questions concerning any of the founders’ personal assignments should be directed to the person concerned. We also reminded her that a so-called expose on Alt News’ founders had been published by The Pamphlet without either of the concerned persons being approached for a response — a violation of basic journalistic ethics.
In her final response, Mehta did not address the question of ethics. Instead, in a demand that many may find bizarre, she asked this correspondent, “as a responsible employee”, to take her questions to the Alt News directors.
At this point, we felt there was no point continuing the conversation.
We will update our article if The Pamphlet answers Alt News’ questions on whether Savitr Analytics and The Pamphlet are connected in any way, and whether Alok Bhatt, BJP’s new IT cell member who continues to remain away from X, holds a position at The Pamphlet.
Social Media Posts Answer the Question
The connection between The Pamphlet and Alok Bhatt is one of internet’s worst kept secrets, it seems. We found several instances on social media where well-known faces from the Right-wing ecosystem tagged Alok Bhatt alongside members of The Pamphlet team — whether to thank them for invitations to Delhi Shabdotsav 2026, where The Pamphlet Panchayat featured on the itinerary, or in connection with other events involving the organisation.
On January 5, 2026, Right-wing influencer Abhijit Iyer-Mitra, who was recently criticised for comparing Newslaundry journalists to prostitutes, thanked The Pamphlet team — including its editor Nirwa Mehta, anchor Shreya Arora, and Bhatt — for inviting him to speak at The Pamphlet Panchayat.
Responding to Iyer-Mitra, Nirwa Mehta and another The Pamphlet employee, Pratibha, thanked him for being a part of the session. The exchange is significant because it can be seen as an acknowledgement by the Pamphlet editor and another employee of Bhatt being a part of the organisation.
Delhi Shabdotsav 2026 was a three-day cultural and literary festival held from January 2 to January 4, 2026, organised by Suruchi Prakashan with the support of the department of art, culture and languages of the Delhi government. The Pamphlet was the digital partner at the event and hosted ‘The Pamphlet Panchayat’ at the fest. The Pamphlet team held and moderated several discussions over the three days, including those with Sanjeev Newar, Vijay Patel, and Subhi Vishwakarma. The subjects of the discussions ranged from ‘Love Jihad: factsheet’ to ‘Bharat’s Hostile Neighbourhood & Need to Regain Shatrubodh’.
We went through the images posted on Shabdotsav’s website and found that Bhatt was present at the event.
The link between Alok Bhatt and The Pamphlet becomes more apparent in another conversation on X in which Iyer-Mitra directly addressed Mehta as Pamphlet and Alok Bhatt’s ‘staff’. Iyer jokingly rebuked Mehta for liking a certain kind of car. Tagging Bhatt, he wrote, “Do @Pamphlet_in and @alok_bhatt @shreya_arora22 approve of these disgusting and extremely hateful statements by their staff?” Mehta responded to Iyer-Mitra’s post, but did not object to the ‘staff’ reference.
On June 1, 2023, a little more than a year after The Pamphlet’s inception, one @saket71 posted a picture with Ashish Nautiyal, who was working at The Pamphlet then, and called him a ‘Media Mughal’. He later tagged Alok Bhatt and Shiv Mishra, praising them for “putting a great team together.”
Such a pleasure to meet the young stars of @Pamphlet_in , @RitikaChandola @himanshi__bisht and the whole team. Such a great young team, full of hope and dreams, and a visible sense of great camaraderie. Kudos to @alok_bhatt and @shivkmishr for putting a great team together. https://t.co/NnmHkA9rQO
— saket साकेत ಸಾಕೇತ್ 🇮🇳 (@saket71) June 1, 2023
Several people have congratulated Alok Bhatt at various points of time upon The Pamphlet reaching certain milestones.
To sum up, what raises serious questions about the BJP’s decision to name Bhatt as its social media co-convenor is not just his past social media conduct, but also the opacity surrounding his professional associations. One organisation he appears to be associated with, The Pamphlet, does not publicly disclose its ownership, editorial team, board or funding sources. Without any apparent source of funding, it starts off as a 20-member organization. Who pays their salary? How are establishment costs met? There are no answers. Again, another corporate entity closely linked to him, Savitr Analytics, has no website or public online presence despite reporting Rs 2.7 crore in operational revenue in 2025.
Things get murkier when one takes into account the desperate efforts by Bhatt’s associates to conceal his association with The Pamphlet, evident in the organisation’s refusal to answer direct questions regarding this.
In other words, a man linked to organisations with questionable records, and whose involvement with a pro-government outlet is abundantly visible in public, but markedly absent from the outlet’s own disclosures, has now been given a formal position in the BJP’s social media cell.

Tropical Storm Dujuan is skirting the coast of Japan and despite avoiding a direct landfall, is still expected to leave its mark. Dujuan briefly reached typhoon status on Friday before weakening to a tropical storm again on Sunday morning. But it is expected to restrengthen back to a typhoon by Tuesday morning. Sustained winds could reach 80mph (129km/h), with gusts approaching 100mph.
Although mainland Japan has avoided a direct hit, Dujuan’s track takes it across the Izu Islands, where evacuation warnings are in place. Heavy rain, flooding and landslide alerts are widespread, with high waves adding another threat to exposed coastal areas and islands.
Some exceptional rainfall totals are expected, with about 200mm (7.9in) possible along the southern coasts of the Chubu and Kanto regions in just 24 hours – roughly equivalent to the average rainfall for the entire month of September. The Tokyo metropolitan area is among the areas facing the heaviest rain, with some models suggesting nearly 90mm could fall within six hours on Monday evening. Further south, the Izu peninsula could receive more than 80mm in just three hours – 38% of the month’s usual rainfall in a single evening. Dujuan is expected to continue north-eastwards before dissipating in the north-west Pacific later this week.
The Atlantic hurricane season remains unusually quiet, despite Tropical Storm Fay developing south-west of the Azores over the weekend. Fay is not expected to strengthen further, extending the record for the latest first hurricane to form in a hurricane season during the satellite era. The previous date record was 11 September, set in 2002 with Hurricane Gustav and equalled in 2013 with Hurricane Humberto.
South-west Europe may get one last taste of summer with a blast of heat this week. Temperatures across Spain and Portugal will rise significantly above the monthly norm, to the low to mid 30s celsius. Even in north-west Spain, in Santiago de Compostela highs could reach about 35C (95F) on Tuesday, about 12C above the typical daytime high. Heading into the weekend, warmth will spread into central Europe, but most likely with less intensity than earlier in the week across the Iberian peninsula.

Brazilian serial killer lived in the woods and was nicknamed "mosquito"
A man who Brazilian authorities say killed 16 people lived in the woods to avoid capture and was nicknamed “mosquito” by locals because of his frail build, the Brazilian police investigator responsible for his arrest said Monday
SAO PAULO -- A man who Brazilian authorities say killed 16 people lived in the woods to avoid capture and was nicknamed “mosquito” by locals because of his frail build, the Brazilian police investigator responsible for his arrest said Monday.
Douglas Garcia, the investigator who led the two-day pursuit for 33-year-old Jorlan Lopes da Silva that ended on Sep. 13, told The Associated Press that the suspect used to hide in the thick bush in his own makeshift camps. The killings linked to da Silva occurred within the last three months in the isolated region of Mulungu in Brazil’s northeastern state of Paraiba.
“That allowed him to evade capture for years,” Garcia said. “Jorlan lived mostly in the woods, that’s why it was so hard to find him and link him to crimes that didn’t seem to be connected at first.”
Garcia said police finally saw the link between da Silva and other crimes after he shot an 18-year-old dead in a public square. The investigator said the serial killer claims he has only attacked criminals, but evidence collected thus far shows that was not the case.
Garcia also said da Silva is providing evidence he committed more crimes than those he is being prosecuted for but added he cannot discuss further details as some investigations continue and others are being reopened.
The investigator said the identity of the victims and details about their deaths are being kept confidential so the prosecution can do its work.
Da Silva was captured wearing a black dress with white stripes, a wig and painted nails. He was carrying a baby that authorities confirmed was not related to him, but they did not provide any other details.
“This is a very different person, he said he killed for the first time at age 13,” Garcia said. “We caught him because he wasn’t able to reach his tent in the woods, so he, out of desperation, got that disguise, took that baby that is not his and was ultimately arrested,” Garcia said.
Police said at the time that da Silva was a member of a criminal gang that has killed dozens of people in the region. He denies any affiliation with local gangs and told investigators upon his arrest that he was “in a personal war.”
The region of Mulungu, where the recent killings took place, lies 2,500 kilometers (1,553 miles) north of Rio de Janeiro.

Snapdeal parent AceVector has set a price band of ₹30-₹32 per equity share for its IPO, valuing the company at up to ₹1,741.4 Cr ($181.7 Mn) at the upper end.
The IPO comprises a fresh issue of shares worth ₹287 Cr and an offer for sale of up to 4.16 Cr shares. At ₹32 per share, the size of the IPO is ₹420 Cr.
The IPO will open for public subscription on Friday (September 25), following anchor bidding on Thursday (September 24). It will close on September 29. AceVector’s shares are expected to list on the BSE and NSE on October 5.
AceVector reduced the fresh issue by ₹13 Cr from the ₹300 Cr proposed in its UDRHP after raising the same amount through a pre-IPO placement. It also cut the OFS component by 34.9% from the earlier proposed 6.39 Cr shares.
SoftBank’s Starfish I Pte Ltd, AceVector’s largest shareholder and part of its promoter group, will sell up to 2.76 Cr shares through the OFS. At the upper end of the price band, the stake sale will fetch Starfish up to ₹88.3 Cr.

Messi in Argentina squad for farewell friendly
- Published
Argentina have named Lionel Messi in their squad for a friendly against Benin in October in a match which is set to be the forward's farewell to international football.
Messi announced his retirement from Argentina duty in August in the wake of his country's defeat by Spain in the 2026 World Cup final and after saying he was considering his future in football following the death of his father, Jorge.
The 39-year-old, who captained Argentina when they won the 2022 World Cup, said the decision to stop playing for La Albiceleste hurt him "deeply" but that he had "given it my all" and had "nothing left to give".
Messi, an eight-time Ballon d'Or winner who currently plays for Inter Miami, is Argentina's all-time leading scorer and most-capped player, having scored 125 goals in 207 appearances.
"We made the decision to invite the best player in the world, the symbol of our national team, our captain, Lionel Andres Messi, so that he can have the farewell he truly deserves on 6 October here in Argentina," said Argentine FA president Claudio Tapia.
River Plate's Estadio Monumental in Buenos Aires, which has an 85,000 capacity, will host the game against Benin.
Argentina's 2022 World Cup winners have also been invited to the match, which Tapia said would be an "unforgettable" occasion.

As Indian startups graduate from venture-backed bets to public-market businesses, the finance function is undergoing a sea shift. As startups scale, raise capital and navigate complex regulations, CFOs are seen balancing technology, strategy, compliance and growth. Finance leaders are increasingly expected to build systems and processes that allow companies to grow without losing control. Technology is becoming central to this transition. Whether it's automation, real-time reporting, ERP systems, or data-led decision-making, finance teams are juggling to optimise for speed, visibility, and precision. This made us question: how are CFOs redesigning financial workflows with automation? Where are they deploying AI? And how are they measuring the returns from new products, expansion and technology investments? Therefore, Inc42, in collaboration with Avalara, is launching The CFO Code, a series that goes inside the minds of finance leaders at some of India’s most ambitious tech startups. In this three-article series, three CFOs from India’s leading tech startups will share their insights and playbooks and explain the nuances of how today’s finance leaders are helping build companies for scale. “Today, the CFOs are transitioning from retrospective general-ledger bookkeepers to real-time growth co-pilots and transaction technologists driving global expansion. I hope The CFO Code series uncovers how finance leaders are becoming the co-author of business models, international pricing strategies, and go-to-market architectures right from day one,” said Dulles Krishnan, VP, go-to-market and general manager, India, Avalara. As Indian businesses expand globally, finance leaders are increasingly shaping international pricing, go-to-market strategies and cross-border operations, while navigating complex, rapidly changing regulations. The next evolution is about operating at transaction speed, using technology and AI to embed compliance and financial controls directly into business workflows, without adding complexity to the core systems. The CFO Code series will look at the systems these leaders are putting in place, the decisions they are making and the frameworks they are using to navigate growth, compliance and capital discipline. Each story will introduce the CFO and the company they are building for, while examining how their role differs from that of a traditional finance head. More importantly, the stories will lay the groundwork for modern finance. Inside The CFO Playbook The CFO Code will explore the changing role of finance leaders across four key areas. Growing Role Of Finance In Business Leadership: How CFOs are moving beyond finance to shape capital allocation, profitability, compliance and strategic decision-making. How The CFO Role Is Evolving On The Ground: How CFOs are working across product, technology, fundraising and operations as startups scale. Finance Stack, Processes And Decision Frameworks: How ERP, automation and AI are reshaping financial processes, cost management, unit economics and risk. The New CFO Playbook: How AI, evolving investor expectations and automation are turning CFOs into increasingly strategic co-pilots to the CEO. The series will also explore the challenges that come with this expanded mandate. Scaling operations without losing control, moving quickly while remaining audit-ready and navigating regulatory uncertainty are becoming part of the CFO’s everyday operating reality. Breaking Down Three CFO Playbooks In the upcoming weeks, the CFO Code will break down three finance playbooks of India’s leading tech startups that are navigating growth, complexity and the changing demands of the modern CFO. Decoding MoEngage’s Global CFO Playbook Narasimha Reddy, CFO & Head of Strategy at MoEngage, will unpack the toughest stretch of the company’s decade-long fundraising journey, his approach to keeping global compliance simple, and his take on AI. He will also share what he believes will set the next generation of CFOs apart. Building LeadSquared’s Finance Engine Chandra Sahal, CFO at LeadSquared, will take us inside the company’s finance overhaul, from bringing month-end visibility down from weeks to days to reshuffling the budget after an unexpected AI tool shift. Sahal will also discuss managing currency and geopolitical risks across the US and Middle East, the cost of delaying finance infrastructure, and how AI is reshaping the CFO role. How The CFO Role Is Changing At Perfios Prashant Mahagaonkar, Group CFO at Perfios, will draw on 25 years in finance to unpack M&A integration, founder-CFO dynamics, AI versus automation, cost discipline and ERP trade-offs. He will also explore how the CFO role has evolved from financial oversight into a strategic decision-making function. When India’s CFOs Talk Finance The CFO Code brings together leading finance minds to decode how the role is changing, from fundraising and financial infrastructure to AI, compliance, risk and strategic decision-making. Through conversations with experienced CFOs, the series will uncover the lessons, frameworks and decisions shaping the future of finance in India. Talking about the critical role of compliance in this journey, Krishnan said, “We want founders and finance leaders to see cross-border compliance not as a post-facto bureaucratic roadblock; it is an active driver of margin protection, engineering velocity, and enterprise valuation.” According to Krishnan, strong financial and compliance systems give founders greater visibility, help investors assess the quality of growth and can become a real advantage when the company is raising capital or preparing for an acquisition. So, if you’re a founder, finance leader or business builder looking to understand the evolving role of finance and compliance, follow Inc42’s CFO Code and learn from those shaping the future of finance in India.

This past summer, Samsung launched the Galaxy Watch9 alongside the Galaxy Watch Ultra2, its more rugged, shock-resistant smartwatch for outdoor adventures.
The Watch9 is the everyday option, and it’s a solid smartwatch and fitness tracker with a plethora of health features. It’s available in a 40-mm size in cream and graphite, and a 44-mm size in graphite and silver, starting at $80. Compared with last year’s Galaxy Watch8, it’s a modest update, though. There’s a faster processor, a slightly larger battery capacity, and an expanded suite of wellness metrics.
After two weeks of testing the 40-mm model, I wouldn’t necessarily upgrade to the Watch9 from the Watch8. But if you have an older Galaxy Watch or you’re invested in Samsung’s ecosystem and are looking for a smartwatch, the Watch9 is the best choice.
A Familiar (Squircle) Face
The Galaxy Watch’s main hardware update is its new processor. It now utilizes Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Wear Elite platform, which Samsung claims enhances CPU and GPU performance along with efficiency. In testing, the watch responded smoothly when scrolling menus, launching apps, and dismissing notifications.
Wear OS 7 also adds more customizable widgets and live updates from compatible apps. One of the more exciting new additions is raise-to-talk for Gemini. Lift your wrist toward your mouth, and you can start talking to Google’s AI assistant. The Google Pixel Watch has had this feature for two generations now, so I’m happy to see Samsung finally catch up.
Samsung has also slightly increased the battery capacity. The 40-mm model has a 390-mAh battery (up from 325 mAh), while the 44-mm models get a 445-mAh cell (up from 435 mAh). Unfortunately, that doesn’t translate to an improvement in battery life, which is probably because it’s being used to power the watch’s expanded suite of health features (more on that later). Samsung still estimates up to 30 hours of battery life, but I averaged closer to 25 hours with Always-On Display enabled. That’s enough to get through a full day and night, but not enough to make charging something you can forget about. A full recharge also took me about 100 minutes on average, which is significantly longer than the 45 minutes it takes the Pixel Watch 5 to reach a full charge.

In Summary
- New Apple CEO, John Ternus, announced a range of products at the Surprise and Shine event.
- While most of the focus was on the iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable phone, there was much more to the event than just devices and a CEO debut.
- We bring you eight takeaways that were buried in the buzz around the new devices, which might have escaped your attention.
It might not have surprised too many people – the leaks messed that up – but Apple did a fair bit of shining at its recent Surprise and Shine event. The event, which also marked John Ternus’ debut as Apple CEO at a launch, went on expected lines, with Apple revealing new AirPods, Apple Watches, new iPhone Pros and, of course, the iPhone Duo, which has grabbed the most attention. There was, however, much more to the event than just the launches. Here are our eight biggest takeaways from the day on which the world saw Apple’s new foldable and the CEO on stage:
Table of Contents
New Era? Presentation-wise, Apple is still Cook-ing (Pun intended)
Yes, it was John Ternus who held the reins at Surprise and Shine. But in terms of presentation style, the template that was followed was still from the menu of the preceding chef, Tim Cook. We had multiple speakers, elaborate backdrops, and a similar race through a number of products, leaving the most time for the star of the show (it was the Air last time around, the Duo this time). Yes, in terms of presentation style, Apple remains well ahead of the competition, although we miss the wit and humor of the past; this launch was more from the Cook manual than the Ternus one.
No surprises (Sigh)…
It’s been a while since Apple surprised the Dickens out of us at a launch, but in recent years, the brand’s product announcements have often been leaked out well in advance. And that was pretty much true this time around. From the iPhone Duo to the shades of Burgundy to the fact that there would be no suffix-less iPhone at the event, the leak community got a lot of things right, which, as we have said in the past, takes some of the mystique and surprise out of the event. Mind you, Apple did pull one rabbit out of its hat.
…except for the AirPods 5
There were no suffix-less iPhones at Surprise and Shine, but there sure were suffix-less AirPods. And while most of the noise was about Apple’s first foldable, the AirPods 5 might have emerged as the silent, value-for-money heroes of the show. While most people had been expecting new AirPods Pro with perhaps a camera built into them, Apple brought in a new version of the classic AirPods, complete with better ANC and battery life, even while retaining the “open” fit and, surprise, surprise, the same price tag as its predecessors. Not too many noticed…until the price of the Duo was announced, and suddenly a device with no price increase became the belle of the tech ball.
Hooray, we will now have TWO iPhone launches every year
Surprise and Shine marked the beginning of a new iPhone era, in which Apple will release its iPhones in two tranches over a twelve-month period. While Apple has released iPhones at two different times of the year in the past, the second launch has generally been a relatively low-profile and soft one (of the SE and ‘e’ mainly). That is set to change now. Even if Apple does a soft launch for the iPhone 18, the iPhone Air 2 and the iPhone 18e, rather than a full-fledged event, the fact is that close to half of the iPhone portfolio will be launched in the second half of the year, and the remainder in the first half of the next year. The iPhone schedules just got tweaked.
Apple is getting REALLY serious about AI (no, really, this time)
Two years ago, Apple launched the iPhone 16 series, saying it had been designed from the ground up for Apple’s avatar of AI, Apple Intelligence. However, AI is one area where the Cupertino brand has been found trailing the competition. So it was not surprising that the brand was clearly out to write a new chapter at Surprise and Shine. Every device it announced – iPhones, Apple Watches, AirPods – had a strong element of AI, which different presenters stressed would work wonderfully well, even while preserving the users’ security. Well, we have heard that a few times in the past, but never in such a comprehensive manner. Is Apple finally going to crack the AI puzzle? Based on what we saw, it would be no Surprise if it went on to Shine in that department in the coming months.
Whoop, Whoop, the Apple Watch is now a full-fledged fitness and health device, and is targeting Whoop
It started out trying to be a computer on your wrist, complete with apps, notifications and alerts, but the Apple Watch has of late graduated (or been demoted, depending on your perspective) to being mainly a health and fitness tracking device. And Surprise and Shine saw this trend continuing, with most of the talk about the Apple Watch 4 Ultra and Apple Watch Series 12 revolving around better sensors and measurement. The highlighting of features like Readiness Scores and Health Age seems to indicate that the Cupertino brand now has the screenless Whoop, which popularised these features, in its sights.
The narrative is unmatched, but is now very hardware-driven!
Processors, camera apertures, health sensors, ANC, battery life…these formed the major part of the narrative around Surprise and Shine, showing how Apple’s has shifted from storytelling to specs at its launches in recent times. This might be fine for some, but we do miss the time when an announcer would walk us through nuances of design and amazing (or they called amazing, and often, unbelievable) features on devices.
Yes, Apple remains the lord, master, and commander of product launches, but we prefer tales to tech, and a live presenter on stage to edited videos, no matter how sleekly edited. The fact that the Duo section stood out from the others because of its stress on design and UI only reinforces our belief that Apple might perhaps reconsider going back to its storytelling roots, and leave the specs on the spec sheet, rather than on the speech notes. Everyone else talks specs anyway.
Cosmic orange is out of the Apple cosmos… and Black is back!
This was so typically Apple. After making orange the color of the last twelve months, courtesy of the Cosmic Orange variant of the iPhone 17 Pro series, and making a number of brands come out with orange phones and other devices (JBL even had a pair of headphones in orange), the Cupertino giant pushed the shade out of its color palette. It also brought back the one color that everyone had missed in the Pro series – Black. Henry “Any Color As Long As It Is Black” Ford and AC/DC would approve of the return of the color, and so do we. We are not shedding any tears for orange, although we suspect those orange Pros are going to have great antique value some day.
And one more thing…
Craig Federighi’s hair looks as awesome as ever!

Turning your old PC into a media server is easier than it sounds
Just load up your 100-percent legally sourced media files and go!
If you've got an old laptop or desktop PC lying around and collecting dust, especially if it's fewer than ten years old, you can easily breathe new life into it by turning it into a media server. The process is far easier than you may assume. In the span of an afternoon, you can have your own, private Netflix or Spotify alternative that lets you stream your media files to nearly any device in your home.
Nearly any PC can run media server software like Plex or Jellyfin, and even low-end hardware will only miss out on a slim number of features. Moreover, media servers are approachable to both beginners and advanced users. If you're not very technically inclined, you can put Plex on your Windows laptop and call it a day, whereas tech enthusiasts can tinker with specialized Linux distros and Jellyfin servers, or tweak network architecture to optimize every last inch of a media server setup.
While the specifics of media server setup can be somewhat involved, they're certainly not beyond the capabilities of anyone who can click through setup menus and do some light web searching. If you're still not sure, here are the basic things you'll need to worry about when turning a PC into a media server.
Windows can run a server, but Linux is more lightweight
The first choice you'll need to make when setting your old PC up as a media server is whether to run Windows — which is most likely the operating system it came with — or to convert it over to Linux. The good news is, there's not really a wrong choice, regardless of what people online may insist. Linux is far easier to use than is commonly assumed, but there's nothing wrong with sticking to the familiar territory of Windows. The most popular media server software runs on either OS, with the main difference being that Linux is more lightweight and can help breathe new life into older hardware.
Speaking of older hardware, the primary argument for using Linux is that Windows 10 is past its end-of-service date, meaning any computer which cannot be upgraded to Windows 11 is now a major security risk when connected to the internet. If your computer does not support Windows 11, consider running a Linux distro instead. Some versions of Linux are built to host servers, and will help turn your computer into a personal Netflix or Spotify. If you'd like to play around with different media server solutions, a general-purpose server distro like Fedora Server or Ubuntu Server will let you play around with a broad range of options. There are more versions of Linux than you can shake a TV remote at and even more opinions about which is the best, so the best advice is to explore them with your personal needs in mind.
If you choose to keep Windows 11, it's best to reset it before going any further. Back up any data you don't want to lose onto an external SSD or hard drive, then press Win + I to open Settings and head to System > Recovery > Reset PC, following subsequent prompts until the OS resets. This will take a while, up to several hours on low-powered hardware.
Plex or Jellyfin will get you streaming media in no time
Once you've got your clean and shiny operating system ready to go, it's time to load the computer up with media and start streaming it to your household. Depending on the size of your media collection, you'll need quite a bit of storage. While you can serve media from the PC's boot drive, you risk losing all of your files if anything goes wrong. Many home server enthusiasts prefer to use multiple storage drives and redundant solutions like RAID. This takes a bit of setup and gives you less usable storage space overall, but gives you peace of mind in the event of a drive failure or other emergency.
All that's left to do is choose your media server software, with the two most popular choices being Plex and Jellyfin. Plex is the easiest to set up, and you'll rarely have to touch it again after an initial configuration. However, its advanced features are locked behind a steep subscription. Jellyfin is a free and open-source alternative, meaning you'll never pay to use it and you'll have more control over how everything works. On the other hand, you'll need to be a bit more comfortable tinkering with your server and network. Both options offer clients (the app you'll need to stream media from your server) for most major TV platforms, as well as iOS and Android mobile apps.
Media transcoding is the best example of the differences between the two. When a media file is incompatible with one of your devices, both Plex and Jellyfin can use a GPU to transcode it for universal playback. (Although pretty much any PC can run a media server, you will need a dedicated GPU for the best results with transcoding, as CPU-bound transcoding can be slow or glitchy.) Plex makes this process automatic but keeps transcoding CPU-bound, with no hardware acceleration able to take place on your GPU unless you pay for the Plex Pass subscription. Jellyfin gives you both types of transcoding for free, but you'll need to spend a couple of minutes setting it up. But don't worry, Jellyfin doesn't get particularly complex unless you plan to stream media remotely, in which case you'll need to use other software to create a secure tunnel so that you can point it to the internet without getting blasted by malware.
Emby is another popular Plex alternative worth looking into. It sits somewhere between Plex and Jellyfin in terms of ease of use (Jellyfin is actually based on an older open-source version of the software), but has a similar pricing structure to Plex that puts features like hardware transcoding behind a paywall. There's no "right" choice to make, and all of the options will offer you a taste of what they can do for free.

Flooding around the city of Malda in the Indian state of West Bengal since Thursday has had a devastating effect. So far, three deaths have been recorded and many areas are still flooded, with numerous villages affected, along with the region of Bhutni. Erosion from the flooding, reported from Khaskol, led to a disruption in river flow which led to a more severe impact in Bhutni. More than 100 boats have been sent out for evacuation.
At East Basudevpur, a 20ft (6-metre) embankment collapsed, reducing the channel from 550ft to under 150ft, which could lead to further flooding unless repaired. This flooding resulted after the Ganges River rose about 75cm above its “extreme danger” level owing to heavy rainfall.
A swell caused by Hurricane Marie led to significant beach erosion across Orange county in California on 7 September. The erosion formed a cliff edge on some of the beaches, along with exposing old asphalt, pipes and even pieces of an old pier. The flooding caused by the swell damaged homes and vehicles, as well as flooding streets, leaving behind a layer of sand. The swell has been estimated to be between 8 and 10ft tall. Local people say it is not uncommon to see beach erosion, but this has been one of the most severe cases.
After the hottest summer on record for the US, the above average temperatures are expected to continue this week as a heatwave grips many central states. A persistent area of high pressure and a very warm surface after recent heat will help to drive the daytime temperatures widely into the high 30s celsius or up to 40C across Oklahoma, Kansas and nearby states. Models keep the heat locked in through much of the remainder of the month, increasing the risk of wildfires, with other parts of the country already under red flag warnings.

Shares in Grail, the company developing a blood test aimed at detecting many different types of cancer early, when they can be treated more effectively, surged 33% Monday after the Food and Drug Administration posted documents ahead of an advisory committee meeting that suggest the agency may take a favorable view of the test.
The meeting, scheduled for Wednesday, will bring together key experts to discuss the test, known as Galleri. The FDA is not obliged to follow the advice of these panels, but it often does.
Investors had already been bidding up Grail’s stock in anticipation of the meeting. The test is already available as a laboratory-based diagnostic, but FDA approval would be expected to help lead to reimbursement from Medicare and other insurance payers.

On a cold February morning, Jassuram Khanna, a farmer from Sujau village in Chakrata in Uttarakhand, felt a tightness in his chest on his way to the market. After waiting a few minutes, he called his son Suresh to come and take him to the doctor. They hired a private car and went to the local Primary Health Centre (PHC), where the health worker checked his blood pressure and sent him to Vikasnagar, a nearby Tehsil town.
On reaching Vikasnagar’s Community Health Centre (CHC), 55 km away, they found no doctor there. Finally, at around 3 pm, they found help at the Swami Vivekanand Charitable Hospital in Dharamwala, about 70 km from their hometown. This is where Jassuram finally got an electrocardiogram (ECG) done, which indicated he had suffered a heart attack. The doctors rushed him for an angiography, where they found he had a 100% blockage in one of his heart vessels. They performed an angioplasty where a balloon was sent to the blocked heart blood vessel to widen it, and a mesh tube called a stent was placed there. The time taken from his first symptoms at 10:30 am to his first ECG was 4.5 hours, and it would be another 40 minutes before he the angioplasty procedure was done.
The ideal time that guidelines recommend for a patient with a heart attack to get an ECG and have it interpreted is 10 minutes of contact with a medical team.
Jassuram’s long journey for an ECG is typical of what patients in rural areas face.
While poor access to healthcare in rural India is a well-known fact, does living in a city guarantee timely care? In December 2025, Usha Amin, a retired teacher, felt breathless for two consecutive days on her morning walk; she found her pulse to be 33 on her electronic BP machine (normal pulse being 60-80beats/min). Alarmed, she called her son and rushed to the nearest multispecialty hospital in Thane, which falls in the Mumbai Metropolitan Region.
An ECG showed Usha had developed a third degree heart block, a serious condition where the electrical signals from the upper chambers of the heart are completely blocked from reaching the lower chambers of the heart that can lead to cardiac arrest. However the doctor on duty informed them that the cardiologist was unavailable at the moment. Since Amin looked stable, the family was told that there was no need to worry, and she was advised to schedule an appointment with the cardiologist and return the next day. Amin’s daughter, an occupational therapist, realised the possible gravity of the extremely low pulse rate and asked them to go to another hospital’s emergency department, which correctly diagnosed her. They immediately admitted her and fitted her with a temporary pacemaker and scheduled her for surgery to fit a permanent pacemaker the next day. “I feel extremely lucky that my mother did not face complications due to the delay, and we could refer her to another hospital,” her daughter Kritika Amin said.
Heart disease is the most common cause of death in India, accounting for 28.6 lakh deaths according to the Global Burden of Disease, 2021. It is estimated that nearly 27% of all deaths in India are due to heart disease, while 62% of all deaths due to cardiovascular disease (CVD) in the country are premature between the ages of 40 and 69 years. In 2014, the World Economic Forum and Harvard School of Public Health estimated India’s economic loss due to CVD between 2012 and 2030 to be approximately $2.17 trillion--about half of India’s 2025 GDP of $4.5 trillion. Yet, despite the rapid development of medical facilities in the country, there remains a lacuna when it comes to an appropriate and timely response to emergency heart conditions. Here, we look at the various gaps in the healthcare system that delay treatment for heart disease and the cost that we pay for it.
Most PHCs not equipped
The first step in diagnosing a heart attack is undergoing an ECG test, which records the heart’s electrical activity using sticky patches called electrodes, and gives out a report as a wave graph. This test can help diagnose heart attacks, irregular heartbeats (arrhythmias) and problems with blood flow. An ECG can detect a heart attack as ST-segment elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI) cases -- or non-STEMI within minutes, and help doctors plan further treatment. However, even access to this ECG is not common in India.
ECGs are currently available in district hospitals and community health centres in India, which are tertiary healthcare centres. Most primary health centres (PHCs), which are the first point of contact for patients in rural areas and are equipped with medical officers, do not have ECG machines. While the 2025 National Essential Diagnostic List recommends that ECG be available at the PHC level, its implementation is expected to take time, time which millions in India do not have.
Meanwhile the availability in higher centres is also not guaranteed. “ECGs are not available in many of the CHCs here and patients have to travel all the way to the district hospital (2-3 hours away) to get an ECG done, ” said a doctor who works at a non-profit in the tribal district of Surguja in north Chhattisgarh. 
Despite being comparatively inexpensive and easy to conduct, the availability of ECGs is restricted to big metros and hospitals in India, and there is a shortage of trained personnel to interpret the results, says Yogendra Singh, director-interventional cardiology at Max Healthcare, Dehradun. “If a patient gets chest pain in Uttarkashi [in Uttarakhand], he has to travel at least 40-50 km to get an ECG done without which he cannot even be given an Ecospirin [a blood thinner]”, he says, emphasising the need to make ECGs available and accessible to people to detect heart attacks early.
Doctors are not necessary to be present to read the ECGs, several studies (here and here) have shown how tele-ECGs, conducted by frontline health workers, can be electronically sent to doctors and nurses for further interpretation and advice, saving crucial time and money, in reaching higher centres.
Heart attack mortality
Indians suffer from heart disease about 10 years before the Western population, while our deaths due to heart attacks is twice that of Sweden, even as their patients are 15 years older, said S. Ramakrishnan, senior cardiologist at the All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), New Delhi.
While the average age at first heart attack in Western Europe, China, and Hong Kong is 63 years, it is 53 years in South Asia, and about 10% of our patients are below the age of 40 years. A number of factors, like high blood pressure, poor cholesterol control, diabetes, sedentary lifestyles, high abdominal fat, poor diet, as well as genetic factors, play a role, along with lifestyle factors such as smoking and prolonged stress. Poverty also plays a role -- poor people are more likely to consume tobacco and alcohol and not consume fruits, vegetables, fish and fibre -- and this increases risk for heart disease.
What’s worse is that most people do not know that they are at risk for heart disease due to inadequate screening and poor awareness. “In India, major heart attacks and death are often the first symptoms of heart disease,” said Dr. Ramakrishnan. Despite having 315 million with high blood pressure and 101 million with diabetes according to the Indian Council of Medical Research’s INDIAB study, there is low awareness of blood pressure and blood glucose, even among those with the disease, and 57% of the population does not meet the WHO guidelines for physical activity.
Further, various studies have shown that patients with heart disease in India have a higher proportion of STEMI cases. STEMI is a more severe type of heart attack caused by the complete blockage of a coronary artery, restricting blood to the major part of the heart and requiring urgent emergency care. The studies also show that STEMI patients in India are likely to be poorer, show symptoms late, get inappropriate treatment and have a higher likelihood of dying within a month of the first month.
While timely treatment of STEMI cases in India will improve the quality of life and also save lives, “the most common treatment an average Indian gets for a heart attack is no treatment,” says Dr. Ramakrishnan. Either patients do not reach the hospital in time, or the hospitals they reach do not have the infrastructure or expertise to treat heart attacks, he added. Late treatment increases the risk of death and complications, increases chances of muscle damage and even if the patient survives, he or she ends up having heart failure, adds.
‘Time is muscle’
When it comes to the heart, cardiologists often like to use the phrase ‘time is muscle.’ Every minute of delay in getting treatment causes irreversible death of the heart muscle. Restoring blood supply to the heart can reduce damage to the heart, improve survival rates and prevent deaths.
In STEMI cases, for example, the key treatment is reperfusion, which involves opening the blocked blood vessel. This can be done either by giving thrombolytic therapy, which is drugs that bust the clots in the artery or through primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) or an angioplasty. While PCI is the gold standard of treatment, a very small percentage of Indian patients get PCI as treatment, and even getting thrombolytic therapy in the treatment window is not widespread. Various registry databases show that only 5 to 10 in 100 patients undergo timely PCI while 36-60 out of 100 undergo thrombolysis.
Another approach of combining the two, is called pharmaco-invasive therapy, where thrombolytic drugs are given to the patient till the patient can be transferred to a hospital with a cath lab. This has been successfully implemented as a hub-and-spoke model in many parts of the country.
In other cases such as in conduction defects, cardiac muscle dies because of the irregular pumping of the heart. Immediately addressing this via drugs or a temporary pacemaker ensures that the damage to the heart muscle is kept to a minimum.
In case of any emergency heart condition, detecting and treating immediately is of paramount importance to ensure that as much of the heart muscle as possible can be saved.
Treatment windows
The most critical time for intervention is between 1-3 hours of the heart attack. The ideal time to conduct an angioplasty is within 120 minutes or two hours of the first medical contact. Treatment most beneficial within three hours of a heart attack.
Jassuram and his son had to waste four and half precious hours travelling from one centre to another before getting the treatment that could save his life.Most Indian patients reach the hospital between 6 hours on average, and up to 12 hours in the hilly States of India, according to various heart registries, after suffering significant damage to their heart muscles. A study in Denmark has shown that a one hour delay in starting treatment after the first contact in the health system leads to a 15% increase in deaths within three-and-a-half years, while it is doubled if the delay is of three hours.
Treatment window in the Indian context
| Metric | Target time | Description |  | 
| Door-to-Needle (Thrombolysis) | ≤30 minutes | From hospital arrival to starting thrombolysis at spoke/non-PCI centres |  | 
| Door-to-Balloon (primary PCI) | ≤90 minutes | Arrival at PCI-capable hub to balloon inflation |  | 
| First Medical Contact (FMC) to Reperfusion | ≤120 minutes | FMC to PCI or thrombolysis; ≤90 min preferred for direct PCI |  | 
| Symptom Onset to Reperfusion | Within 12 hours | Best <6 hours; pharmacoinvasive PCI 3-24 hours post-thrombolysis |  | 
| First Medical Contact-to-Needle (prehospital) | ≤120 minutes | Community-level goal for thrombolysis initiation |  | 
Source: Guidelines by Cardiological Society of India, American Heart Association, TN-STEMI model, National STEMI guidelines
Why the delays
Lack of awareness: A 2023 study, which audited civil-registered premature (30–69 years) deaths due to acute cardiac events or strokes in Faridabad, Haryana, found that only about 11% of the patients reached an appropriate health facility within one hour. About 4 in 10 of them did not reach the correct facility due to a delay in recognising the symptom or its seriousness; 2 in 10 did not reach the correct facility due to a delay in reaching the hospital -- due to lack of transport, absence of an attendant or reaching a centre without appropriate facilities -- and lastly 1 in 10 due to unaffordability or lack of a specialist.
This was similar to what was found by analysing the results of the CREATE registry -- a prospective study of 20,937 acute coronary syndrome (ACS) patients across 89 Indian hospitals between 2001-2005 -- poor awareness of symptoms, logistical challenges in reaching the hospitals and health system gaps were key reasons patients got delayed treatment.
“Sometimes there is ignorance, sometimes there is denial, [patients think] that it will get relieved with local treatment or an antacid,” says H. S. Isser, professor and head of cardiology, at Vardhman Mahavir Medical College and Safdarjung Hospital, Delhi. If the heart attack is very severe, the patient may collapse and is immediately rushed to the nearest hospital, but if the symptoms are mild, like sweating, pain and breathlessness, patients often try home remedies and wait for one or two hours before reaching the hospital, he notes.
Lack of cath labs in public settings, over-crowded tertiary care centres: Even when patients reach hospitals, many hospitals are not equipped with ECG machines or the manpower to interpret them. Even if ECGs are available, patients are often referred to higher centres that have cardiologists and cath labs, where angioplasties are conducted. There are about 2,500 cath labs in the country, most of them in the metros of the developed States of Maharashtra, Kerala, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu and New Delhi.
Thrombolysis use is also limited because non-specialist doctors do not want to risk giving clot-busting drugs, which can have side effects like internal bleeding, without the presence of cardiologists. There are about 6,500 cardiologists in India, less than 0.45 per 100,000 population and most of them are concentrated in urban cities.
Also, despite the increasing number of cath labs, 90% of them are in the private sector, and most States, especially in the North and the East, have to make-do with having only one tertiary centre in the State capital with a cath lab-- leading to overcrowding and long waiting times for patients.
Unaffordability: Even if the treatment is accessible and available, the question that bogs down most families is how expensive it would be. Given the lack of diagnostic facilities in the public sector and long waiting lines, most patients rely on private hospitals for hospitalisation of cardiac conditions, but this has led to high out-of-pocket expenses in patients. Nearly half of heart patients experience catastrophic health expenses -- when the health expense is greater than 40% of the family’s annual income -- due to hospitalisation, while 43% face it due to outpatient expenses.
The Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (AB-PM JAY), India’s flagship health insurance scheme, has improved access to heart procedures that were out of reach for average Indians -- the rate of angioplasties rose by 61% and angiographies by 132% -- after the launch of the scheme in Kashmir, notes a 2025 study. While this is a welcome change, there is an over-reliance on the private sector -- 79% of all cardiac procedures under the scheme are conducted in the private sector. This has led to cases of malpractice on one hand and denial of the scheme on the other -- hospitals in several States have protested nonpayment of dues and refused to provide treatment under PMJAY, leaving millions without coverage.
Many patients we met outside Delhi’s public hospitals claimed to have been told the scheme is not available in the private hospitals in their districts, which forced them to seek care in crowded public hospitals, even if they face delays. One patient, 57-year-old Raiz, suffered a heart attack on December 30 in Bulandshahr’s Shikarpur but came all the way to Delhi government’s Govind Ballabh Pant Hospital 100 km away, because the treatment would be free of cost. Raiz, a labourer, had first done preliminary tests including an ECG and 2D ECHO at Jaypee Hospital, Chitta, but refused further treatment when he was told that an angiography would cost ₹30,000. While the hospital is empanelled under the PMJAY scheme for cardiology according to PMJAY’s website, Raiz says the hospital said they do not accept Ayushman Bharat card patients and Raiz decided to wait. Like most Indian patients who set out on a journey, he tried to attend to all his unfinished business first, which included getting one of his daughters married. A heart attack that should have been attended to within the first two hours, would only be treated a month later.
Sheespal Bhagel, head of medical operations at Jaypee Hospital says, “Our name has changed from Jaypee Hospital to Manush Jaypee Hospital on January 14, 2026 which has caused a change in the status on the [PMJAY] portal. We have sent applications to Lucknow so that the hospital, with its new name, is empanelled again.”
After a heart attack
Once a person has a heart attack, they have to take medicines for life. There is, however, no mechanism to ensure patients have access to affordable drugs in the public system. “Patients do not get their prescribed medicines in PHCs or CHCs but have to travel all the way to the district hospital to get them,” says the Chhattisgarh doctor. Given the cost, intermittent unavailability of medicines and the time involved, most patients have to buy the drugs out-of-pocket from the private sector, he adds.
The situation is not better in Delhi’s tertiary care hospitals, which cater to patients within the State and other neighbouring states. Many of the patients we met at the cardiology OPD of Delhi’s tertiary care hospitals did not know whether they had suffered a heart attack; they had been going from hospital to hospital without a clear diagnosis or a plan. It took them weeks to get their reports ready and get a chance to see the doctor while the waiting time for procedures was in weeks or months.
At AIIMS Delhi, the waiting period for cardio-thoracic and vascular surgery is up to two years due to heavy patient load, according to an answer given in Parliament in July 2025, by Prataprao Jadhav, Union Minister of State in the Health Ministry. Just a few metres away is another government tertiary care hospital, Vardhman Mahavir Medical College and Safdarjung Hospital, with a fully equipped 12 bedded ‘Heart Command Centre’ that is trying to reduce delays in treatment for heart patients. While the patients in general emergency patients may suffer delays in getting identified and referred for angioplasty, they get quickly triaged and receive thrombolysis and angioplasty here. The centre boasts of four cath labs with two being available 24/7.
“This is a rare kind of set-up in the public setup; we do 20 angioplasties daily out of which 5-10 are heart attack patients receiving emergency angioplasties,” said Dr. Isser. The hospital, which gets patients from Delhi and other North Indian states, has a capacity of 110 beds for cardiac patients but sometimes faces a shortage, he says.
What if heart patients did not have to travel long distances to other cities and were treated near their homes? That is a question waiting to be answered.
(Swagata Yadavar is an independent journalist. swagatayadavar@gmail.com)

Meta founder and CEO Mark Zuckerberg has gone to great lengths to hype the security of its new AI assistant Muse, claiming it is “built from the ground up for privacy and security.” A zero-day vulnerability that gives locally run apps and terminal commands complete control of the agent raises serious doubts. Further raising questions, Amazon on Sunday began blocking Muse from its site.
Meta introduced Muse a few weeks ago. The assistant “books appointments, fills out forms and handles customer service,” “proactively takes tasks off your plate,” and can “make purchases, generate images, create documents, and connect with your favorite apps and services.” The macOS app (curiously, there’s no Windows version) also works with a user’s WhatsApp, email, calendar, and social media accounts. When a task requires a tool that doesn’t exist, Muse creates one on the fly.
Meta doth hype Muse security too much
Of course, for Muse to do any of these things, users must first give it access to their accounts. This includes authenticating the assistant to each service and, because the app runs on macOS, giving it permissions to a broad range of operating system-restricted device resources like writing files to disk, accessing the mic and camera, and monitoring location and calendars. Apple has spent years developing these defenses to prevent installed apps or commands entered into the terminal from accessing these resources, clearly because the company considers them a security threat. Muse completely undoes these default measures.
The zero-day allows any app or terminal command to gain access to the token that authenticates users to their Muse account. Meta developers designed the assistant so that any locally installed app or executed code, regardless of the macOS permissions it has, can change a long list of undocumented settings. Most of them are fairly innocuous, such as controlling dark mode. One setting, however, is anything but innocuous. It allows processes to change the endpoint where transcription occurs. Normally, it’s a server address operated by Meta. Attackers can exploit this flaw by changing the location to their own endpoint. Once that happens, the attackers have the token that gives complete control over the Muse account.

Did you know that an Indian woman scientist had a notable role to play in the development of anti-epileptic drugs and anti-malarial drugs? That the same woman also told us most of what we needed to know about the medicinal plants in the subcontinent?
By the standards of her time, unlike other women scientists, Asima Chatterjee did get recognition for her research while she was alive, but it cannot be said that she received the adulation and celebration that her male peers did. That doesn’t make Asima Chatterjee any less tall a figure in the history of Indian science, and the nation must be grateful for her pioneering work in organic chemistry and the sub category of phytomedicine – using plant extracts to treat various conditions, even prevent them.
109 years ago, Asima Chatterjee was born, on September 23. Her love affair with chemistry began at a young age and she went on to pursue this, with a Bacherlor’s degree and a masters in the subject. At a time when few women were able to take up higher education, she went on to complete her Doctor of Science degree in pre-independent India, specialising in phytochemistry. History records her as the first Indian woman to be awarded a Doctor of Science by any Indian university. She went on to gain expertise in research methodology at the University of Wisconsin, Madison and the California Institute of Technology, working with international experts in the field before returning to India.
She took a great interest in a sector that sought to harness the natural plant biodiversty of India and phytochemistry skills to develop newer compounds and drugs that could be used to treat people. Today plant-based extracts form key elements of critical drugs. Plant-derived drugs range from pure compounds extracted from herbs to complex botanical extracts approved as prescription medications. Chatterjee sank herself into the development of clinically useful drugs from indigenous plants – striking success with isolating the chemical constituents of Marsdenia tinctoria – which led to the formulation of the anti-epileptic drug later marketed as Ayush- 56.
Chatterjee also made huge breakthroughs in developing anti-malarial drugs derived from plant extracts. But the greatest achievement that she is credited with is her extensive research on the chemistry of alkaloids found in Caranthus roseus, or the Madagascar periwinkle, which contributed leaps to the understanding of compounds with anti-cancer properties. No less important is the foundation she laid for modern pharmaceutical chemistry, utilising physical and chemical methods to to determine the complex molecular structures of numerous organic compounds, and recording her methodology meticulously.
Beyond her pioneering work in the lab, Chatterjee was also an ace institution builder and educationist. During her academic career, she served as a professor of chemistry at the University of Calcutta at a time of intense gender barriers in academia, and was later appointed as the Khaira Professor of Chemistry, a prestigious chair in the varsity.
Her work in science was recognised with a Padma Bhushan in 1975, Chatterjee creating a record here too, being the first woman scientist to achieve this honour. She was the first female scientist to be elected as the General President of the Indian Science Congress Association and was also a Fellow of the Indian National Science Academy. No wonder then that she was the first female recipient of the Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar Prize in Chemical Sciences (1961), India’s top science award, introduced in 1958. She was also awarded the prestigious CV Raman Award and PC Ray Award.
Today, as the debate rages about bringing scientific vigour and scientifically validating traditional systems of medicine in the country, Chatterjee was a beacon even in this area, her work bridged the gap between traditional Ayurvedic knowledge and modern rigorous chemical analysis, to benefit humanity. Legacy
But Asima Chatterjee’s achievements cannot be confined to just the scientific arena, her immense achievement must also be counted at a time when formidable gender barriers stood in the way of female achievements, breaking the glass ceiling and making it possible, even inspiring, generations of women scientists to make their bold foray into the sciences. Being that rare Indian women scientist who got substantial recognition during their lifetime, in the scientific world, and yet she was largely missing from mainstream narratives, and global histories of science.
But today, we say her name, properly celebrate her legacy. Asima Chatterjee, exceptional chemist, phytochemist and extraordinary pioneering scientist who opened the portals the world of science for generations of women. Say her name, say Asima Chatterjee.
