- After French President Emmanuel Macron said France was providing two-thirds of all intelligence to Ukraine on Jan. 15, 2026, a rumor gained traction that this was because Ukraine had given false intelligence to the U.S., which the United States then leaked to Russia, revealing the U.S. as an unreliable intelligence partner for Ukraine. The rumor continued to circulate in September 2026.
- Snopes could find no evidence confirming the rumor Ukraine had shared false information with the U.S. Instead, this part of the claim came from an apparent misunderstanding of a Jan. 16, 2026, interview on a French news television channel.
- In that interview, Vincent Crouzet — a former intelligence officer at the Directorate General for External Security (DGSE), France's foreign intelligence agency — said, without citing any sources, that Ukrainian intelligence officials suspected the U.S. had leaked information to Russia, causing Ukraine to stop sharing intelligence with the United States. In an X post two days later, Crouzet appeared to deny the claim that those leaks involved intentionally false information.
- Snopes first contacted Crouzet in January 2026 and reached out to him again in late September to ask about his evidence for these alleged leaks and whether there was any indication they involved Ukraine intentionally feeding the U.S. false information. We had not received a reply before publication but will update this story if we learn more.
In September 2026, a claim recirculated online that Ukraine had allegedly given the U.S. false intelligence that the United States then leaked to Russia, which revealed the U.S. as an unreliable intelligence partner.
Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, starting a war that is ongoing as of this writing.
For example, one X user, whose post had been viewed more than 8 million times at the time of publication, wrote (archived), "France and Ukraine fed Trump false intelligence to test whether he would leak it to Putin—and he did."
An Instagram user then posted a screenshot of that X post (archived). The caption said the claim fueled "speculation that Trump or people around his administration were leaking intelligence to Moscow," but added that it "has not been proven."
(X)
The rumor first spread at the start of 2026, shortly after French President Emmanuel Macron said France was providing two-thirds of Ukraine's intelligence on Jan. 15. Social media users then suggested the reasoning behind the French-Ukrainian intelligence partnership was the alleged leak of false Ukrainian intelligence from the U.S. to Russia. Posts making the claim featured on X, Substack, Medium, Bluesky and Reddit.
Several posts, including one on Facebook (archived), featured a screenshot of a since-deleted X post by user Luc Rombout, which read:
Interesting message on French newschannel LCI:
"Ukrainian intell services sent false strategic info to US intell services... and observed that the information had been relayed to RUS and was used by RUS forces."
=> total replacement of US as Intell partner with FRA, GBR, DEU [France, the U.K., Germany]
"Trump is leaking intelligence about our allies to Russia," the Facebook post's caption read.
Snopes could find no evidence confirming the rumor Ukraine had shared false information with the U.S. Instead, this claim appeared to stem from a misunderstanding of an interview that aired on Jan. 16, 2026, on the French news television channel LCI.
The interview subject was Vincent Crouzet, who formerly worked at the Directorate General for External Security (DGSE), France's foreign intelligence agency. He said in the interview, without citing his sources, that Ukrainian intelligence officials suspected the U.S. had leaked information to Russia, causing Ukraine to stop sharing intelligence with the United States.
Asked to clarify his assertion that the U.S. had leaked Ukrainian intelligence to Russia, Crouzet said in a Jan. 18, 2026, X post (archived), which in English reads, "No, I did not say that: I said Ukrainians suspected risks of information leaks from the U.S. to the Russians."
Snopes first contacted Crouzet in January 2026 and then reached out to him again in September to ask him what evidence he could provide that Ukrainians suspected intelligence leaks from the U.S. to Russia and whether there was any reason to believe Ukraine had fed the U.S. false information. We also contacted the White House for a comment on the rumor. We will update this report if we receive any responses.
Due to the fact that we could not verify or disprove these details independently, we did not give this report a rating.
The interview that sparked the rumor
The rumor spread, in part, via the screenshot of the X post by Rombout, who identified himself on his LinkedIn page as the head of a crisis management center in Belgium.
Rombout's post appeared to reshare a video clip posted on the 24H Pujadas account. 24H Pujadas is a program on LCI, considered reputable in France.
The clip itself was genuine and not created or altered using an artificial intelligence tool. Snopes identified an X post by the TV program 24H Pujadas with the video clip (archived) and a full video of the segment on the day it aired, Jan. 16, 2026. The presenter on that day was French journalist Yves Calvi.
Rombout seemingly deleted his original X post that made the claim. In a later post, he said in French that he was quoting the discussion in the French news program, implying that the claim did not originate with him.
A review of the televised interview showed Crouzet saying, in the context of discussing Macron's speech announcing France was now providing two-thirds of Ukraine's intelligence, that two Ukrainian intelligence officials had decided to stop sharing intelligence with the U.S. due to a lack of trust (emphasis ours):
So this announcement went a bit under the radar, yet it is essential. It is essential in two ways. First because it marks the divorce between Ukrainian intelligence and U.S. intelligence, because if we [France] supply two-thirds of Ukraine's intelligence, I can well imagine that the last third is supplies by other European partners — in this case, Germany and the U.K.
When did this divorce happen? It happened on Feb. 28, 2025, during the famous session in the Oval Office, which created a break in the trust between Ukrainian intelligence and U.S. intelligence, to the point where the two leaders of Ukrainian intelligence — so, Vasyl Malyuk for the SBU [Security Service of Ukraine] and Kyrylo Budanov ... you can see them on the screen ... for the GUR [Main Directorate of Intelligence, military intelligence] — decided to no longer share effective intelligence they had with their U.S. partner due to U.S. leaks to Moscow.
Rombout's X post seemingly misinterpreted some details. At no point did Crouzet say Ukraine had fed the U.S. false information and then tracked that information to Russia. We first reached out to Rombout in January and then contacted him again in September for his response to our findings about the possible translation error. We will update this report if we receive a response.
For further reading, Snopes examined a rumor spread by Russian hackers that 1.7 million Ukrainians died or went missing during the war with Russia.

Miffed over Rs 10,000, employee sets boss's Surat shop on fire, causes Rs 24 crore loss
A Surat textile market fire initially thought to be an accident was later found to be alleged arson over a Rs 10,000 payment dispute. Police arrested accountant Vinod Pandit Sawale, accusing him of targeting his employer's shop, with the blaze gutting 14 shops and destroying textiles worth around Rs 24 crore.
A dispute over a delayed payment of Rs 10,000 spiralled into a massive fire after an accountant allegedly took matters into his own hands to settle the score, gutting 14 shops and destroying textiles worth around Rs 24 crore at Surat's Shyam Sangini Textile Market. After days of investigation, police said the September 9 blaze in the Saroli area was not an accident, but a planned act of arson allegedly carried out by the employee against his employer.
The Surat Crime Branch has arrested 33-year-old Vinod Pandit Sawale in connection with the fire. Police said Sawale had worked as an accountant at a shop on the market's sixth floor and was allegedly angry with the owner over around Rs 10,000 that he claimed was pending.
According to the police, Sawale had joined the shop in April 2026 on a salary of around Rs 30,000. A dispute later developed between him and the shop owner over his work, following which he left the job. Police said the alleged dispute over the unpaid amount left him angry and prompted him to plan the arson.
Investigators also said this was not his first attempt. Sawale had allegedly tried to set the shop on fire earlier, but the attempt failed. He then allegedly returned with a second plan -- this time using around Rs 150 worth of petrol.
HOW THE FIRE WAS ALLEGEDLY SET
CCTV footage showed a man with his face covered by a white handkerchief entering the market with a bag slung over his shoulder. Police said the man was later identified as Sawale.
According to the police, Sawale bought around Rs 150 worth of petrol from a petrol pump in Devadh village. He carried the fuel in a plastic bag and a bottle and reached the market at around 9 pm on September 8.
He waited near a staircase on the fifth floor until around 12.30 am, when the market had become deserted. Police said he then sprinkled petrol on textile boxes and parcels kept outside the shop and set them on fire before fleeing.
The flames spread rapidly, engulfing several shops. Around 14 shops were gutted and textiles and other goods worth crores of rupees were destroyed. Firefighters battled the blaze for around 38 hours, according to the police account.
1,500 CCTV CAMERAS HELPED CRACK CASE
After the fire, Saroli Police registered a case against an unidentified person and began investigating. The Crime Branch examined footage from more than 1,500 CCTV cameras installed under Surat Police's 'Vishwas Project' Phase 2.
Investigators tracked the suspect's movements and analysed his entry and exit routes through backward and forward tracking. The CCTV trail eventually led police to Sawale.
Police said that after a video of the fire went viral on social media and he learnt that an FIR had been registered, Sawale switched off his mobile phone and fled Surat with his wife and child.
He first travelled to Rajasthan's Khatu Shyam temple and later went to Ayodhya, police said. When he eventually returned to Surat, investigators received information about his whereabouts. A Crime Branch team deployed for Ganpati security arrangements arrested him near Flower Garden in Dindoli.
Sawale was subsequently handed over to Saroli Police Station.
Rs 10,000 DISPUTE, RS 24 CRORE LOSS
Surat Additional Police Commissioner Karanraj Vaghela said the fire had caused an estimated loss of around Rs 25 crore, while the police investigation put the value of the destroyed textiles at around Rs 24 crore.
Police are questioning Sawale to establish the details of the alleged conspiracy and how the petrol was procured. Investigators are also examining the role of the petrol pump operator who allegedly sold him the fuel.
The accused was also taken back to Shyam Sangini Textile Market for reconstruction of the sequence of events. During the exercise, he was seen with his hands folded.
What began, according to the police investigation, as an alleged dispute over Rs 10,000 had ended with a fire that destroyed around Rs 24 crore worth of textiles.

It was at the 1992 Olympics in Barcelona when the mutterings about a new "secret weapon" started.
Dozens of Great Britain athletes had been taking a new product that increased muscle mass and improved athletic performance – a "wonder pill" that didn't fall foul of any doping rules.
They were talking about creatine.
Now found in tubs and bags on many supermarket shelves and tagged in your social feeds, it is the supplement of choice for millions of people and one of the most scientifically researched.
But back then, when it came on the scene at the very top of British elite sport, there were suspicions and stigma around the use of any substance described as 'performance enhancing' – even if it was legal.
From the minute an athlete wakes, to the moment they go to bed, they are thinking about how they can optimise their performance and recovery.
Today, creatine is just one of a long list of supplements taken by elite athletes in this pursuit of marginal gains. Some help with muscle size and strength, while others correct deficiencies in the diet.
"There are various reports in the literature of some studies that say maybe up to 90% of athletes take supplements. I often jokingly say that means 10% are lying," says Prof Graeme Close, professor of human physiology at Liverpool John Moores University.
"The sports teams that I've worked in, I think that's probably closer to 100% of athletes will be taking some form of supplementation."
So, what do supplements actually do and why do athletes take them? And in the world of strict liability, where elite athletes are solely responsible for what they put in their bodies, how do they make sure they stay clean?
While experts like Close advocate for seeking to meet nutritional needs through food in the first instance, it may not always be possible or practical to do this - and that is where supplements come in.
Take, for example, creatine, which is found naturally in meat and fish.
"You would need the best part of a kilogram of raw chicken a day to get the amount of creatine you need," says Close. But it is unsafe to eat raw poultry because of the food poisoning risk from harmful bacteria.
Creatine is a natural compound in the body produced in the kidneys, liver and pancreas. It is a quick source of energy for muscles, which is especially important for short-duration, high intensity activities such as sprinting.
Its big break as a supplement came in the 1990s when two scientists who had been researching it for two decades shared their findings with Steve Jennings, whose Maxim sports nutrition company supplied products to the British Olympic team.
During the 1992 Barcelona Games, investigative reporter Doug Gillon had learned of a 'secret trial' involving British athletes and seen a box of their Ergomax C150 – effervescent creatine tablets. He wrote that if the scientists' claims - that creatine could improve explosive athletic performance by 1-3% - were true, then "sport may never be the same again".
In terms of sport supplements and nutrition, he was right. By the time of the next Olympics in 1996, an estimated 80% of athletes were taking creatine, and since then it has become mainstream, with research suggesting there may be cognitive benefits as well as physical.
According to the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition, the creatine breakthrough of the 1990s had "launched a new era in sports nutrition" and "sparked exploration into other supplements".
The global dietary supplements market size was valued at $209.5bn (£154bn) in 2025 and is projected to grow to $431.7bn (£317.4bn) by 2033, according to Grand View Research., external
Close, who oversaw nutrition for last year's British and Irish Lions rugby union tour, sees supplements as the "final piece of the jigsaw" rather than a starting point.
"What we're talking about is small margins of benefit, where actually these athletes who focus on the food, I think what you often find is that they've got the big-ticket items right," he says.
"So they're seeing great performance benefits because their overall diet is immaculate.
"They might be missing out on the one per-centers, but they've really nailed the 99 per-centers. And they often do better than those who chase the one per-centers but have not given enough attention to the 99 per-centers."
Australian cyclist Nicole Frain agrees, adding: "I'm a pretty big believer that they are called sport supplements. They are there to supplement the things you already do right.
"I don't think supplements are the answer to fix my problems.
"You need to be eating a balanced diet, training well, sleeping right, recovering well, hydrating – all of those things – before we add in all of the extras."
Close puts protein powders top of the list of supplements taken by athletes he works with, followed by creatine and vitamin D.
Protein powders maximise muscle repair and contribute to muscle growth, while creatine is a quick source of energy for muscles and important in short-duration, high-intensity activities like sprinting. Vitamin D, meanwhile, is essential for bone health and supports muscle function.
Other popular supplements include carbohydrate gels, which Close says were key in the first sub-two hour marathon run earlier this year by Kenyan long-distance runner Sabastian Sawe.
"As sport nutritionists we were all fascinated at what the fuelling programme was, and it was the sports drinks and gels that played a huge part of that fuelling," Close says.
"There was a calculation done of what it would take to break the two-hour marathon, and that did involve making sure that over 100 grams of supplemental carbohydrate were ingested per hour.
"And the reports coming out of the recent sub-two-hour marathon was that it was 110 grams of carbohydrate per hour that was achieved."
Supplements can improve performance, but there is an uneasy ring to describing them as 'performance enhancing' because of the association with banned substances and anti-doping rule violations.
So what determines whether something is on the World Anti-Doping Agency's (Wada) banned list?
"For Wada to put anything on the list, it's got to hit two out of three criteria: dangerous to health, performance enhancing, and against the spirit of sport," Close explains.
"So just because something enhances performance, if it's not dangerous to health and not against the spirit of sport, Wada will not touch it.
"So creatine is a good example.
"Though something like an anabolic steroid, where it's against the spirit of sport to be injecting yourself for a performance benefit, it's dangerous to health and it's performance enhancing - that hits all three."
But taking a supplement still carries anti-doping risks.
"No guarantee can be given that any particular supplement is free from prohibited substances," UK Anti-Doping advice states, urging athletes to "be vigilant" in using them.
And if you test positive for a prohibited substance, consuming it unintentionally can result in the same four-year ban as if you deliberately took it.
There are supplement-testing programmes which batch test products before they are sold to make sure they do not contain any Wada-prohibited substances.
One of those is Informed Sport, which says as many as one in 10 supplements is contaminated with ingredients and compounds prohibited in sport and points to a study carried out by the Anti-Doping Knowledge Centre that showed product contamination was responsible for 8% of all anti-doping violations between 2005 and 2022.
While Informed Sport is a very well used system among athletes, Wada makes it clear that quality assurance schemes can reduce but do not eliminate the risk of an anti-doping infringement.
If you do accept the risk, you need to be organised to keep track.
In the case of Great Britain rower Heidi Long, it takes a spreadsheet.
"I've recorded the batch number of every product that I've taken and its expiry date because if you take it after the expiry date the Informed Sport [certification] is no longer viable," she says.
Close says he has also done site visits to factories to see where the supplements are made to check the manufacturing processes because "the risk of failing a drugs test is huge".
There are risks to the general population too, he adds, saying: "You can be buying supplements off the internet that are made in somebody's garage and you've got no idea of the manufacturing processes."
He points to studies on creatine products which have found there is no creatine in them and so "you're completely wasting your money" and that in the worst case scenario it may contain substances that are dangerous to your health.
"So it is really important that the message is that while they can play a small role, the safety considerations are the key factor," he says.
There is, however, more than one way for an elite athlete to chase a competitive edge – and some are going back to basics.
For every trending supplement, there is an unprocessed, wholefood alternative – from the anti-inflammatory benefits of turmeric, staving off cramp with pickle juice or consumption of high-nitrate foods like beetroot before competition.
It is what Close calls a "food-first" or "food-only" approach and something he says every athlete should use as a starting point.
The latest to have its moment in the spotlight is an ancient Ethiopian grain called teff.
Used for thousands of years in traditional east African diets, teff is now making its mark globally in performance nutrition.
In comparison to other popular grains like wheat, rice and quinoa, teff has a high mineral content and is rich in calcium, iron and vitamin C. Naturally gluten-free and good for the gut, it is also unique for being a 'complete' protein, meaning it provides all nine essential amino acids required for human nutrition.
These superfood credentials have caught the attention of some of the world's best athletes over the years, from Olympic champion marathon runner Haile Gebrselassie to seven-time Grand Slam singles champion Venus Williams, and it is now becoming a more common sight on UK supermarket shelves.
British boxer Fran Hennessy was introduced to teff by her nutritionist and it is now part of her daily routine.
"I've never looked back," she says. "What I'm putting in my body is good fuel and energy and teff has so much. It energises you so much before a workout and it gives you the fibre you need."
As well as boosting her performances, Hennessy credits teff with being key to recovery.
She says: "Each meal I'm having there's a reason behind and everything that's in it there's a reason behind... I know what I'm putting in my body is fuelling me, recovering me, energising me."
Cost is another consideration when athletes are deciding on supplements.
"The supplement industry is really expensive," says Long. "And we're definitely not made of money. So I think it's really picking and choosing when you want to put that investment in."
She says it makes sense to have more supplements around racing time "when the performance is super critical and very time dependent".
"[But] on a daily basis if I can get the protein intake from my dinner and a glass of milk or yoghurt and breakfast then actually I was going to be eating that food anyway so it's not as expensive."
And then there is taste.
"I would much rather enjoy a coffee in the morning with friends or while I'm working rather than have one of the gels," she says. "Some of the gels ... you'll end up holding your nose when you take it.
"I guess it's just like the enjoyment of what you're taking, you know, it's nicer to eat food than it is to take supplements."

Bushra Bano cleared the Uttar Pradesh Public Service Commission examination in 2017 with Rank 6, becoming a PCS Officer and later a sub-divisional magistrate. She studied on her own, without coaching, while working full-time and raising two children with her engineer husband. She sat for the UPSC exam twice — in 2019 and 2021 — before securing Rank 234 and clearing the Indian Police Service.
On September 14, 2026, she was transferred from her post as additional SP of Kharagpur in West Bengal’s Paschim Medinipur district, a day after propaganda news channels and Right-wing accounts targeted her for using the Arabic words, ‘Assalamu Alaikum’, ‘Jazakallah’, and ‘Inshallah’, in a video.
In the clip, Bushara is heard commending a government-aided residential coaching academy for minorities, women and SC/ST students at Aligarh Muslim University. While she spoke, she said the three phrases in Arabic. She said, “Assalamu Alaikum. My name is Bushra Bano… ” at first. Towards the end, she said, “…If they (the students) stay and study through the RCA then Inshallah many more people will move forward like me and get the opportunity to serve their country.” At the end she ended her video by saying, “Thank you, Jazakallah”.
“Assalamu Alaikum” is a common greeting which means “Peace be upon you”; “Inshallah” translates to “God willing”, and the phrase “Jazakallah” means “May God Reward You”. The reader might note that these are not religious phrases but greetings and wishes.
A simple video, made by a Muslim IPS officer who used a few Arabic phrases, sent ripples across the Right-wing ecosystem. On September 13, propaganda outlet Sudarshan News, which has its own national TV channel, shared the video on X and said, “Starting with ‘Assalamualaikum,’ slipping in ‘Inshallah’ midway, and wrapping up with ‘Jazakallah’, Bushra Bano… shared how she came from Saudi Arabia and became an IPS officer in India… She made full use of the scheme being run by the government at Aligarh Muslim University.”
“अस्सलाम वाले कुम” से शुरू कर बीच में “इंशाल्लाह” कहते हुए “जज़ाकल्लाह” पर किया खत्म,
खड़गपुर में एडिशनल एसपी के तौर पर तैनात बुशरा बानो ने बताया कि सऊदी अरब से आ कर वो कैसे भारत में बनीं IPS..
सरकार द्वारा अलीगढ़ मुस्लिम यूनिवर्सिटी में चलाई जा रही स्कीम का उठाया भरपूर फायदा.… pic.twitter.com/foYKjihMV2
— Sudarshan News (@SudarshanNewsTV) September 13, 2026
Soon, a barrage of online trolls started targeting Bano. An X handle called @HinduLegalFund posted on X that a complaint had been filed with the West Bengal home secretary regarding the video. “She began with Assalamualaikum, used Inshallah, ended with Jazakallah — and did not use Vande Mataram or Jai Hind…” the post read. Additionally, it stated that a serving officer should maintain “neutrality and national expressions in public communication”.
Complaint filed with West Bengal Home Secretary regarding IPS Bushra Bano’s official video statement.
She began with Assalamualaikum, used Inshallah, ended with Jazakallah — and did not use Vande Mataram or Jai Hind.
A serving officer representing the Indian state should…
— Hindu Legal Fund (@HinduLegalFund) September 13, 2026
Several Right-wing accounts, including @JaipurDialogues and @MeghUpdates, also shared the video and complained that no ‘Vande Mataram’ or ‘Jai Hind’ had been used by the IPS officer.
A notification issued by the government of West Bengal on Monday stated that Bano, alongside two other WBPS officers, was being transferred to a different posting “in public interest”. She has been made the deputy commandant of the state armed police 4th battalion. The notification does not state any reason behind the transfer.

Subhendu Mandal posted as Addl DC, Chandannagar

It should be common knowledge that Arabic is a language and Islam is a religion. Muslims use Arabic extensively for religious purposes, but Arabic is not synonymous with Islam. In other words, none of these expressions is simply a ‘Muslim word’ in the narrow linguistic sense. They are Arabic phrases whose meanings and histories intersect with Islamic religious usage, but they are not exclusive to Islam. The tradition of greeting a person with ‘Peace be upon you’, for example, exists in other languages and religious traditions — the Hebrew expression ‘shalom aleichem’, for example, literally means ‘peace be upon you’ and is common in Jewish religious literature. None of this, however, came in the way of pro-BJP handles slamming the officer for her alleged religion posturing.
Sudarshan News editor Suresh Chavhanke, whose history of peddling misinformation and communal propaganda is well documented, called Bano’s case ‘UPSC Jihad’.
Even if one were to accept this as an instance of religious posturing, it would hardly be the first time a police officer has done so. What stands out, however, is how differently such conduct is received depending on the community to which the officer belongs.
In May 2026, IPS officer C V Anand invited priests to perform a puja in his office on the day he took charge as director general of police of Telangana.

Anand wrote, “As per the muhurtham , I reached the DGP office at Lakdikapul with my family , took the salute and followed the pujari into the dgp chambers where the puja and blessings were done.”
It was a very busy and perhaps the biggest day for me and my family . As per the muhurtham , I reached the DGP office at Lakdikapul with my family , took the salute and followed the pujari into the dgp chambers where the puja and blessings were done.

More such instances are not difficult to find.
In Uttar Pradesh’s Sambhal, a circle officer named Anuj Chaudhary, who was an accused of firing during the violence at the Shahi Jama Masjid in November 2024, was pictured joining a Hindu religious procession in January 2025. He was accused of participating in religious rituals while on duty and violating service conduct rules. A complaint was filed by retired IPS officer and Azad Adhikar Sena president Amitabh Thakur, following which a probe was launched.
The same year, on Holi, Chaudhary had stated: “Holi comes once a year, Jumma comes 52 times. If you want to serve sevai, you must also eat gujiya.” Again, an investigation was initiated, and Chaudhary was eventually given a clean chit.
In May 2025, he was transferred from Sambhal to Chandausi, some 30 km away. Three months later, in August, Chaudhary was promoted to the role of additional superintendent of police (ASP). His colleagues and senior officers, including SP K K Bishnoi and ASP Rajesh Kumar Srivastava, marked the occasion with a felicitation ceremony.
Was there no outrage when Anuj Chaudhary carried a mace and marched in a religious procession in uniform? There was, from one section, but he went on to be promoted. Bano’s case panned out differently. The principle, presumably, is that the same rules apply to everyone. In practice, however, some seem to be considerably more equal than others. And if Bushra Bano’s transfer was, as the government put it, “in public interest”, one is left wondering exactly which ‘public’ that interest was meant to serve.
Bano’s transfer set off a series of critical reactions from the Opposition. Several politicians alleged that the transfer was a direct fallout of her use of Arabic phrases. Comparing the incident with Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s inauguration of the Parliament “with sengol & bare chested sadhus”, Trinamool Congress MP Mahua Moitra remarked, “…We are a nation gone mad, poisoned with hate & bigotry. God Save India”.
For a country whose Prime Minister inaugurated new Parliament with sengol & bare chested sadhus, transferring a Muslim IPS officer for saying Assalamalaikum & Inshallah is ridiculous. We are a nation gone mad, poisoned with hate & bigotry. God Save India.

Former Jammu and Kashmir chief minister Mehbooba Mufti also criticised the move, saying the transfer, which was followed by the West Bengal CM “calling an election a ‘test’ of Muslim loyalty”, was “a veiled threat to the community”. “…First our food, clothes and marriages , now even our vocabulary and our votes are being policed”, she added.
Congress MP Imran Pratapgarhi took to X to condemn the move. “A hate-mongering TV channel first sensationalized that video by posting it and incited online trolling against the female IPS officer, and instead of standing by her, the state government transferred her the very next day. What kind of India are you building, @narendramodi ji? @IPS_Association, are you watching this?”, he wrote.

Hong Kong workforce to shrink by 20,000 yearly as key sectors face shortages
Predicted 2028 shortfall will narrow to 130,000, but key sectors like aviation, tech, healthcare and construction still face a crunch
Hong Kong’s workforce is forecast to shrink by around 20,000 a year until 2028 despite measures to import labour and talent, with shortages remaining most acute among skilled technical workers.
A government report on manpower projections on Tuesday found that although the labour shortfall would narrow to 130,000 by 2028, down by nearly a third from the original estimate of 180,000, the city would continue to face critical manpower challenges across key sectors.
“Due to economic transformation, the adoption of AI [artificial intelligence] and various talent and labour importation measures, the predicted manpower shortfall in 2028 will narrow to 130,000, but most critical industries, especially innovation, aviation, construction, city operations and healthcare, still face a manpower crunch,” said Acting Secretary for Labour and Welfare Ho Kai-ming.
“The adoption of AI is expected to accelerate and companies are likely to take a more cautious approach when hiring for entry-level positions. We believe demand for these roles will ease and some clerical jobs will undergo restructuring. Overall, fresh graduates and middle-aged clerical staff are expected to be most impacted.”

If the tech industry sought to create a method of seducing users into sending their deepest, most sensitive secrets to a server in a faraway data center, it would be hard-pressed to create a better honeypot than an AI chatbot.
OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Anthropic’s Claude, Google’s Gemini, and their countless smaller competitors have become therapists, sounding boards, and virtual confession booths for millions of people around the world. Almost all of those AI models are set by default to collect and store that highly private data with, in many cases, no restrictions on how it’s shared or sold, used to further train the tools, or handed over to any lawsuit plaintiff or law enforcement agency that demands it through a legal process.
“You have this intelligent thing staring back at you, and you’re basically telling it, one question at a time, every possible thing there is to know about your life,” says Matt Green, a privacy- and security-focused computer science professor at Johns Hopkins University. “You're giving it this huge profile on you.”
A decade ago, text messages represented perhaps the most personal, sensitive data that most people shared from their devices, says cryptographer and software developer Moxie Marlinspike. The surveillance dangers invited by unprotected texting are what pushed him in 2014 to create Signal, the end-to-end encrypted messenger now used by well over a hundred million people. Now, he says, that critical point of privacy vulnerability has shifted to people’s interactions with AI.
“Those same things I was concerned about with messaging are happening in the AI space, but several orders of magnitude more significantly,” says Marlinspike. “People are integrating AI into their personal lives. They talk with it about their deepest insecurities, their finances, their health, their relationships.”
So earlier this year, Marlinspike launched Confer, an AI chatbot designed to allow users to ask it anything while preserving their privacy, using cryptography to technically prevent the service’s own server from being able to surveil or log their conversations. “Confer is designed to be a service where you can explore ideas without your own thoughts potentially conspiring against you someday,” he wrote in a blog post introducing it.
Marlinspike’s private AI tool is, in fact, just one standout among a new generation of AI services that promise to remedy the pervasive privacy invasion that these chatbots represent. Some advertise that they never record conversations as a policy. Others offer to anonymize them. A few, like Confer, seek to create actual technological guardrails that restrict their own access to users’ secrets.
The result of that nascent competition to create less surveillance-prone AI is a growing crowd of tools, often ones that offer confusing assurances for users as they seek to adopt an increasingly unavoidable technology without losing control of their secrets. Here’s WIRED’s guide to using AI with your privacy intact.
Zero Data Retention
When you start typing into one of the big three AI chatbots—ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini—it’s safest to start with a baseline expectation of approximately zero real privacy from anyone who is determined to access your conversation records and has a legal path to obtaining them. That includes the owner of the service, advertisers or other companies they partner with, contractors who help fine-tune the systems, law enforcement agencies, or even someone who manages to subpoena the records as part of a civil lawsuit.
The simplest, strong exception to that rule is a contract between you—or more likely, your employer—and an AI provider that legally prevents them from retaining those records, a provision that’s come to be known as zero data retention, or ZDR. OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google all offer ZDR policies for their enterprise versions, which when enabled generally require that they immediately delete records of users’ interactions with a chatbot as soon as they’re processed.
Even these ZDR policies, which are only available for paid enterprise and developer accounts rather than for average users, have significant exceptions. Anthropic, for instance, doesn’t offer ZDR for its most sophisticated “Mythos-class” models like Fable 5.1, due to what it describes as the potential for misuse like scamming or hacking and even “autonomous misbehavior,” such as AI agents independently hacking targets to carry out their unwitting users’ requests, as has occurred in several high-profile AI-driven breaches.
OpenAI also announced last month that its ZDR implementations will analyze user activity prior to deletion—on the customer’s systems rather than its own, it says—and, if it detects abuse, flag it for the customer organization. OpenAI says its system, known as Private Safety Processing, will even alert OpenAI’s staff if it detects abuse in some cases, though without revealing the content of the conversation to them. Google, too, warns that it logs some Gemini prompts for abuse monitoring even with ZDR enabled, but without the user’s Google ID or IP address included—though that “sanitized” data can in some cases still pinpoint a particular person when the request itself includes identifiable information.
Policies, Promises, and Proxies
Regardless of those protections and exceptions, the paid, enterprise-level, contractual promises of ZDR are out of reach for the vast majority of non-corporate AI users. Instead, many consumer-targeted AI services ask us to settle for the far weaker, pinky-swear promises they’ve made not to log our conversations.
Privacy-focused cloud services company Proton, for instance, offers the AI chatbot Lumo, which it describes as “AI where every conversation is private.” That privacy, however, isn’t based on the technical guarantees of end-to-end encryption, like Proton’s other services such as Proton Mail and Proton Drive. Instead, it simply promises not to log users’ conversations, and users have to trust that Proton will adhere to that privacy policy—which, in Proton’s case, is at least backed by the company’s long track record as a privacy-focused company. “A promise is not as good as a mathematical guarantee,” Yen told WIRED in an interview last month, “but a promise made by the right people is still actually quite substantial.”
Other privacy-focused AI services like Venice.ai and Duck.ai, the AI chatbot offered by long-running private search engine DuckDuckGo, offer similar vows about keeping no logs of your conversations. Both services, however, relay your chat requests to other services such as Claude or ChatGPT, essentially acting as a proxy for your conversation that limits what information the underlying AI model can collect about you.
(Duck.ai lets the user choose which third-party model they’re using. Venice.ai appears to automatically route conversations to different services based on the request, without always making clear to the user which one it’s using, as well as answering queries with an AI model hosted on its own infrastructure in some cases. Venice.ai also touts other privacy features, like using “trusted execution environment” systems to cryptographically prevent logging of conversations—more on that below—but when WIRED attempted to reach out to Venice.ai’s staff to ask more questions about these privacy features, its AI response bot only repeatedly referred us to a nonworking email address.)
Using an anonymity proxy offers some privacy protection compared with using ChatGPT or Claude directly. Yet when they relay your requests to those services, Duck.ai and Venice.ai’s own promises about their retention of data become significantly less meaningful, points out Johns Hopkins’ Green. That’s because your chat messages can still be collected by that underlying AI model and, even stripped of any identifying metadata, those messages can often contain identifiable information.
Ask about the best coffee shops in your neighborhood, for instance, and you’ve immediately revealed information about where you live, Green points out. “All that stuff tied together is basically a fingerprint for you,” says Green.
Trusted Execution Environments and On-Device AI
Far better than privacy promises, policies, or anonymizing relays are actual technological restrictions that prevent an AI service from reading your conversations—a guarantee that the service not only does not snoop on or record your chats, but that it cannot. That’s where cryptography comes in.
Unlike encrypted messaging or storage, where the server hosting a service never sees any unencrypted data, interactions with an AI model can’t yet be truly end-to-end encrypted like a Signal or WhatsApp conversation. Currently, working AI models can only process unencrypted prompts. So instead, some AI services are offering the next best thing, what’s known as a trusted execution environment, or TEE. In that system, the server running the AI model uses a hardware setup—most often Nvidia’s Confidential Computing—in which the user’s queries are processed on isolated hardware, and the server can cryptographically prove that the rest of the system has no access to that segregated enclave of secrets.
Confer, the private AI chatbot launched by Signal creator Moxie Marlinspike, uses that Nvidia-based TEE setup— along with an authentication system based on passkeys and open-source code that anyone can audit—to offer what are perhaps the strongest consumer-level privacy protections currently available in an AI chatbot.
Meta, too, uses a TEE to offer a more private version of the Meta AI chatbot included in WhatsApp—a privacy system that Confer’s Marlinspike has said he is helping Meta to develop. Start typing into the “Ask Meta AI or Search” bar in your WhatsApp app, and an “Ask” button will appear on the right side of the text field with the Meta AI logo. Tap it and then tap the speech bubble with a lock that appears on the top right of that Meta AI chat screen, and you’ll enter a new chat screen that’s protected with a TEE system, which Meta says prevents it from keeping any record of it. That Incognito system is by no means truly end-to-end encrypted like the rest of WhatsApp’s messaging, but it appears to be Meta’s attempt at integrating AI into WhatsApp while approximating the privacy promises it offers to users in their conversations with other humans.
Unlike the Meta AI integrated into WhatsApp, Meta’s newer AI agent called Muse doesn’t yet offer a TEE-based privacy system. Instead, it promises only to run in a segregated virtual machine (VM) in the cloud, where Meta says its ad systems won’t be able to access your data and you can opt out of your data being used to train Meta’s AI. The company says, however, that it’s working on releasing Muse Confidential VM later this year, which Meta tells WIRED “is intended to cryptographically and verifiably prevent Meta from accessing data” in a user’s Muse virtual machine.
Apple also offers a privacy-preserving AI system of its own design with some TEE-like properties, what it calls Private Cloud Compute (PCC), to enforce its promise that it can’t read users’ conversations with its Apple Intelligence AI service. When you ask Apple Intelligence or Siri a query that’s processed on its servers, your personal device cryptographically checks that the server is running an unaltered version of Apple’s PCC code, which is designed to keep no logs and isolate your data from any remote access. (It’s also possible to ask Apple Intelligence or Siri to query ChatGPT or other third-party AI services. When you do, just as with other tools that relay your queries, you won’t get that same PCC level of protection, but Apple will also check with you before sending your request to a third-party service.) For most simple queries, however, Apple uses a more limited, on-device AI model that doesn’t share any of your secrets beyond your phone, computer, or smartwatch, but also isn’t as fully featured as a typical server-based model.
On that note, there are plenty of other AI tools that run locally on your computer, too, such as Ollama, LMStudio, or LocalAI. All of them ensure—by the simple fact that no data ever leaves your computer—a level of privacy that’s tough to obtain with any cloud-based AI tool. But Green warns that what you gain in privacy with locally hosted artificial intelligence, you lose in, well, intelligence. Expect these self-hosted AI tools to be frequently stumped and to hallucinate far more often than the modern, cloud-hosted AI models most users are accustomed to. “You can run these on any laptop,” Green says. “They’re just dumb as rocks.”
The Price of Privacy
That intelligence-versus-privacy question is, of course, just one of the trade-offs that privacy-conscious AI users face as they choose their preferred tool. Price is another.
Confer, for instance, uses a freemium model, charging $34.99 a month for its cheapest tier after users run out of the roughly 20 to 25 queries a day it offers for free. That’s more than the $20 a month Claude and ChatGPT charge for their cheapest paid tiers. But Marlinspike says that price premium in fact captures the actual cost of running an AI model without the subsidies that come from an expectation of future profits from data collection or advertising. “It’s more expensive, but it's the real cost,” Marlinspike says, “whereas other paid providers are subsidizing the cost with monetization of our data in one way or another.”
Given the serious energy and hardware costs of running frontier AI models, the advent of more privacy-preserving AI raises the question of how companies that don’t monetize user data will sustain themselves, Green notes. Without those data-collection-driven profits, he says, it’s not yet clear whether companies that provide more private AI services will find a sustainable business model—or whether some will eventually give up or even undermine their data protection promises down the road.
In other words, AI that doesn’t exploit your data is possible. But it may be far pricier than you think. “If you want real privacy,” Green says, “you might have to pay for it.”

Balrampur police did not confirm what caused the death of the girl but said that after she fell unconscious, she was taken to hospital where she was declared dead.

At first, the girl gains her consciousness back as teacher takes a round of the class, failing to notice her. She sits straight, only to fall back again on her bench within seconds. Later, the teacher notices and attends to her, as the entire class gathers around the desk.
Several posts on social media claimed that she allegedly suffered a heart attack due to loud music from the DJ passing nearby. However, the police has not yet confirmed the cause.
The girl was a student of Divine Public School in the district. Police said that she allegedly fell unconscious in her classroom on Monday due to unknown reasons, following which she was taken to a hospital where doctors declared her dead.
The claim that the girl died due to the loud sound of a DJ during the Ganesh idol immersion on September 21 went viral on social media, prompting police to take cognisance of the matter and conduct an inquiry.
Police added that the girl's family did not approach them after the incident. When cops got in touch with the girl's family, they told them that they had already performed her last rites and did not want any action in the matter.
Police said they are examining CCTV footage and conducting a detailed investigation into various aspects of the incident.

- Posts pointing out several alleged contradictions in German politician Alice Weidel's politics and personal life circulated in 2026.
- The rumor stems from a meme claiming Weidel is the first leader who is anti-immigration yet has an immigrant wife, supports anti-LGBTQ+ policies but is a lesbian, and opposes adoption for LGBTQ+ families despite having adopted two children.
- According to media profiles of the couple, Weidel's romantic partner is Sri Lankan-born but of Swiss citizenship, and they are raising two sons in Switzerland. We were unable to determine the exact nature of the couple's legal marriage status or details of the children's adoption process at this time.
- Weidel has expressed anti-immigration views and has called "traditional" families a "societal ideal." She has said in an interview that advocating for traditional families makes "no contradiction" with own life.
- Because we have not been able to confirm certain details of Weidel's family life, we have not rated this claim. Snopes has reached out to Weidel's party, Alternative for Germany, to learn more and will update this report if, or when, additional information surfaces.
In August and September 2026, a popular meme claimed to show the alleged contradictory positions of Alice Weidel, leader of the far-right German political party Alternative for Germany, known in Germany by the abbreviation AfD. The meme states that Weidel is anti-immigration yet has an immigrant wife, supports anti-LGBTQ+ policies but is a lesbian, and opposes adoption for LGBTQ+ families despite having adopted two children.
The claim states:
Alice Weidel becomes the first leader in the world who is anti-immigration but has an immigrant wife, is anti-LGBTQ+ but is a lesbian herself, opposes LGBT adoption but has adopted two children, and is a hardcore German nationalist but lives in Switzerland.
While Weidel has stood by her party's positions on immigration and LGBTQ+ issues—while expressing minor disagreements on occasion—we have not been able to verify certain details of her personal life directly from her, and as a result we have relied on her interviews and reporting from other sources. Snopes reached out to AfD to learn more and will update this post accordingly. Until we have more information, we will keep this claim unrated.
Below we break down the truth behind several of the above claims. The above meme is largely true in that Weidel has a Sri Lankan-born wife with Swiss citizenship, while also supporting anti-immigration policies. Despite her party's anti-LGBTQ+ policies, she has said there is "no contradiction" between her personal life, her belief that same-sex couples deserve equality, and her public advocacy for a "traditional" family.
While Weidel is at the time of this writing the most prominent leader internationally associating with a party that contradicts her personal lifestyle, she is not the only public figure to follow this pattern. For example, U.S. President Donald Trump's ally and former Acting Director for National Intelligence, Richard Grenell, is openly gay despite having opposed pro-LGBTQ+ policies.
Weidel's family life
A 2021 interview with the German politician's Sri Lankan-born wife, Sarah Bossard, noted that the couple was in a registered partnership. We should note that as of July 1, 2022, same-sex marriages are 
In a televised interview, Weidel said Bossard, whom she referred to as her wife, became Swiss through adoption as a child, not through "migration":
INTERVIEWER: You brought your wife along; she was born in Sri Lanka. Is that sort of thing ever discussed at home — given that it touches on something fundamental?
WEIDEL: It's not about skin color. And my wife — as you've just done yourself — is labeled as having a "migration background." My wife is Swiss and was adopted; consequently, she doesn't view herself as having a migration background.
In a 2021 interview, Bossard noted that she grew up in Biel, Switzerland. A 2025 NBC News report said the couple resided in Willerzel, a village in Switzerland. A 2025 Time magazine profile noted they have a home in Switzerland and their sons attend school there.
According to The New York Times, they are raising two sons together. According to the Financial Times, their sons are adopted. Pink News, an outlet focused on LGBTQ+ news, said Bossard gave birth to the sons and Weidel adopted them. Snopes was unable to determine the exact circumstances of the sons' adoption and whether they are biologically related to either parent.
AfD's positions on LGBTQ+ rights, immigration and adoption
Weidel's AfD party opposes same-sex marriage and does not support same-sex adoption, according to German news outlet DW. The party website states:
We, the AfD, as the only serious political force, have the will to counter the family policy failures of recent decades with clear political measures. We will put the family, consisting of father, mother and as many children as possible, back in the center of political and social thinking and action. With us, parents get the best possible conditions for starting and managing a family and our children the best possible chances of good and healthy development.
Weidel addressed her party position in an interview:
Well, we live in a completely different reality now. Same-sex relationships should be treated as equal. But if I, as a politician, speak of a societal ideal—and that happens to be the traditional family—then I am entitled to advocate for it. There is no contradiction there.
Weidel also said the party position "was written by conservatives who might not see things exactly the way I do. As for me personally ... my children have the best upbringing and the best foundation — let them write whatever they want. I live a different reality."
She has also reportedly said, "I'm not queer, I'm just married to a woman who I've known for 20 years."
In a 2021 interview, Bossard criticized a campaign against marriage equality in Switzerland:
The campaign is not only distasteful, but completely misses our reality of life. I would have wished the committee would have more closely experienced the people and life constellations that it is criticizing. But that also shows what is still going on in the minds of some people. This is why marriage equality is an important step towards changing that.
AfD has a firm anti-immigration policy and calls for more local skilled workers. In 2025, in an interview with billionaire Elon Musk, Weidel said former German Chancellor Angela Merkel "ruined" the country after she "opened our borders through illegal immigration." Weidel also said Germany allowed migrants to "throw away" their passports and papers before entering the country in order to avoid deportations.
Snopes has previously reported on false claims that migrants committed mass sexual assaults in Germany.
Snopes reporters Laerke Christensen and Aleksandra Wrona provided the German translations in this report.

Government hospitals across Tamil Nadu are facing a shortage of surfactant medicines, a critical and life-saving medicine for pre-term babies.
The shortage has been persisting for the past few months, and several Special Newborn Care Units (SNCUs) at government hospitals have been flagging it up for the Health Department.
Doctors said surfactant medicines are essential to inflate the lungs of pre-term babies in need of the therapy. They utilised external bovine or porcine surfactants (intratracheal) in pre-term babies. These surfactants were part of the speciality drug rate contract purchases of the Tamil Nadu Medical Services Corporation (TNMSC).
Inquiries with a number of hospitals and doctors revealed that a number of centres were facing short supply of surfactants in the past few months. Official sources confirmed that government hospitals, among them medical college hospitals in Theni, Dharmapuri, Tiruppur, Cuddalore, Tiruvannamalai, Vellore and Karur districts and in Chennai, reported surfactant vial shortage, while some hospitals said they had uninterrupted supply.
A doctor, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the shortage prevailed in the past three to four months owing to a number of factors. “First, we got no allotment. Secondly, some centres miscalculated their requirement, which is based on the average number of pre-term babies delivered, and thirdly, there was higher utilisation. This is a life-saving medicine essential to inflate the lungs of pre-term babies who are otherwise solid,” he said.
A doctor at another hospital said continuous supply was not assured, and shortage occurred frequently. “Currently, we are borrowing from other sub-centres which are referring babies to us. It is very difficult for us to manage newborn units without surfactants. Sometimes, we purchase them privately using SNCU funds to save the babies,” another doctor said.
A senior paediatrician said that after 34 weeks of gestation, the foetal lungs are generally mature enough to support exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide after birth. “However, in very pre-term babies, the alveoli, which are the tiny air sacs in the lungs, may not be sufficiently mature to function effectively on their own. Surfactant, a substance produced in the lungs, helps keep the alveoli open. But in babies born very prematurely, not enough surfactant may be produced, making it difficult for them to maintain adequate oxygen levels. Depending on the baby’s condition, doctors may use respiratory support such as CPAP or a mechanical ventilator. Surfactant is delivered directly into the lungs through the endotracheal tube to prevent hyaline membrane disease.”
Lung maturity in a newborn is critical as decreased oxygen could cause hypoxia and conditions such as retinopathy of prematurity and hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy, he said.
A Health Department source denied that there was any shortage. “There was no procurement delay. Some centres may have miscalculated their requirement, resulting in shortage, or may have utilised more vials. In such circumstances, they have obtained the required supply from neighbouring facilities. A six-month purchase order, worth nearly ₹9 crore, has been issued. Additionally, operational costs are provided for paediatricians to make local purchases whenever required,” he said.
Another official said the TNMSC has issued purchase orders and it will be supplied within two days. Officials said Cuddalore faced shortage and arrangements were made to send supplies from Coimbatore. The situation was being closely monitored, they said.

India survived a major scare on Tuesday, edging Japan by two runs in a rain-curtailed one-off T20I at the Sano International Ground.
A wet outfield delayed the start by three hours, reducing the contest to five overs per side. India captain Shreyas Iyer won the toss and opted to bat, but what was expected to be a routine outing for the defending T20 World Cup champion quickly turned into a test of adaptability.
India, ranked No. 1 in the world, struggled on an unfamiliar surface that was slow, low and offered sharp turn and occasional extra bounce. Fresh from playing on batting-friendly pitches against Afghanistan, its batters found the conditions in Sano difficult to read.
Sanju Samson and Abhishek Sharma tried to attack from the outset, but the approach quickly backfired. By the end of the third over, India had lost three wickets, with Samson, Abhishek and Ishan Kishan back in the dugout.
Japan captain Kendel Kadowaki-Fleming was excellent with his bowling changes and field placements, using spin throughout the innings.
Shreyas was the exception. He resisted the temptation to play big shots, instead relying on singles and twos to keep India moving. His measured approach helped India recover and finish on 32 for four.
Japan’s chase was similarly difficult. India’s spinners, led by Axar Patel, kept the batters tied down and made the most of the sluggish surface.
Fleming briefly shifted the momentum, taking 10 runs off Ravi Bishnoi in the third over. But his dismissal in the fourth left Japan needing too much with too little time.
Axar held his nerve in the final over, conceding only six runs to defend eight and seal a two-run win. Japan needed four from the final ball but could manage only one.
Shreyas, named Player of the Match, praised Japan’s approach.
“It was turning square, was a very difficult surface to bat. It was important to take singles and rotate the strike. I just decided to play on the merit of the ball. That worked out pretty well. I always keep saying that five-over games can go anywhere. Kudos to them, their approach was impeccable. For us, it was great practice,” he said.
Fleming said he was proud of Japan for taking India to the final ball.
“Extremely proud. When it gets that close, it’s actually a little bit tougher to take, and the emotions are running pretty high in our group. But the fact that we were able to run the best team in the world, in my opinion, to the last ball of a game is pretty special,” he said.
“To hear someone like Shreyas talking about the progression of Japan cricket is still quite surreal. So, extremely proud of our group and the broader cricket community that we were able to make this game happen.”
Japan, Fleming added, entered the chase believing it had a chance despite India’s formidable spin attack.
“We ran in and we knew that anything is possible was the attitude. They’ve got some world-class spinners, Axar, Washington and Ravi Bishnoi bowling on our spinning wicket. We knew it was going to be an extreme challenge, but at six and a half an over your mind does sort of wander and think you get a couple out of the middle and you never know,” he said.
Both teams will now head to the Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya. India will enter the quarterfinals, while Japan will face Afghanistan and Nepal in the group stage.

MUMBAI: “I made a mistake by telling him to tolerate the situation.” This was the regret expressed by the mother of IIT Bombay student Sahil Wakode, who was found dead in his hostel room last week.
Sahil’s parents on Tuesday demanded the arrest of the institute’s director Shireesh B Kedare and professor Suryanarayana Doolla, news agency PTI reported.
Sahil’s mother, Sonali Wakode, said she and her husband had met their son in his hostel room on September 13, when he told them he was being tortured and harassed.
Speaking to ANI, she said they tried to reassure him and advised him to focus on his studies, believing he had a bright future ahead.
“We tried to give him moral support and advised him to focus on his studies because he had secured admission to IIT and had a bright future ahead. In hindsight, I feel that telling him to tolerate the situation was our mistake,” she said.
She added, “We persuaded him, told him that he was doing great and his future was bright. Probably, that’s where we faltered as parents. Had we taken him back home with us, our child would have been alive today. 
We know how the system works, but he was just a 19-year-old kid.”
The parents made the remarks after visiting the Mumbai Police Crime Branch office, where they demanded a thorough investigation into the circumstances surrounding their son’s death and action against those found responsible, news agency PTI reported.
Sonali claimed Sahil had told his parents that he was being tortured, abused and humiliated on the basis of his caste, PTI reported.
“He specifically told us that professor Suryanarayana Doolla would say, ‘I am from an upper caste and you are from a lower caste.’ According to what Sahil told us, this had been continuing for around three months,” she claimed.
Sahil’s father Ravindra Wakode also alleged that Doolla had told his son that he belonged to an upper caste while Sahil belonged to a lower caste.
“He used to tell him that he is from the upper caste while Sahil is from the lower caste. He also told him, ‘I will implicate you in some wrong thing and will remove you.’ This had been happening for the past three months,” Ravindra said.
He said that when Sahil narrated his ordeal, he advised him to tolerate the situation for the sake of his future.
“When he narrated his ordeal, I advised him to bear it a bit for the sake of his future,” he said, speaking to ANI.
The parents demanded the immediate arrest of Kedare and Doolla.
Sahil’s mother said she had full faith in the Crime Branch and wanted the allegations recorded in the FIR to be examined thoroughly.
“I have full faith in the Crime Branch and request that the investigation into my son Sahil’s death be completed fairly, thoroughly, and strictly in accordance with the FIR,” she said.
“The allegations and circumstances recorded in the FIR must be properly investigated, and appropriate action should be taken against those found responsible,” she added.
The mother also objected to the institute’s initial claim that Sahil had allegedly been caught using an AI platform during an examination.
She said anyone making allegations of cheating must provide evidence and questioned what she described as a change in IIT Bombay’s position on the matter.
“I am also concerned by what appears to be a change in IIT Bombay’s position or statements regarding these allegations. I request the authorities to examine this carefully and determine whether such allegations have any evidentiary basis or whether they are diverting attention from the issues raised in the FIR,” she said.
Ravindra also defended his son’s academic record, saying Sahil had cleared the JEE Advanced examination without using unfair means or cheating.
“My child was good at academics. It’s not easy to crack JEE Advanced. Look at his All India rank. He didn’t clear JEE Advanced by using unfair means or cheating,” he said.
Meanwhile, a senior Crime Branch official said the statements of Sahil’s parents had been recorded, PTI reported.
Statements of IIT Bombay officials, including professor Doolla, were yet to be recorded and they would be summoned for questioning soon, he said.
IIT Bombay has said Prof Suryanarayana Doolla was temporarily relieved of his administrative duties pending an investigation.
He continues as a professor and head of the Department of Energy Science and Engineering.
The institute has also apologised for its earlier communication about the circumstances preceding Sahil’s death, saying those details remained subject to investigation.
Sahil, a second-year BTech student in the Department of Energy Science and Engineering, was found hanging in his hostel room on the Powai campus on September 18 evening, hours after being caught allegedly using a mobile phone to access ChatGPT during a mid-semester examination.
The allegations made by Sahil’s parents are part of the ongoing Crime Branch investigation.

Throughout 2026, people shared a rumor alleging Denver Broncos quarterback Bo Nix responded to U.S. President Donald Trump calling a reporter a pig. According to social media users' posts, the NFL quarterback publicly rebuked Trump, saying that "staying silent makes me part of the problem."
For example, on Sept. 20, a Facebook post (archived) read, "BREAKING NFL NEWS: Broncos star Bo Nix breaks his silence in shocking video response after 'Little Pig' comment to a female reporter shocks T.r.u.m.p — NFL superstar condemns disrespect towards women and sparks nationwide outrage."
The post featured a meme showing side-by-side images of Nix and Trump, with a purported Nix quote reading as follows:
When I watched that clip, something in me snapped. I play this game with fire and pride, but I was raised to respect every woman who cheers, works, and sacrifices behind the scenes. If a man with that much power can mock and demean them in front of the world, then staying silent makes me part of the problem. And I refuse to be part of that.
Other examples of the claim appeared on Facebook, Instagram and Threads. Snopes readers also searched this website in September 2026, specifically asking, "Did Bo Nix stand up for a female reporter?"
We first used search engines such as DuckDuckGo, Google and Yahoo to locate possible evidence from credible sources about Nix publicly commenting on Trump. If the story was true, journalists with reputable news outlets, such as The Associated Press or Reuters — or sports blogs — would have widely reported on it. That was not the case.
The rumor about Bo Nix responding to Trump was fictional, and as a result we've rated the claim false.
The claim appeared to take inspiration from a real remark Trump made in November 2025 while aboard Air Force One, when he told a female reporter asking a question, "Quiet. Quiet, piggy." 
People.com, citing a journalist's X post, reported the female journalist Trump addressed as "piggy" was Bloomberg reporter Catherine Lucey. The subject matter of Lucey's question pertained to asking Trump about his past relationship with deceased convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
We emailed the Denver Broncos to ask if the organization would like to address the fake Nix quote and will update this article if we receive further details.
Digging into the rumor
In addition to social media posts, the untrue rumor about Nix publicly rebuking Trump appeared on a handful of generic-looking WordPress blogs. Those blogs lacked author names and credible information about their founding. An examination of the blogs found they were not reputable outlets, for example such as well-known newspapers or established news websites, or websites for local or national TV channels.
A scan of the text in one blog article with the artificial intelligence detection tool Pangram displayed the results, "We believe that this entire text is AI," as well as, "100% of this text is AI."
Snopes doesn't depend solely on AI detection tools, which vary in reliability, and instead considers the tools' results as one of several data points toward judging an image's authenticity. For Pangram, we bear in mind the platform's strong performance in third-party and internal evaluations, as well as criticisms of the tool.
Creators of content like the fabricated Nix quote capitalize on social media users' willingness to believe and share the made-up stories, profiting from advertising revenue on external websites to which the posts link. (Snopes has previously reported on the business strategy.)
The fictional story about Nix standing up for women resembled glurge, which Dictionary.com defines as "stories, often sent by email, that are supposed to be true and uplifting, but which are often fabricated and sentimental."
For further reading, we previously reported about whether Broncos head coach Sean Payton fired two players for refusing to stand for the U.S. national anthem.

Even as climate change is emerging as a significant driver of vector-borne diseases as it alters ecological and climatic conditions that influence mosquito proliferation and virus transmission, a study by the Centre for Climate Change Research at the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology (IITM), Pune, has confirmed strong seasonality in dengue transmission in Keralam. Nearly 60% of dengue cases in the State occur during the southwest monsoon (June-September) season, closely mirroring the State’s rainfall cycle.
The study, titled ‘Climate-informed dengue prediction and future risks under a changing monsoon climate in Keralam,’ identified rainfall, humidity and the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) as the key drivers of dengue transmission. It also pointed out that climate change and shifting monsoon patterns can increase dengue incidence in the State.
The study, conducted in collaboration with experts from the Department of Atmospheric and Space Sciences, Savitribai Phule Pune University; ICMR-National Institute of Translational Virology and AIDS Research, Pune; School of Public Health, Kerala University of Health Sciences (KUHS); Government Medical College, Thrissur; and KUHS, found that dengue cases begin rising in May and peak during the southwest monsoon, particularly in June and July.
Long-term risk planning
Future simulations using different machine-learning models suggest that dengue risk in Keralam could increase by 16-20% during 2021-2040 and by up to 113% by 2081-2100 under low- to high-emission pathways, underlining the need for climate-informed dengue early warning systems and long-term risk planning.
A key contribution of the study, published in GeoHealth, a peer-reviewed, open-access scientific journal, is the inclusion of El Niño-Southern Oscillation as a predictor of dengue risk. Both El Niño and La Niña were found to influence dengue risk depending on regional climate responses, although La Niña events, generally associated with cooler and wetter conditions, were found to be of relatively lower risk than El Niño.
Locally, warmer temperatures of 30.5°C-32.5°C and moderate humidity of 66%-79% during the pre-monsoon season, along with moderately high monsoon rainfall of 180-450 mm a month, were found to favour higher dengue incidence.
Peak and weaker phases
According to climate scientist Roxy Mathew Koll of IITM, Pune, who led the study, the model can predict the peak and weaker phases of dengue transmission more accurately when high-resolution climate and epidemiological data are available. Such data are particularly important at the block level in Keralam because of variations in maritime and orographic influences, monsoon rainfall and its active and break phases.
For instance, the southwest monsoon is generally more vigorous in northern districts, while southern districts experience more intense spells during the northeast monsoon. Changes in atmospheric pressure, temperature and relative humidity during the active and break phases can influence localised mosquito breeding and dengue risk, Mr. Koll said. The same modelling approach could potentially be extended to other vector-borne diseases by incorporating detailed temperature, rainfall and epidemiological data, he said.
Post-monsoon dengue
Post-monsoon dengue also showed considerable year-to-year variability, possibly reflecting differences in the spatial distribution of monsoon rainfall. The Keralam dengue model could be further strengthened through enhanced disease surveillance, better representation of vector biology and socio-demographic factors, and continuous validation.
The researchers also cautioned that changes in circulating dengue virus strains could trigger sudden surges in cases, while the future deployment of vaccines currently in development could substantially reduce dengue risk. Despite these limitations, the model demonstrated reasonable forecasting accuracy and provided region-specific insights that could support early warning systems and public health planning. Given the marked spatial variation in monsoon characteristics and dengue distribution across Keralam, more localised studies using high-resolution climate and epidemiological data could further improve dengue forecasting and risk assessment, said the researchers.
