J. D. Vance and Abdul El-Sayed have very little in common ideologically and seem to like each other even less. As part of a nasty exchange of personal insults last month, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Michigan implied that Vance’s grandfather would disapprove of the vice president’s Indian American wife. In response, Vance called El-Sayed “very, very evil” and warned him to “keep my wife’s name the hell out of your mouth because she’s way out of your league.” Yet even as Vance and El-Sayed are happy to trade schoolyard taunts, they can agree on at least one thing: that guilt by association is a contemptible means of scoring cheap political points.
“I’m tired of this guilt-by-association thing,” El-Sayed complained earlier this year, when he was asked about his decision to campaign alongside Hasan Piker, an internet shock jock who has said that “America deserved 9/11,” described allegations of sexual violence on October 7 as “rape fantasies,” and praised Mao Zedong as “one of the great leaders of the world,” among many other charming bon mots. Despite repeated calls from within his own party to renounce Piker, El-Sayed refuses to do so.
Vance is facing a similar situation with his friend Tucker Carlson. Vance “doesn’t believe in guilt-by-association cancel culture,” a spokesperson said in September 2024, after the then-senator appeared onstage with the conservative podcast host. In the years since his firing from Fox News, Carlson has lauded a Holocaust denier as “the most important historian in the United States,” accused a small Jewish sect of orchestrating the war in Iran, and praised Vladimir Putin as “the most effective leader in my lifetime.” Carlson, whose show returns again and again to the supposed perfidy of the Jews, has become the country’s highest-profile promoter of anti-Semitism. He recently held a friendly conversation with a guest who claimed that algebra was “fake math” created for “goy slaves.”
Vance was asked directly about his relationship with Carlson at a White House press conference earlier this month. “Tucker is a friend, despite the fact that we disagree on a number of things,” the vice president said. “And I’m not going to play the game where I throw friends under the bus because I have political disagreements with them. I think that is a terrible place for the United States to go.”
El-Sayed and Vance would have us believe that their troublesome friends are no different from the people in our own lives whose political views we abhor but whom we nonetheless love and appreciate. “If I had to choose between betraying my country and betraying my friend, I hope I should have the guts to betray my country,” the English writer E. M. Forster wrote in 1938 as Europe hurtled toward war. It’s a noble sentiment, a paean to friendship over tribe. But Piker and Carlson are not the equivalent of your crazy uncle. And El-Sayed and Vance are not regular citizens; they’re political figures whose judgment and choices affect other Americans’ lives. One’s choice of friends is in fact an excellent sign of character, and in this respect, both Vance and El-Sayed have demonstrated a conspicuous lack of it.
The tactic known as “guilt by association” evokes the legacy of Senator Joe McCarthy, whose feral zeal for exposing Communists, real or imagined, was so era-defining that it inspired the attachment of an ism to his surname. McCarthy’s sin wasn’t his anti-communism, however—there were indeed highly placed Soviet agents in the federal government. It was his recklessness and lack of concern for the truth. There has to be a reasonable middle ground between conducting a witch hunt and blatantly ignoring someone’s willingness to fraternize with genuinely disreputable people.
Now that their associations are in the spotlight, El-Sayed, Vance, and their respective ideological compatriots are eager to minimize them. In a softball interview with Piker several months ago, the Pod Save America host Jon Favreau, a prominent liberal opinion-shaper, said that he wants Democrats to take the “Don’t Talk About Hasan Piker For A Day Challenge.” Asked about Piker’s remarks concerning 9/11, El-Sayed tried to depict himself as a victim of the “cancel culture that all of us agreed was a bad idea back in 2020, but we seem to want to bring back.” A “Vance ally” echoed a similar sentiment to The Washington Post about the vice president’s relationship with Carlson, saying, “We’re done with the canceling, period.”
No one should accept these evasions. In April, El-Sayed deployed Piker to boost support among young voters at Michigan State and the University of Michigan. In the final hours before polls closed, El-Sayed appeared at a pool party with Piker and other internet influencers in Detroit.
Vance’s association with Carlson goes much deeper. In a 2021 interview recalling the time they first met, Vance described their immediate recognition of each other as “the guy who’s exactly right about what’s going on in the country.” Carlson helped persuade Donald Trump to select Vance as his running mate; Vance hired Carlson’s son as his deputy press secretary. When Vance guest-hosted Charlie Kirk’s show after the conservative activist’s assassination, one of the first people he invited into the vice-presidential suite was Carlson. (At Kirk’s funeral six days later, Carlson delivered a eulogy that seemed to imply that the Jews had murdered Kirk just as they had Jesus Christ.)
The most obvious reason El-Sayed and Vance haven’t disowned their noxious friends is that both Piker and Carlson command large audiences. Politics is about winning votes, and a moral miscreant’s is worth the same as a saint’s. Other politicians have done much worse than associate with the likes of Piker and Carlson.
What’s more troubling is that El-Sayed and Vance both appear to sympathize with at least some of what their influencer friend espouses. On multiple occasions, Vance has shown that he either doesn’t understand or doesn’t care about anti-Semitism. He once dismissed outrage over a group of Young Republicans joking about gas chambers as “pearl clutching” and characterized attempts to sideline bigots from the conservative movement as “endless, self-defeating purity tests.” One might think that Carlson’s frequent attacks on Vance’s boss, up to and including that Trump “should be removed from office immediately,” would have persuaded Vance, purely out of his own self-interest, to disavow Carlson. That he hasn’t done so indicates the high value he places on his association with him.
If not for such data points, Vance’s friendship with Carlson would be easy to dismiss as misplaced affection for someone who helped advance his career. But Vance is on the record stating otherwise. Late last year, he said,
I find the idea that Tucker Carlson—who has one of the largest podcasts in the world, who has millions of listeners, who supported Donald Trump in the 2024 election, who supported me in the 2024 election—the idea that his views are somehow completely anathema to conservatism, that he has no place in the conservative movement, is frankly absurd.
This implies that Holocaust denial, claims of Jewish disloyalty to the United States, veneration of Putin, and a host of other poisonous ideas are welcome in the conservative movement. Even the white-nationalist influencer Nick Fuentes is fed up with Vance’s disingenuousness. “JD Vance panders to the far right but simply doesn’t want the baggage of associating with the far right,” Fuentes told The New York Times. “If he has a problem with ‘antisemites,’ then he should start by disavowing his best friend Tucker Carlson.”
A similar ideological affinity appears to exist between Piker and El-Sayed, whose past statements on 9/11 and terrorism more broadly have a way of creating a moral equivalency between the United States and its Islamist enemies. “Today, I mourn the 3K lives, 6K injuries, & infrastructural devastation in NYC, perpetuated ignorantly in the name of my faith,” El-Sayed tweeted five years ago on the 20th anniversary of the attacks. “Tomorrow, I’ll mourn ~1M lives, millions of injuries, & infrastructural devastation in 3 countries, perpetuated ignorantly in the name of my country.” Earlier this year, after a Hezbollah-inspired terrorist rammed his car into a Detroit-area synagogue where 140 preschool-age Jewish children were playing, El-Sayed said that “hurt people hurt people,” a reference to the fact that the attacker had lost four relatives in an Israeli air strike. (In a clumsy attempt at an apology, El-Sayed stubbornly refused to acknowledge the odious logic of his remarks, allowing only that he had chosen to administer “the right medicine at the wrong time.”)
Like Prince Hal banishing Falstaff from the royal court, sometimes ending a friendship is a sign of the maturity necessary to lead. Barack Obama made just such a choice in 2008 after the hateful and conspiratorial remarks of his longtime pastor, Jeremiah Wright, were exposed to the world. Obama’s relationship with Wright was much more intimate than that between El-Sayed and Piker or Vance and Carlson; he had sat in Wright’s pews for decades, and Wright had baptized his children. And yet Obama ultimately turned his back on Wright, saying that the preacher’s divisive, anti-American “rants” were “an insult to what we’ve been trying to do in this campaign.” Obama understood that as long as he was associated with a character like Wright, he could never be a credible advocate for the national unity he claimed to seek.
J. D. Vance and Abdul El-Sayed each face a much easier decision—and each has failed to make the right one. It’s a testament to Americans’ increasing tolerance for extremism that both men seem to be getting away with it.

The 50th episode of The Health Wrap by The Hindu explores longevity, healthspan and factors that influence health as people age.
Ramya Kannan, Health Editor, The Hindu, speaks to Navin Gnanasekaran, longevity physician and head of Radiology, Apollo Hospitals, Chennai, about healthy ageing and the distinction between lifespan and healthspan.
India’s population is ageing. According to the United Nations Population Fund’s India Ageing Report 2023, the share of people aged 60 and above is projected to increase from 10.5% in 2022 to 20.8% by 2050. The episode discusses what this demographic change means for maintaining health and functional ability in later life.
The conversation covers racquet sports as a key form of physical activity, along with nutrition, sleep, muscle strength, stress, metabolism, inflammation and cognition. It also examines the importance of establishing sustainable health habits.
Physical activity is a key part of the discussion. The World Health Organisation recommends at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity or 75 minutes of vigorous activity a week for adults, along with muscle-strengthening activities on two or more days. For older adults, the guidelines also recommend activities that improve balance and help prevent falls.
Racquet sports are discussed as one form of physical activity. Dr. Gnanasekaran looks at how they can combine exercise with social interaction and cognitive engagement.
The episode also discusses whether longevity advice needs to account for Indian lifestyles and health needs, including food habits, physical activity and other aspects of daily life.
The discussion focuses on the practical aspects of maintaining health and physical function as people live longer, and on the difference between simply extending lifespan and maintaining health during those additional years.

The Press Is Not the Root of Trump’s Problems
He’s in a predicament of his own creation.
This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.
President Trump is going through a rough patch—in foreign relations, in the economy, in the courts, and in election outlook—and he believes that he has found the culprits: CNN, MS NOW, and Politico. On Friday, Trump said he was banning the three outlets from the White House “as a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS” and warned that more bans could come. When he feels beleaguered, he tends to lash out at familiar enemies, especially reporters. The idea that negative coverage is to blame for his predicament is perversely flattering. But Trump’s true scourge is reality, not how the news is covering it.
Although the decision is part of a gradually intensifying attack on free speech, as I noted last month, it has drawn particular pushback. This morning, five major TV networks (including Fox News) agreed to suspend pool coverage of the president and White House events after CNN was blocked from its previously assigned spot in a pool rotation today. The three banned outlets also sued over their exclusion. How such a suit will fare is unclear; Trump banned the Associated Press from the White House press pool last year after it refused to adopt his renaming of the Gulf of Mexico, and a lawsuit challenging the ban is still pending.
After Trump committed a Kinsley gaffe on Friday by calling his move “the ban on the free press,” he tried to clean up his spin this morning. “The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish. It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS,” he wrote, claiming that it “is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!” This is nonsense. Trump has every right to hate the way he’s covered, but if the government has the power to decide what is fake and what is true, then the press is not free.
Trump’s post demonstrates his talismanic belief in the power of news coverage. The president himself has been obsessed with attention—how to get it and how to shape it—for his entire life, and he is a relic from an era when the media were so dominant, and had such control over the means of reaching an audience, that they seemed to shape reality. They are much diminished today, occupying a strange, unstable role: strong enough to be blamed for both Trump’s rise and his downfall, yet weak enough that they can be threatened with relative impunity. Though Trump’s attacks on free speech are unlike any in living memory, his is not the first administration to believe that its problems are about messaging and coverage. In 2012, Barack Obama said that the biggest mistake of his first term “was thinking that this job was just about getting the policy right,” because “the nature of this office is also to tell a story to the American people.” A decade later, Joe Biden’s administration was convinced that negative coverage of inflation and Biden’s age were bigger problems than inflation or the president’s evident frailty.
Now Trump is making the same misjudgment. He is not unpopular because of Politico, an outlet that focuses largely on Washington machinations, or because of MS NOW or CNN, two cable channels that—as he is fond of pointing out—have relatively small audiences for television. The media cannot be “failing” and all-powerful at the same time. Trump is unpopular because (to name a few big reasons) he is losing a war of choice to Iran, making inflation worse without seeming to care how voters feel, overreaching with draconian immigration enforcement, and focusing on vanity projects that don’t matter to voters.
Ironically, Trump is committing the same error as many liberal critics of the press, who seem to believe that popular support for the president would have collapsed long ago if the media had used harsher words to describe him. But the idea that tougher coverage would have stopped him is fantasy. Although the press has made many mistakes in how it has reported on the president, including giving him hours of uninterrupted TV air time in 2016, downplaying bigoted remarks, and “sanewashing” some statements, Trump has also received more intensive investigation and negative coverage than any president in American history.
Some of that coverage has surely been hackish partisanship—which is protected by the First Amendment too—but much of it has been earned. Newspapers, magazines, wire services, and TV networks have turned out a series of scoops about the chaos inside the administration, Trump’s policy errors, and the pervasive corruption around him. In late 2023, The Atlantic published a set of prescient essays considering what would happen if Trump won back the White House. Voters had even lived through one Trump presidency already. They had access to the relevant information before they voted him in again.
Believing that Americans might have chosen differently if only The New York Times had abandoned its obtuse headline conventions is comforting to some Trump critics, because it puts the blame on the press rather than acknowledging that a majority of those who voted wanted Trump. By the same token, Trump would rather blame news outlets he does not like than confront the reality that some of those same voters are rejecting him because of his choices.
The president faces an additional risk in trying to ban these three outlets. He detests adversarial coverage, but he desperately desires attention. This afternoon, Trump spoke with reporters outside the White House. Usually, his comments are captured by the boom mics from the pool TV team, but without their presence today, he was inaudible. Censorship can silence anyone, it turns out—even the censor.

What Were My Dreams Trying to Tell Me?
By Ayad Akhtar
When I was 20 years old, I started to sense a hole inside me. The feeling was utterly concrete, though the result of no medical condition that any of the various doctors I saw could identify. The hole felt like a viscous emptiness—a paradox, admittedly, as any real emptiness should have felt like nothing. This was a nothing, but its nothingness very much felt like something—and something that was growing …
My friends found my behavior disturbing. I was missing class in college, showing up to theater rehearsals drunk. I knew she was right. Even sleep was now fraught with violent, terrifying dreams—of rocket ships out of control, conflagrations and invasions, and, yes, holes into which I would disappear. Meet the Scottish teenagers poised to represent Uganda
- Published
Teenage brothers Olly and Seb Fisher are closing in on their dream of international recognition - but it won't come from their homeland of Scotland.
Instead, the Partick Thistle duo are in line to play for Uganda.
They believe they would become the first white players ever to represent the African nation, thanks to their mother Kate being born there.
"My gran and grandad lived out here for, I think, four or five years," Olly, 18, tells BBC Sport Scotland. "My grandfather came out here to teach in a school then my mum was born here. So, it's a bit of a strange one."
The siblings became aware of interest from Uganda about six months ago, following a chance conversation some time before between their father and a football consultant at a game in Nigeria.
And, at the start of August, they were invited to attend under-20 and under-17s training camps.
They spent last week in Jinja in the country's eastern region and will stay on for one more week, with the pair saying they're "shocked" and "honoured" at the call-ups.
"I couldn't believe it," 16-year-old striker Seb said. "It's one of those things you look at and you're shocked. You can't believe it. Most other people couldn't as well."
Goalkeeper Olly had a similar reaction. "A real mixture of emotions," he said. "I was quite shocked. I didn't really think that this was a possibility but I was honoured to be asked to represent Uganda. I thought it was a real big opportunity."
Mum Kate is "ecstatic" and "thinks it'd be a great experience for us", adds Seb.
'The other boys have been brand new'
There is another Scottish link with Uganda, with former Hearts and Ghana midfielder Laryea Kingston currently coach of Uganda's under-20s.
And he is the one who believes the Fisher brothers are on the verge of making history.
"Coach Kingston was saying we'd be the first white boys to play for Uganda, which would be history in the making," Seb explained. "It is very special."
And Olly added: "It's never been done before, so definitely it is very special."
The pair feel like they're making connections with the African nation, having been reared on stories about Uganda from their grandparents.
And even though they have been training in oppressively warm conditions, they are embracing the opportunity.
"Everyone has been brilliant, welcoming, really great," Seb said. "The other boys have been brand new with us. Some of the boys actually come from the same area where my mum was born. So, they were all talking about that."
The boys will return to Scotland soon, combining training and playing with Thistle with university and school, but are planning to rejoin their new international team-mates in the near future.
Olly hopes to be part of his squad if they qualify for the Under-20's Africa Cup of Nations early next year, and Seb could be in the Under-17 squad for November's World Cup in Qatar.
"That's what you want as a footballer, being in an international environment," Seb said. "It makes you a better player and hopefully it does for the two of us, and I think it will, and benefit us very much going back to Scotland playing at Thistle."

The 51st episode of The Health Wrap by The Hindu explores what constitutes a healthy diet amid the growing focus on protein, along with recent developments in osteoarthritis research, corneal donation and rabies prevention.
Ramya Kannan, Health Editor, The Hindu, and Zubeda Hamid, Senior Assistant Editor, The Hindu, discuss nutrition, weight management, osteoarthritis, corneal donation and transplantation, and rabies prevention.
Protein has become a major focus of nutrition advice, particularly on social media. The episode discusses the role of protein in the diet and why a healthy diet needs to be considered as a whole rather than through the lens of a single nutrient or product.
The conversation also looks at what happens to protein consumed in excess of the body’s requirements. Unlike carbohydrates and fat, protein is not stored in the body as a dedicated reserve. Amino acids from protein are used for functions including tissue repair, muscle maintenance and the production of enzymes and hormones, while excess intake can be used for energy or other metabolic processes.
The episode examines the role of diet and exercise in weight management, including research suggesting that combining dietary changes with physical activity can help support sustained weight loss. It also discusses why overall dietary patterns matter when assessing healthy eating.
Another segment looks at new research into osteoarthritis and cartilage regeneration. The research involves stromal-cell extracellular vesicles derived from menstrual blood and their potential role in cartilage repair. The findings are preliminary and are discussed in the context of ongoing research into new approaches to osteoarthritis care.
The episode also examines challenges in corneal donation and transplantation. Despite the potential of donated corneas to restore vision, some donated tissue does not reach patients who need it. The discussion looks at gaps in the process and the need to improve the use of donated corneal tissue.
Rabies prevention is another focus of the episode. The discussion looks at dog vaccination as an important part of preventing human rabies, given the role of dogs in transmission of the disease.
The episode can also be viewed here at The Hindu health page along with the full playlist of The Health Wrap .

Apple is working on a new fitness tracker with a screenless design, similar to the one made by Whoop, according to a report from Bloomberg. A prototype of the device reportedly has “a thin fabric band with a sensor-equipped computing module.”
Apple is reportedly working on a Whoop-like fitness tracker
The screenless fitness tracker is still in an early stage of development, according to Bloomberg.
The device is in an early stage of development and likely wouldn’t arrive before 2028 if Apple decides to release it, Bloomberg reports. In addition to Whoop’s lineup of 5.0 bands, the company also sells MG — or “medical grade” — variants with a built-in EKG feature. The bands are designed to be worn continuously, as they offer more than 14 days of battery life.
As pointed out by Bloomberg, Apple has added several features already offered by Whoop to its new Apple Watch Series 12, including continuous heart rate tracking. Apple’s Health app also now has a “readiness score” used by Fitbit, Oura, and Whoop, which is supposed to tell you how “ready” you are to work out based on several factors, along with an estimate of your biological age.

These play-it-safe updates aren’t very exciting, but they’re also usually all upside—you get a year or two’s worth of technological improvements for the same price you would have paid for the older version yesterday. Unfortunately, 2026’s unprecedented memory crunch has upended that standard operating procedure.
The new Mac mini starts at $899 for a version with 16GB of RAM and 256GB of storage, a $300 increase for the same memory and storage specs you could get in the $599 M4 Mac mini in 2024.
The M4 Mac mini was a great general-purpose desktop computer and one of the best values Apple had ever offered in a desktop Mac. The M6 Mac mini is only one of those things. I’ll let you guess which.
Note that this review is specifically for the M6 version of the Mac mini. We didn’t get an M5 Pro Mac mini to review, but we’ll talk more about how its pricing and performance fits in for our Mac Studio review.
Design
The M4 Mac minis gave the computers their first full redesigns in nearly 15 years, so it’s not too surprising that the new Mac minis don’t change anything. Compared to the older Intel and M1/M2-era versions, they’re slightly taller (2 inches, up from 1.4), but they have a smaller 5×5-inch footprint (down from 7.7 inches squared). The system is actively cooled, with a fan vent on the bottom to make sure that whatever chip is inside can run at high sustained clock speeds (passively cooled Apple Silicon Macs like the MacBook Air have always been a bit slower than actively cooled Macs with the same chip).
All Mac minis have two 10 Gbps USB-C ports and a headphone jack on the front, and a 2.5 Gbps (default) or 10 Gbps (optional) Ethernet port and HDMI port on the back. Both also have three Thunderbolt ports on the back, but these are Thunderbolt 4 on the M6 Mac mini and Thunderbolt 5 on the M5 Pro version. That means the M6 mini’s ports top out at 40 Gbps, while the M5 Pro mini supports up to 120 Gbps speeds.
The Mac mini’s ports. No USB-A, but otherwise not bad for a system this small.

Realistically, there aren’t a ton of things on a Mac that can use all that bandwidth, especially since Apple doesn’t support external GPUs. But you do need a Thunderbolt 5 Mac to daisy-chain multiple computers together to form a compute cluster, so if that’s something you’re interested in, keep it in mind when you buy—maybe you’re buying multiple desktops, or maybe you already have an M5 Pro or M5 Max MacBook Pro you’d like to test the feature with.
The only real gripe with this design continues to be its bottom-rear-mounted power button; apparently, complaints about this are being sent to the same trash can Apple has always used for complaints about the Magic Mouse’s bottom-mounted charging port. It doesn’t come up often in everyday use if you just let your Mac go to sleep rather than shutting it down. But the positioning problem does really call attention to itself when you pair a TouchID-equipped external keyboard with the mini, since it requires a quick double-tap of the Mac’s power button before the sensor will work.
Meet the M6
Apple’s first M6-series chip is making its debut in the humble Mac mini, and the chip looks like the biggest upgrade Apple’s lower-end chip has gotten since the M4 generation added extra efficiency cores.
The headliner is the presence of two of Apple’s so-called “Super” cores, Apple’s nomenclature for P-cores that are even faster than its typical P-cores. Those are added on top of four P-cores and six E-cores for a total of 12 CPU cores. M4 and M5 both had 10 CPU cores. In the M4, these were split between four regular P-cores and six E-cores, whereas the M5 split them between four super cores and six E-cores (the M5’s cores were referred to as P-cores when it launched but were rebranded later when the M5 Pro and Max came out). The M1, M2, and M3 generations all used four P-cores and four E-cores.
The M6 has fewer super cores than the M5 but the same number of E-cores and four additional P-cores. While they’re apparently no longer “super,” the P-cores still perform well enough to ensure that the M6’s multi-core performance is better than M5’s overall.

Apple has mixed super cores with both other kinds of cores before, but this is its first chip to include all three kinds at once. To get around the awkwardness this might create at the CPU scheduler level, the built-in powermetrics tool suggests that Apple is still treating the M6 like a chip with just two types of cores. The six E-cores are all gathered together in one cluster, and the two Super cores and the four P-cores are all lumped together into a second six-core cluster called the “PS cluster.”
Powermetrics also reports that both the P- and S-cores have the same peak and minimum clock speeds, unlike in the M5 Pro and M5 Max where they’re different clusters with different clock speeds (both P- and S-cores in M6 range from 1.44 GHz to 4.79 GHz). The sysctl utility also suggests they share the same 20MB pool of L2 cache, up from 16MB for the 4-core Super cluster in the M5 (the E-core cluster has a bit more L2 cache, too, 8MB up from 6MB in the M5). The Super cores do have more L1 instruction and data cache, so they are definitely still different cores, and there are likely other differences that we can’t detect using software-level tools. But if you were wondering how macOS was going to treat a chip with three different kinds of CPU cores at a software level, the answer is “to act like it still has two different kinds of cores.”

The M6 gets additional GPU cores for the first time since the M2, increasing the count from 10 cores to 12. These cores include improved versions of the integrated neural accelerators Apple introduced in the M5-series GPU for speeding up AI and machine-learning workloads like ray-tracing and MetalFX upscaling. A “Dual 16-core Neural Engine” also bumps the number of Neural Engine cores from 16 to 32. Saying you have 2×16 of something strikes me as a roundabout way of saying you have 32 of something, but I suppose the end result is the same either way.
One small wrinkle in the M6 variants the Mac mini uses: The basic 16GB Mac mini offers 153 GB/s of memory bandwidth, the same amount as the M5. The 24GB and 32GB versions offer 170 GB/s, an 11 percent increase that should marginally improve graphics performance and the speed of any local AI models you run on this machine. Our review unit is the 24GB version.
What of the M6 Pro, M6 Max, or M6 Ultra? If the rumors are true, the M6 could end up being a lonely chip.
Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reports that Apple isn’t planning a full M6 chip generation and that it could skip directly to M7 branding for the Pro, Max, and Ultra chips. That would be a first for the company, which skipped shipping an M4 Ultra but has otherwise shipped a baseline, Pro, and Max-series chip in each generation so far.
But it makes sense for a couple of reasons. The first is that most of the M6’s gains can be attributed to its extra CPU and GPU cores relative to the M5, and the M5 Pro, M5 Max, and M5 Ultra all obviously still have more of both kinds of cores than the M6 does. The second is that it’s still pretty early for TSMC’s 2 nm process, following three generations where Apple used versions of TSMC’s 3 nm process, and Apple is probably fighting with every other fabless chipmaker on Earth to reserve capacity. Apple could be sticking with smaller, simpler 2 nm chips for now and saving its bigger and more complex chips for later, when capacity will be higher, yields will be better, and costs may be lower.
Performance
The new mini re-uses the launch strategy for last year’s Mac Studios, which used an M4 Max in the base model and an M3 Ultra in the top-tier configurations. The basic Mac mini uses the brand-new M6, while the semi-professional Mac mini tier gets the M5 Pro that we saw in MacBook Pros back in the spring.
This means the M6 mini has newer tech than the more-expensive M5 Pro mini—and marginally better single-core CPU performance, too. The M6’s single-core is roughly 8 to 10 percent faster than the M5 family’s in our benchmarks; graphics performance is also up by roughly 10 percent. In multi-core CPU benchmarks, the M6’s performance is roughly 20 percent faster than the M5.
But for heavy multi-core performance, having more cores is still more important than using the newest cores. The M5 Max (which uses the same 18-core CPU block as the M5 Pro, so it’s a decent stand-in) is still generally 60 or 70 percent faster than the M6 in our multi-core benchmarks.
If you’re comparing the last-generation mini to this one, the upgrades over the M4 are pretty substantial. Single-core CPU performance improves by between 20 and 30 percent in most tests, while both graphics performance and multi-core CPU performance are up by between 50 and 80 percent—and occasionally even more, in some tests. The M6 does nearly as well as the M4 Pro in the Blender benchmark and beats the M5 by around 40 percent, again suggesting that this benchmark in particular is benefiting from the GPU cores’ built-in Neural Accelerators.
Usually at this point we would talk about the chip’s estimated power consumption using the powermetrics tool, a built-in utility that gives clock speed and power consumption data for the CPU and GPU cores in Macs. This is a software-based reporting tool, which makes it imperfect for comparisons between chip generations. But it does at least give us some vague estimate of Apple’s power efficiency.
For the M6, powermetrics doesn’t actually report CPU power levels. It appears in the tool’s logs, but the value is always “0.” I’ve asked Apple whether this is a bug or an intentional behavior change (it still works fine for M5-generation chips), and I’ll update this if I get a response.
About that price
The $599 M4 Mac mini was a tiny, affordable desktop computer with as much speed and memory as most people need for general-purpose computing. You could quibble with the 256GB base storage, but it was still the most usable the basic Mac mini had ever been.
The M6 mini’s $899 starting price sets us way back. That’s a $300 increase in just under two years for a computer that has a faster chip in it but otherwise shares the key specs and most of the capabilities.
One could argue that this merely resets Mac mini pricing back to where it was circa 2020. A base M1 Mac mini cost $699 to start, and upgrading to 16GB of RAM added another $200. It just feels like a big step back, given how great the M4 mini was.
If you need a desktop computer right now for anything from basic browsing to less-intensive local AI models, this is still Apple’s most affordable computer (chatbots and image generation should run pretty well on it; more intensive coding-centric models will be a bit squeezed for RAM and memory bandwidth, even at 32GB). And even the $599 M4 mini was undercut by the kind of lowest-common-denominator cheap mini PCs you could get on Amazon. It’s just hard to swallow the current price, given how much better it was not all that long ago.
The good
An impressively fast and quiet little computer that can fill roles from “entry-level desktop” to “midrange coding and video editing rig.”
M6 is a big step up for Apple’s entry-level chip, with more CPU and GPU cores and other improvements.
Large improvements over the M4 mini, thanks to a two-generation silicon jump.
The bad
Zero upgradability, aside from what you can add with external accessories. What you buy is what you have until you buy the next thing.
256GB of storage in the base model is low, especially if you want to play games or run any kind of AI models locally.
Power button on the bottom is mildly inconvenient on the occasions you have to interact with it.
M6 version can’t be daisy-chained together with Thunderbolt 5 to join a compute cluster.
The ugly
The memory crisis means we can’t have nice things unless we’re willing to pay out the nose for them.
Andrew is a Senior Technology Reporter at Ars Technica, with a focus on consumer tech including computer hardware and in-depth reviews of operating systems like Windows and macOS. Andrew lives in Philadelphia and co-hosts a weekly book podcast called Overdue.

The Manipur Police arrested two persons, including a 40-year-old woman, from Thoubal district’s Lilong on September 14 in connection with the seizure of addiction-causing pharmaceutical drugs. The police found in their possession 50 boxes containing 15,000 capsules of “Tramadol Hydrochloride Tramanil”, weighing about 7 kg.
Also Read: Highest prevalence of opioid use disorders in eastern parts of India: UNODC report
The consignment, allegedly for illegal distribution to specific clients, was seized almost a month after a youth died at a drug rehabilitation centre in the State’s capital, Imphal. He had reportedly been injecting crushed tablets of Tapentadol, an opioid analgesic thrice as potent as Tramadol.
These incidents and the admission of another Tapentadol user at the drug rehabilitation centre with a serious infection due to injections confirmed what anti-narcotic officials and counsellors suspected — drug addicts were shifting to opioid analgesics available as prescription pain management medication from heroin and other narcotic substances made costlier by the ongoing ethnic conflict in Manipur.
“We are investigating to ascertain the source and intended destination of the Tramadol capsules and to determine the extent of involvement of the arrested duo in the possession or distribution of the pharmaceutical drug,” a Manipur police officer said.
The police and drug enforcement agencies in Manipur said data on seizures of opioid analgesics sold or ferried illegally in the State were not immediately available. They, however, said the price factor could have dictated the shift from methamphetamine and heroin, locally known as No. 4.
High prices
The prices of narcotic substances increased sharply after Manipur spiralled into seemingly unending violence in May 2023. According to reports in the local media, a vial of heroin, for instance, costs almost ₹5,000. A strip of Tramadol or Tapentadol costs between ₹40 and ₹400 depending on strength, brand, and manufacturer.
“Tramadol and Tapentadol are painkilling compounds derived from opium alkaloids. Taken for pain relief, they cause a sense of well-being, but can develop dependence if these are taken continuously for a few weeks,” Krishanu Krori, a Guwahati-based medicine specialist, told The Hindu.
“Addicts increase the dosage through injections after typically starting with 50-100 mg. Apart from a sense of euphoria, they develop disinterest in daily activities, withdrawal from family and society, and a craving for violence,” he said.
Counsellors in Manipur said pharmacists should strictly observe prescription requirements and health authorities should monitor emerging patterns of Tramadol and Tapentadol misuse. Hospitals and rehabilitation centres also need updated guidance on dependence, withdrawal, and complications associated with its misuse and injection, they said.
Opioid analgesics have become a worry for enforcement agencies beyond India’s northeastern region too. In August, the Directorate of Revenue Intelligence (DRI) unearthed an organised network involved in the clandestine manufacture, concealment, and illegal export of such drugs, a scheduled psychotropic substance, to African countries.
The seized items included 1 lakh Tramadol Hydrochloride tablets, 1 lakh Tapentadol tablets, machinery, and raw materials. The DRI sleuths arrested three key members of the syndicate during the operation at the Mumbai Air Cargo Complex.

The death of an Anna University student at Government Kilpauk Medical College Hospital (KMCH) on Friday (September 18, 2026), due to scrub typhus, has once again brought this bacterial infection to the fore. University authorities have said they have started screening students for scrub typhus as well, along with dengue and leptospirosis
What is scrub typhus?
Scrub typhus is a bacterial infection caused by the bacterium Orientia tsutsugamushi. It is spread by the bite of infected larval mites or chiggers -- it is not a mosquito-borne disease.
Scrub typhus is a major public health burden in South and Southeast Asia. A 2021 systematic review noted that scrub typhus, a common acute febrile illness, is “a grossly under-recognised public health problem in India.” It stated that the proportion of scrub typhus among acute undifferentiated febrile illness (AUFI) studies was 25.3%, and community seroprevalence was 34.2%. The review also noted that the disease causes severe morbidity and accounts for a large number of deaths, with its bueden “underappreciated.”
A 2025 multi-centre study of 587 children with acute encephalitis syndrome (AES) from Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, and Tamil Nadu revealed that scrub typhus is now the most common infectious cause of AES in southern India.
What are the symptoms?
Symptoms usually begin within 10 days of infection. The United States Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) lists symptoms of scrub typhus as: fever and chills, headache, body aches and muscle pain, a dark, scab-like region at the site of the chigger bite (also known as eschar), mental changes ranging from confusion to coma, enlarged lymph nodes and a rash.
Timely treatment is critical. If left untreated, severe illness from scrub typhus infection can lead to acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), shock, meningitis and kidney failure, which can be fatal, notes a research paper, Incidence of Scrub Typhus in Rural South India published in The New England Journal of Medicine last year.
In India, there is a high mortality of scrub typhus, primarily due to late diagnosis and treatment.
How is it diagnosed and treated?
Since the symptoms of scrub typhus are common to those of several other diseases, diagnosis is often delayed. A blood test (IgM ELISA or PCR) can help confirm the diagnosis.
Scrub typhus should be treated with the antibiotics doxycycline or azithromycin. If the treatment is begun in time, it is effective. Results of a trial carried out in seven centres in India, published in 2023, in which patients were randomly assigned to receive a combination therapy of doxycycline and azithromycin, showed faster resolution of complications compared with two other arms where patients were given monotherapy with either doxycycline or azithromycin. The frequencies of respiratory, renal, hepatic, and central nervous system complications were lower in the combination-therapy group than in either of the monotherapy groups.
How can it be prevented?
There is no vaccine as yet for scrub typhus. The infection is not contagious.
Chiggers live in areas with lots of grass, thick vegetation, agricultural fields, plant litter and bare soil across rural areas of Asia, and usually feed on small mammals such as rats and shrews.
Keeping oneself safe from bites through protective clothing, covered footwear and the use of insect repellent may help. Ensuring surroundings are clean and well maintained can also go some way towards reducing mite habitats.
“Early diagnosis and prompt treatment can significantly reduce complications and mortality. Establishing good surveillance and instituting appropriate control measures are urgently needed,” the 2021 review notes.

Houthis try to push deeper into western Yemen, upending life, witnesses tell NPR
The capture of Western Yemen is making the country's humanitarian crisis worse
DUBAI, United Arab Emirates — As Houthi fighters swept into the western Yemeni port city of Mokha earlier this month, Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces abandoned their armored vehicles and aid groups say families fled with no time to grab their clothes.
Around 125,000 people were displaced in just a matter of days, says the U.N. World Food Programme.
The U.N. says most healthcare facilities in Mokha immediately shut down, but Mokha's General Hospital remained open as staff treated patients who cannot leave.
"There are pregnant women who need urgent care. There are women who need cesarean sections. There are children who need treatment and patients with medical conditions who simply cannot wait," says Sarah Ahmed, a health promotion supervisor with the aid group, Doctors Without Borders, in Mokha's General Hospital.
In a voice memo shared with NPR by the aid group, she says Mokha's hospital staff are focusing on only the most essential services, including caring for babies in the neonatal intensive care unit, or NICU.
Even before the latest fighting, which comes after years of civil war, Yemen was among the world's poorest countries. Years of conflict have led to widespread hunger with some 22 million people — half the population — in need of humanitarian aid.
The current fighting shattered a yearslong truce, and plunged Yemen back into conflict at a time of severe funding shortages and as the U.S. is mired in another Gulf conflict, with Iran. Aid groups say Yemen needs urgent attention and millions more in funding now.
Meanwhile, the World Health Organization says it can no longer transfer patients from Mokha to the government stronghold of Aden in the south, and that the city of Taiz quote "must plan for isolation" as roads to Aden come under fire.
Loading...
As fighting intensifies, crisis to worsen
Doctors Without Borders is one of several aid groups warning that the needs of people in western Yemen will grow as more people are displaced from the frontlines of fighting.
The Houthis, who are supported by Iran, say the Saudi Air Force has launched hundreds of airstrikes across areas of western Yemen since the group captured territory on Sept. 10 and 11, including Mokha. The U.N. confirms some civilian casualties from those airstrikes, as well as hundreds of people wounded in the fighting.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree says the group seized 5,400 square kilometers (about 2,100 square miles) of western territory, including Mokha and islands in the Bab el-Mandeb strait in the Red Sea.
The Houthis' capture of these territories from Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces helps the group, which already controls Yemen's capital, Sanaa, further consolidate control of this key waterway, where they've attacked Saudi oil tankers and blocked them from transiting.
Loading...
The Houthis have also hit Saudi air bases, as well as Saudi oil sites. Saudi Arabia says the Houthis targeted the Saudi capital, Riyadh, over the weekend with missiles, marking the first such attack on the city in years.
Additionally, the Houthis released video of the group downing a Saudi F-15 U.S.-made fighter jet. The Saudi government has yet to comment on that attack, and the fate of the pilots remains unknown.
At the same time, Saudi Arabia says Iran-backed militias in Iraq used drones to hit several areas of its east-west pipeline, which was being used to transport Saudi crude and bypass closures in the Strait of Hormuz. NPR has examined satellite images showing damage to the pipeline's pumping stations.
Those attacks, coupled with the ongoing U.S. war with Iran, have pushed Brent crude past $100 a barrel and diesel to record highs in the U.S.
Houthi leader, Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, released a video message telling Yemenis in western and southern provinces who are fleeing that they are not the target.
"The targets have always been the military build-ups brought by the Saudi aggressor to kill our people," he said, adding that the Houthis target Saudi air bases because they are used to attack Yemen, and Saudi oil sites because they are the kingdom's source of wealth and funding for attacks on Yemen.
Senior Houthi official Mohammed al-Bukthi told NPR this month that the group is imposing a blockade on Saudi oil carriers in Bab el-Mandeb to force Saudi Arabia to lift its air and sea blockade of Houthi areas.
Saudi Arabia and the U.S. say the Houthis receive arms and training from Iran. Officials in Iran do not deny supporting the Houthis, but say the group operates independently.
A Saudi official told NPR the Houthis recently met with White House officials in Oman and told them their attacks are only on Saudi ships, and that they would not attack U.S. or Israeli ships as they had done in previous years to protest the Israeli war in Gaza. The official, who spoke anonymously to discuss security matters, says the U.S. informed the Saudi crown prince about the meeting, and that the U.S. has increased the number of its military experts in Saudi Arabia to assist with planning and to provide intelligence regarding the locations of Houthi forces and weapons depots.
Displacement mostly now in western Taiz
Some of the fiercest clashes now are in Taiz, a southwestern governorate along Bab el-Mandeb, and where the port city of Mokha was captured.
Francesco Galtieri, the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) representative in Yemen shared the story of a single mother burnt by shelling as she fled Mokha with her four daughters, and of another woman who gave birth without any medical care in the open air.
"Unfortunately, currently we estimate around 2,000 pregnant women on the move," Galtieri told reporters during a press conference.
Aid groups, like the Norwegian Refugee Council, tell NPR they're rushing to set up new displacement camps with water, food and mattresses in parts of the governorate of Taiz.
"It's a very dynamic, moving, massive scale of displacement," says Alison Bottomley, an advocacy advisor with the Norwegian Refugee Council in Yemen.
She says people have arrived at camps that are already full of displaced people, and so had to keep walking.
"They move on or they try to find someone in the local villages that will help them. But people are also sleeping under trees. Like they're just waiting on the side of the road," she says.
Many people cannot leave Taiz. The roads to the government stronghold of Aden in the south are under missile fire, says Faisal al-Ossari, who leads the human rights group "The protection of freedoms of Taiz"— and is opposed to Houthi rule.
Others NPR reached in the city of Taiz, which remains under government control, say there have been clashes nearby as the Houthis try to advance.
"There have been attacks on the outskirts of the city, with some kids hit in their spines and facing a lifetime of disability," says Shaef al-Jabri, a Yemeni aid worker in Taiz.
Similarly, Mohammed Radman, with Yemen's Human Access aid group, says the Houthis are trying to take more territory in Taiz. He spoke with NPR from the southern al-Maafer region of the governorate of Taiz.
"We have more than 30 displacement camps here and surrounding areas, with 10,000 families," he said, adding that around 6,000 of these families are newly displaced.
Funding isn't enough for Yemen's needs
The United Nations says only 20% of its funding needs for Yemen have been met this year. Aid groups say far more is needed to reach people displaced this month alone.
"We know how to respond to the needs, we're able to do it, but we really lack the money, the funding that we need to do at the scale that's required now," says Bottomley of the Norwegian Refugee Council.
Doctors Without Borders says years of funding cuts have already left health facilities with little capacity to absorb a new wave of conflict.
Similarly, Prosper Global, formerly known as Mercy Corps, says more aid is needed for their teams in Taiz who are seeing families arriving to safer areas with no more than what they could carry and without enough food, shelter or money to meet their basic needs.
But many cannot wait for the aid to arrive. The U.N.'s International Organization of Migration says that over the course of four days last week, more than 2,400 people fled Yemen altogether, crossing by sea to Djibouti in the Horn of Africa. Most have been women and children, the U.N. refugee agency, UNHCR, says.
Anas Baba in Gaza City, Ahmed Abu Hamda in Cairo and Abu Bakr Bashir in the U.K. contributed reporting.

Dozens of people in the US have filed personal injury lawsuits against the manufacturers of widely used GLP-1 drugs, including Ozempic, Wegovy and Mounjaro, alleging that they were not adequately warned about the risk of a rare form of sudden vision loss.
The condition, known as nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION), affects the optic nerve and can cause sudden, painless loss of vision. Researchers have been examining a possible connection between GLP-1 medicines and NAION, but so far no study has established that the drugs cause the condition, ABC reported.
A potential safety signal was first reported in 2024 following observations at a single health centre in Boston. Since then, researchers and regulators have continued to assess whether there is a link between the medicines and the eye condition.
Novo Nordisk, which makes Ozempic and Wegovy, said it takes “all reports of adverse events very seriously” but disputed the allegations made in the lawsuits.
“Novo believes the personal injury lawsuits filed in the U.S. are without merit and are vigorously defending them,” a company spokesperson told ABC News.
The company added, "Novo is committed to patient safety and continuously monitors the safety profile of our GLP-1 RA products. Should emerging safety data warrant further action, appropriate measures will be implemented in accordance with regulatory requirements.”
Eli Lilly, the manufacturer of Mounjaro and Zepbound, also said it continuously monitors the safety of its medicines.
“Patient safety is Lilly’s top priority. We actively monitor, evaluate, and report safety information for all our medicines to the FDA. As part of our routine safety review process, we have ongoing discussions with regulators regarding potential safety topics, and we will continue to review data, including any data regarding ophthalmic issues," a company spokesperson told ABC News.
Vision-related problems are already included among the possible side effects of the medicines. However, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) does not currently require manufacturers to specifically mention NAION as a risk on their labels.
The FDA's Sentinel Initiative is conducting a review to assess the possible safety signal involving GLP-1 drugs and NAION. The review is still under way.
"The FDA routinely monitors the safety of drug products postmarketing. The FDA identifies safety signals from a variety of sources, evaluates the available data and takes regulatory actions when appropriate,” an FDA spokesperson said in a statement provided to ABC News.
Regulators in some other countries have taken a different approach based on their assessment of the available evidence.
The European Medicines Agency and Australia's Therapeutic Goods Administration have both required drugmakers to include warnings about a potentially increased risk of NAION with certain GLP-1 medicines.
Both regulators have described NAION as a rare possible side effect.

Here is a story that on the face of it seems so wildly unlikely it can only be true. Indeed, the very concept of a romantic documentary sounds almost oxymoronic, an indication of how much nonfiction films have become synonymous with grim histories full of suffering and injustice. Let’s hope this sweet work, directed by Orlando von Einsiedel (who’s made his share of hardcore, suffering-intensive docs including Oscar-winning short The White Helmets) launches a new trend in nonfiction film-making for stuff that makes you happy-cry.
The basic meet-cute happened in 1975, when PK (played by Chirag Lobo in the film’s extensive re-enactments) met Lotta (Mina Dale) in Delhi. He was a poor street artist, a Dalit, the lowest possible caste, once called Untouchables. The real PK Mahanandia appears on screen to explain how he had left his rural village for Delhi in order to get away from all that caste hierarchy. When he met Lotta he pretty much knew he’d met the woman of his dreams because he’d been carrying a horoscope his father had commissioned for him when he was a baby that prophesised he’d fall in love with a woman whose family owned a jungle. Lotta, a backpacker from Sweden, hailed from a clan back home that owned a forest, so that was good enough for PK to believe he’d met his fate. After a chaste holiday romance bloomed between these two crazy kids, she went back to Sweden and he decided to bicycle the 6,000 miles all the way there from India to prove his love.
As we hear the now elderly young lovers describe what they were thinking at the time, we watch Lobo and Dale act out the journey, with poor PK getting into a few scrapes that set him back a few steps as he plods his way westward. Some of the most touching interludes are the interactions he has with strangers along the way that seem incredibly naturalistic and semi-improvised. Cynics might quibble that one can’t help wondering what darker parts of the story have been left out, and note that the actors chosen to play the lovers are a few notches more conventionally beautiful than the actual people – but every love story has its soft focus, flaw-concealing fudges so we’ll let it slide here.

The leaders of France and Canada have pledged closer ties to grapple with rising geopolitical tensions, climate change and the erosion of democratic values, after they met in a French territory off Canada’s Atlantic coast.
The two leaders’ visit to Saint-Pierre and Miquelon – the first by a French president since 2014 and the first by a Canadian prime minister – came just weeks after Donald Trump posted an image showing the islands, as well as all of Canada and other countries in North America, covered by the US flag.
Ottawa has been seeking closer ties with the EU amid an increasingly acrimonious trade war with the US.
“Our societies are being shaken by new storms: the upheavals, caused by climate change, the erosion of democratic norms, and new threats to our sovereignty,” Canada’s Mark Carney said in a statement alongside France’s Emmanuel Macron on Sunday. “The time has come to strengthen our ties.”
Macron added that the two allies agreed to forge closer ties in sectors ranging from space and climate to energy.
“We both believe in democracy, the rule of law, respect for international law, respect for free and fair trade, science as the basis for our decisions, and the strategic autonomy that we defend,” the French president said.
Diplomats said the visit by Macron, who was en route to the annual UN general assembly of world leaders, had a symbolic weight following Trump’s social media post.
The image Trump shared showed the US flag draped over a map of the US, Canada, Greenland, Iceland, Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean, and was labelled “United States of America”. It included Saint-Pierre and Miquelon and French Caribbean territories.
Responding to questions on Trump’s post, Macron dismissed any notion that the territories could not be French and said he did not need to reaffirm that point every day just because “people have strange ideas or say strange things”.
For France, Saint-Pierre and Miquelon is strategically important due to its location on the doorstep of the US and the Arctic.
The territory also occupies a key place in France’s cooperation with Canada, including over energy.
Macron, whose government is facing increased pressure at home over rising fuel prices, said the talks had opened the door for bilateral discussions aimed at sealing concrete deals. 
Paris hopes Canada will broaden its exports of liquefied natural gas to Europe rather than primarily to Asia.
“Canadian liquefied natural gas projects can help. They are important for Europe,” Macron said.
The two leaders also discussed Canada’s relationship with the EU after the bloc proposed that Ottawa become its first associate member, something Macron said France supported.
Trump threatened the EU with “serious tariffs” and a halt to trade after the proposal – an idea he derided as “laughable”.
Any move towards deeper integration is likely to face hurdles. More than a decade after the EU and Canada agreed to the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement, and nine years after its provisional application began, several EU member states have yet to ratify the accord, including France.

Fintech major PhonePe on Tuesday (September 22, 2026) announced that it has secured in-principle approval from the Central Bank of the UAE for two key operating licences, marking its first international expansion footprint.
The in-principle approval covers retail payment services and card schemes (RPSCS), as well as stored value facilities (SVF), the company said in a statement.
The digital payments firm will now work towards obtaining final approval before commencing commercial operations in the United Arab Emirates.
Upon securing final regulatory clearances, PhonePe plans to partner with regional banks, licensed payment service providers, and local technology vendors.
The company also intends to explore opportunities to support the UAE's domestic payment rails, Aani and Jaywan, by leveraging its full-stack technology platform.
"The country’s vision and regulatory environment make it an ideal setting for our international journey. As the UAE advances toward an interconnected, digital-first economy, PhonePe aims to be a committed, long-term partner supporting its evolving ecosystem. By combining world-class technology with local partnerships, PhonePe intends to support the strong economic and trade corridors connecting the UAE, India, and global markets, while striving to deliver elevated everyday payment experiences across the Emirates," Ritesh Pai, CEO and Executive Director, International Payments at PhonePe, said.
At present, PhonePe enables outbound Indian travellers in the Emirates to scan local QR codes and make instant payments across NEOPAY and Network International terminals through a partnership with NPCI International Payments Limited (NIPL).

Nasdaq sets record high on AI optimism, oil drops below $100
NEW YORK, Sept 22 : The tech-heavy Nasdaq hit an intraday record high for the first time since June on Tuesday, while oil prices hit two-week lows as supply showed signs of improving in the Middle East.
Tech stocks reclaimed the spotlight as AI demand showed no signs of abating and corporate earnings stayed resilient.
"We maintain our constructive outlook on the AI trade, supported by rising adoption and monetization, as well as growing capital spending," said Ulrike Hoffmann-Burchardi, CIO Americas and Global Head of Equities at UBS’ Chief Investment Office.
The Nasdaq Composite rose 0.40 per cent, to 27,231.59 while the S&P 500 was roughly flat and the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.40 per cent.
MSCI's gauge of stocks across the globe rose 0.92 points, or 0.08 per cent, to 1,153.33. The pan-European STOXX 600 index rose 0.2 per cent.
Falling oil prices added to risk appetite after a senior Iranian official told Reuters on Tuesday that Tehran can reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days if the United States eases military pressure and lifts its blockade on Iranian ports.
Three sources briefed on the matter also told Reuters that Saudi Arabia has restarted operations at its East-West Pipeline and could resume exports from the Red Sea port of Yanbu later on Tuesday.
U.S. crude was last down 0.47 per cent at $95.33 a barrel and Brent fell to $99.92 per barrel, down 0.43 per cent on the day.
TRUMP-XI MEETING AWAITED
Attention is turning to a meeting between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping later this week, with investors watching for any indications that the leaders of the world's two largest economies can prevent a further deterioration in relations.
Xi arrives in Washington on Wednesday for the first time in more than a decade, helping fuel optimism that a trade truce between the two countries will be extended and there could be potential cooperation over AI.
"For markets, the big question is what’s going to happen when the current one-year trade truce expires in November, and whilst the general tone remains positive, there still isn’t an agreement yet," Deutsche Bank strategist Jim Reid said.
RATE HIKES ON THE WAY
German and US bond yields fell in line with oil. That said, investors are pricing in another round of rate hikes from major central banks, which could limit the decline in debt yields.
US 10-year Treasury yields were down 0.17 basis points on the day at 4.961 per cent.
The dollar gained 0.17 per cent on the euro to $1.1441 and was down 0.03 per cent at 157.33 Japanese yen.
The Bank of Japan raised rates last week to a 31-year high but two dissenting votes and a lack of explicit hawkish guidance disappointed investors, which has left the yen vulnerable and kept traders on alert for signs of official intervention.
"FX intervention remains a blunt tool to prop up currencies, and without a forceful monetary policy response it will be difficult for Japanese authorities to rein in the selloff in the yen," said Matthew Ryan, head of market strategy at Ebury.
The Federal Reserve, by contrast, raised rates last week and warned its fight against inflation was not over, keeping the door open to further tightening.

Richard Marles says the Department of Defence is examining how F-35 fighter jet parts bound for the US from Australia were unexpectedly diverted to Hong Kong.
The acting prime minister said “very much everything that has occurred at the Australian end” will be reviewed, however, he claimed the technology parts were not “sensitive”, as first reported by Politico over the weekend.
The parts, which were being transported by another unknown third party on behalf of manufacturer, Lockheed Martin, still remain unaccounted for months later following their unplanned diversion to Hong Kong.
The last known location of the fighter jet components – in Hong Kong, a special administrative region of China – has sparked concern that some of the program’s technology secrets could have been exposed.
“We are examining [Australia’s involvement], but the point I would make here is that we are confident about the way in which we’ve engaged with the program, and through the US’s prime contractor, Lockheed,” Marles said on Tuesday.
“My understanding is that there is a sense of comfort, and we’re not talking about sensitive equipment here, or sensitive parts.
“Ultimately, though, this is an issue which is going to be managed by the United States and by Lockheed in terms of what has occurred.”
Politico reported sources said the “sensitive” shipment contained on of the jet’s canopies, which reportedly contains stealth technology.
The Guardian has contacted the Pentagon.
While many details have not yet been revealed, Michael Shoebridge, a director for Strategic Analysis Australia who has worked in intelligence agencies, said there were two reasons why China, or another adversary, would want F-35 parts – to reverse engineer them, or to learn how to better exploit and attack them.
Shoebridge added the shipment’s pitstop in Hong Kong was “such an unexpectedly stupid thing” for the manufacturer or Australia to do.
“This is an act of incredible ineptitude and stupidity, and so it’s more the Chinese taking advantage of an incredible stroke of luck brought to them by the stupidity of the people involved,” he said.
Last week, the US State Department announced that the Trump administration would continue with the sale of 48 F-35s to Saudi Arabia, despite reported concerns from the US intelligence community that China could obtain some of the stealth technology.
Australia was one of the early development partners in the F-35. The program spreads the development, supply, management and sustainment of the fighter jets across different countries.
More than 70 Australian companies have production and sustainment contracts with the F-35 program. In excess of 700 of the fighter jet’s “critical pieces” are manufactured in Victoria alone, according to the state government. Australia also hosts a regional distribution hub for F-35 parts in New South Wales.
Australian companies involved in the program’s supply chain have been awarded contracts valued at over $5.2bn, as of September 2025.
Shoebridge said the missing shipment of parts could mean the whole multibillion-dollar fleet is vulnerable to adversaries.
“They’re all now carrying the risk of whatever vulnerabilities this has brought to the to the aircraft,” he said.
“So it’s not just a US-Australia issue. It’s every operator of the F3-5 program [that] has an interest in understanding what happened and what was potentially exposed.”

The story uses screenshots and not the actual viral video in view of its sensitive nature.
A 12-second long video is going viral on social media where a woman is seen bathing in river water while wearing a bikini.
The video was posted on September 15 by X user Barkha Trehan, who describes herself as ‘Activist | Voice Of Men | President, Purush Aayog’. She wrote, “Location : Haridwar. Madam: My Body My Choice. Your take ??” The video garnered over 1 million views. (Archive)
In her X bio, Trehan identifies herself as a “men’s rights activist” and the “president of Purush Aayog”. She also claims to be a TEDx speaker and a “Hindu entrepreneur”; she apparently also “directed a documentary titled The Curse of Manhood”.
Media outlet News 18 Hindi published a report with screenshots from the video pointing out that it had angered social media users. (Archive)
This same video was posted by content creator Piyali Banerjee, where she questioned the “basic decency” and “knowledge of clothing” of the woman.
Other social media users also shared the same video with similar captions, questing the woman for wearing a bikini in Haridwar, with misogynistic comments about her character.
The video is also viral on Instagram.
Fact Check
To verify its authenticity, we ran a reverse image search on a few keyframes from the viral clip. This search led us to a reel posted on Instagram on August 18. The 21-second long reel was uploaded by an account named ‘ishika_pandit’. It showed the same woman bathing at the same spot, but wearing completely different clothes.
This video matched the background of the viral clip with the steel railing on the river and the foundations of a bridge clearly visible in the background. The woman’s hand gestures also mirror the viral video, and the same two men are visible in both videos.
Based on these similarities, it can be concluded that the video uploaded on August 18 is the original footage. The woman in the original video is seen wearing a yellow suit, and not a bikini. Thus, the viral clip is a doctored version of the original video, manipulating the attire of the woman.
Some social media users highlighted the possibility of the viral clip being an AI-generated deepfake, claiming that the woman’s clothes had been purposely changed from a suit to a bikini. (Archive)

Taking a safe bet here that most of you who have heard of Louise Joy Brown have not heard at all of Jean Purdy, or her role in the birth of Baby Brown. Louise Brown was the first baby born of an IVF procedure on July 25, 1978. But this might not have been a joyful story, but for Jean Purdy.
Like all the heroines in this column, Jean Marian Purdy, a clinical embryologist and a critical part of the development of in vitro fertilisation, remained uncredited for a long while. Born in Cambridge, U.K., she went to work with physiologist Robert Edwards and gynaecologist Patrick Steptoe at the Physiological Laboratory in Cambridge. They were working on a high-risk experiment and taking medical science where it had never been before – who would have thought babies could be created in test tubes before the trio managed to show that it is possible.
Purdy trained as a nurse in Addenbrooke Hopsital in Cambridge, and joined Edwards in 1968 as a research nurse and quickly became indispensable to the team. Going back to study the records later, scientists established that it was Purdy who managed the laboratory, prepared and tested culture media, and recorded and organised the data of the early IVF work in the lab. Besides this, the records also put her at the centre of patient care, in this case, supporting women who volunteered their eggs and wombs at a time when public sentiment was entirely against it.
Purdy was the first to recognise and describe the formation of the early human blastocyst – the cluster of cells that forms five or six days after a sperm fertilises an egg, in the culture, a key milestone in pre-implantation development. It represents the early stage of embryonic development, where the embryo implants itself into the wall of the uterus to establish a pregnancy. Purdy was the first to see the embryonic cells successfully dividing in the lab, soon these cells would go on to become on 25 July 1978, she was the first to see the embryonic cells that would become Louise Brown. This moment is significant, because it was the first indication that their pioneering technique had worked.
That was not all; between 1970 and 1985, until her death, she co-authored 26 academic papers with Edwards and others in leading journals, including Nature, documenting methods, outcomes and sophistication that made IVF safe and more reliable.
After NHS funding for IVF was withdrawn following early successes, Purdy helped establish the world’s first dedicated IVF clinic, Bourn Hall Clinic near Cambridge in 1980, and served as its technical director. Again, she helped standardise medical protocols for IVF and scale up treatment, overseeing the birth of more than 500 IVF babies before her death from cancer at just 39 years, in 1985.
In their article The Oldham Notebooks: an analysis of the development of IVF 1969–1978. V. The role of Jean Purdy reassessed, archived in PubMed, Martin H. Johnson and Kay Elder, look at her body of work in early fertility care. The authors pored over the Oldham Notebooks - 21 handwritten laboratory notebooks and loose records kept primarily by Purdy between 1969 and 1978. They concluded that: “Purdy’s interests were clearly focused on the research and development aspects, especially those exploring viable embryo development and improved transfer procedures. For example, in a film made in 1980 (Williams, 1980), she talks about a modification to the transfer cannula that she was trying. Thus, whilst Edwards provided the ideas and the intellectual stimulation and Steptoe the authoritative clinical skills, it is arguable that without Purdy’s systematic approach and dedicated contributions, the project at Oldham may have faltered.”
Despite all this, centuries of sexism weighing in on the scientific community, a classic example of the Matilda Effect, her role was minimised in public memory for decades. Even though Edwards and other colleagues objected to it, Purdy’s name was omitted from a commemorative plaque installed at Oldham Hopsitals, associated with IVF’s breakthrough. Correspondence from Edwards archived at Cambridge later described Purdy as “crucial” to their work, underscoring how her erasure contradicted the team’s own view of her importance. In fact, Edwards’ own records state his growing confidence in her and her essentiality in the team: Purdy was “being ‘particularly good with the patients’, and her ‘cooperation had become crucial. It was no longer just Patrick and me. We had become a threesome’.
However, only Edwards was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for IVF. While recognition for the work that Purdy did, has grown only recently, thanks in good measure to the research of Johnson and Elder, some things cannot be corrected any more. Now, some museums and clinics cite Purdy as the first clinical embryologist, and other institutions have begun naming awards and exhibitions after her. Sidelined again, this time, though her collaborators acknowledged her work, Purdy’s contributions were callously and credit consistently denied.
Though belated, it’s now time to undo the wrongs. It is time to say her name! Say Jean Purdy, shout it out from the rooftops!
