For example, GoPro sent a Laowa 7.5-mm lens for me to test with. When HyperSmooth is on, that's the equivalent of shooting with a 23-mm lens on a full-frame camera. With HyperSmooth off, it becomes a 20-mm lens. I bring this up mainly because if you want to go really wide on the ILS, you'll need a very, very wide lens (fisheye lenses are probably your best bet).
Now for the downside to the ILS: There are no electrical contacts, which means lenses that rely on electronic focus or aperture control probably won't work. For example, my all-time favorite MFT lens, Panasonic's original 20-mm pancake, won't work on the ILS because there's no manual aperture ring.
Your best bet is to stick with fully manual lenses that have a mechanical aperture ring. There aren't many, but there are enough with quality glass to cover a good range of focal lengths. GoPro's Abe Kislevitz put together a nice collection of lenses that he has tested with the Mission 1 Pro ILS, along with his recommendations for various shooting scenarios. Be aware that the camera is sold body-only, and so far, we haven't seen any bundles from GoPro or resellers that include a lens.
And yes, you have to manually focus. I could drop some jokes here about kids today not knowing how to do it, but the truth is, I shoot vintage manual-focus lenses all the time on my Sony A7R II. While I've shot sports and wildlife with these lenses and had a pretty high success rate, I struggled to focus on the ILS.
The problem with focusing on the ILS is the small screen. It's hard to see, not just in bright daylight. It's just really small. There is focus peaking, which uses color banding to indicate what's in focus, but it can be hard to see exactly where it ends, and I've learned from my Sony not to fully rely on peaking.
You can zoom in to get very precise focus, which is what I do on the Sony, but again the small screen makes it hard to see. Worse, for filmmakers especially, you have to have the camera at eye level to focus it well, which limits your shooting ability (or you get to contort into all sorts of weird poses). I would love to see the next Mission 1 Pro ILS get a tilting screen; it's not waterproof anyway, so it doesn't seem like there would be a need to reengineer. GoPro no doubt would suggest using the app on my phone, as it does make it considerably easier to focus, but then you need a cage, and then a handle, and at that point most of the Mission 1 Pro ILS' size advantage is gone; you might as well get a Panasonic GH7, which has an even larger sensor.
Ultimately, while focusing on the small screen is challenging, using a phone or other external monitor sidesteps that issue (and is what pro filmmakers do anyway), but the inability to control the lens iris electronically feels like a bigger limitation since it eliminates a significant number of lenses. It would be nice to see a future Mission 1 Pro ILS support at least electronic connectors for aperture and manual focusing on lenses that require it.
Shooting With the Mission 1 Pro ILS
Once you get past the hurdle of manual focusing, there's a lot to love about the ILS footage. Testing it reminded me more than anything of the Blackmagic Pocket Cinema Camera from several years ago. I can't believe this tiny little thing can match the quality of those early Blackmagic cameras.

Inside Max: The Russian super-app that could spy on millions in Putin’s ‘digital gulag’
The Russian President has ordered officials to switch to Max to restrict the use of foreign software, according to Ukrainian intelligence. Alex Croft reports
Every new digital device in Russia is mandated to come equipped with a messenger app named Max.
But beneath its innocuous white-and-blue logo lies software that experts warn could allow the Kremlin to dramatically expand its capacity to spy on the Russian public.
The app, launched last year by Russian tech company VK, is not only a space for messaging and video calls but serves as a broader information system with the capacity to perform rigid surveillance on citizens.
New research conducted by academics has found tens of millions of people use the platform, which has the potential to serve as a “backdoor” to sweeping invasions of privacy that “undermine the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of information”.
The study conducted by academics at the University of Michigan, University of Calgary, Georgia Institute of Technology, and the Indian Institute of Technology, added that the “Android security model does not have any built-in mechanisms to constrain or audit a super-app”.
By downloading the app, researchers found that Max can screenshot users’ devices and the contents of mini-apps without their knowledge.
Even more worryingly, the app is also able to impersonate users without them knowing and has access to all information stored in apps including messages and payments.
The app also has the capacity to inject code into the mini-apps, which can be used to launch cyberattacks, one of the academics behind the study, Roya Ensafi, told The Guardian.
“What Max provides is the cleverest and also the scariest tactic by authoritarian governments” to surveil their citizens, she said.
The Independent previously spoke to analysts who predicted the app could work as a “spy programme”, allowing Russia’s FSB security service to establish rigid surveillance and that encrypted messaging apps such as WhatsApp would be banned.
With servers based in Russia, Max is subject to Russian law, which grants the FSB to have access to certain materials.
WhatsApp - the global messenger app used by more than 70 per cent of Russians - was banned in February 2026, pushing people towards using Max.
Telegram has faced a reduction in service, with the Russian government saying it has been used for violations of Russian law.
In June 2025, Max had one million users. By October this had climbed to 50 million, in December it rose to 75 million and by March 2026, this number had skyrocketed to 100 million, although the numbers are released by Max and have not been independently verified.
Russian opposition journalist Andrey Okun said last year that Max would be central to the Kremlin’s dream of constructing a “digital gulag”.
Writing for the Republic website, he said in comments reported by The Times: “This will be a sterile space in which the authorities have complete control over the leisure time, motives and thoughts of citizens.”
Experts on Russian technology and surveillance say that the introduction of the app, which is said to have been developed on Vladimir Putin’s orders, is only the latest step in repeated measures to ramp up its ability to monitor the entire Russian online sphere.
“This is a normalisation of Russia's surveillance of its internet use… it's part of a long, long process,” Keir Giles, author of Russia’s War on Everybody, told The Independent.
“The perceived threat from Western communications technology is not something that's new. It's something that has always been a focus for the Russian security services.”
Moscow’s security industry has for decades been frustrated by Russian citizens using foreign software such as Google, Skype and Hotmail, all of which made it much more difficult to read their messages, Mr Giles explained.
Western communications technologies have always been perceived as a threat by Russian security services. After years of trying to clamp down on services such as WhatsApp, the latest move to push Russians towards Max is “really just tidying up at this point”, he added.
Popular apps such as WhatsApp - a messenger owned by Meta, which is designated as an extremist organisation by Russia - have now been banned.
“It would be disruptive and unpopular to [ban it] without having a replacement available,” Mr Giles added.
Mark Galeotti, a veteran observer of Russian security and politics and director of Mayak Intelligence, told The Independent : “The Russian state looks keen to be using sticks rather than carrots... just to kind of drive people towards Max.”
Pushing users towards Max is unlikely to have a significant impact on Russian opposition and activism against the government, Prof Galeotti explained, because they tend to avoid WhatsApp in favour of “more seriously secure” apps such as Proton Mail and Signal.
But it may prompt a significant change in “casual dissent”, he added. “That's where it might have a freezing effect: people who might be under other circumstances willing to send messages with slightly scurrilous content about the Kremlin might think twice.”
Russia previously attempted to block the Telegram messaging app in 2018. But the attempt failed, and did not practically affect the availability of Telegram in Russia, leading it to be officially unblocked two years later. However, it is subject to restrictions.
Max has been contacted for comment.

The future is looking increasingly bleak for Germany’s automotive industry. Since the turn of the century, car makers have been among the crown jewels of the German economy, punching above their weight in terms of investment and innovation. But those companies are now facing multiple problems at once, from declining demand at home and stronger competition from abroad to the cost of punitive and arbitrary new tariffs, on top of preexisting structural challenges like an aging workforce and a slow recovery from COVID.
Total automotive sales in Europe have fallen from a peak of almost 18 million in 2019 to around 13 million in 2025, and some share of that smaller market is increasingly going to new entrants from China, which has its own spare automotive production capacity problem to worry about. And while the US market has always been the most profitable for German car exports, that was before the imposition of new import tariffs, which currently stand at 25 percent but could be subject to change at any time.
Factory closures now seem not just possible but likely, something that would have been unthinkable just a few years ago. Earlier this summer, news emerged that Volkswagen Group is considering closing four of its German factories to prepare for the future. Things have not gotten much better for VW Group in the months since that news broke.

IIT Bombay student death: Maharashtra minister says caste angle being politicised
A Maharashtra minister has alleged that politicians are giving a casteist colour to the IIT Bombay student's suicide case. The remark comes amid protests, a police case against a professor and demands for a fast-track probe.
Maharashtra minister and Shiv Sena leader Pratap Sarnaik on Tuesday alleged that some politicians were trying to give a casteist colour to the death by suicide of an IIT Bombay student, even as the case continued to draw protests and calls for a speedy investigation.
Sahil Ravindra Wakode, 22, a second-year BTech student in the Department of Energy Science and Engineering, was found hanging from a ceiling fan in his hostel room on IIT Bombay's Powai campus on the evening of September 18. His death has led to student protests and a police case against a professor under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita and the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, based on a complaint by his parents alleging caste discrimination and harassment.
"His father has complained about the casteist angle. Some political people are trying to give casteist colour to the issue. This is wrong. This should not happen in the education sector," Sarnaik said.
Shiv Sena spokesperson Shaina NC said the crime branch was properly carrying out its investigation in the case. She also demanded that the case be fast-tracked so that justice could be delivered to the student's family.
IIT Bombay on Monday removed Suryanarayana Doolla as dean of Administrative Affairs after protests by students and political activists over Wakode's death. A case of abetment and caste discrimination had been registered against him.
According to investigators, CCTV cameras inside the examination hall captured Wakode's movements before a professor approached him and led him away from other students after he was allegedly caught copying. Later footage showed him walking across the campus to his hostel room after leaving the examination hall. He was not seen leaving his room after that.
Earlier, IIT Bombay Faculty Forum president Dr Rajkumar Pant had said that the student had not approached the institute's SC/ST cell with any complaint in the recent past. The case has since led to protests, political reactions and an ongoing investigation into the allegations made by Wakode's family.

Landslide warnings remained in force on Tuesday after the 25th typhoon of the season left thousands without power and ruined holiday plans
Nearly 2 million people were instructed to evacuate their homes in low-lying coastal areas, or be prepared to move at short notice, after the Japan Meteorological Agency had warned that the typhoon posed an “imminent threat to life”.
While the evacuation order has since been lifted, authorities are still warning residents to beware of landslides in areas where heavy rain has destabilised hillsides.

A British woman kidnapped in Malawi last week has been rescued by police after a shootout in which four of her alleged abductors were killed.
Nusrat Osman was abducted outside her home in the southern city of Blantyre on 11 September at about 12.30pm. Police had offered a reward of 30m Malawi kwacha (£12,950) for information leading to her rescue and the arrest of the perpetrators.
Malawian police announced Osman’s rescue late on Thursday in a statement. “There was an exchange of fire between police and kidnappers, who were armed with [an] AK47 rifle and a Girsan Regard MC pistol. In the process, the criminals got shot and were taken to hospital where they succumbed to their injuries.” it read.
A police officer, deputy inspector general Mlowoka Noel Kayira, was also shot during the operation. “He is currently receiving medical attention at the hospital and is in a stable condition,” police said.
Osman, a 47-year-old auditor and mother of two, was safe and “not too shaken” after her ordeal, her brother Shobi Jiwa told the Sun, expressing his gratitude to Malawi’s police.
Jiwa reserved special thanks for Kayira. “He is the hero of our family. He’s the hero of the country,” he said. “He’s the hero of the world, actually, for putting his life at risk and taking a bullet into himself for my sister.”
Kidnappings are rare in Malawi, which has experienced a rise in pickpocketing and house burglaries by often armed men in recent years amid unstable, crisis-ridden economic conditions.
The landlocked southern African country is one of the world’s poorest nations, with a population of about 22 million and an average annual income of just $672, according to the World Bank.
In 2024, a country report by the US state department’s diplomatic security service said: “Kidnappings are not a widespread concern in Malawi, and there have been no recent high-profile incidents involving westerners.
“Historically, expatriates have not been significant targets for kidnappings in the country. When kidnappings do occur, they often involve members of the Asian business community rather than foreign travellers or residents.”
Osman, who is originally from Leicester, worked for a local audit firm and had lived in Malawi with her husband and children for several years. Before her rescue, her family said they had not had any news of her, including any contact from the kidnappers demanding a ransom.
Her husband, Nazil Osman, told the local news outlet Nyasa Times: “I don’t know where she is or how she is. My wife is an auditor, and I have no issues with anyone.”
Her brother told the Sun on Tuesday: “My sister has been missing for five days with no trace or call,” adding that the family could not think of a motive for her kidnapping.
Police did not say whether information received in response to the offered reward had led to Osman’s rescue, adding that investigations were ongoing and more details would be shared “in due course”.

Robotaxis aren't always a smooth ride - here's what passengers should look out for
Waymo, Zoox and Tesla have all faced challenges.
Autonomous car manufacturers have long claimed that self-driving vehicles would reduce traffic accidents. Thus far, the stats are largely in their favor. According to a report by the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS), Google's Waymo robotaxis were involved in roughly 65 percent fewer car crashes than human drivers last year. Waymo's own internal statistics, meanwhile, claim that the autonomous vehicles (AVs) reduce accidents with serious injuries by 94 percent. Some critics are understandably dubious, however, noting that more testing needs to be done before anyone can meaningfully certify these safety gains.
A September 2026 report by TechCrunch adds further fuel to the AV skepticism fire. Using exclusive OSHA data, the publication reported that Waymo and Zoox, the steering wheel-free robotaxi company owned by Amazon, caused dozens of injuries to test drivers while training their autonomous vehicles last year. According to the report, drivers experienced sprains and whiplash due to sudden stopping and other mistakes while training AVs to drive around major cities. TechCrunch noted that the dataset is somewhat incomplete, due in large part to the narrowness of OSHA's reporting mandates. Inside sources noted that injuries continued to occur at Zoox throughout 2026, although little is known about the results of Waymo's more up-to-date tests.
The report is just one of several data points that have raised questions about the immediate feasibility of self-driving vehicles. Tesla's robotaxis, for instance, recorded more accidents than their human counterparts during their rollout in Austin, Texas. Meanwhile, news reports are flush with anecdotes of AVs plowing over traffic barriers, swerving into oncoming traffic, running red lights and driving into police standoffs. And while these issues occur relatively infrequently, some experts are concerned that they are likely to become more pronounced as the technology spreads.
Assessing safety records
Autonomous vehicles struggle when road conditions become uncertain. In July 2026, Amazon's Zoox recalled over a hundred vehicles because they failed to identify smoke, following an incident where a software glitch caused a vehicle to drive into an active emergency. A few months earlier, Waymo issued a similar recall after several taxis drove into flooded streets. Tesla, which recently launched its Cybercab robotaxi service, faced a federal probe over its self-driving software's struggles in reduced-visibility environments. Other examples include a Waymo recall for driving into closed roads and construction zones, the breaking of school bus safety regulations, and interference with first responders.
One of the most dangerous safety issues are autonomous vehicles' penchant for sudden stops. According to TechCrunch, brake jabs were the most common cause of injury for AV testers, often caused by phantom debris. A report by researchers at the University of California Irvine further underscores the issue, noting that AVs often make dangerous stops when detecting harmless objects on the side of the road. Tesla, meanwhile, faced a four-year-long NHTSA probe over phantom braking issues.
Software glitches can also cause robotaxis to suddenly stop in traffic. For instance, Zoox contractors told TechCrunch that the company's software systems sometimes shut down, causing a sudden and dangerous stop.
System malfunctions and situational factors, such as power outages, can also cause your robotaxi to block traffic. In Wuhan, China, a system malfunction caused at least 100 robotaxis to stop in the middle of the road. Similar traffic congestion has occurred in San Antonio, Los Angeles, San Francisco and Atlanta, to name a few.
This shouldn't scare you away from using robotaxis. Instead, it is a reminder that the technology is far from infallible. As a passenger, you should always approach an autonomous ride with an appropriate amount of caution, and stay on the lookout for potential warning signs.
What to do when your Robotaxi acts up
But how can you tell that your ride is on a one-way street to Dangertown? Of course, erratic behavior like unpredictable swerving, unreasonable speeds, breaking traffic laws and sudden braking are obvious red flags. But more subtle issues may point to larger issues. Taking unnecessarily complex routes and missing stops can indicate problems. Technical glitches with your app or your car's display screen can be equally reflective of a potential software mishap.
Ultimately, the most important question may be whether you are prepared to respond during a malfunction. Luckily, most robotaxis allow users to end their rides if they detect a problem. Waymo, for instance, provides a Pull Over command in its phone application and in-car display. When pressed, the robodriver will navigate to a safe stopping place. If you have trouble finding the feature, check your display's cabin preferences section.
Similarly, Tesla's Cybercab service provides a Pull Over option in its app and vehicle touchscreen. You can also press the Stop button between the cabin overhead lights. Zoox, meanwhile, provides an Emergency Call Button in its overhead section. Pressing the button will connect you to Zoox Support, who will bring you to a safe stopping point. Knowing the protocols of your selected taxi service is essential to ensuring you stay safe whenever an algorithm takes the wheel.
If your robotaxi does get in an incident, treat the crash like you would any other car accident. Observe standard safety precautions and call 911 if you or anyone else is seriously injured. For the most part, your robotaxi should automatically contact its support service to help manage the situation. However, if the service fails to reach out, contact the company via their app to initiate its accident protocol.

Trump heads to U.N. looking for wins after a rough week
President Trump touted his war in Iran in his speech before the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday, claiming the U.S. acted while other world leaders hesitated.
"I hope the Europeans realize that Iran's goal was to complete their mad dash to a nuclear bomb from behind this conventional ballistic missile shield, if they had succeeded, that wicked regime would have been free to spread terror and death forever, knowing that any attempt to stop them would face an arsenal of nuclear annihilation," he said.
Trump spent the beginning of his speech touting the U.S. economy, his immigration policy, and the drop in violent crime.
"The entire world is being lifted by the wealth, strength, spirit, and momentum of a newly energized and a very powerful United States of America," Trump said.
President Trump is addressing world leaders at the U.N. General Assembly after a challenging few weeks with a series of legal and political setbacks. He's also riding a wave of low approval — below 40% — thanks in part to growing concerns about the economic fallout from the Iran war. He's also facing blowback after banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House. The news organizations have sued to regain access.
Less than two months from the midterm elections, Trump is looking for wins as he kicks off a high-profile week of diplomacy at the U.N. before hosting Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington.
In his speech, Trump painted himself as a peacemaker, highlighting peace deals he's announced around the world while defending his Iran policy.
"The president will highlight how he has, and his administration, have confronted complex problems head-on around the world," U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Mike Waltz told reporters, adding later: "He will touch on the importance of ensuring that Iran never has a nuclear weapon."
Undoubtedly, leaders will be eager to hear what the U.S. president has to say. He often makes news.
The first time he addressed the U.N. General Assembly in 2017, Trump threatened to totally destroy North Korea. The second year he boasted that his administration had accomplished more than any other in American history. Some leaders laughed out loud.
Last year, Trump blasted the U.N. and told leaders "your countries are going to hell."
"What is the purpose of the United Nations?" Trump asked. "It has such tremendous, tremendous potential. But it's not even coming close to living up to that potential."
Speaking of wins, Trump may want to tout his recently announced new deal with Denmark over security of Greenland.
He will also defend his decision to strike Iran. Interestingly, he'll be doing so in front of Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, who is expected to speak after Trump on Wednesday.
Much of the diplomacy will be happening on the sidelines of the event.
Trump is expected to meet with Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, as well as Gulf leaders, and Venezuela's interim President Delcy Rodríguez.
The importance of those meetings speaks to the changing role of the UN as an institution, said Richard Fontaine, who served in the George W. Bush White House and now runs the Center for a New American Security, a Washington, D.C.-based think tank focused on national security issues.
"The meat of the diplomacy will be done in the private meetings, not at the U.N. Security Council or in the U.N. General Assembly," Fontaine said.
The U.N. security council has also struggled to come to agreement on key issues.
Another issue at the top of the agenda is artificial intelligence. A U.N. panel recently called for stronger safeguards on artificial intelligence agents.
Leaders are expected to try to come to some kind of global agreement on guardrails around the advancing technology.
The dilemma is that so many of these issues revolve around China and President Xi won't be there, said Heather Conley, who worked on European issues in the Bush State Department.
"So this is the challenge," Conley said. "In many ways we have global leaders coming to New York to offer their own set piece speeches, how they look at the world. But the world will not be looking towards New York on Wednesday and Thursday of this week. They're going to be looking at Washington."
That's because Xi will not be traveling to New York. He will instead be traveling to Washington, D.C. for a state dinner with Trump.

Why a new Pakistan-China border pact has irked India
- Published
For decades, India has refused to recognise a Pakistan-China boundary in a disputed part of the Himalayas that Delhi claims as its own.
But last week, Pakistan and China formalised a boundary in a remote part of the mountainous region, drawing a sharp response from Delhi.
The two countries signed the Pakistan-China Boundary Joint Commission, an agreement which Pakistan described as a "significant milestone" that would deepen cooperation on border management, trade and connectivity between India's regional rivals.
Delhi rejected the move as having no legal basis, saying it did not recognise any Pakistan-China boundary located in territory it claims as Indian.
The announcement comes at a particularly sensitive moment.
India and China are seeking to stabilise their relationship after years of military tensions along the Line of Actual Control (LAC), the disputed line separating their forces along much of their Himalayan frontier. At the same time, Beijing and Islamabad are deepening cooperation along a neighbouring stretch of the frontier that India also claims.
"There is no boundary between Pakistan and China. We reject the so-called Joint Commission, which is without any legal basis," Indian foreign ministry spokesman Randhir Jaiswal said.
The commission concerns the Pakistan-China frontier, including the Shaksgam Valley, a roughly 5,180 sq km tract that Pakistan ceded to China in 1963 but which India claims as part of its territory in Ladakh.
India says the territory was part of the former princely state of Jammu and Kashmir and was illegally occupied by Pakistan before being ceded to China. The Indian government has never recognised the agreement and considers it illegal and invalid.
This history explains the particular sensitivity of Wednesday's announcement.
"Pakistan has no locus standi to enter into arrangements concerning Indian territory under its illegal and forcible occupation," the Indian foreign ministry said.
Pakistan says Jammu and Kashmir remains a disputed territory, and argues that India therefore has no standing to challenge its 1963 boundary agreement with China. It regards the agreement as valid.
Jabin T Jacob, professor at the Department of International Relations and Governance Studies at Delhi's Shiv Nadar University, said the new development represented the revival of an old mechanism rather than an entirely new arrangement.
"A joint boundary commission is provided for in the 1963 Sino-Pak Agreement, the only issue at hand is the timing of its operationalisation," he told the BBC.
He said there could be several reasons for the timing, including China's broader effort to demarcate its boundaries and a desire to institutionalise exchanges and movement along a frontier at a time when Pakistan's other borders have experienced conflict and instability.
Jacob said India should be "worried" by the development. More importantly, he said, the move appeared to disregard a provision in the 1963 treaty itself.
Article 6 of the agreement provided for its renegotiation once the Kashmir dispute was settled with whichever country ultimately controlled the territory, Jacob said.
For India, Jacob said, the problem is compounded by the international information environment.
"China's relative dominance of the international media and information landscape - [with] CGTN, CRI, presence on social media - relative to India allows it to put forward its narrative and maps globally while India is limited to fulminations that other world capitals are likely to ignore," he said.
That concern is distinct from the practical management of the frontier itself. Pakistan and China already have extensive infrastructure and connectivity links across the region, including the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) and the Karakoram Highway.
Husain Haqqani, former Pakistani ambassador to the US and now a senior fellow at Anwar Gargash Diplomatic Academy and Hudson Institute, said the new commission was both practical and political.
"It is a combination of both," Haqqani told the BBC. "It is a mechanism to enhance border and boundary cooperation, prevent illegal crossings and protect the strategic infrastructure tied to CPEC."
He said it also served as a signal to India that Beijing continued to view Kashmir through the Pakistani prism.
"China has never accepted India's position on Kashmir and China views Gilgit-Baltistan from the Pakistani, not Indian prism," Haqqani said, referring to the region in Pakistan-administered Kashmir that borders China and which India claims as part of its territory.
Haqqani said Islamabad's position had evolved in response to developments in Indian-administered Kashmir.
"Pakistan still maintains that the final status of Jammu and Kashmir is yet to be decided," he said. "But since India has made internal changes - for example, the abrogation of Article 370 - in its part of Kashmir, Pakistan sees no issue with simply institutionalising what has been de facto with China since 1963."
For Beijing, the arrangement also fits into a broader pattern of using its relationships with neighbouring states to manage and signal its position towards India.
Haqqani said reassurance to Pakistan on Kashmir was of both strategic and geopolitical value to Beijing.
"On the strategic front it further deepens ties with Pakistan and on the geo-strategic front it reinforces for India its fear of a two-front threat from China and Pakistan, which pleases Pakistan and benefits China."
The timing of the statement, say experts, is also significant.
"China always plans its decisions months, if not years, in advance so the decision to operationalise a joint boundary commission must have been made some time back," says Haqqani.
"The release of this information was timed for after President Xi Jinping's recent Brics summit trip to send Pakistan a message of reassurance in the strategic partnership, and India a reminder that multilateral engagement does not translate into any change in China's vision for South Asia."
But Jacob cautioned against interpreting every aspect of the development as a direct military move against India.
"There aren't any immediate or apparent implications for the LAC as of now," he said.
That suggests that the significance of last week's announcement may lie less in an immediate change to the disputed Himalayan frontier than in the gradual institutionalisation of arrangements that India has consistently rejected.
India's position, Jaiswal said, remained "clear and consistent": any attempt to legitimise what Delhi considers Pakistan's illegal occupation of Indian territory is unacceptable and has no bearing on India's sovereignty.
But Haqqani believes the dispute goes beyond the legalities of borders.
"The key disagreement between India and China about the border and boundary is geo-strategic, not cartographic," he said. "So there is a limit to what border negotiations and border management mechanisms can achieve."
Pakistan, he added, remained "China's secondary deterrent against India" - and Beijing's engagement with Islamabad would continue to send that message to Delhi.

A video is going viral on social media (here, here, and here) claiming that Prime Minister Narendra Modi said he would eliminate poverty from the country in one stroke. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows Prime Minister Narendra Modi saying that he will eradicate poverty from the country at once.
Fact: The viral video is presented out of context to make it appear that Prime Minister Narendra Modi said he would eradicate poverty from India in a single stroke. In the original video, PM Modi was referring to Congress leader Rahul Gandhi’s earlier statement about eradicating poverty and questioning the claim, rather than making the claim himself. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to an extended version of the same video uploaded on Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s official YouTube channel on 14 April 2024, titled “PM Modi addresses a public meeting in Hoshangabad, Madhya Pradesh”. According to the video description, PM Modi addressed a public meeting in Hoshangabad ahead of the 2024 Lok Sabha elections and paid tribute to Dr Babasaheb Ambedkar on his birth anniversary. At the 28:05 timestamp, PM Modi can be heard referring to a statement by Congress leader Rahul Gandhi, saying that Gandhi had claimed he would eradicate poverty from the country in a single stroke.
PM Modi said, “Modi’s guarantee begins where expectations from others end. That is why a desperate Congress is making announcements that even its own leaders fail to comprehend. The Congress ‘Prince’ made a declaration that would make you laugh too: he claimed he would eradicate poverty from the country in a single stroke. The entire nation is astonished to hear this. People ask where this ‘royal magician’ has been hiding all these years. Fifty years ago, his grandmother had announced the eradication of poverty. Before 2014, they ran the government via remote control for a decade. And now, they claim to have found a magic mantra that can do the job in one stroke. Where did they get this ‘one-stroke’ mantra? Tell me, isn’t this a mockery of the poor? Isn’t this an insult to the poor? You tell me, can poverty really be eliminated in a single stroke? What are they saying? Who would trust them? It is because they make such claims that they become a laughingstock across the country; the nation does not take them seriously.”
We also found that the Bharatiya Janata Party’s (BJP) official YouTube channel uploaded the same video on the same day, featuring a longer version of the viral clip.
The full transcript of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s speech at the Hoshangabad rally was also available on his official website. The transcript confirms that PM Modi was referring to Rahul Gandhi’s claim about eradicating poverty in a single stroke, rather than making the claim himself, as the viral video suggests.
A few days before PM Modi’s rally, Rahul Gandhi said at a rally in Anupgarh, Rajasthan, “The Congress government will give one lakh rupees annually to one woman in every family. One lakh rupees, or 8,500 rupees every month, will be deposited into your bank account every year, and in one fell swoop, we will eradicate poverty from India.”
To sum up, PM Modi did not say he would eradicate poverty in one stroke; he was referring to Rahul Gandhi’s earlier statement.

The Enforcement Directorate (ED) has chargesheeted EaseMyTrip cofounder and chairman Nishant Pitti in the Mahadev online betting app money laundering case, accusing him of facilitating the entry of alleged illegal betting proceeds into the Indian stock market through FPIs. The ED filed its fifth supplementary prosecution complaint before a special PMLA court in Raipur on September 10, according to The Indian Express. This is the sixth chargesheet filed by the agency in the wider money laundering investigation. The agency also provisionally attached demat shares belonging to Pitti worth ₹59.6 Cr under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA). It has sought the court’s permission to confiscate the shares, alleging that they constitute proceeds of crime. Responding to Inc42, Pitti said he was not aware of any chargesheet and had not been summoned by the jurisdictional court. “I have always strived to uphold the highest standards of governance and ethics in my professional and personal dealings,” Pitti said, adding that all his transactions comply with applicable laws and that his assets were acquired through lawful sources of income and formal banking channels. He further said he would contest any contrary allegations before the courts and expressed confidence that the legal process would establish the facts. Pitti also urged against speculation around ongoing judicial proceedings. "I shall submit detailed evidence to establish my bona fide conduct, in accordance with the procedure prescribed by law," he added. Separately, EaseMyTrip said it had not received any formal communication regarding legal proceedings against the company or Pitti. “Easy Trip Planners Limited has not received any formal intimation of legal proceedings against the company or its director, Mr Nishant Pitti,” an EaseMyTrip spokesperson said. Pitti’s name first surfaced in the ED’s investigation last year. In April 2025, the agency conducted searches at multiple locations linked to Pitti and EaseMyTrip across Delhi NCR, Mumbai, Chandigarh, Ahmedabad, Indore, Jaipur, Chennai, and Sambalpur. Pitti was subsequently questioned by the agency. The ED alleged then that Pitti was connected to a network of operators accused of using betting proceeds to manipulate the stock prices of several listed companies. At the time, EaseMyTrip denied any direct or indirect association with the Mahadev betting app or any other betting platform and said it was cooperating with the authorities. ED’s Mahadev Betting Case Probe The latest development comes after Mahadev betting app promoter Sourabh Chandrakar was detained by the Royal Oman Police earlier this year following an Interpol Red Notice issued at the request of the ED and the Chhattisgarh Police. Indian authorities are seeking his extradition or deportation. In March, the ED provisionally attached properties worth ₹1,700 Cr belonging to Chandrakar and entities allegedly linked to him in Dubai and New Delhi. The assets included 18 luxury properties in Dubai, including villas and apartments in Burj Khalifa, Dubai Hills Estate, Business Bay, and SLS Hotel & Residences, besides two properties in New Delhi. The agency alleged that the properties were acquired using proceeds from illegal betting operations and held through entities controlled by Chandrakar and his associates. According to the latest available figures cited in the chargesheet report, the ED has arrested 14 people and attached assets worth ₹1,885 Cr in the case so far. Shares of EaseMyTrip were trading 2.41% higher at ₹5.94 on the BSE at 14:35 IST.

Jenee Gragston dropped to the ground and held on to the grass as if it could save her life. She yelled to her family members to get down. She later told me that she didn’t know where the bullets were coming from, but she knew they were close. When the firing stopped, the cries began. She could hear her 4-year-old nephew howling: “Get it off me! Get it off me!” She wasn’t close enough to see what had happened, but it looked like he had blood on his chest. A teenage boy was lying near the child. The teenager “never screamed or anything,” she said. “I can still see all of it.”
It was a Saturday afternoon, mid-August in Lexington, Kentucky. Hundreds of people had gathered in Charles Young Park to celebrate what’s called East End Day—a combination of family reunions, live music, and lots of food. I grew up going to festivals in that park, though I lived on the west side of town, in the Charlotte Court housing projects.
Kentucky isn’t the most dangerous place in America, but it’s up there, with the 14th-highest rate of gun deaths. Twelve years ago, my uncle was murdered in Lexington. Three years ago, my sister’s husband was shot and killed there. I worry about my brother, who still lives there. He had gotten himself off the streets for a while, but is now back living in the city. Lexington had recently seen a hard-won drop in gun deaths—last year was the fourth straight year of declines in gun violence among young people. This spring and summer set a record of 190 straight days without a homicide. Then came the East End Day shooting, which killed that teenager, 16-year-old Di’Zhon Robertson, and wounded four others—including the 4-year-old, who was shot in the leg. The next weekend, another person was killed. The weekend after that, four separate shootings left two more dead.
Gragston was selling Polish sausages in the park. She’d paid more than $300 for the grill, $300 for the sausages, more than $1,000 in fees, $75 for the booth. Business was good; some people returned for seconds. Her husband, her kids, and other family members had come to help her set up her tent. Her 4-year-old nephew was handing customers sodas and water bottles. On the basketball court nearby, Devine Carama was talking with a group of young people. Carama is the director of ONE Lexington, a city-funded program that tries to prevent gun violence by mentoring at-risk boys. He, too, threw himself down when he heard gunfire. “I almost got shot that day,” he told me. Two people near him were hit—a man and his girlfriend. Carama and others tried to bandage the man’s leg; he told me he could see a glimmer of bullet or bone through the blood.
A day later, 18-year-old Jametrius Griffin turned himself in and was charged with murder. According to court testimony, Griffin’s younger brother had gotten into an argument; punches were thrown, and the younger brother fell or was pushed. When Griffin saw that, he yanked out a gun and started firing.
For the past three years, Robertson had participated in ONE Lexington’s summer youth program, which offers workshops on building emotional and social skills, as well as college-campus visits. “He wasn’t a street kid,” Carama said. Griffin’s younger brother was in ONE Lexington, too—in its school mentoring program. The organization had also helped Griffin get a job at UPS. The group’s work seemed to be making a difference. And then a fight left one young man dead, one wounded, and one in prison.
In many ways, Lexington feels like a small town, where everyone knows everyone. I went to middle school with Griffin’s lawyer, Daniel Whitley, who has a big reputation locally for representing people accused of murder—and for winning their cases. The week after the shooting, I spoke with Whitley and with Griffin’s mother, Jay-Me Baxter, on a video call.
“A bunch of bullshit” was how Baxter described the park shooting, “because everybody’s friends and everybody’s family.” She said her youngest son told her he had been bullied by Di’Zhon Robertson and others. The day after the shooting, she made the same argument in a video she posted on Facebook that outraged many in the community. She suggested that her older son had had no choice and said she didn’t care “who makes it home as long as mine do.” (I tried to reach Robertson’s mother through family members to see if she would talk with me about what happened to her son; her sister replied that the family didn’t want to relive it. But friends and family members described the teenager as quiet, observant, and “very respectful.”)
“I’m like, Shit, I know Di’Zhon’s mama,’” Baxter told me—the other mother was close friends with her own sister. Baxter said she had had a conversation with her about the beef between the boys, and assumed the issue had been settled. Griffin loved football, and he had started college at Kentucky State University. “But you know them kids,” she said. “They be doing stuff in silence.” Her son must have been simmering with fury.
I knew Baxter’s family growing up—she’s a year older than me, and they, too, lived in the Charlotte Court housing projects. She didn’t remember me, but she knew my brother. Her mother was white, and had nine children. Baxter, the third-oldest, is half Black, like her younger siblings. But the oldest two are white. Her mother used to cry, Baxter told me, because “the white kids didn’t ever live with us.” In our majority-Black neighborhood, a white mother with mixed-race kids stood out. Baxter remembers people throwing rocks through their windows and a lot of name-calling—“white bitch.” Her family was poorer than many others, but people in the neighborhood assumed that she was privileged, and tormented her for it. “That white mama, man,” she said. “You know what I’m saying?”
That kind of bullying is part of the pain of being impoverished. You feel so low, you desperately want to make someone else feel lower.
Baxter is a single mother, and Griffin is the oldest of her five children. Like my own mother, she lost custody of her kids because of drugs—she signed over her parental rights to her mom. She told me the story as if she was discussing a character in a book: “Jay-Me got in trouble. Jay-Me started using drugs, cocaine specifically.” Like my mother, Baxter was a victim of sexual abuse. She grew up watching her mother “get beat by men. I done been touched by men, and I never told my mama until a couple months before she died.”
It took Baxter seven years to stop using drugs and get her kids back. Those kids needed her, yet she kept choosing drugs over them, she said, as her voice cracked and tears hit her cheeks. “That hurts, because I can’t believe I did that.” I’ve heard those same words from my own mother and watched her cry for the same reason.
Before Baxter signed over her rights, she said, she asked her mother to promise that what she’d experienced as a little girl wouldn’t happen to her kids. She wanted to break the cycle of violence, poverty, and dysfunction that is the inheritance of so many children. “I’m not a gun mama,” Baxter told me, but she believes in “stepping in the street” to fight. “I’ve been fighting all my life,” she said.
Backgrounds like these are so common in Whitley’s line of work that he seemed to tune out our conversation. At one point on the video call, we heard the sound of snoring. Baxter joked about it: “Listen to him. My lawyer tiiiiiired.” We continued talking for a few more minutes and never heard from him again. “Night night, Daniel,” she said before we hung up. He called me back later, apologized for not saying goodbye, and said he hadn’t been asleep.
Despite the pity I felt for Baxter and her family, I felt more for those shot by her son, and their families.
Di’Zhon Robertson’s uncle Tyrone Johnson officiated his funeral, and told me that the church was full of people “struggling with their emotions.” I was told by attendees that the teenager’s grieving mother had to be pulled off the coffin. Damon Williams Jr., a 14-year-old wounded in the shooting, was hit in the thigh. He had been planning on joining his middle school’s football team this season. Lakeisha Martin was shot in the stomach and the sternum. East End Day, her older brother Isaiah Barron told me, “is a day for our community that we look forward to every year.” Martin was in the hospital for 21 days and will be unable to work for months.
The day of the shooting, Jenee Gragston rushed to the hospital as her nephew went into surgery. She told me the police said she should leave her tent, and could return later to retrieve everything. But when her husband went back to the park, almost everything was gone. The cooler with the meat. The grill, the propane tank, even her prescription eyeglasses. Other tents had been robbed as well. Gragston told me that she was grateful her nephew was okay, but that she would never go to one of the park festivals again.
Lexington is trying hard to reduce this kind of gun violence. Mayor Linda Gorton told me the city has handed out free gun locks and offered to buy back guns from residents, among other interventions. Through ONE Lexington, it offers groceries, hotel stays, and educational funds to people affected by gun violence. The city relocated a family whose house had been shot up, Gorton said. Still, she conceded, “there are times when we cannot control every human being’s behavior.”
It doesn’t help that Kentucky has such lax gun laws. Just this year, state legislators dropped the age required to carry a concealed firearm from 21 to 18. When I was growing up in Lexington, gun violence was even worse. Whenever you have a community of young men who feel powerless and disrespected, who have been raised to protect themselves and their families from perceived threats, and who believe words can’t save them but a gun might, then death will follow. The story of what happened in Lexington this summer is particularly tragic because so many had worked so long and so carefully to make a difference. But a gun changes everything in a moment.
Carama, of ONE Lexington, told me he has more friends who are dead than alive. He, too, said that “a lot of it is out of our control,” and that there’s only so much someone from outside a young person’s family can do. You can monitor a kid all you like, but if he has a gun, “you got a split second to react.” Ultimately, he said, “you can’t prevent everything. It’s just not possible.”
In Jay-Me Baxter’s account, she tried, in her way, to intervene. “The mamas grew up together,” she told me. “This could’ve been prevented.” But it wasn’t.

Indian nationals travelling to Malaysia have been warned against using the country's 30-day visa-free entry facility to look for employment. The High Commission of India in Kuala Lumpur said it had observed a “noticeable increase” in Indian nationals entering Malaysia through the visa-free route to seek jobs. In an advisory posted on X on Tuesday, the mission said some travellers were being misled by “unscrupulous agents” making false employment promises. The warning comes as Malaysia continues to allow Indian passport holders visa-free entry for up to 30 days. Malaysia's official immigration information says the exemption remains in place until December 31, 2026. The High Commission said the 30-day facility is intended for tourism and social visits and does not permit employment. Indian nationals travelling to Malaysia for work must instead have the required employment documentation, including a valid work permit or Visa With Reference (VDR). The Malaysian Immigration Department also states that a Visa With Reference is used for purposes including work, subject to the required approval. The Indian mission warned that people attempting to use the tourist facility to find employment could face overstaying, illegal status, exploitation, detention and legal action. The High Commission separately advises Indian workers planning legal employment in Malaysia to travel with a valid Malaysian visa and employment-related documents. The mission has also advised genuine tourists to carry documents that can be verified by Malaysian immigration authorities. These include a confirmed return ticket, hotel booking and a passport valid for at least six months. Indian passport holders must also submit the Malaysia Digital Arrival Card (MDAC) online three days before arrival. Malaysia's official guidance lists the same requirements for Indian travellers entering under the visa waiver. The High Commission's advisory follows previous instances in which Indian travellers faced entry-related issues in Malaysia over suspected job-seeking, inadequate accommodation proof, insufficient funds or missing return tickets. The mission's latest warning specifically highlights the risks of relying on agents promising employment and travelling under a facility that does not authorise work. For Indians travelling to Malaysia for employment, the High Commission's existing guidance recommends having the appropriate visa, employment contract and employer details before departure. Ready-to-heat meals are convenient, quick, and easy to prepare. Never frozen. Proteins in particular are surprisingly well textured. Can be prepped in an air fryer to good effect. Free consult with a dietitian.
TIRED
Meals are still too reliant on microwaves. Reheated meals have inherent limitations, especially with texture. Many meals lean on fat and sodium for flavor.
Like many children of the West Coast, I am a sucker for teriyaki salmon—a Japanese classic that slid easily into the menu of funny little bento shacks owned by former surfers named Dan or Dave.
And so maybe I was a prime target for a teriyaki salmon and “forbidden rice” meal from Factor, HelloFresh’s ready-to-heat meal delivery service. Factor preps and cooks its meals freshly in a commissary kitchen and then, through the magic of modified atmosphere packaging, Factor ships this meal in the mail without the indignity of freezing. All I have to do after that is heat it up.
What surprised me is how good the salmon tasted, even after being reheated. After air-frying my meal with the sauce drizzled on top, the salmon remained flaky and mild, without rubber or mush. The rice was al dente, lightly crisped. I’ve tested nearly every meal delivery service in existence, and one of the most interesting developments in food tech over the past decade has been the rise of the fully prepared, ready-to-heat meal that’s actually palatable.
With Factor, HelloFresh’s ready-to-heat meal delivery service, I’ve witnessed this process in real time. Over the six years since the meal kit giant acquired Chicago-founded Factor (previously Factor 75), Factor’s meals have evolved from their roots as essentially protein pills in TV dinner form to something much more sophisticated. It’s also expanded to include flatbread pizzas and frankly delicious smoothies and juice blends.
Not every meal tasted as good as that salmon, of course. And at around $13–17 a serving for dinner, Factor is more expensive than scratch cooking but less expensive than delivery. The cost is comparable, perhaps, to the ready-to-heat meal boxes you might find in your local supermarket deli section, except delivered to your door. Factor also tends to offer steep discounts for the first week or month.
After testing four different deliveries of Factor meals over the past two years, here’s my experience.
Factor by the Numbers
Specs
Cost per meal
$13—17 per serving (usually closer to $14), plus $10+ shipping
Meal plan options
Choose anywhere from four to 24 meals a week
Lowest-cost plan at full price
$70 for four meals, not including shipping
Size of weekly menu
100+ meal options, plus juices, smoothies, protein shakes, breakfasts, and desserts
Gluten-free meals?
Most meals made without gluten, but not in a certified gluten-free facility
Plant-based meals?
About a dozen vegetarian or vegan meal options
Other dietary plans or restrictions
Meal filters include high protein, low calorie, low carb, low sodium, and keto
Prep time
A few minutes in the microwave (or less than 10 minutes in an air fryer)
How Factor Works and Who It’s For
Like all prepared meal delivery services, Factor is a lot like ordering a week’s worth of meals from a restaurant—in this case, one of HelloFresh’s regional kitchens. Factor’s website will ask you a few questions about your preferences, ranging from allergens to whether you’re looking to up your protein levels or lose weight.
Then you’ll be asked to choose the number of meals you want to order a week—and the day you want them delivered. In general, the more meals you order per week, the less they cost. Most fall in a modest 600-calorie range. The following week, a box arrives at your door with your chosen selection of meals, plus some ice packs.
Factor’s selling point over other ready-to-heat meal kits has always been twofold. One is that its meals are friendly to keto and other versions of high-protein and carb-conscious diets, which goes back to the company’s founding 15 years ago by a fitness-obsessed MMA fighter. The other is that its microwaveable meals have never been frozen, leaving open the possibility for actual texture in one’s meal—a light crispness to the green beans, say, or the grill char and soft give of a medium-rare filet mignon.
Meals can include classic Midwestern meats and twos, but also barramundi filets topped with a “Niçoise” olive topping, Caribbean-spiced chicken thighs, and the occasional premium-priced filet mignon with truffle butter. More than half of meals contain 30 grams or more of protein, and more than half are no-gluten-added, usually with rice or potato sides. (Though take note that Factor is not prepared in a fully gluten-free facility.)
In the past couple years, Factor has also branched out to add more fresh ingredients and even baked goods. There are calzones now. Flatbread pizzas. Mixable salads and warmable soups, each available as a dinner option. But there’s also a world of market add-ons, including smoothies, protein shakes, and downright terrific juice blends.
How Does Factor Taste?
Over the past two years, I’ve tried about three dozen Factor meals, ranging from breakfast pancakes to meals involving steaks, shrimp, and pork chops. The results, after reheating in an oven, air fryer, or microwave, are not quite the same as a fresh-cooked meal, including meal kits you prepare yourself using HelloFresh’s other services. Any meal that looks like it might be mushy probably is. But proteins in particular fare quite well, whether shrimp or fish or pork chops.
Heated, frozen, then reheated chicken breast tends to have the character of wet chalk. But a never-frozen chicken breast from Factor had the texture of … wait for it … chicken breast. Shrimp is plump. And the tenderness, juiciness, and blessed pinkness of a truffled medium-rare filet mignon slab from Factor was nothing short of startling after I steamed it in the microwave, according to Factor’s instructions.
But the results are even better when I ignore Factor’s instructions and cook for eight minutes at 340 degrees Fahrenheit in an air fryer, specifically the Ninja Crispi (7/10, WIRED Recommends) that allows me to put wet ingredients below the crisper plate, and proteins or potatoes atop the crisper. This leads to light browning on a pork chop, but especially much better crispness on green beans or carrots or potato sides. When left to my own devices, this is kinda the only way I want to heat a prepared meal, and I will continue to lobby for Factor to add air fryer instructions.
But while Factor fares better than most prepared meals I’ve tested, it hasn’t solved every issue inherent in ready-made delivery meals. Some of the gluten-free dishes, and anything that looks like a hash or ragu, can struggle with texture. For every crisp green bean or air-fryer-charred broccoli, there’s slightly gummy pasta or limp zucchini. As a rule of thumb, it’s best to steer toward dishes with rice and potato as starches.
Meals can also lean a bit too hard on sodium, especially an otherwise nicely browned calzone filled with meatballs and mozzarella. But most meals still didn’t edge much over a third of the daily recommended sodium intake, and for those watching their diet, Factor does offer an unusual perk: a free 20-minute consult with a dietitian. I took advantage of this with HelloFresh’s sister plan, Green Chef, and got surprisingly helpful advice on fiber and protein needs.
Juice Worth the Squeeze
But for a moment, I’d like to talk about juice.
One of the most delicious things I’ve ever tasted was a sweetly coral-colored elixir poured from a chilled glass carafe at a Georgian bakery in Northeast Philadelphia. The drink was, according to my server, nothing special: a proprietary blend of juices made from fresh strawberries and other “delicious fruits.” I’ve been chasing that high ever since—but am usually sorely disappointed by the tepid, stale bottles that clog the fridge case at your average natural grocer.
I’ve often resorted to juicing fruits myself, which takes some effort and cleanup. But I was genuinely surprised to get some of that same fix from Factor, via the company’s add-on six-juice variety pack. Dang if a vibrant cucumber-apple-pineapple “gut greens” juice blend from Factor didn’t put supermarket juice blends to shame: a mix of tropical brightness, apple sweetness, savory spinach, and a prickle but not a stab wound of mint and ginger.
A Green Supreme smoothie fared equally well, and I also enjoyed an apple-kale-wheatgrass bottle to a shocking degree—again for its balance of savor, sweetness, and brightness. Some of the juice flavors leaned a little too hard into turmeric, and the option of 2-ounce ginger-turmeric-lemon wellness shots seemed a little silly. But in all, fresher-than-expected juice delivery is a boon, available for around $3 per 12-ounce bottle in the multi-packs—better than at many health food stores.
Tacked onto an eight-meal plan, those juices and smoothies can make Factor feel like a downright wholesome option for breakfast and a work lunch. If a microwave meal will always be graded on a curve, the trade-off is ease: a full meal with meat and sides that arrives premade at your door, awaiting a turn in the air fryer.

Mum's viral barefoot race sparks debate over India's education crisis
- Published
Despite having no training, or even a pair of running shoes, Ramabai Ranveer sprinted barefoot to victory in her first-ever race in August.
The 47-year-old widow had entered a 3km (1.86-mile) community run with a single goal: winning the prize money to help pay for her two daughters' education.
When she crossed the finish line first, Ramabai from Maharashtra in western India was delighted. The 3,000-rupee ($31; £23) prize would help her buy books and study materials for her daughters.
It was not much money. It would not come close to covering the cost of higher education in India, or even a course at the coaching centre where one of her daughters is preparing for a government recruitment examination.
But videos of her barefoot run spread rapidly on social media and in newspapers, striking a nerve as India's education system faces unusual scrutiny.
"Is it glory or a source of shame for us as a society?" one social media user remarked.
Soon, a woman who had never imagined becoming a runner was being held up as a symbol of something much bigger: the extraordinary lengths some Indian families go to in the hope that education will give their children a better life.
For Ramabai, the decision to run was simple.
"My elder daughter came to me early in the morning and said, 'Mummy, I want to take part in a running race'," she told BBC News Marathi from her home in Beed district.
"I asked her where it was and she said it was nearby. She told me that if she won the prize money, it would help with her education."
Her younger daughter, Arati, lives in Nanded and was struggling to afford books.
"I couldn't send her money to buy books and because of that she didn't speak to me on the phone for eight days," Ramabai said. "So I decided I had to run and win the race."
When her slippers kept slipping off, she removed them, gathered her sari and ran barefoot, pulling ahead to win the women's 30-60 category.
Her elder daughter, Pooja, also won a prize after finishing second in her age group. But she reserved her praise for her mother, describing her as courageous.
Ramabai has been the family's sole provider since her husband died in 2012.
"I did whatever work I could find," she said. "I picked soybeans and chickpeas in other people's fields. I also collected turmeric, processed it and sold it."
She left school when she was 13. Her daughters, she says, should have the opportunities she never had.
"I believe that as long as I am alive, I should do everything I can to give my daughters a good education."
That aspiration is shared by millions of Indian families. But getting a child through the education system and into a secure career can involve years of preparation, intense competition and, for many families, considerable expense.
One of Ramabai's daughters is preparing for police recruitment and the other for the civil services - two fiercely competitive routes into the security and social status associated with a coveted and secure government job.
Millions of young Indians spend years preparing for such examinations, often paying for coaching and study materials. But faith in the system has been shaken by repeated allegations of question-paper leaks and other irregularities.
The controversies have fed a wider sense of frustration among young Indians over education, jobs and the increasingly uncertain promise of a secure future. That frustration has also fuelled student-led protests and youth movements demanding changes to India's education system.
For families such as Ramabai's, education is something they make sacrifices for every day.
After her husband's death, she took whatever work she could find. She now cooks at the coaching centre where one of her daughters prepares for police recruitment.
Ramabai's run also drew the attention of authorities. Earlier this month, Chief Justice of India Surya Kant directed local officials to provide her with financial assistance of 50,000 rupees.
But Sukhadeo Thorat, a former chairman of the University Grants Commission, says the family's story points to broader structural challenges.
"If a woman is compelled to struggle so hard for her daughters' education, it shows that government education schemes are not reaching people adequately," he said. "Both the central and state governments run a variety of schemes. The problem is that implementation remains weak."
For Ramabai, though, the debate is secondary. What matters most is ensuring her daughters have a better future.
"I don't want them to go through the hardships I have faced," she said. "I don't want them to struggle through mud or travel under the scorching sun and rain. Whatever I have suffered, I don't want my daughters to suffer the same."
Additional reporting by Laignee Barron.

How ‘national security’ has become Trump’s crutch for getting his way in Washington
Congress sees through Trump’s ‘idiotic’ justification for fortifying every inch of Washington, D.C., but the president is pushing ahead with it anyway, writes John Bowden
Donald Trump announced on Sunday that he would be placing a sniper’s nest in the front of Arlington National Cemetery.
In any other moment, the act would have been truly confusing. Presidents are not generally known for advertising the whereabouts of specific U.S. military fortifications, even those placed in such scenic and somber locations. But Trump’s announcement followed a pattern: His planned fortification of this hallowed ground comes as the president has leaned into national security and his role as commander-in-chief to justify his physical transformation of the nation’s capital and the White House.
On Truth Social, the president wrote Sunday that he was transforming his planned “triumphal arch” into another D.C. military installation, complete with “large numbers of drones, plus Snipers.” If that sounds familiar, it’s because he recently attempted the same transformation with the plans for his White House ballroom, now dubbed a “DronePort” in several seemingly AI-generated mockups of the structure planned for the grounds of the former East Wing.
Despite Congress turning up its nose at the prospect of providing money for the White House’s construction plans under the guise of security funding, Trump’s aim seems to be clear: Presenting his desired development projects as crucial to national security — and painting his critics as standing in the way of protecting Washington, D.C.
The northern Virginia congressman representing the region, which includes Arlington National Cemetery, Rep. Don Beyer, responded to that attempt to establish that pretext on Sunday and he called it “idiotic.”
“Putting a drone-launching site directly in the landing path for DCA [airport] is a stupid, dangerous, and unworkable idea.Trump clearly expects to lose a lawsuit and therefore wants to set up a pretext to argue that the arch is tied to national security. Which is obviously idiotic,” said the congressman.
Transforming the nation’s capital and its surrounding areas, including parts of Maryland and Virginia, under the banner of “security” has been one of Trump’s main focuses since returning to the White House. In an unprecedented move last year, he deployed National Guard troops to Washington D.C. and a handful of other cities with the mission of stopping waves of crime and lawlessness that Trump promised were washing over liberal cities nationwide.
In reality, troops around D.C. spent much of their time on these same beautification projects; they picked up trash, raked leaves, replanted grass, and so on. More smoke-and-mirrors to achieve Trump’s dream of a squeaky-clean seat of power.
Trump even used a variation of this explanation on Monday when he gave his supposed reasoning for banning MS Now, CNN, and Politico from the White House, calling them a “threat to democracy.”
“[The] Kennedy Center will next become a national security issue as well. We need a drone port on roof and ammo in the basement,” wrote one X user on Sunday.
To the administration, the lack of official justification for the necessity of these fortifications doesn’t seem to matter. The White House sought to quickly shovel money for the White House ballroom/”DronePort” into the second Republican reconciliation package passed by Congress this summer, which broke a deadlock on ICE and Border Patrol funding.
That effort failed, but there doesn’t seem to be any effort by any arm of the administration, including the Pentagon, to try and justify the need for these new fortifications, including backing up Trump’s assertion that the military had requested his proposed changes to the White House in the first place.
Trump’s ballroom will likely continue as long as a court does not block the administration from using privately-raised funds and other money diverted from the Secret Service and White House Military Office for its construction. But the arch is another story; a number of groups have already filed to block its construction, and a federal judge has refused to allow the administration to begin major construction projects on the plot without providing notice to the court.
Bizzarely, after a year of DOGE taking an axe to whole federal agencies and sub-agencies, and the president’s radical transformation of departments like Education and Defense, the real test of Trump’s executive power in front of the courts may end up being fought around his D.C. beautification efforts. A relatively small part of the president’s agenda, they’ve still consumed much of the president’s attention as his renovation efforts around the city have been the most direct, immediate and viewable extension of his political will.
How much of that will survives after November is another story.
