TOI correspondent from Washington:
 Critics are calling out the Trump administration for hypocrisy and double standards after MAGA supremo Donald Trump announced a potash (fertiliser) deal on Monday with Belarus, a close ally of Moscow, days after he signed a bill which would punish India if it buys Russian energy.
Arising from his spat with Canada, which supplies 85 per cent of US-needed potash, a key farming input, Trump announced with his customary fanfare that Washington is working on a “massive Deal” to purchase potash from Belarus at prices “substantially less” than what Washington currently pays Ottawa, calling it good news for American farmers. The move will affect New Delhi because Belarus is also an established supplier of potash to the Indian agricultural market.
The apparent double standard is already drawing flak in diplomatic circles. Evan Feigenbaum, a former administration official and a South Asia analyst, has pointed to the contradiction between Washington’s pressure on India over Russian energy and Trump’s willingness to pursue Belarusian potash and said the appearance of “double standards and apparent hypocrisy” can affect perceptions of the US as a negotiating partner.
But as has become normal with many announcements by the MAGA boss, he appears to have jumped the gun on the issue – if he's not posturing – because Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko said there was little or no spare potash available for western markets and his country’s production was already contracted. “Even if we wanted to supply other markets we simply don’t have the volume,” Lukashenko said, according to reports from Minsk.
Potash is not quite oil or gas, but in agriculture it has a comparable strategic character. Potassium is one of the three major plant nutrients, alongside nitrogen and phosphorus. It helps regulate water uptake, photosynthesis and enzyme activity and improves crop quality, disease resistance and yields.
And the global concentration is striking. Canada, Russia and Belarus are the dominant players in the international potash market. Canada alone accounts for about one-third of global supply and is by far the principal supplier to the US Trump's gambit therefore amounts to using a trade war with one major supplier to seek leverage through another supplier that happens to be aligned with a notional geopolitical adversary who is frequently helped through the backdoor.
This is because Belarus is landlocked, and European sanctions have restricted its traditional export routes. So any significant new flow of Belarusian potash to the US would face complicated logistics and could require transit through infrastructure and ports of Russia, the very country Trump is trying to squeeze in an effort to end its war with Ukraine.
For New Delhi, the question is not simply whether Trump can secure cheaper potash for American farmers; it is whether Washington – by rearranging the global fertilizer market for its own agricultural survival amid a cratering of ties with Canada – ends up making Indian farmers pay more.
India requires roughly 4-5 million tonnes of potash a year and is among the world's largest importers. Although India's supply is now diversified among Canada, Russia, Israel, Jordan and others, Belarus is an important source.

Easy for anyone to use. Consistently perfect prints. Enclosed chamber for temperature control. New tool-free nozzle-swap feature. AMS add-on makes multicolor printing a breeze.
TIRED
Speed causes a lot of shaking—needs a very stable surface to sit on. Filament waste disposal makes a mess. Fumes from high-temperature filaments are still very intense.
Does the average consumer actually need a 3D printer? Isn’t it just for people who want to sell fidgets at the flea market, design obscure brackets in CAD, or print groups of Warhammer figurines?
Yes, they do, and no, it isn’t.
Photograph: Kat Merck
In my four weeks of testing the Bambu Lab P2S Combo, I have printed a sponge holder for my kitchen sink; caps and parts for my hydroponic gardens; various clips and hangers; a Mason jar lid organizer; a shovel; a couple of funny signs; plant pot coasters; a shoehorn; truck bed tie-downs; a pair of earrings; and, of course, a Benchy—every piece perfectly smooth and looking like it was purchased from a store. Owning a 3D printer is like having an Amazon fulfillment center right in your house.
While I'm no stranger to 3D printing—I owned the open-frame Bambu Lab A1 before I started testing 3D printers—I have never used a machine as easy to operate as the P2S. In fact, when we reviewed Bambu Lab’s P2S predecessor, the popular and bestselling P1S, earlier this year, tester Brad Bourque declared it the easiest-to-use 3D printer he’d ever tried, claiming its lack of complicated steps and futzing has changed the way he thinks about 3D printing.
The P2S builds on the already excellent P1S design with a new 5-inch color touchscreen, tool-free nozzle swapping, a beefed-up 1080p 30-frames-per-second camera with improved AI failure detection, and a redesigned airflow system. I wasn’t exactly in love with the latter, but one complaint for a system with thousands of failure points is more than enough to earn the P2S a solid A-grade.
Detail of identical pigeon figurine printed on white Bambu Lab PLA: A1 on left, P2S on right.
Photograph: Kat Merck
Photograph: Kat Merck
It Really Is That Easy
If you own another brand of mid- or lower-tier 3D printer, any Bambu Lab machine will already feel like an upgrade. Much like an iPhone, any Bambu Lab printer will work seamlessly right out of the box, with easy-to-use software and intuitive design elements. With a little assembly, you’re ready to go.
The large touchscreen allows you to perform many functions and troubleshooting right on the machine. These printers are easy for even the most clueless newbie to use and understand—so much so that some call the company “the Apple of 3D printing.” (Even better, the company’s free, flagship Bambu Studio software is open source.)
What makes both the P1S and P2S worth the upgrade from the A1 is the enclosed chamber that provides environmental control for acrylonitrile filaments like ASA and ABS, which require high temperatures to melt and are notoriously prone to warping. In the P2S, Bambu Lab incorporates a new airflow system that switches modes depending on the filament—it pulls in cooler air for more easily melted PLA, or retains air (and therefore heat) for ASA and ABS.
However, I did notice that when printing in ASA (note that the P2S comes with only a rough-textured build plate; I had to buy the smooth $30 engineering plate separately), the resulting fumes were overwhelming—I had to close the door, open the windows, and turn on an air purifier. There is a carbon filter in the back of the device, but during high-heat prints, the airflow is supposed to circulate inside the unit; instead, it seemed to leak out around the door and other cracks.
Video: Kat Merck
Fumes are emitted from all 3D printers, so this is not really a flaw on the company’s part, just an indication that the redesigned airflow system has room for improvement. Make sure you keep the printer in a room with a door that can close if you’re printing with any kind of impact-modified plastics. Bambu Lab’s helpful Wiki also offers a 3D-printable exhaust kit that can redirect fumes outside.
And speaking of locations, you will also want to ensure the 15 x 16 x 19-inch P2S is on a very firm surface—perhaps even on the ground. At 600 mm per second, the nozzle moves vigorously, which will shake whatever it’s on. I was using a low wooden table, but since I found myself using the printer near-daily, the shaking eventually loosened the table’s leg joints, resulting in multiple X-Y axis error messages on the machine. Research showed this to be a somewhat common issue, almost always resolved by finding a firmer surface.
I was not able to test the AI failure detection, as none of my 30-plus prints failed (aside from a couple of mismeasurements on my end), but I did have occasion to view through the 1080p camera—if you download the free Bambu Handy app, it will store a little time-lapse video of your object being printed, which is fascinating to watch.
In Living Color
The “Combo” in the name refers to the Automatic Material System (AMS) that sits on top of the printer. (You can also buy it separately at $299.) It holds four spools of filament that auto-feed to your project—a game changer if you’re printing something with multiple colors. Without it, a multicolor print would necessitate stopping the print, removing the spool of filament, and installing a new one on the side. For the P2S, the AMS also has the ability to dry the filament—this removes any absorbed ambient moisture that would create steam when heated and mess up your print.
The AMS add-on allows for seamless multicolor prints.
Photograph: Kat Merck
I tested the P2S on the West Coast in late summer, when the humidity was very low, so my filament stayed below 40 percent relative humidity, according to the built-in hygrometer—it didn’t need drying. However, if you live in a humid region, springing for the AMS will be a massive time-saver.
With the P1S, if you needed to swap out a different nozzle, it was something of an ordeal—you basically have to unplug everything and take apart the assembly with screws. On the P2S, the front of the nozzle head is magnetic and pops right off—simply unclip the old nozzle and clip in the new one. Another massive improvement if you find yourself swapping nozzles often.
The P1S’s automatic nozzle cleaning function that “poops” filament blobs out the back of the machine is still in effect on the P2S. I’d been warned, but I was still surprised to see the amount of detritus it left on the floor, especially during multi-color prints. I highly recommend that a “poop chute” or collection basket be one of your first prints. (And there are plenty of fun designs for using the waste filament blobs once they’ve accumulated, from creative games to a “poop Atlas” filament waste world map.)
Do You Really Need One?
Yes, unless you need a dual-nozzle printer or a commercial-grade unit that can also laser cut and engrave—features this printer doesn’t offer. The ability to print and customize useful household and garage objects, art projects, and toys easily and quickly—with minimal fuss—makes the P2S worth every penny. This is doubly so if you have some basic engineering skills, as importing files into Bambu Studio is a cinch.
Bambu Lab-brand filaments start at about $15 a roll with spool. Note that we flagged some app inconsistencies when using non-Bambu filaments with the P1S, but I did not have any non-Bambu filaments on hand to test in the P2S, so I can’t vouch for whether this issue has been fixed.
While the P2S may well be overkill if you only want to print the occasional fidget or figurine, if you regularly find yourself in need of some annoyingly specific organizer, replacement cap, or bracket, this machine could well pay for itself over time in both convenience and material costs.
Kat Merck is a commerce editor for WIRED, where she covers smart bird feeders, indoor gardening systems, kitchen composters, and all things sustainable home tech. A survivor from a prison cell in Nigeria where 37 suspected illegal goldminers died while in the custody of a paramilitary group this week has recounted his panic and struggle for breath, as police on Friday fired teargas at people protesting against the deaths.
Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) – a paramilitary group that works with police – initially blamed the deaths in Minna, the state capital of the mineral-rich state of Niger, on a disease outbreak.
However, an intelligence report seen by Agence France-Presse said preliminary information suggested that overcrowding and inadequate ventilation were responsible.
Dauda Shehu, a survivor from the cell, told journalists at a hospital on Friday: “We were jam-packed in the cell, no ventilation for us to breathe well. All of a sudden we realised that we could not breathe and we were all scampering for where to get fresh air, we even appealed to them several times, banged the cell door, but they refused to answer us.”
A video shared online showed the bodies of dozens of young men clad only in shorts, most of whom appeared to be teenagers, sprawled on the ground out in the open. Volunteers wearing gloves can be seen standing over the dead, while veiled women try to identify the bodies of their relatives. Voices shouting curses on those responsible can be heard in the background.
Protests over the deaths broke out on Thursday evening in Minna. On Friday dozens of young people, including miners and their relatives, gathered near the NSCDC’s office in the city. Police cordoned off the area and attempted to disperse the protesters by firing teargas.
A Reuters witness saw security forces fire live rounds as protesters – some armed with sticks, machetes and traditional hunting rifles – called for justice. Some protesters tried to set fire to government buildings in the Tunga neighbourhood. “We are not thieves – we are simply seeking a way to make a living by mining,” Yusuf Auwal, a miner who joined the protesters, told Reuters. At least one body lay on the streets. Soldiers and police officers patrolled Minna to try to restore order.
The NSCDC said the detainees had been held in raids on suspected illegal mines on 15 and 16 September in the Wushishi-Lukoto area west of Minna. Nigeria’s interior minister, Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo, ordered the immediate suspension of Niger state’s NSCDC commandant, Suberu Siyaka Aniviye, pending the outcome of a full investigation.
Niger state, which is Nigeria’s largest and more than twice the size of Belgium, is rich in minerals and attracts thousands of artisanal miners, most lured by gold.
Police and the NSCDC did not initially provide a precise number of deaths but the state governor, Mohammed Umaru Bago, later confirmed 37 people had died.
“It’s so sad, it’s so tragic,” he said, adding an inquiry into the deaths had already started work. He declared three days of mourning and postponed the start of campaigning for elections due in January. The men were buried on Thursday, according to Islamic tradition, without any forensic investigations.
The scramble for gold reserves dug up in illegal mines in Niger state is fuelling violence by criminal gangs, according to officials and experts. The gangs tax the miners and demand a cut from the extracted ore as a levy to allow them access to the pits.
Most of the illegally mined gold is smuggled to the United Arab Emirates, where it is laundered into the global supply chain in Europe, the US, Asia and South Africa, according to a 2024 Swissaid report.
Apart from gold, the state of Niger sits on deposits of other minerals including tantalite, copper and lithium, which are in strong demand for use in electric vehicles and clean energy technology.
Agence France-Presse and Reuters contributed to this report

Thousands of patients in India are diagnosed with melanoma, a type of skin cancer, each year. While melanoma is far less common here than in Western populations, it is far from rare and the way it presents in our patient population makes it uniquely difficult to detect early. Too many patients come to us when the disease is already advanced, precisely at a time when treatment options have never been more powerful or more personalised. This contrast between available therapies and the stage at which patients are diagnosed defines one of the most pressing challenges in melanoma care in India today.
Why melanoma gets missed
The warning signs most people associate with skin cancer come from research developed for fairer-skinned populations, where melanoma tends to appear on sun-exposed areas as an irregular or darkening mole. That picture does not reflect what clinicians see in India.
Melanoma here, most commonly presents on the soles of the feet or beneath the nails, sites that are rarely examined and even more rarely associated with cancer. This condition is called acral lentiginous melanoma, a subtype that accounts for 35 to 60% of cases in dark-skinned individuals. Such lesions are frequently mistaken for bruises, fungal infections, or diabetic ulcers, and by the time a biopsy is taken, the disease has often progressed.
Mucosal melanomas, a rare type of cancer that starts in the mucous membranes, are highly aggressive with a very low chance of recovery and produce few early warning signs. Most are diagnosed only after spread has occurred.
Any pigmented lesion that changes or persists, wherever it appears on the body, deserves investigation rather than reassurance.
A decade of transformation
When I began my oncology career, managing advanced melanoma meant offering patients limited and rarely durable options. That has fortunately changed significantly.
The foundational shift came from James Allison and Tasuku Honjo, whose discoveries on CTLA-4 and PD-1 earned them the 2018 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Their research established the principle of immune-checkpoint blockade: rather than attacking a tumour directly, we can sometimes release the biological brakes that stop the patient’s own immune system from doing so. The results can be extraordinary. Former U.S. President Jimmy Carter was diagnosed at 91 with melanoma that had spread to his liver and brain. Surgical resection of liver disease, stereotactic radiation for the brain, and immunotherapy with the checkpoint inhibitor pembrolizumab produced a durable remission, and he lived to 100.
Precision medicine has reshaped the approach in parallel. Some melanomas carry specific mutations, particularly in the BRAF pathway, that can be directly targeted with molecularly designed therapies. This is where next-generation sequencing, or NGS, becomes critical. In simple terms, it reads the genetic blueprint of a patient’s tumour and identifies the alterations that should guide treatment, turning what was once a single clinical decision into a detailed, individualised process.
The melanoma story is not over; it is only becoming more exciting. TIL therapy takes tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes, expands them in the laboratory, and reinfuses them in far greater numbers, a step toward truly personalised cellular treatment. In August 2026, intismeran, a personalised mRNA vaccine built from the patient’s own tumour sequence, was combined with pembrolizumab in high-risk melanoma patients after surgery. The results were striking: a significant reduction in recurrence compared with pembrolizumab alone, making it the first positive late-stage trial of a personalised mRNA cancer vaccine, though survival data remain pending.
What still needs to change
All of these advances deliver their best results when treatment begins early. The more sophisticated our therapies become, the more clearly we see that they work best before the disease has spread. In India, awareness and referral gaps continue to push diagnosis toward advanced stages.
Recalibrating public health messaging to reflect how melanoma actually presents in Indian patients is a start. Faster pathways from primary care to specialist centres matter equally. More fundamentally, India needs a national melanoma registry, stronger epidemiological and genomic data, more clinical trials in Indian patients, and deeper international collaboration. The advances of the past decade are genuinely extraordinary. Whether they reach the patients who need them comes down to one thing: a diagnosis early enough to act on.
(Prof. Jyoti Bajpai is director – medical precision immuno-oncology, Apollo Hospitals, Mumbai & Western Zone. drjyoti_ba@apollohospitals.com)

New Delhi, Sep 22: The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) has advised the public, healthcare professionals, pharmacists, retailers and hospitals against the indiscriminate use of painkillers and antibiotics, highlighting the associated risk of chronic kidney disease and other renal complications.
In a circular dated September 21, the drug regulator called for rational, safe and responsible use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and antibiotics, besides strict adherence to prescription requirements and stronger antimicrobial stewardship.
The circular issued by Drugs Controller General (India) Dr Rajeev Singh Raghuvanshi said that import, manufacture, sale and distribution of drugs are regulated under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and the rules framed under it.
"As per the said rules, all drugs including non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and antibiotics are required to be sold and distributed in the country on prescription of an RMP/specialist only," it said.
The CDSCO said various drugs, including NSAIDs and antibiotics, have been placed under Schedules G, H, H1 and X of the Drugs Rules, 1945, considering their potential risks, and require appropriate medical supervision.
"Most of NSAIDs are included in the Schedule H of Drugs Rules, 1945. Thus, they are not to be sold by retail without the prescription of a Registered Medical Practitioner as is required in Rule 97 of Drugs Rules, 1945," the circular said.
It added that most antibiotics are included in Schedule H1 and carry warnings that they are dangerous to take except in accordance with medical advice and should not be sold by retail without the prescription of a registered medical practitioner.
"In view of the above, it is mandatory to ensure that these drugs shall only be used when clinically indicated, in the appropriate dose and for the appropriate duration, and under the supervision of a Registered Medical Practitioner," it said.
For the general public, the CDSCO advised that NSAIDs or painkillers and antibiotics should not be taken "indiscriminately, repeatedly or for prolonged periods without medical advice".
It also said antibiotics should not be used for self-medication or for conditions where antibiotic treatment is not clinically indicated, "such as most uncomplicated viral infections".
The regulator advised people to take prescribed antibiotics strictly as advised and not share them with others or use leftover medicines.
Individuals, "particularly those with pre-existing kidney disease or other risk factors for renal impairment", have been advised to inform their healthcare professionals before using NSAIDs.
"The public is advised to seek medical advice where pain, fever or other symptoms persist or recur rather than repeatedly using painkillers or antibiotics on their own," the circular said.
For healthcare professionals, the CDSCO said NSAIDs and antibiotics should be prescribed only when clinically indicated, after considering the patient's clinical condition, age, comorbidities, concomitant medicines and relevant risk factors.
It advised that "the lowest effective dose for the shortest appropriate duration" should be considered when prescribing NSAIDs, particularly for patients at increased risk of renal impairment.
The circular also called for appropriate precautions in patients with renal impairment, dehydration, cardiovascular disease or other conditions that may increase the risks associated with NSAID use.
On antibiotic use, it said these drugs should be prescribed judiciously and in accordance with applicable antimicrobial stewardship principles, taking into consideration the likely causative organism, site and severity of infection and, wherever appropriate, relevant microbiological investigations and local susceptibility patterns.
"Unnecessary combination therapy, inappropriate antibiotic selection, incorrect dosing and unnecessarily prolonged duration of antibiotic treatment should be avoided," it said.
The CDSCO also directed pharmacists, retailers and distributors to strictly comply with statutory requirements relating to the sale and distribution of Schedule H, H1 and other prescription drugs.
"Schedule H/H1 drugs shall not be sold at retail except in accordance with the applicable provisions of the Drugs Rules, 1945," it said, adding that pharmacists and retailers should not encourage or facilitate self-medication with antibiotics or prescription-only NSAIDs.
Hospitals and healthcare institutions have been advised to strengthen systems for rational prescribing and monitoring of NSAIDs and antibiotics and promote antimicrobial stewardship, prescription review and appropriate patient counselling.
The Drugs Control Authorities in the states and Union Territories have also been asked to create awareness among healthcare professionals, pharmacists, retailers and the general public regarding the risks associated with indiscriminate use of NSAIDs and antibiotics, and ensure compliance with applicable provisions.
"In view of the above, all concerned are advised to take necessary steps to promote rational, safe and responsible use of NSAIDs and antibiotics, and to prevent avoidable adverse drug reactions, renal complications and antimicrobial resistance," the circular said.

Shares of insurtech company Turtlemint soared 9% to touch an intraday high of ₹142.90 apiece on the BSE today. The shares pared some of the gains later, closing 6.6% higher at ₹139.75 apiece. At the time, Turtlemint’s market capitalisation stood at ₹4,115.34 Cr ($431 Mn). The rally today comes days after brokerage Motilal Oswal initiated a “buy” rating for the stock and set a price target (PT) of ₹180 on the stock. This implies a 22% upside from today’s close. Motilal Oswal said that the PoSP-driven premiums are growing at nearly twice the industry rate. The company, with its presence across 19,186 pin codes, is well-positioned to capture this opportunity. The brokerage further said, “While we expect 1.3–1.5 Lakh partner additions annually, active DPs are poised to grow at about 24% FY26–29 CAGR, driven by Turtlemint’s training-led activation engine and strong partner retention.” As per Motilal Oswal, Turtlemint’s key margin opportunity lies in controlling corporate overheads with partner payouts accounting for most direct costs. As growth shifts from adding partners to improving their activation and productivity, the brokerage expects operating leverage to improve, with corporate overheads projected to grow at a 6% CAGR between FY26-29. This is expected to help Turtlemint achieve adjusted EBITDA breakeven in FY27 while expanding margins to around 11% by FY29. The development comes a month after Jefferies initiated coverage on the company with a ‘Buy’ rating and a price target of ₹190. Founded in 2015, Turtlemint operates an insurance distribution platform, connecting consumers with insurers through a network of financial advisors for car, bike, health, and term life insurance. The company made its market debut on the exchanges on June 29. Its shares were listed at ₹134.90 on the NSE, an 11.25% discount to the IPO price of ₹152. On the BSE, the stock debuted at ₹136.20, down 10.4% from the issue price earlier in June. On the financial front, Turtlemint managed to trim down its Q1 FY27 net loss 19% to ₹37.8 Cr from a loss of ₹46.7 Cr in the same quarter last year. Operating revenue jumped 40% to ₹294.1 Cr in the quarter under review, from ₹210.5 in Q1 FY26.

The unequal impact of the climate crisis on the world’s poorest people, including those in tropical areas, has been highlighted by new research that finds they will be among the last to feel the benefits if global greenhouse gas emissions are cut to net zero.
Temperatures have risen more significantly in tropical areas relative to their historic range than at higher latitudes, including in wealthier countries in Europe and North America.
A team of Australian climate scientists found this inequality would not be reversed if global emissions reached net zero – the implicit goal of the landmark 2015 Paris agreement – and could take “many decades to begin to reverse” if carbon dioxide was drawn from the atmosphere under a “net-negative emissions” plan.
The research coincided with the UN’s refugee agency releasing a report showing how the climate crisis was increasing the risk of people becoming stateless.
The climate inequality study, published in the journal Environmental Research Letters, was led by Dr Andrew King and colleagues at the University of Melbourne. They looked at three sets of computer modelling experiments of the likely temperature changes if global emissions reached net zero and overlaid the results with countries’ gross domestic product.
“If we follow a path that is close to net zero, then the inequality we see in present day warming persists indefinitely,” King said. “The wealthier countries that have caused more of the problem are not those that are the most exposed, even beyond net zero. The regions that have not caused the warming are those that experience the most warming.”
King said the fate of the planet’s poorest regions, which tend to be concentrated closer to the equator, would depend on how much greenhouse gas was emitted before the world reached net zero.
“Even when we get to net zero, we have still emitted an enormous amount of carbon into the atmosphere and its effects will continue for centuries. We can’t easily undo all that damage,” he said. “Getting to net zero sooner means we are less likely to have that long-term warming after net zero. We need to get to net zero sooner to limit that inequality.”
King said tropical ecosystems, such as some coral reefs, had mostly evolved to exist in a narrower temperature range than ecosystems at higher latitudes and would continue to be heavily affected for longer as the world cut emissions.
A separate report on the impact of climate change on the stateless, commissioned by the UN refugee agency and released with the Peter McMullin Centre on Statelessness, called on nations to support “the continuity of statehood” for countries facing extreme climate damage. It said those at risk included Pacific islands that were losing land to rising seas.
The agency estimated about 4.5 million people were stateless but said it accepted the number was probably much larger as stateless people were “invisible to official statistics”.
The report said the climate crisis risked creating more stateless people through displacement after climate-driven disasters such as fire, flood and sea level rise.
University of Melbourne Associate Prof Radha Govil, a report co-author, said there was a correlation between the regions most affected by climate change and statelessness.
The report recommended countries should be helped to digitise citizenship records, and steps should be taken to ensure children were afforded citizenship if they were left without parents after a disaster.
It said the risks to children were increased if mothers were not given the same rights as fathers to confer their own nationality to their children.
“The recommendations we have set out are absolutely doable,” said Govil. “They can stave of this risk of statelessness and get ahead of this problem.”

20 December 2024 was a crucial moment for Luxembourg in supporting WHO and strengthening global public health, to make progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals in 2025–2028. A Strategic Partnership Framework (SPF) with the Ministry of Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Affairs was signed amounting to €46.5 million – the largest-ever agreement WHO has had with Luxembourg. Furthermore, the first-ever multiyear agreement with the Ministry of Health and Social Safety €1 million was launched, as the country’s first voluntary contribution to WHO.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General greets with Luxembourg's Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety and Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. © MAE Luxembourg
“From now till 2028, this contribution will help finance priority areas in Luxembourg’s collaboration with WHO” said Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety during the bilateral meeting, “notably for sanitary crisis preparedness and response and the fight against health inequalities, with a special focus on gender.”
The amount of €46.5 million contains fully flexible and thematic funding, and allocations for the Universal Health Coverage Partnership, tropical disease research and polio eradication. The fully flexible funding enables WHO to allocate the money to the areas of highest need.
“By signing two new partnership agreements, we have reaffirmed Luxembourg's continued support for the WHO and its mission,” said Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. “This reflects our strong commitment to promoting global health and multilateralism. We launch these agreements with WHO because we believe the best way to avoid is to prevent.”
To support the achievement of WHO’s priorities, the strategic partnership framework with Luxembourg includes support for WHO’s core work to develop, deliver and implement high-quality technical products – the guidelines, norms and standards on which many countries rely.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General, remarked how symbolic it was that the agreements were signed on the International Day of Solidarity. They are “a strong statement of solidarity by Luxembourg, not just with WHO, but with the people of the world”, said Dr Tedros.
Xavier Bettel, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus and Martine Deprez at the signing ceremony. © MAE Luxembourg
WHO and Luxembourg continue their historical strategic partnership, collaborating to fulfill a shared mission to promote, provide and protect health.

Heroes star Hayden Panettiere died from 'toxic' mix of drugs, including fentanyl: coroner's report
Coroner's office rules actor's August death an accident
The recent death of Hayden Panettiere has been ruled accidental and attributed to "toxic effects" of a mix of drugs, including fentanyl, according to the Greenville County Coroner's Office.
The actor, known for roles in TV shows like Heroes and Nashville, died on Aug. 16 at a Greenville, S.C., residence where she'd been staying.
Upon arriving at the scene, emergency responders had found Panettiere in cardiac arrest and were unsuccessful with their resuscitation efforts, according to the office.
Following a joint investigation by the office alongside the Greenville City Police Department, "the cause of death has been ruled as toxic effects of fentanyl, 4-ANPP, Alprazolam, Methocarbamol, and Quetiapine," the office confirmed to CBC News in an official statement on Tuesday.
Quetiapine is an antipsychotic medication used to treat schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and major depression and Alprazolam is used to treat anxiety and panic disorders as well as anxiety caused by depression.
Methocarbamol is a muscle relaxant, while 4-ANPP is a compound linked to the production of fentanyl, a powerful opioid.
During the autopsy, "no signs of trauma were discovered that would have contributed to the death," the statement added.
The television and film performer, who died days ahead of her 37th birthday, had openly discussed personal struggles with early fame, addiction and mental health, including postpartum depression following the birth of her daughter in 2014.
Panettiere spoke and wrote candidly about her life, including in interviews and in her recent memoir, This Is Me: A Reckoning.
Her death unleashed a flood of tributes and remembrances from co-stars and fans.

Snopes contacted the retailer to ask if the company created it. We also reached out to an eBay seller specializing in Walmart pins, including the 9/11 design in question, to ask for more details about it and where it was acquired. We will update this article if we receive a response.
Snopes found the pin listed for sale by eBay seller UpNorth Mercantile. One listing that was deactivated on Aug. 31, 2026, showed the pin retailing for $14.99. It appeared there had been a quantity of 30 available that either sold out or were unlisted by the seller.
The same seller showed two live auctions for the pin with bids of more than $100 each, as of this writing. UpNorth Mercantile's eBay store showed dozens of collectible Walmart pins for sale, including the alleged 9/11 pin and other variations of Walmart's smiley face logo.
Smiley was first introduced in 1990, according to Walmart's own timeline. It became the mascot for the brand's signature "Rollback" price-cut promotions in 1996, then was sidelined in 2006 due to a trademark war. In 2016, Walmart's then-chief marketing officer Tony Rogers proclaimed the return of Smiley.
He said, "We first introduced Smiley in 1990 and, since then, he has been a widely recognized symbol for low prices. In fact, nearly 70% of our customers still associate Smiley with savings at Walmart even though he's been behind the scenes for the past decade."
Walmart lightly documents its employee lapel pin culture on the corporate website, which says:
Lapel pins may be small, but they hold big meaning! We use them to celebrate and commemorate. They show off our goals and our wins. They honor hometowns and heroes. Pins are our love language, our very own cultural currency.
The website describes an annual event called Associates Week, scheduled around the time of the company's shareholders conference, as a "pin lover's paradise." According to Walmart, Associates Week brings together employees from across the globe, during which "pin trading becomes a common language."
One of the Reddit threads featuring the 9/11 pin appeared in the r/WalmartEmployees subreddit, where current and former workers discuss working for the company.
A search within the subreddit for conversations about employee pins yielded a wide variety of results, showing the prevalence of pin culture at the corporation. Users posted images of the 9/11 pin by itself or of one attached to a jacket.
(Pangram)
Snopes ran images of the pin through Pangram, an artificial intelligence detection service, including those taken from the various social media posts and eBay listings.
All versions came back with results that declared no generative AI was used to create the images. It's important to note that such tools are not always reliable. None of the pictures we checked showed any signs of being AI-generated.
In sum, it appears that photos of the lapel pin in question are authentic and specimens of the pin itself are available for purchase on eBay as of this writing, but it was not possible to verify that it was an official offering from Walmart's own line of employee pins, as online posts claimed.

A US military plane crashes near a US air base in Germany, injuring the pilot
An American military aircraft has crashed at a U.S. air base in western Germany, injuring the pilot
BERLIN -- An American military aircraft crashed at a U.S. air base in western Germany on Tuesday, injuring the pilot, the American military said.
In a statement, the U.S. Air Base Spangdahlem said that the pilot ejected and was receiving medical care. The air base did not give any further details.
The local German district, where Spangdahlem is located, had said earlier that fire and emergency teams responded to the incident. Local authorities said they were unable to provide any further information about the accident.
Spangdahlem is home to an F-16 fighter jet squadron with about 20 aircraft, the German news agency dpa reported.
The squadron, which supports U.S. Air Force and NATO missions worldwide, is the centerpiece of the air base. The base has about 5,000 military and civilian employees, plus their family members, according to the latest figures. The U.S. air base also employs between 700 and 800 Germans.
The U.S. Air Force has maintained a presence in Spangdahlem since the mid-1950s. Along with Ramstein near Kaiserslautern in southwestern Germany, Spangdahlem Air Base is considered one of the most important airfields for the U.S. military in the region.

The United States will be allowed to establish military bases at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig and expand its activities at Pituffik Space Base under a new security agreement signed by US President Donald Trump, Denmark and Greenland on Tuesday (September 22).
The agreement, signed on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York, strengthens US military access to Greenland while keeping the territory under Danish control.
The pact also sets out security conditions for any future independence of Greenland, including a requirement that an independent Greenland remain part of NATO.
“It's going to be a long-term, fantastic relationship,” Trump said at the signing ceremony.
Trump said the agreement would give the United States “permanent control over security and all other needs” in Greenland.
“No US adversary will ever be permitted to establish a military presence in Greenland any more, or make sensitive investments there without our express written approval,” Trump said in his UN speech before the signing.
Here is what the US-Denmark-Greenland agreement means:
Under the agreement, the United States will be allowed to establish military bases at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig.
Washington will also be permitted to modernise and expand its activities at Pituffik Space Base, the US military installation in northwestern Greenland.
The agreement allows US aircraft to fly over and land in any territory in Greenland, including its territorial waters.
Trump had earlier said the US would begin developing a “large military presence” in Greenland, including “building two very major military bases.”
The agreement also allows the United States to establish its Golden Dome defence system in Greenland.
The provision would give Washington an expanded role in the island's air and missile defence architecture, amid growing US concerns about security in the Arctic and North Atlantic.
The pact also says that no state that is not a NATO member will be allowed to establish its own manned or unmanned military installations in Greenland.
A major provision of the agreement deals with Greenland's possible future independence.
If Greenland exercises its right to become independent, Denmark and Greenland must work together to ensure that the independent Greenlandic state agrees to remain in NATO, including by applying to become a member of the alliance.
The independent state would also be expected to honour the defence agreement.
The provision links Greenland's future security arrangements to the NATO alliance even if its constitutional relationship with Denmark changes.
The agreement also introduces restrictions on foreign investment in sensitive sectors.
Investors from countries outside NATO and the European Union will be barred from certain sensitive sectors in Greenland, with the agreement citing potential security threats.
The parties also agree to work together to counter espionage in Greenland.
Despite the expanded US military role, the agreement places conditions on how Washington exercises its access rights.
It states that US access must be exercised in a manner that respects Greenlandic society and the Greenlandic way of life.
Denmark will also continue to strengthen its own security posture in the Arctic.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte welcomed the agreement, saying it would enhance collective security.
The agreement, he said, supports “a safer and more stable future for us all.”
The pact places NATO at the centre of the security framework for Greenland and the wider Arctic region.
The agreement comes after months of tension over Trump's repeated calls for the United States to acquire Greenland.
Trump had argued that US control of Greenland was necessary to prevent Russia or China from gaining a stronger foothold in the Arctic. His demands strained relations with Denmark, a NATO ally, and triggered a wider diplomatic dispute within the alliance.
The new agreement does not transfer Greenland to the United States. Instead, it expands Washington's military access and security role while leaving the territory under Danish sovereignty.
The agreement is subject to the necessary parliamentary procedures in the Kingdom of Denmark together with Greenland.
Its provisions therefore still face the required domestic approval processes before they can take full effect.

The latest PlayStation update made PSSR 2.0 the default for PS5 Pro owners
The newer upscaler now kicks in automatically, but only for games that already support PSSR.
One of the PS5 Pro's graphical improvements is much more noticeable thanks to Sony's latest PlayStation 5 system update, as system software 26.06-14.00.00 enables Enhance PSSR Image Quality by default. Games that are based on the original version of PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution will now take advantage of Sony's newer upscaler without the owner needing to know about a fairly obscure toggle.
There is an important limit, though: games that don't already support PSSR aren't affected. The update is not suddenly adding AI upscaling to everything in the PlayStation library, and not every game with a "PS5 Pro Enhanced" badge is using PSSR to begin with.
The enhanced PSSR and its system-level override arrived in March. Sony calls it "upgraded" or "enhanced" PSSR rather than PSSR 2.0, and the newer version takes a different approach to both the neural network and overall algorithm. Until now, PS5 Pro owners who wanted to apply the enhanced model to games built around the original PSSR tech had to enable the setting themselves.
PSSR 2.0 is mostly about cleaning up the first version
PSSR is Sony's machine-learning upscaler for PS5 Pro. It allows games to be rendered at a lower resolution and then upscaled to a higher output resolution, allowing developers to push for better visuals without the full performance cost of natively rendering at that higher resolution.
The initial release wasn't always elegant. Our PS5 Pro review noted some games had shimmering textures and distortion around fine text, which can be hard to ignore once you've spotted them.
According to Sony, the enhanced version offers fine detail clarity, image reconstruction and stability in motion. Developers who've used it have noted less flickering and afterimages, and more refined details like hair and foliage. The technology is an outgrowth of Project Amethyst, Sony's graphics research with AMD, which has also helped with AMD's machine-learning graphics on PC.
Games that support the newer version will use it by default, but you aren't trapped into the newer version for older games that weren't built to support it. If you're experiencing any unexpected visual effects, go to Settings > Screen and Video > Video Output > Enhance PSSR Image Quality and disable the override to keep PSSR 1 games using their original tech. Make sure you're running games in Pro or Quality mode to take advantage of the improvements.
The update does more than change PSSR's default
Sony didn't explain why it took some six months to enable this setting by default, and hasn't claimed that every PSSR title will look better in every circumstance.
Meanwhile, PS5 Pro owners aren't getting all the attention. The same update introduces an on-screen voice chat indicator to display the name of the person speaking, along with an option to select where this indicator will appear.
The Welcome Hub also gets a Community Activity widget. Trending Now displays 10 multiplayer games or modes that are attracting a lot of players, and Top 10 displays the most popular games from the last week in your region.

How the race they said women couldn't run took centre stage
- Published
For 32 years, the women's 800m was absent from the Olympics, with its competitors deemed too frail. Now, it is one of the most hotly anticipated events on the track.
This extraordinary story starts at the 1928 Olympic Games, which represented a huge - if temporary - step forward for women's sports.
The Amsterdam Games were the first to allow women to compete in track and field events. Five women's events were added to the programme - the 100m, high jump, discus, 400m hurdles and, controversially at the time, 800m.
The progress, however, was temporary.
German athlete Karoline Lina Radke, external became the first woman to win Olympic gold in the 800m - but she would also be the last for another 32 years.
The event was removed from the Games after reports - later proven to be false - claimed competitors suffered extreme exhaustion after the race, and the International Olympic Committee decided women were too frail to compete, external over the two-lap distance.
Fast forward almost 100 years and the event now gets headline status at major events.
In recent times, it's been the battle between Britain's Olympic 800m champion Keely Hodgkinson and the Swiss European champion Audrey Werro that has captivated fans.
So how did the 800m become the 'one to watch'? BBC Sport spoke to the women who helped shape the race to find out.
'You don't realise what you've done'
It was the 1964 Tokyo Olympics, and Ann Brightwell (nee Packer) had just crossed the finish line of the women's 800m to take gold - and set a new world record.
In doing so, Brightwell became the first British woman to win an Olympic gold on the track, in a time of two minutes 01.1 seconds.
She told BBC Sport: "My husband, who was my fiance then, said to me, 'you don't realise what you've done'.
"I didn't give it a thought at the time… but now I realise I played a very small part in women running longer distances."
But the controversy hadn't completely gone away. Brightwell knew all about the claims that had seen women unable to compete for 32 years after the 800m was removed from the Olympics.
Brightwell adds: "Men weren't happy about women competing in these very high profile events…we were considered too frail and too delicate.
"And they took it upon themselves to make it look really bad. They were saying women were collapsing on the way round. But it was all a lie."
After 1928, women's middle-distance shrunk into the shadows for the next few decades.
The 800m was finally reintroduced to the Olympic programme in 1960 and, four years later, the then-22-year-old Brightwell went to her first Olympics, fitting training around her job as a teacher.
"Many people in my era either had to take unpaid leave or resign, or they got sacked because they were trying to juggle their sports with their career," she said.
"My school was very tolerant towards what I was doing, so I was fortunate."
Going out for a run around the local streets or countryside - which seems so commonplace today - was unusual in the era Brightwell was competing.
"If I just felt like an easy run, I would run around my village, around the streets… people commented on it or tooted their horns. And it was funny looking back, but it never troubled me," the now 84-year-old told BBC Sport.
Brightwell's 800m time of 2:01.1 stood for almost three years, before Australian Judy Pollock broke that with a new time of 2:01 flat in 1967.
The next target was to go under two minutes.
Breaking 'sub-two' - and a stubborn world record
"Records are great and medals are the best, but when you break a barrier it's a fantastic feeling," said Christina Boxer-Cahill (nee Boxer).
It was at the 1979 European Cup final in Turin that Boxer-Cahill looked up at the clock and realised she'd gone under two minutes.
She added: "I knew this would probably be my last chance, because there were other girls in Britain trying to do it."
In 1971, Germany's Hildegard Falck, external had become the first woman to break the two-minute barrier.
Eight years later, it was the 22-year-old Boxer-Cahill who became the first British woman to do so, in a time of one minute 59.05 seconds.
"It's a bit like when Roger Bannister broke four minutes for the mile. Once he'd done it everybody did it because you see what's possible," Boxer-Cahill, who is now 69 years old, told BBC Sport.
"I just think I'm so fortunate that I was in a sport where everybody accepted that you have men and women's races in the Olympics."
From 1971 to 1983, the women's 800m world record would be broken six times.
But the 1983 record stands to this day.
It belongs to Czech athlete Jarmila Kratochvilova, who ran a time of one minute 53.28 seconds at a meeting in Munich.
Kratochvilova's record has been questioned, with claims it was assisted by her country's doping regime that existed at the time, something she has strenuously denied.
In 2017, European Athletics proposed wiping out records set before 2005 - sending a strong signal that records set before then were disputable.
Several Soviet satellite states - including East Germany - are known to have been operating state-sponsored doping programmes throughout the 1980s.
At the 1988 Seoul Olympics, Boxer-Cahill finished fourth in the 1500m, behind a Russian athlete who was later banned for doping.
Boxer-Cahill said: "I was running during that Eastern Bloc era when, you know, they've looked back and some of the performances, there's sort of a cloud over it.
"I'd just have loved to have been on that rostrum. I wish the Eastern Bloc system hadn't been there, but that's what it was.
"Politics in sport, when you're the performer, it frustrates you. But if you get too frustrated, all it's going to do is upset your own performance."
Women's 800m 'stronger than ever'
"We've got not just two but several girls who are running under two minutes every time they turn out," Brightwell told BBC Sport.
"It's stronger than it's ever been."
Kratochvilova's 43-year-old record is looking increasingly precarious.
The 800m European champion Werro has come closest, running a time just 0.42 seconds shy of the record at the Zurich Diamond League.
Keely Hodgkinson, the current 800m indoor world record holder, told BBC Sport earlier this year that she's never felt closer to breaking the outdoor record.
She said: "I really do believe we can break it, but a lot of things have got to come together."
Hodgkinson is one of six athletes competing in the 800m at Athlos, the all-female athletics event taking place in London, on Friday.
"I do think the [800m] world record will go in the next year or two, and hopefully this season, because we're on a real high, aren't we?" Boxer-Cahill told BBC Sport.
"If it happens towards the end of the season, 2026 [would be] the year of women's 800m running."

It has become increasingly common for AI firms to announce that their latest and most capable models engaged in unauthorized real-world hacking. Google, which has been slow to release frontier Gemini models in recent months, has been absent from the “rogue AI” conversation until now. Following a Wall Street Journal report, Google has confirmed that Gemini models hacked three companies during a May 2026 test, but the nature of the intrusion isn’t as troubling (or impressive) as previous AI hacks.
The hack took place during a test conducted by cybersecurity firm Irregular. A collection of Gemini models were taking part in a “capture the flag” exercise intended to test the AI’s cybersecurity capabilities in a closed environment. The AI was instructed to retrieve information from a fake company (which shared a name with a real company) within this environment. Irregular was not supposed to allow the model to operate outside its servers, but due to a misconfiguration, Gemini was able to access the Internet.
When Gemini started snooping around the web, it targeted real infrastructure instead of the fakes. For one of the three hacks, Gemini simply guessed passwords until it accessed a company’s online services. In the other two instances, Gemini searched public software repositories until it found login credentials for companies that had been accidentally included.
In all three test runs, Google’s models reportedly stopped after realizing they had accessed a real company’s servers. At that point, Irregular changed its configuration to prevent the AI from accessing the Internet. Apparently, Irregular didn’t initially consider this event worthy of further investigation—it didn’t even tell Google about the hacks until July, following the news of other AI hacking incidents. After becoming aware of the event, Google notified the companies so they could (we hope) improve their password security.

“Merz cancelled a planned trip to New York to speak before the UN general assembly, already anticipating he would need to be in Berlin to grapple with the state elections’ aftermath.
Now, more than ever, he will have his work cut out for him after just 16 months in office.”
Instead, Germany will be represented by its foreign minister, Johann Wadephul, who will speak later this week.
In other very important news, the escalators at the UN HQ appear to be functioning absolutely fine on Trump’s arrival, in sharp contrast to last year’s incident.
US ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz also seems to be very happy about this fact.
Let’s hope the teleprompter is ready for Trump’s speech, too.
'Settle the war,' Trump says is his message to Putin
Meanwhile, Trump is arriving at the UN HQ right now.
Our colleagues on the US blog will cover him in more detail here, but I will pick up all his Europe-related comments here.
After very brief doorstep comments – almost exclusively mocking CNN - he answers a reporter’s very loud question by saying his message to Putin is: “settle the war.”
Guterres also talks about the importance and relevance of the UN in today’s world, as he argues that:
“The world does not need the weaker United Nations. It needs the UN strong enough to face the world as it is, and determined enough to build the world as it should be.”
He says that in his 10 years he has learned that “the greatest power is not the power to dominate; [but] the power to build a future that works for everyone.”
“Our shared future will be forged by whether humanity can govern power wisely, by upholding the law before impunity becomes normalised, by ending wars, before they consume generations. By tackling inequality, before societies fracture. By accelerating climate action, before tipping points are crossed, and by governing artificial intelligence before it governs us.
This is the challenge before this General Assembly, the United Nations and humanity itself.”
He signs off declaring his resolve to follow these principles in the last 100 days in the office, and pledging he will always keep championing them even once he left the post.
“I will continue to stand up for the values of the United Nations Charter, and I will never, ever give up,” he declares to warm applause and a standing ovation.
UN general assembly president and Bangladeshi foreign minister Khalilur Rahman is next to speak, with US president DonaldTrump expected near the top of the hour.
In a paragraph that would look ridiculous in 2016 – but very much does not in 2026 – UN secretary-general António Guterres has issued a stark warning on the escalation of autonomous technology.
“Artificial intelligence must be shaped by humanity, with humanity and for all humanity. And as we confront the challenges ahead, let us not retreat from two fundamental principles. Let’s say with one voice, children must never become the test subjects for unregulated systems.
And let us resolve that life and death decisions must never be surrendered to machines. Killer robots must have no place in our future.”
Guterresalso speaks at length about the prospect of AI, and risks associated with its rapid rise, just as “the very developers building these systems are now pulling the alarm.”
He says that “governments must assume their responsibilities” to scrutinise AI and work on “transparency, trust and cooperation.”
“Not despite geopolitical rivalry, but precisely because of it.
At a pivotal moment during the cold war, strategic rivals came to recognise the need to manage shared existential risks. They built mechanisms to reduce misunderstandings, manage escalation and prevent catastrophe. At that time, it was the nuclear armament. Today, artificial intelligence demands the same clarity of purpose and sense of urgency.”
UN's Guterres speaks about Middle East, Ukraine in opening address
UN secretary general António Guterres is now speaking in the opening debate of the UN general assembly.
He warns that “across the Middle East, conflicts are cascading,” as he urged leaders to use the week in New York “for de-escalation and dialogue.”
Continuing on the Middle East, he says “all the fighting must stop, and humanitarian aid must flow.”
He specifically picks up on “the devastating situation in the occupied Palestinian territory,” saying that in the three years following the “abhorrent terror attacks” on 7 October, “what followed was an onslaught on Palestinians and Gaza” at scale that has no comparison.
“Violence, displacement and settlement expansion by Israel in the occupied West Bank are bulldozing the path to peace and raising the spectre of ethnic cleansing. We cannot allow the two state solution to disappear before our eyes,” he warns.
He then turns to Ukraine, talking about how “Russia’s full scale invasion has subjected a sovereign country to a brutal war, in blatant violation of the charter.”
“Civilians continue to be killed far from the frontlines, mainly in Ukraine, but also more recently in parts of Russia. Homes, energy and water systems and transport have come under repeated attack, threatening food and energy supplies and supply chains globally.”
He also mentions the crises in Sudan and Myanmar, and talks about the need to reform the UN security council by adding a permanent seat for an African nation.
Swedish prosecutors to probe election fraud allegations
Swedish prosecutors are investigating possible election fraud that has raised uncertainty about the recent election there.
A preliminary investigation into potential election fraud in Borlange, a town in the largely rural county of Dalarna, central Sweden, might still affect the final result. Sweden’s election review board could decide on a re-run or recount of the vote, which elects 11 members of parliament, if it decides the result is suspect.
Reuters, citing local media, reports that the prosecutor’s investigation centred on the election of Mohamed Abdukardir Ali, a Left Party candidate for parliament. Ali told Swedish TV that the allegations were false.
Reuters is carrying a Kremlin read-out of a call between Russia’s president Vladimir Putin and Saudi crown prince Mohammed bin Salman. It said the two leaders held a detailed exchange of views on the situation in the Middle East, and “the importance of ensuring the safe and unimpeded passage of vessels through the region’s international waterways was emphasised.”
Just a quick note with bit of guidance on timings today, as we are inevitably looking at events across the ocean.
Donald Trump’s speech to the UN general assembly is expected around 10am New York time. That’s 3pm UK, 4pm in most of Europe.
Our US blog colleagues will cover it in excruciating detail if you don’t want to miss a single thing, but rest assured I will pick up key bits on Europe here.
And if you want to plan further ahead:
The Greenland deal signing ceremony is expected around 10.30am (3.30pm UK, 4.30pm Europe).
And Trump’s sit-down with Zelenskyy will be around 13.15am New York time, so 6.15pm UK, 7.15pm Europe.

There's always a danger in over-complicating products. Simple is so often best. The apocryphal story of NASA spending millions crafting a space pen while Soviet cosmonauts used a pencil is often cited as a prime example, even if it's actually not true. Perhaps it's not surprising that Dyson has got into hot water trying to reinvent the electric toothbrush.
The Chinese invented the first bristle toothbrush during the Ming dynasty. That concept muddled along quite nicely until 1937, when Tomlinson Moseley filed a patent for the earliest electric toothbrush. After more than 400 years, the Motodent marked the beginning of an evolutionary shift from manual brushing to powered oral care.
Having had considerable success reimagining established product categories such as stick vacuums and premium hair dryers—though not so much air-purifying headphones—the company earlier this month, with great fanfare, unveiled the next leap forward for teeth: the $499 Dyson CameraJet with a tiny camera to aim streams of rinsing fluid into the gaps between your teeth.
Others, like the Waterpik Sonic-Fusion 2.0, have already been daring (or foolhardy) enough to combine brushing and water flossing. However, Dyson upped the ante further by adding a macro-lens camera, allowing its “Gap Optical Targeting system,” trained on 470,000 dental images, to identify within 100 milliseconds precisely where to squirt fluid from the 12.5 milliliters of mouth rinse stored in its on-board reservoir.
It's taken Dyson six years, 38 patents, and an awful lot of money to make this camera-squirt-brush doohickey work. However, something has gone badly wrong with the CameraJet. So wrong that despite James Dyson globally launching the product at a Paris event mere weeks ago, you can no longer, as far as WIRED can ascertain, buy the CameraJet anywhere.
The CameraJet launched in US stores on September 8. Just a day later, reports began outlining the first user complaints of water in the battery compartment and failures within 30 seconds of use. Consumer Reports' own review unit stopped working less than 24 hours after unboxing. On September 11, French outlet Numerama reported that the French Dyson site and stores had reportedly stopped selling the toothbrush. By September 15, stores in the US, UK, and Singapore, where Dyson's headquarters now reside, had followed suit.
Despite the product disappearing from shelves and online stores, Liv Thomas, the company's head of Beauty Communications, insists to WIRED that the CameraJet hasn't been recalled. Instead, the gadget is “experiencing strong demand globally” and “shortages of supply as we are in the process of scaling up production." Units will reappear supposedly in “the coming weeks.” But what about the multiple reports of breakages, leaking, and battery failures in multiple countries?
“We have identified a single component issue affecting a small number of early batches,” Thomas says. “We have isolated those batches and are supporting affected customers.”
Thomas confirmed that Dyson would not answer questions on where—if anywhere—the Dyson CameraJet was still on sale worldwide. Nor would Dyson confirm when it stopped shipments of the product. Thomas also confirmed that Dyson refuses to detail what the faulty “single component” is, what problem it's causing for the CameraJet, or how many units have been affected globally. Dyson also refused to comment on why it had not issued a formal recall of these faulty early batches of the $500 device.
Dyson Reddit forums have lit up, with names such as “ScameraJet” being bandied around, along with one disgruntled buyer commenting: “Bought two of these and both of them have stopped working. Since I bought it in the UK and wasn’t planning to return it and have thrown the packaging away, I can’t even return them. Disappointed that they scammed so good. Unbelievable that it lasted just two weeks.”
Kyle Wiens, CEO of the repair company iFixit, feels the problem may well be leaking.
“This sounds like a waterproofing issue. Making products at scale with the tolerances required to waterproof are hard,” he says. “My guess without getting a chance to look at a failed unit is that we either have a tolerance issue where some parts aren't mating perfectly, or a failure in the adhesive curing process, either during manufacturing or in shipping.”
Wiens says this adhesive-curing failure can happen in such a way that a product can pass factory testing fine, but then heat or humidity (or both) during shipping causes a problem.
Adam Toner, founder and technical director of Ripcord Designs, a UK-based electronic design consultancy that has worked with multinational companies including Formula One Management and Panasonic, also thinks water is the CameraJet's problem.
“On a product like this, there just should never be any water ingress into the internals,” he says. “I don't have one in front of me, but I've seen a few videos and people explaining how you change the battery. Once you pull the battery off—which is where people say they're seeing water—it looks like there is probably access from that battery compartment into all of the internals of the device.”
The CameraJet not charging, overheating, or failing to start—all of that can be explained by water getting into the device, Toner says. He suspects the problem could be as benign as a faulty gasket or O-ring.
If water getting in does turn out to be an issue for the CameraJet, as these experts suggest, this begs the obvious question: How on earth has Dyson managed to spend six years developing a teched-up toothbrush, designed to be dunked in water every use, and that carries liquid around in it, yet fail to make it waterproof?
Wiens believes the CameraJet chaos could force a well-overdue rethink for Dyson.
“Clearly they didn't plan for this to happen," he says. "They should take this opportunity to invest in repairability. Making products easier to fix also makes them easier to rework when manufacturing defects occur. Dyson is way behind the industry on making repair parts and information available for their products. This should be a wake-up call for them to step up.”
